# PGWP Refusals for Non-Credit Programs in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/pgwp-non-credit-program-refusals-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-08-23
Author: Go Far Global Team

> > This guide is for international graduates in Canada who are about to apply for a PGWP.

# PGWP Refusals for Non-Credit Programs in 2026

*As of August 23, 2026.* Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is refusing Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) applications from graduates of non-credit programs after a June 2026 update to its eligibility page, and it has frozen the eligible field-of-study list for all of 2026.

> This guide is for international graduates in Canada who are about to apply for a PGWP. It explains why non-credit, ESL, and general-interest programs are being refused, and how to confirm your program qualifies before you apply.

## TL;DR

A PGWP is only issued for a program that leads to a degree, diploma, or certificate | Non-credit, ESL/FSL, and general-interest courses do not qualify | IRCC clarified this on its eligibility page around June 24, 2026 | The eligible field-of-study list is frozen from January 21, 2026 with no additions or removals | Language proof is mandatory: Canadian Language Benchmark 7 for university grads, CLB 5 for college grads

## Why is IRCC refusing PGWPs for non-credit programs?

IRCC is refusing these applications because a PGWP is only issued for a completed program of study that leads to a degree, diploma, or certificate at a designated learning institution. Around June 24, 2026, IRCC updated its [post-graduation work permit eligibility](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html) page to state plainly that general-interest programs, English or French as a Second Language (ESL/FSL) programs, and other non-credit courses do not meet that bar. IRCC has described the change as a clarification of a longstanding requirement, not a brand-new rule. In practice, graduates whose transcripts show audit or non-credit status are now being refused, even when they studied full time and held a valid study permit the whole time.

## What counts as a non-credit program?

A non-credit program is any course of study that earns no academic credit toward a recognized credential. These programs can still be full time and expensive, but they do not lead to a degree, diploma, or certificate that the school records on an official transcript. The most common examples caught by the 2026 clarification are language-upgrading courses, general-interest and personal-enrichment classes, and continuing-education courses taken on an audit basis. A credit-bearing program, by contrast, appears on your transcript with earned credits and results in a credential you can name on your [work permit application](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation.html).

| Program type | Leads to a credential? | PGWP eligible? |
|---|---|---|
| Bachelor's, master's, or doctoral degree | Yes | Yes |
| College or polytechnic diploma or certificate | Yes | Yes, if the field of study qualifies |
| ESL or FSL language program | No | No |
| General-interest or personal-enrichment course | No | No |
| Audited or non-credit continuing education | No | No |

## What are the PGWP eligibility rules in 2026?

To qualify for a PGWP in 2026, you must have graduated from a program at a designated learning institution that is at least eight months long and leads to a degree, diploma, or certificate. You must apply within 180 days of getting confirmation that you completed your program, and your study permit must have been valid at some point during those 180 days. You also have to prove language ability with a test taken within the last two years, and non-university graduates must have studied in an [eligible field of study](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility/field-of-study.html). The language floor is Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7 for university graduates and CLB 5 for college and other non-university graduates, measured across reading, writing, listening, and speaking.

## Does the field-of-study requirement apply to me?

It depends on your credential. If you graduated with a bachelor's, master's, or doctoral degree from a university, the field-of-study requirement does not apply and you can qualify regardless of your program subject. If you graduated from a college, polytechnic, or any other non-university program, you must have studied in a field on IRCC's eligible list to receive a PGWP. On January 21, 2026, IRCC froze that list for the year, meaning no fields will be added or removed in 2026. The freeze locks the list that took effect after the June 2025 update, so the fields that qualify today are the fields that will qualify for the rest of the year.

## How do I confirm my program qualifies before applying?

Check four things before you submit, because a refusal cannot be appealed to a tribunal and restarting can cost you months of work authorization. First, confirm your transcript shows a completed credential, not an audit or non-credit result. Second, confirm your school is a designated learning institution and your program is at least eight months. Third, if you did not earn a university degree, match your program against the eligible field-of-study list using its Classification of Instructional Programs code. Fourth, book a valid language test dated within two years and confirm you meet CLB 7 or CLB 5 for your credential type. When any of these is unclear, have a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) review your transcript before you file.

## Frequently asked questions

### What happens if my PGWP is refused?

A PGWP refusal does not carry a right of appeal to the Immigration and Refugee Board. Your practical options are to restore your status if you are still eligible, apply for a different type of work permit, or reapply with stronger evidence if the refusal came from a missing or misread document. You cannot keep working on an expired permit while you sort this out.

### Can I restore my status after a PGWP refusal?

You may be able to restore your temporary resident status within 90 days of it expiring if you still meet the conditions of your stay. Restoration does not let you work until a new permit is approved, so many graduates apply for restoration and a fresh work permit together. Speak to a representative quickly, because the 90-day window is strict.

### Did IRCC freeze the list of PGWP-eligible programs for 2026?

Yes. On January 21, 2026, IRCC announced it will not add or remove any eligible fields of study for the PGWP in 2026. The list that applies now is locked for the year, which gives college and non-university graduates a stable target but no chance for a newly added field to help them mid-year.

### What is the new rule for PGWP in Canada?

There is no single new rule in 2026. The refusals stem from a June 2026 clarification that a PGWP is only issued for a program leading to a degree, diploma, or certificate, plus the language and field-of-study requirements that took effect earlier. The practical effect is that non-credit, ESL, and general-interest students who could once slip through are now refused.

### Will Canada extend PGWP in 2026?

A PGWP is issued once per study credential and cannot simply be extended. If your PGWP is ending, you generally need a new basis to keep working, such as an employer-supported work permit or a provincial nomination. Some graduates with a valid job offer move onto an employer-specific permit before the PGWP expires.

## Sources

- [Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html), IRCC eligibility page
- [Work in Canada after you graduate](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation.html), IRCC PGWP overview
- [Eligible fields of study for a PGWP](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility/field-of-study.html), IRCC field-of-study list

# Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot 2026: 2,970 Spots

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/francophone-minority-communities-student-pilot-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-08-19
Author: Go Far Global Team

> A new annual intake of 2,970 study permit applications under the Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot opens on August 26, 2026 and runs to August 25, 2027.

# Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot 2026: 2,970 Spots

*As of August 18, 2026.* A new annual intake of 2,970 study permit applications under the Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot opens on August 26, 2026 and runs to August 25, 2027.

> This guide is for French-speaking students from 33 eligible countries who want to study in French outside Quebec and move on to permanent residence. It covers the exact eligibility conditions in the signed public policy, the country list, the language score you need, and the money you must show.

## What is the Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot?

The Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot (FMCSP) is a temporary public policy from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) that creates a study-to-permanent-residence pathway for French-speaking international students. It targets applicants from world regions with historically high study permit refusal rates, defined as regions where most member countries of l'Organisation internationale de la Francophonie had a refusal rate of 60% or more when the original policy took effect on August 26, 2024. Students accepted under the pilot study in French at designated learning institutions outside Quebec, and a companion public policy gives them access to permanent residence and open work permits after they earn their Canadian credential.

## Who is eligible for the Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot?

You must be a citizen of one of 33 listed countries, hold a letter of acceptance from a participating institution, meet a French language standard, and show specific funds. The program you enrol in must be postsecondary, taught more than 50% in French, at least two years long on a full-time basis, and lead to a diploma or degree. Your letter of acceptance must come from a designated learning institution (DLI) that has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with IRCC to take part in the pilot, and it must state that you are applying under the FMCSP. A letter from a non-participating school does not qualify you, no matter how strong the rest of your file is.

| Requirement | Standard set by the public policy |
|---|---|
| Citizenship | One of 33 listed countries in Africa, the Middle East or the Americas |
| Institution | Designated learning institution outside Quebec with an IRCC Memorandum of Understanding |
| Programme language | Taught more than 50% in French |
| Programme length | At least two years, full-time |
| Programme outcome | Leads to a diploma or degree |
| Language score | Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens (NCLC) 5 in all four abilities |
| Funds | First-year tuition and travel, plus 75% of the local low income cut-off (LICO) |

## Which countries qualify for the FMCSP in 2026?

Thirty-three countries qualify, grouped into three regions in the public policy text. In Africa the list covers Bénin, Burundi, Burkina Faso, Cabo Verde, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Comoros, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Republic of the Congo, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Côte d'Ivoire, Madagascar, Mali, Mauritania, Mauritius, Morocco, Niger, Rwanda, São Tomé and Principe, Senegal, Seychelles, Togo and Tunisia. In the Middle East it covers Egypt and Lebanon. In the Americas it covers Haïti, Dominica and Saint Lucia. The list is fixed by the policy and is based on refusal-rate data from when the pilot first launched, so it does not expand as conditions change.

## What language score do you need for the FMCSP?

You need a minimum of NCLC 5 in each of the four abilities: speaking, listening, reading and writing. The score must come from a designated language-testing organization using a general French proficiency test approved under subsection 74(3) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. NCLC 5 is a lower bar than many economic immigration streams require, which is deliberate, because the pilot exists to reduce barriers rather than raise them. Note that the requirement is a floor in every ability, not an average. A strong speaking score does not compensate for a reading score below 5, and a single ability below the threshold takes your application outside the public policy.

## How much money do you need to show for the FMCSP?

You must demonstrate two separate things. First, the ability to cover your first year of tuition and your travel costs. Second, available financial resources totalling at least 75% of the low income cut-off associated with the municipality where your institution's main campus sits. This is a departure from the standard study permit route, where applicants generally show a fixed national cost-of-living figure. Because the FMCSP threshold is tied to the LICO for a specific municipality, the amount you need varies with where you will actually live. Confirm the figure for your campus city before you assemble proof of funds, and keep the funds available rather than merely showing a one-time balance.

## How many FMCSP applications will IRCC accept in 2026?

IRCC will accept a maximum of 2,970 study permit applications from new applicants abroad between August 26, 2026 and August 25, 2027. That figure matches the cap for the previous year, which ran from August 26, 2025 to August 25, 2026, and it makes this the third consecutive annual intake since the pilot launched in August 2024. The cap applies only to Part A of the policy, meaning first-time applicants applying from outside Canada. Study permit renewals from students already in Canada under the pilot fall under Part B and are not counted against the annual cap.

| Intake year | Application window | Cap |
|---|---|---:|
| Year 2 | August 26, 2025 to August 25, 2026 | 2,970 |
| Year 3 | August 26, 2026 to August 25, 2027 | 2,970 |

## When does the Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot expire?

Part A, the intake for new students applying from abroad, expires on August 25, 2027. Parts B and C run considerably longer. They stay in effect until the companion permanent residence public policy expires or is revoked, and that policy is currently set to expire on November 30, 2032. Part B covers study permit renewals for students already in Canada under the pilot, and Part C covers accompanying family members applying for work permits, study permits, visitor visas, extensions or restoration of status. IRCC states that the policy may be revoked at any time without prior notice.

## What advantage does the FMCSP give over a normal study permit?

The pilot waives the requirement to prove you will leave Canada at the end of your authorized stay. Under the ordinary rules, paragraph 20(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and paragraph 216(1)(b) of the Regulations require a study permit applicant to satisfy an officer that they will depart. Dual intent refusals on that ground are a leading cause of rejection for applicants from the listed countries. The FMCSP exempts principal applicants and accompanying family members from that test, which removes the single most common reason these applications fail. The pathway to permanent residence after graduation is the second advantage.

## What mistakes disqualify FMCSP applicants?

Most failures under this pilot are eligibility mismatches that an applicant could have caught before paying a fee. The public policy is a conditions-based instrument, so an officer works through the listed requirements and stops at the first one your file does not meet. There is no discretion to approve a one-year programme or a letter from a school outside the Memorandum of Understanding list. Check the five items below against your file before you apply.

1. **Choosing a programme shorter than two years.** One-year certificates and diplomas do not qualify, regardless of the institution.
2. **Applying to a school without an IRCC Memorandum of Understanding.** Being a designated learning institution is necessary but not sufficient. The school must be a signatory to the pilot.
3. **A letter of acceptance that does not name the FMCSP.** The policy requires the letter to indicate you are applying under the pilot.
4. **A programme taught mostly in English.** More than 50% of classes must be taught in French.
5. **Using a language test that is not approved.** The result must come from a designated testing organization using a general French test approved under subsection 74(3) of the Regulations.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I study in Quebec under the FMCSP?

No. The pilot exists to support Francophone minority communities, which by definition sit outside Quebec. Your designated learning institution's main campus must be located outside Quebec and the institution must have signed a Memorandum of Understanding with IRCC to participate.

### Does the FMCSP lead to permanent residence?

Yes, through a companion public policy. Students who obtain a Canadian credential while participating in the pilot can access permanent residence and open work permits under the separate updated public policy for FMCSP graduates, which is currently set to expire on November 30, 2032.

### Can my spouse come with me and work?

Part C of the public policy covers accompanying family members. It lets them apply for work permits, study permits, temporary resident visas, extensions of temporary resident status or restoration of status with the same exemption from the requirement to prove they will leave Canada.

### Is NCLC 5 the same as an IELTS score?

No. The Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens is the French-language benchmark system, separate from the Canadian Language Benchmark used for English. You must take an approved general French test from a designated testing organization. English test results do not satisfy this requirement.

### What happens when the 2,970 cap is reached?

IRCC stops accepting new Part A applications for that intake year once the cap is met. Applications are counted against the year in which they are received, so applying early in the window matters. The next window opens the following August 26 if the policy is renewed.

### Do renewals count against the annual cap?

No. The cap applies to Part A only, which covers first-time applicants applying from outside Canada. Study permit renewals filed from inside Canada by students already in the pilot fall under Part B and are not counted.

- [Updated public policy on permanent residence and open work permits for FMCSP graduates, IRCC](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-instructions-agreements/public-policies/pr-francophone-minority-communities-student-pilot-2026.html)

# A70 Open Work Permit: Working While Your Inland PR Application Processes

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/a70-open-work-permit-inland-pr-2026
Category: Work Permits
Published: 2026-08-11
Author: Go Far Global Team

> If your permanent residence application is in progress inside Canada, there is a specific open work permit that becomes available once IRCC decides you are eligible for your PR class.

*As of August 11, 2026. Based on the restructured officer instructions Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada published on August 10, 2026.*

If your permanent residence application is in progress inside Canada, there is a specific open work permit that becomes available once IRCC decides you are eligible for your PR class. It runs under section 207 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations with the administrative code A70, it is exempt from a Labour Market Impact Assessment, and it is unrestricted: no named employer, no occupation limit, no location condition.

IRCC rebuilt its officer instructions for this permit on August 10, 2026, splitting one dense page into an overview and four class-specific pages. Nothing about eligibility changed, but the restructure is a good moment to explain a permit that confuses almost everyone who encounters it, mostly because it is neither the spousal open work permit nor a regular employer permit.

## What is the A70 open work permit?

**Short answer:** An unrestricted open work permit for people in Canada who have been determined eligible as members of certain in-Canada permanent residence classes. Four groups qualify under section R207: spouses and common-law partners in the Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada (SCLPC) class, protected persons including Convention refugees and successful Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) applicants, people approved for humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) consideration, and the in-Canada family members of all of the above.

The word doing the work is "determined eligible." This permit is not triggered by filing a PR application; it is triggered by IRCC's first-stage decision on it. For spousal applicants that decision is [approval in principle](/news/approval-in-principle-aip-canada-2026), the milestone where an officer confirms the relationship qualifies before the final admissibility checks.

One legal quirk worth knowing: under section R202, protected persons and H&C applicants who receive this permit do not become temporary residents merely by holding it. The permit authorizes work; it does not by itself confer status.

## How is A70 different from the spousal open work permit?

**Short answer:** Timing and trigger. The spousal open work permit (SOWP) is available to inland spousal applicants early, while the sponsorship application is still being assessed. The A70 permit becomes available later, at approval in principle, and it is the mechanism that keeps you working from that milestone through to landing. Many spousal applicants hold a SOWP first and transition to, or renew into, the A70 stage without ever knowing the codes differ.

For the other classes there is no earlier equivalent: a successful PRRA applicant or an H&C-approved applicant reaches work authorization through A70, not through any spousal-style early permit.

| | Spousal OWP | A70 permit |
|---|---|---|
| Who | Inland spousal applicants | All four R207 classes |
| Trigger | Sponsorship application submitted | Determined eligible / approved in principle |
| Restriction | Open | Open, unrestricted |
| Covers protected persons and H&C | No | Yes |

If you are a spousal applicant deciding what to apply for today, our [spousal open work permit guide](/news/spousal-open-work-permit-canada-2026) covers the early-stage permit; this article covers what happens after the first-stage approval.

## What must spousal applicants show?

**Short answer:** Three things at the time the work permit is decided: you are the spouse or common-law partner of your sponsor and live with them in Canada; your SCLPC application has been approved in principle; and you hold valid temporary resident status, are on maintained status, or are eligible for restoration. The application must be filed online through the IRCC Secure Account or the Authorized Paid Representative Portal, with paper reserved for the narrow accessibility exceptions in the regulations.

The status requirement carries an important safety valve. Under the public policy that facilitates the SCLPC class, the requirement to hold valid status can be waived, which is what allows out-of-status spouses inside Canada to remain in the inland process and still reach work authorization. If you are out of status, that waiver is the difference between this pathway and having no pathway, and it is worth professional eyes before you file anything.

## Who qualifies under the other three classes?

**Short answer:** Protected persons under R207(c), meaning people with protected status under subsection A95(2) such as Convention refugees and successful PRRA applicants. H&C-approved applicants under R207(d), whether the exemption was granted on your request under A25(1), on the Minister's initiative under A25.1(1), or under a public policy under A25.2(1). And under R207(e), the in-Canada family members of anyone in the classes above, which is how a whole household reaches work authorization once the principal applicant clears eligibility.

The family-member provision is the least known of the four. A spouse or dependant of a protected person or H&C applicant, physically in Canada, can hold their own unrestricted open work permit while the family's PR application completes processing.

## What changed on August 10?

**Short answer:** Structure, not substance. IRCC replaced the single instruction page, previously titled "Applicants in Canada: Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemption code A70," with an overview page and four class-specific pages, one each for the spousal class, protected persons, H&C applicants, and in-Canada family members. The department describes the change as extensive updates for navigation and clarity, using its standardized format, with updated language and links.

Restructures like this matter for one practical reason: officers now work from cleaner, class-specific checklists, which tends to make assessments more consistent. They also tell you where IRCC's attention is. This is the second major instruction rebuild in two months touching inland applicants, after the July updates to the humanitarian and compassionate pages.

## When should you apply, and what can go wrong?

**Short answer:** Apply once you have the approval-in-principle or eligibility letter, not before. An A70 application filed ahead of the first-stage decision fails its core requirement. The common failure modes are applying too early, letting status lapse without being eligible for restoration in a class where the waiver does not apply, and assuming the permit itself grants status when, for protected persons and H&C applicants, it does not.

Timing the application well means watching your PR file for the eligibility decision. That letter is the trigger, and processing your work permit starts from when you apply, not from when you became eligible.

Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto, and inland PR files with work authorization questions are core casework for us. If you are unsure whether your file has reached the trigger point, or your status has lapsed while waiting, [book a consultation](/book). For where your PR application sits in the queue, see our [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) pages.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is LMIA exemption code A70?

A70 is the International Mobility Program administrative code for open work permits issued under section R207 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations to in-Canada permanent residence applicants who have been determined eligible in their class. It covers spouses and partners in the SCLPC class after approval in principle, protected persons including successful PRRA applicants, people granted humanitarian and compassionate relief, and their in-Canada family members. The permit is exempt from the Labour Market Impact Assessment and is unrestricted, meaning no employer, occupation, or location conditions. IRCC reorganized its officer instructions for A70 into class-specific pages on August 10, 2026.

### Can I work while waiting for my inland PR application?

It depends on the stage and the class. Inland spousal applicants can seek a spousal open work permit while the application is still in first-stage processing, then move to the A70 permit at approval in principle. Protected persons, successful PRRA applicants, and H&C-approved applicants reach work authorization through A70 once determined eligible, and their in-Canada family members qualify alongside them. Before the trigger point, work authorization depends on whatever permit you already hold. The A70 permit then carries you from the eligibility decision to landing, and it is renewable through that window.

### Does an open work permit under R207 give me status in Canada?

Not by itself, for two of the four classes. Section R202 states that applicants issued a work permit under R207(c), protected persons, or R207(d), H&C applicants, do not become temporary residents by reason only of the permit. The permit authorizes work while the PR application completes. Spousal-class applicants are differently placed, since their eligibility requires holding valid status, being on maintained status, or being eligible for restoration, with the status requirement waivable under the SCLPC public policy for out-of-status spouses. If your status situation is complicated, get advice before filing rather than after a refusal.

### How do I apply for the A70 work permit?

Online, through your IRCC Secure Account or through the Authorized Paid Representative Portal if a licensed representative files for you. Paper applications are limited to the accessibility exceptions in sections R9.4 and R9.5, and applications cannot be made at a port of entry. Apply after your PR file has been determined eligible, since the officer decides the work permit against your class criteria at the time of decision. Spousal applicants should be living with their sponsor in Canada and hold, or be able to restore, temporary status unless the public policy waiver applies to them.

## Sources

- [Permanent resident (PR) applicants in Canada [R207, A70]](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/applicants-canada.html), IRCC program delivery instructions
- [Spouse or common-law partner class (SCLPC) [R207(b), A70]](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/spouse-a70.html), IRCC program delivery instructions
- [Program delivery update, August 10, 2026](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/updates/2026-pr-in-canada-a70.html), IRCC
- [Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, section 207](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-227/section-207.html), Justice Laws Website

# Manitoba Work Permit Extension 2026: Workforce Transition Bridge

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/manitoba-workforce-transition-bridge-2026
Category: Provincial Nominee Programs
Published: 2026-08-11
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada signed a temporary public policy on July 6, 2026 giving open work permits to up to 2,700 Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program candidates, including workers whose permits have already expired.

# Manitoba Work Permit Extension 2026: Workforce Transition Bridge

*As of August 18, 2026.* Canada signed a temporary public policy on July 6, 2026 that gives open work permits to up to 2,700 Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program candidates, including workers whose permits have already expired.

> This guide is for temporary foreign workers in Manitoba who hold a provincial support letter and are waiting on permanent residence. It explains exactly who the Manitoba Workforce Transition Bridge covers, which documents Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) requires, and what to do if your status has already lapsed.

## What is the Manitoba Workforce Transition Bridge public policy?

The Manitoba Workforce Transition Bridge (MWTB) is a temporary public policy signed on July 6, 2026 under section 25.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). It lets IRCC issue open work permits to a defined group of up to 2,700 temporary foreign workers in Manitoba who the province has already screened as strong permanent residence candidates. The policy replaces the earlier Temporary Public Policy to Facilitate Work Permits for Prospective Provincial Nominee Program Candidates and keeps those same workers employed while their files move toward permanent residence. IRCC published the policy text on August 5, 2026, and it expires on December 31, 2027.

## Who qualifies for an open work permit under the Manitoba bridge?

You qualify under one of three situations, and all three require the same two supporting letters. In every case you need a support letter from the Government of Manitoba issued on or before December 31, 2025 confirming you were screened and placed in the Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program (MPNP) Expression of Interest (EOI) pool on or before that same date, plus a letter of employment from your current employer. What differs between the three groups is your status history: whether you hold a valid work permit now, held one on May 7, 2024 that has since expired, or were working under maintained status after filing a renewal on or before May 7, 2024.

| Your situation | Status requirement | What you must apply for |
|---|---|---|
| Group 1 | Hold a valid work permit now | Work permit under s.200 or s.201 plus a temporary resident extension under s.181 |
| Group 2 | Held a valid work permit on May 7, 2024, now expired | Work permit under s.200 plus an extension under s.181 or restoration under s.182 |
| Group 3 | Authorized to work under s.186(u) on May 7, 2024 after filing a renewal on or before May 7, 2024 | New work permit under s.200 plus an extension under s.181 |

## What documents do you need for the Manitoba Workforce Transition Bridge?

You need two documents beyond the standard work permit application. The first is a support letter issued by the Government of Manitoba on or before December 31, 2025. That letter must state that Manitoba screened you and placed you in the MPNP Expression of Interest pool on or before December 31, 2025. Manitoba signed a letter of intent with IRCC setting out its role in this facilitation, so the letter has to come from the province rather than from an employer or a consultant. The second document is a letter of employment from your current employer. Both letters must be submitted with the application. Missing either one takes you outside the public policy entirely.

## What if your Manitoba work permit already expired?

Group 2 exists specifically for workers who lost status. If you held a valid work permit on May 7, 2024 and it has since expired, the policy exempts you from several requirements that would normally block a restoration application. IRCC waives the section 182 rule that you must apply for restoration within 90 days of losing temporary resident status, and it waives the requirement that you complied with every other condition imposed on you. It also waives paragraph 200(3)(e), which normally bars a work permit for anyone who worked or studied without authorization or breached a previous permit condition. This is the most consequential part of the policy, because it reaches people who would otherwise have no route back to authorized work.

## Which requirements does IRCC waive under this policy?

The exemptions differ by group. For Groups 1 and 3, IRCC waives paragraph 200(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, the provision that requires an applicant to fall within a described class in order to be issued a work permit. Group 2 receives a wider set of exemptions because those applicants have already lost status. Alongside paragraph 200(1)(c), Group 2 is exempt from the section 182 restoration deadline and conditions, from paragraphs 199(a) to (i) governing who may apply for a work permit from inside Canada, and from paragraph 200(3)(e) on unauthorized work or study. Everything not listed still applies, including medical admissibility, criminality and security screening.

## How long does the Manitoba Workforce Transition Bridge last?

The policy took effect the day it was signed, July 6, 2026, and expires on December 31, 2027. IRCC states plainly that it may be revoked at any time without prior notice, so the expiry date is a ceiling rather than a promise. The cohort is capped at up to 2,700 workers, and Manitoba controls who enters that cohort through the support letters it issued on or before December 31, 2025. If you did not receive a provincial support letter by that date, no later letter makes you eligible. Apply as early as your circumstances allow rather than waiting for the expiry date to approach.

| Milestone | Date |
|---|---|
| Support letter and EOI pool placement deadline | December 31, 2025 |
| Policy signed and in effect | July 6, 2026 |
| Policy text published by IRCC | August 5, 2026 |
| Policy expires | December 31, 2027 |
| Maximum cohort size | 2,700 workers |

## What mistakes cost applicants the Manitoba bridge work permit?

Four errors account for most avoidable refusals under a facilitation policy like this one, and all four are documentation problems rather than eligibility problems. The Manitoba Workforce Transition Bridge is a conditions-based policy, which means an officer checks each listed condition against your file and stops the moment one fails. There is no discretion to accept a support letter dated after the deadline or an employment letter from a former employer. Review the four items below against your package before you submit, because a refusal here can leave you without status while you start over.

1. **Submitting a provincial letter dated after December 31, 2025.** The date on the letter is a hard condition, not a guideline. A letter issued in 2026 does not qualify you.
2. **Applying for the work permit without the paired status application.** Every group must also apply for an extension under section 181, or restoration under section 182 for Group 2. A work permit application on its own does not satisfy the conditions.
3. **Sending an old employment letter.** The policy requires a letter from your current employer. A letter from a previous job does not meet the condition.
4. **Assuming the exemptions cover admissibility.** Medical, criminal and security requirements are untouched. The policy exempts specific regulatory provisions and nothing more.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does the Manitoba Workforce Transition Bridge give permanent residence?

No. It issues an open work permit only. The policy is designed to keep you working and in status while Manitoba and IRCC assess you for permanent residence through the Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program. Permanent residence remains a separate application with its own requirements.

### Can I change employers on this work permit?

Yes. The policy issues an open work permit, which is not tied to a single employer. You still need a letter of employment from your current employer at the time you apply, because that letter is one of the eligibility conditions.

### What happens if I never received a Manitoba support letter?

You are not eligible. The support letter had to be issued on or before December 31, 2025 and had to confirm placement in the MPNP Expression of Interest pool by that same date. Manitoba is not issuing new letters for this policy, so there is no way to join the cohort now.

### Does this policy apply outside Manitoba?

No. It applies only to candidates screened and supported by the Government of Manitoba. Other provinces run their own Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) streams and are not covered by this public policy.

### Can my spouse get a work permit through this policy?

The public policy text addresses the principal applicant. Family members follow the ordinary rules for spousal open work permits and dependant study permits, which depend on your occupation and permit type. Have your specific family situation assessed before you file.

### How many people will actually get a permit?

Up to 2,700. That is a ceiling on the cohort Manitoba supports, not a guarantee that every applicant is approved. Each application is still assessed against the policy conditions and general admissibility.

## Sources

# OINP Expression of Interest: How to Register for the 2026 EOI Pool

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/oinp-expression-of-interest-2026
Category: Provincial Nominee Programs
Published: 2026-08-05
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Ontario opened the Expression of Interest portal for its new Ontario Workforce Priority stream on August 4, 2026.

*As of August 5, 2026. Checked against Ontario's published application process for the Ontario Workforce Priority stream.*

Ontario opened the Expression of Interest portal for its new Ontario Workforce Priority stream on August 4, 2026. Registering an Expression of Interest (EOI) is now the only way into the Ontario Immigrant Nominee Program (OINP), because every other stream is closed.

Most of what you will read about the OINP EOI describes the old system. The guides ranking for it were written when Ontario ran nine categories and candidates could register themselves. Neither is true anymore. Under the new stream you cannot start the process at all until your employer acts first, and there are three separate deadlines that can end your registration before Ontario ever looks at it.

## What is an OINP Expression of Interest?

**Short answer:** An EOI is a free profile you register in Ontario's e-Filing Portal telling the province you want to be considered for a nomination. It is not an application. Ontario scores every profile in the pool, then issues invitations to apply to the highest-ranked candidates in periodic draws. Only after you receive an invitation do you submit an actual application and pay a fee.

The distinction matters because registering costs nothing and guarantees nothing. Ontario states plainly that you should not register if you do not meet the stream criteria: if you are invited and then cannot prove what you claimed, the application is refused and the fee is not refunded.

## Who can register an EOI right now?

**Short answer:** Skilled and intermediate workers with a qualifying Ontario job offer, and self-employed physicians who meet the College and Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP) requirements. Everyone else is out for now, because the Ontario Workforce Priority stream is the only stream open and the other eight closed in June 2026.

Self-employed physicians are the exception to almost every rule here. They register without a job offer and without an employer, provided they are members in good standing with the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, hold a certificate of registration in an eligible class, and are eligible to bill OHIP.

For everyone else, the sequence is the thing people get wrong. Your employer registers in the Employer Portal and submits a job offer for your position. That generates a job offer ID. You cannot register an EOI without it.

## What deadlines can end your EOI before a draw?

**Short answer:** Three, and two of them are easy to miss. You have 30 calendar days from your employer submitting the job offer to register your EOI. A registered EOI stays in the pool for 12 months and is then removed automatically. After an invitation, you have 17 calendar days to submit and pay, but you cannot submit until your employer files their own application, and they have 14 days to do it.

| Clock | Who it applies to | Length | What happens if you miss it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Job offer to EOI registration | You | 30 calendar days | The job offer expires and your employer must submit a new one |
| EOI validity in the pool | You | 12 months | The EOI is automatically removed from the selection pool |
| Employer application after invitation | Your employer | 14 calendar days | You cannot submit your own application |
| Your application and payment | You | 17 calendar days | The invitation lapses |

The last two run at the same time and depend on each other. Your 17 days start when the invitation is issued, but Ontario blocks submission until your employer has filed their application for approval of the employment position. You can build your application during those 17 days. You cannot press submit. An employer who takes their full 14 days leaves you three. Agree a filing date with your employer before you register, not after the invitation lands.

One more trap sits in the job offer itself. If your employer needs to change the wage or the National Occupational Classification (NOC) code on the offer, they have to withdraw it and submit a new one, and you then have to register a brand new EOI. Your place in the pool does not survive the correction.

## How many points is the OINP EOI scored out of?

**Short answer:** Job-offer candidates are scored out of 130 points and self-employed physicians out of 115, because the wage factor does not apply to them. Points come from employment factors, education, language, and where in Ontario the job sits. Ontario has not published a cut-off for the new stream, because it has not run a draw yet.

The single largest swing for most candidates is geography. A work location in Northern Ontario earns the full 15 regionalization points. Toronto earns zero. Eastern Ontario, Southwestern Ontario, and Central Ontario outside the Greater Toronto Area each earn 10, and the GTA outside Toronto earns 5. Two identical candidates can sit 15 points apart on the location of the job alone.

Language is the next largest lever at 15 points for Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 9 or higher, with a further 10 available for a second official language at CLB 6 across all four abilities. Ontario work experience in the offered position tops out at 18 points.

## Does registering an EOI cost anything?

**Short answer:** No. Ontario charges nothing to register an Expression of Interest. The application fee only arrives if you are invited to apply, and it is paid at that point. Any service charging you to register an EOI is charging for form-filling, not for access.

That is worth stating plainly because the free registration step is where paid intermediaries cluster. What you are buying, if you buy anything, is judgement about whether your profile is competitive and whether your employer can actually meet the employer-side requirements. The registration itself is a form.

## What happens after Ontario invites you?

**Short answer:** An invitation is not a nomination. You submit an application with documents proving every scoring factor you claimed, your employer submits their application for approval of the employment position, and Ontario assesses both. If Ontario nominates you, you then apply to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) for permanent residence, and IRCC makes the final decision.

Everything you attested to in the EOI has to be evidenced. Ontario is explicit that receiving an invitation does not mean you will be nominated, and that not all applicants who meet the criteria will be invited.

Self-employed physicians have an extra option at the nomination stage: they can choose to be nominated through the federal Express Entry system, which adds 600 points to an Express Entry profile. If you take that route and let the Express Entry profile lapse after nomination, you start the whole OINP process again from a new EOI.

## Where can you get help deciding if it is worth registering?

**Short answer:** The registration is free, so the question is not whether to register but whether your profile is competitive and whether your employer can carry their half. Those are the two places these applications fail, and both are answerable before you start.

Look hard at the employer side first. They must be registered, willing to file within 14 days of an invitation, and able to meet the requirements for approval of the employment position. A candidate with a strong score and a disengaged employer does not get nominated.

Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto. If you want your score estimated and your employer's position assessed before you commit, [book a consultation](/book). For the full stream requirements and the closed-stream transition, see our [Ontario Workforce Priority Stream guide](/news/oinp-workforce-priority-stream-2026), and for draw activity our [OINP news tracker](/news/ontario-oinp-overhaul-2026).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How to express interest in OINP?

Your employer starts it. They register their business in the OINP Employer Portal and submit a job offer for your position, which produces a job offer ID. You then sign in to Ontario's e-Filing Portal, enter that job offer ID and your email address, and register your Expression of Interest within 30 calendar days of the offer being submitted. Registration is free. Self-employed physicians are the exception and register without an employer or job offer, provided they meet the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario and OHIP billing requirements. Registering does not guarantee an invitation.

### What is the EOI score for OINP?

Under the Ontario Workforce Priority stream, job-offer candidates are scored out of a maximum 130 points and self-employed physicians out of 115, since the hourly wage factor does not apply to them. Points come from the NOC TEER category and occupational category, hourly wage, Ontario work experience, Canadian earnings history, legal status, education, Canadian credentials, official language ability, and the region of Ontario where the job is located. Ontario has not published a cut-off score for this stream because no draw has been held since it opened on August 4, 2026. Cut-offs from the closed streams do not carry over.

### What are the latest OINP news for 2026?

Ontario rebuilt the program this year. Amendments to Ontario Regulation 422/17 came into force on June 25, 2026, removing the existing eight streams and creating the Ontario Workforce Priority stream in their place. Ontario updated its web pages with the new eligibility criteria on July 20, and opened the Expression of Interest portal on August 4, 2026. No invitations have been issued under the new stream yet. Ontario describes this as Phase 1 of a two-phase redesign, so further changes are expected. Registrations under the closed streams that never received an invitation were withdrawn.

### Does OINP EOI expire?

Yes. Your EOI registration stays valid for 12 months while you wait for an invitation to apply, and Ontario removes it from the selection pool automatically after that. An EOI can also be withdrawn earlier, either by you or by the program, and Ontario notifies you when that happens. There is a separate and shorter deadline before the EOI even exists: the job offer your employer submits expires if you do not register within 30 calendar days, and they must then submit a new one. If your employer changes the wage or NOC code, the offer is withdrawn and you must register a new EOI.

## Sources

- [Ontario Workforce Priority stream](https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontario-workforce-priority-stream), Government of Ontario
- [2026 Ontario Immigrant Nominee Program Updates](https://www.ontario.ca/page/2026-ontario-immigrant-nominee-program-updates), Government of Ontario
- [OINP invitations to apply](https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontario-immigrant-nominee-program-oinp-invitations-apply), Government of Ontario
- [Ontario Immigrant Nominee Program](https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontario-immigrant-nominee-program-oinp), Government of Ontario

# IMM 5476 2026: Use of a Representative, Version 11-2025 Only

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/imm-5476-use-of-a-representative-guide
Category: Immigration Process
Published: 2026-08-04
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Which sections of IMM 5476 you actually complete, how the November 2025 version change affects old copies, and the difference between IMM 5476 and IMM 5475.

# IMM 5476 2026: Use of a Representative, Version 11-2025 Only

*As of August 31, 2026.*

IMM 5476 is the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) Use of a Representative form. The current release is 11-2025, last updated November 2025. IRCC's form page still says previous versions were accepted until 12 March 2026. That date has passed. File 11-2025 only. An older PDF from a third-party site will not do.

## TL;DR

Use IMM 5476 version 11-2025 only. The March 12, 2026 window for old versions is closed | You may appoint only one representative per application | All IRCC and Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) correspondence goes to the representative, not to you | Paid representatives must be in good standing with the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC), a Canadian law society, or the Chambre des notaires du Québec | IMM 5475 releases information only. It does not let someone conduct business on your file

## What is IMM 5476 and when do you use it?

**Short answer:** IMM 5476 authorizes a named person to conduct business with IRCC and the CBSA on one specific application. Complete it only if you are appointing a representative, updating that person's contact details, cancelling an appointment, cancelling one representative and appointing another, or withdrawing yourself as a representative. You are not obliged to hire anyone. IRCC treats applicants with and without a representative the same. A representative does not get special attention, faster processing, or a better outcome.

The live form and instructions are on the IRCC [Use of a Representative Form (IMM 5476)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5476.html) page, dated 12 December 2025 on the page stamp, with the PDF last updated November 2025. Download it on a computer. IRCC says the form may not open on tablets or phones. Open it in Adobe Acrobat Reader version 10 or higher.

Once appointed, the representative receives all correspondence from IRCC or the CBSA in place of you, not in addition to you. You can appoint only one representative at a time for each application. Dependent children aged 18 or older must complete their own copy if a representative is also conducting business on their behalf.

## Which sections do you fill in?

**Short answer:** You never complete every section. Section A identifies the applicant and is always required. Section E is the applicant declaration and is always required, except when a representative who is withdrawing cannot get the applicant's signature and signs the declaration in section D instead. Sections B, C, and D depend on the action. Filling in the wrong block, or skipping E because the form looks done, is how files get sent back.

| What you are doing | Sections to complete |
|---|---|
| Appointing a representative | A, B, E |
| Updating a representative's contact information | A, B, E |
| Cancelling a representative | A, C, E |
| Cancelling one representative and appointing another | A, B, C, E |
| Withdrawing yourself as a representative | A, D, E |

Section D belongs to the representative, not to the applicant. Signatures are section E. If you are both cancelling and appointing, check the matching box and complete A, B, C, and E.

On a sponsorship application, a spouse or common-law partner included in the same request signs in the box on this form and does not file a separate copy. On any other application, a spouse or common-law partner needs a separate authorization even if they are on the same file. That split is easy to miss.

## Who counts as a paid representative?

**Short answer:** Anyone who charges a fee or receives any other compensation for representing or advising you. The test is payment, not job title. If someone else pays the representative, IRCC still treats that person as paid. Paid representatives who are not in good standing with a designated body cause the application to be returned. Unpaid representatives are friends, family, or professionals who will not charge or receive consideration. IRCC will deal with an unpaid representative you appoint. You do not have to pay someone to act for you.

Paid representatives IRCC will deal with:

- consultants who are members in good standing of the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC)
- lawyers and paralegals who are members in good standing of a Canadian provincial or territorial law society, and students-at-law under their supervision
- notaries who are members in good standing of the Chambre des notaires du Québec, and students-at-law under their supervision

Anyone who represents or advises you for payment without being an authorized representative, or without a specific agreement with the Government of Canada, is breaking the law. That covers advice given before or after an application is made. Confirm standing on IRCC's [learn about representatives](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigration-citizenship-representative/learn-about-representatives.html) page before you write a name in section B. Put the membership ID on the form as it appears on the organization's list. If you appoint a student-at-law, include the supervising lawyer's information and membership ID. The supervising lawyer must also sign.

A Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) is a CICC member. Go Far Global is a licensed firm. Verify any consultant the same way you would verify us, using the public register, not the person's website. We published a separate [guide to verifying a licensed consultant](/news/how-to-verify-licensed-immigration-consultant-canada).

## How is IMM 5475 different from IMM 5476?

**Short answer:** IMM 5475 is the Authority to Release Personal Information to a Designated Individual. It lets IRCC give someone information about your application, such as status. That person cannot conduct business on your behalf. IMM 5476 is the form that grants the power to act. If you only want a relative to check a file, use IMM 5475. If you want a consultant or lawyer to submit documents and answer IRCC, use IMM 5476, and accept that mail then goes to them.

The [IMM 5475 page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5475.html) last updated the PDF in May 2021. The form page stamp is 30 September 2024. Choosing 5476 when you wanted 5475 is how people stop receiving their own letters.

## How do you download and sign the current form?

**Short answer:** Download IMM 5476 from the official [IRCC form page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5476.html) on a desktop. The current PDF is version 11-2025. Save it, then open it in Adobe Acrobat Reader 10 or higher. Do not use a phone, a browser PDF viewer, or a commercial form-filling site. Those copies are often years out of date.

If you submit through a portal or secure account, IRCC accepts a wet (hand) signature, an e-signature, or a thumbprint if the person cannot make a mark. E-signature includes a typed name, Adobe Fill & Sign or DocuSign, a scan or image of a signature, or a check box as indicated. If you submit outside a portal or secure account, IRCC wants a wet signature. A scanned wet signature is acceptable. A thumbprint is acceptable if the person is illiterate or cannot make a mark for a physical reason.

Download the PDF from that IRCC page. The current file is version 01-11-2025. That is the file to keep.

## How do you submit IMM 5476, including after you have already applied?

**Short answer:** If the immigration or citizenship application is not in yet, upload IMM 5476 with the online package, or send it with a paper package to the address in that application's guide. If the application is already in, submit the form through the IRCC web form, or mail it to the office that is processing the file if you know the address. You must notify IRCC if the representative's contact information changes, if you change representatives, or if you cancel the appointment.

The web form IRCC points to is [Client Contact form 71](https://secure.cic.gc.ca/ClientContact/en/Application/Form/71). Use it for a form that is late to a file that is already in processing. Do not assume a portal upload is still open after you hit submit on the main application.

Keep a copy of what you sent. If you appoint someone and then hear nothing, the first check is whether correspondence is landing in the representative's inbox instead of yours.

## What gets an application returned?

**Short answer:** Naming a paid representative who is not in good standing. Using a pre-11-2025 PDF after 12 March 2026. Appointing two people on one application. Completing the wrong sections. Skipping the signatures in section E. Using IMM 5475 when you needed 5476, or the reverse. Forgetting that an 18-year-old dependant needs their own form. Those are paperwork errors. IRCC can return the whole application for them.

Before you name anyone, confirm CICC, law-society, or Chambre standing yourself. Then be clear about what you are signing. IMM 5476 redirects correspondence and hands over the authority to act. If all you wanted was a status check, that is IMM 5475.

We are Go Far Global, a licensed Canadian immigration firm. If you want a representative named on IMM 5476 who is on the public register, [book a consultation](/book). We will tell you whether you actually need 5476, 5475, or neither.

## Sources

- [Use of a Representative Form IMM 5476 (IRCC, page dated 2025-12-12, form 11-2025)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5476.html)
- [Authority to Release Personal Information IMM 5475](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5475.html)
- [Learn about representatives](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigration-citizenship-representative/learn-about-representatives.html)
- [IRCC web form to submit IMM 5476 after filing](https://secure.cic.gc.ca/ClientContact/en/Application/Form/71)

# IMM 5444: PR Card Application and Appendix A Explained (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/imm-5444-pr-card-application-guide
Category: Permanent Residence
Published: 2026-08-04
Author: Go Far Global Team

> A guide to IMM 5444 and Appendix A, the residency obligation calculation that decides permanent resident card renewals under section 28 of IRPA.

*As of August 3, 2026. Checked against the current form release (09-2024) published by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada.*

# IMM 5444 Explained: PR Card Renewal, Appendix A, and Why You Probably Should Not Download the PDF

IMM 5444 is the Application for a Permanent Resident Card or Permanent Resident Travel Document. It is the form behind every permanent resident (PR) card renewal, replacement and first issue.

It is also a form most applicants no longer need to download. [Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship.html) now runs PR card applications through the Permanent Residence portal, where you complete a digital version of IMM 5444 on screen. IRCC's own guidance says not to fill out the PDF if you are applying online. Yet the results ranking for this form still push the PDF, including a copy sitting in a university repository and another in an unrelated cloud storage bucket.

The part that actually decides these applications is Appendix A, the residency obligation calculation. That is where this guide spends most of its time.

## Where can I get the IMM 5444 form?

**Short answer:** For almost everyone, you do not download it at all. Sign in to the Permanent Residence portal and complete IMM 5444 as a digital form inside your application. IRCC states directly on the form page that you should not fill out the PDF if you are applying online. The downloadable PDF, currently dated 09-2024, exists for the narrower set of applicants who are still eligible to file on paper.

If you do need the paper route, take it from IRCC's [IMM 5444 page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5444.html) rather than anywhere else, complete it electronically, and use the form's validation button before printing and signing. Its companion instruction guide is Guide 5445, which carries the document checklist and the photo specifications.

Copies circulating on third-party sites are the main risk here. Some indexed versions of this form are old enough to still carry the Citizenship and Immigration Canada name, a department that was renamed in 2015.

## What is Appendix A, the residency obligation of IMM 5444?

**Short answer:** Appendix A is the residency obligation section. It asks you to list every trip you took outside Canada in the past five years, with dates and destinations, so IRCC can calculate how many days you were physically present in Canada. Every adult permanent resident renewing a card completes it. It is the section that decides the application.

The standard comes from section 28 of the [Immigration and Refugee Protection Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/i-2.5/section-28.html): you must be physically present in Canada for at least 730 days within every rolling five-year period. That is two years out of five, and the days do not have to be consecutive.

Accuracy matters more than the total. Officers cross-check what you declare against border crossing records, and an omitted trip reads as a misrepresentation rather than as a rounding error. Reconstruct your travel from passport stamps and boarding passes, and if you are missing records, you can request your own entry and exit history from the Canada Border Services Agency before you file.

## Which absences still count toward the 730 days?

**Short answer:** Three categories of time abroad count as if you had been in Canada. Days accompanying a Canadian citizen spouse or common-law partner, or a parent if you are a child. Days employed full-time outside Canada by a Canadian business or the public service. And days accompanying a permanent resident spouse, partner or parent who is themselves employed full-time outside Canada by a Canadian business or the public service.

These exceptions are narrower than they sound. "Canadian business" has a specific statutory meaning, and being paid by a Canadian company while working abroad indefinitely for a foreign client does not automatically qualify. Assignments structured as a temporary posting from a Canadian operation, with a expectation of return, sit far more comfortably inside the provision.

| Situation | Counts toward 730 days? |
|---|---|
| Physically in Canada | Yes |
| Accompanying a Canadian citizen spouse, partner or parent abroad | Yes |
| Employed full-time abroad by a Canadian business or public service | Yes |
| Accompanying a PR spouse, partner or parent who is so employed | Yes |
| Working abroad for a foreign employer | No |
| Living abroad while holding Canadian property or paying Canadian tax | No |

If your count falls short, do not simply file and hope. Humanitarian and compassionate considerations can be raised, and there is an appeal route to the Immigration Appeal Division, but both work far better as a prepared argument than as a reaction to a refusal.

## What is a Permanent Resident Travel Document, and when do you need one?

**Short answer:** A PR travel document (PRTD) is a single-use document that lets a permanent resident board a commercial carrier back to Canada when they are outside the country without a valid PR card. IMM 5444 covers both applications, which is why the form's title names them together. You apply for a PRTD from outside Canada, through a visa office.

The practical trigger is a card that expires while you are abroad. A PR card cannot be renewed from outside Canada, so if yours lapses during a long trip, the PRTD is how you get home. The same residency obligation applies, and the officer assessing your PRTD is making the same 730-day calculation.

Permanent residents who can reach Canada by land or sea from the United States are in a different position, since carrier document requirements apply to commercial air travel.

## Why does my IMM 5444 say in progress?

**Short answer:** "In progress" means IRCC has accepted your application into processing and is working through it. It is a normal status, not a warning sign, and it typically persists for most of the processing period. It does not indicate a problem, a request for more documents, or a decision either way.

Status labels in the portal move slowly and in coarse steps, which makes them a poor guide to how your file is actually doing. If your application has passed the posted processing time and the status has not shifted, the informative move is to request your file notes rather than to keep refreshing the portal. Those notes show which checks are complete and which are outstanding, and they are free to request. Our guide to [GCMS notes](https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/gcms-notes-canada-immigration-guide) covers how to file that request.

## What if your residency count falls short?

Do not file and hope. An application that discloses fewer than 730 days invites a residency determination, and a negative one can put your status itself at risk rather than just delaying a card. The options that exist, humanitarian and compassionate considerations or an appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division, work far better as a prepared argument submitted with the application than as a response to a refusal.

Count carefully first, including the absences that still qualify as presence. If the total is close to 730, the exact dates matter and reconstructing them from border records is worth the effort.

If someone is filing on your behalf, they need [IMM 5476](/news/imm-5476-use-of-a-representative-guide), the Use of a Representative form, which IRCC updated in November 2025.

Our [PR card renewal](/immigration/extensions/pr-card-renewal) page covers the renewal process and current [processing times](/immigration/processing-times). If your count is short or your absences depend on one of the statutory exceptions, Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto and you can [book a consultation](/book).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Where can I get the IMM 5444 form?

Most applicants no longer download it. IRCC processes permanent resident card applications through the Permanent Residence portal, where you complete IMM 5444 as a digital form on screen, and IRCC's guidance says not to fill out the PDF if you are applying online. If you are among the applicants still filing on paper, download the current PDF, dated 09-2024, only from IRCC's own page on canada.ca, and read it alongside Guide 5445. Avoid third-party form sites and cached copies: some indexed versions are old enough to carry the pre-2015 Citizenship and Immigration Canada branding.

### Why does my IMM 5444 say in progress?

"In progress" simply means your application has been accepted into processing and IRCC is working on it. It is the normal status for most of the time your file is open, and it does not signal a problem or a pending request. Portal statuses update in coarse steps and lag the actual work on your file, so they are not a reliable way to judge progress. If you have passed the posted processing time, request your GCMS notes through a free Privacy Act request. Those notes show which checks have been completed and which remain outstanding, which the status label never does.

### What is appendix a residency obligation of IMM 5444?

Appendix A is the residency obligation section of the permanent resident card application. It requires you to list every trip outside Canada over the past five years and calculate the total days you were physically present in Canada. Under section 28 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, you must be present at least 730 days in every rolling five-year period. Certain absences count as presence: accompanying a Canadian citizen spouse, partner or parent, being employed full-time abroad by a Canadian business or the public service, or accompanying a permanent resident family member who is. Declare every trip, since officers cross-check against border records.

### How to apply for a PR card renewal?

Apply through the Permanent Residence portal. Create or sign in to your account, start a permanent resident card application, and complete the digital IMM 5444 along with Appendix A, the residency obligation calculation. You will upload a copy of your current or expired card, identity documents, and photographs meeting IRCC's specifications, which are set out in Guide 5445. Apply before your card expires where possible, because a card cannot be renewed from outside Canada: if it lapses while you are abroad, you need a permanent resident travel document instead. Reconstruct your five-year travel history carefully before you begin.

## Sources

- [Application for a Permanent Resident Card or Permanent Resident Travel Document (IMM 5444)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5444.html), IRCC
- [Guide 5445: Applying for a permanent resident card](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5445-applying-permanent-resident-card-card-first-application-replacement-renewal-change-gender-identifier.html), IRCC
