# H&C Processing Time in 2026: IRCC Publishes More Than 10 Years

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/humanitarian-compassionate-processing-time-2026
Category: Permanent Residence
Published: 2026-07-31
Author: Go Far Global Team

> IRCC publishes a processing time of more than 10 years for humanitarian and compassionate permanent residence, the top of its published scale. Many pages still quote 18 to 24 months. Here is the published figure, the two-stage structure, and the July 22, 2026 change to H&C requests made inside public policy applications.

# H&C Processing Time in 2026: IRCC Publishes More Than 10 Years

*As of July 31, 2026.* Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) publishes a processing time of more than 10 years for humanitarian and compassionate applications, which is the top of its published scale and far beyond the 18 to 24 months quoted on many law firm and agency pages.

> For people who have filed a humanitarian and compassionate application or are considering one. This covers the published timeline, what the two stages actually are, the July 22, 2026 change to H&C requests made inside public policy applications, and the bars that stop an application being examined at all.

## How long does a humanitarian and compassionate application take in 2026?

More than 10 years, according to IRCC's own figures. IRCC's processing-times data, last updated July 7, 2026, lists humanitarian and compassionate permanent residence at **more than 10 years** both inside Quebec and in the rest of Canada. That is not a typo and it is not our estimate. It is the figure IRCC publishes. Several widely circulated pages, including one currently ranking on the first page of Google for this question, state 18 to 24 months. That figure does not match what IRCC publishes today. If you are planning around an H&C application, plan against the published number, and check the live tool before relying on any figure, including this one.

| Permanent residence stream | IRCC processing time, July 7, 2026 |
|---|---|
| **Humanitarian and compassionate, outside Quebec** | **More than 10 years** |
| **Humanitarian and compassionate, Quebec** | **More than 10 years** |
| Canadian Experience Class | About 6 months |
| Federal Skilled Worker | About 7 months |
| Provincial Nominee Program, base | About 12 months |
| Spouse or partner outland, outside Quebec | About 17 months |
| Spouse or partner inland, outside Quebec | About 27 months |
| Parents and grandparents, outside Quebec | About 30 months |
| Caregivers | About 79 months |

## Why does IRCC publish "more than 10 years" instead of a number?

Because it is the ceiling of the published scale, not a precise estimate. Six of the 28 permanent residence categories in IRCC's data carry the identical "more than 10 years" value: humanitarian and compassionate inside and outside Quebec, self-employed persons, the start-up visa, dependants abroad in Quebec, and protected persons in Canada in Quebec. When a queue runs past the top of the range, every category in that position reports the same ceiling. So the honest reading is not "exactly ten years." It is that IRCC will not commit to a figure inside its published range, and that H&C now sits with the most heavily backlogged streams it administers rather than anywhere near mainstream economic processing.

## What are Stage 1 and Stage 2 in an H&C application?

Two separate decisions, and people routinely mistake the first for approval. IRCC's instructions state that once an applicant is found eligible to have an application assessed, the H&C application is processed in two stages. **Stage 1**, also called approval in principle, is the H&C assessment of the exemptions you requested. **Stage 2** is the final decision on the permanent residence application itself. A positive Stage 1 assessment is a decision on your H&C grounds, not a grant of permanent residence, and IRCC's instructions contemplate interim documentation at that point and address what happens if the applicant has left Canada. A positive Stage 1 can also be revisited: the instructions direct decision-makers to act where it appears an applicant used fraud or misrepresentation to obtain one.

## What changed for H&C requests on July 22, 2026?

IRCC published new instructions covering H&C requests made inside applications under in-Canada permanent residence public policies, and the effect is that those requests do not get their own decision. The Minister can create temporary public policies under section 25.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) to grant permanent residence to people in similar circumstances. If you apply under one of those and also ask for H&C consideration, IRCC's position is that while a decision is being made on the public policy application, **applicants are not entitled to an additional, distinct decision** on whether to grant permanent residence on H&C grounds. Officers must acknowledge the request in the refusal letter, refuse the public policy application while identifying the requirement you failed, and tell you that to have H&C assessed you must re-apply on H&C grounds and pay the applicable fees again.

### Why that matters in practice

It removes a fallback many applicants assumed they had. Asking for H&C "in the alternative" inside a public policy application does not preserve an H&C decision. It produces a refusal plus an invitation to start over, at your own cost, and any new H&C application then joins the queue described above.

## Who cannot apply for H&C?

Several groups are barred, and in the clearest cases IRCC's instructions say the application should not be examined at all. If you already have a pending H&C application, a second one should not be examined, with the instructions noting there are no exceptions and the fee and application returned. If you are found inadmissible under sections A34, A35 or A37 of IRPA, covering security, human or international rights violations, and organized criminality, an exemption may not be requested and the application should not be examined, again with no exceptions. Where such inadmissibility is suspected but not determined, the file goes to the Centre of Expertise in Security Cases and the fees are kept. A separate 12-month bar applies to people who have made a refugee claim, subject to two exceptions.

| Situation | Effect on the H&C application |
|---|---|
| Pending H&C application already on file | Not examined, no exceptions, fee and application returned |
| Found inadmissible under A34, A35 or A37 | Not examined, no exceptions |
| Suspected A34, A35 or A37 inadmissibility | Referred to the Centre of Expertise in Security Cases, fees kept |
| Refugee claim made, inside the 12-month bar | Barred, subject to the exceptions below |
| Medical condition posing a risk to life | Exception to the 12-month bar |
| Best interests of a child (BIOC) | Exception to the 12-month bar |

## What does an H&C application cost, and is the fee refundable?

Fees must be paid up front and you do not get them back if you are refused. IRCC's instructions are explicit that for in-Canada requests under subsection A25(1), fees must be collected before the application can be examined, under subsection A25(1.1) and section R307 of the Regulations. For applicants overseas, the processing fee for the permanent resident visa must be paid before the application may be considered, and **the fee cannot be refunded even if the application is refused**. The one carve-out in the instructions is that there are no processing fees where someone applies in the refugee classes overseas and requests H&C consideration. Given the published timeline, treat the fee as spent at the moment you file.

## Can you stay in Canada while waiting for an H&C decision?

An H&C application does not by itself give you status in Canada. It is a request for an exemption so that a permanent residence application can be considered, not a temporary status document and not a stay of removal. IRCC's processing instructions deal separately with post-removal assessment and with how H&C applications relate to a pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA), which are different mechanisms with their own rules. If you are out of status or facing removal, the interaction between H&C, PRRA and removal is the part to get professional advice on, because filing an H&C application is not a substitute for maintaining status.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Stage 1 approval for H&C?
Stage 1, or approval in principle, is IRCC's decision on the humanitarian and compassionate exemptions you asked for. It is not a grant of permanent residence. Stage 2 is the separate, final decision on the permanent residence application.

### Who is not eligible for H&C?
People with a pending H&C application, people found inadmissible under sections A34, A35 or A37 of IRPA, and people inside the 12-month bar following a refugee claim, unless the medical-risk or best-interests-of-a-child exception applies.

### Can I stay in Canada while waiting for H&C?
An H&C application does not grant status or halt removal on its own. Maintaining your own status, or addressing removal through the appropriate mechanism, is a separate matter from the H&C application.

### What is the new IRCC update for H&C in 2026?
On July 22, 2026, IRCC published instructions confirming that where H&C is requested inside an in-Canada permanent residence public policy application, no separate H&C decision is issued. The public policy application is refused and the applicant is told to re-apply on H&C grounds and pay the fees again.

### Is the H&C processing time really more than 10 years?
That is the figure IRCC published as of July 7, 2026, for both Quebec and the rest of Canada. It is the top of IRCC's published scale rather than a precise estimate, and five other backlogged categories carry the same value.

### Can I file a second H&C application while one is pending?
No. IRCC's instructions state a second application should not be examined where one is already pending, with no exceptions, and the fee and application are returned.

## Sources

- [H&C: In-Canada PR granting public policies where H&C requests were also made](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/humanitarian-compassionate-consideration/processing/in-canada/pr/hc-requests.html) (published July 22, 2026)

# Study Permit Financial Checks Tightened: What IRCC Changed on July 24, 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/study-permit-financial-checks-tightened-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-07-30
Author: Go Far Global Team

> IRCC updated its officer instructions for assessing study permit finances on July 24, 2026. The thresholds did not move. What changed is that officers are now directed to verify the source and history of your funds, not just the balance.

# Study Permit Financial Checks Tightened: What IRCC Changed on July 24, 2026

*As of July 30, 2026.* Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) updated the instructions its officers use to assess study permit finances on July 24, 2026, and the shift is from checking how much money you have to checking where it came from and whether it is really yours.

> For study permit applicants and the people funding them. This covers what officers were told to look at, the 6-month bank statement rule, the documents that count, and the refusal mechanics most guides never mention.

## What changed for study permit financial checks on July 24, 2026?

IRCC revised the [program delivery instructions for assessing a study permit application](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/assessing-application.html), and the page carries a July 24, 2026 date. The substance is about verification rather than amounts. Officers are now directed to assess both the amount and the source of an applicant's funds, and to satisfy themselves that there is a probability of those funds being available and accessible. The instructions state that reviewing and verifying the history of funds, together with supplementary individual or family financial and employment documentation, may be necessary to ensure that only genuine students capable of supporting themselves are approved. The cost-of-living thresholds did not change on that date. What changed is the depth of scrutiny applied to proving them.

## What does IRCC actually require you to prove?

Three things, and the statutory wording matters. [Section 220 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/assessing-application.html) says an officer shall not issue a study permit unless the applicant has sufficient and available financial resources, **without working**, to pay tuition, to maintain themselves and any accompanying family members, and to pay transportation to and from Canada. The phrase "without working" is the one applicants underestimate. A plan to cover living costs through on-campus or off-campus work does not satisfy R220. You must also only demonstrate funds for the **first year** of study, regardless of how long the program runs.

### IRCC's own worked example

The instructions give a single student entering a 4-year degree in Ontario with annual tuition of CAD $15,000. That applicant must show the first year of tuition, meaning CAD $15,000, **not** the CAD $60,000 covering all four years, plus living costs and travel.

## How many months of bank statements does IRCC want?

Six months. The instructions list bank statements, from a Canadian or foreign bank account, for the past 6 months, and add a detail that trips people up: the statements must include the month the application was submitted or the month prior. A six-month history that ends three months before you file does not meet the wording. This is also where the tightened source-of-funds review bites. A balance that appears shortly before filing, with no history explaining it, is exactly the pattern the July 24 instructions direct officers to examine. If a family member deposited the money, expect to document their income as well as the transfer.

## What documents count as proof of funds?

IRCC lists nine acceptable forms of proof, and two of them explicitly cannot stand alone. The instructions frame this as demonstrating your overall financial capacity rather than producing one decisive document, so most approved files combine two or three of the items below. A [GIC](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/get-documents/financial-support.html) plus six months of statements is the most common pairing, and a sponsor letter is never sufficient by itself. Match each of the three R220 costs, meaning tuition, living expenses and travel, to at least one document rather than assuming a single large balance covers all three.

| Accepted proof | Notes |
|---|---|
| Bank statements for the past 6 months | Must include the month of submission or the month prior |
| Guaranteed investment certificate (GIC) | From a participating Canadian financial institution |
| Proof of a Canadian bank account in your name | If you have already transferred money to Canada |
| Proof of paid first-year tuition and housing | Must be accompanied by other proof of living and travel costs |
| A letter from the person or institution giving you money | Must be accompanied by other supporting documents |
| Student or education loan from a bank | Private or foreign lender |
| Proof of funding within Canada | Scholarship or Canadian-funded educational program |
| Financial documents related to a pension | |
| Proof of income from rental properties | |

Scholarships, fellowships, assistantships and support in kind may also be considered. One trap worth naming: international students in Canada are **not** eligible for the Canada Student Loan Program, so it cannot form part of your proof.

## How much money do you need to show in 2026?

For applications submitted on or after September 1, 2025, a single applicant outside Quebec must show CAD $22,895 for living expenses for the first year, on top of tuition and return travel. Be careful with figures you find in search results. Google's own answer panel for this question is currently still displaying the previous table, which topped out at $20,635 for a single applicant, and several education and agency pages repeat it. The amounts below are [the current ones](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/get-documents/financial-support.html). Quebec sets its own, higher requirement.

| Family members, including the applicant | Amount required per year, excluding tuition and travel |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | $22,895 |
| 2 | $28,502 |
| 3 | $35,040 |
| 4 | $42,543 |
| 5 | $48,252 |
| 6 | $54,420 |
| 7 | $60,589 |
| Each additional member beyond 7 | $6,170 |

## Are the cost-of-living amounts actually law?

No, and this is the most useful thing to understand about how these files get decided. [IRCC's instructions](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/assessing-application.html) state plainly that the cost-of-living amounts are policy guidelines set through Ministerial direction, and are **not** established by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or its Regulations. Officers apply them using discretion. In practice that cuts both ways. Meeting the number exactly does not guarantee approval if the source of funds looks unreliable, which is precisely what the July 24 update targets. It also means the assessment is of your overall financial capacity, not a single balance on a single day.

## What if your country has foreign exchange controls?

IRCC has a separate rule for this, and it is largely absent from the guidance published elsewhere. Where a student depends on funds subject to foreign exchange controls, officers should require one of three things: a letter from a Canadian financial institution confirming the funds for the entire upcoming academic year are on deposit in the applicant's name, a bank draft in convertible currency for the year's required funds made payable jointly to the school and the applicant, or written assurance from the applicant's bank that sufficient funds are on deposit together with confirmation from the foreign exchange control authorities that the applicant will be permitted to export an adequate sum. If you are applying from a country with capital controls, plan for this before you file.

## On what grounds can an officer refuse a study permit for finances?

Section R220 is the operative ground, and there is a technical limit on a second one that matters if you are challenging a refusal. Where an applicant cannot demonstrate sufficient and available financial resources, officers are directed to refuse under R220. The instructions add that paragraph R216(1)(b) **cannot be cited exclusively** as a refusal ground for failing to meet financial resources. It can only be selected in addition to R220. A refusal resting on R216(1)(b) alone for financial reasons is inconsistent with IRCC's own instructions, which is worth knowing before you decide whether to reapply or seek review.

## Who is exempt from showing proof of funds?

A small number of applicants. IRCC's instructions remind officers that temporary public policies and pilot programs may exempt applicants from the proof-of-funds requirement, or apply different amounts. Two are named: the temporary measures to reunite families of Indigenous people separated by Canada's border, and the Francophone Minority Communities Student Pilot (FMCSP). Officers are told to check whether an applicant falls under one of these before assessing against the standard thresholds. For the FMCSP specifically, paragraph R216(1)(b) cannot be used as a refusal ground at all.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you show proof of funds for a Canada study permit?
Through documents that show both an adequate amount and a credible source: 6 months of bank statements ending in the month you apply or the month before, a GIC, a Canadian bank account, paid tuition receipts, a loan, or a sponsor letter backed by that sponsor's own financial and employment documents.

### How much money do you need for a study permit in Canada?
A single applicant outside Quebec needs CAD $22,895 for living costs for the first year, plus first-year tuition and return travel, for applications submitted on or after September 1, 2025. Quebec sets separate, higher amounts.

### What is the minimum bank balance for a student visa in Canada?
There is no single minimum balance. IRCC assesses overall financial capacity against the cost-of-living amount for your family size, plus tuition and travel, and the money has to be available without working.

### How many months of proof of funds does Canada need for a study permit?
Six months of bank statements, and they must include the month you submitted the application or the month immediately before it.

### Does a large recent deposit hurt your application?
It can. The July 24, 2026 instructions direct officers to review the history and source of funds, so an unexplained lump sum shortly before filing invites questions. Document where it came from and the sender's ability to provide it.

### Can you use a study permit extension to fix a proof-of-funds problem?
No. The financial requirement applies to the application in front of the officer. If your funds no longer meet the threshold, address the underlying documentation rather than assuming an extension is assessed more leniently.

## Sources
- [Study permits: Assessing the application](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/assessing-application.html) (program delivery instructions, updated July 24, 2026)
- [Study permit: Proof of financial support](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/get-documents/financial-support.html)
- [Study permit: Get the right documents](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/get-documents.html)

# Canada Passport Renewal 2026: Online, In Person, by Mail and Urgent

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/renew-canadian-passport-online-2026
Category: Citizenship
Published: 2026-07-30
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Online passport renewal opened to all eligible adults on July 28, 2026. The rule that disqualifies the most people is the one almost no coverage leads with: if your passport expires more than 6 months from now, you cannot renew online. And applying cancels the passport you are still carrying.

*As of August 11, 2026. Checked against Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada's current passport program pages.*

Canada has three ways to renew an adult passport: online, in person, and by mail. Online renewal opened nationally in July 2026 and the daily application caps that throttled it at launch are gone, but the eligibility rules for the online route are stricter than most people expect, and one of them is the opposite of what intuition says: if your passport still has more than six months left, you cannot renew it online.

This guide covers who qualifies for each route, what renewal actually costs after the March 2026 fee increase, how long each option takes right now, and the urgent services that exist when a trip is close.

## Can you renew your Canadian passport online?

**Short answer:** Yes, if you clear every item on a strict list. You must be renewing your own adult passport, applied for when you were 16 or older; it must be a regular blue passport, valid for 5 or 10 years, showing your place of birth, and issued within the last 15 years. Your home and mailing address must be in Canada, your passport must expire within the next 6 months or have already expired, and you must not need it for travel in the next 20 business days.

The six-month rule surprises people. Renewing early is normally sensible, but the online system rejects passports with more than six months of validity left. If yours expires next year and you want it renewed now, you are applying in person or by mail.

Two more things before you start. You need a digital photo that meets the government's specifications, taken by a commercial photographer or by someone else following the rules. And your current passport is cancelled the moment you apply, not when the new one arrives, so you cannot book flights on the old document while you wait.

## Who cannot renew online at all?

**Short answer:** Anyone outside Canada, since online renewals are only delivered to Canadian addresses. Anyone whose current passport was issued more than 15 years ago, was a temporary or diplomatic document, or does not show place of birth. Anyone applying for a child: children's passports are never renewed, and every child application is a new application. And anyone changing their name, which also requires a new application rather than a renewal.

If you fall outside the online rules, you have not lost anything: the in-person and mail routes take the same application form, and in person is currently the fastest standard option anyway.

## How long are Canadian passport renewals taking right now?

**Short answer:** The published service standards are 20 business days plus mailing time for online and mail applications, and 10 or 20 business days for in-person applications depending on where you apply, with the 10-day standard at passport offices and certain Service Canada Centres. On top of those standards, IRCC is currently warning of mail delivery delays following the Canada Post labour disruption, which affects any passport being mailed rather than picked up.

| Route | Published standard | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Online | 20 business days + mailing | Delivery to Canadian addresses only |
| In person, passport office | 10 business days | Pick-up available; proof of travel may be required |
| In person, Service Canada Centre | 10 or 20 business days | Depends on the location's service level |
| By mail | 20 business days + mailing | Same form as in person |
| Urgent pick-up | End of next business day | In person, with proof of travel, extra fees |
| Express pick-up | 2 to 9 business days | Slower at some locations |

If mail disruption is a concern for your timeline, applying in person at a location that offers pick-up removes Canada Post from the equation entirely.

## What is the fastest way to renew a Canadian passport?

**Short answer:** Urgent pick-up service, which delivers a passport by the end of the next business day. Below that sits express pick-up at 2 to 9 business days, and an emergency service exists for weekends and statutory holidays. All of these require applying in person, documentation proving the urgency, usually proof of travel, and additional fees on top of the regular passport fee.

Two caveats from IRCC's own guidance. Some locations take at least 3 or 4 business days to process express applications rather than 2, so if you are cutting it close, the specific office matters. And you can request faster service after you have already applied through a normal route if your travel date moves, rather than starting over.

The practical rule: if your trip is inside two weeks, do not apply online. Online applications cannot be expedited into a pick-up, and your old passport is already cancelled once you have applied.

## Can you walk into Service Canada for passport renewal?

**Short answer:** Yes. Passport offices and many Service Canada Centres accept walk-in passport applications, and no appointment is required at most locations, though booking one where available shortens the wait. The 10-business-day processing standard applies at passport offices, while some smaller Service Canada Centres forward applications for processing and carry the 20-day standard instead.

Bring the completed form rather than expecting to fill it out there, plus your photos, references and fee payment. If you need urgent or express service, walk-in at a full passport office is the only way to access it, and you should bring evidence of your travel date.

## How many months before expiry can you renew?

**Short answer:** There is no minimum wait and no penalty for renewing early: you can renew a Canadian passport at any point, and unused validity on the old passport is not added to the new one. The only timing constraint is the online route's requirement that the passport expire within 6 months or already be expired. In person and by mail, you can renew whenever you choose.

The reason to renew well before expiry is other countries' rules, not Canada's. Many destinations require six months of validity beyond your travel dates, so a passport with five months left can be refused boarding even though it is not expired. Check the entry requirements for your destination before deciding the renewal can wait.

An expired passport is not a problem for renewing: passports issued within the last 15 years qualify for renewal whether or not they have expired.

## How much does passport renewal cost in 2026?

**Short answer:** Most passport fees increased on March 31, 2026, so figures in articles written before that date, and many still ranking in search results, are out of date. The current fee depends on whether you choose a 5-year or 10-year passport, whether you are in Canada or abroad, and whether you add urgent, express or weekend service, each of which carries its own additional fee. Check the exact current amounts on [IRCC's passport fees page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-passports/fees.html) before you pay.

Two payment details catch people out. Many in-Canada passport services cannot be paid online, so confirm your payment options before attempting to pay. And the 10-year passport costs meaningfully less per year of validity than the 5-year, which is why most adults choose it.

## What do you need to submit with a renewal?

**Short answer:** The adult renewal form, your current or expired passport, two identical passport photos taken within the last six months (or one digital photo for online renewals), two references who have known you for at least two years, and the fee. Renewals do not require the guarantor and citizenship documents that first-time applications do, which is what makes renewal the simpler process.

References cannot be family members, and your photographer's information has to appear on printed photos. For the online route, the digital photo has its own specification and is checked when you upload it.

If any of your details have changed in a way the form cannot capture, or your passport is damaged, lost or stolen, you are outside the renewal process and into a new application, which brings back the guarantor requirement and proof of citizenship.

## Where can you get help with a passport tied to an immigration file?

**Short answer:** For a routine renewal, you do not need help: the process is designed for individuals and no representative can speed it up. Where advice earns its place is when a passport interacts with an immigration application, because a renewal at the wrong moment can strand a valid visa or permit in a cancelled document.

If you hold a temporary resident visa, a work or study permit, or a permanent residence application in progress, the passport you renew is not automatically linked to them. A visa in an expired passport is not transferred; you travel with both documents or apply to have the visa reissued. Permit holders need their immigration documents updated to reflect the new passport number for some transactions.

Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto. If your passport renewal touches an active immigration file, [book a consultation](/book) before you apply. For Canadian citizenship questions that precede a first passport, see our [citizenship application guide](/news/canadian-citizenship-application-2026), and for current IRCC queues our [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) pages.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I walk into Service Canada for passport renewal?

Yes. Walk-in service is available at passport offices and many Service Canada Centres, and it is the only way to access urgent and express processing. Full passport offices work to a 10-business-day standard and offer pick-up, which also avoids the current Canada Post delivery delays. Smaller centres may forward your application and carry the 20-day standard instead, so check what service level your location offers before choosing it. Bring your completed form, photos, references, payment, and proof of travel if you intend to request faster service. Appointments are optional but shorten waits where offered.

### How long are Canadian passport renewals taking right now?

The published standards are 20 business days plus mailing time for online and mail applications, and 10 or 20 business days in person depending on the location. IRCC states it is processing applications normally but warns of mail delivery delays following the Canada Post labour disruption, which adds unpredictable time to anything delivered by mail. If your timeline is tight, an in-person application with pick-up is currently the most predictable route, and express pick-up shortens processing to 2 to 9 business days at most locations for an additional fee.

### How many months before expiry can I renew my Canadian passport?

You can renew at any time, with no minimum and no penalty beyond losing whatever validity remained on the old passport, since unused time is not carried over. The exception is the online system, which only accepts passports expiring within the next 6 months or already expired. Renewing early matters mostly because many countries require six months of passport validity beyond your travel dates, so a passport that is technically valid can still be inadequate for a trip. Passports issued within the last 15 years remain eligible for renewal even after they expire.

### What is the fastest way to renew my Canadian passport?

Apply in person at a passport office and request urgent pick-up, which delivers by the end of the next business day, with proof of travel and additional fees. Express pick-up takes 2 to 9 business days, though some locations need at least 3 or 4. An emergency service covers weekends and statutory holidays. None of these are available through the online or mail routes, and an online application cannot be converted to urgent processing, so if a trip is close, in person is the only sensible choice. If you already applied and your travel moved up, contact IRCC to request faster service on the existing application.

- [Renew a passport online in Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-passports/renew-adult-passport/submit-form-fees/renew-online.html), IRCC

# Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP) Canada 2026: Eligibility by Program

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/bridging-open-work-permit-bowp-canada-2026
Category: Work Permit
Published: 2026-07-30
Author: Go Far Global Team

> A bridging open work permit lets you keep working while IRCC decides your permanent residence application. Which document unlocks it depends on your PR program, and two widely repeated eligibility rules do not appear in IRCC's instructions at all.

# Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP) Canada 2026: Eligibility by Program

*As of July 30, 2026.* A bridging open work permit lets you keep working while Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) decides your permanent residence application, and the document that unlocks it is different depending on which program you applied under.

> For workers in Canada with a permanent residence application in progress and a work permit running out. This guide sets out what IRCC actually requires for each of the eight programs, and dates the October 2021 change that made two still widely repeated eligibility rules obsolete.

## What is a bridging open work permit (BOWP)?

A bridging open work permit is an open work permit for people already in Canada who have a permanent residence (PR) application in progress. IRCC describes it as a permit that "lets you keep working while you wait for the results of your permanent residence application." Open means it is not tied to one employer, so you can change jobs without a new permit. It exists to close the gap between a work permit that is about to expire and a PR decision that has not arrived yet. It is not a separate immigration program and it does not speed up your PR application. It is a temporary permit that depends entirely on your PR application staying alive.

## Who is eligible for a BOWP in 2026?

Four conditions apply across almost every program. You must live in Canada when you apply, and for the federal and non-Quebec provincial streams you must intend to live outside Quebec. You must be the principal applicant on the PR application, not a spouse or dependant. You must have submitted a complete PR application that passed IRCC's completeness check. And your status must be one of three things: valid temporary resident status with a valid work permit, an expired work permit where you maintained your status as a worker, or eligibility to restore your status and get a work permit. What differs by program is the fourth item, the document that proves your PR application has reached the right stage.

## Which document do you need for each PR program?

The trigger document is where most applications go wrong. Some programs release the BOWP at acknowledgement of receipt (AOR), which is the letter confirming your PR application passed the completeness check. Others hold it until approval in principle (AIP), a later and more substantive decision confirming you meet the PR eligibility rules. The Quebec streams key off a Certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ) instead of either. And one pilot that opened in 2025 does not qualify for a BOWP at all, which catches out applicants who assume every caregiver stream works the same way. Find your program in the table below before you file anything.

| PR program you applied under | Document IRCC requires | Extra condition |
|---|---|---|
| Express Entry: Federal Skilled Worker (FSW), Canadian Experience Class (CEC), Federal Skilled Trades | Acknowledgement of receipt (AOR) | Passed completeness check |
| Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) via Express Entry | AOR plus nomination letter | No employment restrictions on the nomination |
| Provincial Nominee Program not via Express Entry | AOR plus nomination letter | Passed the eligibility assessment |
| Quebec skilled worker class | Certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ) plus PR application number letter | Must intend to live in Quebec |
| Quebec investors | CSQ plus PR application number letter | Must live in Quebec |
| Home Child Care Provider or Home Support Worker Pilot (2019 to 2024) | Approval in principle (AIP) letter | 6 months of qualifying work experience |
| Caring for children or people with high medical needs | Approval in principle (AIP) letter | Applied before June 18, 2019 |
| Agri-Food Pilot | Approval in principle (AIP) letter | Principal applicant only |
| **Home Care Worker Immigration pilots (opened 2025)** | **Not eligible for a BOWP** | See other work permit options |

For the Quebec streams, the PR application number on that letter begins with the letter E. For Express Entry and PNP streams, submitting an Express Entry profile to the pool is not the same as applying for permanent residence, and it does not make you eligible.

## Is there a 4-month rule for applying for a BOWP?

Not any more. This one is worth explaining properly, because the rule was real and it is now obsolete. Until 2021, you could only apply for a BOWP if your work permit was set to expire within four months. IRCC removed that requirement in October 2021, in the same change that added the Quebec Skilled Worker Class and extended eligibility to people on maintained status or eligible for restoration. No four-month window appears anywhere in [IRCC's current BOWP instructions](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/pr-work-permits/bridging.html). The rule survives online because firm websites never updated, and Google's AI Overview now repeats it, sourced to those sites rather than to IRCC. If your permit has more than four months left, you are not too early.

## Do you need to be holding a valid work permit right now?

Not necessarily, and this is the other half of the same 2021 change. Much of the published guidance says a BOWP requires a valid work permit, which was correct before October 2021, when the old rules denied a BOWP to anyone whose work permit had already expired. IRCC's current instructions list three acceptable positions, and only the first involves a valid permit. You can have valid status with a valid work permit. You can have an expired work permit where you maintained your status as a worker by applying to extend before it expired. Or you can be eligible to restore your status and get a work permit. A lapsed permit is no longer an automatic disqualification.

## When should you apply for a BOWP?

Apply before your current work permit expires. That is the practical rule, because applying before expiry is what lets you keep working under maintained status while IRCC processes the new permit. IRCC's guidance is explicit that if you are not yet eligible for a BOWP, you should not let your work permit lapse while waiting for an invitation to apply. Extend your existing work permit instead, which may require your employer to obtain a new Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or submit a new offer of employment. IRCC does not publish a BOWP-specific processing time. A BOWP is processed as a work permit application from inside Canada, so check [IRCC's processing times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) for the current figure, which IRCC revises monthly.

## Can you leave Canada while your BOWP is being processed?

You can travel, but the risk is real and IRCC words it carefully. You may leave Canada temporarily while your PR application is processed. If your work permit expires while you are outside Canada, or if you leave after it has expired, you lose your temporary resident status, and on return you cannot work until the new permit is approved. For the provincial nominee streams IRCC goes further: you must be in Canada with valid temporary resident status when IRCC makes a decision on your BOWP, or the application may be refused. So the danger is not the trip itself. It is being outside Canada, or out of status, at the moment your permit expires or your decision lands.

## How much does a BOWP cost in 2026?

A BOWP costs $255 in government fees, made up of the $155 work permit processing fee and the $100 open work permit holder fee. IRCC requires both, and the open work permit holder fee is the one applicants most often miss, which can render an application incomplete. There is no separate BOWP fee and no premium for bridging. If you are also restoring your status as a worker, that is a different and higher fee combination of $401.25, which covers restoration at $246.25 plus the $155 work permit.

| Item | Fee (CAD) |
|---|---:|
| Work permit processing fee | 155 |
| Open work permit holder fee | 100 |
| **BOWP total** | **255** |
| Restore status as a worker, including new work permit | 401.25 |

Current amounts are on [IRCC's fee list](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/information/fees/fees.asp).

## How do you apply for a BOWP?

You apply using the instructions for extending or changing the conditions on your work permit, not through a dedicated BOWP form. Three things have to be right. Select "Open work permit" as the type of work permit. Pay both the work permit processing fee and the open work permit holder fee. Upload your trigger document, meaning your AOR letter, AIP letter, nomination letter or CSQ, in the "Client information" field of your document checklist. In most cases you must apply online, and IRCC allows a paper application only if you have problems applying online. Applicants under the Quebec skilled worker and Quebec investor streams must also answer yes to the portal question asking whether IRCC has told you that you are approved in principle for permanent residence.

## What is the AOR trap for PNP applicants who did not use Express Entry?

Receiving your AOR does not mean your BOWP is moving. IRCC states this directly for provincial nominee applicants outside Express Entry: the AOR letter "doesn't mean your BOWP application is being processed," and IRCC will not begin processing the BOWP until it has reviewed your PR application and confirmed you meet the basic PR eligibility requirements under the PNP. In practice that means you can hold an AOR, have filed a correct BOWP, and still be waiting on a step that has not started. Plan your work permit expiry around the eligibility assessment rather than around the AOR date. There is also a separate 2026 measure allowing some PNP candidates to get a work permit without an AOR, which is worth checking against your own file.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long is a bridging open work permit valid?
IRCC does not publish a fixed validity period on the public BOWP page, and the expiry is set by the officer against your pending PR application. Its operational comparison table for the Quebec skilled worker stream does give a figure: 24 months from the date of issue, with extensions issued for 12 months, and officers free to use discretion based on current processing times. Treat that as the shape of it rather than a guarantee for every stream, and check the permit itself when it arrives.

### Can a BOWP be rejected?
Yes. The most common grounds are failing one of the status conditions, submitting before your PR application passes the completeness check, missing the open work permit holder fee, or being outside Canada or out of status when IRCC decides.

### Can I leave Canada while waiting for a bridging open work permit?
You can, but if your work permit expires while you are away, or you leave after it has expired, you cannot work on return until the new permit is approved. For provincial nominee streams you must be in Canada with valid status when the decision is made.

### How long does a bridging open work permit take?
IRCC does not publish a BOWP-specific figure. It is processed as a work permit from inside Canada, so use IRCC's processing times tool for the current estimate rather than relying on a number quoted on a third-party site.

### Can a bridging open work permit be extended?
A BOWP is tied to your pending PR application, so it is not extended indefinitely. If your PR application is still in progress and your BOWP is running out, speak to a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) about your options before it expires.

### Does my spouse get a work permit too?
A BOWP is for the principal applicant. A spouse or common-law partner may qualify for their own open work permit under separate rules, which changed in January 2025, so their eligibility has to be assessed on its own.

# Approval in Principle (AIP) in Canada: What It Means in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/approval-in-principle-aip-canada-2026
Category: Sponsorship
Published: 2026-07-29
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Approval in principle confirms IRCC accepted your sponsor and your relationship as genuine, but not your medical or security checks. What the letter actually unlocks, how it differs from your AOR, and the one situation where you cannot get an open work permit without it.

# Approval in Principle (AIP) in Canada: What It Means in 2026

*As of July 29, 2026.* Approval in principle means Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has accepted that you meet the permanent residence eligibility rules, but your medical, security and background checks are still open.

> For sponsored spouses and partners waiting on a decision. This guide explains what the approval in principle letter actually confirms, why it is not the same thing as your acknowledgement of receipt, and the one situation where you genuinely cannot get an open work permit without it.

## What does approval in principle (AIP) mean in Canada?

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) defines it precisely. Your application is "approved in principle (AIP)" if you have received a letter from IRCC stating that you meet the permanent residence eligibility requirements, but you still have to pass the medical, security and background checks for you and, if needed, your family members. In a spousal sponsorship file, that means two things have been settled: your sponsor was approved as a sponsor, and IRCC accepted your relationship as genuine. Nothing else is final. Approval in principle is a first-stage decision, not permanent residence, and it does not by itself give you status in Canada.

## Is AIP the Atlantic Immigration Program or approval in principle?

Both, and that is why searching for it is confusing. The acronym AIP carries two unrelated meanings in Canadian immigration. Approval in principle is a first-stage decision on a permanent residence application. The [Atlantic Immigration Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/atlantic-immigration/how-to-immigrate.html) is an employer-driven permanent residence program for New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador. IRCC's own processing-times data feed uses the key `aip` for the Atlantic Immigration Program, which is why search engines routinely return Atlantic Immigration Program pages and its 26-month processing time to people who are asking about a first-stage sponsorship decision. The two have no relationship. If you are a sponsored spouse, the Atlantic Immigration Program's timeline tells you nothing about your file.

| Term | What it is | Who it applies to |
|---|---|---|
| Approval in principle (AIP) | First-stage decision on a permanent residence application | Sponsored spouses, partners, and other PR applicants |
| Atlantic Immigration Program (AIP) | Employer-driven PR program in the four Atlantic provinces | Skilled workers and graduates with an Atlantic job offer |

## How long does approval in principle take in spousal sponsorship?

IRCC does not publish a processing time for the approval in principle stage. It publishes one figure for the whole application, from submission to final decision. Any "AIP takes 4 to 9 months" figure you find online is a third-party estimate, not an IRCC service standard, and IRCC does not commit to it. What IRCC does publish, updated July 7, 2026, is the total spousal sponsorship processing time. Treat approval in principle as an unscheduled milestone somewhere inside these windows rather than a date you can count on.

| Application type | IRCC processing time (July 7, 2026) |
|---|---:|
| Spouse or partner in Canada, outside Quebec (inland) | About 27 months |
| Spouse or partner abroad, outside Quebec (outland) | About 17 months |
| Spouse or partner in Canada, Quebec | About 32 months |
| Spouse or partner abroad, Quebec | About 33 months |

Check the live figure on IRCC's [processing times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) before you rely on any number, including these. IRCC revises them monthly.

## What is the difference between AOR and approval in principle?

They are different letters arriving at different stages, and people mix them up constantly. The acknowledgement of receipt (AOR) is an administrative confirmation. IRCC states that the AOR letter means an officer has reviewed your application package and confirmed that it is complete, and that the application number on it starts with the letter F. It says nothing about whether you qualify. Approval in principle is a substantive decision that comes later and confirms you meet the eligibility rules. Getting an AOR is not approval of anything. Getting approval in principle is approval of eligibility only.

| | Acknowledgement of receipt (AOR) | Approval in principle (AIP) |
|---|---|---|
| What it confirms | Your package is complete | You meet PR eligibility rules |
| Decision type | Administrative | Substantive, first stage |
| Still outstanding | Everything | Medical, security, background checks |
| Unlocks the open work permit | Yes, if you hold valid status | Yes, and it is required if you are out of status |

## Do you need approval in principle to get a spousal open work permit?

For most applicants, no, and this is the single most common piece of outdated advice on the subject. If you hold valid temporary resident status, IRCC's rule is that once you get your AOR letter, you can apply for an open work permit. You do not wait for approval in principle. Older forum threads still say the opposite because that was the rule before the inland open work permit pilot changed it. There is one real exception. If you do not have valid temporary resident status and your permanent residence application is being processed under the spousal public policy, IRCC states you must wait until you have received your approval in principle letter to be eligible to apply for an open work permit. Out-of-status applicants in that situation also cannot apply online.

### If you are out of status

You apply on paper, and your package must include a letter explaining that you cannot apply online because you are out of status, plus a copy of your approval in principle letter. Full requirements are on IRCC's [spousal open work permit page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/spouse-common-law-partner-canada-open-work-permit.html).

### If your status expires within two weeks

You can apply for the work permit without an AOR at all, but only if both conditions are met: your work permit, study permit or temporary resident status expires in two weeks or less, and you applied for permanent residence under the Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada class (SCLPC) or the family class as a spouse, common-law or conjugal partner.

## What happens after approval in principle?

Your file moves to the checks that were still open when the letter was issued. IRCC completes medical, security, criminality and background screening on you and any family members included in the application. If your medical exam has expired by this point, you will be asked to redo it. You may receive requests for updated police certificates or additional relationship evidence. Once the checks clear, IRCC issues the final decision and, for applicants in Canada, confirms permanent residence. You can also extend an open work permit granted under this public policy for two more years if you received your AOR, and your permanent residence application is still being processed with no decision made.

## What can still go wrong after approval in principle?

Approval in principle is reversible, which is why treating it as the finish line is a mistake. Eligibility was approved on the evidence in front of the officer at that moment. A failed medical, a security or criminality concern, or new information about the relationship can all still sink the application. Separation or divorce after approval in principle ends the basis for a spousal application entirely, and you are obliged to tell IRCC. Misrepresentation discovered later can trigger a five-year bar. The practical rule is simple: keep your medical valid, respond to every IRCC request inside the deadline, and report any change in your relationship or address promptly.

1. Medical results expire or come back with an inadmissibility finding.
2. Security or criminality screening raises a concern for you or a dependant.
3. The relationship ends, or IRCC receives information suggesting it is not genuine.
4. You miss a request for additional documents and the file is refused for non-response.
5. Undisclosed information surfaces and is treated as misrepresentation.

## How much does spousal sponsorship cost in 2026?

Sponsoring a spouse or partner costs $1,260 in government fees. IRCC publishes this as a bundled amount covering the sponsorship fee, the principal applicant processing fee, and the $600 right of permanent residence fee, rather than as separate line items. The right of permanent residence fee can be paid later, which brings the upfront amount down to $660. The totals are identical whether your partner is in Canada or abroad. The open work permit is billed separately at $155 for the work permit plus the $100 open work permit holder fee. Biometrics add $85 per person. None of these figures change based on whether you have reached approval in principle.

| Item | Fee (CAD) |
|---|---:|
| **Spousal sponsorship, including right of permanent residence fee** | **1,260** |
| Spousal sponsorship, without right of permanent residence fee | 660 |
| Right of permanent residence fee | 600 |
| Work permit | 155 |
| Open work permit holder fee | 100 |
| Biometrics, per person | 85 |

Current amounts are on IRCC's [fee list](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/information/fees/fees.asp).

## Frequently asked questions

### What is AIP in spousal sponsorship?
It is the first-stage decision confirming that your sponsor qualifies and IRCC accepts your relationship as genuine. Medical, security and background checks remain outstanding after it is issued.

### How long does it take to get approval in principle in spousal sponsorship?
IRCC does not publish a timeline for this stage. It publishes a total processing time of about 27 months for inland applications outside Quebec and about 17 months for outland applications outside Quebec, as of July 7, 2026.

### What is an approval in principle letter from IRCC?
It is a letter stating you meet the permanent residence eligibility requirements while the medical, security and background checks are still pending. Out-of-status applicants must attach a copy of it to a paper open work permit application.

### Who is the principal applicant in spousal sponsorship in Canada?
The principal applicant is the person being sponsored, not the sponsor. The sponsor is the Canadian citizen or permanent resident who submits the sponsorship undertaking.

### Does approval in principle give me status in Canada?
No. It is a decision on eligibility for permanent residence, not a grant of temporary or permanent status. You must maintain your own valid status or apply for restoration if you have lost it.

### Can approval in principle be revoked?
Yes. It can be reversed if a check comes back negative, the relationship ends, or IRCC receives new information that changes the eligibility assessment.

# CAQ Quebec 2026: Quebec Acceptance Certificate for Students

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/caq-quebec-acceptance-certificate-2026
Category: Study in Canada
Published: 2026-07-24
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Certificat d'acceptation du Quebec (CAQ) is the provincial document you need before IRCC will issue a study permit for Quebec. What it costs in 2026, how long it lasts, the documents required, and how it differs from a CSQ.

*As of July 24, 2026.*

If you plan to study in Quebec, you need a document that students heading to any other province never encounter: the Certificat d'acceptation du Québec (CAQ), or Quebec Acceptance Certificate. Quebec selects its own temporary immigrants, so the province approves you first and the federal government approves you second. Miss this step and your study permit application goes nowhere.

One thing to clear up immediately: "CAQ" also stands for Coalition Avenir Québec, the provincial political party. This guide is about the immigration document.

## What does CAQ mean in Quebec immigration?

**Short answer:** CAQ stands for Certificat d'acceptation du Québec, the Quebec Acceptance Certificate. It is a provincial document issued by the Ministère de l'Immigration, de la Francisation et de l'Intégration (MIFI) confirming Quebec accepts you as a temporary resident to study or work there. You need it before Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) will issue your study permit.

Quebec is the only province that runs its own selection process for temporary residents. Under the Canada-Quebec Accord, the province decides who it accepts, and Ottawa handles admissibility, security, and medical screening afterward. The practical effect is a two-stage approval: Quebec first, then the federal government.

You apply for the CAQ online through MIFI's portal. The province publishes the process on its [temporary selection application page](https://www.quebec.ca/education/etudier-quebec/demande-selection-temporaire) and a general overview at [Studying in Québec](https://www.quebec.ca/en/education/study-quebec). Note that Quebec's most detailed pages are published in French, which is worth knowing before you start.

## How long is a CAQ valid?

**Short answer:** A CAQ for studies is generally issued to cover the length of your academic program, and it is commonly valid for up to 49 months. If your program runs longer, or if you change programs or institutions, you apply to renew or amend the certificate before it expires.

Validity is tied to your program, not to a fixed calendar period. A two-year college diploma typically receives a CAQ covering that program plus a short buffer. Because your study permit cannot extend beyond the validity of your provincial certificate, an expiring CAQ effectively caps your permit.

| Situation | What you do |
|---|---|
| Program finishes before the CAQ expires | No action needed |
| Program extends beyond the CAQ | Apply to renew before it expires |
| You change institution or program | Apply to amend or reapply |
| Program is 6 months or less | You may be exempt entirely |

Confirm current validity periods on the province's official pages before you rely on any figure, since Quebec has adjusted its temporary immigration rules repeatedly through 2025 and 2026.

## What documents do you need to obtain a CAQ?

**Short answer:** You generally need a letter of admission from a Quebec institution, a valid passport, proof you can cover tuition and living costs, and a completed online application. MIFI sends you a personalized document checklist after you pay, because required documents vary by applicant.

The core set is predictable:

1. **Letter of admission** from a recognized Quebec educational institution
2. **Valid passport** for you, and identity documents for any accompanying family
3. **Proof of financial capacity** covering tuition, living expenses, and return transport
4. **Completed online application** submitted through MIFI's portal
5. **Payment** of the processing fee

MIFI generates a personalized checklist in your online file once payment clears, which is the list that actually governs your file. Documents in a language other than English or French usually require a certified translation. Do not assemble your package from a third-party checklist alone, since the province adjusts requirements without much notice.

## How much does a CAQ cost in 2026?

**Short answer:** The CAQ processing fee rose to CA$135 effective January 1, 2026, according to figures reported for the current schedule. You pay online by credit card, and the fee is charged per applicant rather than per family.

The fee is separate from, and additional to, the federal study permit fee you pay IRCC later. Budget for both.

| Cost | Amount (CAD) |
|---|---|
| CAQ processing fee (2026) | $135 |
| Federal study permit application | Paid separately to IRCC |
| Biometrics, if required | Paid separately to IRCC |
| Certified translations | Varies by document |

Fee schedules change at the start of the calendar year, so verify the current amount on Quebec's official application page before paying. Quebec has raised immigration-related fees more than once in recent years, and a stale figure repeated on a third-party site is a common source of underpayment, which gets applications returned.

## What is the difference between a CAQ and a CSQ?

**Short answer:** A CAQ is temporary and a Certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ) is permanent. The CAQ supports a study permit or work permit for a defined period. The CSQ is Quebec's selection certificate for permanent residence, and it is the document you need before applying to IRCC for permanent resident status through a Quebec stream.

Students confuse these constantly, and the distinction matters because they sit at opposite ends of the immigration journey.

| Feature | CAQ | CSQ |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Temporary stay (study or work) | Permanent residence selection |
| Leads to | Study permit or work permit | Permanent residence application |
| Duration | Tied to your program or job | Used once for a PR application |
| Typical stage | Before you arrive to study | After you qualify through a Quebec stream |

If your longer-term plan is to stay in Quebec permanently, the CSQ is what you eventually pursue, often through the Programme de l'expérience québécoise (PEQ) or the skilled worker stream. We cover both in our guides to the [Quebec Experience Program](/news/peq-quebec-experience-program-2026) and the [Programme de sélection des travailleurs qualifiés](/news/pstq-quebec-skilled-worker-program-2026), and the [Arrima portal](/news/arrima-quebec-immigration-portal-2026) is where skilled worker profiles are submitted.

## Can you study in Canada without a CAQ?

**Short answer:** Yes, in two situations. If your program in Quebec lasts six months or less and you will finish within your authorized stay, you generally need neither a CAQ nor a study permit. And if you study anywhere in Canada outside Quebec, the CAQ does not apply to you at all.

The six-month exemption is the one most people ask about. Quebec institutions including Polytechnique Montréal confirm that foreign nationals taking a program of six months or less, completed inside their authorized period of stay, can study without a CAQ or a study permit. The exemption is narrower than it sounds: if you intend to extend, transfer into a longer program, or work on campus, you will need the full documentation.

Studying outside Quebec removes the question entirely. A student heading to Ontario, British Columbia, or Alberta deals only with IRCC and applies directly for a [study permit](/immigration/study-permit) without any provincial certificate.

## How do you apply for a CAQ, step by step?

**Short answer:** Accept your admission offer, apply online through MIFI's portal, pay the fee within one hour of submitting, upload the personalized document list MIFI generates, then wait for your attestation before you apply to IRCC for the study permit.

The sequence matters, because each step gates the next:

1. **Receive and accept** your letter of admission from a Quebec institution
2. **Submit** the online temporary selection application through MIFI
3. **Pay** the processing fee online by credit card, generally within one hour of submitting the form
4. **Upload** the personalized document list that appears in your file, typically within about 48 hours of payment
5. **Receive** your CAQ attestation in your online file
6. **Apply to IRCC** for your study permit, attaching the CAQ

Processing times vary. HEC Montréal advises students to expect the attestation in roughly 25 business days, though this fluctuates with volume and time of year. Apply as early as your admission letter allows, because the federal study permit stage still lies ahead of you and IRCC processing for the [study permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html) adds further weeks.

## What happens if your CAQ is refused or expires?

**Short answer:** A refusal usually reflects incomplete documents, insufficient proof of funds, or doubts about your intent to study. You can correct and reapply. If a valid CAQ expires while you are still studying, apply to renew it before the expiry date, since your study permit cannot outlast it.

Quebec does not run a formal appeal process for a refused CAQ in the way a court would. In practice the route forward is a stronger reapplication that addresses whatever the province flagged. Financial capacity is the most common weak point, particularly where funds arrived recently or come from a third party without clear documentation.

Timing is the other frequent failure. Because the CAQ gates the study permit, and the study permit gates your arrival, a late renewal cascades into a loss of status. Diarize the expiry date the day you receive the certificate.

## Should you get help with a Quebec student application?

Most students complete the CAQ themselves, and for a straightforward file that is reasonable. The cases worth a second opinion are the ones where something is unusual: funds held by a relative, a previous refusal from any country, a program change mid-study, or an accompanying spouse who wants to work.

A licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) can tell you honestly whether your file needs help or whether you are fine on your own. If you want that review before you submit, [book a consultation](/book) and we will go through your situation.

## Sources

- Gouvernement du Québec, [Demande de sélection temporaire pour études](https://www.quebec.ca/education/etudier-quebec/demande-selection-temporaire)
- Gouvernement du Québec, [Studying in Québec](https://www.quebec.ca/en/education/study-quebec)
- Government of Canada, [Study permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html) (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada)
