# IRCC Returned Your Application as Incomplete? What the 2026 Federal Court Ruling Means for You

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/ircc-returned-application-incomplete-what-to-do-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-07-18
Author: Go Far Global Team

> A reported December 2025 Federal Court decision holds that IRCC returning an application as "incomplete" can be challenged in court. Here is what changed, the strict 15 or 60 day deadline to act, and how to decide between resubmitting and seeking judicial review.

*As of July 18, 2026.*

If Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) sent your file back with a letter saying it was "incomplete" and never entered processing, you used to have very little recourse. A Federal Court decision reported in early 2026 changed that. This article explains what the ruling reportedly held, the deadlines that now matter, and how we help clients decide what to do next.

## What does it mean when IRCC returns an application as "incomplete"?

**Short answer:** It means IRCC decided your application did not meet the completeness requirements in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), so the file was never accepted into processing and was sent back to you.

A return is different from a refusal. With a refusal, an officer reviewed your case on its merits and said no. With a return, an officer looked only at whether the package was complete, decided it was not, and stopped there. The practical damage can still be serious. A return can cost you your place in the queue, and in Express Entry it can cost a locked-in age factor or a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score tied to a specific invitation. It can also mean paying the application fees again when you resubmit.

For years IRCC treated these returns as routine administrative acts with little room to argue. The reported 2026 ruling reframes that.

## What did the Federal Court actually decide in 2026?

**Short answer:** In a decision reported as Devgon v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 FC 2005, the Court held that IRCC's decision to return an application as "incomplete" is an administrative decision that can be judicially reviewed for reasonableness and fairness.

According to the decision and legal analyses, the case was decided on December 18, 2025 by Justice Battista and was widely reported around January 17, 2026. The Court rejected IRCC's argument that returning a file is a non-justiciable clerical act outside the reach of judicial review. The reasoning, as reported, is that an officer cannot impose completeness requirements beyond those set out in the published document checklist and the regulations. Procedural-fairness letters and internal instructions cannot, on their own, redefine what makes an application "complete".

In Devgon, the point of contention was reportedly a one-year gap in a curriculum vitae (CV) that the checklist did not require to be gap-free. The applicant's file was returned over something the published requirements did not actually demand.

There is no confirmed IRCC policy change in response as of July 2026. The ruling is the development to watch, not a new IRCC rule.

## Does this apply to every "incomplete" return?

**Short answer:** No. Some returns are still plainly correct, and only the questionable ones give you a realistic argument.

It helps to separate the two situations honestly.

| Situation | Typical outcome | What it means for you |
|---|---|---|
| Missing required signature | Legitimately incomplete | The return is likely correct; fix and resubmit |
| Unpaid mandatory fee | Legitimately incomplete | The return is likely correct; pay and resubmit |
| An entirely missing required form | Legitimately incomplete | The return is likely correct; add the form and resubmit |
| A requirement the officer imposed that is not in the checklist | Debatable | This is the Devgon scenario; may be unreasonable |
| Missing supporting "documents" when the rules asked only for "information" | Debatable | Reportedly examined in a related 2026 decision drawing an information versus documents distinction |

If your return is in the top three rows, the fastest path is usually to correct the file and resubmit. If it is in the bottom two rows, you may have grounds to challenge the return rather than simply accept it. This is where a careful reading of your specific return letter against the exact checklist matters, and it is worth getting that read quickly.

## What are my options if my application was returned?

**Short answer:** You generally have three: resubmit, request reconsideration, or file for leave and judicial review at the Federal Court. Each has trade-offs.

**1. Resubmit.** This is the simplest option. You fix whatever was flagged and send the package back in. The downside is that you re-enter the queue and may lose the processing time you had already built up. If your file was returned over a genuine gap like a missing signature, resubmitting is usually the sensible move.

**2. Request reconsideration.** You ask IRCC to look again. There is no statutory right to reconsideration, and historically the success rate has been low. It can be worth a try in narrow cases, but do not count on it, and do not let the reconsideration clock run out your court deadline.

**3. File for leave and judicial review.** This is the avenue the reported ruling opened up. It is strongest when the requirement that triggered the return was not in the checklist. You ask the Federal Court for leave (permission) to review IRCC's decision, and if leave is granted the matter proceeds to a hearing.

You do not have to pick only one path in your head before getting advice. What you cannot do is wait, because the court option is on a strict clock.

## How long do I have to challenge the return in court?

**Short answer:** The deadline to file the Application for Leave and for Judicial Review is 15 days if the matter arose inside Canada, and 60 days if it arose outside Canada. Extensions are possible only for "special reasons".

This is the single most important number in this article. The 15-day clock is short and it is strict. If your return arose inside Canada and you spend three weeks deciding whether to try reconsideration first, you may have already lost the ability to go to court. Missing the deadline does not automatically end your options, because the Court can extend time for special reasons, but you should never plan around getting an extension.

Because the window is so tight, the safest step is to have a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) or an immigration lawyer read your return letter promptly, ideally within days of receiving it, so the deadline is protected while you weigh the options.

## What does the Federal Court process look like?

**Short answer:** You file the Application for Leave, the Court reviews it on the documents, and if leave is granted a hearing follows, commonly 30 to 90 days later, judged on the reasonableness standard.

Here is the shape of it, drawn from the Federal Court's own practice guidance and the reported decision. First you file the Application for Leave and for Judicial Review within the applicable 15 or 60 day deadline. The leave stage is usually decided on the written record, and there is typically no hearing at that point. If the Court grants leave, a hearing is scheduled, commonly in the range of 30 to 90 days later. At the hearing the standard is reasonableness, meaning the question is whether IRCC's decision to return your file was reasonable, not whether the judge would have decided it the same way.

If you succeed, the usual result is that the return is set aside and your application is sent back for reconsideration, often by a different officer. Winning judicial review does not hand you an approval. It puts your application back in line to be assessed properly. That distinction matters, and we make sure clients understand it before they spend money on litigation.

## How is a returned application different from a refusal?

**Short answer:** A return is a completeness decision made before processing; a refusal is a merits decision made after review. They lead to different next steps.

If your application was actually refused rather than returned, the analysis in this article is not the right playbook for you. Refusals turn on the reasons an officer gave after assessing your case, and the strategy to reapply is different depending on the stream. For refusals specifically, our guides on a [study permit refused in Canada](/news/study-permit-refused-canada-reasons-reapply) and a [work permit refused over Labour Market Impact Assessment issues](/news/work-permit-refused-canada-lmia-issues-reapply) walk through the reasons and how to respond. Read the letter you received carefully. The words "returned" and "not accepted into processing" point to a completeness issue; the words "refused" and "not satisfied" point to a merits decision.

## Should I just resubmit to be safe?

**Short answer:** Sometimes yes, sometimes no, and the difference usually comes down to what you lose by re-entering the queue.

Resubmitting is genuinely the right answer when the return was correct and the cost of restarting is low. It is the wrong answer when a return over a non-checklist requirement would cost you a locked-in CRS score, an age factor, or a place in a time-sensitive process, and where the return itself looks unreasonable. In those cases, quietly resubmitting can throw away the very leverage the reported ruling created.

Timelines also feed this decision. If current processing for your stream is long, losing your queue position is more costly, which can tilt the balance toward challenging the return rather than restarting. You can check where things stand on our [processing times page](/immigration/processing-times) as one input into that call. None of this is a formula, which is exactly why a quick professional review is worth it before the 15-day clock runs.

## Where does Go Far Global fit in?

**Short answer:** We read your return letter against the exact checklist and regulations, tell you honestly which of the three paths fits, and protect the deadline while you decide.

We are a licensed Canadian immigration firm led by a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC). When a client brings us a returned application, our first job is to figure out whether the return was legitimate or questionable, because that single answer drives everything that follows. We will not tell you to litigate a missing signature, and we will not tell you to quietly resubmit when a return looks unreasonable and you have real value at stake.

If you are not yet sure where you stand, our [free assessment](/assessment) is a good first step to map your situation. If you already have a return letter in hand and a 15-day clock ticking, book a [paid consultation](/book) so we can review the letter properly and act in time. We cannot promise any outcome, and no honest firm can. What we can do is make sure the decision you make is an informed one, made before the deadline rather than after it.

# Quebec Experience Program (PEQ) Reopens: The 2026 Guide for Graduates and Workers

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/peq-quebec-experience-program-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-07-18
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Quebec Experience Program reopened on July 2, 2026 as a temporary two-year window that ends July 2, 2028. Here is a plain reading of the two streams, the French levels, and how the Quebec selection certificate leads to federal permanent residence.

*As of July 18, 2026.*

The Programme de l'experience quebecoise (PEQ), or Quebec Experience Program, is open again. It reopened on July 2, 2026 at 8:30am Montreal time after being closed for about thirteen months, and Quebec has framed this reopening as a temporary window rather than a permanent restoration. If you graduated from a Quebec institution recently, or you have been working in Quebec on a temporary permit, this is one of the more direct routes to a Quebec selection certificate, and there are firm deadlines you need to know.

## What is the PEQ and why does it matter in 2026?

**Short answer:** The PEQ is Quebec's experience-based skilled-worker pathway for people already established in the province, and in 2026 it reopened only as a temporary two-year window that closes permanently on July 2, 2028.

The PEQ selects economic immigrants who already live, study, or work in Quebec, based on their Quebec experience and their French rather than on a points score. It had been suspended on October 31, 2024 and was officially closed on November 19, 2025. Quebec announced the reopening on May 5, 2026 and released full details in June 2026. After the window sunsets on July 2, 2028, the Programme de selection des travailleurs qualifies (PSTQ), or Skilled Worker Selection Program, becomes Quebec's sole skilled-worker selection pathway. If you want the points-based sibling of the PEQ, we cover it separately in our guide to the [PSTQ](/news/pstq-quebec-skilled-worker-program-2026).

Because Quebec runs its own economic immigration under the Canada-Quebec Accord, PEQ applicants do not compete in the federal Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) used by Express Entry. That system is for provinces outside Quebec.

## When can I apply, and is there a cap?

**Short answer:** The first application period runs from July 2 to October 31, 2026, and there is no application cap for this period.

You must use the June 2026 versions of the forms. Older versions of the forms are not admissible, and using an outdated form is an avoidable way to have an application rejected. Below is a timeline of the key dates.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| October 31, 2024 | PEQ suspended |
| November 19, 2025 | PEQ officially closed |
| May 5, 2026 | Reopening announced |
| June 2026 | Full details and new forms released |
| July 2, 2026 (8:30am Montreal time) | PEQ reopens |
| October 31, 2026 | End of first application period (no cap) |
| July 2, 2028 | PEQ closes permanently |

## What are the two PEQ streams?

**Short answer:** There is a Quebec Graduates stream (Diplomes du Quebec) and a Temporary Foreign Workers stream, each with its own eligibility rules and its own French requirement.

The Graduates stream is for people who earned a qualifying Quebec credential. The Workers stream is for people who built up qualifying Quebec work experience. A few acronyms in the table below deserve a plain expansion up front. A DEC is a Diplome d'etudes collegiales, a technical college diploma. A DEP is a Diplome d'etudes professionnelles, a professional diploma, and for the PEQ it must be at least 1,800 hours. FEER stands for Formation, etudes, experience et responsabilites, the Quebec skill tiers, and tiers 0 to 3 cover management, professional, technical, and skilled roles. NCLC stands for Niveau de competence linguistique canadien, the Canadian language benchmark scale used in French. With those defined, here is the core of each stream.

| Requirement | Quebec Graduates | Temporary Foreign Workers |
|---|---|---|
| Qualifying basis | Quebec bachelor's, master's, doctorate, DEC, or DEP of at least 1,800 hours | At least 2 years of full-time Quebec work in a FEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 occupation |
| Timing | Completed the program within the last 36 months | Experience acquired by November 19, 2025, within the 3 years before applying |
| Current status | Legally in Quebec when applying | Must currently hold a qualifying FEER 0 to 3 job when applying |
| French (main applicant) | NCLC 7 speaking and listening; NCLC 5 reading and writing | NCLC 7 speaking and listening only |
| Prior work experience | Not required | Central to eligibility |

You apply through the stream that matches your situation.

## What does the Graduates stream require in detail?

**Short answer:** You need a qualifying Quebec credential completed within the last 36 months, you must be 18 or older, you must have studied full-time in Quebec while living there for at least half of the program, and you must intend to work for a Quebec employer.

Beyond the credential, the Graduates stream asks that you were 18 or older, studied full-time in Quebec, lived in Quebec for at least 50 percent of the length of the program, and are legally in Quebec at the time of application. You must intend to work for a Quebec employer, which means self-employment does not satisfy this stream. No prior Quebec work experience is required.

There is one change in 2026 that matters to a lot of graduates. The old requirement to have completed three years of full-time study in French has been removed. Graduates now meet the French condition through the language levels described below rather than through a study-in-French rule. If you studied in English but have strong spoken and written French, this change may open the stream to you.

## How much French do I actually need?

**Short answer:** The main applicant generally needs Niveau de competence linguistique canadien (NCLC) 7 in speaking and listening, with the reading and writing requirement depending on the stream.

The NCLC is the Canadian language benchmark scale used in French. For the Graduates stream, the main applicant needs NCLC 7 for speaking and listening, which is roughly Cadre europeen commun de reference (CEFR) level B2, and NCLC 5 for reading and writing, which is roughly B1. For the Workers stream, the main applicant needs NCLC 7 for speaking and listening only, with no written French requirement.

| Person | French requirement |
|---|---|
| Main applicant, Graduates stream | NCLC 7 speaking and listening; NCLC 5 reading and writing |
| Main applicant, Workers stream | NCLC 7 speaking and listening only |
| Accompanying spouse or partner | NCLC 4 speaking (about CEFR A2) |
| Dependent children | No French requirement |

An accompanying spouse or partner needs NCLC 4 in speaking, which is roughly CEFR A2. Dependent children have no French requirement.

## Does a CSQ mean I have permanent residence?

**Short answer:** No. A Certificat de selection du Quebec (CSQ) is Quebec's selection decision, and it is a step toward permanent residence, not permanent residence itself.

The path runs in two stages. First, Quebec selects you and issues a Certificat de selection du Quebec (CSQ), or Quebec selection certificate, which you submit through the [Arrima portal](/news/arrima-quebec-immigration-portal-2026) under the Canada-Quebec Accord. Second, the CSQ holder applies to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), the federal department, for permanent residence, and IRCC runs the security and medical checks. The CSQ is not permanent residence. You are only a permanent resident once IRCC approves that second, federal application.

Since April 2026, CSQ applicants can access a transitional open work permit while the federal permanent residence application is processed. We do not publish a fixed federal processing figure here, because that number moves; if you want a current view of timelines, check our [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) page rather than relying on a static estimate.

## PEQ or PSTQ: which one is for me?

**Short answer:** The PEQ fits Quebec graduates and experienced temporary workers with strong spoken French who are already in Quebec, while the PSTQ is the broader points-based program and will be Quebec's only skilled-worker pathway after July 2, 2028.

The PEQ is experience and language based. The PSTQ is points-based, broader in who it can reach, and it is the program that continues after the PEQ window closes. From June 10, 2026, Quebec splits its CSQ allocations equally between the PEQ and the PSTQ through 2029, so both programs will be issuing selection certificates side by side for the next few years.

For context, Quebec's 2026 to 2029 orientations set an overall permanent-resident target near 45,000 per year. There is also a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) freeze in Montreal and Laval that runs through December 31, 2026, which affects employer-driven hiring in those two areas during the same period.

## What if I do not qualify for the PEQ?

**Short answer:** If you have strong French but do not meet the PEQ's Quebec-based conditions, the federal Express Entry French-language draws are often the better route, because they have carried some of the lowest CRS cut-offs.

The PEQ rewards people who are already rooted in Quebec through study or work. If you are not in that position, a PEQ application will not succeed without those Quebec ties. People with strong French who fall outside the PEQ should look closely at the federal Express Entry French-language category, which has repeatedly drawn candidates at lower CRS scores than the general draws. That is a different system with different rules, and the right choice depends on your profile.

## How can Go Far Global help with a PEQ application?

**Short answer:** We are a licensed Canadian immigration firm led by a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC), and we help Quebec graduates and temporary workers read these rules correctly the first time.

The PEQ window is real but finite, and the details, the form versions, the FEER tier of your job, the exact French benchmarks, are where applications succeed or fail. If you are not sure whether the PEQ, the PSTQ, or a federal Express Entry route fits you best, start with our free [assessment](/assessment). If you want a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant to review your specific case in depth, you can book a paid [consultation](/book). The consultation is a paid service, and we will tell you honestly which pathway gives you the strongest shot.

- [PEQ conditions de selection, Diplomes du Quebec, Quebec.ca](https://www.quebec.ca/immigration/permanente/travailleurs-qualifies/programme-experience-quebecoise/conditions-selection/diplomes-quebec)

# IRCC Pauses Parent and Grandparent Sponsorship: What the July 15, 2026 Announcement Means

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/ircc-pauses-parent-grandparent-sponsorship-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-07-17
Author: Go Far Global Team

> IRCC paused all new Parents and Grandparents Program intake on July 15, 2026: no new interest to sponsor forms and no new invitations, until further notice. What it means for the 60,500 families in the queue, and why the Super Visa is now the main path.

*As of July 17, 2026.*

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) announced on July 15, 2026 that it is pausing all new intake for the Parents and Grandparents Program (PGP) until further notice. The department will not accept new interest to sponsor forms and will not send new invitations to apply. Families already in the system keep their place, and processing of existing applications continues. For everyone else, the [Super Visa](/immigration/super-visa) is now the practical way to bring parents and grandparents to Canada.

## What did IRCC announce on July 15, 2026?

**Short answer:** IRCC formally paused new intake for the Parents and Grandparents Program. No new interest to sponsor forms will be accepted and no new invitations to apply will be issued, until further notice. Processing of applications already in the system continues.

The notice came from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada under Minister Lena Metlege Diab. The department said interest in the program consistently exceeds the available spaces, and framed the pause as a step toward a sustainable system with more predictable timelines for families already waiting. No end date was announced.

## Was the program not already frozen?

**Short answer:** In practice, yes. No new intake has opened since fall 2020, and ministerial instructions in effect since January 1, 2026 already blocked new applications. The July 15 announcement turns that de facto freeze into official policy and stops even the annual invitation rounds that drew from the 2020 pool.

The last time Canada accepted new interest to sponsor submissions was October 13 to November 3, 2020, when 203,213 families filed forms. Every invitation round from 2021 through 2025 drew from that same 2020 pool. Anyone who did not file in 2020 has had no way into the program for almost six years. What changed on July 15 is that IRCC will no longer invite anyone at all, including sponsors still waiting in the 2020 pool.

## What happens to applications already in the system?

**Short answer:** They continue. IRCC says it will keep processing the roughly 60,500 applications in the queue and plans to admit up to 15,000 parents and grandparents in 2026.

Applications submitted after invitations in earlier rounds, including the 2025 round, remain in process. No files are being returned or cancelled. Current [processing times](/immigration/processing-times/parent-grandparent) are long: about 30 to 33 months outside Quebec, and more than five years for Quebec (roughly 65 to 66 months) because of the separate Quebec selection stage.

## Why is Canada pausing parent and grandparent sponsorship?

**Short answer:** Demand massively exceeds a shrinking number of spaces. The admissions target has been cut by more than half in two years while tens of thousands of files sit in the queue.

| Measure | Figure |
|---|---|
| 2024 PGP admissions target | 32,000 |
| 2025 PGP admissions target | 24,500 |
| 2026 PGP admissions target | 15,000 (held at 15,000 per year through 2028) |
| Applications in queue (July 2026) | About 60,500 |
| Last new intake | Fall 2020 (203,213 interest to sponsor forms) |
| Processing time outside Quebec | About 33 months |
| Processing time for Quebec | About 66 months |

With the 2026 to 2028 Immigration Levels Plan holding admissions at 15,000 per year, the existing queue alone represents about four years of admissions. That is the math behind the pause: inviting new sponsors would add files to a line that is already years long.

## What is the Super Visa, and is it a real alternative?

**Short answer:** The Super Visa is a multi entry visitor visa for parents and grandparents that allows stays of up to five years per entry, with no annual cap. It does not lead to permanent residence, but it stays open and processes in months, not years.

IRCC itself points affected families to the Super Visa. Key features as of July 2026:

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Who qualifies | Parents and grandparents of Canadian citizens and permanent residents |
| Stay per entry | Up to 5 years |
| Validity | Multi entry, up to 10 years |
| Annual cap | None |
| Medical insurance | Minimum CAD $100,000 coverage valid for at least 1 year, from a Canadian insurer or an OSFI authorized foreign insurer (foreign insurers accepted since January 28, 2025) |
| Income requirement | The host child or grandchild must meet the income threshold; since March 31, 2026 IRCC calculates it more flexibly |
| Typical processing | Roughly 2 to 4 months depending on country |

The trade offs are real. A Super Visa holder is a visitor, not a permanent resident, has no provincial health coverage, and depends on private insurance. But for families who were waiting on a lottery that may not return for years, a renewable five year stay is the path that actually works today. Our [Super Visa insurance guide](/news/super-visa-insurance-canada-2026) covers costs and providers.

## What should families do now?

**Short answer:** If you are already in the PGP queue, keep your file current and wait. If you are not, apply for a Super Visa instead of waiting for an intake that has no reopening date.

Practical steps:

1. **Already invited and applied:** your application keeps processing. Keep your address, family details, and documents up to date with IRCC, and respond quickly to any request.
2. **Filed interest to sponsor in 2020 but never invited:** the pause means no invitation is coming for now. Treat the Super Visa as your working plan rather than a backup.
3. **Never entered the pool:** the Super Visa is the route. Confirm the host meets the income threshold, buy qualifying insurance, and file a complete application.
4. **Verify announcements at the source:** reopening rumours circulate every year. Only canada.ca announcements count.

Go Far Global is a Toronto based immigration firm led by a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC). We prepare Super Visa applications end to end, including the insurance and income documentation that causes most refusals, and we monitor IRCC announcements daily. Start with a [free assessment](/assessment) or [book a consultation](/book).

- [IRCC notice: Canada takes steps to responsibly manage the Parents and Grandparents Program (July 15, 2026)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/responsibly-manage-parent-grandparent-program.html)
- [Super Visa eligibility, canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/eligibility.html)
- [Super Visa insurance change (OSFI authorized foreign insurers), canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/change-health-insurance-requirement-makes-super-visa-more-accessible.html)
- [Super Visa income requirement change, canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/changes-parents-grandparents-super-visa-income-requirement-calculated.html)

- [CIC News coverage of the pause](https://www.cicnews.com/2026/07/canada-shuts-door-to-sponsoring-parents-and-grandparents-for-permanent-residence-0778003.html)

# Saskatchewan SINP 2026 Changes: What They Mean for Applicants

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/saskatchewan-sinp-2026-changes
Category: News
Published: 2026-07-15
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Saskatchewan cut its 2026 SINP allocation to 4,761 nominations, reserved half for priority sectors, and capped food service, trucking, and retail. Here is who is affected and how to respond.

*As of July 15, 2026.*

Saskatchewan reshaped its provincial immigration program for 2026, and the changes are significant. A smaller nomination pool, hard caps on certain sectors, staggered application windows, and tighter rules for graduates who studied elsewhere all landed at once. If you were planning to apply through the Saskatchewan Immigrant Nominee Program (SINP), the pathway that made sense in 2025 may look different today.

This guide walks through what actually changed, who each change affects, and the practical steps you can take. We only use the numbers Saskatchewan and IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada) have confirmed.

## How many nominations does the SINP have for 2026?

**Short answer:** For 2026 the SINP has an initial allocation of 4,761 nominations, a sharp reduction from prior years. The province split that pool by policy: at least 50 percent is reserved for priority sectors, and no more than 25 percent goes to capped sectors. The remaining share covers everything else. A smaller allocation means the province is choosier about who it nominates, and it is steering most of its capacity toward the occupations Saskatchewan considers most in demand. Applicants outside those priority sectors face more competition for fewer spots.

The Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) is how a province selects skilled newcomers who fit its labour market. When the allocation drops, the province does not treat every applicant equally. It ranks its priorities and reserves capacity accordingly. That is the single most important thing to understand about SINP 2026: the allocation is smaller, and it is not distributed evenly.

## Which sectors are capped in the 2026 SINP, and by how much?

**Short answer:** Three sectors carry hard caps in 2026. Food Service and Accommodation is capped at 15 percent, which is roughly 714 nominations. Trucking is capped at 5 percent, about 238 nominations. Retail Trade is also capped at 5 percent, about 238 nominations. Once a capped sector reaches its ceiling, no further nominations go to it that year, regardless of how strong the remaining candidates are. If you work in one of these sectors, timing and preparation matter more than ever, because you are competing for a fixed and limited number of spots.

| Sector | Cap (share of allocation) | Approximate nominations |
|---|---|---|
| Food Service and Accommodation | 15 percent | about 714 |
| Trucking | 5 percent | about 238 |
| Retail Trade | 5 percent | about 238 |
| Priority sectors (combined) | at least 50 percent reserved | at least about 2,381 |
| Capped sectors (combined) | no more than 25 percent | up to about 1,190 |

The priority sectors, which keep the largest reserved share, are the ones Saskatchewan is actively recruiting for. If your occupation sits in a priority or non-capped sector, you are in a much stronger position under the 2026 rules.

## When can capped-sector applicants apply in 2026?

**Short answer:** Capped sectors no longer have open, year-round intake. They use staggered intake windows. The 2026 capped-sector intake opened around July 6 to 7, 2026. Priority and non-capped sectors keep continuous, year-round intake, so those applicants can submit whenever they are ready. For capped-sector applicants, this means you cannot apply on your own timeline. You have to be document-ready before a window opens, because spots can fill quickly once intake begins and the sector cap can be reached inside a single window.

This is a real shift in behaviour. In prior years, many capped-sector candidates could take their time assembling a file. Under the 2026 model, a strong but late application can miss the window entirely. Treat every intake date as a deadline, not a suggestion, and have your language results, work-experience proof, and employer documents finalized well in advance.

## What is the work-permit timing rule for capped sectors?

**Short answer:** For capped sectors only, the employer must have an identified candidate whose work permit expires within the next 6 months. In other words, the province is prioritizing people already working in Saskatchewan who are close to running out of status. Priority and non-capped sectors have no such work-permit timing restriction, so overseas candidates and those with longer permit validity can still apply through those streams. If you are in a capped sector but your permit does not expire within that 6 month window, this pathway is not open to you right now.

This rule effectively narrows capped-sector nominations to a specific group: workers already in the province who need to secure permanent status soon. It rewards people who are settled and employed locally, and it closes the door to fresh overseas applicants in those three sectors.

## How do the 2026 changes affect PGWP holders who studied outside Saskatchewan?

**Short answer:** Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) holders who studied outside Saskatchewan and have worked 6 months in their field can no longer apply through the Saskatchewan Experience pathways. They are now limited to certain subcategories: Student, Health Talent, Agriculture Talent, Tech Talent, and International Skilled Worker: Employment Offer. If you graduated from a school in another province and moved to Saskatchewan to work, this is a meaningful narrowing of your options, and you will need to check whether your occupation fits one of those remaining subcategories.

Here is what that looks like in practice.

| Your situation | Saskatchewan Experience pathways | Remaining subcategories |
|---|---|---|
| Studied in Saskatchewan | Generally still available | Plus the standard streams |
| Studied outside Saskatchewan, worked 6 months in field | No longer available | Student, Health Talent, Agriculture Talent, Tech Talent, International Skilled Worker: Employment Offer |

If you studied outside the province, do not assume your Saskatchewan work experience alone qualifies you the way it once did. Confirm which of the remaining subcategories you can realistically enter before you build your file.

## What does the International Skilled Worker: Employment Offer sub-category require?

**Short answer:** This sub-category is one of the pathways still open to affected PGWP holders, and it has clear thresholds. You need at least 60 points on the SINP point assessment grid, at least 1 year of work experience in your intended occupation within the past 10 years, and a language score of at least Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 4. Meeting all three is the baseline to be considered. The point grid weighs factors like education, work experience, language ability, and connection to Saskatchewan, so a genuine job offer plus solid credentials is what moves you toward the 60 point mark.

A quick reference for the three thresholds:

| Requirement | Minimum |
|---|---|
| SINP point assessment grid | at least 60 points |
| Work experience in intended occupation (past 10 years) | at least 1 year |
| Language score | at least CLB 4 |

CLB 4 is a modest language bar compared with federal Express Entry expectations, so language is rarely the blocker here. The point total and the qualifying job offer are usually what decide whether this pathway works for you.

## What should applicants do now?

**Short answer:** First, identify whether your occupation sits in a priority, capped, or other sector, because that determines your intake timing and your odds. Capped-sector applicants should prepare a complete file ahead of the next intake window and confirm the employer meets the 6 month permit rule. PGWP holders who studied outside Saskatchewan should check which remaining subcategory fits. Everyone benefits from confirming their eligibility against the current SINP criteria before spending money on documents. A short, honest assessment early can save months of effort spent on a pathway that has quietly closed.

The 2026 rules reward preparation and punish delay. The applicants who do best are the ones who know exactly which stream applies to them, have their documents ready before a window opens, and are not relying on a pathway that changed under them. If you are not sure where you stand, our evergreen [Saskatchewan PNP guide](/immigration/provincial-nominee/saskatchewan) breaks the streams down in more detail, and a [free assessment](/assessment) will tell you which 2026 subcategory, if any, you actually qualify for.

Immigration rules change, and 2026 is proof of how fast that can happen. The safest move is to check your eligibility against the current criteria before you commit time and money. You can [take our free assessment](/assessment) to see where you stand, or [book a consultation](/book) with one of our RCICs (Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultants) to map the pathway that fits your situation.

# Express Entry Senior Managers Category 2026: Who Qualifies and Recent Draws

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/express-entry-senior-managers-category-2026
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-07-15
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada's new 2026 Express Entry "Senior managers with Canadian work experience" category invites C-suite executives with at least 12 months of Canadian experience. Two draws have run, with the CRS cut-off dropping from 429 to 392.

*As of July 15, 2026.*

If you already run a Canadian business unit, lead a hospital department, or sit in a C-suite chair here in Canada, there is a new door into permanent residence built for people like you. Canada added a "Senior managers with Canadian work experience" category to Express Entry as part of its 2026 category-based selection overhaul. This guide from our licensed RCIC (Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant) team explains exactly who qualifies, which four occupations count, and what the first two draws tell us about your odds.

## What is the new senior managers Express Entry category for 2026?

**Short answer:** It is a category-based selection stream that Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) announced on February 18, 2026, as part of a wider overhaul of Express Entry categories. Under category-based selection, IRCC invites candidates who meet a specific goal rather than only inviting the highest Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) scores in the general pool. This category targets senior executives who already have Canadian experience in top-tier management roles. It sits alongside the other 2026 categories and runs its own dedicated draws, so a strong candidate can receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA) at a CRS score lower than the general cut-off.

Category-based selection lets Canada steer invitations toward the workers its economy needs most. For 2026, senior management joined that list for the first time, recognizing that experienced executives create jobs and anchor investment.

## Which occupations qualify for the senior managers category?

**Short answer:** Four TEER 0 (Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities level 0) senior-management occupations under the 2021 National Occupational Classification (NOC) qualify. These are C-suite and senior executive roles, not front-line supervisors or middle managers. If your job title is director, vice-president, chief officer, or general manager over a major function or organization, you likely fall into one of these four codes. Your actual duties, not just your title, must match the NOC description. IRCC checks the main duties on your reference letters against the code you claim.

| NOC 2021 code | Occupation |
|---|---|
| 00012 | Senior managers, financial, communications and other business services |
| 00013 | Senior managers, health, education, social and community services and membership organizations |
| 00014 | Senior managers, trade, broadcasting and other services |
| 00015 | Senior managers, construction, transportation, production and utilities |

## What are the eligibility requirements for this category?

**Short answer:** You need at least 12 months of Canadian work experience in one of the four eligible occupations within the past 3 years. This is the key difference from some other 2026 categories: the experience must be Canadian, not foreign. You also need an active Express Entry profile and must already be eligible under one of the programs the profile serves, such as the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) or the Federal Skilled Worker Program. Meeting the category requirement does not by itself create program eligibility; it only makes you selectable for that category's draws once you are already in the pool.

A short checklist of what IRCC looks for:

- At least 12 months of full-time (or equivalent part-time) Canadian experience in NOC 00012, 00013, 00014, or 00015, gained in the last 3 years.
- An active Express Entry profile.
- Eligibility under an Express Entry program (CEC, Federal Skilled Worker, or Federal Skilled Trades).
- Language and other minimum program criteria already met.

Note the January 2026 change: IRCC raised the minimum experience for occupation-specific categories from 6 months to 12 months. If you were counting on the old six-month rule, you now need a full year.

## What draws have been held and what were the CRS cut-offs?

**Short answer:** Two senior-manager draws have run so far in 2026. Round 402 on March 5, 2026 issued 250 ITAs at a CRS cut-off of 429. Round 426 on July 10, 2026 issued 500 ITAs at a lower cut-off of 392. The cut-off fell by 37 points between the two rounds, and the number of invitations doubled. That downward trend is encouraging for candidates who sit in the 390s, though a single trend is not a guarantee that future draws will stay this low. Cut-offs can rise again if the pool of eligible senior managers grows.

| Draw | Date | ITAs issued | CRS cut-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Round 402 | March 5, 2026 | 250 | 429 |
| Round 426 | July 10, 2026 | 500 | 392 |

You can estimate where you stand today with our [free CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator). It scores your age, education, language results, and Canadian experience the same way IRCC does, so you can see whether you are within reach of the recent 392 mark before you commit to a full application.

## How does this category differ from the general Express Entry pool?

**Short answer:** In a general draw, IRCC invites the top CRS scores across the entire pool, and the cut-off often sits well above 480. In a category draw, IRCC only compares candidates who meet the category requirement, which shrinks the competing group and usually lowers the cut-off. That is why the senior-manager draws landed at 429 and then 392, below typical general-draw scores. The catch is that you must genuinely qualify: your Canadian experience has to fall inside one of the four senior-management NOC codes, and IRCC will scrutinize your reference letters and duties to confirm it.

This is also why documentation matters so much for executives. Senior roles are easy to mislabel. A "manager" who supervises a small team may actually fall under a different, ineligible NOC. Getting the code right the first time protects you from a refusal after months of waiting.

## What should senior managers do to prepare?

**Short answer:** Start by confirming your NOC code against your real duties, then gather clean proof of at least 12 months of Canadian experience. Reference letters should list your title, dates, hours, salary, and a duty list that mirrors the NOC 00012 to 00015 descriptions. Improve any weak CRS factor, especially language, since a higher language score can add dozens of points. Keep your Express Entry profile active and accurate so you are in the pool when the next senior-manager draw runs. If your score is close to the recent 392 cut-off, small gains can make the difference.

Practical steps to take now:

- Pull your reference letters and check the duties against the exact NOC code you plan to claim.
- Retake a language test if a higher score would lift your CRS meaningfully.
- Confirm your education credential assessment is current if you rely on foreign education points.
- Keep your profile updated as your experience and family situation change.

Getting the occupation classification right is the single most common failure point for executive applicants, and it is exactly where a licensed consultant earns their keep.

## Is the senior managers category worth pursuing?

**Short answer:** For genuine senior executives with Canadian experience, yes. The category creates a dedicated invitation path with cut-offs well below general draws, and the second round already dropped to 392 while doubling invitations to 500. That combination points to real opportunity for C-suite candidates who might otherwise wait a long time in the general pool. The main risk is misclassification, not competition. If your role clearly fits one of the four codes and you have 12 months of clean Canadian experience, this is one of the strongest 2026 pathways available to executives.

Every profile is different, and one wrong NOC choice can undo a strong application. If you want a clear read on whether you qualify and how to strengthen your CRS, [take our free assessment](/assessment) and our licensed RCIC team will review your case, or [book a consultation](/book) to map out your next steps.

# Express Entry Transport Category 2026: Your Low-CRS Path to PR

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/express-entry-transport-category-2026
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-07-15
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada's 2026 Express Entry Transport category targets four aviation and mechanic occupations, and your qualifying experience can be earned entirely outside Canada. Here is who qualifies and how to get ready before the first draw.

*As of July 15, 2026.*

If you fix aircraft, fly planes, or repair heavy vehicles, Canada has a 2026 Express Entry pathway built for you. The Transport occupations category is one of the routes under category-based selection, and it carries a real edge over the general pool: your qualifying work experience can be earned entirely outside Canada. That single fact opens permanent residence to skilled tradespeople who have never set foot on Canadian soil.

This guide walks through who qualifies in 2026, which occupations made the list, why truck drivers are no longer part of it, and how to get your profile ready before the first Transport draw runs. As a licensed RCIC (Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant) firm, we deal with these files every week, so everything below reflects the current rules from IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada).

## What is the Express Entry Transport category in 2026?

**Short answer:** The Transport category is a targeted stream inside Express Entry that lets IRCC invite candidates working in specific transportation occupations, separate from general draws. Canada renewed its category-based selection categories for 2026, and the announcement came on February 18, 2026. Transport is one of those categories. Instead of ranking every candidate together, IRCC runs occasional category rounds that invite only people who qualify under the chosen theme, often at a lower CRS (Comprehensive Ranking System) score than a general round would require. That lower bar is the whole point.

Category-based selection sits on top of the existing Express Entry system. You still need a profile under an eligible program, and you still compete on your CRS score. The difference is the pool you are competing against: a smaller, targeted group instead of the entire pool. You can estimate where you stand using our [free CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) before you do anything else.

## Which occupations qualify for the 2026 Transport category?

**Short answer:** The 2026 Transport category targets four occupations, all defined under the 2021 NOC (National Occupational Classification). They cover pilots and flight instructors, aircraft mechanics and inspectors, avionics technicians, and automotive, truck, and bus mechanics. Each occupation has a specific NOC code, and your work experience must fall under one of these codes to be considered. If your job title does not map to one of the four codes below, this category is not your route, though other Express Entry pathways may still fit.

Here are the four eligible occupations for 2026:

| NOC code (2021) | Occupation | TEER | Field |
|---|---|---|---|
| 72600 | Air pilots, flight engineers and flying instructors | TEER 2 | Aviation |
| 72404 | Aircraft mechanics and aircraft inspectors | TEER 2 | Aviation |
| 22313 | Avionics and related aircraft instrument and electrical technicians | TEER 2 | Aviation |
| 72410 | Automotive service technicians, truck and bus mechanics and mechanical repairers | TEER 2 | Ground transport |

TEER refers to the Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities tiers that replaced the old NOC skill levels. All four occupations sit in TEER 2, which typically means an apprenticeship, college program, or several years of specialized on-the-job training.

## Are truck drivers still eligible for the Transport category?

**Short answer:** No. Truck drivers, formally transport truck drivers under NOC 73300, were REMOVED from the Transport category for 2026. They were eligible in 2025, but they do not appear on the 2026 list. This is the single biggest change to the category this year, and it catches many applicants off guard. If your experience is as a long-haul or transport truck driver, you cannot use this category in 2026, even though you could have last year. You would need to qualify through a different Express Entry program or a Provincial Nominee Program stream instead.

Category lists are reviewed each year, so an occupation being in for one cycle is no guarantee it stays in the next. That is exactly what happened here. We flag this because families sometimes build a whole plan around a 2025 rule that no longer holds. Always confirm the current-year list before you commit.

## What are the eligibility requirements for 2026?

**Short answer:** You need at least 12 months of full-time work experience, or the equal amount in part-time, in one of the four eligible occupations within the past 3 years. You must have an active Express Entry profile under an eligible program, and you must receive an ITA (Invitation to Apply) in a category-based round. As of January 2026, IRCC raised the minimum experience for occupation-specific categories from 6 months to 12 months, so the old half-year threshold no longer applies. All three conditions have to be met at once.

The requirements in plain terms:

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Work experience | At least 12 months full-time, or equal part-time, in one eligible occupation |
| Reference period | Within the past 3 years |
| Continuity | Does not need to be continuous |
| Location | Can be gained anywhere in the world |
| Profile | Active Express Entry profile under an eligible program |
| Invitation | Must receive an ITA in a category-based round |

One nuance worth stressing: your qualifying experience does not need to match the primary occupation listed on your Express Entry profile. If your main NOC is something else but you also have 12 months in an eligible Transport occupation within the last 3 years, you can still be considered under this category.

## Why is foreign experience such a big advantage here?

**Short answer:** Because the qualifying experience can be gained outside Canada, and it counts fully. Most Canadian PR pathways, especially the CEC (Canadian Experience Class), require experience earned inside Canada. The Transport category does not. An aircraft mechanic in Manila, a pilot in Dubai, or a bus mechanic in Nairobi can all count their home-country experience toward this category. Combined with the chance of a lower CRS cut-off in a category round, this makes Transport one of the most accessible routes for skilled workers who have never worked in Canada.

To put the advantage in context, category draws can invite candidates at a lower CRS score than general or CEC draws, because the pool is smaller and targeted. That means a score that would fall short in a general round might still earn an ITA in a Transport round. You can read more about how the whole system fits together on our [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) overview.

## Has IRCC held a Transport draw in 2026 yet?

**Short answer:** No. As of mid-July 2026, IRCC has not yet held a Transport-specific category-based round this year. That means there is no published 2026 cut-off score for this category, and anyone quoting one is guessing. The absence of a draw is not bad news. It is a window. Candidates who enter the pool now, with a complete profile and verified documents, are the ones positioned to receive an invitation when the first Transport round runs. The applicants who wait until a draw is announced are usually too late to prepare.

Getting draw-ready means a few concrete steps: confirm your language test results, get an Educational Credential Assessment if you were trained abroad, gather reference letters that prove your 12 months in the eligible occupation, and submit an accurate profile under an eligible program. Miss one piece and an ITA can slip away.

## How should you get ready before the first draw?

**Short answer:** Build a complete, accurate Express Entry profile now and make sure your documents prove your eligible experience. Confirm your job maps to one of the four NOC codes, gather employment letters showing at least 12 months in the past 3 years, complete an approved language test, and get your foreign credentials assessed. Then keep your profile active so you are in the pool the moment IRCC runs a Transport round. Preparation done early is what turns a category announcement into an actual invitation rather than a missed chance.

A licensed RCIC can check that your reference letters describe the right duties, that your NOC choice will survive scrutiny, and that your profile maximizes your CRS. Small errors, a wrong NOC or a vague employer letter, are the most common reasons strong candidates get passed over or refused.

Not sure whether your occupation and experience line up with the 2026 Transport category? The fastest way to find out is to [take our free assessment](/assessment), or [book a consultation](/book) with one of our licensed consultants and we will map your exact path.

# TCF Canada 2026: Score Chart to CLB/NCLC and Express Entry Points

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/tcf-canada-score-chart-clb-express-entry-2026
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-07-13
Author: Go Far Global Team

> TCF Canada is one of only two French tests Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) accepts for permanent residence, and the points it earns can decide whether your Express Entry...

As of July 13, 2026.

TCF Canada is one of only two French tests Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) accepts for permanent residence, and the points it earns can decide whether your Express Entry profile gets an invitation. This guide gives you the exact TCF Canada score chart converted to NCLC (Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens, the French equivalent of the Canadian Language Benchmark, or CLB), how many Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points French is worth, and how TCF Canada compares to TEF Canada.

## TL;DR

**TCF Canada (Test de connaissance du français) is one of two French-language tests IRCC accepts for Express Entry and permanent residence, alongside TEF Canada.** | It tests four abilities: listening, reading, writing, and speaking. IRCC converts each score to an NCLC level, the French equivalent of the CLB. | Reaching NCLC 7 or higher on all four abilities earns you extra CRS points: 25 points if your English is CLB 4 or lower, or 50 points if your English is CLB 5 or higher. | For a general Express Entry profile you need NCLC 7 across all four abilities (TEER 0 or 1 jobs); NCLC 5 is the floor for TEER 2 or 3 jobs. | Your test results are valid for two years from the test date, so book with your invitation timeline in mind.

## What is TCF Canada?

TCF Canada (Test de connaissance du français pour le Canada) is a standardized French-language test built specifically for Canadian immigration. It is administered by France Éducation international, and IRCC accepts it for Express Entry, Canadian permanent residence, and citizenship applications. The test measures four separate abilities: listening (compréhension de l'oral), reading (compréhension de l'écrit), writing (expression écrite), and speaking (expression orale).

For French, IRCC accepts exactly two tests: TCF Canada and TEF Canada. If you want the French-language points on your profile, one of these two is mandatory. There is no way to self-declare French ability or use a school transcript instead.

## How do TCF Canada scores convert to NCLC?

IRCC does not use your raw TCF Canada score directly. It converts each ability to an NCLC level, which is the French counterpart of the CLB used for English. Listening and reading are scored on a numeric scale up to 699; speaking and writing are scored on a 0 to 20 scale.

| NCLC level | Speaking | Listening | Reading | Writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 and above | 16 to 20 | 549 to 699 | 549 to 699 | 16 to 20 |
| 9 | 14 to 15 | 523 to 548 | 524 to 548 | 14 to 15 |
| 8 | 12 to 13 | 503 to 522 | 499 to 523 | 12 to 13 |
| 7 | 10 to 11 | 458 to 502 | 453 to 498 | 10 to 11 |
| 6 | 7 to 9 | 398 to 457 | 406 to 452 | 7 to 9 |
| 5 | 6 | 369 to 397 | 375 to 405 | 6 |
| 4 | 4 to 5 | 331 to 368 | 342 to 374 | 4 to 5 |

Your profile uses the NCLC level for each ability separately, so a strong listening score cannot lift a weak writing score. IRCC looks at your lowest ability when it checks whether you meet a program minimum.

## How many CRS points is French worth?

French is one of the most efficient ways to raise a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score, which is why French-only category draws have cut off far below general draws. There are two places French earns points.

First, French counts as a language just like English, feeding the core human-capital and skill-transferability points. Second, there is a dedicated additional-points bonus for French ability on top of that:

- **25 points** if you score NCLC 7 or higher on all four French abilities and your English is CLB 4 or lower (or you have no English result).
- **50 points** if you score NCLC 7 or higher on all four French abilities and your English is CLB 5 or higher on all four abilities.

The maximum French bonus is 50 points, not more. This bonus is a major reason a candidate with strong French can clear a French category-based draw that an English-only candidate cannot. If you are weighing where to spend your effort, see our guide on [how to improve your CRS score](/news/how-to-improve-crs-score) and how [category-based selection](/news/express-entry-category-based-selection-2026) works.

## What NCLC level do you actually need?

The NCLC level you need depends on your program and the skill level of your job under the National Occupational Classification (NOC). For a general Express Entry profile in a TEER 0 or 1 occupation, you need NCLC 7 on all four abilities. For a TEER 2 or 3 occupation, the floor drops to NCLC 5. To claim the French additional-points bonus, the bar is NCLC 7 across every ability, whatever your job. The table below sets out each case.

| Your situation | Minimum French level (all 4 abilities) |
|---|---|
| Express Entry, TEER 0 or 1 job | NCLC 7 |
| Express Entry, TEER 2 or 3 job | NCLC 5 |
| Targeting the French category bonus | NCLC 7 |

If your goal is the French category draws or the 50-point bonus, aim for NCLC 7 on every ability, since a single ability below 7 disqualifies you from the bonus even if the other three are strong.

## TCF Canada vs TEF Canada: which should you take?

Both are accepted equally by IRCC, and neither earns more points than the other for the same NCLC level. The right choice comes down to test format and where you feel more comfortable.

- **TCF Canada** uses multiple-choice questions for listening and reading, plus a separate writing and speaking session. Many candidates find the multiple-choice format more predictable.
- **TEF Canada** uses a different scoring scale and question style. If you have already prepared with TEF materials, switching may not be worth it.

Compare the [TEF Canada score chart](/news/tef-canada-score-chart-clb-2026) side by side before you book. If you are still deciding between French and English routes altogether, our [CELPIP vs IELTS comparison](/news/celpip-vs-ielts-canada-2026) covers the English side.

## How do you book TCF Canada?

You book TCF Canada through an approved test centre. When you register, choose the "TCF Canada" version, not the general TCF, because IRCC only accepts the Canada version for immigration. Bring the same valid passport you will use on your application, since IRCC matches the name and document number on your test result to your profile.

A few practical points:

- Results are valid for **two years** from the test date. If your result expires before you submit, you must retake the test.
- You can retake TCF Canada to improve a score; IRCC uses your most recent valid result that you enter in your profile.
- Book early. If you are already in the Express Entry pool, a strong French result can be the difference in a French category round, and those run on IRCC's schedule, not yours.

French is a long game for many applicants, so pairing test prep with a realistic plan matters. Our overview of [learning French for immigration](/news/learning-french-immigration) and the [Francophone Mobility work permit pathway](/news/francophone-mobility-pr-pathway-2026) show how French can open doors beyond Express Entry.

## Frequently asked questions

**Does IRCC accept the regular TCF, or only TCF Canada?**
Only TCF Canada. The general TCF and other TCF versions are not accepted for Express Entry or permanent residence. Register specifically for the Canada version.

**How long are TCF Canada results valid?**
Two years from the date of the test. If your result is older than two years when you submit your application, IRCC will not accept it.

**Can French alone qualify me for Express Entry?**
Yes. You can meet the language requirement with French only, provided you reach the minimum NCLC level for your program and job. Adding even a modest English result can raise your bonus to the larger 50 points.

**Is TCF Canada easier than TEF Canada?**
Neither is officially easier, and both convert to the same NCLC levels. TCF Canada's multiple-choice format for listening and reading suits some test-takers better, but the best choice depends on your own strengths.

**How many CRS points do I get for French?**
Up to 50 additional points: 25 if you have NCLC 7+ in French and weak or no English, or 50 if you have NCLC 7+ in French and CLB 5+ in English, plus the regular language points French earns on your profile.

## How do you make your French result count?

The applicants who benefit most from French are the ones who test strategically: they target NCLC 7 across all four abilities to unlock the bonus, then time the result so it is valid when a French draw lands. As a licensed Canadian immigration firm, we help candidates decide whether French is worth the investment for their profile and map it to the right Express Entry round. If you are planning a French test, book a consultation with our team.

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Express Entry: Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/criteria-comprehensive-ranking-system.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Understand Express Entry: Additional points](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/works.html)

# Proof of a Genuine Relationship for Canada Spousal Sponsorship (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/genuine-relationship-spousal-sponsorship-canada-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-07-08
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Most spousal sponsorship refusals do not come from missing forms; they come from an officer not being convinced the relationship is real.

As of July 8, 2026.

Most spousal sponsorship refusals do not come from missing forms; they come from an officer not being convinced the relationship is real. This guide explains what Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada means by a genuine relationship, exactly what evidence proves one, and why applications get refused.

## TL;DR

**Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) approves a spousal sponsorship only when the relationship is both genuine and not entered into primarily to gain immigration status.** | Strong applications show a mix of evidence: joint finances, proof you live together, a history of communication, photos together over time, joint travel, and statements from people who know you as a couple. | A genuine relationship can be refused on the evidence alone, without any finding of fraud, so thin or inconsistent documentation hurts real couples too. | Common-law partners must prove at least 12 continuous months of living together; conjugal partners must show why they could neither marry nor live together.

## What does IRCC mean by a "genuine relationship"?

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) uses a two-part test: your relationship must be genuine, and it must not have been entered into primarily to obtain permanent residence. An officer weighs the whole picture, including how you met, how your relationship developed, and how you live as a couple now. A real relationship with weak documentation can still be refused, because the officer can only assess what you submit, so the burden is on you to prove it clearly.

## What evidence proves a genuine relationship?

The strongest applications combine several types of evidence that together tell a consistent story over time, rather than a single document. Officers look for financial interdependence, shared living, ongoing contact, and recognition of your relationship by others.

| Evidence type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Financial | Joint bank accounts, shared bills, beneficiary designations, money transfers |
| Cohabitation | Shared lease or deed, mail to the same address, joint utilities |
| Communication | Call and message logs across the relationship, not just recent |
| Social recognition | Photos together over time, with family and at events, joint travel |
| Third-party proof | Statutory declarations from friends and family, wedding evidence |

## Why do spousal sponsorship applications get refused?

A relationship can be refused as not genuine on the evidence alone, without any finding of fraud, so thin or inconsistent documentation is enough to sink a real relationship. Officers refuse when the file has large unexplained gaps, when dates or facts contradict each other, or when interview answers do not match the application. Relationships that developed very quickly, involve a large age or background difference, or have little communication history draw closer scrutiny, so those couples should document even more carefully rather than less.

- Too little evidence, or evidence only from the last few months
- Inconsistencies between forms, documents, and interview answers
- Little proof of communication or time spent together
- Unexplained factors that officers associate with marriages of convenience

## How much evidence is enough?

Quality and consistency matter more than volume, so a focused set of documents that spans the whole relationship beats a large pile from a single month. Show the arc of the relationship: how you met, key milestones, and daily life together now. Include a written relationship history that ties the documents together and explains anything unusual, so the officer does not have to guess.

## What about common-law and conjugal partners?

If you are not married, you can be sponsored as a common-law partner if you have lived together continuously for at least 12 months, or as a conjugal partner if you are in a marriage-like relationship but could not live together or marry, often due to legal or immigration barriers in your country. Common-law partners prove cohabitation with shared documents covering the full 12 months, while conjugal partners must also explain the specific barrier that kept you apart.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the single most important type of evidence?**
There is no single document. Officers want a consistent mix showing financial ties, cohabitation, communication, and social recognition across the whole relationship.

**Can a real couple be refused?**
Yes. If the evidence is thin, inconsistent, or does not cover enough time, an officer can refuse even a genuine relationship, which is why thorough documentation matters.

**Do we need to be married to sponsor a partner?**
No. You can sponsor a spouse (married), a common-law partner (12 months of cohabitation), or a conjugal partner (a marriage-like relationship with a barrier to marrying or living together).

**Will we be interviewed?**
Not always. IRCC interviews some couples when the officer needs more assurance, and inconsistent answers at an interview can lead to refusal.

## Building a file an officer can approve

The couples who get approved are the ones who prove their story rather than assume it is obvious, with evidence that spans the whole relationship and a clear written history tying it together. As a licensed Canadian immigration firm, we help couples build a spousal sponsorship file that answers an officer's doubts before they arise. If you are preparing a sponsorship application, book a consultation with our team.

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Sponsor your spouse, partner or child](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Sponsor your spouse, partner or child: Who you can sponsor](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/who-you-can-sponsor.html)

# After Your ITA: The Express Entry e-APR Application Step-by-Step (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/express-entry-after-ita-eapr-guide-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-07-08
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Getting an Invitation to Apply is the milestone every Express Entry candidate waits for, but it starts a 60-day clock and the hardest paperwork of the whole process.

As of July 8, 2026.

Getting an Invitation to Apply is the milestone every Express Entry candidate waits for, but it starts a 60-day clock and the hardest paperwork of the whole process. This guide walks you through exactly what to do after your Invitation to Apply, from the document checklist to the fees to what happens once you submit.

## TL;DR

**After an Invitation to Apply (ITA), you have 60 days to submit a complete electronic application for permanent residence (e-APR) through your online account.** | The core documents are your language test, Educational Credential Assessment (ECA), proof of funds, police certificates, medical exam, work reference letters, passport, and photos. | Government fees are about CAD $990 processing plus a $600 Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF) per adult, plus $85 biometrics per person; a single applicant must also show $15,263 in settlement funds. | After you submit, you get an Acknowledgement of Receipt (AOR), give biometrics, complete a medical exam, pass background checks, and finally receive a passport request and Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR).

## What happens after you get an ITA in Express Entry?

When you receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA), Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) opens a 60-day window for you to submit a complete electronic application for permanent residence, called the e-APR, through your online account. Everything you claimed in your profile now has to be proven with documents. If you cannot gather everything in time or your situation changed, you can decline the ITA and return to the pool instead of submitting a weak application.

## What documents do you need for the e-APR?

You need documents that prove every part of your profile: your identity, language ability, education, work history, funds, and admissibility. Missing or inconsistent documents are the top reason applications are refused or delayed, so gather them before the clock runs down.

| Document | Proves |
|---|---|
| Language test (IELTS, CELPIP, or TEF/TCF) | Your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) language points |
| Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) | Foreign education for CRS points |
| Proof of funds | You can support yourself and your family |
| Police certificates | Admissibility (criminality) |
| Medical exam | Admissibility (health) |
| Work reference letters | Your claimed skilled work experience |
| Passport and photos | Identity |

## How much does the Express Entry PR application cost?

The main government fees are about CAD $990 for processing plus a $600 Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF) per adult, and $85 for biometrics per person, so a single adult pays roughly $1,675 in government fees. On top of that, you must show settlement funds, which is money you keep, not a fee: $15,263 for a single applicant, rising with family size. Budget separately for third-party costs like the language test, ECA, medical exam, and translations. Fees can change, so confirm current amounts on the official IRCC fee schedule before you pay.

## What happens after you submit the e-APR?

After you submit and pay, IRCC sends an Acknowledgement of Receipt (AOR), then moves your file through a set sequence: you give biometrics, complete your medical exam if you have not already, and IRCC runs security and background checks. When everything clears, you receive a passport request (PPR) and your Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR). Most complete Express Entry applications are processed within about six months, though individual files vary.

- Acknowledgement of Receipt (AOR) confirms your application is in the queue
- Biometrics instruction letter arrives shortly after AOR
- Medical exam is validated (upfront exams speed this up)
- Security, criminality, and background checks run in the background
- Passport request (PPR) and COPR are the final steps

## Can you decline an ITA if you are not ready?

Yes, you can decline an Invitation to Apply and your profile goes back into the pool, keeping your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score and eligibility. This is the right move if you cannot get a key document, like a police certificate or ECA, within the 60 days, because submitting an incomplete or inaccurate application risks a refusal. You can be invited again in a future round if your score stays competitive.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long do I have to submit after an ITA?**
You have 60 days from the date of your Invitation to Apply to submit a complete e-APR.

**What is an e-APR?**
The electronic application for permanent residence, the full application you submit online after your ITA, with all supporting documents uploaded.

**What happens if I miss the 60-day deadline?**
Your invitation expires. You can decline before it expires to return to the pool, or wait for a new invitation if your score remains competitive.

**Do I need a medical exam before I apply?**
You can complete an upfront medical exam before submitting, which often speeds up processing, or wait for IRCC to request one after you apply.

## Turning your ITA into a submitted application

The candidates who clear the 60-day window without stress are the ones who prepared their documents while still in the pool, so the ITA becomes a formality, not a scramble. As a licensed Canadian immigration firm, we help candidates assemble a complete, consistent e-APR that stands up to an officer's review. If you just received an ITA or expect one soon, book a consultation with our team.

## Sources

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Apply for permanent residence through Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/apply-permanent-residence.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Proof of funds](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/proof-funds.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Express Entry: Police certificates](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/police-certificates.html)
