# Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR) Can Still Be Cancelled: Why It Is Not a Guarantee (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/confirmation-of-permanent-residence-copr-cancelled-2026
Category: Immigration
Published: 2026-06-21
Author: Go Far Global Team

> A Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR) is not a guarantee that you are a permanent resident of Canada.

A Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR) is not a guarantee that you are a permanent resident of Canada. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) can reopen your file, reassess it, and cancel both your COPR and your permanent resident visa before you land, and in narrow cases even after. You become a permanent resident (PR) only when you complete your landing, and until that moment your approval can still be pulled.

*As of June 21, 2026.*

## Does a COPR guarantee permanent residency in Canada?

No. A Confirmation of Permanent Residence confirms that IRCC approved your application, but it does not make you a permanent resident, and it is not a guarantee. You become a permanent resident only when you complete your landing, either at a port of entry or through the online Permanent Residence Confirmation Portal. Until that step is finished, IRCC can reopen your file and cancel the approval. The document is also stamped not valid for travel, because it records your approval rather than serving as a travel document. The permanent resident visa that comes with it, or an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA), is what actually lets you travel to Canada.

## What is a Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR)?

A Confirmation of Permanent Residence is the document IRCC issues when it approves your permanent residence application, for example after an Express Entry round. It records your personal details, the program you were approved under, and an expiry date. Applicants who need a visa also receive a permanent resident visa, often called a counterfoil, in their passport. The COPR is generally valid for one year, and IRCC cannot extend it, so you must travel to Canada and complete your landing before it expires. If it expires before you land, you usually have to apply for permanent residence again from the start. IRCC explains the document on its [Confirmation of Permanent Residence page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/permanent-residents/status/copr.html).

## When do you actually become a permanent resident?

You become a permanent resident at the moment you complete your landing, not when you receive your COPR. Landing happens in one of two ways. If you are outside Canada, an officer examines you at a port of entry when you arrive, checks your documents, and admits you as a permanent resident. If you are already in Canada, you confirm your status online through the [Permanent Residence Confirmation Portal](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/pr-confirmation-portal.html). Once your landing is complete, your COPR becomes valid as proof of permanent resident status until your PR card arrives. Before that step, your status is still pending, and your approval can be withdrawn.

## Can IRCC cancel your COPR after it is issued?

Yes. IRCC can reopen an approved application, reassess it, and cancel your COPR and permanent resident visa, and it does this in real cases. A cancellation letter typically states that the documents in your possession have been cancelled, that the application has been re-opened and is being reviewed, and that the documents are not valid for travel. You are then told to return the COPR and the visa counterfoil. This most often happens before landing, while your status is still pending. Even after landing, permanent residence can be challenged in narrow situations, mainly where IRCC later finds misrepresentation or serious inadmissibility, through a separate process.

## Why would IRCC reopen and cancel a PR application?

IRCC reopens and cancels an approved application when something changes or comes to light that affects your eligibility or your admissibility. The reason is not always misconduct on your part. The most common triggers are a change in your circumstances, new information that contradicts your file, a document problem, or a concern about misrepresentation.

| Trigger | Example |
|---|---|
| Changed circumstances | A marriage breakdown in a spousal case, a withdrawn job offer, a new dependant |
| Document or eligibility problem | Missing or inconsistent documents, an expired requirement, a failed condition |
| New inadmissibility | A criminal charge, a medical issue, or a security concern arising after approval |
| Misrepresentation concern | A false statement or a fake document found in the application |
| Procedural review | IRCC reopens the file to correct an error or apply a fairness step |

## What does a COPR cancellation letter mean?

A COPR cancellation letter means IRCC has taken back your approval for now and put your application back into review. It tells you three things: your COPR and visa counterfoil are cancelled, your application has been re-opened and is being reviewed, and the documents are not valid for travel. It usually directs you to follow the instructions in a Ready for Visa letter and to return the cancelled documents. It does not automatically mean your application is refused, but it does mean you are not cleared to travel or land, and you must wait for IRCC's decision on the reopened file. Acting on the letter quickly matters.

## What should you do if your COPR is cancelled?

Read the letter carefully, do exactly what it instructs, and respond by the deadline. Return the cancelled COPR and visa counterfoil if asked, and do not try to travel or land on cancelled documents, because that can lead to a refusal or a finding against you. Gather any documents IRCC requests and answer every question honestly and completely. Because a reopened file can end in a refusal, a procedural fairness letter, or a misrepresentation finding with a five-year bar from Canada, get advice from a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) or an immigration lawyer before you reply. A careful, honest response is your strongest protection.

## How do you protect your PR approval until you land?

Keep everything in your application true and current until your landing is complete. Do not change the facts your approval was based on, and if something genuinely changes, such as a relationship ending, a birth, or a lost job offer, tell IRCC rather than hiding it. Never use false documents or make a false statement, because misrepresentation is the fastest way to lose an approval and earn a five-year ban, a consequence IRCC describes in its guidance on [protecting yourself from fraud](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/protect-fraud.html). Land before your COPR expires, since IRCC will not extend it. No agent or consultant can guarantee your permanent residence. Honest, accurate guidance can only help you follow the process correctly and avoid the mistakes that get a file reopened.

Go Far Global is a licensed RCIC firm in Toronto, and our consultants help applicants protect their approval all the way through to landing.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does COPR mean PR is approved?

Receiving a COPR means IRCC approved your permanent residence application, but it does not make you a permanent resident on its own. You become a permanent resident only when you complete your landing at a port of entry or through the Permanent Residence Confirmation Portal. Until then, your approval is still subject to review.

### What happens after you receive a Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR)?

After you receive your COPR, you must travel to Canada, or confirm your status online if you are already inside Canada, and complete your landing before the COPR expires. An officer or the online portal verifies your documents and admits you as a permanent resident. Only then does the COPR become valid proof of your status.

### Does getting my eCOPR mean I am a permanent resident?

No. The electronic Confirmation of Permanent Residence (eCOPR) is the digital version of the document, and receiving it means your application was approved. You are a permanent resident only after you confirm your landing, either at the border or through the Permanent Residence Confirmation Portal. The eCOPR by itself does not complete the process.

### How long is a COPR valid in Canada?

A COPR is generally valid for one year from the date it is issued, and IRCC cannot extend it. You must travel to Canada and land before it expires. If your COPR expires before you complete your landing, you usually have to apply for permanent residence again from the beginning.

### Can IRCC take back permanent residence after you land?

In narrow situations, yes. After you land, your permanent residence can be challenged mainly where IRCC later finds misrepresentation or serious inadmissibility, and this is handled through a separate process rather than a simple cancellation. Most cancellations happen before landing, while the COPR is still in your possession and your status is pending.

# How Many Hours Can International Students Work in Canada? 2026 Off-Campus Rules

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/international-student-off-campus-work-hours-canada-2026
Category: Immigration
Published: 2026-06-21
Author: Go Far Global Team

> International students in Canada can work up to 24 hours per week off campus during an academic session, and full time during scheduled breaks.

International students in Canada can work up to 24 hours per week off campus during an academic session, and full time during scheduled breaks. You do not need a separate work permit to work off campus if your study permit allows it and you meet the conditions. This guide explains the hour limits, who qualifies, and the mistakes that put your study permit at risk.

*As of June 21, 2026.*

## How many hours can international students work off campus in Canada?

Eligible international students can work up to 24 hours per week off campus while their academic session is in progress. This limit became permanent in November 2024, replacing the previous 20-hour cap. The 24 hours is a hard weekly ceiling, not an average, so you cannot work 10 hours one week and 38 the next to balance it out. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) treats any week above 24 hours as a breach of your study permit conditions. During scheduled school breaks, such as the summer or winter holidays, you can work more than 24 hours and even full time. IRCC sets out the rule on its [work off campus page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html).

| Period | Off-campus hours allowed |
|---|---|
| Regular academic session | Up to 24 hours per week |
| Scheduled break (summer, winter holidays) | Full time, no weekly limit |
| Before your program starts | Not allowed |
| During an authorized leave from studies | Not allowed |

## Who is eligible to work off campus without a work permit?

You can work off campus without a separate work permit only if you meet every condition IRCC sets. You must be a full-time student at a Designated Learning Institution (DLI), enrolled in a post-secondary academic, vocational, or professional program that is at least six months long and leads to a degree, diploma, or certificate. Your studies must have already started, your study permit must state that you are allowed to work off campus, and you must have a [Social Insurance Number (SIN)](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/sin.html). If any one of these conditions is missing, you cannot work off campus on your study permit alone.

## Can you work full time during scheduled breaks?

Yes. During a scheduled break in your program, such as the summer holiday or the winter break, you can work unlimited hours off campus, including full time. The break must be a real scheduled break in your study calendar, you must be a full-time student before and after it, and you must be returning to studies afterward. You cannot treat your final term or a personal gap as a break. If you take an [authorized leave from your studies](https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/study-permit-authorized-leave-150-days-2026), that is not a break, and you cannot work at all during it.

## What happens if you work more than 24 hours a week?

Working more than 24 hours per week off campus during an academic session breaks the conditions of your study permit. The consequences are serious. IRCC can find you non-compliant, which can lead to the loss of your student status, a refusal of a future study permit or work permit, a refused Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), and in some cases a requirement to leave Canada. Officers can cross-check your hours against tax records and your employer's payroll. The record does not forgive an honest mistake, so track your hours carefully and keep them under the limit every single week.

## Can you work on campus and off campus at the same time?

Yes, but the 24-hour weekly limit still applies to your off-campus hours. On-campus work has no set hour limit under IRCC rules, so a student can hold an on-campus job and an off-campus job at the same time. Only the off-campus hours count toward the 24-hour weekly cap. If you work both, count only the off-campus portion against the limit, and make sure your study permit authorizes off-campus work before you take an outside job.

## Do you still need a co-op work permit in 2026?

In many cases, no. As of April 1, 2026, post-secondary international students no longer need a separate co-op work permit for a required work placement, as long as the placement is 50% or less of the total program hours, a change IRCC explains on its [work as an international student page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work.html). If your placement is larger than that, or you are in a program type that is not covered, you still need a co-op work permit. A required placement is authorized separately, so its hours do not count against the 24-hour off-campus limit. We cover this in our guide on the [co-op work permit change](https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-co-op-work-permit-eliminated-2026).

## When can you start working as an international student?

You can only start working on or after the first day your study program begins, as set out in IRCC's [off-campus work conditions](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html#who-can). You cannot work before your program start date, even if you already have your study permit, your SIN, and a job offer. Working early is one of the most common ways students breach their conditions in their first weeks in Canada. Your right to work also ends if you stop studying full time, switch to part-time without an approved reason, or finish your program, so confirm your status before you keep working after a program ends.

## How do you stay compliant with your work hours?

Track every off-campus hour by week, never cross 24 hours during a session, and only work full time during a genuine scheduled break. Keep your study permit handy so you can confirm it authorizes off-campus work, and keep proof of your enrolment and your work schedule. If your hours, your enrolment, or a leave creates any doubt, speak to a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) before it shows up on a future application. A clean compliance record protects your study permit, your PGWP, and your path to permanent residence.

Go Far Global is a licensed RCIC firm in Toronto, and our consultants help international students protect their status every week.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I work 40 hours a week as an international student in Canada?

Only during a scheduled break. During a regular academic session, the off-campus limit is 24 hours per week, and working 40 hours would breach your study permit. During the summer or winter break, you can work full time, including 40 hours or more, as long as you are a full-time student before and after the break.

### What are the new work rules for international students in Canada in 2026?

The off-campus limit is 24 hours per week during academic sessions, made permanent in November 2024. As of April 1, 2026, post-secondary students no longer need a co-op work permit for a required placement that is 50% or less of program hours. The basic eligibility rules still apply: full-time enrolment, a qualifying program, a started program, and a Social Insurance Number.

### Can international students work unlimited hours during breaks?

Yes. During a scheduled break in your study program, eligible international students can work unlimited hours off campus, including full time. You must be a full-time student before and after the break and be returning to studies, and the break must be a scheduled one in your academic calendar.

### Do off-campus hours include on-campus or co-op work?

No. The 24-hour weekly limit applies only to off-campus work. On-campus work has no set hour limit, and a required co-op or internship placement is authorized separately, so neither counts toward your off-campus 24 hours.

### Can I average my work hours across weeks?

No. The 24-hour limit is a hard ceiling for each week during a session. You cannot average hours, so working fewer hours one week does not let you work more than 24 the next. Every week must stay at or under 24 hours.

## Sources

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Work off campus as an international student](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Work as an international student or recent graduate](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work.html)
- Service Canada, [Social Insurance Number](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/sin.html)

# How to Extend Your Visitor Visa in Canada 2026: Visitor Record, Timing, and Costs

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/extend-visitor-visa-canada-visitor-record-2026
Category: Immigration
Published: 2026-06-21
Author: Go Far Global Team

> To extend your stay in Canada as a visitor, you apply for a visitor record, not a new visitor visa.

To extend your stay in Canada as a visitor, you apply for a visitor record, not a new visitor visa. A visitor record is the document that sets how long you can legally stay, and you apply for it online from inside Canada before your current status expires. Most visitors are admitted for six months, and a visitor record lets you ask Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) for more time.

*As of June 21, 2026.*

## What is a visitor record, and how is it different from a visitor visa?

A visitor record is a document IRCC issues to extend your stay inside Canada as a visitor. It is not a visa. A visitor visa, formally a Temporary Resident Visa (TRV), is the entry document in your passport that lets you travel to Canada. A visitor record does not let you travel; it sets a new date by which you must leave. Many people search for how to extend a visitor visa when what they actually need is a visitor record, because the TRV only controls entry while the visitor record controls how long you can remain. If your TRV has expired but you are still in Canada legally, you only need a new TRV when you plan to leave and return.

| Document | What it does | When you need it |
|---|---|---|
| Visitor visa (Temporary Resident Visa, TRV) | Lets you travel to and enter Canada | Before you arrive, or before you re-enter after leaving |
| Visitor record | Extends how long you can stay inside Canada | When you want to stay past your current authorized period |

## How do you extend your visitor visa in Canada?

You extend your stay by applying online for a visitor record through your IRCC secure account. You complete the application to change conditions or extend your stay, upload your documents, pay the fee, and submit before your current status ends. IRCC sets out the steps and forms in [Guide 5551](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5551-applying-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada.html) and on its [visitor record how-to-apply page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay/apply.html). You apply from inside Canada, and you should not leave the country while the application is in progress, because leaving can end the maintained status that protects you while you wait.

The core form is the Application to Change Conditions, Extend My Stay or Remain in Canada (IMM 5708), completed inside the online application. Have your passport, your current status document, and proof that you can support yourself ready to upload.

## When should you apply to extend your stay?

Apply at least 30 days before your current status expires. IRCC recommends this window so that your application is submitted while you still hold valid status. If you apply before your status ends, you keep what is called maintained status, previously called implied status, which lets you stay in Canada legally under the same conditions until IRCC makes a decision, even if your original period runs out while you wait. If you apply after your status has already expired, you lose that protection and may need to apply to [restore your status](https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/restoration-of-status-canada-2026) instead.

## How much does a visitor record cost in 2026?

The government fee for a visitor record is 100 Canadian dollars. If you have not given biometrics in the last 10 years, you may also need to pay the biometrics fee of 85 Canadian dollars. Most visitors extending from inside Canada are not asked for new biometrics, but the online system will tell you if you are. There is no separate processing fee beyond these amounts for a standard visitor extension.

| Item | Fee (CAD) |
|---|---:|
| Visitor record (extend your stay) | $100 |
| Biometrics, if required | $85 |
| Total if biometrics are required | $185 |

## How long does a visitor record extension take to process?

Processing times for a visitor record change with application volume, and IRCC publishes the current estimate on its [check processing times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html). Online visitor extensions have recently taken several months, so apply early rather than close to your expiry date. While you wait, maintained status keeps you legal in Canada as long as you applied before your previous status expired and you remain in the country.

## How long can you extend your stay as a visitor?

A visitor record usually extends your stay for up to six months from the date of the decision, though IRCC can grant a shorter or longer period based on your situation and the validity of your passport. You should ask for the amount of time you genuinely need and show that you have the funds to support yourself for that period. There is no fixed cap on how many times you can apply, but each application must show a genuine reason to remain a temporary visitor and that you will leave at the end.

## Can you work, study, or leave Canada on a visitor record?

No. A visitor record does not let you work or study in Canada. If you want to work, you need a [work permit](https://www.gofarglobal.com/immigration/work-permit); if you want to study a program longer than six months, you need a [study permit](https://www.gofarglobal.com/immigration/study-permit). A visitor record also does not guarantee re-entry. If you leave Canada, you need a valid visitor visa (TRV) or an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA), depending on your nationality, to come back, and leaving while your extension is pending ends your maintained status.

## What should you do to avoid losing your status?

Apply for the visitor record online at least 30 days before your current status expires, stay in Canada while the application is processed, and keep proof that you applied on time. Set a reminder well ahead of your expiry date, because the single most common mistake is applying late and falling out of status. If your status has already lapsed, you have 90 days to apply to restore it as a visitor, with an extra restoration fee. If your case is complex, speak to a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) before you submit.

Go Far Global is a licensed RCIC firm in Toronto, and our consultants handle visitor extensions and status problems every week.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long can you extend a visitor record in Canada?

A visitor record usually extends your stay for up to six months from the decision date. IRCC can grant less or more depending on your reason and how long your passport is valid. You can apply again before each new period ends, as long as you remain a genuine temporary visitor.

### Can I leave Canada while waiting for a visitor record extension?

You can leave, but it is risky. Leaving Canada while your visitor record application is pending ends your maintained status, and you will need a valid visitor visa or eTA to return. If you must travel, wait for a decision first where possible.

### How long does it take to get a visitor record extension in Canada?

Processing times vary with volume, and recent online visitor extensions have taken several months. Check the current estimate on IRCC's processing times tool, and apply early so that maintained status covers you while you wait.

### What is a valid reason to extend a visitor visa in Canada?

Common accepted reasons include continuing a family visit, recovering from a medical issue, waiting on another application, or tourism that runs longer than planned. You must show that you are a genuine temporary visitor, that you can support yourself, and that you will leave at the end of the extended stay.

### Do I need a new visitor visa to extend my stay?

No. To stay longer inside Canada you apply for a visitor record, not a new visitor visa. You only need a new visitor visa (Temporary Resident Visa) if you leave Canada and need to re-enter.

## Sources

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Extend your stay in Canada (visitor record)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Visitor record: How to apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay/apply.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Guide 5551: Applying to Change Conditions or Extend Your Stay in Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5551-applying-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Check processing times](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html)

# Canada's 150-Day Study Leave Rule: Why a Valid-Looking Permit Won't Protect You (June 2026 IRCC Update)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/study-permit-authorized-leave-150-days-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-21
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada's 150-day authorized-leave rule for study permits: who qualifies, why you cannot work during a leave, and how to keep status past 150 days.

An authorized leave from your studies in Canada protects your study permit for only 150 days. Thousands of international students take a break each year for medical, family, or personal reasons, and most assume the permit keeps protecting them as long as the card has not expired. That assumption is now risky. On June 18, 2026, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) updated the manual its officers use to judge whether a student is following the rules, and it tightened the language around the one number that decides everything: 150 days.

You can take an authorized leave from your studies for up to 150 consecutive days and keep your study permit valid, but only if your Designated Learning Institution (DLI) approves the leave and the reason qualifies. During the leave you cannot work, on or off campus, even if your permit says you can. If you have not resumed studies within 150 days, you must restart classes, change to another status such as visitor or worker, or leave Canada. Stay past 150 days without doing one of those, and you are out of status, even though your study permit card still looks valid.

*As of June 21, 2026.*

## What is the 150-day authorized leave rule for study permits?

The 150-day rule is the limit IRCC places on how long an international student can pause active studies without losing their student status. If your school approves the leave and the reason is valid, your study permit stays valid for up to 150 consecutive days from the day your studies stopped. Cross that line without resuming studies or switching to a new status, and you are no longer maintaining the conditions of your permit. The rule has existed for years inside IRCC's instructions to officers; the June 2026 update wrote it down more clearly and confirmed officers can audit it.

The clock starts on the date you stopped actively studying, not the date your school formally records the leave. A leave is measured in consecutive days, so a five-month gap across two terms can quietly exceed the limit. IRCC lists the conditions every student must keep on its [study permit conditions page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/while-you-study/study-permit-conditions.html), and actively pursuing studies sits at the top of that list.

## What changed in IRCC's June 2026 study permit update?

On June 18, 2026, IRCC revised the internal manual officers use to assess study permit compliance. It did not create a new law. It clarified three things that were already true but often ignored: authorized leave is capped at 150 days, the right to work is suspended for the entire leave, and a co-op or internship work permit cannot be used during a leave either. It also reminded officers that they can run checks and ask for proof that a leave was genuine and approved.

For students, the practical effect is that enforcement is now explicit. Before this update, someone who stretched a break or worked during a leave might have slipped through. After it, an officer reviewing your file, your [study permit extension](/news/extend-study-permit-canada-2026), your [Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP)](/news/pgwp-post-graduation-work-permit-canada-2026), or your permanent residence application has a written instruction to flag exactly these gaps.

## What counts as an authorized leave from your studies?

An authorized leave is a break your DLI approves for a genuine reason. IRCC accepts reasons that include medical issues or pregnancy, a family emergency, the death or serious illness of a family member, and a school-initiated change such as a deferred program start or a change of institution. A break you take on your own, without your school approving it, is an unauthorized leave, and it puts your status at risk from the first day.

The reason matters as much as the paperwork. Taking time off to travel, to work more hours, or because you changed your mind about a program does not qualify. Your school decides whether to grant the leave, and IRCC can later ask to see that approval.

| Situation | Authorized leave? | Can you work? |
|---|---|---|
| Medical reason or pregnancy, approved by your DLI | Yes, up to 150 days | No |
| Death or serious illness of a family member | Yes, up to 150 days | No |
| Your school defers your program start date | Yes | No |
| You change to a new DLI and there is a gap | Yes, if documented | No |
| You take time off to work or travel | No | No, and your status is at risk |
| Break longer than 150 consecutive days | No longer valid | No |

## Can you work during an authorized leave?

No. Your permission to work, whether on campus, [off campus](/news/international-student-off-campus-work-hours-canada-2026), or through a co-op work permit, is suspended for the full length of an authorized leave, even if your study permit still shows that you are allowed to work. Working during a leave is one of the clearest ways to break the conditions of your permit, and after the June 2026 update it is one of the first things an officer is told to check. The safe rule is simple: if you are on an authorized leave, you are not working in Canada.

This catches many students off guard because the study permit card itself does not change during a leave. The card may still read that off-campus work is allowed up to the weekly limit. That printed condition does not apply while your studies are paused, and a co-op work permit is treated the same way, so a work placement cannot continue through a leave.

## What happens after 150 days?

Once your authorized leave passes 150 consecutive days, your study permit is no longer valid for staying in Canada as a student. You then have three choices: resume full-time studies at a DLI, apply to change your status to another type such as a visitor or a worker, or leave Canada. If you do none of these and remain in Canada, you are out of status the day after the 150th day, regardless of the expiry date printed on your permit.

Being out of status is serious. It can lead to enforcement action, and it weakens future applications for a PGWP, permanent residence, or any other immigration benefit, because every later application asks whether you have always complied with your conditions.

## How do you change to visitor status before the leave runs out?

If you cannot resume studies before 150 days, the most common option is to apply for a Visitor Record so you can stay in Canada legally as a visitor. You apply online through the change of conditions process, and you should submit it before your study permit stops being valid so that you keep maintained status while IRCC decides. A Visitor Record does not let you work or study, but it keeps you in the country lawfully while you plan your next step.

Apply through IRCC's process for changing conditions or extending your stay, set out in [Guide 5552](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5552-applying-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada-student.html), or follow the steps to [extend your stay as a visitor](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay.html). If you submit before your current status ends, you benefit from maintained status and can stay in Canada while the application is processed. If you plan to leave and return, review IRCC's guidance on [travelling outside Canada as a student](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/travel-outside-canada.html) before you book anything.

## How does IRCC check whether your leave was authorized?

IRCC can audit your compliance at any time, and the June 2026 manual reminds officers that this power is real. An officer can ask for documents that prove your leave was genuine and approved, including an enrolment letter, your transcripts, a leave-approval letter from your DLI, a doctor's note, or a withdrawal letter from your school. These checks can happen during a routine review or when you apply for an extension, a work permit, or permanent residence.

Keep every document that supports your leave. If your school approved a medical leave, store the approval letter and the medical note together. If you cannot show that a gap was an authorized leave, IRCC can treat it as a period when you were not complying with the conditions of your permit.

## What should international students do right now?

Plan any break around the 150-day limit, get your school to approve it in writing before you stop studying, and do not work during the leave. If a break will run long, file for a Visitor Record before your study permit stops being valid so you keep maintained status. Keep every supporting document. If your situation is complex, or a past gap might look like an unauthorized leave, speak to a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) before you submit your next application.

A few concrete steps:

- Confirm the start date of your leave and count 150 consecutive days from there.
- Get a written leave approval from your DLI before the break begins.
- Stop all work, including any co-op placement, for the entire leave.
- If you will not resume studies in time, apply for a Visitor Record early, while your status is still valid.
- Save enrolment letters, transcripts, leave approvals, and medical notes in case IRCC asks.

Go Far Global is a licensed RCIC firm in Toronto, and our consultants read every IRCC update directly from the source.

## Frequently asked questions

### What counts as an authorized leave from your studies?

An authorized leave is a break that your Designated Learning Institution (DLI) approves for a genuine reason. IRCC accepts reasons such as medical issues or pregnancy, a family emergency, the death or serious illness of a family member, and a school-initiated change such as a deferred start date or a change of institution. A break you take without your school approving it is unauthorized and puts your study permit at risk immediately.

### Can I work during an authorized leave from studies?

No. Your right to work on campus, off campus, or through a co-op work permit is suspended for the entire authorized leave, even if your study permit still says you can work. The suspension lasts the full leave, and working during it breaks the conditions of your permit.

### How long can an authorized leave last in Canada?

An authorized leave can last up to 150 consecutive days without affecting the validity of your study permit, as long as your DLI approves it and the reason qualifies. The count starts on the day you stop actively studying. If you have not resumed studies within 150 days, you must change status or leave Canada.

### What if my study permit looks valid but I stopped studying?

The expiry date on the card does not protect you. If you stopped actively studying and your authorized leave has passed 150 days, you are out of status even though the permit card still looks valid. You need to resume studies, change to another status such as a visitor or worker, or leave Canada to stay compliant.

### Can I change my status to visitor if I need more time?

Yes. You can apply for a Visitor Record to remain in Canada as a visitor. Submit the change of conditions application before your study permit stops being valid so that you keep maintained status while IRCC decides. A Visitor Record does not allow you to work or study.

### Can I leave and come back to Canada if I have a study permit?

Yes, if your study permit is still valid you can usually re-enter Canada, but you also need a valid travel document for the trip back, either a visitor visa (Temporary Resident Visa) or an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA), depending on your nationality. A study permit by itself is not a travel document. If you are on an authorized leave, leaving and returning does not reset the 150-day limit, which keeps counting while you are away.

## Sources

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/while-you-study/study-permit-conditions.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Guide 5552: Applying to Change Conditions or Extend Your Stay in Canada as a Student](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5552-applying-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada-student.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Extend your stay in Canada as a visitor](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [International students travelling outside Canada and then re-entering](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/travel-outside-canada.html)

# Canada Wants to Bring Back Express Entry Job Offer Points in 2026: For High-Wage Jobs Only

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/express-entry-job-offer-points-high-wage-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-19
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Job offer points are back on the table for Express Entry, and they could matter a lot for your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score.

Job offer points are back on the table for Express Entry, and they could matter a lot for your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score. But there is a catch that most headlines skip: under what Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has proposed, those points would only reward people working in or holding an offer for a high-wage occupation.

**Short answer:** This is a proposal, not a rule. IRCC consulted the public on bringing back job offer points, but only for high-wage jobs, as part of a larger Express Entry overhaul. The consultation closed on May 24, 2026, no regulation has been published, and no start date has been set. If you already hold an Invitation to Apply (ITA), the rules from your draw still apply to you.

*As of June 18, 2026.*

## What is Canada proposing for Express Entry job offer points?

IRCC wants to reintroduce CRS points for a valid job offer, after removing them in March 2025. The difference this time is the filter: the points would attach to a new high-wage occupation factor rather than to any job offer. The proposal appears in IRCC's [public consultation on Express Entry reforms](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry-reforms.html), which ran from April 23 to May 24, 2026.

In plain terms, the government wants to steer permanent residence toward higher earners and the jobs that pay them, on the theory that wage level is a stronger predictor of how well a newcomer does in the Canadian economy than some of the points the system rewards today.

## Why were job offer points removed in the first place?

IRCC dropped the arranged-employment CRS points in March 2025 over fraud concerns. Job offers are easy to fake, and the bonus they carried, up to 200 points for some senior roles and 50 points for most others, created a strong incentive to buy or fabricate one. Removing those points took that incentive away, but it also stripped score from honest candidates who had real offers, and it pushed several draw cut-offs higher as that source of points left the pool.

The proposed comeback tries to solve that by tying the points to wage data instead of to the existence of an offer alone. A high-wage role is harder to fake because the salary has to match published wage benchmarks, which lowers the fraud risk the earlier rule could not control.

## What is the high-wage occupation factor?

The high-wage occupation factor is the heart of the proposal. It would award extra CRS points to candidates whose Canadian work experience or job offer sits in an occupation that pays above the national median wage, sorted into three tiers. IRCC has said the official list would be built from Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) wage data and the Government of Canada [Job Bank](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/trend-analysis/search-wages), which tracks median wages by National Occupational Classification (NOC) code.

| Wage tier | Threshold | Example occupations |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 | At least 2x the national median wage | Physicians, university professors |
| Tier 2 | At least 1.5x the national median wage | Engineers, teachers, transportation managers |
| Tier 3 | At least 1.3x the national median wage | Other above-median skilled roles |

Higher tiers would carry more points than lower ones. IRCC has not published the exact CRS values for each tier, so anyone quoting a specific number is guessing.

## Which occupations would benefit?

The factor would reward roughly four in ten of the occupations Canada already prioritizes. Of the 89 occupations currently flagged for priority processing, about 37 sit high enough on the wage scale to gain an extra boost under the proposed regime.

That is the real story behind the punchy headlines. Bringing back job offer points sounds like good news for everyone, but the design favours doctors, engineers, senior managers, skilled trades in well-paid niches, and similar earners. A skilled worker in a lower-paid occupation would see little or nothing from this specific factor, even with a genuine job offer.

## What would count as a qualifying job offer?

IRCC has said the definition is still being written. Based on its public statements, a qualifying offer would likely need to be full-time, in a high-wage occupation, and supported by a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or a valid LMIA exemption, broadly in line with the current [job offer requirements](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/job-offer.html) for Express Entry.

The government has also said it is weighing whether to widen LMIA exemptions for offers where the fraud risk is low. None of that is settled, so treat any specific claim about LMIA rules under the new factor as a forecast, not a fact.

## Is this confirmed, and when would it start?

No, and this is the single most important thing to understand before you make any decision based on it. As of June 18, 2026, the high-wage occupation factor and the return of job offer points are proposals that IRCC put out for public comment, not rules that exist. What is certain is that job offer points were removed in March 2025 and that the government formally proposed bringing them back for high-wage roles. What is not certain is the start date, how many points each tier would carry, or which occupations would make the final list. Until a regulation is published, nothing here changes how your profile is scored.

| Status | Detail |
|---|---|
| Confirmed | Job offer points were removed from the CRS in March 2025 |
| Confirmed | IRCC proposed bringing them back for high-wage occupations and ran a public consultation (April 23 to May 24, 2026) |
| Not confirmed | Any start date, the exact point values, or the final list of qualifying occupations |
| Not confirmed | The final job offer and LMIA rules under the factor |

IRCC officials have pointed to a 12 to 18 month window for the full set of Express Entry reforms, while suggesting the high-wage factor could arrive sooner. No official date exists. You can track real changes through IRCC's [rounds of invitations](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/submit-profile/rounds-invitations.html) page, which is updated after each draw.

## How does this fit the bigger Express Entry overhaul?

The job offer points proposal is one piece of a much wider plan IRCC put out for [consultation on the federal high-skilled programs](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry.html). The department wants to simplify how it selects skilled workers and tilt the Comprehensive Ranking System toward economic outcomes such as wages, rather than credentials that have proven weaker at predicting how well a newcomer does after landing. The other proposed pieces include:

- Merging the Federal Skilled Worker Program, the Canadian Experience Class, and the Federal Skilled Trades Program into a single Federal High-Skilled class.
- A single set of entry requirements: at least one year of skilled work experience (NOC TEER 0 to 3), language at Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 6, and education equal to a Canadian high school diploma, verified by an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA).
- A review of bonus points that have been flagged as weak predictors of success, including points for a sibling in Canada, for Canadian study, and for a spouse's French ability.

We cover the full picture in our guide to the [Express Entry overhaul and the proposed Federal High-Skilled class](https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/express-entry-overhaul-2026-federal-high-skilled-class), and the proposed single unified pathway and eligibility floor in our [Express Entry reforms 2026 overview](/news/express-entry-reforms-2026-unified-pathway).

## What should you do right now?

Plan around what is real today, not around a proposal that has no date. The factors that decide your score under the current rules are the same ones that would help you under the proposed rules, so the smart move is to strengthen those now and treat the high-wage factor as a possible bonus rather than a plan. A few practical steps:

- Maximize the CRS factors you control now: language test results, your ECA, and Canadian work experience. These matter under both the current rules and the proposed ones. Use the official [CRS criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html) to find your weak spots.
- Check where your occupation sits on the wage scale through Job Bank, so you know whether a high-wage factor would help or pass you by.
- If a high-wage job offer is realistically within reach, it could become valuable. If it is not, do not reshape your whole plan around a rule that may never apply to you.
- Do not pay anyone who promises you guaranteed job offer points or a confirmed start date. Neither exists.

Because the rules are moving, a short review with a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) can save you from chasing points you will not get. Go Far Global is a licensed RCIC firm in Toronto, and our consultants read every IRCC update directly from the source.

## Frequently asked questions

### What are the changes in Express Entry 2026?

The biggest proposed change is a restructuring of the system: merging the three federal high-skilled programs into one class, adding a high-wage occupation factor, bringing back job offer points for high-wage roles only, and reviewing bonus points such as those for a sibling in Canada or a spouse's French. These are proposals under consultation, not rules in force.

### Is Canada removing Express Entry?

No. Canada is proposing to restructure how Express Entry selects candidates, not to shut it down. The pool, the CRS, and the draws would continue, with different scoring and a single high-skilled class replacing the current three programs.

### Is the CRS expected to drop in 2026?

Cut-off scores rise and fall draw by draw and depend on category, pool size, and the number of invitations issued, not on the proposal itself. Category-based draws can have lower cut-offs than general draws. Watch IRCC's rounds of invitations for the actual numbers rather than predictions.

### Will bringing back job offer points raise my score?

Only if your job, or your job offer, is in a high-wage occupation as the government defines it. Under the current proposal, a job offer in a lower-paid occupation would not earn the new points, even if the offer is genuine.

### How many permanent residents will Canada admit in 2026?

The 2026 to 2028 Immigration Levels Plan sets the permanent resident target at 380,000 for each of 2026, 2027, and 2028, down from 395,000 in 2025.

## Sources

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Consultation on potential Express Entry reforms](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry-reforms.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Consultation on reforms to the federal high-skilled programs and the CRS](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Express Entry: Comprehensive Ranking System criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html)
- Government of Canada, [Job Bank wage data](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/trend-analysis/search-wages)

# Lost Canadians Citizenship Certificate Suspension, Reversed (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/lost-canadians-citizenship-certificates-suspended-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-16
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has suspended a batch of citizenship certificates issued under the new Bill C-3 "lost Canadians" rules and is asking some...

*As of June 26, 2026.*

> **Update (June 26, 2026):** Ottawa has reversed course. The people who were ordered to surrender their certificates received revalidation letters dated June 19, 2026 from the Registrar of Canadian Citizenship, confirming that the evidence supports their claim and that the certificate "shall not be cancelled." On June 23, Immigration Minister Lena Diab said she had ordered her department to investigate after learning "something" had happened, and on June 25 Prime Minister Mark Carney said the affected new Canadians "deserve answers." IRCC is still reviewing the roughly 4,100 citizenship-by-descent claims made under Bill C-3 and has temporarily paused finalizing new descent certificates. The full timeline is below.

In June 2026, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) suspended a batch of citizenship certificates issued under the new Bill C-3 "lost Canadians" rules and asked a few dozen recipients to surrender them while it reviewed their files, then reversed that surrender demand about a week later. The notices went out over the weekend of June 14, 2026, and they have alarmed thousands of people who only recently received proof that they are Canadian. This guide explains exactly what happened, who is affected, why IRCC is doing it, whether the demand can be challenged, and the steps to take if you received a notice.

> Who this is for: anyone who obtained a Canadian citizenship certificate by descent under Bill C-3 since December 2025, especially U.S.-born descendants of Canadians, and anyone advising them.

## Has the citizenship certificate suspension been reversed?

Short answer: Yes, for the people who were told to surrender their certificates. On June 22, 2026, the federal government walked back the surrender demand. The few dozen recipients who had received surrender letters earlier in June were sent new letters confirming that their citizenship claims remain valid, so they no longer have to hand in their certificates. IRCC has said a certificate will not be suspended unless its review turns up a problem with a document already issued. Two things are still open: the department is reviewing roughly 4,100 citizenship-by-descent claims made under Bill C-3, and it has temporarily paused finalizing new descent certificates while that review continues. On June 23, 2026, Immigration Minister Lena Diab told reporters she had ordered her department to investigate after learning "something" had happened, without saying what, and on June 25 Prime Minister Mark Carney said the affected new Canadians "deserve answers." The government has not yet detailed what triggered the reviews.

## What did IRCC do to the lost-Canadian citizenship certificates?

Short answer: On June 15, 2026, the federal government suspended a group of citizenship certificates issued under the new citizenship-by-descent provisions and sent affected people a notice asking them to surrender their certificate during an investigation. IRCC also paused issuing new certificates under those provisions. Between December 15, 2025 and March 31, 2026, the department issued 4,075 citizenship certificates under the new rules, and nearly half of them, about 1,955, went to applicants born in the United States. CBC and CTV News first reported the suspensions after recipients received the notices. A citizenship certificate is the document that proves your status, so a suspension does not by itself erase citizenship, but it removes the proof and signals that the file is under review. You can read what a certificate is on the IRCC [proof of citizenship](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/proof-citizenship.html) page.

## Who is affected by the citizenship certificate suspension?

Short answer: A specific group, not everyone with a certificate. The review targets people who received a proof of citizenship by descent under Bill C-3 between mid-December 2025 and the end of March 2026, and in particular those whose applications relied on secondary evidence of a Canadian parent or grandparent rather than original vital-statistics records. Many of those affected are U.S.-born children and grandchildren of Canadians. If you are a citizen because you were born in Canada, or you became a citizen through the regular grant process, or you received your certificate under the older descent rules, this review does not apply to you. The table below sums up who is and is not in scope.

| Situation | In this review? |
|---|---|
| Certificate by descent under Bill C-3, Dec 2025 to Mar 2026 | Yes, likely |
| Application used secondary proof of a Canadian parent or grandparent | Yes, the main target |
| Citizen by birth in Canada | No |
| Citizen by regular grant (naturalized) | No |
| Certificate issued under the older descent rules | No |

## Why is the government asking for the certificates back?

Short answer: IRCC says the proof was incomplete. The notices state that the certificate must be surrendered during an investigation because the application did not include proof of the Canadian family link from original sources, such as vital statistics, and did not explain why the original documents were not provided. In plain terms, the department is now questioning whether the evidence it accepted at approval was strong enough, and it wants to re-examine those files. Confirm your own status only through official channels, starting with the IRCC [check if you may be a citizen](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility/already-citizen.html) page.

## Can IRCC legally make you surrender the certificate?

Short answer: It is contested, and there is a real counter-argument. IRCC's own document checklist for proof of citizenship (form CIT 0014) lists "any other evidence" as an acceptable category of proof of a parent's Canadian citizenship. The Federal Court has repeatedly held that applicants are entitled to rely on the instructions the department publishes, most recently in Somers-Edgar v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2026 FC 417. If IRCC approved an application on the basis of alternative evidence that its own checklist allowed, a challenge to the later surrender demand may have merit. This is a legal question, and a certificate-surrender review that could reach the Federal Court is the kind of matter where a Canadian immigration lawyer, not only a consultant, should be involved.

## What should you do if you received a surrender notice?

Short answer: Take it seriously, but do not act without advice. A surrender notice carries a deadline, and missing it without a response puts your position at risk. Before you reply, preserve every document related to your application and every communication you have received from IRCC. Gather original vital-statistics records if you have not already done so. A licensed immigration representative can review the notice, assess the strength of your evidence, and help you draft a response that protects rather than weakens your position. Here is a practical order of steps:

1. Keep a complete copy of the notice and your full application, including everything you submitted and every IRCC communication.
2. Note any deadline in the notice and do not let it pass without a response.
3. Do not destroy your records, and get advice before handing over your only proof of status.
4. Gather original vital-statistics documents if you can, including long-form birth certificates for yourself and for your Canadian parent or grandparent, plus marriage records that connect the names.
5. Speak with a licensed immigration representative before you reply, so your response protects your position rather than weakening it.

## What is Bill C-3 and citizenship by descent?

Short answer: Bill C-3 restored Canadian citizenship to many "lost Canadians." For years, a "first-generation limit" meant a Canadian citizen born outside Canada could not automatically pass citizenship to a child also born outside Canada. Bill C-3 changed that, recognizing citizenship by descent for people who had been cut off by the limit. The law took effect in late 2025, and IRCC began issuing certificates under it in December 2025. The current suspension affects certificates issued in that first window, not the underlying right that Parliament restored. To see how citizenship is established and proven, start with the IRCC [Canadian citizenship](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship.html) hub.

## Common Questions About Canada's Lost Canadians Citizenship Certificate Suspension

These are the questions people most commonly ask after the June 2026 suspension. In short, the suspension affects only people who received a Bill C-3 descent certificate between December 2025 and March 2026 and whose applications relied on secondary evidence of a Canadian parent or grandparent. If you were born in Canada, or you became a citizen through the standard grant process, you are not in this group. A suspended certificate is not the same as revoked citizenship, but it removes your proof of status and triggers a formal review. If you received a notice, the practical steps are in the section above. The questions below address the most specific scenarios.

**Did the government reverse the citizenship certificate suspension?**

Yes, in part. Recipients who had been told to surrender their certificates received revalidation letters dated June 19, 2026 confirming their claims stand and that the certificate "shall not be cancelled," and Ottawa walked back the surrender demand the following week. IRCC is still reviewing about 4,100 Bill C-3 descent claims and has paused finalizing new descent certificates, so confirm your own status through official IRCC channels before you act.

**Does this affect my citizenship if I was born in Canada?**

No. Being born in Canada makes you a citizen regardless of this review, and your provincial or territorial birth certificate is your proof. The suspension is limited to certain proof-of-citizenship certificates issued by descent under Bill C-3.

**I got my certificate under Bill C-3. Is my citizenship cancelled?**

Not automatically. IRCC has suspended the certificate and opened a review, which is different from revoking citizenship. Your status is under question while the department re-examines the proof, so the priority is to respond properly and strengthen your evidence, ideally with advice.

**How do I prove Canadian citizenship by descent?**

The strongest proof is original vital-statistics records: a long-form birth certificate for you, a long-form birth certificate for your Canadian parent or grandparent, and the marriage or name records that link them. IRCC's checklist also recognizes other evidence, which is at the centre of the current dispute.

**Can I still apply for citizenship by descent right now?**

IRCC has paused issuing new certificates under the descent provisions during this review, so timelines are uncertain. Check the official IRCC pages for the current status before you apply, and confirm exactly which documents your file will need.

**I was born before 2009 to a Canadian parent. Am I affected?**

It depends on your facts. The current review focuses on Bill C-3 descent certificates issued from December 2025 onward. Earlier rules and dates can change your situation, so confirm your specific case rather than assuming.

## How can a licensed immigration consultant help you respond to a citizenship certificate surrender notice?

Short answer: The danger here is responding the wrong way to a government notice. Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto, regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). If you received a surrender notice, we help you read it correctly, gather the original vital-statistics documents that strengthen your file, and prepare a complete, well-documented response within the deadline. If your case looks headed for a Federal Court challenge, we will tell you plainly and help you involve an immigration lawyer. [Book a consultation](/book) before you reply to IRCC.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. Citizenship status and government investigations are serious legal matters. Confirm the current rules for your situation with a licensed immigration lawyer or RCIC, and on the official IRCC website, before you act.*

# Canada Immigration Changes in 2026: What's New for Newcomers

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-immigration-changes-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-15
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada has rewritten large parts of its immigration system for 2026.

*As of June 14, 2026.*

Canada has rewritten large parts of its immigration system for 2026. Permanent resident admissions are capped at 380,000 and held there through 2028, temporary residents are being cut back, and a run of rule changes has hit Express Entry, study permits, the super visa, the Start-Up Visa, and asylum law. This guide collects the changes that actually matter for applicants, with the date each took effect and the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) source for every one.

> Who this is for: anyone planning a Canadian application in 2026, or already in the queue, who needs the current rules in one place. Each section links to the official IRCC page so you can confirm the detail for your own case.

## What are the biggest Canadian immigration changes in 2026?

Short answer: The through-line is a smaller, more selective system. The 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan holds permanent residence at 380,000 a year and lowers temporary resident intake. Selection now favours people with in-demand skills, Canadian experience, and strong language scores. Around that core, IRCC has paused the Start-Up Visa, capped study permits, changed how the super visa income test works, limited settlement services, raised several fees, and brought in new asylum rules under Bill C-12. The table below is the quick version, and each change has its own section under it.

| Change | In effect | Who it affects |
|---|---|---|
| PR target held at 380,000 | 2026-2028 | All permanent residence applicants |
| Express Entry category draws and reform | Ongoing in 2026 | Express Entry candidates |
| Start-Up Visa closed to new applicants | January 1, 2026 | Immigrant entrepreneurs |
| Study permit cap and PAL rules | 2026 intake | International students |
| Super visa income test recalculated | March 31, 2026 | Parents and grandparents, their hosts |
| Co-op work permit no longer required | April 1, 2026 | International students in placements |
| Settlement-service time limits | Phasing in (Budget 2025) | Economic immigrants |
| Bill C-12 asylum measures | March 26, 2026 | Asylum claimants |
| Iran special measures extended | To March 31, 2027 | Eligible Iranian nationals in Canada |

## How many permanent residents will Canada admit in 2026?

Short answer: The target is 380,000 permanent residents for 2026, down from 395,000 in 2025, and IRCC plans to hold that same level through 2027 and 2028. The plan also reduces temporary residents, including international students and temporary workers, to bring the temporary share of Canada's population below 5% by the end of 2027. For applicants, fewer spots means more competition and a clearer tilt toward economic candidates who already live and work in Canada. You can read the targets in the [2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/corporate-initiatives/levels/supplementary-immigration-levels-2026-2028.html). One bright spot for people already here: IRCC plans to move up to 33,000 temporary workers to permanent residence across 2026 and 2027, which our [temporary-to-permanent pathway guide](/news/canada-tr-to-pr-pathway-33000-workers-2026) covers in detail.

## What changed for Express Entry in 2026?

Short answer: Selection moved toward targeted categories, and a bigger reform is in consultation. Through 2026, IRCC has leaned on category-based draws that invite candidates in priority groups rather than the whole pool, adding new categories in February 2026 for fields such as healthcare, trades, education, and French-language ability. In parallel, IRCC ran a public consultation on reshaping Express Entry and the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS), which proposes new weighting for wages and language and would fold the Federal Skilled Worker, Federal Skilled Trades, and Canadian Experience Class programs into one. Nothing in the reform is law yet, but the direction is set. Track live cut-offs on the IRCC [rounds of invitations](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/submit-profile/rounds-invitations.html) page and the [2026 Express Entry reform consultation](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry-reforms.html), and see our [Express Entry overview](/immigration/express-entry) for how the streams compare.

## Is the Start-Up Visa still open in 2026?

Short answer: It is closed to new applicants. IRCC stopped accepting new Start-Up Visa applications on January 1, 2026, and designated organizations stopped issuing commitment certificates after December 31, 2025. There is one exception with a hard deadline: founders who already hold a valid 2025 commitment certificate must submit their permanent residence application by June 30, 2026. IRCC has said it is building a new high-impact entrepreneur pilot to replace the program, with details still to come. The official [Start-up Visa Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/start-visa.html) page confirms the closure, and our [Start-Up Visa 2026 guide](/news/canada-start-up-visa-2026-paused-what-next) walks through what existing applicants and future founders should do.

## What are the 2026 study permit cap changes?

Short answer: The cap is tighter and the paperwork is mandatory. For 2026, IRCC expects to issue up to 408,000 study permits, including about 155,000 to newly arriving international students, as study-permit holders fall from over one million in early 2024 toward the government's targets. Most applicants now need a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) or Territorial Attestation Letter from the province or territory before they apply. Without a valid attestation letter, IRCC will not process most new study permit applications. The details by province are in the IRCC notice on [2026 allocations under the international student cap](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/2026-provincial-territorial-allocations-under-international-student-cap.html), and our [study permit cap guide](/news/canada-study-permit-cap-pal-2026) explains how to get a PAL.

## How did the super visa income requirement change?

Short answer: It got easier to meet. As of March 31, 2026, IRCC changed how it calculates family income for the super visa, the multiple-entry visa that lets parents and grandparents of Canadian citizens and permanent residents stay for long periods. A host can now combine their income with the income of the visiting parent or grandparent to reach the minimum, and IRCC can look at either of the two previous tax years rather than only the most recent one. The change is meant to make the program reachable for more families. Confirm the current income table on the IRCC notice, [changes to the super visa income requirement](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/changes-parents-grandparents-super-visa-income-requirement-calculated.html), and see our [super visa guide](/immigration/super-visa) for the full checklist.

## What other 2026 changes should newcomers know about?

Short answer: Several smaller updates carry real weight depending on your situation. As of April 1, 2026, eligible post-secondary international students no longer need a separate co-op work permit for required placements. IRCC is also phasing in time limits on federally funded settlement services for economic immigrants under Budget 2025. Intake to the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots has remained paused since December 19, 2025. Bill C-12 became law on March 26, 2026, tightening asylum eligibility. IRCC also extended special work permit measures for eligible Iranian nationals to March 31, 2027. Each update below includes its IRCC source.

- Co-op and internship work permits: as of April 1, 2026, eligible post-secondary international students no longer need a separate work permit for placements required by their program. One study permit now covers the placement. See the IRCC [co-op work permit notice](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/simplifying-co-op-work-permit-requirement-post-secondary-international-students.html).
- Settlement services: IRCC is introducing time limits on how long economic immigrants can use federally funded settlement services, a measure announced in Budget 2025. Details are in the [settlement-service eligibility notice](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/changes-settlement-service-eligibility-economic-immigrants.html).
- Home Care Worker pilots: IRCC paused new intake to the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots on December 19, 2025, and they did not reopen in March 2026, per the [home care pilots notice](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/pausing-home-care-worker-immigration-pilots-application-intake.html).
- Asylum law: Bill C-12 became law on March 26, 2026, adding eligibility limits such as a bar on claims made more than one year after entry and on certain claims by people who crossed between ports of entry. Read the IRCC backgrounder on the [Bill C-12 measures](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/2026/03/new-immigration-and-asylum-measures-from-bill-c-12-the-strengthening-canadas-immigration-system-and-borders-act-have-become-law.html), or our plain-language [Bill C-12 explainer](/news/bill-c12-canada-immigration-law-2026).

## Did Canada change immigration measures for Iranian nationals in 2026?

Short answer: Yes, and the support was extended. On March 4, 2026, IRCC extended its temporary special measures for Iranian nationals already in Canada. Eligible people who hold a work permit issued on or before February 28, 2025, can apply to extend it, and those measures now run until March 31, 2027, with standard processing fees. Iranians who want to extend a visitor stay or a study permit can apply through the regular IRCC processes. The full details are in the IRCC notice, [Canada extends special measures for Iranian nationals](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/canada-extends-certain-temporary-special-measures-iranian-nationals.html), and our [Iran special measures guide](/news/canada-iran-special-measures-2026-changes) breaks down who qualifies.

## What are the most common questions about Canada's 2026 immigration changes?

The questions below address the most common concerns applicants have about Canada's 2026 immigration system. Each answer draws directly from official IRCC notices and the 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan cited in this article. Immigration rules change often, so confirm current requirements on the official IRCC website or with a licensed representative before you apply.

**What are the new immigration changes for 2026?**

The headline changes are a permanent residence target held at 380,000, lower temporary resident intake, Express Entry category draws plus a proposed reform of the points system, the Start-Up Visa closing to new applicants, a tighter study permit cap with mandatory attestation letters, an easier super visa income test from March 31, 2026, and new asylum rules under Bill C-12. Several fees also rose in spring 2026.

**How many people will get PR in Canada in 2026?**

Canada plans to admit 380,000 new permanent residents in 2026, down from 395,000 in 2025, and intends to hold that level through 2028. The mix leans toward economic immigrants, especially those already working in Canada.

**Is TR to PR coming back in 2026?**

There is no general temporary-to-permanent program open to everyone in 2026. IRCC has committed to moving up to 33,000 temporary workers to permanent residence across 2026 and 2027 through existing economic streams and targeted measures, rather than a broad public pathway like the 2021 one.

**Which province is easiest to get PR in Canada in 2026?**

There is no single easiest province, because each Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) targets different occupations and has its own cut-offs, and 2026 allocations were reduced across the board. The province where you have a job offer, work experience, or family ties is usually your strongest route. A licensed consultant can match your profile to the provinces where you actually qualify.

Short answer: With this many moving parts, the risk is applying under a rule that has already changed. Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto, regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). We confirm which 2026 rules apply to your situation, find the pathway that still fits, and prepare a complete application so a stale assumption does not cost you. [Book a consultation](/book) and we will build a plan around the current rules.
