# Canada Immigration Medical Exam (IME): Panel Physician, Tests, and Validity

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-immigration-medical-exam-panel-physician-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-13
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Most permanent residence applicants need an Immigration Medical Exam (IME), and some temporary residents do too.

*As of June 13, 2026.*

> This guide is for people applying for permanent residence, a work permit, or a study permit who have been told they need a Canada Immigration Medical Exam, or who want to know if they do. You will learn who needs the exam, what an approved panel physician checks, the tests involved, how long results stay valid, what you pay, and when to do the exam upfront instead of waiting for a request. Every fact here is checked against canada.ca.

## Who needs an immigration medical exam for Canada?

Most permanent residence applicants need an Immigration Medical Exam (IME), and some temporary residents do too. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) uses the exam to check whether you are inadmissible to Canada on health grounds. If you apply for permanent residence (PR), you and your family members must complete an IME, even family members who will not come with you. Temporary residents such as visitors, students, and workers generally do not need one unless they will work in a job where public health must be protected, such as health care, child care, or primary and secondary school settings, or they have lived in or travelled to a designated country or territory for six months or more in a row in the year before coming to Canada. IRCC sets these rules on its [medical exams page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams.html).

| Your status | Do you need an IME? |
|---|---|
| Permanent residence applicant (and accompanying or non-accompanying family) | Yes, in almost all cases |
| Visitor, student, or worker staying six months or less | Usually no, unless the job protects public health |
| Visitor, student, or worker staying more than six months | Yes, if you lived in or visited a designated country for six months in the prior year, or will work in a public-health job |
| Parent and grandparent super visa applicant | Yes |
| Refugee claimant at a port of entry | Yes, within 30 days of being told |

## What is a panel physician, and can you use your own doctor?

A panel physician is a doctor that IRCC has approved to perform immigration medical exams, and no, you cannot use your own family doctor. Only a doctor on the official panel physician list can do the exam, because the results have to be recorded and submitted in a standard format that IRCC accepts. Your regular doctor, however well qualified, is not authorized to complete an IME. The panel physician also does not decide your application. They perform the exam and send the results to IRCC, which makes the final admissibility decision and contacts you in writing if there is a problem. You locate an approved doctor through the official [find a panel physician](https://secure.cic.gc.ca/PanelPhysicianMedecinDesigne/en/Home) tool, which lists approved clinics by country and city.

## What tests are included in the immigration medical exam?

The immigration medical exam includes a review of your medical history, a physical examination, and, depending on your age and other factors, a chest X-ray and laboratory tests. The panel physician completes a medical history questionnaire with you about any past or current conditions, then performs a physical exam that records measures such as your height, weight, and vision, and takes your photograph for the file. Depending on your age, you may be sent for chest X-rays and laboratory blood and urine tests, which are routine screening; the physician discusses any abnormal results with you. Screening commonly covers tuberculosis, and IRCC lists active tuberculosis and active syphilis among the infectious diseases it considers. You may be referred to a specialist for more testing if a result calls for it. The full sequence is on the [permanent residence medical examination page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-permanent-residents.html).

| Component | What happens |
|---|---|
| Medical history | The panel physician completes a questionnaire about past and current conditions |
| Physical examination | Height, weight, vision, and a general physical check; your photo is taken |
| Chest X-ray | Required depending on age, mainly to screen for tuberculosis |
| Laboratory tests | Blood and urine tests, depending on age and history |
| Specialist referral | Only if your results need further review |

## How long is an immigration medical exam valid?

An immigration medical exam is valid for 12 months only. If you do not become a permanent resident or arrive in Canada within that window, the results expire and you may need a new exam. For students and workers, the letter of introduction shows the date your results expire if you received it after November 30, 2021. There is also a separate route for people already in Canada: under a temporary public policy in effect until October 5, 2029, you may not need a new exam if you completed one in the last five years, you applied for permanent or temporary residence, you already live in Canada, and your previous exam showed low or no risk to public health or safety. IRCC explains validity on the [medical exams for visitors, students and workers page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-temporary-residents.html).

## When does IRCC ask for your medical exam, and what is an upfront exam?

IRCC either tells you to do the exam after you apply, or you choose to do it before you apply, which is called an upfront medical exam. Many applicants do the exam upfront to speed up processing. As of August 21, 2025, Express Entry permanent residence applicants must do an upfront medical exam first and contact a panel physician directly. For most other permanent residence applications, including spouse, partner, and child sponsorships, you wait for IRCC instructions after you submit a complete application, then complete the exam within 30 days. Temporary residents applying to visit, work, or study can also choose an upfront exam. If IRCC requests the exam and you do not follow the instructions, it may refuse your application. You can confirm [whether you need a medical exam](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-temporary-residents/country-requirements.html) for a temporary stay before you book.

| Approach | Who it fits | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront medical exam | Express Entry applicants (required); visitors, students, workers, and others who want faster processing | Done before or right after applying; contact a panel physician directly |
| Exam requested by IRCC | Most non-Express Entry permanent residence applicants, including family sponsorships | Wait for instructions, then complete within 30 days |

## How much does the immigration medical exam cost?

IRCC does not set the medical exam fee, so the cost varies by clinic and by the tests you need. You pay the panel physician directly at the time of your exam. Your payment covers the doctor or radiologist fee, any special tests or investigations, and any specialists you are referred to. If the panel physician offers vaccines and you choose to receive them, you may pay for those too, depending on the clinic and local practice. Because IRCC does not fix the price, ask the clinic for its current fees when you book your appointment. Note that if IRCC refuses your application after the exam, those fees are not refunded. The medical exam cost is separate from any application or biometrics fees you pay to IRCC.

## What happens after the panel physician sends your results?

After the exam, the panel physician sends your results directly to IRCC, often through an electronic system called eMedical, so you do not get a pass or fail on the spot. The physician gives you a document confirming you had the exam, and you should keep a copy as proof. IRCC then reviews the results and makes the admissibility decision. If officers believe you may be inadmissible on health grounds, they send a procedural fairness letter explaining why, and you can respond with more information before any final decision, as set out in the [medical inadmissibility rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/inadmissibility/reasons/medical-inadmissibility.html). If your exam shows inactive tuberculosis, you may be placed under medical surveillance after you arrive in Canada to ensure you get proper treatment. You are allowed professional advice or representation when you respond, though it is not required.

## How do you find an IRCC-approved panel physician?

You find an approved doctor using the official panel physician list, then book directly with a clinic near you. The list lets you search by country and city, and it shows only doctors IRCC has authorized to perform immigration medical exams. Call the clinic before your appointment to confirm fees, whether it uses eMedical, and what to bring. Bring valid identification, ideally your passport, plus the IRCC medical report form (IMM 1017E or IMM 1020E) if you are not doing an upfront exam, any current medication list and prior medical reports, your glasses or contact lenses, and proof of vaccinations if you have it. If the clinic does not use eMedical, bring four recent photographs. Use the [find a panel physician](https://secure.cic.gc.ca/PanelPhysicianMedecinDesigne/en/Home) tool to start your search.

## How can a licensed RCIC help with your medical exam?

A licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) can confirm whether you need an exam, when to do it, and how it fits the rest of your application, so a timing mistake does not stall your file. In Canada, only an RCIC, a Canadian immigration lawyer, or a Quebec notary can give immigration advice or represent you for a fee. Go Far Global is a Toronto RCIC firm (#R515110), regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). We help you decide between an upfront exam and waiting for an IRCC request, keep your medical results valid against your processing timeline, and prepare a response if a procedural fairness letter ever arrives. Book a consultation at [gofarglobal.com/book](https://www.gofarglobal.com/book).

## What else do applicants ask about the immigration medical exam?

These are the questions newcomers search for most about the Canada immigration medical exam, with short answers drawn from current IRCC guidance. For your own case, confirm the details against the linked canada.ca pages, because requirements can change and depend on your status, age, and where you have lived.

### What are the medical tests for Canada immigration?
The exam covers a medical history questionnaire, a physical examination, and, depending on your age, a chest X-ray and laboratory blood and urine tests. The chest X-ray mainly screens for tuberculosis. You may be referred to a specialist if a result needs more review.

### What can make you fail a medical test in Canada?
You can be found medically inadmissible for three reasons: your condition is a danger to public health, a danger to public safety, or would place an excessive demand on health or social services. The 2026 excessive demand cost threshold is $144,390 over five years. Excessive demand does not apply to refugees and their dependants, protected persons, or certain family-sponsored spouses, partners, and children.

### At what stage does IRCC ask for a medical exam?
It depends on your application. Express Entry permanent residence applicants must do an upfront exam before applying, as of August 21, 2025. Most other applicants wait for IRCC instructions after submitting a complete application, then complete the exam within 30 days.

### How long is an IRCC medical valid?
An immigration medical exam is valid for 12 months. If you do not arrive in Canada or finalize your permanent residence within that period, the results expire and you may need to repeat the exam.

### Can I use my own doctor for the immigration medical exam?
No. Only an IRCC-approved panel physician can perform the exam. Your own family doctor cannot do it, even if they are fully qualified. Use the official panel physician list to find an approved clinic.

## Sources
- [Medical exams, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams.html)
- [Medical examination for permanent residence applicants](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-permanent-residents.html)
- [Medical exams for visitors, students and workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-temporary-residents.html)
- [Find out if you need a medical exam for a temporary resident application](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-temporary-residents/country-requirements.html)
- [Medical inadmissibility](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/inadmissibility/reasons/medical-inadmissibility.html)

# Canadian Citizenship Ceremony and Oath: What to Expect in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canadian-citizenship-ceremony-oath-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-13
Author: Go Far Global Team

> For most applicants, the citizenship ceremony is the last step before becoming a Canadian citizen.

*As of June 13, 2026.*

> You passed the citizenship test and your application is approved. The last thing standing between you and Canadian citizenship is the ceremony. This guide is for permanent residents who are waiting for, or attending, their citizenship ceremony. It covers what happens on the day, how online and in-person ceremonies differ, the current Oath of Citizenship wording, what to bring, and what to do once you are a citizen.

## What happens at a Canadian citizenship ceremony?

For most applicants, the citizenship ceremony is the last step before becoming a Canadian citizen. At the ceremony you take the Oath of Citizenship in front of a citizenship official or judge, and then you receive your citizenship certificate, the document that proves you are a citizen. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) runs ceremonies in two formats, online by video conference and in person, and your invitation tells you which one you are attending. Both formats include registration, speeches, the oath taking, congratulations, and the singing of the national anthem. From the moment you take the oath, you are a Canadian citizen. You can read IRCC's [citizenship ceremony overview](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony.html) for the full outline.

## Is the citizenship ceremony held online or in person?

IRCC holds most citizenship ceremonies online over a video conference platform, and it holds some in person. You do not choose the format yourself at first. IRCC decides and puts the format, along with the date, time, and either a video link or a location, in your invitation. If you are invited to a virtual ceremony but would rather attend in person, or the reverse, you can ask to change the format. You can request a format change only once, and you will be given a new date because you cannot keep the original one. The two formats differ on a few practical points, set out in the [ceremony formats](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/format.html) guidance.

| Detail | Online (virtual) ceremony | In-person ceremony |
|---|---|---|
| How you join | Video link in your invitation | Travel to the location in your invitation |
| Permanent resident (PR) card | You cut it up with scissors at the start | An official collects it at registration |
| Identity check | Done privately on video at registration | Done at the registration table |
| Posture for the oath | You stay seated, including for the oath and O Canada | You stand for the oath and O Canada if you can |
| Citizenship certificate | E-certificate, or paper mailed in 2 to 4 weeks | Paper certificate handed to you, or e-certificate |
| Guests | May watch in the same room, not on a separate device | Allowed if space permits, so check your invitation |

## When will I get my citizenship ceremony invitation?

IRCC invites you to the ceremony after it approves your application, which for most adults happens once you pass the citizenship test. The wait depends on current processing times and your situation, and it can run from a few weeks to a few months. IRCC sends the invitation at least one week before the ceremony date, usually by email and sometimes by phone or mail. Add addresses ending in cic.gc.ca to your safe-sender list and check your spam folder so you do not miss it. Your invitation states the time, date, format, language, and the video link or location.

If you cannot attend on the day, contact IRCC to reschedule rather than skipping the ceremony. If you miss a first ceremony without explanation, IRCC automatically reschedules you and sends a final invitation. You can follow the scheduling status in your citizenship tracker account. The full timing rules are on the [when to go to the ceremony](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/when.html) page.

## What should I bring to my citizenship ceremony?

Bring your ceremony invitation, your permanent resident card even if it has expired, and acceptable identification. Adults need two pieces of identification, and at least one must show both your photo and your signature. If you no longer have your PR card, bring your Confirmation of Permanent Residence instead. For a virtual ceremony, also have your seat number from the first page of the invitation and a pair of scissors, because you cut up your PR card at the start. For an in-person ceremony, bring the signed permission release and consent form if one came with your invitation.

A few extra points to remember:

1. The PR card is surrendered at the ceremony because you no longer need it once you are a citizen.
2. If you became a permanent resident before June 28, 2002, bring your Record of Landing if you still have it.
3. The full checklist is on the [what to bring to the ceremony](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/bring.html) page.

## What is the Oath of Citizenship in Canada?

The Oath of Citizenship is the promise you make to become a Canadian citizen, and taking it is the moment citizenship takes effect. You can swear it or affirm it, in English or in French, and at the ceremony you repeat it after the presiding official. Canada updated the wording in 2021 to add an explicit line recognizing the rights of Indigenous peoples. Many people take the oath together at the same ceremony. The current wording, confirmed on IRCC's [what to expect at the ceremony](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html) page, reads:

> I swear (or affirm) that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to His Majesty King Charles the Third, King of Canada, His Heirs and Successors, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada, including the Constitution, which recognizes and affirms the Aboriginal and treaty rights of First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples, and fulfill my duties as a Canadian citizen.

You can swear the oath if you want to refer to a religious belief, and you may bring your holy book to the ceremony. You can affirm it if you do not want to refer to a religious belief. After the oath, everyone sings the national anthem, O Canada, and you can sing it in English, in French, or bilingually. Who actually has to recite the oath depends on age.

| Age when taking the oath | Must take the oath? |
|---|---|
| Adult, 18 and older | Yes |
| Minor, 14 to 17 | Yes |
| Child under 14 | No, but welcome to attend with the parent who applied |

## What happens after a citizenship ceremony in Canada?

After the ceremony you are a Canadian citizen, and you receive your citizenship certificate, which proves your citizenship and shows the date you became a citizen. You can choose a paper certificate or an electronic certificate (e-certificate). With your certificate in hand, you can apply for a Canadian passport and register to vote. You cannot apply for a passport until you have the certificate, and an e-certificate has to be printed first. Keep the certificate safe and do not laminate it, because lamination can damage it and make the barcode unreadable for passport and other government services.

Plan your travel around this timing. Your PR card is destroyed or collected at the ceremony, and the citizenship certificate is not a travel document, so wait for your Canadian passport before you leave the country. IRCC's [after the citizenship ceremony](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/after.html) page lists every next step, including registering to vote.

## How long does a citizenship ceremony take in Canada?

Both virtual and in-person citizenship ceremonies generally last a few hours, so plan to set the time aside. Your invitation gives the arrival time and the expected duration, and you should check it before the day. That window covers registration, the ceremony itself with speeches, the oath taking, congratulations and the national anthem, plus any video presentations and post-ceremony instructions. At a large virtual ceremony with more than 100 candidates, you may wait up to 30 minutes at the start before officials greet you and let you into the ceremony room.

## What is the dress code for a citizenship ceremony?

There is no uniform. IRCC asks you to wear business attire that suits the occasion and to behave respectfully. You can also wear traditional, religious or ceremonial clothing, head coverings, and the colours red and white. A medical mask or a face covering is allowed, though officials will ask you to remove a face covering briefly during registration to confirm your identity, and they can do this in a private room if you prefer. At an in-person ceremony, do not wear scented products such as perfume or cologne, because they can affect other people.

## Can guests attend an oath ceremony?

Yes. Family and friends can join you. At a virtual ceremony, guests may sit in the same physical room with you to watch, but they must not be disruptive and must not join on a separate device. At an in-person ceremony, whether you can bring guests, and how many, depends on the size of the ceremony and the room setup, so check your invitation for the number. Members of the public and elected officials can also attend most in-person ceremonies to support new citizens.

## Can I take the oath of citizenship online?

Yes. IRCC holds many citizenship ceremonies online by video conference, and you take the oath during that virtual ceremony. You join with the link in your invitation, confirm your identity privately, take the oath, and then sign and return the Oath or Affirmation of Citizenship form. You must sign that form on the day you take the oath, not the day before or after. If you would rather attend in person, you can ask to switch formats once, and IRCC will assign you a new date.

- [Citizenship ceremony: ceremony formats](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/format.html) (IRCC, updated June 4, 2026)
- [Citizenship ceremony: when to go to the ceremony](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/when.html) (IRCC, updated June 12, 2026)
- [Citizenship ceremony: what to bring to the ceremony](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/bring.html) (IRCC)
- [Citizenship ceremony: what to expect and the Oath of Citizenship](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html) (IRCC, updated June 4, 2026)

# How to Apply for OHIP in Ontario 2026: Documents and Wait

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/apply-ohip-ontario-health-card-newcomer-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-12
Author: Go Far Global Team

> You apply for OHIP in person at a ServiceOntario centre. There is no online or mail application for a first health card.

# How to Apply for OHIP in Ontario 2026: Documents and Wait

*As of September 3, 2026.*

Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP) coverage has no waiting period. If you qualify, you are covered from the day ServiceOntario approves the application. You must apply in person. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) does not issue OHIP. The provincial rules below come from Ontario's apply and documents pages.

## TL;DR

No OHIP waiting period: eligible people are covered once ServiceOntario approves the file | Apply in person at a ServiceOntario centre, not online | Bring a completed Registration for Ontario Health Insurance Coverage form plus 3 identification documents | Presence test: 153 days in any 12-month period, and 153 of the first 183 days after you begin living in Ontario | Many full-time work permit holders who work in Ontario for at least 6 months qualify; visitors do not

## How do I apply for an OHIP health card in Ontario?

**Short answer:** You apply in person at a [ServiceOntario centre](https://www.ontario.ca/page/apply-ohip-and-get-health-card). There is no first-card application by mail or through a website. Bring a completed Registration for Ontario Health Insurance Coverage form and three separate identification documents. Staff take your photo and signature. If they approve you, coverage starts that day and the plastic card arrives later by mail. Federal settlement pages still tell newcomers to [learn about health care in Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/settle-canada/health-care.html) and then follow the provincial process. Ontario runs OHIP. IRCC does not.

Book a ServiceOntario appointment if your city offers one, or walk in. Bring originals. Photocopies of status and identity documents are not accepted.

## How do you qualify for OHIP in Ontario?

**Short answer:** You must meet the presence rules and at least one status rule on Ontario's apply page. Presence: be physically in Ontario for 153 days in any 12-month period, be physically in Ontario for at least 153 of the first 183 days after you began living in the province, and make Ontario your primary residence. Status examples: Canadian citizen, registered Indigenous person, permanent resident, an IRCC-confirmed permanent residence applicant who has not been refused, a valid work permit holder working full time in Ontario for an Ontario employer for at least 6 months, Live-in Caregiver or Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program permit holders, convention refugees and other protected persons, and some Temporary Resident Permit case types (Ontario lists examples 86 through 95). Visitors from other provinces or from outside Canada do not qualify.

You do not have to finish 153 days before you apply. Ontario says there is no waiting period and you can apply as soon as you arrive if you are eligible. Children need their own IRCC immigration document. Children under 16 do not need separate proof of residency or identity.

| Status | OHIP-eligible on Ontario's list? | Extra condition |
|---|---|---|
| Permanent resident | Yes | Meet presence rules; bring PR proof |
| Approved PR applicant | Yes | IRCC confirmed eligibility to apply and you were not refused |
| Work permit, full time, 6+ months with an Ontario employer | Yes | Spouse and dependants may also qualify |
| Study permit only | Not listed | Use private or school coverage unless you also meet another status |
| Visitor | No | Ontario says visitors do not qualify |

## What documents are needed to apply for OHIP?

**Short answer:** Ontario requires three separate documents: one original that proves Canadian citizenship or OHIP-eligible immigration status, one original or printed or digital document that proves you live in Ontario, and one original that proves your identity with your name and signature. Photocopies are not accepted for the status and identity documents. The [documents needed to get a health card](https://www.ontario.ca/page/documents-needed-get-health-card) page lists examples. Status can be a PR card, Confirmation of Permanent Residence, an eligible IRCC letter, or a valid work permit. Residency can be a lease, utility bill, bank statement, or Ontario driver's licence. Identity can be a passport or another signed photo ID. You cannot use the same paper for two categories.

Download the Registration for Ontario Health Insurance Coverage form from Ontario's [Central Forms Repository](https://forms.mgcs.gov.on.ca/en/dataset/014-0265-82) (form 014-0265) before you go, or fill it at the counter.

## Can I apply to OHIP online?

**Short answer:** No. Ontario's apply page says you must apply in person at a ServiceOntario centre. The infant registration form used in hospital is also not an online first-card path for newcomers. Related searches for "apply for OHIP online" are about driver's licence or health-card renewal for people who already have a card, or about booking a ServiceOntario appointment. A first health card for a newcomer is a counter visit with original documents. IRCC's [Settling in Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/settle-canada.html) hub will not submit the OHIP form for you.

If a website offers to "register OHIP online" for a fee, it is not ServiceOntario.

## Can I get OHIP immediately?

**Short answer:** If you are eligible, Ontario says there is no longer a waiting period and you have immediate health insurance coverage once the application is approved. That replaced the old three-month wait. Immediate means from approval, not from the day your flight landed and not from the day the plastic card arrives in the mail. Keep private travel or newcomer insurance active until ServiceOntario confirms the file. The 153-day presence test is a residency rule you must meet over time. It is not a queue you sit in before you may apply.

Bring every original. An incomplete counter visit delays approval, which delays the start date of coverage.

## Do work permit holders qualify for OHIP?

**Short answer:** Many do, if the work conditions on Ontario's apply page are met. You must be in Ontario on a valid work permit and working full time in Ontario, for an Ontario employer, for at least 6 months. If you meet that test, your spouse and dependants may also qualify. If the permit expired but you hold maintained status, Ontario says you may be eligible and tells you to contact ServiceOntario. Live-in Caregiver and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program permit holders are listed separately. A [work permit](/immigration/work-permit) from IRCC is the immigration document. OHIP is the provincial health plan. One does not replace the other.

Study-permit-only students are not on Ontario's qualifying-status list. Use the school plan unless you also hold a qualifying work status. We are Go Far Global, a licensed Canadian immigration firm. If your permit type is unusual, [book a consultation](/book) before you stand in the ServiceOntario line with the wrong papers.

# Intra-Company Transfer (ICT) Work Permit Canada 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/intra-company-transfer-work-permit-canada-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-12
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Intra-Company Transfer is a work permit that lets a multinational company move an existing employee from a foreign office to its Canadian parent, branch, subsidiary, or...

*As of June 12, 2026.*

> This guide is written for executives, senior managers, and specialized-knowledge employees of multinational companies that are expanding to or already operating in Canada, and for the Canadian employers who want to bring them over. It explains how the Intra-Company Transfer (ICT) work permit lets a qualifying company move an existing employee to a Canadian office without a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA), what the rules expect of you, and how the permit can later support permanent residence.

## What is the Intra-Company Transfer (ICT) work permit?

The Intra-Company Transfer is a work permit that lets a multinational company move an existing employee from a foreign office to its Canadian parent, branch, subsidiary, or affiliate without an LMIA. It sits inside Canada's International Mobility Program (IMP), the group of work permit streams that skip the labour market test because the transfer is treated as a significant benefit to Canada. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) issues the permit, and it is employer-specific, meaning it is tied to the company and the role named in the application.

IRCC records the route under the [LMIA exemption codes for the International Mobility Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/exemption-codes.html), where an intra-company transfer falls under exemption code C12. A separate route under the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) covers [business people who work in Canada under a free trade agreement](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/business-people.html) and includes its own intra-company transferee category for citizens of the United States and Mexico. The general ICT route described here is open to any nationality, as long as the company relationship qualifies.

## Who qualifies for an intra-company transfer to Canada?

The ICT covers three employee categories, and the worker must already belong to one of them at the foreign company. Executives direct the management of the organization or a major component of it. Senior managers run the organization, a department, or a function and supervise professional staff. Specialized knowledge workers hold advanced or proprietary knowledge of the company's products, services, research, systems, or procedures. On top of the category test, the employee must currently work for the foreign company and have worked there continuously, full time, in a similar executive, managerial, or specialized-knowledge role for at least one year within the three years before the application.

| Category | What the role involves | Maximum time in Canada |
|---|---|---|
| Executive | Directs the organization or a major component, sets goals and policies, and works with broad decision-making authority | Up to 7 years |
| Senior manager | Manages the organization, a department, or a function, supervises professional staff, and has authority over staffing decisions | Up to 7 years |
| Specialized knowledge worker | Holds advanced or proprietary knowledge of the company's products, services, or procedures that is uncommon and hard to transfer | Up to 5 years |

The Canadian role must match the category claimed. A senior manager abroad cannot transfer into a junior role in Canada and still qualify, because the position on each side of the move has to line up with the executive, managerial, or specialized-knowledge definition.

## What company relationship does the ICT require?

The transfer only works if there is a qualifying corporate relationship between the foreign company and the Canadian entity. That means the Canadian business must be a parent, branch, subsidiary, or affiliate of the foreign employer, and both must keep doing business for the whole period the worker is in Canada. A shared brand name or a loose commercial partnership is not enough. IRCC looks for real common ownership or control linking the two companies, supported by incorporation papers, ownership charts, and financial records.

A brand-new Canadian office faces an extra test. Because there is no operating history to point to, the company has to show a secured physical location for the business, a realistic business plan, and the financial capacity to start and staff Canadian operations. IRCC wants evidence that the office will actually trade and employ people, not exist only on paper to support a single permit. For a new office, expect to provide a signed lease, projected staffing, and proof of funds alongside the corporate documents.

| Requirement | What it means | Who proves it |
|---|---|---|
| One year of qualifying employment | Employed full time and continuously by the foreign company in an executive, managerial, or specialized-knowledge role for at least one year in the past three years | Worker |
| Matching Canadian role | The Canadian position is executive, managerial, or specialized knowledge, in line with the category claimed | Worker and employer |
| Qualifying corporate relationship | The Canadian entity is a parent, branch, subsidiary, or affiliate of the foreign employer, with proof of common ownership or control | Employer |
| New office viability (if applicable) | A secured physical location, a realistic business plan, and the financial capacity to start and staff operations | Employer |
| Offer and compliance step | The employer submits the offer of employment through the IRCC Employer Portal and pays the employer compliance fee | Employer |
| Biometrics and medical (if applicable) | Provided depending on nationality and length of stay | Worker |

## How long is an ICT work permit valid?

An established company usually receives a permit of one to three years, while a new Canadian office is generally given an initial one year so IRCC can confirm the operation is real before extending it. The permit can be renewed, but there is a ceiling on total time. Executives and senior managers can stay for up to seven years, and specialized knowledge workers for up to five years. Once a worker reaches that maximum, they must spend at least one full year working outside Canada before they can apply again, a rule often called the cooling-off period.

| Situation | Initial permit length | Maximum total stay |
|---|---|---|
| Established Canadian company | 1 to 3 years | Executives and senior managers up to 7 years; specialized knowledge up to 5 years |
| New Canadian office | Generally 1 year to start | Same maximums once the office is trading and staffed |

Because the clock keeps running across renewals, plan the move with the ceiling in mind. If the goal is to stay in Canada for good, the permit years are best treated as a window to build the work experience that supports a permanent residence application, which the [live IRCC processing times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) and your own timeline should inform.

## How does the intra-company transfer process work?

The process runs in two stages, employer first and then worker. The Canadian employer starts by submitting an offer of employment through the IRCC Employer Portal and paying the employer compliance fee, which registers the job and the qualifying relationship before any work permit is filed. The worker then applies for an employer-specific work permit that points back to that offer. Depending on nationality and where the application is made, the worker may also give biometrics or complete a medical exam before the permit is issued.

1. The employer confirms the corporate relationship and, for a new office, prepares the business plan, lease, and proof of funds.
2. The employer submits the offer of employment through the IRCC Employer Portal and pays the employer compliance fee.
3. The worker applies for an employer-specific work permit, online or, for some visa-exempt travellers, at a port of entry.
4. The worker gives [biometrics](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics.html) and completes any required medical exam.
5. IRCC assesses the role against the executive, managerial, or specialized-knowledge definition and issues the permit if the evidence holds up.

## What changed for specialized knowledge in October 2024?

On October 3, 2024, IRCC issued a Program Delivery Update that tightened how officers assess specialized knowledge. The bar is now read more strictly. The worker must show knowledge that is genuinely advanced or proprietary, uncommon both inside and outside the company, and hard to find in the Canadian labour market, not simply skill picked up over a few years on the job. Pay level, the business reason for the transfer, and proof that the knowledge is truly company-specific all carry more weight than before.

Executives and senior managers were not the focus of that change, but specialized-knowledge applications now need stronger, better-documented evidence to succeed. The category still sits within the [International Mobility Program exemption codes](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/exemption-codes.html), but the standard of proof expected for it has risen. If you are transferring on specialized knowledge, build the file around what only your company knows and why a Canadian hire could not replace it.

## Can an intra-company transfer lead to PR in Canada?

Yes, but only indirectly, because the ICT itself is a temporary permit and not a permanent residence (PR) route. The value of the permit for someone who wants to settle is the skilled Canadian work experience it builds. After enough qualifying experience in Canada, that record can support a PR application through Express Entry under the [Canadian Experience Class (CEC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/canadian-experience-class.html), or through a [Provincial Nominee Program (PNP)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html) stream that targets your occupation or region.

PR is always a separate application with its own criteria, and a work permit never converts into permanent residence on its own. Treat the transfer as the first step rather than the finish line. Executives and managers often have strong profiles for Express Entry because of their seniority, while specialized knowledge workers may fit specific provincial streams. The cleaner your Canadian work history and the earlier you map the PR route, the better positioned you are when the permit years start counting down toward the cooling-off ceiling.

## What else do people ask about the ICT work permit?

These are common questions pulled from real searches about intra-company transfers. The answers reflect the rules in force as of June 12, 2026, and flag where IRCC does not publish a fixed figure so you do not plan around a number that does not exist.

### What is the processing time for an intra-company transfer to Canada?

IRCC does not publish one fixed processing time for an intra-company transfer. The wait depends on where the application is made, whether the worker is visa-exempt and can apply at a port of entry, the worker's nationality, and whether biometrics or a medical exam are needed. Check the current estimate on the [official IRCC processing times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) for your country and application type rather than relying on a figure quoted second-hand.

### How does an intra-company transfer work?

A multinational company moves an employee it already employs from a foreign office to a related Canadian office, without an LMIA, under the International Mobility Program. The employee has to fall into the executive, senior manager, or specialized knowledge category and have at least one year of qualifying full-time work with the company in the past three years. The Canadian entity must be a parent, branch, subsidiary, or affiliate of the foreign employer.

### Can an intra-company transfer lead to PR in Canada?

It can, through a separate application. The permit does not grant permanent residence, but the skilled Canadian work experience it produces can later support Express Entry under the Canadian Experience Class or a Provincial Nominee Program stream. You apply for PR on its own once you meet that program's requirements.

### What is the ICT refusal rate in Canada?

IRCC does not publish a single official refusal rate for intra-company transfers, so be wary of any specific percentage you see quoted. From what officers look for, refusals most often come from a weak or unproven qualifying relationship between the two companies, thin evidence on specialized knowledge after the 2024 tightening, or incomplete corporate and financial documents, especially for a new Canadian office. A well-built file that proves the relationship and the role is the best protection.

# TN Visa Canada: The CUSMA Professional Work Permit Explained

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/tn-visa-canada-cusma-professional-work-permit-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-12
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Short answer: Not under that name. "TN visa" almost always means a United States status that lets Canadian and Mexican citizens work in the US.

*As of June 12, 2026.*

> This guide is written for two readers. If you are a United States or Mexican citizen with a job offer in Canada, the permit you want is the CUSMA professional work permit, and that is the focus below. If you are a Canadian citizen wondering about working in the United States, the classic "TN visa" is a separate US process, and we describe it factually so you know which authority to approach.

## Is there a TN visa for Canada?

Short answer: Not under that name. "TN visa" almost always means a United States status that lets Canadian and Mexican citizens work in the US. The Canadian equivalent, for United States and Mexican citizens who want to work here, is a work permit issued under the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), the trade deal that replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). The two move in opposite directions, so the first thing to settle is which way you are going.

If you are heading to Canada, read the next four sections. If you are a Canadian looking south, skip ahead to the US section. We keep them apart on purpose, because the rules, the forms, and the deciding authority are different on each side of the border. The letters "TN" come from "Trade NAFTA," and the category survived the move from NAFTA to CUSMA.

## What is the CUSMA professional work permit?

Short answer: It is an employer-specific work permit that lets an eligible United States or Mexican citizen work in Canada in a qualifying profession without a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA). It sits in the "professionals" category of Canada's International Mobility Program, and it is processed by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). Because the trade agreement already accounts for the labour market effect, the employer is spared the LMIA step that most other work permits demand. The official rules are on the IRCC [Work in Canada under a free trade agreement](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/business-people.html) page.

The permit is temporary and tied to the specific employer and role named in your offer. It does not grant permanent residence and it is not a visa to settle. It is a way for a named company to bring a named professional into a named job, faster than the standard route, because the LMIA is waived.

## Who is eligible for the CUSMA professional work permit?

Short answer: Four things have to line up. You must be a citizen of the United States or Mexico, your occupation must appear on the CUSMA professionals list, you must hold a prearranged job offer from a Canadian employer in that same profession, and you must have the degree or professional credentials the occupation requires. Permanent residents of the US or Mexico do not qualify on residence alone; this route is built on citizenship.

The core requirements:

- **Citizenship** of the United States or Mexico, not permanent residence.
- **A listed profession.** Your occupation must be one of the professions named in the agreement.
- **A prearranged Canadian job** with an employer, in that profession, at the level the role calls for.
- **The right credentials.** The degree, licence, or experience the profession requires.

If your occupation is not on the list, this permit is closed to you, and another work permit category may fit instead.

## How does a US or Mexican citizen apply to work in Canada under CUSMA?

Short answer: The process has two halves, employer first. Your Canadian employer submits an offer of employment through the Employer Portal and pays the employer compliance fee, which produces an offer number. You then apply for the employer-specific work permit using that number, either online before you travel or, depending on your situation, on arrival. IRCC sets out the employer's duties on the [Hire through the International Mobility Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/hire-temporary-foreign/international-mobility-program.html) page.

A few practical points follow from being employer-specific. You can work only for the employer on the permit, in the role it names. If you change employers, you generally need a new permit. Bring proof of citizenship, your job offer, and your credentials, and be ready to show how your occupation matches the listed profession.

## How is the US TN visa different from the Canadian CUSMA work permit?

Short answer: They face opposite directions and answer to different governments. The TN visa carries Canadian or Mexican citizens into the United States and is decided by US authorities. The CUSMA professional work permit carries United States or Mexican citizens into Canada and is decided by IRCC. The same trade agreement underpins both; the United States calls it USMCA, Canada calls it CUSMA, and Mexico calls it T-MEC. The table sets the two side by side.

| Feature | TN visa (to the United States) | CUSMA professional work permit (to Canada) |
|---|---|---|
| Who it is for | Canadian and Mexican citizens | United States and Mexican citizens |
| Where you work | United States | Canada |
| Deciding authority | US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and USCIS | Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) |
| Labour market test | Not required | No LMIA required |
| Employer link | Tied to a named employer and role | Employer-specific |
| Profession list | USMCA professionals list (US side) | CUSMA professionals list (Canada side) |
| Status type | Non-immigrant, no dual intent | Temporary resident on a work permit |
| Staying permanently | Separate US process | Separate Canadian PR application |

The practical takeaway: a US citizen reads the Canada column, and a Canadian citizen reads the United States column. Mexican citizens can appear in either, depending on the direction of the move.

## What does the US TN visa involve for Canadian citizens?

Short answer: It lets a Canadian citizen work in the United States in a listed profession, and it is a US process from start to finish. You apply on the strength of a US job offer in a qualifying occupation, and Canadian citizens usually request TN status at a United States port of entry rather than getting a visa sticker in the passport. The decision is made by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), with policy set alongside US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). Canadian permanent residents are not eligible; the route is for citizens.

Two limits matter. TN is a non-immigrant status, which means it does not carry "dual intent," so it is not designed as a step toward a US green card. And it is profession-bound and employer-specific on the US side as well. Because this is United States immigration, a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant cannot act for you on it. Start with the official USCIS [TN USMCA professionals](https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/tn-usmca-professionals) page and a US immigration attorney.

## Can the CUSMA work permit lead to permanent residence in Canada?

Short answer: Indirectly, yes. The permit itself is temporary, but the skilled Canadian work experience you gain on it can count toward permanent residence later. Time worked in Canada can support an Express Entry profile through the [Canadian Experience Class (CEC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/canadian-experience-class.html), or a nomination under a [Provincial Nominee Program (PNP)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html). Permanent residence is always a separate application with its own criteria; the work permit does not convert into it automatically.

If permanent residence is the goal, treat the CUSMA permit as the first move, not the finish. Keep records of your hours and duties, confirm your occupation's skill level early, and look at the [Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html) streams while you work. The right sequence can turn a temporary professional posting into a durable Canadian future.

## Frequently asked questions

These are the questions we hear most from United States and Mexican professionals looking at Canada, and from Canadians asking about the United States route. Each answer keeps the two directions apart, so you can act on the one that actually applies to your citizenship and your destination.

**Who is eligible for a Canadian TN visa?**

There is no permit literally called a "Canadian TN visa." The Canadian equivalent is the CUSMA professional work permit, open to United States and Mexican citizens whose occupation is on the CUSMA professionals list and who hold a prearranged Canadian job offer in that profession with the required credentials.

**Do Canadians need a TN visa to work in the US?**

A Canadian citizen needs TN status to work in the United States in a qualifying TN profession, but usually not a visa sticker. Canadians typically request TN status at a US port of entry. It is a US process decided by US authorities, not by Canada.

**Can a Canada PR apply for a TN visa?**

No. The TN route is for citizens of Canada, the United States, or Mexico, depending on direction. A Canadian permanent resident who is not also a citizen of one of those three countries cannot use it, on either side of the border.

**Is a TN visa better than an H-1B?**

It depends on the person. TN is faster and cheaper and has no annual cap, but it is profession-bound and is a non-immigrant status with no dual intent. The H-1B allows dual intent, which can suit someone aiming at a US green card. This is a United States comparison, so confirm it with a US immigration attorney.

**What are the disadvantages of a TN visa?**

The main drawbacks are that it ties you to one employer and one listed profession, it is temporary, and it carries no built-in path to permanent residence. On the US side, the absence of dual intent can complicate a later green card. On the Canadian side, the CUSMA permit shares the same employer-specific and temporary limits.

## How can a licensed RCIC help with your CUSMA work permit?

Short answer: On the Canadian side, the details decide the case. Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto, regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). We confirm that your occupation truly matches the CUSMA professionals list, structure the employer's offer of employment and compliance step, prepare the work permit application, and map whether your Canadian experience can later support permanent residence. Because we are regulated for Canadian immigration, we advise on the Canada-bound CUSMA permit, not the United States TN. [Book a consultation](https://www.gofarglobal.com/book) to confirm your route.

# Study Without a Study Permit Policy Ended June 27, 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/study-without-study-permit-policy-ending-june-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-12
Author: Go Far Global Team

> A temporary public policy that has been in place since June 27, 2023 lets eligible foreign nationals who hold a work permit study in Canada without applying for a separate study permit.

# Study Without a Study Permit Policy Ended June 27, 2026

*As of September 10, 2026.* The temporary public policy that let some work permit holders study without a study permit expired on June 27, 2026. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) replaced it on September 4, 2026. This page is the old rule. Current rules: [Work Permit Holders Can Study Without a Study Permit (2026)](/news/work-permit-holders-study-without-study-permit-2026).

> This is a historical record of the June 27, 2023 to June 27, 2026 policy. Do not use it to decide whether you can study today.

## TL;DR

The 2023 policy expired June 27, 2026 and is archived | It only covered work permit files IRCC received on or before June 7, 2023 | IRCC replaced it on September 4, 2026 | The new policy covers any valid work permit, but only for programs of 6 months or less | It runs until December 31, 2027 unless revoked

## What expired on June 27, 2026?

**Short answer:** IRCC’s first [temporary public policy](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-instructions-agreements/public-policies/study-without-study-permit.html) that let eligible work permit holders study without a study permit came into force on June 27, 2023 and expired on June 27, 2026. Canada.ca now marks that instrument archived. It is not in force. Anyone still citing the June 7, 2023 application-date cutoff, or telling workers they can take a program longer than six months on a work permit alone, is describing a rule that ended. If you are choosing a course today, use the [September 2026 successor](/news/work-permit-holders-study-without-study-permit-2026), not this page.

## Who did the expired policy cover?

**Short answer:** Only a narrow cohort. The archived instrument required that IRCC had received the foreign national’s [work permit](/immigration/work-permit) application on or before June 7, 2023, and that the person either held a valid work permit or was authorized to work under paragraph 186(u) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) while an extension filed by that date was in process. Later work permit applicants were never in that policy. In exchange, the old instrument waived all of IRPR 188(1)(a) through (d), so longer programs were possible for that group. That waiver ended with the policy.

| Your situation in 2023-2026 | Covered by the expired policy? |
|---|---|
| Valid work permit, application received on or before June 7, 2023 | Yes, until June 27, 2026 or until the permit expired |
| Extension filed on or before June 7, 2023, working under IRPR 186(u) | Yes, until a refusal, permit expiry, or June 27, 2026 |
| Work permit applied for after June 7, 2023 | No |
| Studying after June 27, 2026 under that instrument | No. The instrument is archived |

## What replaced it on September 4, 2026?

**Short answer:** A new [temporary public policy](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-instructions-agreements/public-policies/study-without-study-permit-2026-2.html), signed August 5, 2026, took effect 30 days later on September 4, 2026. IRCC’s [worker instructions](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/workers-study-without-study-permit.html) now describe that successor. Any valid work permit holder may study a course or program of six months or less without a study permit, including when the course runs past the stay authorized on first entry. The exemption lasts until the work permit expires, or until December 31, 2027, or until IRCC revokes the policy, whichever comes first. Full detail, Quebec CAQ rules, co-op, and Canadian Experience Class (CEC) warnings are on [Work Permit Holders Can Study Without a Study Permit (2026)](/news/work-permit-holders-study-without-study-permit-2026).

| | Expired 2023 policy | Current 2026 policy |
|---|---|---|
| Who | Work permit filed on or before June 7, 2023 | Any valid work permit |
| Program length | Not capped at 6 months in the instrument | 6 months or less |
| What was waived | IRPR 188(1)(a) to (d) | Original-entry timing in 188(1)(c) only |
| Dates | June 27, 2023 to June 27, 2026 | September 4, 2026 to December 31, 2027 |

## Can I still take a short course without a study permit?

**Short answer:** Yes, on two separate tracks. Standing [IRPR paragraph 188(1)(c)](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/sor-2002-227/section-188.html) still lets a foreign national study a course or program of six months or less without a study permit if it will be completed within the stay authorized upon entry. The September 2026 public policy then lets a valid work permit holder take that same six-month cap even when the course runs past the original entry stamp, until the current permit expires. A program longer than six months still needs a [study permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html). Check [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) before you enrol if you need that permit.

## Does studying on a work permit lead to a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP)?

**Short answer:** No. It did not under the expired policy, and it does not under the new one. A Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) is for people who held a study permit and completed an eligible program at a designated learning institution. IRCC’s [PGWP eligibility page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html) treats the study permit as the starting document. Short training taken on a work permit is for the job you already have. If a PGWP is part of the plan, apply for the study permit first and confirm the program qualifies.

## What should you do now if you were studying under the old policy?

**Short answer:** Stop treating June 27, 2026 as a future deadline. That date has passed. If your program is six months or less and you still hold a valid work permit, the [September 2026 policy](/news/work-permit-holders-study-without-study-permit-2026) is the instrument that may cover you now, with no June 7, 2023 cutoff. If the program is longer than six months, you need a study permit. You can hold a work permit and a study permit at the same time if you meet both. Apply on IRCC’s [study permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html) page rather than stretching an archived public policy.

| Situation now | What to use |
|---|---|
| Valid work permit, course 6 months or less | Current 2026 public policy |
| Course longer than 6 months | Study permit |
| Old June 7, 2023 cohort cutoff | Dead. Do not use it |
| PGWP after studying on a work permit only | Not available |

## How can a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) help?

**Short answer:** Go Far Global, a Toronto Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm, can tell you whether your course fits the current six-month work permit exemption or whether you need a study permit. We do not advise from the expired June 2023 instrument. If you started a longer program under that old policy and kept studying after June 27, 2026 without a study permit, get the file reviewed before the next IRCC touch. [Book a consultation](/book). Other updates: [news](/news). Related pathways: [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry), [provincial nominee](/immigration/provincial-nominee), [family immigration](/immigration/family-immigration).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I use my work permit to study in Canada?

Not under the expired 2023 policy. That instrument ended June 27, 2026. Under the replacement policy in force September 4, 2026, yes if you hold a valid work permit and the program is six months or less. Read [the current article](/news/work-permit-holders-study-without-study-permit-2026).

### How long can you study on a work permit?

Under the current policy, six months or until the work permit expires, whichever comes first. The expired policy had no six-month cap in the instrument, but that waiver is gone.

### Can I do a 6 month course on a work permit?

Yes, if you hold a valid work permit. That is exactly what the September 2026 policy covers. IRPR 188(1)(c) also still covers short courses that finish within the stay authorized on first entry.

### Can I convert my work permit to a study permit in Canada?

You do not convert one document into the other. You apply for a study permit while keeping the work permit. Use that route for any program longer than six months.

### Can I have a study permit and work permit at the same time?

Yes, if you meet the conditions of each. That is the route for a program the six-month exemption does not cover.

- [Temporary public policy, signed August 5, 2026](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-instructions-agreements/public-policies/study-without-study-permit-2026-2.html) - in force September 4, 2026
- [Public policy allowing some work permit holders to study without a study permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/workers-study-without-study-permit.html) - current worker instructions, page dated September 9, 2026

# Proof of Funds for Canada PR 2026: How Much You Need and How to Show It

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/proof-of-funds-canada-pr-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-11
Author: Go Far Global Team

> If Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) invites you to apply for permanent residence through Express Entry, you may have to prove you hold enough money to settle here.

*As of June 11, 2026.*

If Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) invites you to apply for permanent residence through Express Entry, you may have to prove you hold enough money to settle here. The amount is fixed by family size and updated once a year. This guide covers who must show settlement funds, the exact 2026 amounts, who is exempt, what kind of money counts, and how to document it the way IRCC wants. There is a rupee-conversion note for applicants from India further down.

## Who needs proof of funds for Canada PR?

You need to show settlement money if you apply under the [Federal Skilled Worker Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/federal-skilled-workers.html) or the [Federal Skilled Trades Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/federal-skilled-trades.html). These two federal streams treat available money as a core eligibility test, because neither one assumes you already earn an income inside Canada. If the system invites you under either program, you must give written proof that the money is real and within your reach. The full rules sit on the [IRCC proof-of-funds page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/proof-funds.html).

## Who is exempt from showing proof of funds?

Two groups do not have to show settlement money. First, candidates applying under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) are exempt, because their Canadian work history stands in for it. Second, anyone who is authorized to work in Canada and holds a valid job offer is exempt, even when they apply through the Federal Skilled Worker or Federal Skilled Trades program. The Express Entry system still asks every candidate for the document, so if you qualify for the carve-out you upload a short letter explaining that you have either a CEC invitation or a valid job offer plus work authorization. Confirm the exemption on the [Express Entry: Canadian Experience Class page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/canadian-experience-class.html).

## How much money do you need by family size?

The amount is based on the size of your family, and IRCC updated the figures on July 7, 2025. The table below shows the minimum you need in Canadian dollars. If you hold more than the minimum, list the full amount in your Express Entry profile. To size your family, count yourself, your spouse or common-law partner, and the dependent children of either of you, even if some of them are Canadian citizens or are not travelling with you.

| Number of family members | Funds required (CAD) |
|---|---|
| 1 | $15,263 |
| 2 | $19,001 |
| 3 | $23,360 |
| 4 | $28,362 |
| 5 | $32,168 |
| 6 | $36,280 |
| 7 | $40,392 |
| Each additional member | $4,112 |

These figures come straight from the IRCC settlement-funds table and change roughly once a year, set at about half of the low-income cut-off totals, so check the current number before you submit.

## How much is that in Indian rupees?

Many Express Entry candidates from India want a rupee figure, so here is a careful one. The single-applicant minimum of $15,263 CAD works out to somewhere around 9 lakh rupees when the Canadian dollar trades in the low 60s of rupees, which is roughly where it has sat recently. Treat that as indicative only. Exchange rates move every day, and IRCC measures the requirement in Canadian dollars, not rupees, so the rupee amount you actually need shifts with the market. Check the live Canadian-dollar-to-rupee rate the week you prepare your bank letters, and keep a comfortable buffer above the minimum. If you are moving from India, our [guide for applicants from India](/immigration/from/india) walks through the wider process.

## What counts as acceptable proof of funds?

Your money has to be liquid, legally yours, and available both when you apply and when IRCC issues your permanent resident visa. That means cash and balances you can readily turn into cash to pay for your family's living costs, even if your family is not coming with you. It cannot be money you borrowed from another person, and it cannot be equity in property or other real estate. If your spouse travels with you, money in a joint account counts, and funds held only in your spouse's name may count if you can prove you have access to them. The [IRCC proof-of-funds page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/proof-funds.html) sets the exact wording for what qualifies.

## Does a GIC or fixed deposit count as proof of funds?

Yes, investment money can count, as long as you can convert it to cash and you back it with an official letter. A Guaranteed Investment Certificate, a fixed deposit, a mutual fund, or a brokerage balance can all qualify when the institution confirms the value and your access to it. The test is the same as for a savings account: the money must be liquid enough to pay for settlement, legally yours, and free of any lock-in that stops you from withdrawing it when you arrive. A term deposit with a hard maturity lock can be a problem, so confirm you can redeem it early if needed. List each investment account on its own institution letter, showing the account number, the balance, and the six-month average. This matters for many applicants from India, where fixed deposits are a common way to hold savings.

## How do you prove your funds to IRCC?

You prove the money with official letters from every bank or financial institution where you hold an account. Each letter must be printed on the institution's letterhead and must include its contact details, your name, and any outstanding debts such as loans and credit-card balances. For every banking and investment account, the letter has to state the account number, the date the account was opened, the current balance, and the average balance over the past six months. A plain screenshot or a mobile-app statement is not enough on its own. Build your document set from the [Express Entry document checklist](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents.html) and the proof-of-funds requirements.

## When must the funds be available?

The money must be available at two moments: when you submit your application and again when IRCC is ready to issue your permanent resident visa. Officers can ask for updated letters late in processing, so you cannot show the balance once and then spend it down. Keep the funds steady from the day you are invited until you land in Canada. A sudden large deposit can also draw questions, because officers check that the money is genuinely yours and not parked temporarily to pass the test. Watch the live cut-offs on the [Express Entry rounds of invitations](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations.html) page to time your profile.

## How much extra should you keep above the minimum?

Aim to hold a clear margin above the figure for your family size, not the bare minimum. Currency swings, bank fees, and a balance that dips for a few days can all pull you under the line at the wrong moment, and officers assess the funds at more than one point. A cushion of a few thousand Canadian dollars gives you room if the exchange rate moves against you or a transfer is delayed in clearing. It also signals that the money is settled and genuinely yours, which is exactly what an officer wants to see. The minimum is a floor, not a target, so treat it that way when you plan your transfers.

## What mistakes get a proof-of-funds letter refused?

The common failures are avoidable. Showing borrowed money is the biggest one, since IRCC explicitly bars funds you cannot legally keep. Counting home equity or property value is another, because real-estate equity does not qualify. Letters that omit the six-month average balance, the account opening date, or the institution's contact details get sent back for correction. A large unexplained deposit just before you apply can trigger a request for an explanation of its source. So can letting the balance fall below the minimum partway through processing. Work out your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) target with our [CRS score calculator](/tools/crs-calculator), then line your funds up before you submit.

## How can an authorized representative help?

Settlement funds are where small documentation errors cause big delays, which is why many applicants use a paid representative. Under Canadian law, only three kinds of people can be paid to represent you: a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC), a lawyer in good standing with a Canadian provincial or territorial law society, or a notary who is a member of the Chambre des notaires du Québec. Go Far Global is an RCIC firm based in Toronto, RCIC number R515110. A licensed representative checks your bank letters against the IRCC list before you submit, so the file does not bounce back. If you are weighing the timing of your move, read our note on the [2026 immigration levels plan](/news/canada-immigration-levels-plan-2026).

## What do applicants ask about proof of funds for Canada PR?

These are the questions Express Entry candidates search most often about settlement money, pulled from live Google results. The short answers reflect the current IRCC rules for the federal economic programs. For fast-moving policy, see our coverage of the [Canada fast-track work permit for AI professionals](/news/canada-ai-professionals-fast-track-work-permit-2026).

**What is the minimum amount for proof of funds in Canada?**

For a single applicant the 2026 minimum is $15,263 CAD, rising with family size to $19,001 for two people and $23,360 for three. IRCC updates the table each year at about half of the low-income cut-off. Always confirm the current figure on the IRCC page before you submit your profile.

**How to show proof of funds for Canada PR?**

You show it with official letters on each bank's letterhead. Every letter lists your name, the institution's contact details, your outstanding debts, and, for each account, the number, the opening date, the current balance, and the six-month average balance. You upload these letters in your Express Entry application after you are invited to apply.

**How does IRCC check proof of funds?**

Officers read your bank letters and compare the balances against the required amount for your family size. They look for steady balances, a genuine source, and legal access to the money. Borrowed funds, sudden large deposits, and home equity raise flags and can lead to a request for more documents or a refusal.

**What can be shown as proof of funds?**

Liquid money you can readily use counts: chequing and savings balances, plus investments you can convert to cash, all evidenced by official bank letters. Cash you cannot document, money borrowed from someone else, and the equity in a house or other property do not count toward the requirement.
