# Canada's Fast-Track Work Permit for AI Professionals (2026): The Global Talent Stream Under AI for All

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-ai-professionals-fast-track-work-permit-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-11
Author: Go Far Global Team

> On June 4, 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney launched "AI for All," Canada's new national artificial intelligence strategy.

# Canada's Fast-Track Work Permit for AI Professionals (2026): The Global Talent Stream Under "AI for All"

**As of June 11, 2026.**

On June 4, 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney launched "AI for All," Canada's new national artificial intelligence strategy. For people searching for a **canada ai work permit**, the headline is this: the government committed to expand and speed up the existing Global Talent Stream (GTS) so highly skilled AI, machine learning, and data science workers can come to Canada faster, and to align permanent residence rules to keep them here. What is actually available to apply for today is the fast-track program that already exists, not a separate new "AI stream." This guide separates what is live now from what is an announced commitment.

## What did Canada announce for AI professionals on June 4, 2026?

The announcement was a national strategy, not a single new visa. AI for All is a five-year plan that the government says targets an additional $200 billion of economic growth, the creation of 250,000 new AI-related jobs over five years, and an increase in AI adoption across the country from just over 12% to 60% by 2034. Inside that plan, the talent measure that matters most to foreign workers is a stated commitment to expand the fast-track stream to accelerate the entry of highly skilled AI workers, and to align permanent residence measures to retain that talent.

The strategy was announced by [Prime Minister Carney on June 4, 2026](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2026/06/04/prime-minister-carney-launches-ai-all-canadas-new-national-artificial), with the detailed plan published by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada in [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all). Other talent measures in the plan include:

- Up to 90,000 AI-related jobs and work placement opportunities for young Canadians.
- Increasing the Canada CIFAR (Canadian Institute for Advanced Research) AI Chairs program from 130 to nearly 200 researchers.
- A $1.7 billion talent attraction strategy first announced in Budget 2025.

The plan does not publish a separate new application form, a separate AI work permit category, or a guaranteed AI-specific processing time. It commits to building on a program that is already running.

## How does the fast-track work permit work today?

The GTS is the live mechanism right now, and it predates this announcement. It is part of the Temporary Foreign Worker Program and is run by Employment and Social Development Canada. It is employer-driven: a Canadian employer applies to hire you, not the other way around. Through the linked Global Skills Strategy, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) aims to process eligible work permit applications within two weeks once the employer side is in place. That two-week target is the closest thing to a published fast-track that exists today.

Here is the order of operations for a [Global Talent Stream](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers/global-talent.html) hire:

1. A Canadian employer applies for a [Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA)](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers.html) through the stream and pays the $1,000 processing fee for the position.
2. The employer agrees to a Labour Market Benefits Plan, which commits them to benefits such as job creation or skills investment for Canadians and permanent residents.
3. Once the LMIA is positive, you apply for the work permit. Under the [Global Skills Strategy](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/hire-temporary-foreign/global-skills-strategy.html), IRCC aims for [two-week processing of eligible applications](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/hire-temporary-foreign/global-skills-strategy/2-week-processing.html).

The "around 20 days start to finish" figure that has circulated in coverage of the June 4 announcement is a reported number, not a guarantee published by IRCC or ESDC for an AI stream. The government's own published target is the two-week work permit processing window.

## Who qualifies for Canada's AI work permit fast-track?

Two-week processing under the Global Skills Strategy applies when the job is classified under Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) category 0 (management jobs) or category 1 (jobs that usually require a university degree) of the National Occupational Classification (NOC). Most AI, machine learning, and data science roles sit in TEER 0 or 1. The stream itself has two routes: Category A, for employers referred by a designated referral partner who are hiring unique and specialized talent, and Category B, for employers hiring highly skilled workers in occupations already on the global talent occupations list. A referral is not required for Category B.

The Category B occupations list already includes the core AI and tech roles. You can confirm your role against the [Global Talent Stream program requirements](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers/global-talent/requirements.html).

| Occupation | NOC code | TEER level | Typical AI focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data scientists | 21211 | 1 | Machine learning, modelling |
| Software engineers and designers | 21231 | 1 | AI systems engineering |
| Software developers and programmers | 21232 | 1 | Model deployment, MLOps |
| Computer engineers | 21311 | 1 | Compute and hardware |
| Cybersecurity specialists | 21220 | 1 | Securing AI systems |
| Mathematicians and statisticians | 21210 (subset) | 1 | Algorithms and statistics |
| Computer and information systems managers | 20012 | 0 | Leading AI teams |

Because data scientists and software roles were already on this list, AI talent could already be hired through the fast-track before June 4. The announcement is about doing more of it, faster, not opening a door that was closed.

## What is live now versus what is an announced commitment?

This is the part that most online summaries blur, so be precise about it before you make any plans. The fast-track stream and its two-week work permit processing target are live and have been for years. The AI-specific acceleration, the broader expansion of the program, and the aligned permanent residence measures are commitments inside a five-year strategy. They are government policy direction, but they are not yet a separate program you can apply to, and no AI-specific timeline has been published beyond the existing two-week target.

| Item | Status | What it means for you |
|---|---|---|
| The fast-track stream (GTS) | Live | You can be hired through it today if an employer applies |
| Two-week work permit processing | Live | Applies to eligible TEER 0/1 jobs with a positive LMIA |
| AI, data and software roles on the occupations list | Live | Already eligible for Category B |
| Expanding the stream to accelerate AI worker entry | Announced commitment | Strategy direction, no separate application yet |
| Aligning permanent residence to retain AI talent | Announced commitment | Detail and timing not yet published |
| A separate "AI work permit stream" | Does not exist | Do not apply to a stream that has not been created |

## How does an AI work permit lead to permanent residence?

A fast-track work permit is temporary, but it is one of the cleaner on-ramps to permanent residence for tech workers. Once you have worked in Canada in a skilled (TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3) job for at least one year, you may qualify under the [Canadian Experience Class (CEC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html), which is managed through Express Entry. Canadian work experience and a valid job also tend to lift your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score, which is the points total IRCC uses to rank Express Entry candidates.

There is a second route worth watching. IRCC runs [Express Entry category-based selection](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/submit-profile/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html), where the Minister invites candidates with work experience in targeted occupations, and science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields have featured in past rounds. The commitment to "align measures for permanent residency" suggests this targeting could lean further toward AI talent, though the specifics are not yet published. To understand the full picture, read [how Express Entry works](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/works.html) before you build a plan around any single category.

## What should AI professionals applying from India do now?

India is one of the countries Canada has signed AI cooperation agreements with since March 2025, and Indian IT and AI talent is a large share of the global pool Canada is competing for. The most useful thing you can do from India today is treat the live fast-track stream as the real path and ignore any agent promising a separate "AI visa." The work permit is employer-led, so a job offer from a qualifying Canadian employer is the thing that opens the fast-track, not a standalone application you file yourself.

Concrete steps to take now:

1. Target employers, not programs. Look for Canadian companies hiring into NOC 21211, 21231, 21232 and similar roles who are willing to run a GTS LMIA. Our guide on [how to get a work permit in Canada](/news/how-to-get-work-permit-canada) explains the employer side.
2. Understand the employer's obligation. The fast-track runs on an [LMIA](/news/lmia-canada-2026), so the employer carries the paperwork and the Labour Market Benefits Plan, not you.
3. Prepare your documents early. Passport, credentials, and proof of experience should be ready so you can move inside the two-week window once the LMIA is positive. Be ready to [give your biometrics](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics.html) promptly.
4. Know the work permit basics. Review how to [apply for a work permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit/temporary.html) and the broader [tech talent pathways Canada is attracting](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/campaigns/tech-talent.html). Country context is in our [immigration from India](/immigration/from/india) page.

Quebec runs a separate provincial pilot for AI, information technology and visual effects workers, governed by Quebec rather than the federal program, with different rules and timelines.

## What else do AI professionals ask about the fast-track?

These are common questions pulled from real searches around the GTS and the AI for All announcement. The short answers below reflect the government rules that are in force as of June 11, 2026, and flag where a figure is a policy direction rather than a current guarantee.

### What is a global talent stream?

The Global Talent Stream is a part of Canada's Temporary Foreign Worker Program that lets approved employers hire highly skilled foreign workers quickly. It is one pillar of the Global Skills Strategy, under which IRCC aims to process eligible work permit applications within two weeks. It is designed to help innovative companies access skilled talent, including AI, data and software professionals, without the long timelines of standard work permit routes.

### Who is eligible for Global Talent Stream Canada?

Eligibility has two sides. The employer must qualify under Category A (referred by a designated referral partner to hire unique and specialized talent) or Category B (hiring for an occupation on the published occupations list, no referral needed). The worker qualifies for two-week processing when the job sits in TEER 0 or 1 of the NOC and there is a positive LMIA in place. Most AI, machine learning and data science roles meet the TEER 0/1 test.

### How much is the Global Talent Stream fee in Canada?

The employer pays a $1,000 LMIA processing fee for each position requested through the program, in Canadian dollars. This is the employer's cost, not the worker's, and it is not refunded if the application is withdrawn, cancelled, or refused. You will separately pay the standard work permit and biometrics fees when you submit your own application after the LMIA is positive.

### Is TR to PR coming back in 2026?

A broad temporary-resident-to-permanent-resident pathway has been discussed for 2026, but there is no open, general TR to PR program you can apply to as of June 11, 2026. For most AI workers, the realistic route is the Canadian Experience Class through Express Entry after about a year of Canadian work, plus category-based selection rounds. Treat any wider TR to PR program as unconfirmed until IRCC publishes the criteria.

### Is 470 a good score for Canada PR?

A Comprehensive Ranking System score of 470 is competitive for many Express Entry draws, but whether it earns an invitation depends on the draw type and the cut-off on the day. Category-based and Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) draws can have very different cut-offs from general draws. Canadian work experience from a fast-track job and a provincial nomination are two of the strongest ways to push a score above the line.

# Spousal Open Work Permit Canada 2026: Who Qualifies Under the New Rules

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/spousal-open-work-permit-canada-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-10
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Yes. A spouse or common-law partner can still get a spousal open work permit in 2026, but only in specific situations.

Yes. A spouse or common-law partner can still get a spousal open work permit in 2026, but only in specific situations. As of June 9, 2026, three separate measures exist, and which one applies to you decides everything. If your partner sponsors you for permanent residence from inside Canada, you most likely still qualify. If your partner works here, you qualify only when their job sits in a higher skill tier. If they study here, you qualify only when their program is on a short approved list. This guide walks each path and links the official rule so you can check your own case.

## What is a spousal open work permit?

A spousal open work permit (SOWP) is a work permit issued to the spouse or common-law partner of someone who already has status in Canada. It is an open permit, so the holder can work for almost any employer, with no job offer and no Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) required. That is what separates it from an employer-specific permit, which names one employer and one job. The label actually covers three different government measures, each with its own rule set: partners of people being sponsored for permanent residence, partners of foreign workers, and partners of international students. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) treats these as separate streams, so a "yes" under one says nothing about the others. The broader [open work permit overview](/news/open-work-permit-canada-2026) covers every category. This page goes deep on the three that involve a partner.

## What changed for spouses on January 21, 2025?

On January 21, 2025, IRCC narrowed two of the three streams at once. Before that date, most partners of foreign workers and most partners of international students could apply. After it, both groups shrank to a defined subset. For workers, the partner now generally qualifies only when the worker holds a high-skilled job. For students, the partner qualifies only when the student is in a master's, doctoral, or select professional program. Dependent children also lost access under the foreign-worker measure on that date. The sponsored-partner stream, the inland family-class route, was left untouched and still runs on its own rules. IRCC has since added smaller 2026 measures for Quebec and British Columbia, covered below. The official eligibility page for [family members of foreign workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/spouses-dependent-children/eligibility.html) sets out the current criteria in full.

| Your situation | Stream | Still open in 2026? |
|---|---|---|
| Partner sponsors you for PR from inside Canada | Inland family class | Yes, broadly |
| Partner is a foreign worker | International Mobility Program | Only if their job is high-skilled |
| Partner is an international student | Student-spouse measure | Only for select programs |

## Path 1: Can a sponsored spouse still get a work permit?

Yes. If your spouse, common-law partner, or conjugal partner is sponsoring you for permanent residence and you live in Canada together, you can apply for a work permit while the application is processed. This is the inland route, the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class, and the January 2025 restriction did not touch it. To qualify, you must be in a genuine relationship with your sponsor, be included in a permanent residence application, hold an Acknowledgement of Receipt (AOR) letter from IRCC confirming the application is in process, and live in Canada with your sponsor. An accompanying dependent child of the principal applicant can also apply. You cannot apply if the permanent residence application was refused, withdrawn, or returned, or if you plan to apply at a port of entry. See the official [sponsored-spouse work permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/spouse-common-law-partner-canada-open-work-permit.html) page, and our guide to the broader [spousal sponsorship process](/news/spousal-sponsorship-canada-2026), for the full steps.

## Path 2: Which spouses of foreign workers still qualify?

This is where the January 2025 change bites hardest. When your partner works in Canada and has not applied for permanent residence, you now qualify only when their job is high-skilled. The National Occupational Classification (NOC) system groups jobs into Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) categories 0 through 5. Your partner's job must be in TEER 0 or 1, or one of a defined set of jobs in TEER 2 or 3. Their permit or work authorization must also be valid for at least 16 months after IRCC receives your application, with narrow exceptions added in 2026. Dependent children are no longer eligible under this measure as of January 21, 2025. The full criteria and the TEER 2 and 3 job list sit on the [family members of foreign workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/spouses-dependent-children/eligibility.html) page.

Two 2026 updates relax the 16-month rule. As of May 25, 2026, the permit does not need 16 months of validity left if the worker was recruited by Quebec as a foreign-trained registered nurse, respiratory therapist, or medical laboratory technologist. As of March 23, 2026, the 16-month rule also does not apply to partners of workers on a significant investment project in British Columbia, whose job can sit at any TEER level.

The rules are wider when your partner has already applied for permanent residence through an economic program such as the Provincial Nominee Program (PNP), the Canadian Experience Class, or a federal skilled stream. In that case the worker's permit only needs to be valid for at least 6 months after IRCC receives your application, and dependent children can still qualify. If your partner works in a lower-skilled job at TEER 4 or 5 and has not applied for permanent residence, you are not eligible under this measure, though an existing permit may sometimes be extended.

## Path 3: Which international students' spouses still qualify?

Since January 21, 2025, only partners of students in higher-level programs qualify. Your student partner must hold a valid study permit and be enrolled in one of the following: a master's degree program that lasts 16 months or longer, a doctoral degree program, an eligible pilot program, or a specific professional degree at a university. If your partner's program is a college diploma, a bachelor's degree outside the listed professional fields, or a shorter master's, you are not eligible under this stream, though another permit type may fit. The complete list is on the [help your spouse or common-law partner work in Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/help-your-spouse-common-law-partner-work-canada.html) page.

Professional degree programs that make a partner eligible include:

- Doctor of Medicine, Doctor of Dental Surgery, and Doctor of Veterinary Medicine
- Bachelor of Law or Juris Doctor
- Doctor of Optometry and pharmacy degrees
- Bachelor of Science in Nursing, Bachelor of Nursing, and related nursing degrees
- Bachelor of Education and Bachelor of Engineering

Once your partner finishes studying and moves onto a [Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP)](/news/pgwp-post-graduation-work-permit-canada-2026), they count as a worker, and the Path 2 rules decide your case instead.

## What does the June 5, 2026 Quebec public policy add?

On June 5, 2026, IRCC signed a temporary public policy for Quebec. It lets spouses and common-law partners of certain temporary workers in Quebec apply for a permit while the province assesses the worker for permanent selection. The worker must hold an eligible Quebec employer-specific permit, have been invited to apply under the Programme de selection des travailleurs qualifies (PSTQ), and have filed their selection application with Quebec. The partner must be included as an accompanying family member on that selection application and hold valid temporary status, or have lost it within the last 90 days and applied to restore it. The policy runs until December 31, 2026. If your partner was invited through Quebec's [skilled worker program](/news/pstq-quebec-skilled-worker-program-2026), read the [Quebec work permit public policy](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-instructions-agreements/public-policies/work-permits-qc-pr-2026-2.html). Applicants type the code PPTR2PRQC2026 in the job-title field of the form.

## How do you apply, and what documents do you need?

Almost all of these applications are filed online through an IRCC secure account. You answer a short set of questions, IRCC builds a personalized document checklist, and you upload your forms and pay the fees. Across the three paths, the documents overlap: proof of your relationship, your partner's status document, and one stream-specific proof. A sponsored partner uploads the Acknowledgement of Receipt letter. A worker's partner uploads the worker's permit or job proof. A student's partner uploads a letter of acceptance, an enrolment letter, or transcripts. Each path also uses a specific code in the job-title box of the form, which the relevant IRCC page spells out. The general steps are on the [apply for a work permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit/temporary/apply.html) page. Only you or an authorized paid representative should submit on your behalf.

## How long does processing take for a spousal permit?

Processing time depends on where you apply and which stream you use, and IRCC updates the estimates regularly, so there is no single fixed number. Inland applications, applications from outside Canada, and student-partner applications each carry their own current estimate. Rather than quote a figure that goes stale, check the live tool. IRCC's [check current processing times](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) page gives the up-to-date estimate for a work permit by country and category. Apply early, keep your partner's status valid, and file before any current permit expires so you can keep working under maintained status while IRCC decides.

## What are the most common SOWP mistakes?

Most refusals and delays trace back to a handful of avoidable errors. The biggest is assuming the old rules still apply: many applicants file under the pre-2025 criteria and get refused because the worker's job is below the skill threshold or the student's program is not on the list. Others miss the worker's 16-month validity requirement, forget the job-title code, or apply at a port of entry when their stream requires an online filing. Weak relationship evidence is another frequent cause. Review the exact criteria for your path before you file.

Common mistakes to avoid:

- Applying under the foreign-worker stream when the worker's job is TEER 4 or 5
- Filing a student-partner application for a program not on the approved list
- Missing the worker's 16-month permit-validity requirement
- Leaving out the job-title code the form requires
- Submitting thin proof of a genuine relationship

## What do spouses ask most about the SOWP?

These are the questions partners raise most often, pulled from live Google results. The short answers below point back to the official rule for your situation, because the correct answer almost always depends on whether your partner sponsors you, works in Canada, or studies here. Use them as a starting point, then confirm the detail on the IRCC page that matches your path.

### What are the new rules for spousal open work permit in Canada?

As of January 21, 2025, two streams tightened. A foreign worker's partner generally qualifies only when the worker's job is high-skilled, at TEER 0, 1, or a select TEER 2 or 3 occupation. A student's partner qualifies only when the student is in a master's of 16 months or more, a doctoral, or a listed professional program. The sponsored-partner stream was not changed.

### How long does it take to get an open work permit for a spouse in Canada?

There is no single fixed timeline. Processing depends on whether you apply from inside or outside Canada and which stream you use, and IRCC revises the estimates often. Check the live processing-times tool for the current figure for a work permit in your country and category, then apply early so you can keep working under maintained status while you wait.

### Who is eligible for SOWP 2026?

Eligibility splits three ways. If your partner sponsors you for permanent residence from inside Canada and holds an Acknowledgement of Receipt letter, you generally qualify. A high-skilled foreign worker's partner qualifies when the job meets the TEER threshold. A student's partner qualifies only for the listed master's, doctoral, and professional programs. A new Quebec measure adds partners of PSTQ-invited workers.

### Can my family come with me on a SOWP?

It depends on the stream. Under the sponsored-partner route, an accompanying dependent child can also apply for a permit. Under the foreign-worker measure, dependent children lost eligibility on January 21, 2025, so usually only the spouse or partner qualifies. Children of workers who applied for an economic permanent residence program may still be covered. Check the rule for your exact path.

# Arrima 2026: How Quebec's Immigration Portal and Expression of Interest Works

# Arrima 2026: How Quebec's Immigration Portal and Expression of Interest Works

As of June 9, 2026, Arrima is the online platform the Government of Quebec uses to manage most of its permanent economic immigration. You create a free Arrima account, complete an Expression of Interest, and Quebec invites the candidates it wants from that pool. This guide explains what Arrima is, how to open an account, how to submit your declaration, what the 30-day acceptance window means, and what happens at the federal level after Quebec selects you. For the eligibility rules and the streams behind it, read our companion guide to the [Quebec skilled worker program (PSTQ)](/news/pstq-quebec-skilled-worker-program-2026).

## What is Arrima and when did Quebec launch it?

Arrima is the secure online service operated by Quebec's immigration ministry for permanent economic immigration. Quebec launched it on August 2, 2018, replacing the older "Mon projet Quebec" intake system. The portal hosts the Expression of Interest (EOI) bank for the Programme de selection des travailleurs qualifies (Skilled Worker Selection Program), along with several other immigration and French-language services. Quebec controls who it selects for permanent residence through its own selection power, which is separate from the federal government. That split matters: Quebec decides who it wants through Arrima, and Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) later decides federal admissibility. An EOI is the free declaration you file in the portal so Quebec can consider you. The system runs in both French and English, and the same account follows you through every stage.

## What can you do inside the Arrima portal?

Arrima is more than a single application form. Once you have an account, you can submit and update an EOI, respond to an invitation, and file a permanent selection application when invited. Quebec also routes other online services through the same portal, including registration for French-language learning support and some temporary immigration steps. You can sign back in at any time to correct your file, track its status, and read messages from the ministry. The table below shows where each stage of the journey sits and who makes the decision at that stage.

| Stage | Platform | Who decides | Your main action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expression of interest | Arrima (Quebec) | You | Create an account and submit your EOI |
| Invitation round | Arrima (Quebec) | Quebec | Quebec ranks the pool and invites candidates |
| Selection application (DSP) | Arrima (Quebec) | Quebec | Accept within 30 days and submit the DSP |
| Quebec Selection Certificate | Arrima (Quebec) | Quebec | Receive your CSQ |
| Permanent residence | IRCC (federal) | IRCC | Apply to IRCC and pass medical, security, and biometrics |

## How do you create an Arrima account and submit an Expression of Interest?

You start by creating a personal account on Quebec's online immigration services page, then completing the EOI form inside it. The declaration asks about your age, education, work experience, French and English language ability, any job offer or family ties in Quebec, and other selection factors. You do not pay a fee to submit the declaration, and submitting one does not guarantee an invitation. Be accurate, because the details you enter feed the score Quebec uses to rank you against everyone else in the pool. The form generally stays valid for a set period, so keep your profile current and update it if your situation changes, for example if you finish a diploma or improve a language test result. Quebec confirms the account and declaration steps on its [Arrima online immigration services](https://www.quebec.ca/en/immigration/online-immigration-services) page, and it details the selection factors on its [expression of interest](https://www.quebec.ca/en/immigration/permanent/skilled-workers/skilled-worker-selection-program/expression-of-interest) page.

## How do Arrima invitations and the 30-day acceptance window work?

Quebec reviews the candidate pool and issues invitations in periodic rounds. It selects people based on its ranking and on its current immigration priorities, so an invitation is not first-come, first-served. If Quebec invites you, you have 30 days from the date on the invitation to accept it through Arrima and submit your permanent selection application. Miss that window and the invitation expires, which means waiting for a future round. The invitation does not by itself grant selection; it only gives you the right to apply. Quebec sets out the acceptance rule on its official [invitation to apply for permanent selection](https://www.quebec.ca/en/immigration/permanent/skilled-workers/skilled-worker-selection-program/invitation) page. We do not publish specific score cutoffs or round sizes here, because those change from round to round and only Quebec's own announcements are reliable.

## What are the DSP and CSQ, and how do they connect?

Once you accept an invitation, you file a Demande de selection permanente (DSP), the permanent selection application, through Arrima. You upload supporting documents, pay Quebec's processing fees, and wait for Quebec to assess your file. If Quebec approves you, it issues a Certificat de selection du Quebec (CSQ), the Quebec Selection Certificate. The CSQ is Quebec's confirmation that it has selected you for permanent residence. It is a provincial document, not a federal visa, and it does not let you live in Quebec on its own. Think of the CSQ as the green light from Quebec that you then carry into the federal stage. To understand the program rules that decide whether your DSP is approved, see the eligibility and stream details in our [PSTQ program guide](/news/pstq-quebec-skilled-worker-program-2026).

## What is the federal permanent residence step after the CSQ?

After Quebec issues your CSQ, you apply to the federal government for permanent residence as a Quebec-selected skilled worker. IRCC runs this stage and checks federal admissibility, which Quebec does not assess. IRCC confirms the process on its [Quebec-selected skilled workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/quebec-skilled-workers.html) page, and it explains the follow-up steps on its [after you apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/quebec-skilled-workers/after-apply-next-steps.html) page. At this stage you sign in to your [IRCC secure account](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/account.html), submit the federal application, and [pay your immigration application fees](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/pay-fees.html). Most applicants must [give their biometrics](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics.html) and complete an [immigration medical exam](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams.html). IRCC also checks security and criminal admissibility, and it can ask for more documents before it approves your file. If you are already working in Quebec while you wait, IRCC has separate instructions for a [bridging work permit for Quebec workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/work-permit-skilled-workers-quebec-pstq.html) who have applied for permanent selection.

Processing times for the federal stage vary, and IRCC publishes current estimates on its website. While your file is in progress, keep your contact details and travel documents up to date, and reply quickly if IRCC asks for anything. Once IRCC approves the application, it confirms your permanent residence and you complete your landing in Canada. From that point you hold the same status as any other permanent resident, with the right to live and work anywhere in the country, including Quebec.

## How does the Arrima Employer Portal work?

Arrima is not only for applicants. Quebec runs an employer side of the portal where approved Quebec employers can search candidate profiles in the EOI bank and connect with people whose skills match their hiring needs. A validated job offer from a Quebec employer can raise a candidate's profile within the selection system, so the employer portal links labour-market demand to the pool of declared candidates. If you have a genuine Quebec job offer, make sure it is reflected accurately in your declaration, because that information can influence whether Quebec invites you. Employers and candidates use the same Arrima system Quebec describes on its online immigration services page, so a real offer should match what you enter.

## What are the most common Arrima mistakes?

The errors that cost applicants the most are usually avoidable. The first is letting an invitation lapse: the 30-day acceptance window is firm, and a missed deadline sends you back to the pool. The second is entering inaccurate details in your declaration, since the score that ranks you depends on what you declare, and a mismatch with your documents can sink the later selection application. The third is treating the CSQ as the finish line. Quebec selection and federal permanent residence are two different approvals, and you still have to satisfy IRCC on medical, security, and biometrics afterward. The fourth is letting a stale profile sit untouched, so a stronger language result or new credential never reaches Quebec. The fifth is paying an unlicensed "agent." Only a regulated representative can legally advise you for a fee, a point we explain in the closing section.

## Arrima FAQ: what else do applicants ask?

Below are common questions people search about Arrima, answered in plain terms. Each answer reflects the Quebec and federal sources listed at the end of this article. If your situation is unusual, confirm the detail against the relevant government page or speak with a licensed representative before you act, because immigration rules and round results can change quickly.

### What is arrima in Canada?

Arrima is the Government of Quebec's online immigration platform, launched on August 2, 2018. It hosts the EOI system for Quebec's permanent skilled worker selection and several other online immigration and French-learning services. Quebec uses it to receive candidate declarations, rank them, and send invitations. It is specific to Quebec and is separate from the federal Express Entry system that the rest of Canada uses.

### What are the requirements for arrima?

To use Arrima you create an account and submit a declaration covering your age, education, work experience, language ability, and any Quebec job offer or ties. Submitting the form is free and open to candidates interested in Quebec's skilled worker selection, but it does not guarantee an invitation. The detailed eligibility criteria and streams belong to the program itself, which we cover in our [PSTQ program guide](/news/pstq-quebec-skilled-worker-program-2026).

### What happens after I get an Arrima invitation?

After an invitation, you have 30 days from the invitation date to accept it in Arrima and submit your permanent selection application (the DSP), with documents and Quebec fees. Quebec assesses the file and, if approved, issues a Quebec Selection Certificate (CSQ). You then apply to IRCC for federal permanent residence, where you complete biometrics, a medical exam, and security checks.

### What is the minimum score for arrima Quebec?

Quebec does not publish a single fixed minimum score for Arrima. It ranks the candidate pool and sets invitation thresholds round by round, based on its priorities and the candidates available at the time. Because cutoffs move between rounds, the only reliable figures are the ones Quebec announces for each round on its official selection program pages.

# PSTQ 2026: Quebec's Skilled Worker Selection Program, Streams, and How to Apply

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/pstq-quebec-skilled-worker-program-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-10
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The PSTQ (Programme de sélection des travailleurs qualifiés, or Quebec Skilled Worker Selection Program) is Quebec's main route to permanent immigration for skilled workers, whether...

*As of June 9, 2026.*

> **Related:** Quebec's experience-based pathway, the PEQ, reopened for a two-year window on July 2, 2026. See our [Quebec Experience Program (PEQ) 2026 guide](/news/peq-quebec-experience-program-2026).

The PSTQ (Programme de sélection des travailleurs qualifiés, or Quebec Skilled Worker Selection Program) is Quebec's main route to permanent immigration for skilled workers, whether you are already in Quebec or applying from abroad. You apply by creating a profile in the Arrima system and submitting an expression of interest. Quebec invites the highest-ranked profiles in periodic rounds, invited people file a permanent selection application, and those approved receive a Quebec selection certificate. Only then do you apply to the federal department, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), for permanent residence. French ability is now central to who gets invited. This guide explains the program, the four streams, the points and French levels, and a new June 2026 bridging work permit for invited workers.

## What is the PSTQ?

The PSTQ is the program Quebec uses to select skilled workers for permanent residence. It replaced the older Programme régulier des travailleurs qualifiés (PRTQ) on November 29, 2024, and now covers all occupations on the Quebec job market through four streams. Quebec, not the federal government, runs the selection: it decides who is invited, assesses your application, and issues a selection certificate. The federal side handles the final permanent residence step. The program is open to people inside Quebec and to applicants abroad, and the first step for everyone is the same: submit an expression of interest in Arrima. You can read Quebec's overview on the official [PSTQ program page](https://www.quebec.ca/en/immigration/permanent/skilled-workers/skilled-worker-selection-program).

## What are the four PSTQ streams?

The PSTQ has four streams, each built around the kind of occupation you intend to work in. Quebec sorts your main occupation using its National Occupational Classification (NOC) code and the related "training, education, experience and responsibilities" (FEER, equivalent to the federal TEER) category. You apply under the stream that matches your occupation, and you must meet both the general requirements and that stream's specific rules. General requirements apply to everyone: you must be 18 or older, intend to settle and work in Quebec, sign a Financial Self-Sufficiency Contract showing you can support yourself for three months, and obtain the attestation of learning democratic and Quebec values. The table below summarizes the four streams.

| Stream | Who it targets | French requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Stream 1: Highly qualified and specialized skills | Main occupation in FEER category 0, 1 or 2, with a qualifying diploma, where no Quebec practice licence is required | Oral French level 7 or higher and written French level 5 or higher on the Échelle québécoise |
| Stream 2: Intermediate and manual skills | Intermediate and manual occupations needing a high school or vocational diploma | Spoken French level 5 or higher |
| Stream 3: Regulated professions | Occupations on the Ministère's list of regulated professions, where a Quebec licence or recognition of equivalence is needed | Level 7 oral and level 5 written for FEER 0, 1, 2; level 5 spoken for FEER 3, 4, 5 |
| Stream 4: Exceptional talent | People with an achievement on the Ministère's list, or a positive opinion from a partner in strategic economic sectors, research, arts or sports | No fixed French level stated on the requirements page; selection rests on exceptional achievement |

You can confirm each stream's exact rules on Quebec's [PSTQ requirements page](https://www.quebec.ca/en/immigration/permanent/skilled-workers/skilled-worker-selection-program/requirements).

## Which PSTQ streams require French, and at what level?

Streams 1, 2, and 3 each require French from the principal applicant, at a level that depends on the stream and the FEER category of your occupation. Stream 1 asks for oral French at level 7 or higher and written French at level 5 or higher on the Échelle québécoise des niveaux de compétence en français. Stream 2 asks for spoken French at level 5 or higher. Stream 3 follows the FEER category: oral level 7 and written level 5 for categories 0, 1 and 2, and spoken level 5 for categories 3, 4 and 5. Stream 4, Exceptional talent, is assessed on achievement, and the requirements page does not state a fixed French level for it, though French is central to selection across the program. An accompanying spouse or common-law partner is asked to show spoken French at level 4 or higher. Quebec accepts specific tests and diplomas as proof, listed on its requirements page. If you are building a French record while working in Canada, our guide to the [Francophone Mobility permanent residence pathway](/news/francophone-mobility-pr-pathway-2026) explains how French-speaking work experience can help.

## How does Arrima work, from declaration of interest to CSQ?

Arrima is Quebec's online platform for the PSTQ. You create an account and submit a declaration of interest, also called an expression of interest, with your age, education, work experience, French level and occupation. Your profile is scored and ranked in Quebec's database. In each invitation round, Quebec targets a stream and a profile, then invites the people with the highest scores until it reaches its target number. If you are invited, you have 30 days to accept in your Arrima account. After you accept, Quebec sends instructions to submit a Demande de sélection permanente (DSP), the formal permanent selection application. Quebec examines that file, and if it approves, it issues a Certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ). Our companion explainer on the [Arrima Quebec immigration portal](/news/arrima-quebec-immigration-portal-2026) walks through account setup. Quebec describes the round process on its [PSTQ invitation page](https://www.quebec.ca/en/immigration/permanent/skilled-workers/skilled-worker-selection-program/invitation).

## What happens after you receive a CSQ?

A Certificat de sélection du Québec is Quebec's decision that it has selected you, but it is not permanent residence by itself. With a valid CSQ you submit a complete permanent residence application to the federal government. At this stage IRCC checks admissibility: it reviews your documents, runs security and criminal background checks, and confirms your identity. Most applicants give fingerprints and a photo, so plan to [give your biometrics](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics.html) once IRCC asks. You and your family members usually also complete an [immigration medical exam](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams.html) with an approved panel physician. The federal process for Quebec-selected applicants is set out on the [Quebec-selected skilled workers process](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/quebec-skilled-workers.html) page, and overall intake sits within the federal [immigration levels plan](/news/canada-immigration-levels-plan-2026).

## What is the June 5, 2026 bridging work permit for PSTQ candidates?

On June 5, 2026, IRCC signed a temporary public policy that helps PSTQ-invited workers keep working in Quebec while their selection is assessed. If you were invited to apply for permanent selection and have submitted a Demande de sélection permanente, you may apply for an employer-specific work permit that lets you keep working for your Quebec employer for up to 12 months. Your employer does not need a new Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA), and you do not file a new LMIA or Quebec Acceptance Certificate. The same policy lets your spouse or common-law partner apply for an open work permit so families stay together during the assessment, a step we cover in our [spouse open work permit](/news/spousal-open-work-permit-canada-2026) guide. The deadline to apply is December 31, 2026, when the policy expires. See the [IRCC work permit instructions for Quebec skilled workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/work-permit-skilled-workers-quebec-pstq.html) and the [temporary public policy on work permits in Quebec](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-instructions-agreements/public-policies/work-permits-qc-pr-2026-2.html).

## How long does the PSTQ take and what does it cost?

The PSTQ has two stages with separate timelines and fees, and both are set by the governments that run them, so they change over time. The Quebec stage covers your Arrima profile, the invitation, your permanent selection application and the CSQ; Quebec sets those processing fees and publishes them on its own pages. The federal stage covers your permanent residence application after the CSQ; IRCC sets those fees and processing times and updates them on canada.ca. Because both change, you should confirm the current amounts and timelines directly on the government pages rather than relying on figures quoted elsewhere. The federal step for Quebec-selected applicants, including how to apply and what to pay, is described on the [Quebec-selected skilled workers process](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/quebec-skilled-workers.html) page.

## What are the most common PSTQ mistakes?

The most frequent mistakes come from treating the PSTQ like a one-step program or underestimating French. People assume a CSQ is permanent residence, when it is only Quebec's selection and must be followed by a federal application. Others let the 30-day window to accept an invitation lapse, which voids their expression of interest. A weak French record is the single biggest gap, since French level decides both eligibility and ranking. Watch for these errors:

- Treating the CSQ as final and skipping the federal permanent residence application to IRCC.
- Missing the 30-day deadline to accept an Arrima invitation, which removes your profile.
- Declaring a main occupation in the wrong stream, or one you no longer intend to practise.
- Filing French test results below your stream's required level.
- Forgetting the Financial Self-Sufficiency Contract or the attestation of Quebec values.

## What else do skilled workers ask about the PSTQ?

These are common questions from skilled workers comparing the PSTQ with other routes to permanent residence in Canada. The answers below are short and point to the government pages that set the rules. Immigration policy changes often, so confirm details against the official Quebec and federal pages before you act, and treat any score or timeline you read elsewhere as informal until a government page confirms it.

### What is the minimum score for arrima Quebec?

There is no single fixed pass mark published ahead of time. Quebec ranks declarations of interest by score, then in each round invites the highest-scoring profiles in a targeted stream until it reaches its target number. The minimum score for that round is simply the score of the last person invited, so it changes from one round to the next and from one stream to another. Quebec states that comparing minimum scores between streams is not useful.

### What happens after I get an Arrima invitation?

You have 30 days from the invitation date to accept it in your Arrima account. Once you accept, Quebec sends a second message explaining how to submit your Demande de sélection permanente. You file that application with supporting documents, and if Quebec approves it, you receive a Certificat de sélection du Québec. With the CSQ you then apply to IRCC for permanent residence. If you do not respond within 30 days, your expression of interest becomes void and is removed from the database.

### Who is eligible for the Quebec skilled worker program?

To qualify you must be at least 18, intend to settle in Quebec to work, and meet both the general requirements and your stream's specific rules. Streams 1, 2, and 3 set a French requirement at a level that depends on your occupation; Stream 4, Exceptional talent, is assessed on achievement and states no fixed French level. You also sign a Financial Self-Sufficiency Contract showing three months of funds and obtain the attestation of learning democratic and Quebec values. Your occupation determines which of the four streams applies to you.

### How can I get PR in Quebec?

For skilled workers, the main route is the PSTQ. Submit an expression of interest in Arrima, wait for an invitation, file your Demande de sélection permanente, and obtain a Certificat de sélection du Québec. The CSQ is Quebec's selection decision; it does not grant status on its own. You then apply to the federal government for permanent residence, and IRCC decides admissibility through document, security and medical checks before approving.

### Is it easier to get PR in Quebec?

Quebec runs its own selection, so the criteria differ from federal Express Entry, and there is no guarantee one route is easier. The PSTQ now puts French at the centre of both eligibility and ranking, so a strong French profile in an in-demand occupation helps. Remember that Quebec selection and federal permanent residence are two separate approvals, and you must pass both to settle permanently in Quebec.

Go Far Global is a licensed Canadian immigration firm in Toronto (RCIC #R515110). Under Canadian law, only a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) licensed by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC), a Canadian lawyer, or a Quebec notary may act as your paid representative. Our team can review your Arrima profile, confirm which PSTQ stream fits your occupation and French level, and prepare both your Quebec selection file and your federal permanent residence application. We do not promise invitations or approvals; Quebec and IRCC make those decisions on their own criteria.

# Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) 2026: Communities, Eligibility, and How to Apply

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/rural-community-immigration-pilot-rcip-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-09
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) is a federal pathway that offers permanent residence (PR) to skilled workers who want to work and settle in smaller and more remote...

*As of June 9, 2026.* The Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) gives skilled workers a path to permanent residence through a job offer from a designated employer in one of 14 participating rural communities, with no Express Entry profile and no Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score required.

> This guide is for foreign workers who want Canadian permanent residence (PR) through a rural job offer. It covers the 14 communities, the exact eligibility rules, the community-recommendation step, fees, and how the program differs from Express Entry.

## What is the Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP)?

The Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) is a federal pathway that offers permanent residence (PR) to skilled workers who want to work and settle in smaller and more remote Canadian communities. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) chose 14 communities that showed they can support and benefit from skilled migrants. Each community approves certain local employers to hire foreign workers for jobs they cannot fill locally. The pilot launched on January 30, 2025, and replaces the former Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot (RNIP), which stopped taking new applications in August 2024. RCIP is employer-driven and community-driven, so the process starts with a job offer rather than an online points ranking. The full federal framework is published on [Canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration.html).

## Which 14 communities are in the RCIP?

There are 14 designated RCIP communities across six provinces: Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia, plus Nova Scotia. Each community runs its own local economic development organization, sets its own priority sectors, and maintains its own list of designated employers and open jobs. You must have a job offer inside one of these 14 communities to apply. The official list and the link to each community's website are on the [IRCC job-offer page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration/job-offer.html).

| Province | RCIP community |
|---|---|
| Nova Scotia | Pictou County |
| Ontario | North Bay |
| Ontario | Sudbury |
| Ontario | Timmins |
| Ontario | Sault Ste. Marie |
| Ontario | Thunder Bay |
| Manitoba | Steinbach |
| Manitoba | Altona/Rhineland |
| Manitoba | Brandon |
| Saskatchewan | Moose Jaw |
| Alberta | Claresholm |
| British Columbia | West Kootenay |
| British Columbia | North Okanagan Shuswap |
| British Columbia | Peace Liard |

## Who is eligible for the Rural Community Immigration Pilot?

To apply for PR under the RCIP, you must have a valid job offer from an approved local employer in one of the 14 communities, hold at least one year (1,560 hours) of related paid work experience in the past three years, prove your language ability with an approved test, hold a Canadian educational credential or the foreign equivalent, and show enough settlement funds to support your family. The work experience can be from inside or outside Canada, but it must connect to the job being offered. International graduates of a publicly funded school in the community may be exempt from the work-experience requirement. These rules are set out on the [IRCC eligibility page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration/eligibility.html).

| Requirement | RCIP rule |
|---|---|
| Job offer | Genuine, full-time, non-seasonal offer from an approved employer in the community |
| Work experience | 1 year (1,560 hours) of related experience in the past 3 years |
| Eligible jobs | National Occupational Classification (NOC) TEER 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 (with limits at TEER 4) |
| Language | Approved test result less than 2 years old |
| Education | Canadian credential or an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) for foreign study |
| Settlement funds | Proof of funds unless already working in Canada on a valid permit |

## What language score does the RCIP require?

The minimum language score depends on the National Occupational Classification (NOC) Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) category of your job offer. For a TEER 0 or 1 job, you need Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 6. For a TEER 2 or 3 job, you need CLB 5. For a TEER 4 or 5 job, you need CLB 4. You must meet the minimum in all four abilities: reading, writing, listening, and speaking. Accepted tests are CELPIP-General, IELTS General Training, and PTE Core in English, or TEF Canada and TCF Canada in French. Results must be less than two years old when you apply, per the [IRCC language page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration/eligibility/language-test.html).

| Job offer NOC TEER | Minimum language level |
|---|---|
| TEER 0 or 1 | CLB 6 |
| TEER 2 or 3 | CLB 5 |
| TEER 4 or 5 | CLB 4 |

## How much money do you need for RCIP settlement funds?

You must prove you have enough money to support yourself and your family after you arrive in Canada, unless you are already working in Canada on a valid work permit. The amount depends on your family size and is updated each year. As of the figures last updated July 29, 2025, a single applicant needs 10,507 Canadian dollars, rising to 27,806 Canadian dollars for a family of seven, with 2,831 Canadian dollars added for each extra person. Your family size must include your spouse or common-law partner and all dependent children, even those who are already Canadian citizens or are not moving with you. The official figures are on the [IRCC proof-of-funds page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration/eligibility/proof-funds.html).

| Family members | Funds required (CAD) |
|---|---:|
| 1 | $10,507 |
| 2 | $13,080 |
| 3 | $16,080 |
| 4 | $19,524 |
| 5 | $22,143 |
| 6 | $24,975 |
| 7 | $27,806 |
| Each additional | +$2,831 |

## How do you apply for the RCIP step by step?

The RCIP is employer-led, so you cannot submit a federal application until a community recommends you. First, find and accept a genuine job offer from one of the community's approved employers. The employer then sends a community-recommendation application to the local community organization. The community checks that the job is in a priority sector or occupation, that the offer is real, and that you meet every pilot requirement. If it agrees, it issues a community recommendation. Only then do you submit your PR application to IRCC. The full sequence is described on the [IRCC job-offer page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration/job-offer.html).

1. Secure a full-time, non-seasonal job offer from an approved employer in an RCIP community.
2. The employer submits a community-recommendation application on your behalf.
3. The community verifies the offer, your eligibility, and that the job meets a local priority.
4. You receive a community recommendation if approved.
5. You apply to IRCC for permanent residence and pay the fees.

## How much does the RCIP cost?

The RCIP uses the standard IRCC permanent residence fees for economic programs. As of April 30, 2026, the processing fee for the principal applicant is 990 Canadian dollars, and the same 990 Canadian dollars applies to an accompanying spouse or common-law partner. Each accompanying dependent child costs 270 Canadian dollars. The Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF) is 600 Canadian dollars per adult and is paid before PR is granted. A single applicant therefore pays about 1,590 Canadian dollars in federal fees. The amount owed is based on the fee in effect when you pay, not when you apply. Always confirm current amounts on the [IRCC fee list](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/information/fees/fees.asp).

| Fee item | Amount (CAD) |
|---|---:|
| Principal applicant processing | $990 |
| Spouse or common-law partner processing | $990 |
| Dependent child processing (each) | $270 |
| Right of Permanent Residence Fee (per adult) | $600 |
| Single applicant total (processing + RPRF) | $1,590 |

## How is the RCIP different from Express Entry?

The RCIP does not use Express Entry, a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score, or an Expression of Interest (EOI) ranking. There is no points draw and no cut-off score. Your route to PR is a designated job offer plus a community recommendation, not a ranked pool. This makes the pilot useful for applicants whose CRS score is too low for federal Express Entry draws but who can secure a genuine rural job offer. The trade-off is that you must commit to living and working in a small community, and the application cannot start until an approved employer hires you and the community recommends you. Express Entry programs are managed separately by IRCC at [Canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html).

## How did the RCIP perform in its first year?

The RCIP opened to its first communities in 2025 and welcomed more than 1,000 newcomers to permanent residence during its first year of operation. Ontario communities such as Sudbury and Thunder Bay issued the highest volumes of community recommendations, reflecting strong local labour demand. Because each community sets its own employer list and priority occupations, the number of openings and the speed of recommendations vary widely between communities. The pilot is scheduled to continue through 2026 and is one of the regional economic pathways IRCC reports on in its annual planning to Parliament. The program overview and current status are maintained on [Canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration.html).

## Frequently asked questions

### Who is eligible for rural community immigration pilot?

You are eligible if you have a valid job offer from an approved employer in one of the 14 RCIP communities, at least one year (1,560 hours) of related work experience in the past three years, an approved language test result meeting the level for your job's TEER category, a Canadian educational credential or a foreign-equivalent assessment, and enough settlement funds. International graduates from a local publicly funded school may be exempt from the work-experience requirement. See the [IRCC eligibility page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration/eligibility.html).

### Is IELTS required for RCIP?

IELTS is not the only option. You must take an IRCC-approved test, which for English means CELPIP-General, IELTS General Training, or PTE Core. French speakers can take TEF Canada or TCF Canada. The minimum level depends on your job's NOC TEER category: CLB 6 for TEER 0 or 1, CLB 5 for TEER 2 or 3, and CLB 4 for TEER 4 or 5. Results must be less than two years old when you apply.

### What are the 11 communities for the rural and northern immigration pilot?

The 11-community figure refers to the older Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot (RNIP), which closed to new applications in August 2024. Its successor, the RCIP, has 14 designated communities, not 11. The RCIP communities are Pictou County, North Bay, Sudbury, Timmins, Sault Ste. Marie, Thunder Bay, Steinbach, Altona/Rhineland, Brandon, Moose Jaw, Claresholm, West Kootenay, North Okanagan Shuswap, and Peace Liard.

### What are the criticisms of RCIP?

Some local RCIP organizations have publicly warned about employers allegedly charging applicants money in exchange for a job offer endorsed under the pilot. Paying for a job offer is not allowed, and a recommendation obtained that way can lead to refusal or removal. A genuine offer comes from a designated employer at no cost to the worker. If an employer asks you to pay for a position or a community recommendation, treat it as a warning sign and verify the employer through the community's official website.

### Is TR to PR coming back in 2026?

The Temporary Resident to Permanent Resident (TR to PR) pathway is a separate program from the RCIP and is managed by IRCC on its own schedule. If you are in a rural community on a valid work permit, the RCIP itself can be your route to PR through a designated employer and a community recommendation, without waiting for any temporary-to-permanent stream to reopen. Always confirm the status of any pathway directly on [Canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada.html).

### Which province is easy to get PR in Canada in 2026?

There is no single easiest province, because each economic program has different demand and criteria. The RCIP spreads opportunity across Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, and Nova Scotia, and your best province depends on where an approved employer will hire you. For applicants with a lower CRS score, a rural job offer through the RCIP can be more attainable than a federal Express Entry draw, since it does not rank candidates by points.
