# Manitoba PNP (MPNP) 2026: Streams, EOI Points, Draws, and How to Apply

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/manitoba-pnp-mpnp-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-09
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program (MPNP) is Manitoba's economic immigration stream that lets the province nominate skilled workers, graduates, and business investors for...

*As of June 9, 2026.* The Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program (MPNP) ranks candidates on a 900-point Expression of Interest (EOI) grid and issued 906 Letters of Advice to Apply in its largest single draw of the year on May 7, 2026.

> This guide is for skilled workers, international graduates, and entrepreneurs who want a Manitoba provincial nomination toward Canadian permanent residence. You will learn the active streams, how the EOI points system works, the recent 2026 draws, the fees, and the step-by-step application process.

## What is the Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program (MPNP) in 2026?

The Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program (MPNP) is Manitoba's economic immigration stream that lets the province nominate skilled workers, graduates, and business investors for Canadian permanent residence (PR). Manitoba launched the first Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) in Canada in 1998. To select candidates, Manitoba runs an Expression of Interest (EOI) pool: you submit a free online profile, receive a ranking score out of 900 points, and the province issues a Letter of Advice to Apply (LAA) to the highest-ranked or targeted candidates. A provincial nomination adds 600 points to a candidate's Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score in the federal Express Entry system, which effectively guarantees an invitation to apply for PR. For 2026, the federal government allocated 91,500 nominations across all provinces, up from 55,000 in 2025.

## Which MPNP streams are open in 2026?

The MPNP runs three main streams in 2026, each split into pathways for different candidate profiles. The Skilled Worker Stream serves workers already in Manitoba and qualified workers abroad with a connection to the province. The International Education Stream serves recent graduates of Manitoba post-secondary institutions. The Business Investor Stream serves entrepreneurs and farm investors who will start or buy a business in Manitoba. Each stream has its own eligibility rules, but every candidate first submits an EOI profile and waits to be invited. The table below summarizes the active streams and pathways.

| Stream | Pathway | Who it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Skilled Worker Stream | Skilled Worker in Manitoba (SWM) | Temporary workers and graduates already employed in Manitoba |
| Skilled Worker Stream | Skilled Worker Overseas (SWO) | Qualified workers abroad with a Manitoba connection or direct invitation |
| International Education Stream | Career Employment Pathway | Manitoba graduates with a one-year job offer in their field |
| International Education Stream | Graduate Internship Pathway | Master's and doctoral graduates completing a Mitacs internship |
| International Education Stream | International Student Entrepreneur Pilot | Graduates launching a Manitoba business |
| Business Investor Stream | Entrepreneur Pathway | Investors starting or buying a Manitoba business |
| Business Investor Stream | Farm Investor Pathway | Investors establishing a farm operation in rural Manitoba |

## Who is eligible for Manitoba PNP?

Because the MPNP is an economic program, every applicant must be an employable, adaptable skilled worker with job-ready English or French, enough settlement funds, and a genuine intention to settle in Manitoba. Eligibility depends on the stream. Skilled Worker in Manitoba applicants need ongoing employment with a Manitoba employer, usually after six months of continuous work. Skilled Worker Overseas applicants must show an established connection to Manitoba, such as a close relative or supporter who has lived in the province for at least a year, prior study or work in Manitoba, or a direct invitation through a Strategic Recruitment Initiative. International Education Stream applicants must have graduated from an eligible Manitoba institution. All Skilled Worker applicants must also score at least 60 points on the MPNP self-assessment grid to be allowed to apply.

### Language and education minimums

Language is scored by Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB), a federal scale that maps your IELTS General Training or CELPIP-General result to a band. For occupations classified at National Occupational Classification (NOC) TEER 4 or 5, the minimum is CLB 4. Most professional and skilled-trade roles need CLB 5 or higher. Education must be assessed against Canadian standards, usually through an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) for credentials earned outside Canada.

## How do MPNP Expression of Interest (EOI) points work?

The MPNP scores each EOI profile out of a maximum of 900 points across six factors: language proficiency, age, work experience, education, adaptability, and a risk-assessment deduction. Adaptability carries the most weight at 500 points, which rewards a long-term Manitoba job offer, close family ties, prior Manitoba study or work, or a Strategic Recruitment invitation. Connections to other provinces can deduct up to 200 points. Your profile stays in the pool for one year, and you can hold only one active EOI at a time. Reaching the 60-point self-assessment threshold lets you apply; the 900-point EOI grid then decides your rank in the pool. The table below shows the maximum points per factor.

| EOI factor | Maximum points |
|---|---:|
| Language proficiency | 125 |
| Age | 75 |
| Work experience | 175 |
| Education | 125 |
| Adaptability | 500 |
| Risk assessment (deduction) | -200 |
| Maximum total | 900 |

## What were the recent Manitoba PNP draws in 2026?

In 2026, Manitoba shifted from broad highest-score draws to targeted occupation-specific and Strategic Recruitment rounds, so most 2026 draw notices no longer publish a single lowest-score cutoff per category. The largest round of the year was Draw #270 on May 7, 2026, which issued 906 Letters of Advice to Apply, including 431 to occupation-specific candidates in education roles such as teachers and early childhood educators. Manitoba invited more than 7,700 candidates across 2025 and holds a 2026 federal allocation of roughly 6,239 nominations. Of the 906 LAAs in Draw #270, 326 went to candidates who declared a valid Express Entry profile number. The table below lists the most recent confirmed 2026 draws.

| Draw | Date | LAAs issued | Notable detail |
|---|---|---:|---|
| #271 | May 21, 2026 | 96 | Skilled Worker Stream, Strategic Recruitment; International Education not eligible |
| #270 | May 7, 2026 | 906 | Largest 2026 round; 431 to education occupations; 326 Express Entry profiles |
| #269 | April 23, 2026 | 308 | 192 to health occupations; 105 Express Entry profiles |

## How long does Manitoba PNP take to process?

The MPNP currently states that its processing commitment exceeds six months from the date you submit a complete application, because of high application volumes. The full timeline is longer once federal steps are added. After you receive a Letter of Advice to Apply, you have 60 days to submit your complete MPNP application. Once Manitoba nominates you, you apply to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) for permanent residence. Express Entry-aligned PR applications are processed within published service standards once submitted, while non-Express Entry (paper-based) provincial nominee applications take longer. Plan for roughly 12 to 24 months total from EOI submission to a PR decision, depending on stream, document readiness, and whether you apply through Express Entry.

## How much does the Manitoba PNP cost in 2026?

The MPNP charges a non-refundable provincial application fee of $500 CAD for most streams. The Business Investor Stream and the International Student Entrepreneur Pilot cost $2,500 CAD because of the added due-diligence review. These provincial fees are separate from the federal permanent residence fees you pay to IRCC after Manitoba nominates you. Federal economic-class fees increased on April 30, 2026. The principal applicant now pays a $990 processing fee plus the $600 Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF), for a combined $1,590 CAD. Additional family members each pay their own processing fees. The table below summarizes the main costs.

| Fee | Amount (CAD) | Paid to |
|---|---:|---|
| MPNP application (most streams) | $500 | Manitoba |
| MPNP application (Business / Student Entrepreneur) | $2,500 | Manitoba |
| Federal PR processing fee (principal applicant) | $990 | IRCC |
| Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF) | $600 | IRCC |
| Federal combined (principal applicant) | $1,590 | IRCC |

## How do I apply to the Manitoba PNP in 2026?

You apply to the MPNP in two phases: the Expression of Interest, then the full provincial application, followed by the separate federal PR application. The process is the same across Skilled Worker pathways, with stream-specific documents required at each stage. Follow these steps:

1. Confirm you meet at least 60 points on the MPNP self-assessment and have an eligible stream connection.
2. Take an MPNP-approved language test (IELTS General Training or CELPIP-General), valid within two years.
3. Submit your free EOI profile online and receive your ranking score out of 900.
4. Wait in the pool. If invited, you receive a Letter of Advice to Apply.
5. Submit your complete MPNP application within 60 days, with the $500 fee and all documents.
6. Receive your provincial nomination certificate after assessment.
7. Apply to IRCC for permanent residence, either through Express Entry (where the nomination adds 600 CRS points) or the non-Express Entry paper process.

## How does the Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) work for Manitoba?

The Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) is a permanent federal pathway launched in 2025 that succeeds the closed Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot (RNIP). It is run by IRCC, not the MPNP, but three Manitoba communities participate: Brandon, Steinbach, and Altona/Rhineland. RCIP gives skilled foreign workers a route to PR if they have a genuine job offer from a designated employer in a participating community plus a community recommendation from the local economic development organization. The pilot covers 14 communities across Canada. Core requirements include at least one year (1,560 hours) of qualifying work experience in the past three years, a Canadian Language Benchmark level set by the job's NOC TEER (CLB 4 to CLB 6), an education credential or ECA, and settlement funds scaled to family size. The table below lists the participating communities.

| Province | RCIP communities |
|---|---|
| Manitoba | Brandon, Steinbach, Altona/Rhineland |
| Ontario | North Bay, Sudbury, Timmins, Sault Ste. Marie, Thunder Bay |
| Nova Scotia | Pictou County |
| Saskatchewan | Moose Jaw |
| Alberta | Claresholm |
| British Columbia | West Kootenay, North Okanagan-Shuswap, Peace Liard |

## What do applicants most often ask about the Manitoba PNP?

These are the questions Canadians and newcomers ask most often about the Manitoba Provincial Nominee Program (MPNP). Answers reflect current program rules as published by Manitoba Immigration and IRCC. For guidance specific to your immigration profile, consult a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC).

### Who is eligible for Manitoba PNP?
Because the MPNP is an economic program, all applicants must be employable, adaptable skilled workers with job-ready English or French, sufficient settlement funds, and a genuine intention to settle in Manitoba as permanent residents. Skilled Worker applicants must also score at least 60 points on the MPNP self-assessment and meet a stream connection, such as ongoing Manitoba employment, an established connection for overseas applicants, or graduation from a Manitoba institution.

### Is Manitoba still doing PNP?
Yes. The MPNP is active in 2026 and held its largest draw of the year on May 7, 2026, issuing 906 Letters of Advice to Apply. Manitoba nominates several thousand candidates each year and held a 2026 federal allocation of roughly 6,239 nominations. The program continues to run regular EOI draws.

### How much time does Manitoba PNP take?
The MPNP's published processing commitment exceeds six months from the date a complete application is submitted, due to high application volumes. Once Manitoba nominates you, you apply separately to IRCC for permanent residence. Counting the EOI wait, provincial assessment, and federal PR processing, plan for roughly 12 to 24 months in total, depending on your stream and whether you apply through Express Entry.

### What is the cut off for Manitoba PNP points?
You must score at least 60 points on the MPNP self-assessment worksheet to be eligible to apply. If you score below 60, you cannot apply. Separately, your Expression of Interest profile is ranked out of a maximum 900 points, and Manitoba invites the highest-ranked or targeted candidates. In 2026, many draws are occupation-specific, so the province does not always publish a single category cutoff.

### Is IELTS required for Manitoba PNP?
A language test is required, but not specifically IELTS. The MPNP accepts IELTS General Training (English) or CELPIP-General (English), and for French it accepts the TEF or TCF. Your results must be from a test taken no more than two years before you submit your MPNP online application.

### Which province gives PR fastest?
There is no single fastest province; processing depends on the stream, your profile, and whether you apply through Express Entry, which carries faster federal service standards than the paper process. Manitoba's MPNP processing commitment exceeds six months at the provincial stage. Programs like Saskatchewan's SINP and Manitoba's MPNP run frequent draws, but speed varies by occupation demand and draw targeting rather than by a fixed ranking.

# Alberta PNP (AAIP) 2026: Streams, Draws, Eligibility, and How to Apply

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/alberta-pnp-aaip-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-06-09
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Alberta Advantage Immigration Program (AAIP) is Alberta's Provincial Nominee Program (PNP).

*As of June 9, 2026.* Alberta plans to nominate 6,403 people for permanent residence through the Alberta Advantage Immigration Program in 2026, and the Alberta Opportunity Stream draw on May 27, 2026 invited 993 candidates at a minimum score of 51.

> This guide is for skilled workers, international graduates, and entrepreneurs who want Alberta to nominate them for Canadian permanent residence. It covers the current streams, the 2026 draw history with cut-off scores, eligibility, fees, and how the application works step by step.

## What is the Alberta Advantage Immigration Program (AAIP)?

The Alberta Advantage Immigration Program (AAIP) is Alberta's Provincial Nominee Program (PNP). It is an economic immigration program run by the Government of Alberta that nominates people for permanent residence so they can live and work in the province. AAIP does not grant permanent residence on its own. Alberta selects you, and then Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) decides your federal permanent residence application. A provincial nomination is a recommendation to the federal government that you can fill a labour gap in Alberta. The program is sometimes still called the Alberta Immigrant Nominee Program (AINP), its former name. The provincial overview is published on the official [Alberta Advantage Immigration Program page](https://www.alberta.ca/alberta-advantage-immigration-program), and IRCC explains the federal side on its [provincial nominee](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html) page.

## Is Alberta PNP still open in 2026?

Yes. AAIP is open and actively issuing invitations in 2026. The province is working through a large Expression of Interest (EOI) pool, runs draws as labour-market needs require, and has set a 2026 nomination allocation of 6,403 spaces across all streams. As of early June 2026 the worker streams held tens of thousands of candidates in the EOI pool, and Alberta continues to draw from them on no fixed schedule. AAIP draws are not regularly timed. The province selects candidates as it needs to, based on EOI score rankings, provincial labour priorities, available nominations, and current application volumes. You can confirm the live status, remaining spaces, and recent activity on the official [AAIP processing information](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-processing-information) page before you apply.

## What streams does AAIP have?

AAIP runs eight streams, split into four worker streams and four entrepreneur streams. The worker streams cover most skilled workers and graduates already in Alberta or in the federal Express Entry pool. The entrepreneur streams cover people who want to start, buy, or run a business or farm in the province. Each stream has its own eligibility rules, fees, and selection process, and most worker streams now run through the ranked EOI intake system. The table below lists every current stream and who each one targets, drawn from the provincial [AAIP application streams](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-application-streams) page.

| Category | Stream | Who it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Worker | Alberta Opportunity Stream | Workers in Alberta with a valid work permit and an eligible job offer |
| Worker | Alberta Express Entry Stream | Candidates already in the federal Express Entry pool, in priority occupations |
| Worker | Rural Renewal Stream | Candidates with a job offer in a designated rural Alberta community |
| Worker | Tourism and Hospitality Stream | Workers with a full-time job offer in Alberta tourism and hospitality |
| Entrepreneur | Rural Entrepreneur Stream | People starting or buying a business in a rural Alberta community |
| Entrepreneur | Graduate Entrepreneur Stream | Graduates of approved Alberta post-secondary institutions starting a business |
| Entrepreneur | Foreign Graduate Entrepreneur Stream | Foreign graduates launching a start-up with a designated agency |
| Entrepreneur | Farm Stream | Experienced farmers buying or starting a farm in Alberta |

## Who is eligible for Alberta PNP?

Eligibility depends on the stream, but most applicants qualify through one of two routes. The Alberta Opportunity Stream is for people already working in Alberta on a valid work permit with a full-time job offer in an eligible occupation. Language requirements scale by National Occupational Classification (NOC) category. Roles in NOC Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) levels 0, 1, 2, and 3 need Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 5 in each skill, while TEER 4 and 5 roles need CLB 4. The Express Entry Stream is for candidates who already have an active federal profile with a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score of at least 300, in an occupation Alberta is targeting. The Opportunity Stream rules are set out on the [Alberta Opportunity Stream eligibility](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-alberta-opportunity-stream-eligibility) page.

### Alberta Express Entry priority pathways

Within this stream, the province targets specific groups through dedicated pathways and priority sectors. These include the Dedicated Health Care Pathway, the Accelerated Tech Pathway, the Law Enforcement Pathway, and priority sectors such as construction, agriculture, aviation, and manufacturing. The detailed rules are on the [Alberta Express Entry eligibility](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-alberta-express-entry-stream-eligibility) page.

## How does the AAIP EOI ranking and scoring work?

Most AAIP worker streams use a ranked EOI system rather than first-come, first-served intake. You submit a profile, the province scores and ranks it, and only the highest-ranked candidates in each draw receive an invitation to apply. Your EOI score combines factors such as education, language ability, Alberta work experience, and a valid job offer. Alberta then issues invitations based on your score ranking, its labour-market priorities, the nominations it has left, and how many applications it is already processing. A higher EOI score and an occupation in a priority sector both improve your odds. Submitting an EOI does not guarantee an invitation, and the cut-off score changes from draw to draw. The selection mechanics are described on the [AAIP processing information](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-processing-information) page.

## What were the recent Alberta PNP draws and cut-off scores?

Alberta runs frequent, targeted draws rather than one large round. In 2026 it has held separate draws for the Alberta Opportunity Stream, the Rural Renewal Stream, and several Express Entry Stream pathways and priority sectors, each with its own minimum score. Cut-offs have been low compared with the federal pool, often between 48 and 55, because AAIP scores on a different scale. The table below shows the most recent draws recorded on the provincial processing page. Always check the live [AAIP processing information](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-processing-information) page for the latest round, since draw dates and scores change week to week.

| Draw date | Stream or pathway | Minimum score | Invitations |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| June 2, 2026 | Express Entry, Priority Sectors (Manufacturing) | 53 | 49 |
| May 29, 2026 | Express Entry, Accelerated Tech Pathway | 55 | 200 |
| May 27, 2026 | Alberta Opportunity Stream | 51 | 993 |
| May 25, 2026 | Rural Renewal Stream | 50 | 83 |
| May 22, 2026 | Express Entry, Priority Sectors (Agriculture) | 48 | 76 |

## How much does an AAIP application cost?

AAIP charges separate fees for submitting an Expression of Interest and for the application itself, and the amounts differ for worker and entrepreneur streams. Effective April 7, 2026, Alberta introduced a $135 non-refundable Worker Expression of Interest (WEOI) fee, charged whether or not you receive an invitation. The worker stream application fee is $1,500. Entrepreneur streams cost more, with a $3,500 application fee. These are provincial fees only. You also pay separate federal fees to IRCC when you apply for permanent residence after a nomination. The table below summarises the provincial costs published on the [AAIP updates](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-updates) page.

| Fee | Amount (CAD) | Applies to |
|---|---:|---|
| Worker Expression of Interest fee | $135 | Worker streams (from April 7, 2026) |
| Worker application fee | $1,500 | Worker streams |
| Entrepreneur application fee | $3,500 | Entrepreneur streams |

## How does AAIP connect to Express Entry and the 600 points?

The Alberta Express Entry Stream is enhanced, meaning a nomination is tied to the federal selection system. If Alberta nominates you and you accept, you receive 600 additional points on your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score. That is the maximum a nomination can add, and you can only receive it once. With 600 extra points, you are effectively guaranteed an invitation to apply for permanent residence in the next federal round. IRCC explains this on its [get or confirm a nomination](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees/express-entry/get-confirm-nomination.html) page, and the point allocation is set out in the [Comprehensive Ranking System criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html). Base or non-Express Entry nominations work on paper instead and do not add CRS points, as described on the IRCC [Provincial Nominee Program Express Entry process](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees/express-entry.html) page.

## How do I apply for Alberta PNP?

For the worker streams, you apply in two stages. First, you submit a ranked EOI profile and wait to be invited. Second, if you receive an invitation to apply, you submit a full application with documents and fees within the deadline. The general steps are below, but always confirm the current process on the official [AAIP application streams](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-application-streams) page, since intake rules change.

1. Confirm which stream fits your situation and check the eligibility page for that stream.
2. Build or update your federal Express Entry profile if you are applying through that stream.
3. Submit a Worker Expression of Interest and pay the $135 WEOI fee.
4. Wait for a draw. If your score meets the cut-off, you receive an invitation to apply.
5. Submit the full application with supporting documents and the $1,500 worker application fee.
6. If nominated, apply to IRCC for permanent residence and pay the federal fees.

## What is the Rural Community Immigration Pilot, and is Alberta in it?

The Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) is a separate, federal permanent residence pathway launched by IRCC in 2025, replacing the older Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot. It offers permanent residence to skilled workers who want to live and work in one of 14 designated rural communities across six provinces. In Alberta, the only participating community is Claresholm, which launched its pilot on April 29, 2025. To qualify you need a job offer from a designated employer in the community, a recommendation from that community's economic development organization, qualifying work experience, language and education that meet the pilot's thresholds, and proof of settlement funds. The federal rules are on the [Rural Community Immigration Pilot](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration.html) page and the [Rural Community Immigration Pilots who can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-franco-pilots/rural-immigration/eligibility.html) page.

| Province | RCIP communities |
|---|---|
| Ontario | North Bay, Sudbury, Timmins, Sault Ste. Marie, Thunder Bay |
| Manitoba | Steinbach, Altona/Rhineland, Brandon |
| British Columbia | West Kootenay, North Okanagan-Shuswap, Peace Liard |
| Alberta | Claresholm |
| Saskatchewan | Moose Jaw |
| Nova Scotia | Pictou County |

## Frequently asked questions

**Who is eligible for PNP in Alberta?**

Most people qualify through the Alberta Opportunity Stream or the Alberta Express Entry Stream. The Opportunity Stream needs a valid Alberta work permit, a full-time job offer in an eligible occupation, and Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 4 or 5 depending on your National Occupational Classification (NOC) level. The Express Entry route needs an active federal profile with a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score of at least 300 in an occupation Alberta is targeting. Entrepreneur and rural streams have their own rules.

**Is Alberta PNP still open?**

Yes. AAIP is open and issuing invitations in 2026, with a nomination allocation of 6,403 spaces. The province draws from its candidate pool as labour needs require, so there is no permanent closure, but individual streams can fill or pause. Check the [AAIP processing information](https://www.alberta.ca/aaip-processing-information) page for live status and remaining spaces.

**What is the lowest score for PNP Alberta?**

Alberta scores candidates on its own EOI scale, not the federal Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS), so the numbers look low. In recent 2026 draws, minimum scores ranged from about 48 for the Express Entry agriculture priority sector to 55 for the Accelerated Tech Pathway. The cut-off changes every draw and differs by stream, so there is no single fixed minimum.

**What is the AOS Alberta draw 2026?**

AOS refers to the Alberta Opportunity Stream. In 2026 the province has held Alberta Opportunity Stream draws from its EOI pool. The most recent recorded round, on May 27, 2026, invited 993 candidates at a minimum score of 51. Draw dates and scores are not fixed and are published on the official AAIP processing page.

**Which province gives PR fast?**

Speed depends on your profile, not just the province. An enhanced Alberta nomination adds 600 Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points, which usually guarantees a federal invitation in the next round and is one of the faster routes once you are nominated. Federal processing after a provincial nomination is generally quicker for Express Entry-linked applications than for base, paper-based nominations. Each province sets its own occupation rules, so the right choice depends on your job, language, and experience.

# Licensed Immigration Consultant vs Ghost Consultant: How to Choose a Real Representative (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/licensed-immigration-consultant-vs-ghost-consultant-2026
Category: Guides
Published: 2026-06-07
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Only an RCIC, a lawyer, or a Quebec notary can legally charge to handle your Canadian immigration application. Here is how to verify yours and avoid ghost consultants.

*As of June 7, 2026.*

Choosing who handles your Canadian immigration file is one of the highest-stakes decisions you will make. A licensed representative can guide your application correctly. An unauthorized "ghost consultant" can sink it, get you banned, and take your money with no recourse. This guide explains who may legally charge you for immigration advice, how to verify them in minutes, the real penalties for using an unauthorized rep, and what the new rules coming into force on July 15, 2026 change.

## Who can legally charge you for Canadian immigration advice?

Short answer: Three categories of professionals may charge a fee to advise on or represent your Canadian immigration or citizenship application. First, a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) in good standing with the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). Second, a lawyer who is a member in good standing of a Canadian provincial or territorial law society. Third, a notary who is a member in good standing of the Chambre des notaires du Québec. Ontario paralegals are a narrow exception, not a fourth full category: the Law Society of Ontario limits them to representation before the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB), such as refugee and detention hearings, so they cannot prepare or advise on IRCC applications unless they also hold a CICC licence. Anyone else who takes money to advise you is operating outside the law, and Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) may return or refuse your application as a result.

## What is a ghost consultant, and why are they dangerous?

Short answer: A ghost consultant is an unauthorized person who takes payment for immigration advice or who completes your application but stays hidden from IRCC. They do not appear on your Use of a Representative form (IMM 5476), so on paper it looks like you did everything yourself. That secrecy is the point. It hides an unlicensed operator from any regulator. Ghost consultants often work from outside Canada, demand cash or untraceable payment such as cryptocurrency, promise guaranteed results, and pressure clients to submit false information. When the file goes wrong, they vanish. You carry the consequences, not them.

## How do I verify an RCIC on the CICC public register?

Short answer: Use the CICC public register to confirm a consultant is licensed and "active." Search the consultant's name or licence number on the CICC website, and confirm the status shows active with no suspension. For a lawyer, check the relevant provincial or territorial law society directory. For a Quebec notary, check the Chambre des notaires du Québec. IRCC's own page, "Find out if your representative is authorized," walks you through exactly which body to check for each type of representative. Verification takes minutes and is free, so do it before you sign anything or send any money.

## Authorized vs unauthorized representatives: what is the difference?

Short answer: An authorized representative is licensed by a recognized regulator, can be named on your IMM 5476, and is accountable for misconduct. An unauthorized representative has no licence, hides from IRCC, and answers to no one. The table below lays out the practical differences so you can tell them apart fast.

| Feature | Authorized representative | Unauthorized (ghost) consultant |
|---|---|---|
| Licensed regulator | CICC, a law society, or Chambre des notaires du Québec | None |
| Listed on a public register | Yes, searchable and verifiable | No |
| Named on IMM 5476 | Yes | Hidden, often absent |
| Accountable for misconduct | Yes, can be disciplined | No recourse |
| Typical payment request | Transparent fee, written agreement | Cash, wire, or crypto, often upfront |
| Guarantees a visa | Never, outcomes depend on IRCC | Often "guarantees" approval |

## What are the penalties for using an unauthorized representative?

Short answer: The risks fall on you, the applicant. If a ghost consultant submits false or misleading information, IRCC can make a misrepresentation finding under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). That commonly means your application is refused and you receive a five-year ban from entering Canada. You also lose whatever fees you paid, and because the ghost operates outside any regulator, you have no professional body to complain to and little chance of recovering your money. A single dishonest filing can cost years of your immigration plans.

## What are the warning signs of a ghost consultant?

Short answer: A few red flags reliably signal an unauthorized operator. Watch for anyone who guarantees a visa or permanent residence, since no honest representative can promise an IRCC outcome. Be cautious if they ask for cash, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency, refuse to put fees in writing, or will not give you a licence number to verify. Other signals include pressure to lie on forms, reluctance to be named on your IMM 5476, no verifiable Canadian office, and vague answers about their qualifications. If a representative dodges your verification questions, stop and check the register before going further.

## What changed in the 2026 CICC regulations?

Short answer: On May 6, 2026, the Honourable Lena Metlege Diab, Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, announced new regulations to strengthen oversight of licensed consultants. The regulations take effect July 15, 2026. They expand the authority of the CICC, strengthen its complaints and discipline process, and add increased penalties for consultants who break the rules. They also give the minister power to appoint someone to take over board duties if the board fails to protect the public interest, and set guidelines for a compensation fund for people who suffer financial loss from a consultant's dishonest acts.

| Change (announced May 6, 2026) | What it does | Effective |
|---|---|---|
| Stronger complaints and discipline process | CICC can act faster on misconduct, with increased penalties | July 15, 2026 |
| Compensation fund guidelines | Helps victims of a consultant's dishonest acts recover losses | July 15, 2026 |
| Ministerial intervention power | Minister can appoint someone to run the board if it fails the public | July 15, 2026 |
| Expanded public register | More information published on each licensed consultant | Beginning April 2027 |

## Does the 2026 rule change protect me from ghost consultants?

Short answer: The 2026 regulations strengthen the system, but they regulate licensed consultants, not unlicensed ghosts. A stronger CICC with sharper discipline powers and a compensation fund gives clients of licensed RCICs more protection if something goes wrong. The expanded public register, planned to start in April 2027, makes verification easier and increases transparency. None of that helps if you hire someone who is not licensed in the first place, because ghost consultants sit outside the College's reach. The new rules raise the value of choosing a verified, licensed representative and verifying them yourself.

## How much does a licensed immigration consultant cost?

Short answer: Fees vary by case type and complexity, so there is no single rate, and you should always get the fee in writing before you start. A licensed RCIC, lawyer, or Quebec notary will give you a clear written service agreement that lists what is included and the total cost. Be wary of anyone quoting a price only verbally, demanding the full amount in cash upfront, or attaching a "guaranteed approval" to the fee. Honest representatives price their work, not the IRCC decision, which they cannot control.

## Can I get free immigration advice instead of paying a consultant?

Short answer: Yes. You can apply yourself using IRCC's free official guides and forms on canada.ca, which set out eligibility, documents, and steps for each program. Some settlement agencies and community organizations also offer free or low-cost help, and they are not charging you for representation. The key legal line is payment: if you pay anyone for advice or representation, that person must be authorized. Free self-help is fine. Paid help from an unlicensed person is not, and it can jeopardize your application.

## How do I report a suspected ghost consultant?

Short answer: Report unauthorized representatives so IRCC and regulators can act. You can submit a complaint about a licensed consultant's conduct to the CICC, and report fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. IRCC's "Protect yourself from immigration fraud" page and its "Report scams, fraud or abuse" page explain how to file a report and what details to include. Reporting protects other applicants from the same operator, even if you have already been affected.

That means our representatives are on the public register, named on your Use of a Representative form (IMM 5476), bound by professional standards, and accountable to a regulator. You can verify us before you ever sign, which is exactly what you should do with any representative. We give you a written fee agreement, honest answers about your real options, and no false promises about IRCC outcomes. # Exchanging Your Driver's Licence in Canada as a Newcomer (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/exchange-drivers-licence-canada-newcomers-2026
Category: Settlement
Published: 2026-06-07
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Driving is one of the first practical problems newcomers face after landing in Canada.

*As of June 7, 2026.*

Driving is one of the first practical problems newcomers face after landing in Canada. You can usually drive on your home licence for a short window, but that window is short and it varies by province. After it closes, you need a licence issued by your province or territory. Some newcomers can swap their foreign licence for a Canadian one with no road test; others have to sit knowledge and road tests or enter graduated licensing. This guide explains the grace period, the International Driving Permit, and how provincial exchange agreements decide whether you test or simply exchange. Licensing in Canada is run by each province and territory, so confirm the rules where you live before you drive.

## How long can I drive on my foreign licence in Canada?

Short answer: You can usually drive on a valid foreign licence for a short time after you become a resident, but the exact period is set by your province or territory, and it is often shorter than people expect. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) states that if you have a valid licence from your home country, you will probably be able to use it to drive in Canada for a short time after you arrive, and it directs you to check with your provincial or territorial government for details. In Ontario the window is 60 days. In Alberta you must exchange within 90 days of moving. Once that period ends, your home licence is no longer valid for driving here, so apply for a provincial licence before the deadline rather than after it.

## Do I need an International Driving Permit (IDP) in Canada?

Short answer: An International Driving Permit (IDP) helps if your licence is not in English or French, but it is a translation, not a licence on its own. IRCC advises that if you plan to use a foreign driver's licence in Canada, you should get an IDP in your home country, because it gives you a translation of your licence into French and English. You must carry it together with your original licence, since the IDP alone has no legal standing. The most important detail is timing: you have to obtain the IDP before you leave home. Canadian offices do not issue IDPs for foreign licences, so a newcomer who skips this step in their home country cannot fix it after arrival.

## Can I transfer my foreign licence to a Canadian one?

Short answer: Often yes, and whether you face a road test depends entirely on where your licence was issued. Provinces sign reciprocal exchange agreements with specific countries, states, and territories. If your licence comes from a jurisdiction on your province's agreement list and you have enough driving experience, you exchange it for a full Canadian licence without knowledge or road tests, usually after a vision test. If your jurisdiction is not on the list, you generally enter the graduated licensing stream and pass the required tests. You surrender your foreign licence when you exchange it, so keep a photocopy for your records before you hand it over.

## Which countries' driving licence can be exchanged in Canada?

Short answer: It depends on your province, because each province keeps its own agreement list, but the common pattern is that long-established licensing countries qualify for test-free exchange. As an example, Ontario has reciprocal agreements with all Canadian provinces and territories, U.S. states, and a set of countries that includes Australia, Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain, Hungary, the Isle of Man, Japan, South Korea, Kosovo, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland, Switzerland, Taiwan, and Ukraine. Other provinces maintain different lists. Verify your own province's current list before you assume your country qualifies, because governments add and adjust agreements over time.

## What is the exchange rule in each province?

Short answer: There is no national driver's licence in Canada, so the rule changes when you cross a provincial border. The table below shows the grace period and exchange path for several provinces. It is a starting point, not a substitute for your province's official page, which always carries the current rule.

| Province | Time to exchange after moving | Exchange path |
|---|---|---|
| Ontario | 60 days | Test-free exchange if from an agreement jurisdiction; otherwise graduated licensing with tests |
| Alberta | 90 days | Exchange from listed jurisdictions; tests if not listed |
| British Columbia | 90 days | Test-free exchange for some countries; others apply through the new-driver process |
| Quebec | Within the first months of residency | Exchange via the SAAQ; agreement countries skip tests, others test |
| New Brunswick | On becoming a resident | Class-for-class exchange for Canada and U.S.; other countries may test |

## Do I have to retake my driving test if I move to Canada?

Short answer: Not when your licence is from a jurisdiction with a reciprocal agreement and you have enough verified driving experience. Drivers from agreement jurisdictions normally pass a vision test and exchange for a full licence with no knowledge or road test. Drivers from non-agreement countries usually start in graduated licensing, where you pass a written knowledge test, hold a learner stage, and then take one or more road tests. Documented years of driving from your home country can shorten the waiting periods inside graduated licensing in some provinces, so bring proof of your driving history. A certified driving record from your home authority is worth requesting before you leave.

## What documents do I need to exchange my driving licence in Ontario?

Short answer: You need your current foreign licence, identity documents, and a certified translation if your licence is not in English or French. Bring your valid foreign driver's licence, a personal identification document that proves your name, date of birth, and signature, such as a valid passport, and proof that you meet residency requirements. If your licence is in another language, a translation from an approved translator is required, and Ontario requires that the translation be dated within six months of when you apply. An IDP can serve as an accepted translation in some cases. Without the translation, the office cannot process a non-English or non-French licence.

## What to bring to replace or exchange a licence at the office?

Short answer: Plan one in-person visit with originals, not photocopies, of every required document. For an exchange you bring the original foreign licence, the original identity document, your residency proof, and the translation or IDP when your licence is not in English or French. You attend a DriveTest centre or a designated ServiceOntario location in Ontario, while other provinces route you through their own licensing offices or insurers, such as ICBC in British Columbia or the SAAQ in Quebec. Check whether your office takes walk-ins or requires an appointment before you go, because policies differ by location and change without much notice.

## How much does it cost to exchange your licence?

Short answer: Costs vary by province and are set by the provincial government or its insurer, so quote the current figure from your own province rather than relying on a number you read online. The total usually combines a licensing or exchange fee, a vision test, and, where required, knowledge and road test fees, plus the cost of a certified translation if your licence is not in English or French. Some provinces fold driver licensing into the public auto insurer, which can change how and where you pay. Because these amounts are updated periodically, confirm the exact fee on your provincial licensing page before your visit so you bring the right payment.

## What if my country has no exchange agreement with my province?

Short answer: You enter the regular new-driver process and earn your licence through graduated licensing. You pass a vision and knowledge test, receive a learner-stage licence, gain supervised experience, then pass road tests to move up. Proof of prior driving experience can reduce some waiting periods, which is why a certified driving abstract from your home country is useful. Treat the timeline as part of your settlement plan, because you may need other transportation while you progress through the stages. The process is the same one Canadian teenagers follow, so instructors and study materials are widely available.

## How does this fit with my immigration status?

Short answer: A driver's licence is a provincial credential and is separate from your immigration status, but you usually have to prove lawful residence to get one. Provinces ask for proof of permanent residence, a study permit, or a work permit when you apply, and the licence you receive may carry an expiry tied to your status. Keep your immigration documents valid and current, because an expired permit can complicate a licence renewal. If you are unsure how your status affects your eligibility or your timeline, a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) can review your file and confirm what each provincial office will expect.

- [Settling in Canada (IRCC, canada.ca)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/settle-canada.html)
- [Exchange an out-of-province or out-of-country driver's licence (Ontario.ca)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/exchange-out-province-drivers-licence)
- [Exchange a licence from outside Alberta (Alberta.ca)](https://www.alberta.ca/exchange-non-alberta-licences)
- [Moving from outside Canada (ICBC, British Columbia)](https://icbc.com/driver-licensing/moving-bc/moving-from-another-country)
- [Exchange a driver's licence (SAAQ, Quebec)](https://saaq.gouv.qc.ca/en/make-appointment/exchange-drivers-licence)

# Biometrics for Canadian Immigration: Fees, Validity, and How to Give Them

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/biometrics-canada-immigration-2026
Category: Guides
Published: 2026-06-07
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Biometrics are the fingerprints and photo that Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) collects to confirm who you are.

*As of June 7, 2026.*

Biometrics are the fingerprints and photo that Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) collects to confirm who you are. Most people applying for a temporary or permanent visa or permit have to give them once per application cycle, pay a set fee, and book an appointment at an approved collection point. This guide answers the questions applicants ask most often, with every fact checked against canada.ca, so you know exactly what to expect before you file.

## What is done during biometrics for Canada?

Short answer: A collection officer takes a digital scan of all 10 of your fingerprints and a digital photo of your face. The appointment is short and routine. You give your biometrics in person at an approved site, present your passport and your Biometrics Instruction Letter (BIL), and the data is sent securely to IRCC to confirm your identity and run background checks. The fingerprints and photo are then used to verify your identity at the border and in future applications. There is nothing to study or prepare for beyond bringing the right documents and having clean, uninjured fingertips on the day. IRCC explains the full process on its official [biometrics page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics.html).

## Who needs to give biometrics in Canada?

Short answer: Most people applying for a visitor visa, a study permit, a work permit, or permanent residence (PR) must give biometrics. This includes applicants for an initial study or work permit and many extensions. You generally provide them if you are between 14 and 79 years old. IRCC confirms there is no upper age limit in the regulations, but it does not collect biometrics from applicants over 79 for most temporary resident streams. Whether you need to give them depends on the program you apply under and your nationality, so check the official [who needs to give their biometrics page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/who-needs-to-give.html) for your exact situation.

## Who is exempt from giving biometrics?

Short answer: Several groups do not have to give biometrics. According to IRCC, you are exempt if you are a Canadian citizen or citizenship applicant (including passport applicants), an existing permanent resident, a child under the age of 14, an applicant over the age of 79, a head of state or head of government, or a visa-exempt national coming only to visit. You are also exempt if you already gave biometrics for a PR application that is still being processed and you then apply for a visitor visa, study permit, or work permit. There is no fee and no biometrics requirement for a transit visa. Confirm your category on the [who needs to give their biometrics page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/who-needs-to-give.html).

## How much do biometrics cost in Canada?

Short answer: The standard biometrics fee is CAN$85 for one person. Families applying at the same time pay a maximum total of CAN$170, and a group of 3 or more performing artists and their staff applying for work permits at the same time pay a maximum total of CAN$255. There is no fee to give biometrics for a transit visa. You pay this fee on top of your application processing fee. The table below sets out the current amounts confirmed on canada.ca.

| Who pays | Biometrics fee |
|---|---|
| Individual applicant | CAN$85 |
| Family applying at the same time (cap) | CAN$170 |
| Group of 3+ performing artists and staff (cap) | CAN$255 |
| Transit visa applicant | No fee |

## How long do biometrics last in Canada?

Short answer: Biometrics given for temporary residence are valid for 10 years. IRCC cannot issue a visa or permit for longer than 10 years from the last date you gave your biometrics, so the validity of your visa or permit cannot exceed the validity of your biometrics. If you apply again within that 10-year window for a temporary visa or permit, you usually do not have to give them a second time. Permanent residence applicants are treated differently and are generally asked to give biometrics with each new PR application. You can check whether yours are still valid using the IRCC online tool, and the rule is set out on the [biometrics page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics.html).

## When in the process do you give biometrics?

Short answer: You give biometrics after you submit and pay for your application, not before. Once IRCC receives your application and the biometrics fee, it sends you a Biometrics Instruction Letter (BIL) confirming you need to provide your fingerprints and photo. The BIL is your authorization to attend a collection site. IRCC tells you to book your appointment as soon as you receive the BIL and provide your biometrics in person. Do not show up without the letter, and always use the BIL from your current application, not an older one, or your appointment will not count toward the file you have open.

## Is biometrics the last step in a Canada visa application?

Short answer: No. Giving biometrics is one step, not the final one. After your fingerprints and photo are collected, IRCC continues processing your file: officers verify your documents, run background and security checks, and complete any required medical and eligibility reviews before a final decision. Biometrics confirm your identity and let those checks run, but they do not approve the application on their own. Processing time after biometrics depends on the program and your country of residence. Track current processing times and your application status through your IRCC secure account rather than guessing from the appointment date.

## What are officers checking when you give biometrics?

Short answer: Your biometrics are used to confirm your identity and support security screening. IRCC and the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) match your fingerprints and photo against immigration and law enforcement records to verify who you are, confirm your immigration history, and identify any prior records that affect admissibility. This protects the integrity of the system and speeds up identity checks when you arrive at the border. The biometrics themselves are biographic identity data, not a judgment on your case. CBSA describes how it uses biometrics at the border on its [biometrics collection and verification page](https://www.cbsa-asfc.gc.ca/security-securite/biometrics-biometrique-eng.html).

## Where do you give biometrics?

Short answer: Where you go depends on where you are. Outside Canada, you give biometrics at a Visa Application Centre (VAC). In the United States, you can go to a designated application support centre or a VAC, but you must already be legally in the US. Inside Canada, you book a free appointment at a designated Service Canada office. In limited cases, you can give biometrics at a port of entry when you arrive, but only if you are eligible to apply for your study or work permit at the port of entry and you start and finish the application there. Find the right site on the official [where to give your biometrics page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/where-to-give.html).

## How do you book and attend your biometrics appointment?

Short answer: After you get your BIL, book an appointment and bring the right documents. Appointments are free, and IRCC warns that you should never pay anyone for one. You must give biometrics in person and make an appointment in advance for a Service Canada office or a US application support centre. Bring two things to the appointment: your BIL and your valid passport. Make sure your eyes are clearly visible with no glare on glasses, and that any cuts on your fingertips have healed, because poor-quality scans can mean a repeat visit. The full checklist is on the [how to give your biometrics page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/how-to-give.html).

## What happens if you miss or delay your biometrics?

Short answer: Delays can stall or sink your application. IRCC cannot finish processing your file until it has your biometrics, so missing the step leaves your application incomplete and can lead to a refusal for not meeting requirements. Book as soon as you receive your BIL, since VAC and Service Canada appointment availability varies by location and can fill up. If you cannot attend on time, rebook through the official tool rather than letting the file sit. Always use the BIL tied to your current application. Confirm timelines and steps for your case on the [how to give your biometrics page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/how-to-give.html).

## How a licensed RCIC can help

Biometrics look simple, but a missed appointment, an expired BIL, or applying under the wrong program can cost months. Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto, regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). We confirm whether you owe biometrics, when in the process you give them, and where to go, then keep your full application on track. Book a consultation at [gofarglobal.com/book](https://www.gofarglobal.com/book).

## Sources

- [Biometrics, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics.html)
- [Who needs to give their fingerprints and photo (biometrics)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/who-needs-to-give.html)
- [Where to give your biometrics](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/where-to-give.html)
- [How to give your fingerprints and photo](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/biometrics/how-to-give.html)
- [Biometrics collection and verification, Canada Border Services Agency](https://www.cbsa-asfc.gc.ca/security-securite/biometrics-biometrique-eng.html)

# CELPIP vs IELTS for Canada: Which English Test Should You Take in 2026?

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/celpip-vs-ielts-canada-2026
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-06-06
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Both CELPIP and IELTS are accepted for Canadian permanent residence, so the question is never which one Canada wants. It is which one fits you.

*As of June 6, 2026.*

Both CELPIP and IELTS are accepted for Canadian permanent residence, so the question is never which one Canada wants. It is which one fits you. The two tests measure the same thing, map to the same Canadian Language Benchmark scale, and carry the same weight in your Express Entry score. The differences are in format, accents, cost, speed, and whether you need a credential that works outside Canada. This guide lays out those differences, shows how the scores convert, and helps you pick.

## What is the difference between CELPIP and IELTS?

Short answer: CELPIP is a fully computer-based Canadian test taken in one sitting; IELTS is a globally recognized test with a separate, human-led speaking interview. The Canadian English Language Proficiency Index Program (CELPIP) uses only North American accents and Canadian everyday scenarios, and you finish all four sections in about three hours. The International English Language Testing System (IELTS) uses a mix of British, Australian, and other accents and splits speaking into a one-on-one conversation with an examiner. The table below sets the two side by side.

| Feature | CELPIP General | IELTS General Training |
|---|---|---|
| Format | 100% computer-based | Computer or paper |
| Sitting | All four skills in one session | Speaking often on a separate day |
| Speaking | Recorded into a computer | Live interview with an examiner |
| Accents | North American only | British, Australian, and others |
| Results | About 3 to 4 calendar days | About 3 to 13 days |
| Cost | Around CAD $280 | About CAD $300 to $320 |
| Recognition | Canadian immigration and some Canadian uses | Immigration, study, and work worldwide |

Fees and timelines change, so confirm the current numbers with the test provider before you book.

## Which test does Canada accept for permanent residence?

Short answer: Both, but you have to take the right version. For immigration you need CELPIP General or IELTS General Training. The IELTS Academic test, used for university admission, is not accepted for Express Entry, and that single mistake forces people to pay and sit again. French equivalents exist too, through the [TEF Canada](/news/tef-canada-score-chart-clb-2026) and TCF Canada, and a strong French result can be worth more in your profile than a strong English one. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) lists the accepted tests and the rules on its [Express Entry language requirements](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/language-requirements.html) page.

## How do CELPIP and IELTS scores convert to CLB?

Short answer: Both feed into the Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB), which is the only score Express Entry actually uses. Your raw CELPIP number or IELTS band is translated into a CLB level for each skill, and your points come from the CLB, not the test. The table shows the conversion for the levels that matter most in Express Entry.

| CLB | CELPIP (each skill) | IELTS Listening | Reading | Writing | Speaking |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 to 12 | 8.5 | 8.0 | 7.5 | 7.5 |
| 9 | 9 | 8.0 | 7.0 | 7.0 | 7.0 |
| 8 | 8 | 7.5 | 6.5 | 6.5 | 6.5 |
| 7 | 7 | 6.0 | 6.0 | 6.0 | 6.0 |

CLB 9 is the tier to aim for, because it unlocks the highest band of Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) language points and the bonus for strong language plus education. Confirm the full chart on the IRCC [language test equivalency charts](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/standard-requirements/language-requirements/test-equivalency-charts.html).

## Is CELPIP easier than IELTS?

Short answer: Neither is easier overall; each suits a different test-taker. CELPIP tends to help people who think in North American English, prefer finishing in one sitting, and are comfortable speaking into a microphone, and its multiple-choice reading and listening mean a misspelled word will not cost you. IELTS tends to help people who read well by scanning for keywords, who prefer talking to a real person, or who simply find the British and Australian accents familiar. Take an official practice test of each before deciding, because your own result on a sample is worth more than any general claim about difficulty.

## Which is cheaper, and how fast are the results?

Short answer: CELPIP is usually a little cheaper and faster. CELPIP costs around CAD $280 and returns results in roughly three to four calendar days, which matters if you are racing a profile expiry or planning a retake. IELTS runs about CAD $300 to $320, with computer-delivered results in a few days and paper-based results closer to two weeks. If speed and a Canada-only purpose are your priorities, CELPIP has a small edge; if you want one credential for several countries, IELTS earns its price.

## Should you take CELPIP or IELTS for Canada PR?

Short answer: Choose CELPIP if Canada is your only goal and a computer-based, single-sitting format suits you. Choose IELTS if you want a credential recognized worldwide, prefer a human speaking examiner, or already trained for it. There is no scoring advantage either way in Express Entry, since both convert to the same CLB. The smarter move is to match the test to your strengths, because a higher CLB on the test that fits you beats a lower CLB on the one that does not. Build your profile through the IRCC [become a candidate](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/become-candidate.html) guidance once your result is in.

## What do applicants most often ask about CELPIP and IELTS?

Short answer: The four questions that come up most are whether CELPIP is accepted for permanent residence, how the two tests compare on score equivalency, whether CLB 7 is hard to achieve, and how long results stay valid. Both CELPIP General and IELTS General Training are fully accepted for Express Entry and most economic immigration programs. Both convert to CLB levels, and CLB 7 (IELTS 6.0 or CELPIP 7 per skill) is the common minimum floor for skilled programs. Results from both tests are valid for two years from the test date for IRCC purposes, and the test must still be valid on the day you submit your application for permanent residence, not just the day you enter your Express Entry profile.

**Is CELPIP valid for 2 years?**

Yes. Both CELPIP and IELTS results are valid for two years for IRCC immigration purposes, and your test must still be valid on the day you apply for permanent residence, not just on the day you submit your Express Entry profile.

**What is CLB 7 equal to in IELTS?**

CLB 7 equals IELTS General Training scores of 6.0 in each of listening, reading, writing, and speaking. In CELPIP, CLB 7 equals a 7 in each skill. CLB 7 is the common minimum for many skilled programs.

**Is CELPIP accepted for permanent residence?**

Yes. CELPIP General is fully accepted for Express Entry and other economic immigration programs. Only the CELPIP General test counts for permanent residence, not the CELPIP General LS version used for citizenship.

**Is it easy to get CLB 7 in CELPIP?**

It is achievable for most candidates with solid everyday English, since CLB 7 is a middle benchmark rather than an advanced one. The bigger challenge is usually reaching CLB 9 for maximum CRS points, which takes targeted practice on whichever test you choose.

## How can a licensed RCIC help you choose between CELPIP and IELTS?

Short answer: The test is only worth what it does to your CRS score, and that is where strategy beats guessing. Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto, regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). We tell you the CLB level your profile actually needs, which test gives you the best shot at it, and whether a French test would lift your score further. [Book a consultation](https://www.gofarglobal.com/book) before you pay for a test that may not be the right one.

## Sources

- IRCC, [Express Entry: language requirements](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/language-requirements.html)
- IRCC, [Language test equivalency charts (CLB)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/standard-requirements/language-requirements/test-equivalency-charts.html)
- IRCC, [Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html)
- IRCC, [Express Entry: become a candidate](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/become-candidate.html)
