# Canada Start-Up Visa 2026: Paused for New Applicants, and What Comes Next

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-start-up-visa-2026-paused-what-next
Category: Immigration News
Published: 2026-05-27
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Canada Start-Up Visa is the country's flagship route for immigrant entrepreneurs, and 2026 brought a major change: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) paused new...

*As of June 14, 2026.*

The Canada Start-Up Visa is the country's flagship route for immigrant entrepreneurs, and 2026 brought a major change: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) paused new intake to the program on January 1, 2026. If you already hold a 2025 commitment certificate, this is good news with a hard deadline, not a closed door, and that deadline is now just weeks away. If you are a founder planning ahead, IRCC is developing new targeted entrepreneur pilots to take its place. This guide explains where the Start-Up Visa stands, what existing applicants need to do, and the routes available to founders who still want to build a business in Canada.

## Is the Canada Start-Up Visa still open in 2026?

__Short answer:__ The Start-Up Visa (SUV) is paused for new applicants as of January 1, 2026. IRCC has stopped accepting new commitment certificates from designated organizations, so you cannot begin a brand-new SUV application right now. There is one important exception: if a designated Canadian venture capital fund, angel investor group, or business incubator issued you a valid commitment certificate in 2025, you can still apply for permanent residence. The pause is a transition, not a permanent cancellation, and IRCC has said it is building new entrepreneur streams to follow.

## I already have a 2025 commitment certificate. What do I do?

__Short answer:__ You are still in the program, and the key date for you is June 30, 2026. If you received a valid commitment certificate from a designated organization in 2025, your application for permanent residence remains open and must be submitted by that deadline. The most important thing is to file a complete, well-prepared application before June 30, 2026, rather than waiting. IRCC has also stopped accepting new applications for the optional Start-Up Visa work permit, so the option to come to Canada early on that permit is no longer open to new applicants. Gather your business documents, language results, and settlement funds proof now, and have everything reviewed before you submit so a fixable error does not cost you your place. You can confirm your status on the Government of Canada [about the start-up visa process](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/start-visa/about.html) page.

## Why did Canada pause the Start-Up Visa?

__Short answer:__ The program grew faster than it could be processed, which created a long queue for applicants. To manage this, IRCC reduced its overall business immigration targets and paused new SUV intake so it can work through existing applications and redesign the program. The government has signalled that it wants future entrepreneur streams to focus on founders with stronger funding and clear economic impact. In plain terms, the pause is meant to reset the program so it works better, and a new, more targeted version is expected rather than a permanent end to entrepreneur immigration.

## What is replacing the Start-Up Visa?

__Short answer:__ IRCC has said it is developing new targeted pilot streams for immigrant entrepreneurs. Details and an opening date have not been published yet, but the direction is clear: the next generation of entrepreneur immigration is expected to prioritize founders with committed capital, proven traction, and businesses that address Canada's economic priorities. For ambitious founders, that is encouraging. The opportunity is not disappearing; it is being reshaped. The smartest move now is to strengthen your business case and funding so you are ready to move quickly when the new streams open. Watch the official [Start-up Visa Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/start-visa.html) page for announcements.

## What were the Start-Up Visa requirements?

__Short answer:__ Knowing the former criteria helps you prepare for what is likely coming. The Start-Up Visa asked for four things: a letter of support from a designated organization, a qualifying business, language ability, and settlement funds. Each applicant in a group of up to five owners had to hold at least 10% of the voting rights, and applicants and the designated organization together had to hold more than 50%.

| Requirement | What it meant |
|---|---|
| Letter of support | Backing from a designated venture capital fund, angel investor group, or business incubator |
| Qualifying business | Incorporated in Canada, each applicant holding at least 10% of voting rights |
| Language | Minimum Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) level 5 in English or French, all abilities |
| Settlement funds | Proof of enough money to support yourself and your family on arrival |

These criteria are a strong guide to the kind of profile the new entrepreneur streams are likely to reward. You can review the former rules on the Government of Canada page for [who can apply for a start-up visa](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/start-visa/eligibility.html).

## What are the alternatives for entrepreneurs right now?

__Short answer:__ Founders who cannot wait have real options. Many provinces run entrepreneur or business streams through their Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) that lead to permanent residence, usually in exchange for investing in and actively managing a business in that province. A business or owner-operator work permit can also let you enter Canada to launch or buy a company now, building a track record that supports a later permanent residence application.

| Pathway | What it offers | Good fit if you |
|---|---|---|
| Provincial entrepreneur streams (PNP) | Provincial nomination leading to Permanent Residence (PR) | Can invest in and run a business in a specific province |
| Business / owner-operator work permit | Temporary entry to start or buy a business | Want to begin operating in Canada now |
| Express Entry (where eligible) | Federal PR through a points system | Have skilled work experience and strong language scores |
| New entrepreneur pilot (upcoming) | A reshaped federal route, expected soon | Have committed funding and a high-impact business |

Each route has its own investment levels, net-worth tests, and conditions, so the right choice depends on your capital, your business, and where you want to settle. Our [work permit](/immigration/work-permit) and [provincial nominee](/immigration/provincial-nominee) overviews are good starting points.

## How can Go Far Global help founders right now?

__Short answer:__ Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto that works with entrepreneurs. If you hold a 2025 commitment certificate, we help you file a clean, complete permanent residence application before the June 30, 2026 deadline. If you are planning ahead, we map the provincial entrepreneur streams and work-permit routes that fit your capital and business, and we help you get ready for the new federal entrepreneur pilot so you can act the moment it opens.

The founders who do best treat this pause as preparation time, not a dead end. [Book a consultation](/book) and we will build a plan around your business and timeline.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. Business immigration programs change frequently. Confirm the current rules for your situation with a licensed representative or on the official IRCC website before you apply.*

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a Start-Up Visa still available in Canada?

The Start-Up Visa is paused for new applicants as of January 1, 2026, so you cannot begin a brand-new application. The exception is founders who received a valid commitment certificate from a designated organization in 2025, who can still apply for permanent residence until June 30, 2026. IRCC has said it is developing new targeted entrepreneur streams, so a reshaped federal route is expected rather than a permanent closure.

### Is Canada closing the Start-Up Visa?

Canada paused new Start-Up Visa intake on January 1, 2026, but framed it as a transition rather than a permanent end. IRCC reduced business immigration targets and is redesigning the program into new targeted entrepreneur pilots expected to focus on founders with committed funding and clear economic impact. Existing 2025 commitment-certificate holders can still apply for permanent residence until June 30, 2026.

### How much money is required for a Canada Start-Up Visa?

Under the former rules, applicants had to prove settlement funds to support themselves and their family on arrival, with the amount scaling by family size, and the business needed real financial backing from a designated organization. Venture capital, angel, and incubator support carried different commitment levels. Because the program is paused and new streams are being designed, confirm the current financial requirements before relying on past figures.

### How do you get a Start-Up Visa in Canada?

When the program was open, you secured a letter of support from a designated venture capital fund, angel investor group, or business incubator, built a qualifying incorporated business, met Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) level 5, and proved settlement funds. New applications are paused as of January 1, 2026. Founders should now prepare for the upcoming entrepreneur pilot or consider a provincial entrepreneur stream instead.

# Caregiver Program Canada 2026: Closed, No March Reopen

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/caregiver-program-canada-2026-closed-alternatives
Category: Immigration News
Published: 2026-05-27
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The caregiver program in Canada is one of the most searched immigration pathways, and the news this year has caused real worry.

# Caregiver Program Canada 2026: Closed, No March Reopen

*As of September 3, 2026.* Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) paused intake to the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots and said the pilots will not re-open in March 2026. Existing files stay in processing. New federal caregiver-pilot applications are not being accepted.

## TL;DR

IRCC notice dated December 19, 2025: pause until further notice | Pilots will not re-open in March 2026 | Hub title: Closed | Last day for the older Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot: June 17, 2024 | Language when the pilots were open: Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 4 in all 4 abilities | Work experience: at least 6 months full-time, or a recent training credential | Job offer wage must meet Job Bank median for that occupation | The pilots do not make you eligible for a bridging open work permit

## Will the caregiver program open in 2026?

**Short answer:** IRCC has not published a 2026 reopening date. The [December 19, 2025 notice](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/pausing-home-care-worker-immigration-pilots-application-intake.html) says intake is paused until further notice and that the pilots' intake will not re-open in March 2026. IRCC will keep processing applications it already received, in line with the 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan. Any future program update will be shared publicly. Treat social posts that name March 2026, 2030, or a secret reopen date as unverified unless they match that notice or the live [Closed pilots hub](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/home-care-worker-immigration-pilots/child-care-home-support.html).

If you already filed a complete application before the pause, wait for IRCC correspondence and [check your application status](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-status.html). If you have not applied, you cannot start a new Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot file on those pages today.

## Is the caregiver program still open in Canada?

**Short answer:** No. The [home care workers (caregivers)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers.html) page marks the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots Closed. The same page marks the Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot Closed, with last day to apply June 17, 2024. The Live-in Caregiver Program is Closed to new applicants unless you already received a work permit under that program based on a labour market impact assessment (LMIA) submitted before December 2014. The Caring for Children Pilot and Caring for People with High Medical Needs Pilot closed on June 17, 2019. The Interim Pathway for Caregivers closed on October 8, 2019. Closed means new intake is not open. It does not cancel a file IRCC already accepted.

| Program | IRCC status on the caregivers hub | Date IRCC names |
|---|---|---|
| Home Care Worker Immigration pilots | Closed | Pause; will not re-open in March 2026 |
| Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot | Closed | Last day June 17, 2024 |
| Live-in Caregiver Program | Closed to new applicants | Exception: work permit from an LMIA submitted before December 2014 |
| Caring for Children / High Medical Needs pilots | Closed | Last day June 17, 2019 |
| Interim Pathway for Caregivers | Closed | Last day October 8, 2019 |

A Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) stream or a temporary [work permit](/immigration/work-permit) is a different application. Those are not the closed federal caregiver pilots. Confirm the live provincial rules before you pay fees. Start with IRCC's [provincial nominees](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html) page and our [provincial nominee](/immigration/provincial-nominee) overview.

## What is the new update for caregivers in Canada?

**Short answer:** The update that is on IRCC paper is the December 19, 2025 pause. IRCC wrote that interest in the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots exceeded the spaces available and that it is pausing intake so it can process the inventory it already has. The [Closed: Immigrate through the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/home-care-worker-immigration-pilots/child-care-home-support.html) page, date modified April 23, 2026, repeats: "The pilots are closed while we focus on processing existing applications." Both streams, Workers in Canada and Applicants not working in Canada, show Closed. The [who can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/home-care-worker-immigration-pilots/child-care-home-support/eligibility.html) page still describes the old tests because IRCC left the instructions up. Those tests do not reopen intake.

When the pilots were taking files, you had to plan to live and work outside Quebec, meet language and education rules, show work experience or training, hold a genuine job offer, and be admissible. Language was [CLB or NCLC level 4 in all 4 abilities](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/home-care-worker-immigration-pilots/child-care-home-support/eligibility/language-test.html), with results less than 2 years old. IRCC lists CELPIP-General, IELTS General Training, PTE Core, TEF Canada, and TCF Canada. Education needed the equivalent of a Canadian high school diploma, shown with an educational credential assessment (ECA) for a foreign credential, less than 5 years old on the date IRCC receives the application. Work experience was at least 6 months, full-time (30 hours per week), continuous, gained after age 18 and within the 3 years before you apply, in the National Occupational Classification (NOC) groups for that pilot. IRCC also accepts a recent, relevant training credential instead of, or with, that experience. Experience you gain after you apply does not count.

A small [out-of-status public policy](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/home-care-worker-immigration-pilots/child-care-home-support/eligibility.html) on the same eligibility page applied only if you were in Canada, entered legally on or before December 16, 2021, lived here continuously, had a work permit at some point in that stay, and were not under a removal order or a refugee claim. That policy does not reopen the pilots. It described who could still use the Workers in Canada stream when intake existed.

| Pilot | Job-offer NOC IRCC names | Experience NOCs IRCC also counts |
|---|---|---|
| Child Care | Home child care providers (NOC 44100). Not a daycare. Foster parent does not count. | NOC 44100. Early childhood educators and assistants (NOC 42202) only as assistant, helper, or worker |
| Home Support | Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations (NOC 44101). Not a nursing home. | NOC 44101. Nurse aides, orderlies and patient service associates (NOC 33102) |

The [job offer](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/home-care-worker-immigration-pilots/child-care-home-support/job-offer.html) page says these pilots do not make you eligible for a bridging open work permit. If you already work for that employer, you need another way to keep status and renew the permit. Use [check processing times](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) for a file already in the system. Do not use a blog clock.

## How much is a caregiver paid in Canada per hour?

**Short answer:** IRCC does not publish one Canada-wide caregiver hourly wage on the immigration pages. For the closed pilots, the job offer had to pay a wage equal to or higher than the Job Bank median wage for that occupation in the province or territory of employment, or the national median if there is no provincial figure. If the employer's workers have a union, the collective agreement applies. That rule is on the [job offer](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/home-care-worker-immigration-pilots/child-care-home-support/job-offer.html) page. It is not a promise of a specific dollar amount. Median wages differ by city and by NOC 44100 versus 44101. Look up the occupation and location on Job Bank, then compare the written offer. A number you saw in a Facebook thread is not the legal wage.

The offer also had to be full-time (at least 30 hours of paid work per week), permanent (no set end date), outside Quebec, outside an institutional setting, and genuine. IRCC will not accept job offers for early childhood educators and assistants (NOC 42202) or nurse aides, orderlies and patient service associates (NOC 33102) as the job offer, even though some of that experience can count. The employer cannot be a recruitment agency, a diplomatic mission, a non-compliant employer, you yourself, or your spouse, common-law partner, parent, grandparent, or child.

If you still want to work as a caregiver in Canada while the pilots stay closed, the path is a separate [work permit](/immigration/work-permit), often tied to an LMIA, not a federal caregiver-pilot PR file. We are Go Far Global, a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm. If you already applied, or you have a job offer and need a permit that is actually open, [book a consultation](/book). Track IRCC clocks on our [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) page. # Canada PGWP Portal Adds a "Proof of Language Proficiency" Field, But Labels It Optional

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/pgwp-proof-of-language-proficiency-upload-field-2026
Category: Immigration News
Published: 2026-05-27
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has finally added a dedicated Proof of Language Proficiency upload field to the online Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP)...

*As of May 27, 2026.*

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has finally added a dedicated **Proof of Language Proficiency** upload field to the online Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) application. That sounds like good news, and it is. The problem is where IRCC put it. The field sits under the heading **"Optional documents"** and shows a red "Not provided" status, so graduates assume they can skip it. For almost everyone, the PGWP proof of language proficiency is not optional. It is mandatory, and a blank field is now one of the fastest ways to get a post-graduation work permit refused.

## What is the new PGWP Proof of Language Proficiency upload field?

__Short answer:__ It is a new row on the PGWP application document checklist, with its own "Upload file" button, where you attach your official language test result. IRCC added it after a wave of refusals, but placed it under the "Optional documents" section rather than the required list. When the PGWP language rule took effect on November 1, 2024, the portal had no obvious slot for test results, so applicants left them out and were refused for "missing" documents the system never clearly requested. The new field fixes the missing-slot problem. It does not fix the misleading label.

## Is the PGWP language test mandatory if the portal lists it as optional?

__Short answer:__ Yes. For almost everyone who applied for a study permit on or after November 1, 2024, the language test is required, regardless of the "Optional documents" heading above the field. If you take that label at face value and submit without a result, you will file an incomplete application and very likely receive a refusal. The "Optional documents" grouping is a portal layout choice, not a statement of immigration law. Treat the Proof of Language Proficiency field as required unless a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) has confirmed a specific exemption applies to you.

> **Warning:** Do not trust the "Optional documents" heading. If you graduated from a PGWP-eligible program and applied for your study permit on or after November 1, 2024, you must upload a valid language test result in this field before you submit. You can confirm the requirement on the official [who can apply for a post-graduation work permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html) page.

## Who needs to provide proof of language proficiency for a PGWP?

__Short answer:__ Almost all PGWP applicants. There are very narrow exceptions, such as certain PGWP-eligible flight programs, but assume the requirement applies to you unless an RCIC confirms otherwise. The level you need depends on what you studied. University degree graduates need Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7, and college or other eligible-program graduates need CLB 5, in all four abilities. The French equivalent is the Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens (NCLC).

| You graduated from | Minimum required | Applies to which abilities? |
|---|---|---|
| University bachelor's, master's, or doctoral degree | CLB / NCLC 7 | All four: listening, reading, writing, speaking |
| College, certificate, diploma, or other eligible program | CLB / NCLC 5 | All four: listening, reading, writing, speaking |
| PGWP-eligible flight program (narrow cases) | May be exempt | Confirm with an RCIC |

You must meet the minimum in every one of the four skills. A strong reading score will not rescue a weak speaking score. The official requirement is set out in IRCC's guidance on how to [get the right documents](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/get-documents.html) for a post-graduation work permit.

## Which language tests does IRCC accept, and how recent must they be?

__Short answer:__ You prove one language, English or French, with an approved test taken within the last two years. Accepted English tests are IELTS General Training, CELPIP-General, and PTE Core. Accepted French tests are TEF Canada and TCF Canada. There are no exemptions for native speakers, so even first-language English or French speakers must submit an official result. Your report must be less than two years old on the day you submit, because IRCC treats an expired report as no report at all.

Approved tests by language:

- **English:** IELTS General Training (not Academic), CELPIP-General, or PTE Core
- **French:** TEF Canada or TCF Canada

As a rough English guide, a university graduate needs about IELTS General Training 6.0 in each band for CLB 7, while a college graduate needs about 5.0 in listening, writing and speaking and 4.0 in reading for CLB 5. On CELPIP-General, that is a 7 or a 5 in each skill. Confirm the exact equivalency for your test before booking, because the official charts are the final word. You can read IRCC's overview of the rules on the [about the post-graduation work permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/about.html) page.

## How do you upload your PGWP language proof correctly?

__Short answer:__ Open your application's document checklist, scroll to "Optional documents," find the Proof of Language Proficiency row, and upload your complete official test report before you pay and submit. Confirm the status changes from "Not provided" to your uploaded file. A blank status at submission is exactly what triggers a refusal, so check it twice.

1. Open your PGWP application's document checklist in your IRCC secure account.
2. Scroll to the **"Optional documents"** section and find the **Proof of Language Proficiency** row.
3. Click **Upload file** and attach your full official test report as a single PDF, not a screenshot of your scores.
4. Confirm the status changes from "Not provided" to show your uploaded file.
5. If you also need to provide proof of your eligible field of study, follow IRCC's instructions on how to [submit your proof of language results](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/apply/special-instructions-upload-proof.html) and keep each required document in the field IRCC specifies.

## What happens if your PGWP is refused?

__Short answer:__ A PGWP refusal is rarely a simple second chance. You have only 180 days from confirmation that you completed your program to apply, a PGWP is normally a once-in-a-lifetime permit, and your status can lapse while the refusal plays out. A single missed field can cost you the Canadian work experience that feeds Express Entry and provincial nominee programs, which is why the first application has to be right.

- **The 180-day window is unforgiving.** You have 180 days from the date you receive confirmation that you completed your program. If a refusal pushes you past that window, you may lose your eligibility entirely. Track current timelines on our [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) page.
- **Your status can lapse.** If your study permit expires while this plays out, you fall out of status. Restoration is sometimes possible within 90 days, but you generally cannot work during that time, and the conditions are strict.
- **You usually get only one PGWP in your lifetime.** Getting it wrong can mean leaving Canada and losing the work experience many permanent residence pathways depend on.

## How can Go Far Global help with your PGWP application?

__Short answer:__ Go Far Global is a licensed RCIC firm in Toronto that reviews post-graduation work permit applications end to end, including language results, CLB levels, field-of-study eligibility, document placement in the portal, and your 180-day timing. We make sure nothing critical is sitting in a field marked "Not provided" before you submit. The graduates who run into trouble are rarely careless. They simply trusted a portal that labelled a mandatory document optional.

If you are graduating soon, or you are partway through a PGWP application and unsure, [book a consultation](/appointment) or read our overview of the [work permit](/immigration/work-permit) and [study permit](/immigration/study-permit) pathways. Your first application is the one that has to be right, so let us check it before IRCC does.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. PGWP requirements change. Confirm the current rules for your situation with a licensed representative or on the official IRCC website before you apply.*

## Frequently asked questions

### Which language is required for IRCC PGWP?

You can prove either English or French; one language is enough. For almost everyone who applied for a study permit on or after November 1, 2024, proof of language proficiency is mandatory for the PGWP, even though the portal lists the upload field under "Optional documents." The only common exception involves certain PGWP-eligible flight programs. The level depends on your studies: Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7 for university degree graduates and CLB 5 for college and other eligible programs, in all four abilities.

### Which language proficiency test is required for PGWP?

There is no single required test. IRCC accepts several approved tests, and you choose one based on the language you prove. For English, you can use IELTS General Training, CELPIP-General, or PTE Core. For French, you can use TEF Canada or TCF Canada. Whatever you choose, your result must be less than two years old on the day you submit your post-graduation work permit application, and you must meet the minimum CLB or NCLC level in all four abilities.

### What is the CLB requirement for PGWP?

The Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) requirement depends on your level of study. University bachelor's, master's, and doctoral graduates need CLB 7. College, certificate, diploma, and other eligible-program graduates need CLB 5. The French equivalent is NCLC 7 or NCLC 5. You must reach the minimum in every one of the four abilities: listening, reading, writing, and speaking. A high score in one skill cannot offset a low score in another, so plan your test preparation around your weakest ability.

### What is CLB 5 language level in IELTS?

For IELTS General Training, CLB 5 corresponds to roughly 5.0 in listening, 4.0 in reading, 5.0 in writing, and 5.0 in speaking. These are approximate benchmarks, and the official IRCC equivalency chart is the final authority, so confirm the exact scores before you book a test date. CLB 5 is the minimum for college, certificate, and diploma graduates applying for a post-graduation work permit. University degree graduates must reach the higher CLB 7 level instead.

### Which language test is eligible for PGWP?

Eligible English tests for the PGWP are IELTS General Training, CELPIP-General, and PTE Core. Eligible French tests are TEF Canada and TCF Canada. The IELTS Academic test is not accepted for the post-graduation work permit, so make sure you book the General Training version. Whichever test you take, the result must be valid, meaning less than two years old, on the day you submit your application, and it must show you met the minimum CLB level for your level of study.

### Which is easier, IELTS or CELPIP?

Neither test is objectively easier; the better choice depends on your strengths. CELPIP-General is fully computer-based, uses Canadian English, and tests all four skills in one sitting, which suits candidates comfortable with North American accents and typing. IELTS General Training offers a paper or computer option and a face-to-face speaking interview, which some candidates prefer. For a PGWP, both are accepted, so choose the format that matches how you perform best. What matters is reaching CLB 7 or CLB 5 in all four abilities, not which test you sit.

# IRCC Releases Updated Processing Times for Temporary Residence Applications (May 2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/ircc-processing-times-update-may-2026
Category: Immigration News
Published: 2026-05-26
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has published its latest temporary-residence processing times, with the weekly categories last refreshed on May 20, 2026.

**Key takeaways**

- IRCC updated its temporary-residence processing times, with the weekly categories refreshed on **May 20, 2026**.
- Visitor visa wait times rose modestly — **one to five days** — but Philippines and U.S. applicants still process in **under three weeks**.
- Inland study permits improved to about **6 weeks** (two weeks faster); results varied by country.
- Inland work-permit processing fell sharply — down roughly **47 days since late March** — now ~32 days below the January baseline.
- Super visas are the standout: Indian applicants are at about **117 days**, down 21 days week-over-week.

---

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has published its latest **temporary-residence processing times**, with the weekly categories last refreshed on **May 20, 2026**. The headline: a small uptick for visitor visas, but encouraging declines across several study-permit, work-permit, and super-visa streams.

Processing times are estimates based on how long IRCC took to finish the most recent applications. They are a planning tool, not a guarantee — but they are the best signal applicants have for what to expect right now.

### May 2026 at a glance

| Category | This update | Notable figure |
|---|---|---|
| Visitor visa (TRV) | Up slightly (1–5 days) | Philippines & U.S. under 3 weeks |
| Study permit | Mixed by country | Inland ~6 weeks (2 weeks faster) |
| Work permit | Improving | Inland down ~47 days since late March |
| Super visa | Improving | India ~117 days (down 21 days) |

## What changed in the IRCC processing times update for May 2026?

Visitor visa (temporary resident visa) wait times **rose modestly across the board this update — by roughly one to five days**. The increase is minor, and some country-specific streams remain very fast: **visitor visas from the Philippines and the United States are processing in under three weeks**.

If you have a trip planned, the practical takeaway is to apply early and submit a complete application with biometrics done promptly — see our live [Canada processing-times tracker](/immigration/processing-times) for the current figure for your country.

## Study permits: mixed, but inland applications sped up

Study-permit timelines were **mixed by country**. A few nationalities ticked upward while others held steady or improved — for example, Pakistani applicants saw their estimate improve to around 8 weeks, while some countries rose by about a week.

The clearest win was **inland study-permit processing, which dropped to roughly 6 weeks — about two weeks faster than the previous update**. That is welcome news for students already in Canada who are extending or changing their status.

Thinking about studying in Canada? Our [study-permit guidance](/immigration/study-permit) walks through eligibility, the documents that prevent refusals, and timing.

## Work permits: the strongest improvement

The work-permit category contained some of the most encouraging data in the entire update. **Inland work-permit processing has plunged by about 47 days since late March**, and now sits roughly **32 days below the January baseline**. Among country streams, Indian applicants held steady at about 9 weeks.

Faster inland processing matters for workers extending a permit or moving employers. If a permit renewal or employer change is on your horizon, our [work-permit team](/immigration/work-permit) can help you file early and avoid status gaps.

## Super visas: the standout success

The **super visa** — which lets parents and grandparents of citizens and permanent residents stay for extended periods — was the clearest improvement of the update. Indian applicants are now at about **117 days, down 21 days week-over-week** and well below the January baseline.

For families planning a long visit from parents or grandparents, that is a meaningful reduction.

## How IRCC calculates processing times

It helps to know how the clock works:

- Your processing time **starts the day IRCC receives your complete application** (including all fees) and **ends when a decision is made**.
- Incomplete applications are the single biggest cause of delay. Missing documents, unpaid fees, or skipped biometrics can reset or stall your file.
- Posted times are based on the past, so they shift weekly as IRCC clears its inventory.

## How to avoid delays

1. **Submit a complete application.** Double-check the document checklist for your specific stream before you pay.
2. **Do your biometrics quickly.** Your file often does not move until biometrics are received.
3. **Respond fast to requests.** If IRCC asks for more documents, a same-week reply keeps your place in line.
4. **Track the live figure.** Posted times change weekly — check the [current processing times](/immigration/processing-times) for your country and category before you plan travel or make commitments.

Need a second set of eyes before you submit? [Book a consultation](/appointment) and we will review your application for the gaps that most often trigger delays or refusals.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why is my Canadian study permit taking so long?

In most cases, delays come from high application volume, additional screening, or document review — not from a weak application. Incomplete files, late biometrics, or unanswered document requests are the most common controllable causes. Submitting a complete application and responding quickly to IRCC keeps your file moving.

### How much time does it take to get a work permit after study in Canada?

It depends on the permit type and where it is processed. As of the May 2026 update, inland work-permit processing improved significantly — down about 47 days since late March. Check the live [processing-times tracker](/immigration/processing-times) for the current estimate, and apply before your current status expires to avoid a gap.

### What is the Canada visitor visa processing time after biometrics?

Your processing time runs until IRCC makes a decision, and your file typically does not advance until biometrics are received — so completing biometrics promptly is key. As of this update, fast streams like the Philippines and the U.S. are under three weeks, while other countries vary. See the current figure for your country on our tracker.

### Where can I find IRCC processing times for 2026?

IRCC updates its estimates regularly — weekly for most temporary-residence categories. You can see the latest country-by-country figures on our continuously updated [Canada processing-times page](/immigration/processing-times).

*Processing times change every week. The figures above reflect IRCC's May 2026 update and are for general guidance only — always confirm the current estimate for your specific application before making plans.*

# Canada Drops Visa Requirement for Eligible Citizens of Indonesia and Malaysia

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-eta-indonesia-malaysia-visa-change-2026
Category: Immigration News
Published: 2026-05-26
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada has made it dramatically easier, and cheaper, for many travellers from Indonesia and Malaysia to visit. As of May 26, 2026 at 5:30 a. m.

**Key takeaways**

- Effective **May 26, 2026 at 5:30 a.m. EDT**, eligible Indonesian and Malaysian citizens can apply for an eTA instead of a visitor visa to fly to Canada.
- You qualify if you have **held a Canadian visa in the past 10 years** OR **currently hold a valid U.S. non-immigrant visa**.
- An eTA costs **CAD $7**, is applied for online, and is usually approved within minutes — versus a visitor visa that costs CAD $100 and can take weeks.
- The eTA only covers **air travel**; anyone arriving by car, bus, train, or boat still needs a visitor visa.
- Travellers who do not meet the conditions still need a visitor visa.

---

Canada has made it dramatically easier — and cheaper — for many travellers from Indonesia and Malaysia to visit. **As of May 26, 2026 at 5:30 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time, eligible citizens of both countries can apply for an electronic travel authorization (eTA) instead of a temporary resident visa (visitor visa) when flying to Canada.** Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) announced the change on May 25, 2026.

For people who qualify, that means swapping a CAD $100 visitor-visa application that can take weeks for a **CAD $7 eTA that is filed online and usually approved within minutes**.

## What exactly changed?

Indonesia and Malaysia have been added to Canada's list of "visa-required" countries whose citizens may instead be eligible for an eTA. This is the same partial-access pathway already offered to travellers from countries such as the Philippines, Brazil, and Morocco.

It is **not** full visa-free access. Instead, it creates a faster lane for lower-risk travellers who have already been screened by Canada or the United States.

### eTA vs. visitor visa at a glance

| | eTA (new option) | Visitor visa (TRV) |
|---|---|---|
| **Who** | Eligible Indonesian/Malaysian citizens flying to Canada | Everyone who doesn't meet the conditions |
| **Cost** | CAD $7 | CAD $100 |
| **Processing** | Usually minutes | Often several weeks |
| **How to apply** | Short online form | Full application + biometrics |
| **Travel mode** | Air only | Air, land, or sea |
| **Validity** | Up to 5 years | Up to 10 years (multiple entry) |

## Who qualifies for the eTA?

You can apply for an eTA — rather than a visitor visa — if you are a citizen of Indonesia or Malaysia, you are **travelling to or transiting through Canada by air**, and you meet **at least one** of these conditions at the time you apply:

- You have **held a Canadian temporary resident (visitor) visa at any point in the last 10 years**; or
- You **currently hold a valid U.S. non-immigrant visa**.

If you meet one of those conditions, you apply for the eTA online, pay the CAD $7 fee, and in most cases receive approval within minutes. The eTA is then electronically linked to the passport you used to apply, and is valid for up to five years or until your passport expires — whichever comes first.

## What has *not* changed

It is just as important to understand the limits of this announcement:

- **Air travel only.** The eTA pathway applies when you fly into Canada. If you arrive by **car, bus, train, or boat**, you still need a visitor visa — even if you meet the conditions above.
- **Everyone else still needs a visitor visa.** Indonesian and Malaysian citizens who have never held a Canadian visa and do not hold a valid U.S. visa must still apply for a visitor visa as before.
- **An eTA is not a work or study permit.** It is a travel authorization. If your purpose is to study or work in Canada, you still need the appropriate permit — but eligible travellers will now receive an eTA rather than a visitor visa as their travel document, which can simplify the process.

## Why Canada made this change

The federal government framed the move as part of its **Indo-Pacific Strategy**, deepening trade, tourism, and people-to-people ties with two of Southeast Asia's largest economies. Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab said the change supports closer relationships in the region while maintaining Canada's border-security standards — the eligibility conditions ensure applicants have already passed a Canadian or U.S. screening.

For families, students, and business travellers from Jakarta to Kuala Lumpur, the practical effect is simpler: a trip to Canada that used to require a full visa application may now take minutes and a few dollars.

## How to apply for your eTA

1. Confirm you meet one of the two eligibility conditions (prior Canadian visa in the last 10 years, or a valid U.S. non-immigrant visa).
2. Apply **only** through the official Government of Canada website. Have your passport, a credit card, and an email address ready.
3. Pay the CAD $7 fee and wait for the confirmation email. Most approvals arrive within minutes, though some applications are referred for additional review.
4. Travel by air with the **same passport** you used to apply — the eTA is linked to it electronically.

> A word of caution: many look-alike websites charge inflated "service fees" for eTAs. The real fee is CAD $7, paid directly to the Government of Canada.

## What this means if you plan to study or work in Canada

If your longer-term goal is a study permit, work permit, or permanent residence, this change does not alter those programs — but it can make your first entry smoother. Our team helps clients from across Southeast Asia move from a first visit to a long-term plan in Canada, including [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry), [study permits](/immigration/study-permit), and [work permits](/immigration/work-permit). If you are weighing your options, [book a consultation](/appointment) and we will map the fastest legitimate route for your situation.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does Malaysian need visa or eTA to Canada?

As of May 26, 2026, Malaysian citizens who are flying to Canada and who either held a Canadian visa in the last 10 years or currently hold a valid U.S. non-immigrant visa can travel on an eTA. Malaysians who do not meet either condition, or who arrive by land or sea, still need a visitor visa.

### Will Malaysia get a visa free to Canada?

Not fully. Malaysia (and Indonesia) now have **partial** eTA access for eligible air travellers, not blanket visa-free entry. Travellers who have not previously been approved by Canada or the U.S. still apply for a visitor visa.

### Who can apply for eTA Canada?

Citizens of eTA-eligible countries — which, as of May 26, 2026, includes eligible citizens of Indonesia and Malaysia — can apply for an eTA to fly to or transit through Canada. Visa-required nationals like these must also meet a condition such as holding a prior Canadian visa or a valid U.S. visa.

### How do I complete a Canada eTA application?

Apply online through the official Government of Canada website using the passport you will travel with, pay the CAD $7 fee, and wait for email confirmation. Approvals are usually issued within minutes, and the eTA stays valid for up to five years.

*This article is for general information and reflects the announcement effective May 26, 2026. Immigration rules change frequently — confirm current requirements on the Government of Canada website or speak with a regulated consultant before you travel.*

# Dual Citizenship US/Canada 2026: Taxes, Voting, Travel, and FBAR Rules

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/dual-citizenship-us-canada-2026
Category: Citizenship
Published: 2026-05-26
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Acronyms used in this guide: IRS (Internal Revenue Service), CRA (Canada Revenue Agency), FBAR (Foreign Bank Account Report, FinCEN Form 114), FATCA (Foreign Account Tax Compliance...

# Dual Citizenship US/Canada 2026: Taxes, Voting, Travel, and FBAR Rules

*As of May 25, 2026.*

*Acronyms used in this guide: IRS (Internal Revenue Service), CRA (Canada Revenue Agency), FBAR (Foreign Bank Account Report, FinCEN Form 114), FATCA (Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act), FEIE (Foreign Earned Income Exclusion), FTC (Foreign Tax Credit), TFSA (Tax-Free Savings Account), RRSP (Registered Retirement Savings Plan), FHSA (First Home Savings Account), RESP (Registered Education Savings Plan), CPP (Canada Pension Plan), QPP (Quebec Pension Plan), OAS (Old Age Security), SSA (Social Security Administration).*

You can hold U.S. and Canadian citizenship at the same time. Both countries permit dual nationality and neither requires renunciation. But the practical realities of dual citizenship, especially the U.S.’s unusual citizenship-based taxation, surprise most new dual citizens. This guide covers everything that changes the day you become a dual citizen: passports, voting, healthcare, banking, taxes, retirement accounts, and how to travel between the two countries.

Written by Rami Mamar, Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) and Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) representative (RCIC-IRB License #R515110), regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC).

---

## Can you hold dual US and Canada citizenship?

> **Short answer:** Yes. Both Canada and the United States fully recognize dual citizenship. Neither country requires renouncing the other citizenship when you naturalize. Canada has permitted dual citizenship since 1977 under the [Citizenship Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-29/index.html); the [Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC)](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=356&top=5) confirms that Canada recognizes all forms of dual or multiple citizenship. As a dual citizen, you hold full rights in both countries: two passports, voting rights in both, and healthcare eligibility where you reside.

**Both Canada and the U.S. recognize dual citizenship.** Neither requires you to renounce the other when you naturalize. | **Travel rule**: enter Canada on your Canadian passport, enter the U.S. on your U.S. passport. U.S. law (8 USC § 1185(b)) technically requires U.S. citizens to use a U.S. passport to enter and exit the U.S. | **U.S. taxes**: the U.S. taxes citizens on worldwide income regardless of residence. You file IRS Form 1040 every year even living in Canada. | **FBAR**: if your foreign (Canadian) accounts total over $10,000 USD at any point during the year, file FinCEN Form 114 separately from your tax return. Failure to file is a $13,000+ penalty per violation. | **TFSAs, FHSAs, RESPs**: NOT recognized as tax-free by the IRS. They create reporting nightmares. RRSPs are protected by the U.S.-Canada Tax Treaty and are simpler. | Most dual citizens living in Canada owe ZERO net U.S. tax due to the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion ($120,000+ in 2026) and Foreign Tax Credit, but they must still file. | Renouncing U.S. citizenship triggers a one-time exit tax on unrealized gains for high-net-worth individuals.

---

## What does dual US-Canada citizenship actually mean?

> **Short answer:** Canada has explicitly recognized dual citizenship since 1977. The U.S. has long permitted it (the Supreme Court ruled in 1967's *Afroyim v. Rusk* that the government cannot strip citizenship for voluntarily acquiring another nationality). Neither government requires you to choose. You hold both citizenships simultaneously, with full rights of each. Practical complications come from each country's tax and reporting rules, not from the citizenship itself.

**Canadian law on dual citizenship**:

- The [Citizenship Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-29/index.html) permits dual (and multiple) citizenship.
- No renunciation required when you acquire another citizenship.
- You retain all rights of a Canadian citizen (passport, vote, healthcare, and more) regardless of how many other citizenships you hold.
- Some countries don't allow their citizens to hold Canadian citizenship; Canada is not the gatekeeper for those countries' rules.

**U.S. law on dual citizenship**:

- The U.S. State Department recognizes dual nationality as permissible.
- U.S. law does not require a U.S. citizen to choose between U.S. citizenship and another nationality.
- When you naturalize as a U.S. citizen, you take an oath that includes renouncing "allegiance to any foreign state", but the courts have held this oath does not require formal renunciation of foreign citizenship.
- The 1967 Supreme Court case *Afroyim v. Rusk* explicitly held that the government cannot strip a U.S. citizen's nationality for voluntarily acquiring another citizenship.

So both countries permit it. The complications come from each country's rules about taxes, accounts, voting, and travel, covered in detail below.

---

## Travel: which passport when?

> **Short answer:** Enter Canada on your Canadian passport. Enter the U.S. on your U.S. passport. Both countries require their citizens to use their own passport when crossing their border. Carry both passports when traveling between Canada and the U.S. You will typically show the Canadian passport at the Canadian border and the U.S. passport at the U.S. border on the same trip.

The legal basis:

- **U.S. law**: 8 USC § 1185(b) requires U.S. citizens to use a U.S. passport to enter and exit the United States. Civil penalties for non-compliance are rare but possible.
- **Canadian law**: Section 4 of the [Citizenship Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-29/index.html) and the Passport Order require Canadian citizens to enter Canada with proof of Canadian citizenship (passport, citizenship certificate + secondary ID, or NEXUS card). See the Government of Canada’s [guidance for dual citizens](https://travel.gc.ca/travelling/documents/dual-citizenship) for full entry requirements.

**Practical travel tips for dual citizens:**

[TABLE]

| Direction of travel | Passport to present |
|---|---|
| Flying from U.S. to Canada | Canadian passport at Canadian arrivals (boarding pass can be either) |
| Flying from Canada to U.S. | U.S. passport at U.S. arrivals (boarding pass can be either) |
| Crossing land border into Canada | Canadian passport or Canadian citizenship document |
| Crossing land border into U.S. | U.S. passport |
| Flying internationally (e.g., to Europe) | The passport with the easier visa requirements for the destination |
| Returning from international travel to U.S. | U.S. passport |
| Returning from international travel to Canada | Canadian passport |

For trips that aren't entry/exit to either Canada or the U.S., you can choose freely. For example, traveling to France or Mexico, both passports give visa-free access; use whichever you prefer (most people use the Canadian passport because it's stronger in fewer destinations).

**NEXUS** is a trusted-traveler program for U.S.-Canada land/air crossings. Dual citizens can apply for NEXUS, which speeds up border crossings significantly.

---

## Can dual citizens vote in both the US and Canada?

> **Short answer:** As a dual citizen, you can vote in U.S. federal, state, and local elections (subject to your U.S. voter registration in a state) AND in Canadian federal, provincial, and municipal elections (subject to your Canadian residency status for some elections). Neither country considers voting in the other an act of allegiance that affects your citizenship.

**U.S. voting**:

- Federal elections (President, Senate, House): you can vote regardless of residence. If you've lived overseas (in Canada), you vote via absentee ballot in the last state you lived in. Use [vote.gov](https://www.vote.gov) or the [Federal Voting Assistance Program](https://www.fvap.gov).
- State and local elections: depends on the state. Most allow former residents to continue voting in state elections; some require continued residency.

**Canadian voting**:

- Federal elections: any Canadian citizen, regardless of residence, can vote. Use [Elections Canada’s online voter registration](https://www.elections.ca) or see [IRCC’s citizenship services](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship.html) for documentation.
- Provincial and municipal elections: typically require residence in the province/municipality.

**Implications**:

- You can vote in both countries' federal elections in the same year if both have elections scheduled.
- Voting in either country has no negative effect on your citizenship in the other.
- Some U.S. states have notification requirements for citizens registering to vote abroad; check your state’s specific rules.

---

## How does U.S. taxation work for dual US-Canada citizens?

> **Short answer:** The United States and Eritrea are the only two countries in the world that tax their citizens on worldwide income regardless of where they live. As a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen living in Canada, you must file an annual U.S. tax return (IRS Form 1040) reporting all your worldwide income, even though all your income is taxed first by the [Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/international-non-residents.html). However, due to the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (~$126,500 in 2026) and the Foreign Tax Credit, most dual citizens owe ZERO net U.S. tax. The complication is the filing burden, not the tax cost.

What you'll file every year as a dual citizen living in Canada:

[TABLE]

| Form | Purpose | When required |
|---|---|---|
| **IRS Form 1040** | Annual U.S. federal income tax return | Always: file if your worldwide income exceeds the filing threshold (about $14,600 USD in 2026 for single filers) |
| **IRS Form 2555** | Foreign Earned Income Exclusion claim | Exclude up to $126,500 USD (2026 limit) of foreign-earned income |
| **IRS Form 1116** | Foreign Tax Credit claim | Credit Canadian taxes paid against U.S. tax owed (alternative or supplement to FEIE) |
| **FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR)** | Report foreign accounts over $10k USD | Required if any combination of foreign accounts exceeds $10k USD at any point during the year |
| **IRS Form 8938 (FATCA)** | Report foreign financial assets | Required if total foreign assets exceed certain thresholds (varies by filing status and residency) |
| **IRS Form 8621** | Passive Foreign Investment Company (PFIC) reporting | Required if you hold Canadian mutual funds or ETFs (these are often classified as PFICs by the IRS, which has punitive tax treatment) |
| **IRS Form 8833** | Treaty-based return position disclosure | Required when claiming certain U.S.-Canada tax treaty benefits |

**FEIE vs. FTC strategy**:

- The FEIE excludes the first ~$126,500 of foreign-earned income from U.S. tax. Simpler to apply but only covers earned income (wages, self-employment).
- The FTC credits Canadian tax paid against U.S. tax owed. More flexible, applying to passive income (dividends, interest, capital gains) as well, but slightly more complex.
- Most dual citizens use FEIE first for wages, then FTC for everything else.

**Critical accounts you'll need to report on FBAR**:

- Canadian checking and savings accounts
- Canadian RRSPs, TFSAs, FHSAs, RESPs
- Canadian brokerage accounts
- Canadian Pension Plan retirement accounts (CPP)
- Any other Canadian financial account where you can make withdrawals

Aggregate the maximum balance of all accounts. If total exceeds $10k USD at any point during the year, file FBAR. Penalty for non-filing is $13,000-$100,000+ per violation; willful violations can be criminal.

---

## How does the IRS treat Canadian retirement accounts like RRSPs and TFSAs?

> **Short answer:** RRSPs are protected by the U.S.-Canada Tax Treaty and are easy; they're treated similarly to U.S. 401(k)s, with growth deferred until withdrawal. TFSAs, FHSAs, and RESPs are NOT recognized as tax-free by the IRS. You'll pay U.S. tax on the growth, file Form 8938 to report them, and possibly classify them as foreign trusts (Form 3520), which is a nightmare. Most cross-border tax advisors recommend dual citizens AVOID TFSAs and similar Canadian-only accounts.

[TABLE]

| Canadian account | IRS treatment | Recommendation for dual citizens |
|---|---|---|
| **RRSP** | Treated similarly to U.S. 401(k) under U.S.-Canada Tax Treaty Article XVIII. Growth deferred; withdrawals taxed | Use freely; standard reporting on FBAR + Form 8938 |
| **TFSA** | NOT recognized as tax-free. May be classified as foreign trust (Form 3520). Growth taxed annually | Avoid unless cross-border tax advisor confirms minimal complexity for your situation |
| **FHSA** | Same as TFSA, NOT recognized as tax-free | Avoid for U.S. dual citizens; use RRSP + HBP instead for first-home savings |
| **RESP** | Treated as a grantor trust. Government grants (CESG) may be considered taxable income to the grantor | Possible but complicated. Many dual citizens use a U.S. 529 plan for kids who attend Canadian universities |
| **Canadian Pension Plan (CPP)** | Standard pension income; reported on Form 1040 | Use freely |
| **Defined-benefit pension (e.g., from a Canadian employer)** | Standard pension; reported when received | Use freely |

The TFSA problem is the #1 surprise for new dual citizens. Most U.S. expats living in Canada either avoid TFSAs entirely or accept the reporting complexity (often $1,500-$3,000/year in cross-border tax preparation fees).

---

## How does healthcare work for US-Canada dual citizens?

> **Short answer:** Canadian provincial health insurance covers most healthcare needs in Canada free at the point of care, once you meet the province's residency requirement (typically 3 months). The U.S. system requires private insurance, Medicare (over 65), or Medicaid (low-income). As a dual citizen, you can use both systems depending on where you live, but they don't overlap; Canadian provincial insurance does not cover treatment in the U.S. (except for emergency stabilization), and Medicare doesn't cover routine treatment in Canada.

**Living in Canada as a dual citizen**:

- Apply for provincial health insurance (OHIP in Ontario, MSP in BC, etc.) once you've met the residency requirement. Free at point of care for medical services.
- Travel insurance for trips to the U.S.; provincial insurance doesn't cover U.S. care (except emergency stabilization).
- If you'll be in the U.S. for long stretches, consider private travel/expat insurance.

**Living in the U.S. as a dual citizen**:

- Private health insurance through employer or marketplace. ACA still applies; no Canadian special treatment.
- Medicare eligibility based on U.S. work history (40+ quarters of contributions) and age 65+.
- Medicaid eligibility based on income; state-by-state.
- If you'll be in Canada for long stretches, Canadian provincial insurance after meeting residency requirement.

**Snowbird (split residence)**:

- Most provinces allow Canadian residents to be away for up to ~7 months/year while maintaining provincial health insurance eligibility. Check your specific province's rules.
- Medicare doesn't cover routine Canadian treatment; you'd need separate private coverage for the Canadian months.

---

## Can dual citizens own property and inherit assets in both countries?

> **Short answer:** You can own real estate, businesses, and investment property in both Canada and the U.S. as a dual citizen with no restrictions. Inheritance flows between the countries cleanly under the U.S.-Canada Tax Treaty, though estate tax (U.S.) and probate (provincial) rules differ. Talk to an estate planner if your net worth is high.

Specific points:

- **Real estate**: You can buy property in either country. Some provinces (BC, Ontario) have foreign-buyer taxes for non-resident purchasers; dual citizens who are Canadian residents are exempt.
- **Investments**: You can hold U.S. brokerage accounts and Canadian brokerage accounts simultaneously. Both report you to the other's tax authority under FATCA (U.S.) and the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) reciprocal agreement.
- **Estate planning**: The U.S. estate tax exemption is currently $13.6 million USD per person (2026); the threshold has been historically high but is scheduled to drop after 2025 unless Congress extends it. Canada has no estate tax but does have deemed-disposition rules: when you die, your unrealized capital gains are treated as realized and taxed. Estate planning across both jurisdictions is best handled by a cross-border specialist.

---

## What about renunciation?

> **Short answer:** You CAN renounce either citizenship, but it's a deliberate, formal process, not automatic. Renouncing U.S. citizenship requires an in-person appointment at a U.S. embassy/consulate, paying a $2,350 USD fee, and may trigger a one-time "exit tax" on unrealized gains for high-net-worth individuals (covered expatriates). Renouncing Canadian citizenship is simpler: Form CIT 0302 plus a $100 fee, with no tax consequences. Most dual citizens do NOT renounce because there's no benefit unless you're trying to escape U.S. tax filing obligations.

**Why people consider renouncing**:

- High-income earners tired of complex U.S. tax filing
- People with substantial Canadian retirement accounts (TFSAs, FHSAs) facing punitive U.S. taxation
- People with U.S. ties so minimal that the filing burden outweighs any benefit

**Why most people DON'T renounce**:

- The right to live and work in both countries indefinitely is valuable
- The Canadian passport is strong; the U.S. passport is also strong; having both is a unique privilege
- Renunciation is irrevocable and triggers an exit tax for high-net-worth individuals
- The filing burden ($1,500-$3,000/year for cross-border tax prep) is manageable for most

**U.S. exit tax (IRC § 877A)**:

- Applies to "covered expatriates": those with net worth ≥ $2 million USD OR average annual U.S. tax liability ≥ $206,000 over the prior 5 years (2026 threshold) OR failure to certify 5 years of tax compliance.
- All unrealized gains over $866,000 USD (2026 exemption) are deemed realized on the day before expatriation, taxed at capital gains rates.
- One-time event, but can be substantial.

If you're considering renunciation, the tax cost analysis is essential; talk to a cross-border tax attorney before scheduling the consular appointment.

---

## What are the most common questions about US-Canada dual citizenship?

> These questions cover the most common concerns for US-Canada dual citizens: tax obligations, how to acquire citizenship in each direction, travel passport rules, how the IRS treats Canadian accounts, children’s eligibility, and total costs. All answers reflect the rules in place as of May 2026. For advice specific to your situation, consult a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) for immigration questions or a cross-border tax specialist for financial matters.

### Can I hold dual citizenship in the U.S. and Canada?

Yes. Both countries fully recognize dual citizenship. Neither requires you to renounce one to acquire the other. The U.S. Supreme Court's 1967 ruling in *Afroyim v. Rusk* settled the U.S. side; Canada's Citizenship Act has explicitly permitted dual citizenship since 1977.

### Do dual citizens pay taxes in both the U.S. and Canada?

You file in both, but you don't pay tax twice on the same income. The U.S.-Canada Tax Treaty + the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion + the Foreign Tax Credit work together so that most dual citizens living in Canada owe ZERO net U.S. tax. The filing burden is real (annual Form 1040, FBAR, possibly 8938 and others), but the tax cost is usually zero or very low. Live in the U.S. as a dual citizen and pay U.S. taxes plus possibly Canadian withholding on Canadian-source income (which is typically refunded under the treaty).

### How do I become a dual citizen of the U.S. and Canada?

The two main paths:

1. **U.S. citizen acquires Canadian citizenship**: Either through (a) Bill C-3 descent if you have Canadian ancestry: file Form CIT 0001, fee $75, ~11 months processing; or (b) immigrating as a permanent resident, living in Canada for 1,095 days within 5 years, then [applying for citizenship](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/apply.html).
2. **Canadian citizen acquires U.S. citizenship**: Marry a U.S. citizen or qualify for a green card through employment or family, live in the U.S. on a green card for 5 years (3 if married to a U.S. citizen), then naturalize.

In both cases, the country you're acquiring doesn't require you to give up the other.

### Is Elon Musk a Canadian citizen?

Yes. Elon Musk holds Canadian citizenship by descent through his mother, Maye Musk, who was born in Saskatchewan. He used his Canadian citizenship to move from South Africa to Canada in 1989 (the move that ultimately took him to the U.S.). He is a triple national (South Africa, Canada, U.S.).

### Do I have to vote in both countries?

No. Voting is a right, not an obligation. You can vote in both, one, or neither. There is no penalty for not voting in either country, and no benefit to voting in one that's lost by also voting in the other.

### Will the U.S. find out about my Canadian bank accounts?

Yes. Under FATCA (Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act), every Canadian bank reports U.S.-citizen account holders directly to the IRS through CRA. There's no hiding from FBAR or FATCA; file properly.

### Can my children inherit both citizenships?

Yes, with conditions. Canadian citizenship inheritance is governed by Bill C-3 (covered in our [hub article](/news/canadian-citizenship-for-americans-2026)). U.S. citizenship by descent (jus sanguinis) requires the U.S.-citizen parent to have lived in the U.S. for at least 5 years before the child's birth, with at least 2 of those years after age 14 (the requirement is more complex for children born abroad; talk to a U.S. immigration lawyer).

### My father was born in Canada: can I get dual citizenship?

Almost certainly yes under Bill C-3. Apply for proof of Canadian citizenship via Form CIT 0001. If your father was a Canadian citizen at the time of your birth, you've been a Canadian citizen since you were born (you just don't have the paper yet). The application takes ~11 months and costs $75 CAD.

### What are the benefits of dual citizenship US and Canada?

- Right to live, work, and study in either country indefinitely
- Two strong passports (Canadian and U.S.) for visa-free travel
- Vote in both countries
- Healthcare options in both systems
- Eligibility for federal jobs in both countries (some have citizenship requirements)
- Right to pass citizenship to your descendants under both countries' rules
- Strategic location for retirement (live in one, summer in the other)

### Why is dual citizenship sometimes considered bad?

The main downsides are:

- **U.S. tax complexity**: annual filing burden, $1,500-$3,000/year for cross-border tax prep
- **TFSA/FHSA complications**: Canadian-only accounts that don't translate to U.S. tax treatment
- **Jury duty obligations**: in both countries, in theory (rarely enforced abroad)
- **Compliance burden**: FBAR, FATCA, possibly multiple state tax filings
- **Mandatory military service** in some countries (not Canada or the U.S.)

For most people, the benefits outweigh the costs by a large margin. The exception is high-net-worth individuals (>$5M) for whom the U.S. filing burden becomes substantial and renunciation can make financial sense.

### Dual citizenship Canada cost: what's the total to acquire it?

If acquiring Canadian citizenship via Bill C-3 descent: **$75 CAD** plus document collection costs ($300-$1,500). If acquiring through naturalization (3 years residency + application): **$630 CAD** for the citizenship application + the cost of becoming a permanent resident (PR) first ($1,365 federal + provincial fees, totaling $5,000-$10,000). If acquiring U.S. citizenship from Canadian side: roughly **$725 USD** for the naturalization application (Form N-400) plus the cost of getting a green card first.

---

## What should new dual citizens do first?

> The following steps address what new dual citizens most often overlook after acquiring citizenship in either direction. None are complicated individually, but missing them can lead to tax penalties, account reporting failures, or avoidable legal costs.

1. **Get both passports issued.** Apply for the Canadian passport once you have your citizenship certificate. Keep both updated and in good condition.
2. **File U.S. taxes immediately.** Even for the year you acquire Canadian citizenship; your worldwide income is reportable to the IRS from day one of U.S. citizenship.
3. **Avoid the TFSA / FHSA trap.** Use RRSPs instead. The TFSA's tax-free growth doesn't help you; it just adds reporting complexity.
4. **Find a cross-border tax preparer.** Look for a CPA or accountant who specializes in U.S.-Canada cross-border filing. Typical fee: $1,500-$3,000 per year. Worth it.
5. **NEXUS enrollment.** Speeds up land/air crossings significantly. $50 USD for 5 years.
6. **Maintain U.S. voter registration.** Use the Federal Voting Assistance Program if you live in Canada.
7. **Update your estate plan.** Both countries' rules apply. A cross-border estate attorney is worth the consultation fee.
8. **Watch your CPP / Social Security contributions.** The Totalization Agreement coordinates the two, so you don't lose retirement credits when you move between countries.

# Americans Moving to Canada: 7 Visa Paths in 2026 (Complete Guide)
