# Canadian Citizenship Test 2026: Practice Questions, Sample Test, and Complete Study Guide

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canadian-citizenship-test-practice-2026
Category: Citizenship
Published: 2026-05-24
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Acronyms used in this guide: IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada), CRS (Comprehensive Ranking System), CLB (Canadian Language Benchmark), PR (Permanent Resident), CRA...

# Canadian Citizenship Test 2026: Practice Questions, Sample Test, and Complete Study Guide

*As of May 24, 2026.*

*Acronyms used in this guide: IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada), CRS (Comprehensive Ranking System), CLB (Canadian Language Benchmark), PR (Permanent Resident), CRA (Canada Revenue Agency), RCIC (Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant), CICC (College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants), IRB (Immigration and Refugee Board).*

About 350,000 permanent residents apply for Canadian citizenship each year. Of the adult applicants between 18 and 54, every single one writes a test based on the **Discover Canada** study guide. The test itself is short (20 multiple-choice questions, 30 minutes, 15 right to pass; see [IRCC test format](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/test/how-it-works.html)), but roughly 10% of applicants fail on the first attempt, almost always because they did not study the right material.

This guide walks through what the test actually covers, how to prepare for free, sample practice questions across every topic area, what happens on test day, and what to do if you fail. It also explains how the test fits into the broader citizenship application so you understand the immigration side of the journey, not just the exam.

Written by Rami Mamar, RCIC-IRB licensed by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (License #R515110). Our team has guided thousands of clients from over 50 countries through Canadian citizenship.

## What Does the Canadian Citizenship Test Actually Test?

> **Short answer:** The Canadian Citizenship Test is a 20-question multiple-choice exam based entirely on the **Discover Canada** study guide, covering rights and responsibilities, Canadian history, government, geography, symbols, the economy, and Indigenous peoples. You need 15 correct answers (75%) to pass.

IRCC ([canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship.html)) uses the test to confirm that adult citizenship applicants have a working knowledge of Canada; its history, values, institutions, and symbols. The questions are not designed to trick you. They are designed to confirm you have actually read the Discover Canada guide.

The single biggest mistake we see at our Toronto office is applicants studying random "Canadian citizenship test 2026" practice apps without first reading the actual Discover Canada PDF. The apps are helpful for drill practice, but the questions on the real test come word-for-word from concepts covered in Discover Canada. If you skip the source material and only memorize app questions, you will see unfamiliar wording on test day and panic.

The Discover Canada guide is free, 68 pages, and available at [canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/discover-canada.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/discover-canada.html). Download it before anything else.

## Who Must Take the Canadian Citizenship Test (and Who Is Exempt)?

> **Short answer:** Adult applicants between ages 18 and 54 must take the citizenship test ([IRCC eligibility page on canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility.html)). Applicants under 18 and applicants 55 and older are exempt and do not write the test at all. Limited medical and accommodation exemptions exist for the 18-to-54 group, granted on a case-by-case basis.

The age rule is strict. If you are 18 to 54 on the date your citizenship application is received by IRCC, you write the test. The cutoff is set when IRCC opens your file, not when you submit it or when you eventually sit the test.

Applicants under 18 are processed as minors using form CIT 0003. They do not write the test. They do not prove language ability.

Applicants 55 and older are exempt from both the test and the formal language proof requirement. They still need to meet the residency obligation (1,095 days physical presence in 5 years), the tax filing requirement, and admissibility checks.

**Limited exemptions for the 18 to 54 group:**

- **Medical exemption.** Documented serious medical conditions that prevent you from taking the test (cognitive impairment, severe anxiety with medical documentation, certain disabilities) can be presented to IRCC with a supporting letter from a treating physician. IRCC reviews each request and decides individually.
- **Reasonable accommodation.** If you can take the test but need accommodations (extra time, a reader, a quiet room, sign-language interpretation), submit the accommodation request with your application. IRCC accommodates regularly for documented needs.

If you are uncertain whether you qualify for an exemption, do not assume; submit supporting documentation with your application and let IRCC decide. Self-exempting because you assume the rules apply to you is a common cause of file delays.

## What Is the Format of the Canadian Citizenship Test?

> **Short answer:** The test consists of 20 multiple-choice questions drawn from Discover Canada, delivered in 30 minutes. You need 15 correct (75%) to pass. Most tests in 2026 are conducted online via Microsoft Teams (per [IRCC test format on canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/test/how-it-works.html)) with webcam monitoring, though in-person tests at IRCC Local Offices are available on request.

Every question is multiple choice with three or four answer options. Some questions have a "select two" format (rare, well-marked when they appear). There is no essay component, no spoken component, and no surprise listening section.

**Format quick reference:**

| Element | Detail |
|--------|---|
| Total questions | 20 |
| Question format | Multiple choice (3 to 4 options each) |
| Time allowed | 30 minutes |
| Pass mark | 15 correct (75%) |
| Topics covered | Rights and responsibilities, history, government, symbols, geography, economy, Indigenous peoples |
| Attempts allowed | 3 within a 30-day window |
| Delivery | Online via Microsoft Teams (default in 2026) or in-person at IRCC Local Office (on request) |

The online delivery uses a Microsoft Teams interface with webcam monitoring (see [IRCC: Take the online citizenship test](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/test/online.html)). You log in at your scheduled time, an IRCC officer verifies your ID over video, and the test launches in your browser. You cannot pause, switch tabs, or have anyone else in the room. The officer monitors your video feed throughout.

In-person tests still exist for applicants who request accommodations or who have weak internet at home. Request in-person at the time you submit your application or when IRCC sends the test invitation. The trade-off is timing: in-person tests can wait 4 to 8 weeks for a slot, while online tests are typically scheduled within 2 to 4 weeks of the invitation.

## How Do I Prepare for the Canadian Citizenship Test?

> **Short answer:** Read the official **Discover Canada** PDF cover-to-cover (free, 68 pages, available at canada.ca). Take the free IRCC self-test at canada.ca to gauge your readiness, then drill with library practice tests (Toronto Public Library, Richmond Public Library, Citizenship Counts, Immigrant Services Calgary). Mobile apps help with repetition but are not a substitute for reading the source.

Here is the study plan we recommend at Go Far Global to clients preparing for the test:

**Week 1: Read the source material.**
Download the Discover Canada PDF from the [IRCC citizenship study page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/test/study.html). Read it from start to finish, not skimming. The guide is structured into 11 chapters covering rights and responsibilities, Canadian identity, history, government, justice, symbols, economy, and regions. Make notes in a notebook on names, dates, and numbers; those are the most common quiz prompts.

**Week 2: Take the official IRCC self-test.**
IRCC publishes a free practice test at [ct-tc.apps.cic.gc.ca](https://ct-tc.apps.cic.gc.ca). It uses the same software as the real test, so the interface feels identical on test day. Score yourself honestly. If you are below 15 correct, return to the chapters where you lost points.

**Week 3: Drill with library and settlement agency quizzes.**
These are all free and high quality:

- **Toronto Public Library**; tpl.ca/using-the-library/new-to-canada/citizenship-test
- **Richmond Public Library**; yourlibrary.ca/citizenship
- **Citizenship Counts**; citizenshipcounts.ca/quiz
- **Immigrant Services Calgary**; immigrantservicescalgary.ca/citizenship-study-quiz

Each library quiz has slightly different question wording, which is good; it forces you to learn the underlying concept rather than memorizing one phrasing.

**Week 4: Use a mobile app for repetition while commuting or relaxing.**
Mobile apps are useful for repeated drilling, especially during downtime. They are not a substitute for reading Discover Canada, but they are excellent for cementing facts after you have read the source.

### Practice Apps Our Clients Have Used Successfully

We are not affiliated with any of the apps below, and we cannot guarantee the quality or accuracy of their practice material. We share them because our citizenship clients have used them to successfully pass the citizenship test. Always verify any practice question against Discover Canada itself before treating it as gospel.

- **Citizenship App**; citizenshipapp.ca; web-based practice platform
- **Canadian Citizenship Test (Bubbling ISO)**; Google Play Store; Android, free with ads
- **CitizenTest.ca Preparation Course**; citizentest.ca/preparation; web-based, free practice plus optional paid coaching

The two iOS and Android apps that consistently rank in the Canadian app stores ("Canadian Citizenship 2026" with 4.9-star ratings and 39,000+ reviews on Apple, and a similar 4.8-star Android version with 14,000+ reviews) are also free and well-reviewed. We mention them here for completeness; no affiliation, no endorsement guarantee.

If you have a learning disability or limited reading comprehension, consider asking IRCC for an oral hearing accommodation instead of the standard written test. The standard is still based on Discover Canada content, but the format is conversational with a citizenship official.

## What Sample Practice Questions Should I Try Before the Citizenship Test?

> **Short answer:** The 35 sample questions below cover every major topic on the citizenship test; rights and responsibilities, history, government, federal elections, justice, symbols, geography, economy, regions, and Indigenous peoples. Each question is followed by the correct answer plus a one-line explanation. These are written in the style of the actual test, but they are not real IRCC test questions.

### Rights and Responsibilities

**Q1.** Which of the following is a responsibility of Canadian citizenship?
- a) Owning property
- b) Speaking French
- c) Obeying the law
- d) Joining a political party

**Answer: c) Obeying the law.** Obeying laws is one of six core responsibilities of Canadian citizenship, alongside taking responsibility for oneself and family, serving on a jury when called, voting in elections, helping others in the community, and protecting and enjoying our heritage and environment.

**Q2.** Which Canadian document outlines the fundamental rights of all Canadians?
- a) The Magna Carta
- b) The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
- c) The Royal Proclamation
- d) The Indian Act

**Answer: b) The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.** The Charter was added to the Canadian Constitution in 1982 (see [Canadian Heritage: How rights are protected in Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/how-rights-protected.html)) and protects fundamental freedoms, democratic rights, mobility rights, legal rights, equality rights, and official-language and minority-language education rights.

**Q3.** At what age can a Canadian citizen vote in a federal election?
- a) 16
- b) 17
- c) 18
- d) 21

**Answer: c) 18.** Federal voting age has been 18 since 1970.

**Q4.** Which of the following is a fundamental freedom protected by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
- a) Freedom of religion
- b) Freedom of expression
- c) Freedom of peaceful assembly
- d) All of the above

**Answer: d) All of the above.** The Charter protects four fundamental freedoms: conscience and religion; thought, belief, opinion, and expression (including freedom of the press); peaceful assembly; and association.

### Canada's History

**Q5.** Who are the three founding peoples of Canada?
- a) French, British, and Aboriginal peoples
- b) Vikings, Inuit, and French
- c) British, Spanish, and Portuguese
- d) French, Dutch, and Italian

**Answer: a) French, British, and Aboriginal peoples.** Discover Canada identifies these as the three founding peoples whose interactions shaped the country.

**Q6.** In what year did Canada become a country through Confederation?
- a) 1812
- b) 1867
- c) 1885
- d) 1905

**Answer: b) 1867.** The British North America Act took effect on July 1, 1867, uniting the Province of Canada (Ontario and Quebec), New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia into the new Dominion of Canada.

**Q7.** Who was the first Prime Minister of Canada?
- a) Sir John A. Macdonald
- b) Sir Wilfrid Laurier
- c) William Lyon Mackenzie King
- d) Pierre Elliott Trudeau

**Answer: a) Sir John A. Macdonald.** Macdonald served as Canada's first Prime Minister from 1867 to 1873 and again from 1878 to 1891. His face appears on the $10 bill.

**Q8.** What major engineering achievement connected Canada from east to west and was completed in 1885?
- a) The Canadian Pacific Railway
- b) The St. Lawrence Seaway
- c) The Trans-Canada Highway
- d) The Welland Canal

**Answer: a) The Canadian Pacific Railway.** The CPR was completed on November 7, 1885, when the last spike was driven at Craigellachie, British Columbia.

**Q9.** When did women in most of Canada first gain the right to vote in federal elections?
- a) 1900
- b) 1918
- c) 1928
- d) 1940

**Answer: b) 1918.** Most Canadian women got the federal vote in 1918, though Indigenous women and some other groups had to wait decades longer. Asian-Canadian women got the vote in 1948, and First Nations women on reserves in 1960.

**Q10.** What famous Canadian battle of World War I is considered a defining moment in Canada's military history?
- a) The Battle of Vimy Ridge (1917)
- b) The Battle of the Plains of Abraham (1759)
- c) The Battle of Queenston Heights (1812)
- d) The Battle of Stalingrad (1942)

**Answer: a) The Battle of Vimy Ridge (1917).** In April 1917, the four divisions of the Canadian Corps fought together for the first time and captured Vimy Ridge from German forces. The victory is often cited as the moment Canada emerged as a nation with its own identity, separate from Britain.

**Q11.** What was the role of Sir Sam Steele in Canadian history?
- a) He led the Canadian Pacific Railway construction
- b) He was a famous officer of the North-West Mounted Police (forerunner of the RCMP)
- c) He served as the first Governor General
- d) He wrote "O Canada"

**Answer: b) He was a famous officer of the North-West Mounted Police.** Sam Steele is one of Canada's most celebrated frontier soldiers and policemen, known for his role in keeping order during the Klondike Gold Rush.

### How Canadians Govern Themselves

**Q12.** What are the three levels of government in Canada?
- a) Federal, Provincial, Local
- b) Federal, Provincial or Territorial, Municipal
- c) National, Regional, City
- d) Crown, Parliament, Senate

**Answer: b) Federal, Provincial or Territorial, Municipal.** The federal government in Ottawa handles national matters, provinces and territories handle areas like education and health care, and municipalities handle local services like transit and garbage collection.

**Q13.** Who is Canada's official Head of State?
- a) The Prime Minister
- b) The Governor General
- c) The King (Charles III)
- d) The Speaker of the House of Commons

**Answer: c) The King (Charles III).** Canada is a constitutional monarchy with the King of Canada (currently Charles III, since September 2022) as Head of State. The Prime Minister is Head of Government.

**Q14.** Who represents the King at the federal level in Canada?
- a) The Prime Minister
- b) The Governor General
- c) The Lieutenant Governor
- d) The Speaker

**Answer: b) The Governor General.** The Governor General performs the King's constitutional duties at the federal level. At the provincial level, each province has a Lieutenant Governor who represents the King.

**Q15.** How many provinces and territories does Canada have?
- a) 10 provinces and 3 territories
- b) 12 provinces and 2 territories
- c) 8 provinces and 5 territories
- d) 11 provinces and 4 territories

**Answer: a) 10 provinces and 3 territories.** The provinces are Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, and Saskatchewan. The territories are Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut.

**Q16.** What system of government does Canada have?
- a) A republic with an elected president
- b) A direct democracy
- c) A federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy
- d) A theocracy

**Answer: c) A federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy.** Canada combines three principles: federalism (powers shared between the federal and provincial governments), parliamentary democracy (an elected House of Commons), and constitutional monarchy (the King as Head of State, subject to the Constitution).

**Q17.** How are members of the House of Commons selected?
- a) Appointed by the Prime Minister
- b) Elected by Canadian voters in federal elections
- c) Appointed by the Governor General
- d) Selected by provincial premiers

**Answer: b) Elected by Canadian voters in federal elections.** Each riding (electoral district) elects one Member of Parliament to the House of Commons.

**Q18.** How are senators selected in Canada?
- a) Elected by Canadian voters
- b) Appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister
- c) Elected by provincial legislatures
- d) Hereditary positions

**Answer: b) Appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister.** Senators traditionally serve until age 75. The Senate gives "sober second thought" to legislation passed by the House of Commons.

### Federal Elections

**Q19.** How often must federal elections be held in Canada (at the maximum)?
- a) Every 2 years
- b) Every 4 years
- c) Every 5 years
- d) Every 7 years

**Answer: b) Every 4 years.** Federal elections must be held at least every 4 years, though they can be called sooner if the government loses the confidence of the House.

**Q20.** What is a "riding" in Canadian elections?
- a) A small town
- b) An electoral district that elects one Member of Parliament
- c) A political party
- d) A government department

**Answer: b) An electoral district that elects one Member of Parliament.** Canada is divided into 338 ridings, each represented by one MP in the House of Commons.

**Q21.** What happens when no party wins a majority of seats in the House of Commons?
- a) A new election is called immediately
- b) The Governor General chooses the Prime Minister
- c) A minority government forms, often relying on other parties to pass legislation
- d) The Senate takes over

**Answer: c) A minority government forms.** A minority government must work with other parties to pass legislation and can be defeated on confidence votes.

### The Justice System

**Q22.** What does the rule of law mean in Canada?
- a) Only wealthy people must obey the law
- b) Everyone, including the government, must obey the law
- c) Police officers interpret the law however they choose
- d) The Prime Minister is above the law

**Answer: b) Everyone, including the government, must obey the law.** The rule of law means no one is above the law, including elected officials and government bodies.

**Q23.** What is the role of the Supreme Court of Canada?
- a) To create new laws
- b) To interpret the Constitution and federal laws
- c) To pass federal budgets
- d) To advise the King

**Answer: b) To interpret the Constitution and federal laws.** The Supreme Court is Canada's highest court and the final court of appeal. It has nine judges, three of whom must be from Quebec.

**Q24.** Which Canadian police force serves as the national police?
- a) The Ontario Provincial Police (OPP)
- b) The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP)
- c) The Sûreté du Québec
- d) The Canadian Forces Military Police

**Answer: b) The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).** The RCMP enforces federal laws across Canada and also provides provincial policing in 8 of 10 provinces (Ontario and Quebec have their own provincial police forces).

### Canadian Symbols

**Q25.** What is the national anthem of Canada?
- a) "God Save the King"
- b) "The Maple Leaf Forever"
- c) "O Canada"
- d) "True North"

**Answer: c) "O Canada".** "O Canada" was officially adopted as the national anthem in 1980. The English lyrics were updated in 2018 to gender-neutral wording ("in all of us command" instead of "in all thy sons command").

**Q26.** When did the maple leaf flag become Canada's official flag?
- a) 1867
- b) February 15, 1965
- c) 1982
- d) 1995

**Answer: b) February 15, 1965.** February 15 is now celebrated as National Flag of Canada Day.

**Q27.** What is Canada's national winter sport?
- a) Skiing
- b) Curling
- c) Hockey (ice hockey)
- d) Snowboarding

**Answer: c) Hockey.** Hockey was officially declared Canada's national winter sport in 1994. The same legislation declared lacrosse Canada's national summer sport.

**Q28.** What is Canada's national summer sport?
- a) Baseball
- b) Lacrosse
- c) Cricket
- d) Soccer

**Answer: b) Lacrosse.** Lacrosse, which has Indigenous origins, was declared Canada's national summer sport in 1994.

**Q29.** What is Canada's official motto?
- a) "Strong and Free"
- b) "From Sea to Sea" (A Mari Usque Ad Mare)
- c) "We the People"
- d) "Peace, Order, and Good Government"

**Answer: b) "From Sea to Sea" (A Mari Usque Ad Mare).** The Latin motto appears on Canada's coat of arms and references the country stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean.

### Geography and Regions

**Q30.** What three oceans border Canada?
- a) Pacific, Atlantic, and Arctic
- b) Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian
- c) Atlantic, Hudson, and Arctic
- d) Pacific, Hudson, and Atlantic

**Answer: a) Pacific, Atlantic, and Arctic.** Canada has the longest coastline of any country in the world, touching three oceans.

**Q31.** What is the capital city of Canada?
- a) Toronto
- b) Montreal
- c) Ottawa
- d) Vancouver

**Answer: c) Ottawa.** Ottawa, in Ontario, has been Canada's capital since 1857 when Queen Victoria chose it.

**Q32.** Which province is the smallest by area?
- a) Prince Edward Island
- b) New Brunswick
- c) Nova Scotia
- d) Newfoundland and Labrador

**Answer: a) Prince Edward Island.** PEI is the smallest province by area (5,660 km²) and population.

**Q33.** Which Canadian province is officially bilingual at the provincial level?
- a) Quebec
- b) New Brunswick
- c) Ontario
- d) Manitoba

**Answer: b) New Brunswick.** New Brunswick is the only officially bilingual province, with both English and French as official languages of the provincial government.

**Q34.** What is the official language of Quebec?
- a) French
- b) English
- c) Both English and French
- d) Indigenous languages

**Answer: a) French.** Quebec's official language is French, enshrined in the provincial Charter of the French Language. French is also a federal official language alongside English.

### Indigenous Peoples

**Q35.** What are the three groups of Indigenous peoples in Canada?
- a) First Nations, Inuit, and Métis
- b) First Nations, Cree, and Inuit
- c) Aboriginal Status, Non-Status, and Métis
- d) First Peoples, Inuit, and Native Canadian

**Answer: a) First Nations, Inuit, and Métis.** The Constitution Act of 1982 recognizes these three groups as Aboriginal peoples of Canada. First Nations live across Canada; Inuit live mainly in the Arctic regions (especially Nunavut); Métis are people of mixed First Nations and European ancestry, historically concentrated in the Prairies.

**Q36.** What was the residential school system in Canada?
- a) A series of free public schools for new Canadians
- b) Government-funded schools that forcibly removed Indigenous children from their families to assimilate them
- c) Boarding schools for the wealthy
- d) Schools that taught Indigenous languages and culture

**Answer: b) Government-funded schools that forcibly removed Indigenous children from their families to assimilate them.** Residential schools operated from the 1870s to the late 1990s, causing severe and lasting harm. Canada formally apologized in 2008, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission released 94 Calls to Action in 2015.

### Canada's Economy

**Q37.** What are the three main types of industry in Canada's economy?
- a) Service, Manufacturing, Natural Resources
- b) Agriculture, Fishing, Forestry
- c) Technology, Healthcare, Education
- d) Banking, Insurance, Retail

**Answer: a) Service, Manufacturing, Natural Resources.** Most Canadians work in service industries (more than 75% of jobs), followed by manufacturing and natural resources (oil, gas, mining, forestry, fishing, agriculture).

**Q38.** With which two countries does Canada have a free-trade agreement under CUSMA (formerly NAFTA)?
- a) United States and Mexico
- b) United Kingdom and France
- c) China and Japan
- d) Germany and Italy

**Answer: a) United States and Mexico.** The Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) replaced NAFTA in 2020 and continues free-trade rules among the three countries.

## What Topics Does Discover Canada Cover?

> **Short answer:** Discover Canada is structured around five broad themes; rights and responsibilities, who we are (identity), Canada's history, modern Canada, and how Canadians govern themselves; supplemented by sections on the justice system, symbols, economy, and regions. Most of your test will draw on the first three themes.

The Discover Canada guide is broken into 11 sections plus a study questions appendix. The high-yield sections (most likely to appear on your test) are:

1. **Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship.** The Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the six responsibilities of citizenship, equality rights, language rights, mobility rights.

2. **Who We Are.** Canadian identity, multiculturalism, the three founding peoples, official languages, Aboriginal peoples (First Nations, Inuit, Métis).

3. **Canada's History.** Confederation in 1867, early explorers (Cabot, Cartier, Champlain), the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1885, the World Wars, women's suffrage in 1918, key Prime Ministers.

4. **Modern Canada.** Post-WWII immigration, Quiet Revolution in Quebec, patriation of the Constitution in 1982, the Charter, Truth and Reconciliation.

5. **How Canadians Govern Themselves.** Constitutional monarchy, parliamentary democracy, three levels of government, separation of powers, the role of the Crown.

The remaining sections (Federal Elections, The Justice System, Canadian Symbols, Canada's Economy, Canada's Regions) carry fewer questions but each can appear on your test. Do not skip them.

## What Happens on Citizenship Test Day?

> **Short answer:** You receive an email notice 6 to 9 months after your application is acknowledged, giving a 30-day window to take the test per [IRCC test invitation guidance](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/test/invitation.html) (3 attempts allowed). Most tests are conducted online via Microsoft Teams. Log in 10 minutes early with valid government photo ID, your invitation letter, and a quiet room. The test itself takes 30 minutes or less, and you receive your result almost immediately.

### Before You Log In

- Read the IRCC test instructions email carefully (it includes the exact link, your test code, and timing rules).
- Test your webcam, microphone, and internet connection the day before. Use a wired connection if possible.
- Have your **passport or PR card** and the **invitation email** open on your phone or printed.
- Sit in a quiet, well-lit room with no other people. Family members cannot be in the room. The officer can ask you to scan the room with your webcam.
- Have a glass of water nearby. No food, no notes, no second device.

### When You Log In

1. Join the Microsoft Teams call at the exact time on your invitation.
2. The IRCC officer verifies your identity over video. They will ask you to show your photo ID and confirm your name and date of birth.
3. The officer explains the rules: 20 questions, 30 minutes, no pauses, no tab-switching, eyes on the screen.
4. They launch the test. You see one question at a time with multiple-choice answers.
5. Click your answer and move to the next question. You can flag and return to questions if time permits.

### After You Finish

- The system tells you immediately whether you passed.
- If you passed, IRCC schedules your oath ceremony 1 to 4 months later.
- If you failed, you receive a notice with the rules for retaking (you get up to 3 attempts within the 30-day window).

Most applicants finish well under the 30-minute limit. The questions are straightforward if you have studied the material.

## What Happens If You Fail the Canadian Citizenship Test?

> **Short answer:** You get up to 3 test attempts within a 30-day window. If you fail the first attempt, IRCC reschedules within days. If you fail all three attempts, you are not refused outright; instead, you are scheduled for a hearing with a citizenship official, where you can demonstrate your knowledge in a conversation rather than a multiple-choice format.

Failing the first attempt is recoverable. IRCC typically reschedules the next attempt within 2 to 4 days, allowing you time to review weak areas. The most common reason for first-attempt failure is exam anxiety combined with insufficient study time on Discover Canada. Use the few days between attempts to read the chapters where you struggled.

Failing twice is more serious but still recoverable. By this point, you should have an RCIC review your study plan and consider whether you have a documented learning issue that qualifies for accommodation. If anxiety or test format is the problem, you can also request the in-person test format for your final attempt.

Failing all three attempts triggers a citizenship hearing. A citizenship official (typically called a Citizenship Judge or a designated officer) interviews you in a structured conversation. They ask the same kinds of questions covered in the multiple-choice test but allow you to demonstrate knowledge through explanation. The pass standard is the same (you must show working knowledge), but the format is friendlier for applicants whose strengths are conversational rather than testing.

Failing the hearing means your citizenship application is refused. You can reapply (pay the full $653 fee again), but you must wait until any underlying issues are addressed; typically more study time and possibly accommodation requests.

## Why Do People Fail the Canadian Citizenship Test?

> **Short answer:** The five most common failure causes are not reading Discover Canada (relying on apps alone), confusing facts from other countries' history with Canadian history, testing English language ability rather than civics knowledge in marginal cases, test-day technical problems on online delivery, and exam anxiety that fogs simple recall.

In rough order of frequency from our Toronto office:

1. **Not reading Discover Canada.** Applicants drill through 500 app questions but never read the source material. They pass the apps and fail the real test because the wording on the actual test follows the guide rather than the apps.

2. **Confusing Canadian history with US or UK history.** Applicants who studied for the US naturalization test or the UK Life in the UK test sometimes mix up dates, prime ministers, and structures. Canadian Confederation was 1867 (not 1776). Canada's founding Prime Minister was John A. Macdonald (not George Washington).

3. **Weak English or French.** The test is administered in English or French. If your reading comprehension in your chosen language is weak, you can mistakenly select wrong answers because you misread the question. Make sure your CLB 4 language proof reflects your actual reading ability.

4. **Technical issues on online delivery.** Webcam dropouts, slow internet, browser crashes, or Microsoft Teams login problems can rattle applicants. If your connection drops, the officer pauses the test and reconnects you. Take a breath, do not panic.

5. **Exam anxiety.** Adults who have not taken a formal exam in 20 years can freeze even with strong preparation. The technique that works: read each question twice, eliminate obviously wrong answers first, then choose the best remaining option.

If you have a documented anxiety condition or other medical issue affecting test performance, request accommodation in advance. IRCC accommodates regularly.

## What Happens After You Pass the Canadian Citizenship Test?

> **Short answer:** After passing the test, your application moves to the oath ceremony queue. Oath ceremonies are scheduled 1 to 4 months after the test pass. You can choose between a virtual ceremony over Microsoft Teams (typically scheduled in 4 to 6 weeks) or an in-person ceremony at a local IRCC office (typically 6 to 12 weeks). At the ceremony, you take the Oath of Citizenship, sign the Oath form, and receive your Canadian citizenship certificate.

The Oath of Citizenship reads:

> "I swear (or affirm) that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to His Majesty King Charles the Third, King of Canada, His Heirs and Successors, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada, including the Constitution, which recognizes and affirms the Aboriginal and treaty rights of First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples, and fulfill my duties as a Canadian citizen."

You take the oath in English or French (your choice). For applicants from a religious tradition that prohibits oaths, the law allows you to "affirm" rather than "swear" the same words.

From the moment the oath is administered, you are a Canadian citizen. You receive your citizenship certificate immediately. You can apply for a Canadian passport that same day if you wish (most clients apply within the first week).

If you currently hold another citizenship, Canada has allowed dual citizenship since 1977. You can keep your original citizenship if your country of origin allows it. Some countries (Iran, China, Saudi Arabia, India, among others) restrict or revoke citizenship when you take another. Check your country of origin's law before the oath ceremony.

## How Does the Citizenship Test Fit Into Your Application?

> **Short answer:** The citizenship test is one of five core requirements in your citizenship grant application; alongside residency obligation (1,095 days physical presence in 5 years), tax filing, language proof, and admissibility. You only sit the test if you are 18 to 54 and your application is complete enough to reach the test stage. Understanding how the test fits into the broader application helps you avoid common errors that delay your file.

### The Five Pillars of an Adult Citizenship Grant

1. **Permanent residence status.** You must be a Canadian permanent resident. Your PR card does not need to be valid (the status persists even if the card expires), but you cannot be under a removal order.

2. **Physical presence: 1,095 days in 5 years (the residency obligation under [IRCC physical-presence rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility.html)).** You must have been physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days (3 years) in the 5 years before applying. Days as a temporary resident before becoming PR count as half-days, capped at 365 half-days (182.5 actual days of credit).

3. **Tax filing: 3 of 5 years.** You must have filed Canadian income taxes (or shown that you were not required to file) for at least 3 of the 5 years before applying.

4. **Language proof: CLB 4.** Applicants aged 18 to 54 must prove English or French ability at CLB 4 in speaking and listening. Acceptable proof includes approved language tests (CELPIP-General, IELTS General Training, TEF Canada, TCF Canada), a Canadian secondary or post-secondary credential taught in English or French, or a government-funded language class certificate.

5. **The citizenship test (this test).** Applicants aged 18 to 54 write the test based on Discover Canada.

If any of these five pillars is missing, your application gets returned without reaching the test stage. The single biggest cause of citizenship application returns in 2026 is incomplete residency calculations.

For a full walk-through of the citizenship grant application end to end, including the current $653 fee structure and the 12-month processing time, see our [Canadian Citizenship Application 2026 Complete Guide](/news/canadian-citizenship-application-2026). For the latest processing-time tracker, see the [Canadian Citizenship Processing Time guide](/news/canadian-citizenship-processing-time-12-months-2026).

### How the Test Fits the Timeline

A typical successful citizenship file in 2026 follows this timeline:

- **Months 0 to 2:** Submit the [citizenship application](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/apply.html), pay the $653 fee, receive Acknowledgement of Receipt (AOR)
- **Months 2 to 6:** Background and residency verification
- **Months 6 to 10:** Test invitation arrives by email
- **Months 6 to 11:** Sit the test (within the 30-day window of your invitation)
- **Months 10 to 14:** Oath ceremony invitation
- **Months 11 to 14:** Take the oath, become a Canadian citizen

The test invitation is the signal that your file has cleared background and residency verification. By the time you receive it, the rest of your application is in good order.

## What Mistakes Do Citizenship Applicants Make Before the Test?

> **Short answer:** The five most common pre-test mistakes are applying before reaching the 1,095-day residency threshold, miscalculating travel history against passport stamps, missing tax-filing years, providing the wrong language test type (Express Entry tests are not always accepted for citizenship), and submitting the wrong fee after the March 31, 2026 fee increase to $653.

In our Toronto office we see these recur week after week:

1. **Applying before reaching 1,095 days physical presence.** Half-days from pre-PR time only count up to 365 half-days. Many applicants think 3 years as a PR equals 1,095 days, but it does not if you traveled. Always run the IRCC Physical Presence Calculator with passport-verified dates.

2. **Missing trips that show on passport stamps.** IRCC pulls your CBSA Integrated Customs Enforcement (ICES) travel history. If you forgot a weekend trip to Niagara Falls (US side) and IRCC sees it on their database, your file goes into secondary review.

3. **Skipping a required tax year.** If you were required to file taxes (any year you earned employment, self-employment, or significant investment income in Canada) and you did not file, your application is held. Filing late is fine; not filing when required is not.

4. **Wrong language test type.** Citizenship accepts CELPIP-General, IELTS General Training, TEF Canada, and TCF Canada. CELPIP-General LS (Listening-Speaking only) is also accepted. IELTS Academic, PTE Core, and Duolingo are not on the citizenship list; even though IELTS Academic is accepted for Express Entry.

5. **Paying the old $630 fee instead of the new $653.** The adult fee changed on March 31, 2026 from $630 to $653. Applications received after that date with the old fee are returned.

These five errors account for the majority of citizenship file returns we see. Reviewing your file with a licensed RCIC before submission catches them before IRCC does.

## What Else Do People Ask About the Canadian Citizenship Test?

*The questions below cover the most common searches Canadians submit about the citizenship test, based on real search data. Each answer reflects current IRCC policy as of 2026. For file-specific advice on your residency calculation, language proof, or application status, consult a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) or visit the [official IRCC citizenship pages](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship.html) at canada.ca.*

### How hard is the Canadian citizenship test?

The first-attempt pass rate is approximately 90%. The test is not designed to fail you. If you read the Discover Canada guide cover-to-cover and take 2 to 3 practice tests, you will almost certainly pass. The 10% who fail almost always either did not read the source or have a language comprehension issue that affects how they read the questions.

### How long should I study for the Canadian citizenship test?

Most adult applicants need 15 to 30 hours of focused study spread over 2 to 4 weeks. That includes reading Discover Canada cover-to-cover (about 6 to 8 hours), taking 3 to 5 practice tests, and reviewing weak areas. Applicants from English-speaking countries familiar with Westminster-style democracy often need less time. Applicants from countries with very different political systems often need more.

### Is the Canadian citizenship test in English or French?

You choose between English and French when you apply. Both versions test the same content from the same Discover Canada guide. There is no advantage to one language over the other; choose the one you read most fluently.

### Can I take the test online from outside Canada?

No. The citizenship test must be taken from inside Canada. Your physical presence in Canada is required during the entire processing period for the citizenship application, with limited exceptions.

### What is on the Canadian citizenship test 2026?

The 2026 test covers the same content as previous years: Canadian rights and responsibilities, history, government and federal elections, justice system, symbols, geography, economy, and Indigenous peoples. The source is the **Discover Canada** study guide, available free at canada.ca. There were no major curriculum changes for 2026.

### Can I retake the citizenship test if I fail?

Yes. You get up to 3 attempts within a 30-day window. Failed attempts are typically rescheduled within 2 to 4 days. If you fail all 3 attempts, you are scheduled for a hearing with a citizenship official rather than additional retakes.

### How quickly will I become a Canadian citizen after passing the test?

Typically 1 to 4 months. After your test pass, you wait for the oath ceremony invitation. Virtual oath ceremonies are usually scheduled 4 to 6 weeks after the test pass; in-person ceremonies 6 to 12 weeks. From the moment the oath is administered, you are a Canadian citizen.

### Will my children automatically become Canadian citizens when I do?

Not automatically. Children who are permanent residents need a separate application (form CIT 0003, $100 fee). Children born in Canada are already citizens by birth. Children born abroad to a Canadian-citizen parent (you, after you take the oath) may be citizens by descent if you are first-generation Canadian.

### Does the citizenship test cover Quebec specifically?

The test covers all of Canada including Quebec. Specific questions about Quebec history (the Quiet Revolution, Bill 101, the Quebec Act of 1774) appear on the test. Quebec has its own immigration selection system, but the citizenship test itself is federal and applies to applicants in all provinces.

### Can I bring notes or my phone into the test?

No. The citizenship test is closed-book. You cannot have notes, phones, books, or any reference material in the room. The officer monitors your environment via webcam during online tests.

## What Are the Next Steps After Passing the Citizenship Test?

The citizenship test is the visible part of citizenship, but it is rarely the part that determines whether your application succeeds. Most applications that fail or get returned do so because of mistakes in the residency calculation, missing tax years, or document issues; long before the test invitation arrives.

If you are within 6 to 12 months of being eligible to apply for citizenship, here is what to do:

1. **Run the IRCC Physical Presence Calculator** at [eservices.cic.gc.ca/rescalc/startBasicCalc.do](https://eservices.cic.gc.ca/rescalc/startBasicCalc.do) with passport-verified dates. Confirm you actually have 1,095 days.

2. **Verify your CRA tax filing record.** Check that you filed for every year you were required to.

3. **Download Discover Canada** and start reading. Even if you are still months away from the test, getting familiar with the material now reduces test anxiety later.

4. **Take a free practice test** at canada.ca to gauge your baseline. If you are scoring under 15 correct, you have time to study before applying.

5. **Book a consultation with a licensed RCIC** if you are unsure about residency timing, tax-filing requirements, language test type, or anything else in your application. The cost of a 30-minute review is a fraction of the cost of a returned application (and the $653 non-refundable fee).

Our team at Go Far Global has guided thousands of Canadian permanent residents through the citizenship grant application from residency calculation through oath ceremony. If you want a written assessment of your file before you submit, [book a consultation](/appointment) and we will tell you whether your application is ready or what you need to fix first.

For the broader citizenship application process beyond the test itself, read our [Canadian Citizenship Application 2026 Complete Guide](/news/canadian-citizenship-application-2026). For the most current processing-time data, see [Canadian Citizenship Processing Time Drops to 12 Months in 2026](/news/canadian-citizenship-processing-time-12-months-2026).

# From Francophone Mobility Work Permit to Canadian PR: The NCLC 5 to NCLC 7 Roadmap (2026)

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/francophone-mobility-pr-pathway-2026
Category: Permanent Residence
Published: 2026-05-23
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Francophone Mobility work permit, also called code C16 or Mobilité Francophone, is the fastest way for a French-speaking foreign worker to start working in Canada outside Quebec...

*As of May 23, 2026.*

The Francophone Mobility work permit, also called code C16 or Mobilité Francophone, is the fastest way for a French-speaking foreign worker to start working in Canada outside Quebec without a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA). What it does not give you, automatically, is permanent residence. The C16 is a closed work permit tied to your employer, with no built-in PR pathway in the regulation. To get from C16 to PR you have to plan a second move, and the rules for that second move are different from the rules for the work permit itself.

This is the gap that catches workers off guard. The work permit accepts NCLC Level 5 in speaking and listening. The Express Entry French-language category draws, which are the cleanest route to PR for a French speaker, require NCLC Level 7 in all four skills. The Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) bonus you get on Express Entry for strong French requires NCLC Level 9. None of these are the same level. Knowing which level matters for which step is the difference between a 14 month PR plan and an 8 month delay you did not budget for.

This guide walks the actual path. Every number, draw, and deadline cited here comes from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) publications or the verified history of Express Entry draws.

## Can you go from Francophone Mobility to PR?

**Short answer:** Yes, but not directly. The C16 work permit does not convert into permanent residence on its own. You apply for PR through a separate program: the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) inside Express Entry, the French-language category inside Express Entry, or a Provincial Nominee Program (PNP). Each one has its own rules and timelines, and the work experience you build on your C16 counts toward the federal options.

The most common mistake is treating the work permit as a holding pattern. It is not. From day one of your C16, you should be planning the PR application you intend to file 12 to 24 months later. That means tracking your work hours, keeping your language test scores current, and watching the draw thresholds in your target category. Workers who wait until their permit is close to expiring start the PR process from behind.

If you do not yet have your C16, our hub article on the [Francophone Mobility Program](/news/francophone-mobility-program) covers eligibility, the LMIA exemption, and the application process. The rest of this guide assumes you either have an approved C16 or are working toward one.

## What is the gap between NCLC 5 and NCLC 7?

**Short answer:** NCLC 5 is conversational oral French; NCLC 7 is solid working-level French in all four skills (speaking, listening, reading, writing). The C16 work permit accepts NCLC 5 in oral skills only. The Express Entry French-language category requires NCLC 7 across speaking, listening, reading, AND writing. That is a real jump.

On the standardized tests IRCC accepts, the score requirements look like this:

| Test | NCLC 5 minimum | NCLC 7 minimum |
|---|---|---|
| TEF Canada, Listening | 181-216 | 249-279 |
| TEF Canada, Speaking | 226-270 | 310-348 |
| TEF Canada, Reading | not required | 207-232 |
| TEF Canada, Writing | not required | 310-348 |
| TCF Canada, Listening | 331-397 | 458-502 |
| TCF Canada, Speaking | 6 | 10 |
| TCF Canada, Reading | not required | 453-498 |
| TCF Canada, Writing | not required | 10 |

If you arrived in Canada on a C16 with NCLC 5, you have already proven oral French. To reach the French-language category in Express Entry, you need to add reading and writing at NCLC 7, plus push your speaking and listening to NCLC 7 as well. Most workers spend 6 to 12 months on this upgrade while they accumulate their first year of CEC-qualifying work experience. The two clocks run in parallel.

## How does C16 work experience count toward Express Entry?

**Short answer:** Every full-time month of skilled work on your C16 counts toward the Canadian Experience Class, the same as any other Canadian work permit. After 12 months of full-time skilled work in a National Occupational Classification (NOC) TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 occupation, you become eligible for CEC and can submit an Express Entry profile.

The rules:

- Work must be full-time (30+ hours per week) OR an equivalent in part-time hours
- The job has to be in a NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 occupation
- The work has to happen on a valid work permit (your C16 qualifies)
- The 12 months has to be acquired in the 3 years before you submit your Express Entry profile
- Self-employment does not count for CEC

This is the unsexy part of the plan. There is no shortcut. You hold the C16, you work in Canada for a year, you collect pay stubs and a reference letter, and you submit Express Entry. Once you have one year of CEC-qualifying experience plus a CRS score competitive enough for the draws, you are in the pool.

With a [CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) you can model your score before submitting. Most C16 holders who came to Canada in their late 20s or early 30s with a bachelor's degree and Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7 English score between 440 and 480 CRS on the regular profile, without the French bonus. The French bonus changes the picture.

## What CRS scores have French-language category draws cut at recently?

**Short answer:** French-language category draws in Express Entry consistently clear at far lower CRS scores than general draws. The lowest French draw on record cut at 336 CRS on February 29, 2024. The most recent French draw in April 2026 cut at 400 CRS, issuing 4,000 Invitations to Apply. Compare that to Canadian Experience Class draws in the same window, which have cleared at 518 to 547 CRS.

IRCC launched category-based Express Entry draws in mid-2023 to fast-track candidates with French-language proficiency and a small number of in-demand occupations. The French-language category, which requires NCLC 7 in all four skills, has been the most consistent of these categories. In 2025, IRCC ran 3 French-language draws that issued a combined 18,500 Invitations to Apply (ITAs), accounting for 37.4% of all Express Entry invitations that year, according to IRCC's draw history.

The practical read: if you can get to NCLC 7 in French, the bar for PR drops by more than 100 CRS points compared to the general program. A profile that would never clear a CEC draw at 535 CRS clears a French-language draw at 400. That is the entire pricing of the French upgrade. It is not just an SEO point.

For a current view of every draw history, see [Canada.ca Express Entry rounds](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html).

## Do you get 50 CRS points for the C16 work permit itself?

**Short answer:** The work permit itself does not give you CRS points. The CRS bonus for French ability requires NCLC 9 (or higher) in French AND comes in two amounts: 25 points if your English is CLB 4 or lower, and 50 points if your English is CLB 5 or higher. These are added to your CRS score in the Express Entry pool, on top of all your other points.

This is the most-misunderstood part of the program. Many candidates assume the C16 itself triggers the bonus. It does not. The CRS bonus is tied to your language test scores, not your work permit type. To earn the 50-point bonus you need:

- French at NCLC 9 in all four skills (TEF Canada: listening 280-297, speaking 349-370, reading 233-247, writing 349-370; or TCF Canada: listening 503-548, speaking 14, reading 499-523, writing 14)
- English at CLB 5 in all four skills (a very low bar; most C16 holders comfortably exceed it)

If you are sitting at NCLC 7 in French and CLB 8 in English, you qualify for the French-language category draws but you do NOT get the 50-point CRS bonus. To get the bonus you have to push French from NCLC 7 to NCLC 9. That is a bigger language jump. Most workers who target the French-language category at NCLC 7 do not bother chasing NCLC 9 because the category draws clear at CRS 336 to 400 anyway.

In short: NCLC 7 opens the category; NCLC 9 adds the score bonus. They are different decisions.

## What is the realistic C16 to PR timeline?

**Short answer:** A typical C16-to-PR timeline runs 14 to 24 months from work permit approval to PR confirmation, assuming you start your French test prep early and meet the one-year Canadian work experience requirement for CEC.

Here is the calendar most successful candidates follow:

| Month | Action |
|---|---|
| 0 | C16 approved, you start working |
| 0-3 | Order CICC-recognized French course materials; book TEF Canada or TCF Canada for month 6-9 |
| 3-6 | Confirm 30+ hours/week, NOC TEER 0-3 work continues; spouse applies for open work permit |
| 6-9 | Sit TEF or TCF Canada exam; target NCLC 7 in all four skills |
| 9-12 | Finish first 12 months of CEC-qualifying work; gather pay stubs, T4, reference letter |
| 12 | Submit Express Entry profile with French test results uploaded |
| 12-14 | Wait for category-based French draw (these run every 2-4 months) |
| 14 | Receive Invitation to Apply (assuming CRS competitive for the draw) |
| 14-20 | Submit complete PR application; biometrics; medical exam; police certificates |
| 20-24 | PR confirmation (current IRCC processing time for CEC files is ~6 months) |

The slowest piece is the IRCC PR application processing after ITA. The fastest piece you control is the language test. If you arrive in Canada with NCLC 5 oral and your reading/writing French is already at NCLC 7, you can compress months 0-9 dramatically and submit Express Entry the day you hit 12 months of work.

For live IRCC processing times across categories see our [processing times tracker](/immigration/processing-times).

## Which PNPs accept French speakers without Express Entry?

**Short answer:** Several Provincial Nominee Programs run dedicated French-speaking streams outside Express Entry. The strongest options in 2026 are Ontario's Franco-Ontarian stream, Manitoba's French-speaking skilled worker streams, New Brunswick's Atlantic and Strategic Initiative streams, and Nova Scotia's Labour Market Priorities stream. Each has different eligibility rules and most do not require Express Entry profile entry.

PNPs are useful when:

- Your CRS is too low for Express Entry draws even with the French boost
- Your employer is in a specific province willing to support a nomination
- You want to lock in a province before applying federally
- You hold a job offer in a non-NOC-TEER 0-3 occupation that the province values

The trade-off is that PNPs tie you to the nominating province. If you nominate in Manitoba and then take a job in Ontario before PR is finalized, IRCC can refuse the application for not living in the province you were nominated to. PNPs work well when your job and life are stable in one province.

Our [Provincial Nominee Program hub](/immigration/provincial-nominee) lists current streams by province with eligibility criteria.

## What happens if your C16 expires before PR is approved?

**Short answer:** You can apply for a Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP) if you have already submitted your PR application and meet a few conditions. The BOWP keeps you working in Canada legally while IRCC processes your PR file. Without a BOWP, an expired C16 means you stop working and either leave Canada or apply for a new work permit.

To qualify for a BOWP from a C16:

- You must be physically in Canada when you apply
- You must have a valid C16 (or other work permit) at the time of BOWP application
- Your PR application must be "in process" with IRCC (Acknowledgement of Receipt issued) under Express Entry CEC, Federal Skilled Worker (FSW), FST, Caregivers, AIP, or Provincial Nominee Program
- Your current work permit must expire within 4 months

The BOWP gives you an open work permit, so you are no longer tied to the C16 employer. That is valuable if the employer relationship has soured or if you want to switch jobs during the PR wait. The downside: BOWP processing itself takes 4 to 6 months in 2026, so timing matters. Apply the day you hit the 4-month threshold.

If you miss the BOWP window, your only options are: leave Canada, restore status (within 90 days, with a fee), or apply for a new employer-specific work permit (which may require a fresh LMIA or a new C16 offer of employment). None of those are ideal mid-PR-application. Plan the BOWP early.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do I get 50 points if I have a Francophone work permit?**
No. The work permit itself does not give CRS points. The CRS bonus for French is tied to your French-language test results, not your permit category. To get the bonus you need NCLC 9 in all four French skills, plus CLB 5 in English. With NCLC 9 French and CLB 5+ English you get 50 CRS points. With NCLC 9 French and CLB 4 or less English you get 25 CRS points. NCLC 7 French (which opens the French-language category draws) does not by itself trigger any CRS bonus.

**Can I get PR with 470 CRS score?**
Yes, in 2026 a 470 CRS score has been comfortably above the cut-off for French-language category draws (which have cleared between 336 and 400 CRS in the last 12 months). It is unlikely to clear a general draw or a Canadian Experience Class draw at current levels (518-547). If your CRS is 470 and your French is at NCLC 7 or above, the French-language category is your route. If your French is below NCLC 7, focus on PNP options instead.

**Can I get PR with CLB 5 in French?**
CLB 5 is not enough to enter the Express Entry French-language category, which requires NCLC 7. However, CLB 5 oral is exactly what the C16 work permit asks for, and once you are in Canada working, you can upgrade your French to NCLC 7 and then enter Express Entry. So the answer is: not directly, but the C16 is your first step toward exactly that PR application.

**How to be eligible for Francophone Express Entry?**
Three requirements stack up: (1) Achieve NCLC 7 in all four French skills, proven by TEF Canada or TCF Canada within the last 2 years. (2) Meet all general Express Entry eligibility for one of CEC, FSW, or FST. For CEC, that means 12 months of skilled Canadian work experience in NOC TEER 0-3 (your C16 work counts). (3) Submit an Express Entry profile. IRCC then runs category-based draws and invites French speakers regardless of CRS rank within the category.

**Can my spouse work on my Francophone Mobility permit?**
Yes. Your spouse or common-law partner is eligible for an open work permit if the principal job offer attached to your C16 is for 6 months or longer. That open work permit lets your spouse work for any Canadian employer in any occupation, including starting their own business. The spouse's open work permit follows the duration of your C16. Importantly, the time your spouse spends working in Canada also counts toward CEC if they later apply for PR.

**Can I extend my work permit with the Francophone Mobility Program?**
Yes, the C16 can be extended for additional terms, provided your employer is willing to submit a new offer of employment through the IRCC Employer Portal, pay the $230 compliance fee again, and continue to offer NOC TEER 0-3 work. The extension is treated as a new work permit application with the same LMIA-exempt C16 code. Apply at least 90 days before your current permit expires. If you have already filed a PR application and your permit is expiring, look at the Bridging Open Work Permit instead, it is usually faster and breaks the employer-specific tie.

**What is the processing time for Francophone Mobility work permit inside Canada?**
IRCC does not publish a fixed processing time for C16 applications, but workers applying from inside Canada generally see decisions in 4 to 12 weeks for a complete file. Outside Canada the range varies widely by country of citizenship; visa-exempt countries can see approvals as fast as 3 to 5 business days after the employer submits the offer of employment, while visa-required countries can wait 8 to 16 weeks. The PR application that follows is where the longer wait lives.

## Need help mapping your C16 to PR?

The Francophone Mobility to PR pathway is one of the cleanest routes to permanent residence available to a French-speaking foreign worker in 2026. It is also one of the easiest to mistime. If you are already on a C16, or you are about to be, the language test booking and the Express Entry profile timing decide your real timeline. We work through this kind of planning with C16 holders every month. [Book a consultation](/appointment) with a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) and we will map your actual numbers against the current draw history.

# Canada Visitor Visa Processing Time 2026 by Country

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-visitor-visa-processing-time-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-05-22
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada visitor visa processing times depend on the country you apply from and how IRCC counts the wait.

# Canada Visitor Visa Processing Time 2026 by Country

*As of September 4, 2026.*

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) processes most visitor visa applications in a few weeks or less, then immediately qualifies that line: times depend on the visa office and extra steps. There is no single global number. Use the official processing-times tool for your country. Visitor visas are still being issued. Approval odds and wait times are different questions.

## TL;DR

IRCC: most visitor visas process in a few weeks or less | Extra time for biometrics, medicals, police certificates, interviews | Clock starts when IRCC has a complete application | Incomplete files can be refused | National approval rate in the last IRCC committee table was 49% in 2025 YTD | Check the live IRCC processing-times tool for your visa office

## How long does it take for a Canada visitor visa to process?

**Short answer:** IRCC's [after you apply for a visitor visa](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/after-apply-next-steps.html) page says they process most applications in a few weeks or less. Processing times depend on the visa office and whether you need extra steps listed on that page. That is not "2 to 8 weeks" as a departmental guarantee. Private sites invent country-day ranges. The number you should use is the [IRCC processing-times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html), visitor visa from outside Canada, for your country of residence. The clock starts when IRCC receives a complete application, including fees. If you apply by mail, it starts when the package arrives.

Biometrics collection can sit in front of that clock. Book the appointment when IRCC asks. Do not treat a forum "15 days from India" as IRCC policy.

## Is Canada issuing visitor visas now?

**Short answer:** Yes. The [apply for a visitor visa](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/apply-visitor-visa.html) process is live. The after-you-apply page is still instructing people through biometrics, completeness checks, and status. IRCC has not closed the visitor-visa line. Temporary public-health measures can sit on that same page (an Ebola-related notice on the copy we fetched ran until 28 September 2026). Those measures are not a blanket visitor-visa freeze. If your country is named in a special notice, read that notice. Everyone else still applies online unless IRCC says otherwise.

Mail delays can slow paper files. IRCC's after-you-apply text encourages online applications.

## Is Canada rejecting a visitor visa in 2026?

**Short answer:** IRCC is refusing a large share of visitor files. The [committee data summary as of 30 April 2025](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/committees/cow-jun-9-2025/data-summary-table.html) showed a Temporary Resident Visa approval rate of 49% for 2025 year to date, down from 51% in 2024. Refusal is a decision, not a processing-time. A long wait is not the same as a refusal. Incomplete applications may be refused, which the after-you-apply page states in plain language. For country issuance volumes, use [visitor visa approval rate by country](/news/canada-visitor-visa-approval-rate-by-country-2026).

Do not confuse a 49% national approval rate with "Canada stopped visitor visas."

## Is a Canada visitor visa easy to get?

**Short answer:** Not if "easy" means most files sail through. A 49% national approval rate is a coin flip at the country level, and some source countries saw issuance volumes collapse after 2023. Officers look at purpose, funds, ties home, and travel history. The after-you-apply page also lists extras IRCC may ask: interview, more documents, medical exam, police certificate. Missing any of those stretches time or ends in refusal. A clean, complete file is the only version of "easier" IRCC will recognize.

We are Go Far Global, a licensed Canadian immigration firm. If you already have a refusal, [book a consultation](/book) before a second submit.

## What is the success rate of a Canada visitor visa?

**Short answer:** The last IRCC committee figure we can cite is 49% approved in 2025 YTD for Temporary Resident Visas, versus 51% in 2024. IRCC does not publish official per-country approval percentages. Success rate is not processing time. A file can be fast and refused. Full rates and issuance volumes: [Canada visitor visa approval rate by country](/news/canada-visitor-visa-approval-rate-by-country-2026).

| Question | Where IRCC answers it |
|---|---|
| How long will this take? | [Processing-times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) |
| When does the clock start? | Complete application received (help centre on processing times) |
| Are visas still issued? | Apply page plus after-you-apply page |
| What share get approved? | Committee table: 49% TRV in 2025 YTD |

## What is the new rule of visitor visa in Canada?

**Short answer:** There is no single 2026 "new visitor visa rule" on the apply page that replaces the TRV itself. What changed around this product is the levels-plan squeeze on temporary residents, higher refusal rates in IRCC's own table, and office-by-office processing. The [2025-2027 supplementary levels information](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/supplementary-immigration-levels-2025-2027.html) set temporary-resident targets. That is why officers are tighter. It is not a new visa category. Super visa, eTA, and visitor records are still different products. Check [after you apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/after-apply-next-steps.html) for the current extra steps, including any temporary health notices.

If you need a parent to stay longer than a standard visit, that is a super visa conversation, not a visitor-visa processing-time conversation. See [super visa insurance](/news/super-visa-insurance-canada-2026) if that is the product.
