# How to Improve Your CRS Score in 2026: Specific Tactics That Add Real Points

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/how-to-improve-crs-score
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-05-10
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) decides who gets invited from the Express Entry pool.

# How to Improve Your CRS Score in 2026: Specific Tactics That Add Real Points

The Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) decides who gets invited from the Express Entry pool. Cut-offs in 2026 sit roughly between 400 and 540 depending on the draw category. If your score is below the recent cut-off, the question is which specific changes give the biggest point return for the effort.

As of May 10, 2026.

This article walks through the moves that actually move the score. Each section gives the point range, the time required, and the cost.

Run your current numbers in [the Go Far Global CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) before reading. You need a baseline to know which tactic helps you most.

## How can you improve your CRS score?

**Short answer:** Top tactics ranked by point gain: Provincial nomination (+600 points, 6-18 months, highest effort), job offer in TEER 0 (+200) or TEER 1-3 (+50), language test improvement (+50-100), French test addition (+50), additional Canadian work experience (+50-80 per year), sibling-in-Canada bonus (+15, free if applicable).

| Tactic | Point Range | Effort | Time |
|--------|-------------|--------|------|
| Provincial nomination | +600 | High (program-specific) | 6 to 18 months |
| Job offer (NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3) | +50 to +200 | Medium | 1 to 6 months |
| Higher language test (CLB 9+ in all four skills) | +0 to +50 | Medium | 1 to 4 months |
| French language test (NCLC 7+) | +25 to +50 | High | 6 to 18 months |
| Additional year of Canadian work experience | +20 to +50 | Low (just time) | 12 months |
| Additional year of foreign work experience | +13 to +25 | Low (just time) | 12 months |
| Spouse's language or education improvement | +10 to +20 | Medium | 2 to 6 months |
| Sibling in Canada (citizen or PR) | +15 | None if applicable | None |
| Canadian credential (Master's, PhD, ECA upgrade) | +15 to +25 | High | 1 to 4 years |

The full points breakdown is published by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) at [canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/criteria-comprehensive-ranking-system.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/criteria-comprehensive-ranking-system.html).

## How much does a provincial nomination boost your CRS score?

**Short answer:** A provincial nomination adds 600 CRS points, more than every other tactic combined. With 600 extra points, almost any candidate clears the next federal Express Entry cut-off. Best provinces by accessibility: Saskatchewan (in-demand occupations), Manitoba (skilled worker overseas), Alberta (priority sectors), and Ontario (employer-driven).

A provincial nomination adds 600 points to your CRS score. That is more than every other tactic combined. With 600 extra points, almost any candidate clears the cut-off in the next federal Express Entry draw.

Provinces nominate candidates through their Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) streams that are linked to Express Entry. The application path is:

1. Create an Express Entry profile.
2. Apply to a specific provincial stream (most provinces have an Express Entry-aligned stream).
3. Receive a Notification of Interest from the province, then submit a full PNP application.
4. After provincial nomination, accept it in your Express Entry profile and receive +600 CRS.

Each province has its own eligibility rules. The most active in 2026 are Ontario Immigrant Nominee Program (OINP), British Columbia (BC PNP), Alberta (AAIP), Manitoba (MPNP), Saskatchewan (SINP), and the Atlantic provinces. The full list is at [canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html).

The downside: PNP applications take 6 to 18 months and most streams require either prior work or study in the province.

## How much does a higher language test score improve your CRS?

**Short answer:** Moving from Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7 (IELTS 6.0 each band) to CLB 9 (IELTS 7.0+ each band) adds approximately 50-100 CRS points once second-language and skill-transferability bonuses stack. This is the second-largest CRS lever after PNP and the most controllable since you can retake the test in 5 days.

Language is the second-largest CRS lever after PNP. Moving from CLB 7 (IELTS 6.0 in all four skills) to CLB 9 (IELTS 7.0+ in listening, 7.0+ in reading, 7.0+ in writing, 7.0+ in speaking) adds:

- Single applicant: roughly +50 CRS
- Married applicant with spouse accompanying: roughly +40 CRS

Moving from CLB 7 to CLB 10 adds another 6 to 10 points on top.

Test cost: $300 to $400 for IELTS General Training or CELPIP General. You can retake as often as you want. Most candidates who hit a wall at CLB 7 see real gains from a single round of focused practice (writing and speaking in particular). [Practice English for free with the Go Far Global IELTS practice tool](/tools/ielts-practice-test).

The IRCC list of accepted tests is at [canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/language-requirements.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/language-requirements.html).

## Does adding a French test improve your CRS score?

**Short answer:** A French test at NCLC 7 (TEF Canada or TCF Canada equivalent) on top of English CLB 9 adds 50 CRS points. Category-based French draws also clear at 100+ CRS below general draws, so a strong French score doubly helps: it adds points AND opens a lower-cut-off draw type.

A French test result at NCLC 7 (TEF Canada or TCF Canada equivalent) on top of an English CLB 9 adds 50 CRS points. The bonus increases to 50 points for category-based French draws on top of the standard scoring.

Practical reality: getting from zero French to NCLC 7 takes a year of consistent study for most adults. If you already speak some French, the test fee ($350-$400) and a few months of focused prep gets you the bonus.

For category-based draws, French speakers have been the largest invited group throughout 2025 and 2026. Cut-offs for French draws have averaged 50 to 100 points lower than general draws.

## How many CRS points does a Canadian job offer add?

**Short answer:** Valid Canadian job offer adds 50 points for National Occupational Classification (NOC) TEER 1, 2, or 3 occupations and 200 points for NOC TEER 0 (senior management). To count for CRS the offer must come from a Canadian employer with a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or an LMIA-exempt designation.

A valid Canadian job offer adds:

- 50 points for NOC TEER 1, 2, or 3 occupations
- 200 points for NOC TEER 0 (senior management) jobs

To count for CRS, the offer needs to come from a Canadian employer with a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA), or it needs to be from an employer where you already have a Canadian work permit and have been employed full-time for at least one year.

Job offers without LMIA support do not count for CRS even if the employer wants to hire you. The exception is work permits issued under specific international agreements (like the Global Talent Stream or Mobilité Francophone) that exempt LMIA but still count.

Full requirements for a qualifying job offer are at [canada.ca: Offer of employment for Express Entry (IRCC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/offer-employment.html).

## How does Canadian work experience add CRS points over time?

**Short answer:** Each additional year of skilled Canadian work experience adds points: Year 1 starts at 35 points, Year 2 jumps to 46, Year 3 to 56, Year 4 to 63, Year 5 to 72. Foreign skilled work experience adds smaller increments. Sometimes the cheapest CRS gain is patience plus continued employment.

Every additional year of skilled work experience adds points. The math:

**Canadian skilled work experience (in Canada, NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3):**
- Year 1: starts at 35 points
- Year 2: 46 points (+11)
- Year 3: 56 points (+10)
- Year 4: 63 points (+7)
- Year 5+: 70 points (cap)

**Foreign skilled work experience (combined with CLB 9+ language and Canadian education or experience):**
- Year 1: 13 points
- Years 2-3: 25 points (+12)
- Year 4+: 50 points

The largest single-year jumps in Canadian work experience come between year 1 and year 3. If you have less than three years of Canadian skilled work, staying employed in Canada is one of the biggest point gains available.

## How does your spouse's profile affect your CRS score?

**Short answer:** If your spouse is accompanying you: spouse CLB 9 in all four English skills adds +10, spouse Master's or PhD adds +10, spouse Canadian work experience adds +10. If you're applying as a single applicant when you have a spouse, you may forfeit accompanying-spouse points but gain higher single-applicant scores in language and education.

If your spouse is accompanying you to Canada, their language ability and education contribute to your CRS:

- Spouse CLB 9 in all four English skills: +10 points
- Spouse Master's or PhD: +10 points (vs Bachelor's at 7 points)
- Spouse one year of Canadian work experience: +5 points

Spouse improvements are usually faster than your own (one test, one document upgrade). If your spouse can boost their language or get a credential evaluated upward, that is often the quickest 10 to 20 points available.

## Does having a sibling in Canada add CRS points?

**Short answer:** Having a sibling who is a Canadian citizen or PR adds 15 CRS points. The sibling must be a blood, half-blood, or adopted brother or sister, aged 18 or older, living in Canada with citizen or PR status. Most candidates overlook this; verify it before paying for any other improvement tactic.

Having a sibling who is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident adds 15 points. The sibling has to be:

- A blood, half-blood, or adopted brother or sister
- Aged 18 or older
- Living in Canada with citizen or PR status
- Related through a common parent or legal adoption

This is a no-effort 15 points if the relationship qualifies. Most candidates miss it because they do not realize half-siblings and adopted siblings count. The proof is a copy of the sibling's PR card or citizenship certificate plus documents linking you both to a common parent.

## How many CRS points does a Canadian credential add?

**Short answer:** Canadian credentials add bonus points beyond foreign education: a 1-2 year Canadian diploma adds +15, a 3-year+ degree, Master's, or PhD adds +30. If you already have foreign education and are considering a Canadian master's, the +30 plus PGWP eligibility is one of the strongest combined CRS boosts available.

A Canadian credential adds points beyond foreign education:

- Canadian one or two-year diploma: +15 points
- Canadian three-year+ degree, Master's, or PhD: +30 points

If you already have foreign education and are studying in Canada, the Canadian credential stacks on top. This is why many candidates pursue a one-year Canadian Master's program: 30 CRS points plus access to a Post-Graduation Work Permit that builds Canadian work experience.

The downside: tuition for international students runs $20,000 to $50,000 per year, plus living expenses. Worth it only if you have a clear path that justifies the investment.

## What does not improve your CRS score?

**Short answer:** Common ideas that do NOT add CRS: volunteer work, self-employment, freelance/contract work without an LMIA, internships that aren't part of a PGWP-eligible program, online degrees from non-Canadian institutions, and CRS coaching services that promise score boosts. Stick to the IRCC scoring tables.

A few common ideas do not actually move the score:

- **Volunteer work**. CRS does not award points for volunteer experience.
- **Self-employment**. Self-employed work does not count as skilled work experience for Express Entry.
- **Online courses or certificates**. Only formal credentials evaluated by an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) organization count for education points.
- **Multiple ECAs**. Only your highest credential counts. Getting a second ECA for a lower-level credential adds nothing.
- **Repeated language tests below your current level**. Only your single highest valid test result counts.

## What is the fastest combined path to a higher CRS score?

**Short answer:** Cheapest, fastest combined path: (1) verify sibling bonus (free, +15 if applicable), (2) retake language test focused on weakest skill (1-3 months, ~$400, up to +50), (3) add French test if you have any French ability (3-6 months, +50), (4) pursue a job offer or PNP nomination if the gap is bigger than language gains can close.

The cheapest, fastest path to higher CRS for most candidates is:

1. Verify the sibling bonus (free, 15 points if applicable).
2. Retake the language test focusing on weak skills (1 to 3 months, ~$400, up to 50 points).
3. Add a French test if you have any French ability (3 to 12 months, ~$400, up to 50 points).
4. Pursue a provincial nomination if you have a tie to a province (6 to 18 months, +600 points if successful).

Together, these moves can take a CRS profile from the low 400s to over 600 in a year, which clears every Express Entry cut-off.

[Run the calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) again after each change to see the score in real time.

## Frequently Asked Questions

The questions below cover what Express Entry candidates ask most when working to raise their CRS score. Each answer reflects current IRCC rules. If your situation involves a prior refusal, misrepresentation finding, or complex family circumstances, a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) can review your specific case.

**How long does it take for my new CRS score to update?**
Update your Express Entry profile right after the new test result or document is issued. The change takes effect in the next draw, usually within two weeks.

**Can I improve my CRS while I am already in the pool?**
Yes. Edit your profile at any time. The new score is used in the next draw.

**Do I need to take the language test again if my score has expired?**
Yes. Language test results are valid for two years from the date of the test. Expired results cannot be used.

**Will my Master's from outside Canada add as many points as a Canadian Master's?**
A foreign Master's (with ECA) adds the same education points (135). The difference is the Canadian credential bonus, which adds 30 more points.

**Does work experience after my profile is created still count?**
Yes. Update your profile when you hit a new milestone (one more year of Canadian experience, for example). The score updates automatically.

**Is it worth waiting for cut-offs to drop instead of improving my score?**
Cut-offs do drop in some draws. Sitting at the same score and waiting is a passive strategy. Active improvement is faster and gives you more control.

## What are the next steps to raise your CRS score?

If you have not already, [calculate your current CRS score](/tools/crs-calculator) and identify which two or three tactics give you the biggest gain. Most candidates find at least two quick improvements once they see the full breakdown: verifying the sibling bonus costs nothing, and a language test retake can add up to 50 points in one to three months. Start with those before committing to longer paths like a French test or provincial nomination.

For a personalized strategy session with a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC), [book a consultation with Go Far Global](/appointment).

# CRS Score by Age 2026: Express Entry Points Table

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/crs-score-by-age
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-05-10
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Age is one of the largest single contributors to the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score.

# CRS Score by Age 2026: Express Entry Points Table

*As of September 3, 2026.*

Age is a core human-capital factor in Canada's Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS). Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) awards the maximum age points from 20 to 29: 110 without a spouse, 100 with a spouse. Points fall each year after 29 and hit zero at 45. There is no Express Entry age ban. You can still enter the pool at 45 or older with 0 age points.

## TL;DR

Maximum CRS age points: 110 without a spouse, 100 with a spouse, ages 20 to 29 | Age 30 drops to 105 / 95 | Age 45 or more: 0 / 0 | IRCC grid last confirmed on the CRS criteria page | Job-offer CRS points were removed on 25 March 2025, so age gaps now have to be filled with language, education, Canadian work, or a provincial nomination

## Can age affect my CRS score?

**Short answer:** Yes. IRCC scores age as part of core human-capital factors. Without a spouse or common-law partner you can earn up to 110 CRS points for age. With a spouse the cap is 100. The peak is 20 to 29. After 29 the grid drops each year. At 45 or more you get 0 age points, with or without a spouse. Age does not stop you from creating an Express Entry profile. It only changes this slice of the score. The live grid is on [Express Entry: Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html). Use IRCC's [check your score](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score.html) tool, or our [CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator), after you read the table below.

Age is calculated on the day IRCC draws your profile, not on the day you first entered the pool. If your birthday is close, run the numbers for both ages before you wait.

## How many points is age in PR?

**Short answer:** Under Express Entry CRS, age is worth up to 110 points without a spouse and 100 with a spouse. That is not the old Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) selection grid, which used a different 67-point pass mark and a smaller age band. If someone quotes "12 points for age" or "67 points," they are mixing systems. Permanent residence through Express Entry uses CRS. IRCC's CRS page lists age beside education, official languages, and Canadian work experience in the same core-human-capital block. The spouse column is lower because some points move to the spouse or common-law partner factors.

Do not add FSW grid points to a CRS total. They are not interchangeable.

| Age | With a spouse or common-law partner (max 100) | Without a spouse or common-law partner (max 110) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 17 or less | 0 | 0 |
| 18 | 90 | 99 |
| 19 | 95 | 105 |
| 20 to 29 | 100 | 110 |
| 30 | 95 | 105 |
| 31 | 90 | 99 |
| 32 | 85 | 94 |
| 33 | 80 | 88 |
| 34 | 75 | 83 |
| 35 | 70 | 77 |
| 36 | 65 | 72 |
| 37 | 60 | 66 |
| 38 | 55 | 61 |
| 39 | 50 | 55 |
| 40 | 45 | 50 |
| 41 | 35 | 39 |
| 42 | 25 | 28 |
| 43 | 15 | 17 |
| 44 | 5 | 6 |
| 45 or more | 0 | 0 |

Source: [IRCC CRS criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html).

## How many points for age in Express Entry Canada?

**Short answer:** Same grid. A 29-year-old with no spouse gets 110. A 30-year-old with no spouse gets 105. That is a 5-point drop on the birthday. With a spouse the same birthday is 100 to 95. From 40 to 41 the drop is 10 points without a spouse (50 to 39) and 10 with a spouse (45 to 35). From 44 to 45 the last 6 or 5 points disappear. IRCC does not give extra age points for Canadian work or a provincial nomination. Those sit in other rows of the same CRS table.

If you are comparing two birthdays, count only this column. Language, education, and Canadian experience do not replace the age cell. They add beside it.

A 35-year-old without a spouse is at 77 age points, 33 below the peak. A 40-year-old without a spouse is at 50, 60 below the peak. That gap is why people ask about French, a second degree, or a Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) after 30.

## Can I get PR after 45 in Canada?

**Short answer:** Yes. IRCC does not set a maximum age to create an Express Entry profile. At 45 or more the age cell is 0, but you can still score on education, language, Canadian work, skill transferability, a sibling in Canada, French-language additional points, or a provincial nomination. A nomination is worth 600 additional CRS points on the same IRCC criteria page. Canadian Experience Class (CEC) also has no age cap in the program rules. [Who can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply.html) is about program eligibility, not a birthday cutoff.

You can also leave Express Entry and use family sponsorship, a caregiver or other public policy if one is open, or a work permit first. None of those is automatic because you turned 45. Run the live CRS grid and a [provincial nominee](/immigration/provincial-nominee) check before you assume the door is closed.

## How do you make up CRS points after age 30?

**Short answer:** IRCC removed job-offer CRS points on 25 March 2025. You cannot buy back age with an arranged employment bonus anymore. The criteria page still scores official languages up to 160 without a spouse, education up to 150, Canadian work experience, skill transferability, and additional points including a provincial nomination and French. Retake language tests if your Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) can still move. A spouse's language and education also score, which is why the principal applicant's age cap is lower when a spouse is included.

Check [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) category-based rounds as well as general draws. Age is not a category. French, healthcare, and trades rounds can invite a lower CRS than the all-program line. We are Go Far Global, a licensed Canadian immigration firm. If age is the cell that is dragging the file, [book a consultation](/book) and we will map language, a PNP, or CEC timing against the current grid.

Do not wait for IRCC to "drop CRS" as a plan. Draws move. The age table does not.

## Sources

- [Express Entry: Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html)
- [Express Entry: Check your score](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score.html)
- [Express Entry: Who can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply.html)

# Canadian Citizenship Application 2026: Requirements, Fees, and How to Apply

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canadian-citizenship-application-2026
Category: Permanent Residence
Published: 2026-05-10
Author: Go Far Global Team

> A Canadian citizenship application turns on one calculation: 1,095 days of physical presence in the five-year eligibility period, of which at least 730 must be days you held permanent resident status.

# Canadian Citizenship Application 2026: Requirements, Fees, and How to Apply

*As of August 15, 2026.*

A Canadian citizenship application rests on one calculation that most applicants get wrong: the physical presence count. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) does not just ask for 1,095 days in Canada. It asks for 1,095 days inside a specific five-year window, of which at least 730 must be days you held permanent resident status. Miss the second half of that rule and the application is refused on a technicality no amount of supporting evidence can fix.

This guide covers the 2026 requirements, the fee, the documents, the online process, and the paper exceptions. It is written for permanent residents who intend to apply within the next few months.

## What changed for Canadian citizenship applications in 2026?

**Short answer:** Two practical changes matter this year. The physical presence calculator moved inside the online account, so online applicants can no longer prepare their calculation on the old standalone tool before opening a file. And IRCC now treats online as the standard route for most applicants while keeping a defined list of situations that still require paper. The adult fee is $653 CAD and the minor fee is $100 CAD.

The calculator change catches people out. IRCC's guidance is explicit that the calculator "is now available in the online account" and that you can only use it after you create your account. You can still check yourself against the [paper-application calculator](https://eservices.cic.gc.ca/rescalc/startBasicCalc.do) beforehand, but the number that goes on an online application has to come from the calculator inside your account.

IRCC also publishes an optional travel journal for tracking trips outside Canada. It helps you build the numbers, and you do not submit it with the application.

## What are the 5 requirements to become a Canadian citizen?

**Short answer:** An adult applicant must hold valid permanent resident status, have 1,095 days of physical presence in Canada during the five-year eligibility period, have filed Canadian income taxes for at least three of those five years where required, prove English or French language ability if aged 18 to 54 on the day of signing, and pass the citizenship test in that same age band. A sixth condition sits underneath all of them: you must not be under a prohibition.

Your permanent resident card does not need to be valid. Your permanent resident status does. Those are different things, and an expired card is not a barrier to applying.

The prohibition rules are the ones people overlook. Most are criminal or security related, inside or outside Canada, and some apply only for a set period. Read IRCC's list of [situations that may prevent you from becoming a Canadian citizen](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility/situtations-prevent-citizenship.html) before you pay anything.

| Requirement | Who it applies to | What IRCC expects |
|---|---|---|
| Permanent resident status | All applicants | Valid PR status when you apply; the card itself may be expired |
| Physical presence | All applicants | 1,095 days in the 5-year eligibility period |
| Days as a permanent resident | All applicants | At least 730 of those 1,095 days held as a PR |
| Pre-PR time in Canada | Temporary residents and protected persons | Each day counts as 0.5, to a maximum of 365 days of credit |
| Income taxes | Applicants required to file | Filed for at least 3 years of the 5 before applying |
| Language ability | Ages 18 to 54 on the signing date | Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 4 in speaking and listening |
| Citizenship test | Ages 18 to 54 on the signing date | Invitation arrives after you submit |
| Adult fee | 18 and over | $653 CAD |
| Minor fee | Under 18 | $100 CAD |

Age is fixed on the day you sign the application, not the day you sit the test. Sign at 54 and you take the test even if you turn 55 before the invitation arrives. Wait until after your 55th birthday to sign and both the test and the language proof fall away.

## How do you calculate the 1,095 days of physical presence?

**Short answer:** Your eligibility period is the five years before the date you sign. Inside it you need 1,095 days of physical presence, and at least 730 of those days must be days you held permanent resident status. Time in Canada as a temporary resident or protected person before you landed counts at half rate, capped at 365 days of credit, which is 730 calendar days at 0.5 each. Time in prison, on parole, on probation, or waiting on a refugee claim decision does not count at all.

The 730-day floor is the rule that ends applications. Someone who studied and worked in Canada for four years before landing cannot stack that pre-PR time to reach 1,095 and apply after eighteen months as a permanent resident. The pre-PR credit tops out at 365 days, and the permanent resident days have to reach 730 on their own.

Two adjustments work in your favour. Days employed outside Canada as a Crown servant, or as the spouse, common-law partner, or child of one, count as a full day each. And time as a protected person counts from the day your refugee claim or pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA) was approved until the day before you became a permanent resident.

IRCC's own advice is to apply with more than 1,095 days in case the calculation runs into a problem. Build a buffer. Pull every passport you held during the window, including expired ones, and reconcile the stamps against flight confirmations rather than memory. Full rules are on the [who can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/who.html) page.

## What documents do you need for a Canadian citizenship application?

**Short answer:** An adult application needs proof of permanent residence, identity documents, every passport held during the five-year window, your physical presence calculation, language proof if you are 18 to 54, your tax filing information, a photo that meets the citizenship specification, and the fee receipt. The online account lists the exact document set for your situation once you open it.

Work from your account's checklist rather than a generic list, because IRCC builds the requirements from the answers you give. The items below are what nearly every adult file contains:

1. **Proof of permanent residence.** Both sides of your permanent resident card, or your Confirmation of Permanent Residence.
2. **Identity documents** showing your name, photo, and date of birth.
3. **Every passport and travel document** you held during the five-year eligibility period, including expired ones, with biographic and stamp pages.
4. **Your physical presence calculation.** Online applicants generate this inside the account. Paper applicants print the calculator result or complete form CIT 0407.
5. **Language proof** if you are 18 to 54 on the signing date. An approved test result, or a Canadian secondary or post-secondary credential taught in English or French.
6. **Tax filing information** for the relevant years. Confirm what you filed in your [CRA account](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-login-services.html) before you answer the tax questions.
7. **A citizenship photo.** The specification differs from passport and permanent resident card photos.
8. **Your fee receipt.**

Documents that are not in English or French need a translation. If your name has changed since your permanent resident document was issued, include the document that links the two names.

## How do you apply for Canadian citizenship online, step by step?

**Short answer:** Confirm your presence and tax record, sit a language test if you need one, create your online account, run the calculator inside it, complete the application, pay $653, upload your documents, and submit. IRCC sends the test invitation after submission, and the file then moves through the test to an oath ceremony.

**Step 1. Check your numbers before you open an account.** Use the paper-application calculator to confirm you are past 1,095 days with at least 730 as a permanent resident. If you are not there yet, wait.

**Step 2. Confirm your tax record.** IRCC asks whether you had to file and whether you did. Check your CRA account and file anything outstanding first.

**Step 3. Book a language test if you need one.** Applicants aged 18 to 54 who do not hold a qualifying Canadian credential need proof at CLB 4 in speaking and listening. Test seats in large cities book out months ahead.

**Step 4. Create the online account and run the calculator inside it.** This is the calculation IRCC works from.

**Step 5. Complete the application.** Expect to supply five years of addresses, work and study history, every trip outside Canada, and your tax filing detail.

**Step 6. Pay and submit.** Upload the document set, review it once, and submit. Corrections after submission go through a separate web form and add time.

**Step 7. Test and oath.** IRCC invites you to the citizenship test after you submit. The test covers rights and responsibilities, history, symbols, geography, and the structure of government, drawn from the [Discover Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/discover-canada.html) study guide. After you pass, you are scheduled for the oath, and you become a citizen when you take it. For current timing at each stage, see [our citizenship processing times tracker](/immigration/processing-times/citizenship).

If you want an authorized representative to help with an online application, note IRCC's rule carefully: you must complete and submit the application yourself. A representative can advise, review, and prepare, and the submission stays in your hands.

## Who still has to apply on paper?

**Short answer:** IRCC recommends online for most applicants and keeps a published list of situations that require paper instead. Check that exceptions list against your own circumstances before you create an account, because starting in the wrong channel costs weeks. Paper applicants use the standalone physical presence calculator printout or form CIT 0407 in place of the in-account calculation.

The exceptions list changes as IRCC extends online coverage, so read the current version on the [how to apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/how.html) page rather than relying on what applied last year. IRCC has said it is working toward everyone applying online.

Paper files take longer and are returned more often for completeness problems, so treat paper as the route you take when a rule sends you there, not a preference.

## How much does a Canadian citizenship application cost in 2026?

**Short answer:** An adult application is $653 CAD, an amount IRCC states includes both the processing fee and the right of citizenship fee. A minor application is $100 CAD and covers the processing fee only. A stateless adult born to a Canadian parent pays $123 CAD. A citizenship certificate, which is proof of citizenship rather than a grant of it, is $75 CAD.

Budget for the language test separately if you need one. Those are private test providers, not an IRCC charge, and they typically run a few hundred dollars.

| Application | Fee (CAD) | What it covers |
|---|---:|---|
| Adult, 18 and over | $653 | Processing fee and right of citizenship fee |
| Minor, under 18 | $100 | Processing fee |
| Stateless adult born to a Canadian parent | $123 | Includes the right of citizenship fee |
| Citizenship certificate (proof of citizenship) | $75 | Proof for someone who is already a citizen |

Fees change without much notice. Confirm the current amount on the [IRCC fee list](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/information/fees/fees.asp) on the day you pay, because paying a superseded amount gets the application returned. If you are looking for proof of an existing citizenship rather than a grant, our guide to the [proof of Canadian citizenship application](/news/proof-of-canadian-citizenship-application-2026) covers that separate process.

## How do you track a Canadian citizenship application?

**Short answer:** Sign in to the same online account you applied through. It reports your progress and tells you the next step at each stage. For files that have run well past the published processing time, a request for your GCMS notes shows the officer's internal comments and is usually more informative than the tracker.

The account is the primary channel. It confirms submission, flags anything IRCC needs from you, and moves through the test and oath stages.

If your file has stalled, the [access to information and privacy](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/access-information-privacy.html) route lets you request the notes on your file. Compare where you sit against the current published times on the [IRCC processing times tool](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) before concluding anything has gone wrong.

## Why do Canadian citizenship applications get returned?

**Short answer:** Returns cluster around the presence calculation, missing or superseded fee payments, photos that do not meet the citizenship specification, gaps in the five-year travel history, and missing language proof for applicants aged 18 to 54. Each one is avoidable in the week before you submit.

The presence calculation is the recurring problem, and the 730-days-as-a-permanent-resident floor is where files fail most often. Applicants who counted pre-PR study or work time at full value, or who assumed the half-day credit was uncapped, arrive at a number that does not survive review.

Everything else on the list is mechanical. Confirm the fee against the current schedule on the day you pay. Ask your photographer for a citizenship photo by name, since the specification differs from a passport or permanent resident card photo. Reconcile every trip against passport stamps rather than recollection. And upload the language proof even if your English or French is obviously fluent in conversation, because the requirement is documentary.

## What happens if you apply with a spouse, parent, or child?

**Short answer:** Families can apply together online, with one constraint that surprises people: there is only one adult per online account. Spouses each hold their own account and link them into a group. Minors are added to a parent's account, unless the minor's situation requires them to apply on their own. Grouping does not make the file faster, and it keeps a household's applications moving as a unit.

Each application is still assessed individually. Every adult meets the presence, tax, language, and test requirements on their own record, and a group application does not let one person's history support another's.

Minors under 18 who are permanent residents apply for a $100 fee and do not take the test or prove language ability. A minor generally needs a parent or guardian who is a Canadian citizen, or who is applying at the same time. Minors have their own physical presence requirement of 1,095 days within a five-year eligibility period that includes at least 730 days as a permanent resident, the same structure as the adult rule.

You can leave a group or remove someone from it inside the online account if circumstances change before submission.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What are the requirements to apply for Canadian citizenship?**
Valid permanent resident status, 1,095 days of physical presence in the five-year eligibility period with at least 730 of those as a permanent resident, tax filings for three of the five years where required, language proof at CLB 4 for ages 18 to 54, the citizenship test in that same age band, and no active prohibition.

**How long does it take to get Canadian citizenship?**
Timing depends on the application type and IRCC's current inventory, and it shifts through the year. We track the current figures on our [citizenship processing times page](/immigration/processing-times/citizenship) and IRCC publishes its own estimate through the processing times tool.

**What documents do I need for a Canadian citizenship application?**
Proof of permanent residence, identity documents, every passport held during the five-year window, your physical presence calculation, language proof if you are 18 to 54, tax filing information, a citizenship photo, and the fee receipt. Your online account lists the exact set for your circumstances.

**Can I apply for citizenship if my permanent resident card is expired?**
Yes. Permanent resident status does not expire with the card. You do need a valid card or a permanent resident travel document to board a commercial carrier back into Canada, so renew it if you plan to travel while the application is in progress.

**How much is the Canadian citizenship application fee?**
$653 CAD for an adult and $100 CAD for a minor. Confirm the amount on the IRCC fee list the day you pay.

**Can I travel outside Canada while my application is being processed?**
Yes. A citizenship application does not restrict travel. You do need to be available for the test and the oath, and you need to maintain your permanent resident status throughout.

**Do my children become citizens automatically when I do?**
No. A child who is a permanent resident needs their own application. A child born in Canada is already a citizen. A child born outside Canada may be a citizen by descent depending on how you acquired citizenship, which our [citizenship by descent guide](/news/citizenship-by-descent-canada-2026) covers.

**Does Canada allow dual citizenship?**
Canada does. Your other country may not. Several countries restrict or withdraw their citizenship when a national naturalizes elsewhere, so check that country's law before you take the oath rather than after.

**How should I prepare for the citizenship test?**
Read Discover Canada end to end. The questions come from it. Public libraries and free practice tools cover the same material, and our [citizenship test practice guide](/news/canadian-citizenship-test-practice-2026) walks through the format.

**Can I get a Canadian passport right after the oath?**
Yes. Your citizenship certificate is the proof that supports a passport application, and you can apply once you have it.

## What should you do next?

**Short answer:** Confirm your physical presence against both thresholds, 1,095 days total and 730 as a permanent resident, before anything else. Then check your tax record, book a language test if you need one, and read the paper-application exceptions to confirm you can apply online.

1. Run the presence calculation and confirm both thresholds, with a buffer above 1,095 days.
2. Check your filing record in your CRA account and file anything outstanding.
3. Book a language test now if you are 18 to 54 without a qualifying Canadian credential.
4. Read the current exceptions list to confirm whether you apply online or on paper.
5. If you want a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) to review your presence calculation and document set before you submit, [book a consultation with Go Far Global](/appointment).

# Becoming a Real Estate Agent in Ontario as a Newcomer: The 2026 Career Pivot That Works

# Becoming a Real Estate Agent in Ontario as a Newcomer: The 2026 Career Pivot That Works

*Sponsored post. The links to [ExamAce](https://examace.ca) in this article are sponsored placements. The free REAT prep is genuinely free and does not require a card.*

**Quick facts:**
- The Ontario real estate licensing path is administered by [RECO](https://www.reco.on.ca) and delivered through [Humber Polytechnic](https://realestate.humber.ca).
- The path opens with the REAT (Real Estate Admission Test), then five pre-registration courses, then 24 months of articling.
- Total cost runs $3,500 to $5,000 in 2026, depending on prep materials.
- No Canadian degree required. No "Canadian experience" prerequisite. No employer sponsorship needed.
- Most newcomers complete the licensing portion in 9 to 12 months alongside a day job.

> **Read this before you pivot:** Real estate agents in Ontario are almost always classified as self-employed independent contractors. Self-employed income **does not count** toward the Express Entry [Canadian Experience Class](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html). If you have not yet secured PR, talk to an [RCIC](/about) before you make this move. Real estate is a strong career play *after* PR, not a path *toward* PR.

Skilled newcomers often land in Canada and find their foreign credentials need 18 to 36 months of recertification before they can earn a comparable salary. Real estate keeps showing up as the fastest practical pivot. We see this in our Toronto practice every month. An internationally trained engineer waits two years for their P.Eng. A foreign-trained pharmacist hits the [Pharmacy Examining Board of Canada](https://www.pebc.ca) wall. An accountant discovers their CPA equivalency requires three more exams. The licensing path to become a registered real estate salesperson in Ontario is structured and predictable, and it starts paying within 12 to 18 months.

This guide is the operator view from Go Far Global's Toronto office. Most of our finance, engineering, and pharmacy clients who pivoted to real estate did so within their first three years in Canada. The licensing structure changed in 2025, the regulator is enforcing more rigorously, and prep material pricing has shifted enough that older guides are misleading. Here is the 2026 reality.

## Why Real Estate Pivots Work for Newcomers

**Short answer:** Three structural reasons — no foreign credential gate (the REAT, courses, and license skip foreign-degree assessment entirely), self-employment dodges the salaried Canadian-experience trap (but self-employed income does NOT count for CEC, a critical immigration caveat), and the GTA market rewards diaspora-community specialists (bilingual agents serving a specific cultural community averaged 22% higher GCI in their first 3 years per RECO 2024 survey).

Three structural reasons, in rough order of importance:

**One: no foreign credential gate.** Engineering, medicine, accounting, and law all require provincial licensing bodies to assess your foreign degree, often through bridge programs that take 12 to 36 months. The Ontario real estate path skips this entirely. You sit the [REAT admission test](https://realestate.humber.ca), you pass, you enrol. Your degree, your country of training, your prior experience are not assessed. You start at the same line as a Canadian-born candidate.

**Two: self-employment dodges the salaried Canadian-experience trap, with caveats.** Most salaried roles in Canada filter applicants by Canadian work history. Brokerages sponsor anyone they think will close deals. They want a book of business, and a Canadian resume is secondary. If you arrive with an active community network from your home country diaspora, you have a real asset that other candidates do not.

**Important caveat for anyone still working through PR:** self-employed real estate income does **not** count as Canadian work experience for the [Express Entry Canadian Experience Class](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html). IRCC excludes self-employment from CEC eligibility. If you have not yet landed PR and you were counting on months selling real estate to feed your CRS profile, that math does not work. Plan around this. Either secure PR before pivoting, or structure at least part of your work as a salaried employee position. Talk to an [RCIC](/about) before making the jump.

**Three: the GTA market rewards diaspora-community specialists.** Iranian, Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Tagalog, and Persian-speaking realtors regularly outperform generalists in their respective community submarkets. A 2024 RECO survey of agent income found that bilingual agents serving a clearly defined cultural community averaged 22% higher GCI (gross commission income) in their first three years than English-only generalists. If you arrived speaking a heritage language and have an existing network, that is a competitive moat.

## The 2026 Licensing Path, Step by Step

**Short answer:** Three phases — Phase 1 the REAT admission test ($115, 100 multiple-choice questions, 90 minutes, 75% pass mark, 30-35% fail rate on first attempt); Phase 2 pre-registration (5 courses delivered by Humber, $2,000 to $2,400, 12 months from REAT to complete with one extension); Phase 3 articling (24 months with two more Humber courses, first listings often within 3 months and commission from month 4).

The Ontario path is run by Humber Polytechnic on contract from RECO. It has three phases.

### Phase 1: The REAT (Real Estate Admission Test)

The REAT is a 100-question, computer-based exam that tests basic financial literacy, math, reading comprehension, and ethical reasoning. There is no prerequisite course. You register with Humber, you sit the exam at one of the testing centres in Toronto, Mississauga, Brampton, Vaughan, Markham, or Hamilton, and you wait for your score.

- **Cost:** $115 (2026)
- **Format:** 100 multiple-choice questions, 90 minutes
- **Pass mark:** 75%
- **Retake:** allowed, with a 30-day waiting period and another $115 fee

The REAT is the single biggest filter. Roughly 30 to 35% of candidates fail on the first attempt according to Humber's own reporting. Most failures are math (mortgage payments, area calculations, commission splits) and tricky-wording reading comprehension. Two weeks of structured prep is enough for almost anyone to pass.

A free starting point. [ExamAce's REAT Prep](https://examace.ca/courses/ontario/reat-prep) gives you 100 practice questions modelled on the actual exam at no cost and no card required. Use it to gauge whether you can sit the test cold or whether you need a focused prep cycle first.

### Phase 2: Pre-Registration (Five Courses)

Once you pass the REAT, you enrol in the Pre-Registration program, which is five courses delivered by Humber:

1. Course 1: Real Estate Essentials
2. Course 2: Residential Real Estate Transactions
3. Course 3: Additional Residential Real Estate Transactions
4. Course 4: Commercial Real Estate Transactions
5. Course 5: Getting Started

Each course has a final exam. The pass mark is 75% across the board. The full pre-registration package costs around $2,000 to $2,400 depending on whether you bundle.

You have 12 months from the REAT to complete pre-registration, with one extension permitted. Most newcomers complete it in 6 to 9 months while still working full-time elsewhere.

### Phase 3: Articling (24 Months)

After Phase 2 you register with a brokerage and become a registered salesperson. The articling phase requires two more Humber courses (the Articling courses) within 24 months of registration. Most agents take their first listings within the first three months and are earning commission income from month four onward.

## The 2026 Cost Reality

For a newcomer running on settlement funds, the difference between $250 a year and $1,000+ on prep materials matters.

Try [ExamAce's free REAT prep](https://examace.ca/courses/ontario/reat-prep) before you commit to anything. 100 practice questions, no payment, no card. If you can hold a 75% on those questions cold, you are ready to register for the actual REAT. If you are landing in the 50 to 65% range, drill the math sections, then drill the ethics sections, then re-test.

## Timeline: From Landing to First Commission

**Short answer:** Typical timeline — months 0 to 1 settle and get SIN/bank/SIN, months 1 to 2 free REAT prep, month 3 sit and pass the REAT, months 4 to 9 pre-registration courses, month 10 sign with a brokerage, months 10 to 11 RECO registration and onboarding, month 12 register as salesperson, months 14 to 18 first commissions land, month 18 to 36 build a book; most clients are profitable by month 18.

For a newcomer who lands in Canada and decides to pivot to real estate:

| Month | Activity |
|---:|---|
| 0 to 1 | Settle, get SIN, open bank account, decide on real estate path |
| 1 to 2 | Free REAT prep (no cost, no commitment); decide if you want a paid prep tier |
| 3 | Sit the REAT, pass |
| 4 to 9 | Pre-Registration courses (5 courses, ~6 months part-time alongside any day job) |
| 10 | Apply to brokerages; sign with one |
| 10 to 11 | RECO registration, insurance, complete onboarding |
| 12 | Start working as a registered salesperson; begin articling courses in parallel |
| 14 to 18 | First commission cheques typically land |
| 18 to 36 | Build a book; complete articling courses; start positioning for broker eventually |

Most clients we work with are profitable in the trade by month 18. Many are at or above their pre-immigration salary by month 30 if they have an active diaspora network to lean on.

## Common Mistakes Newcomers Make

**Short answer:** Top mistakes — treating the REAT as a casual sit (math sections trip up imperial-system newcomers), picking a brokerage on commission split alone (mentorship matters more than percentage in year one), underestimating ongoing costs ($5,000 to $8,000 in year one for insurance, dues, MLS, desk fees), skipping the diaspora network advantage, and letting the 12-month pre-registration window expire.

In rough order of frequency at our office:

1. **Treating the REAT as a casual sit.** The math sections trip up candidates who studied in metric-only systems. Imperial mortgage calculations and cap rates require dedicated drilling. Use the [free REAT prep](https://examace.ca/courses/ontario/reat-prep) to find your weak areas before you book the exam.

2. **Picking a brokerage on commission split alone.** First-year brokerage choice matters more for mentorship than for split percentage. A 50/50 split with a senior agent who actively teaches you is worth more than an 80/20 split where you are alone in a high-volume office.

3. **Underestimating ongoing costs.** RECO insurance, professional dues, MLS fees, and brokerage desk fees can total $5,000 to $8,000 in year one. Have a runway separate from your prep budget.

4. **Skipping the diaspora network advantage.** Newcomers often try to compete in the broad GTA market against incumbents with 10-year client books. Specialise in a community submarket where your language skills, cultural fluency, and existing network are real advantages.

5. **Letting the 12-month pre-registration window expire.** You have 12 months from the REAT to finish pre-registration, with one paid extension. Plan the schedule before you sit the test, not after.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Short answer:** Common answers — PRs and work permit holders both qualify (with the right authorization), no Canadian high school diploma needed, full path takes 9 to 12 months while working a day job, year one income runs $0 to $80,000 with year two typically $60,000 to $120,000 for serious newcomers; CRITICAL: self-employed real estate income does NOT count for Canadian Experience Class — secure PR before pivoting or arrange salaried-employee status.

**Q: Can a permanent resident or work permit holder become a real estate agent in Ontario?**
A: Yes. Permanent residents qualify directly. Work permit holders qualify if their permit allows self-employment or if their brokerage sponsors them as an employee.

**Q: Do I need a high school diploma from Canada?**
A: No. The REAT entry requirement is a high school diploma or equivalent from any country, plus age 18+. Foreign diplomas are accepted without re-evaluation.

**Q: How long does the full path take from start to license?**
A: 9 to 12 months for most candidates working full-time alongside studies. Faster if you can study full-time.

**Q: What is the realistic income in year one and year two?**
A: Year one is highly variable: anywhere from $0 to $80,000 depending on network and effort. Year two for a serious newcomer with an active diaspora network typically lands in the $60,000 to $120,000 range in the GTA. The [Government of Canada Job Bank](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/) lists median annual earnings around $69,000 for NOC 63102 (Real estate agents and salespersons), but the spread is wide.

**Q: How does becoming a real estate agent affect my immigration status or PR application?**
A: The single most-asked question, and the answer is more cautious than most newcomers expect. **Self-employed real estate income does not count toward the [Canadian Experience Class](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html).** IRCC excludes self-employment from CEC eligibility outright. Most real estate agents in Ontario are classified as independent contractors of their brokerage, which puts them in the self-employment bucket for IRCC purposes. PNP treatment of self-employment varies by province and stream, with most streams either excluding it or requiring a full Self-Employed business case. The federal [Self-Employed Persons Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/self-employed.html) is restricted to cultural and athletic categories and does not apply to real estate. **Plan your immigration timeline before you pivot.** If you still need to build Canadian work experience for PR, secure an employee-status arrangement (some brokerages do offer this) or finish your PR application before going self-employed.

**Q: Is real estate a TEER 0 or 1 occupation for federal Express Entry category-based draws?**
A: No. NOC 63102 is TEER 3. It does not qualify for the federal STEM, healthcare, or trades category-based draws. Combined with the self-employment exclusion above, this means real estate is a stronger career pivot **after** PR than as a path **toward** PR.

**Q: Should I do a free trial before paying for a prep platform?**
A: Yes. [ExamAce offers three free courses](https://examace.ca) (REAT Prep, Course 5, and the Complete Exam Review) without a credit card, which is enough to know whether the format works for you before you subscribe.

# PGWP Language Requirements 2026: TEER Categories, CLB Scores, and What to Test

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/pgwp-language-requirements-2026
Category: Work Permits
Published: 2026-05-08
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Until November 1, 2024, the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) had no language requirement.

# PGWP Language Requirements 2026: TEER Categories, CLB Scores, and What to Test

Until November 1, 2024, the [Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation.html) had no language requirement. You graduated from a Designated Learning Institution, applied within the eligibility window, and Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) issued the permit on your academic record.

Since November 1, 2024, every PGWP applicant must show a minimum [Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/language-requirements.html) level tied to the TEER (Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities) classification of the occupation they intend to work in. IRCC did not push the change in the news cycle. Through 2025 we processed a steady stream of refusals where the applicant did not know a test was required.

Below: the thresholds, which tests count, what fails on technicalities, and how to recover if your first attempt lands short.

## What are the PGWP language requirements in 2026?

**Short answer:** Two PGWP thresholds by TEER level — TEER 0/1 (management, engineer, accountant, RN, teacher, software developer) needs CLB 7 (~IELTS General 6.0 each band); TEER 2/3 (administrative officer, electrician, paramedic, chef) needs CLB 5 (~IELTS General 5.0 each band); TEER misclassification is the most common confusion since the level attaches to actual duties not job title.

Two PGWP language thresholds apply in 2026. Which one you hit depends on the [TEER level](https://noc.esdc.gc.ca/Structure/Hierarchy) of your post-graduation occupation:

| TEER level | Typical occupations | Minimum CLB | Approx. IELTS General |
|---|---|---|---|
| TEER 0 or 1 | Management, professional (engineer, accountant, RN, teacher, software developer) | CLB 7 | L 6.0 / R 6.0 / W 6.0 / S 6.0 |
| TEER 2 or 3 | Technical, supervisory, skilled trades (administrative officer, electrician, paramedic, chef) | CLB 5 | L 5.0 / R 4.0 / W 5.0 / S 5.0 |

TEER 4 and 5 occupations (clerical, retail, manual labour) do not support most PR pathways. The PGWP itself can still issue if your study program qualifies, but the work experience you build in a TEER 4/5 job will not count toward most economic PR streams.

TEER misclassification is the most common confusion we see. The TEER level attaches to the **occupation**, not the job title. Two people with "Project Coordinator" on the same offer letter can sit under TEER 1 (NOC 10010 Senior managers, financial, communications and other business services) or TEER 3 (NOC 13100 Administrative officers) depending on actual duties. Cross-reference your duties against the [official NOC matrix](https://noc.esdc.gc.ca/) before you pick a threshold.

## Which Tests Count

**Short answer:** Accepted English tests are IELTS General Training (not Academic — a recurring refusal trap), CELPIP General, and PTE Core (added 2024); French tests are TEF Canada and TCF Canada; results must be less than 2 years old at submission, and Academic versions of IELTS or CELPIP are not accepted for PGWP.

IRCC accepts the same approved language tests for PGWP that it accepts for Express Entry. The list as of 2026:

**English:**
- IELTS General Training (not Academic, this is a recurring trap)
- CELPIP General
- PTE Core (added in 2024 for Express Entry, accepted for PGWP since)

**French:**
- TEF Canada
- TCF Canada

The Academic versions of IELTS and CELPIP serve university admissions. IRCC does **not** accept them for PGWP. We see refusals every quarter where the applicant submitted IELTS Academic scores at CLB 7 equivalent and IRCC refused on test type. A re-test costs roughly $345 and 4 to 6 weeks. Book the General version the first time.

Test results must be **less than 2 years old** at the date of PGWP submission. An IELTS from June 2024 is expired for a July 2026 application.

## When Do You Need to Have the Test

**Short answer:** The language requirement is assessed at PGWP submission, not at graduation or study-permit issue — you can graduate, then test, then apply within the 180-day post-graduation window; you cannot submit test scores after the application, use a Canadian degree as substitute, or use TOEFL/Duolingo (not on the approved list).

Most students get the timing wrong. The language requirement is assessed at the moment of PGWP submission, **not** at graduation and not at the moment your study permit issued.

You can:
- Graduate, then take the test, then apply for PGWP, all within the 180-day post-graduation window.
- Apply for PGWP without taking the test if you intend to work in a TEER 4 or 5 job (with the caveats above).
- Take the test before graduation if you want to lock in scores while you are still in study mode.

You cannot:
- Apply for PGWP and submit test scores later. The application is assessed on what is in the file at submission.
- Use a Canadian degree to substitute for the language test. There is no degree-based exemption for PGWP, unlike some Express Entry streams.
- Use TOEFL, Duolingo, or any other test not on the approved list.

## The Quebec Carve-Out

**Short answer:** Quebec institution graduates working in French in Quebec still face the federal PGWP thresholds, but Quebec provincial work permits and selection certificates layer on top — book an RCIC familiar with Quebec immigration since the federal-provincial overlap creates edge cases.

Graduates from Quebec institutions who plan to work in French in Quebec face a different framework. The federal PGWP thresholds still apply, but Quebec's provincial work permits and selection certificates layer on top, and IRCC weighs the application differently. Book a consultation with an [RCIC](/about) familiar with Quebec immigration if you sit in this category. The federal-provincial overlap creates edge cases that a generic guide cannot safely cover.

## How to Address a Refusal Based on Language

**Short answer:** Recovery steps — order GCMS notes ($5, ~30 days) to confirm the stated CLB shortfall, re-test the correct version (IELTS Academic → IELTS General, PTE Academic → PTE Core), apply for restoration of status within the 90-day window ($229 + $100 fee), then submit a fresh PGWP application with a cover letter explicitly addressing the previous refusal and new scores.

The [Visa Refusal Analyzer](/tools/refusal-analyzer) will walk you through this. Summary:

1. **Request your [GCMS notes](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/access-information-privacy/requests-information-act.html)** ($5, ~30 days). Confirm the officer's stated CLB shortfall. We see cases where the score was fine and the refusal was actually on a different ground.
2. **Re-test for the correct version.** If you submitted IELTS Academic, retake IELTS General. If you submitted PTE Academic, retake PTE Core.
3. **Apply for [restoration of status](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay/restore-status.html)** if you are within the 90-day window. Restoration lets you re-apply from inside Canada after a refusal. Cost: $229 + $100 restoration fee.
4. **Submit a fresh PGWP application** with the correct scores. Address the refusal in a cover letter: "My previous application was refused on [date] because [stated ground]. I have since obtained [date, test, scores], which exceed the CLB [X] threshold for TEER [Y] occupations."

Refusal to re-decision typically runs 5 to 7 months. You have no implied status during that window (refusal terminates implied status the day of decision). You can remain in Canada on visitor status only if you applied for restoration in time.

## Common Mistakes That Cause Avoidable Refusals

**Short answer:** Top avoidable mistakes — booking IELTS Academic instead of General (re-test costs $345 and 4 to 6 weeks), letting tests expire before PGWP submission, splitting scores across two sittings (all four skills must come from the same test date), misreading the TEER level of the target occupation, and applying with no test at all since the November 2024 requirement applies to every PGWP applicant.

In rough order of frequency at our Toronto office:

1. **Booking IELTS Academic instead of General.** Both tests sit on the same shelf at the same testing centres. Confirm "General Training" when you book.
2. **Letting the test expire while waiting to graduate.** A test taken in first year of a 4-year program will be expired by your PGWP submission date. Take it near the end of studies.
3. **Splitting scores across two sittings.** You cannot combine the listening from one test date with the speaking from another. All four skills must come from the same sitting.
4. **Misreading the TEER level of the target occupation.** "Manager" and "coordinator" titles trip people up most often. The actual TEER hinges on whether you supervise staff and what decisions you sign off on.
5. **Applying with no test at all.** The requirement applies to every PGWP applicant since November 1, 2024, regardless of program length, institution, or program type.

## What If You Cannot Hit CLB 7

**Short answer:** If you cannot hit CLB 7 for TEER 0/1, three options — accept TEER 2/3 work (still feeds most economic PR streams), re-test with structured prep (IELTS scores typically move 0.5 to 1.0 bands with focused prep mostly in writing, clients often move from CLB 6 to CLB 8 over three attempts), or switch to French testing where TEF/TCF curves often land higher for Francophone-adjacent backgrounds.

If you keep landing at CLB 5 or 6 and need TEER 0/1 work, you have three options:

**Option 1: Accept TEER 2/3 work for the duration of the PGWP.** Almost every graduate of an English-medium Canadian program clears CLB 5. Canadian work experience at TEER 2/3 still feeds most economic PR streams.

**Option 2: Re-test with structured prep between attempts.** IELTS scores move 0.5 to 1.0 bands with focused prep, most often in writing. We see clients move from CLB 6 to CLB 8 over three attempts in a year.

**Option 3: Switch to French testing.** TEF Canada and TCF Canada produce different score curves than English tests. For applicants from Francophone or Francophone-adjacent backgrounds (parts of the Maghreb, sub-Saharan Africa, the Levant), TEF scores often land higher.

We run language test booking, prep recommendations, and PGWP filing as one workflow. The most common request from current students is a 30-minute PGWP timing review three to six months before graduation, where we cover:

- The TEER level of your target occupation and the CLB threshold that applies
- Test booking calendar and re-test buffer time
- Study permit and visa expiry coordination

# Financial Analyst and Investment Advisor Jobs in Canada 2026: What Newcomers Need to Know About the CIRO Exam Switch

# Financial Analyst and Investment Advisor Jobs in Canada 2026: What Newcomers Need to Know About the CIRO Exam Switch

*Sponsored post. The links to [Ciroexam](https://ciroexam.ca) in this article are sponsored placements. The 25-question CIRE diagnostic is genuinely free and does not require a card.*

**Quick facts:**
- The Canadian Securities Course (CSC) was retired on January 1, 2026.
- It was replaced by the CIRO Proficiency Model: nine role-specific exams.
- The foundational exam is the CIRE (Canadian Investment Regulatory Examination).
- Existing CSC credentials are recognized for a defined transition period, not permanently.
- Canada's financial sector hires about 18,000 net new licensed professionals each year.

Financial analyst jobs in Canada increasingly expect a CIRO exam credential. Canada's financial sector hires in two cycles a year. The fall cycle pulls in graduates and credential-holders for January desks. The spring cycle picks up newcomers and career-switchers for summer onboarding. Major banks, independent dealers, and asset managers add about 18,000 net new licensed professionals each year, and that number has climbed since the post-pandemic recovery.

*As of May 8, 2026.*

If you arrived in Canada with a finance background, an MBA, an accounting designation, or a quantitative degree, finance is a sector where international experience translates cleanly into a Canadian salary. The industry recognizes many foreign credentials, and the [Government of Canada Job Bank](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/) lists thousands of openings for licensed roles each quarter.

One change to understand before you apply: as of January 1, 2026, the credentialing pathway shifted. The Canadian Securities Course (CSC), the entry-level credential for almost every retail-facing investment role for decades, was retired. In its place, the [Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO)](https://www.ciro.ca), the national self-regulator for investment dealers and trading activity, introduced a new proficiency model with nine role-specific exams.

**Is my CSC still valid?** If you completed the CSC before January 1, 2026, CIRO recognizes the credential for a defined transition period in the registration category you held it for. It is not permanent. Anyone who plans to change roles, switch firms, or re-enter the industry after the transition window will write the new CIRE.

This guide covers which finance jobs are hiring, what the CIRO model means for your application, and how to prepare for the foundational CIRE exam without spending $1,000+ on legacy materials.

## Where are the financial analyst jobs in Canada?

**Short answer:** Canada hires ~18,000 net new licensed financial professionals/year: Financial sales rep (National Occupational Classification (NOC) 64409) $52K to $65K + commission, Investment advisor (NOC 11103) $55K to $70K + book, Financial analyst (NOC 11101) $65K to $85K, Securities trader $70K to $90K, Compliance officer (NOC 11201) $75K to $95K, Portfolio manager $90K to $120K+ (requires CFA + Supervisor); Toronto leads volume with Calgary, Vancouver, Montreal, and Ottawa carrying regional books.

NOC codes for licensed investment work, with 2026 salary bands from [Job Bank](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/trend-analysis/search-occupations) and major-bank disclosures:

| Role | NOC code | Typical entry salary | Senior salary | Licensing required |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Financial sales representative | 64409 | $52,000 to $65,000 + commission | $120,000+ | CIRE + Retail Securities |
| Investment advisor (registered representative) | 11103 | $55,000 to $70,000 + book | $250,000+ | CIRE + Retail Securities |
| Financial analyst | 11101 | $65,000 to $85,000 | $130,000+ | CIRE + role-specific |
| Securities trader | 64409 | $70,000 to $90,000 | $200,000+ | CIRE + Trader |
| Compliance officer | 11201 | $75,000 to $95,000 | $160,000+ | CIRE + CCO |
| Portfolio manager | 11103 | $90,000 to $120,000 | $300,000+ | CIRE + CFA + Supervisor |

Toronto's financial district carries the bulk of the volume. Calgary (energy and resources finance), Vancouver (Asia-Pacific desks and resource banking), Montreal (Quebec institutional and pension funds), and Ottawa (federal pension plans) each run their own hiring books. If you are landing through Express Entry or a Provincial Nominee Program, the destination province matters as much as the role.

## What Replaced the CSC in Canada?

**Short answer:** Effective January 1, 2026, the CSC sequence (CSC + CPH + 90-day training) collapsed into the CIRO Proficiency Model with nine exams: CIRE foundation plus role-specific modules: Retail Securities, Institutional Securities, Supervisor, Trader, Derivatives, Director & Executive, Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Financial Officer; retail advisors write CIRE + Retail Securities, traders write CIRE + Trader, compliance officers write CIRE + CCO.

Most foreign finance credentials (CFA, ACCA, CPA from many jurisdictions, MBA from accredited institutions) carry weight on a resume, but none of them substitute for Canadian regulatory licensing. To work in any client-facing or trading-floor role registered with CIRO, you must pass the relevant Canadian proficiency exams.

The 2026 change reshapes that step. Until December 31, 2025, the standard sequence for a new investment advisor was:

1. Pass the Canadian Securities Course (CSC).
2. Pass the Conduct and Practices Handbook (CPH).
3. Complete a 90-day training program with your sponsoring firm.

Effective January 1, 2026, that sequence collapsed into the CIRO Proficiency Model. Instead of a generic securities course followed by a conduct module, every CIRO-registered professional now starts with the Canadian Investment Regulatory Examination (CIRE), then moves to a role-specific exam.

The nine exams under the new model:

1. **CIRE** (Conduct & Industry Regulatory Exam): the foundation every other path requires
2. Retail Securities
3. Institutional Securities
4. Supervisor
5. Trader
6. Derivatives
7. Director & Executive
8. Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)
9. Chief Financial Officer (CFO)

For retail investment advisor work, you write CIRE plus Retail Securities. For a trading desk, CIRE plus Trader. Compliance roles need CIRE plus CCO. The single linear ladder is gone. You write the foundation, then the role-specific module.

## Why Does the CSC Replacement Matter for Newcomers?

**Short answer:** Three shifts: independent prep platforms have entered the market and compressed legacy $1,000+ price points sharply; the CIRE is more conduct-heavy (~40% on PCMLTFA AML, UMIR, NI 31-103 vs CSC product focus); sponsoring firms are still calibrating and walking into interviews already holding CIRE puts you ahead of mid-prep candidates.

Three things shifted that affect anyone pursuing licensing in their first year or two in Canada.

**One:** The old CSC ran about $1,200 with study materials. Many newcomers paid the fee out of settlement funds before realizing they could have spread the cost over a year-long sponsoring-firm offer. The new CIRO model is similarly priced through the legacy provider channel, but independent prep platforms have entered the market and reshaped the cost calculus.

**Two:** The CIRE is more conduct-heavy than the old CSC was. About 40% of CIRE content covers regulatory conduct, anti-money-laundering rules under the [PCMLTFA](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/p-24.501/), Universal Market Integrity Rules (UMIR), and National Instrument 31-103 registration requirements. For someone new to Canadian markets, the conduct learning curve runs steeper than the old CSC's mostly product-focused content. Budget more study hours for conduct than you would expect.

**Three:** Sponsoring firms are still calibrating to the new model. Through the first half of 2026, large banks have run more cautious hiring on unlicensed candidates while they wait for pass rates to stabilize. Walking into an interview already holding the CIRE puts you ahead of candidates who are still mid-prep.

The content cites the underlying regulation directly (IDPC Rules, UMIR, PCMLTFA, NI 31-103) rather than paraphrased summaries. On test day, conduct questions often demand the exact rule citation, so working from the source pays off.
