## How Does the CIRO Exam Fit Your Immigration and Career Plan?

**Short answer:** NOC codes 11101, 11103, and 11201 are TEER 1 occupations qualifying for most Express Entry category-based draws; securing CIRO licensing within your first 12 months improves both Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score and eligibility for in-Canada draws; Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) holders should also note the 2026 PGWP language requirements adding a Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) threshold tied to target occupation TEER level.

If you are still in the immigration phase, NOC codes 11101, 11103, and 11201 are all TEER 1 occupations, which means they are eligible for most Express Entry category-based draws (the [federal STEM draw](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-instructions-agreements/ministerial-instructions/express-entry-rounds.html) does not include finance directly, but the standard [Canadian Experience Class](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html) and Provincial Nominee Program streams do). If you can secure CIRO licensing within your first 12 months in Canada, your CRS score and your eligibility for in-Canada draws both improve.

We see this with clients arriving on a [PGWP](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation.html) after a Canadian master's degree in finance or economics. They have the academic base and the work permit, but they delay licensing because the cost feels steep right after graduation. By month 18, when they start applying for advisor roles, the firms have moved on to candidates who already passed the CIRE. PGWP holders should also be aware of the [2026 PGWP language requirements](/news/pgwp-language-requirements-2026), which add a CLB threshold tied to the TEER level of the target occupation. Writing the licensing exam early, even before a job offer, is a defensible move when prep runs $30 a month instead of $1,000 upfront.

## What Are the Most Common Questions About the CIRO Exam?

**Short answer:** Common answers: non-registered roles (operations, research, technology) need no CIRO exam; CSC holders from before Jan 1, 2026 have a transition period but not permanent grandfathering; plan 80 to 120 hours of structured CIRE study; CIRE is offered in English and French; you can write CIRE without a sponsoring firm but need one to register with CIRO; legacy fees around $300 to $400/attempt; CFA does not exempt you from CIRE.

**Q: Can I work in finance without writing the CIRE?**
A: You can hold non-registered roles (operations, back-office, research support, technology) without any CIRO exam. The moment you give advice, sell securities, or trade on a registered platform, you need the relevant CIRO licensing. Bank teller and basic mutual-fund roles often run through the Mutual Fund Dealers proficiency stream, which is a separate path with its own credentials.

**Q: I passed the CSC before January 1, 2026. Do I need to write the CIRE?**
A: Not immediately, but probably eventually. CIRO published transition provisions that recognize a completed CSC for a defined period, role-specific to how you registered. It is not permanent grandfathering. Many existing CSC holders will need to write the CIRE before the transition window closes to keep their licensing current, especially if they change registration categories. Confirm your specific situation with [CIRO](https://www.ciro.ca) and your sponsoring firm. A practical move for anyone whose career may shift roles in the next few years: write the CIRE now while the prep cost is low, rather than wait for the transition deadline. The free [25-question diagnostic at ciroexam.ca/diagnostic](https://ciroexam.ca/diagnostic) is a fast way to gauge how much study you would need.

**Q: How long does the CIRE typically take to prepare for?**
A: Plan 80 to 120 hours of structured study if you have a finance background and minimal Canadian regulatory exposure. The free [Ciroexam diagnostic](https://ciroexam.ca/diagnostic) gives you a personalized estimate based on your starting knowledge.

**Q: Is the CIRE in English only?**
A: CIRE is offered in both English and French. French-language testing is available through the regulator at the same fee.

**Q: Can I write the CIRE before I have a sponsoring firm?**
A: Yes. The exam does not require sponsorship to write. Registration with CIRO as a licensed individual does require a sponsoring firm, but holding the credential strengthens your applications.

**Q: How much does the CIRE exam cost in 2026?**
A: The CIRE registration fee through CIRO sits in the same band as the legacy CSC exam fee, around $300 to $400 per attempt. The bulk of the cost comes from study materials. Legacy CIRE prep materials list above $1,000. Independent prep platforms like Ciroexam offer the same coverage for $29.99 a month or $249 a year, which covers all nine CIRO exams.

**Q: Is the CIRE harder than the CSC was?**
A: For most candidates, yes, on the conduct side. The CIRE allocates roughly 40% of its content to regulatory conduct, AML rules, UMIR, and NI 31-103. The old CSC was more product-focused. Newcomers should plan extra study time for the conduct sections, which lean heavily on rule citations rather than concepts.

**Q: Does the CFA Charter exempt me from the CIRE?**
A: No. The CFA designation is a globally recognized investment-analysis credential, but it does not satisfy CIRO's regulatory licensing requirement. CFA charterholders working in registered roles in Canada still write the CIRE plus their role-specific exam. The CFA does, however, signal strong analytical depth on a resume and shortens the conceptual prep curve for the CIRE.

**Q: What is NOC 11103 and does it qualify for Express Entry?**
A: NOC 11103 covers Securities agents, investment dealers, and brokers. It is a TEER 1 occupation, which qualifies for the federal Skilled Worker streams under [Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html) and most Provincial Nominee Programs. Holding the CIRE plus relevant Canadian work experience strengthens both your CRS score and your eligibility for category-based draws.

The CIRO transition adds a wrinkle that even Canadian-trained candidates are still working through.

# GCMS Notes: How to Request Your IRCC File for Free in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/gcms-notes-canada-immigration-guide
Category: Refusal Recovery
Published: 2026-05-08
Author: Go Far Global Team

> How to request your GCMS notes free under the Privacy Act, how long they take, and how to read the officer notes that explain a refusal.

*As of August 3, 2026. Reviewed against IRCC's current Access to Information and Privacy guidance.*


When [Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship.html) refuses an application, the letter you receive runs to about a page. It names a regulation, says the officer was not satisfied, and stops. It does not tell you which document fell short, what the officer actually believed about your case, or what you would have to change to succeed next time.

Your GCMS notes tell you all three.

Most sites will also tell you that if you live outside Canada, you have to pay a service or lean on a Canadian friend to get those notes. That stopped being true on July 13, 2022. A regulation called the [Privacy Act Extension Order, No. 3](https://gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p2/2021/2021-07-21/html/sor-dors174-eng.html) gave foreign nationals abroad the right to request their own personal information from federal institutions directly, at no cost. Four years on, the top results for this topic still describe the old rules, and several of them sell the workaround.

This guide covers what is in the notes, how to file the free request yourself, how long it takes, and how to read what comes back.

## What are GCMS notes?

**Short answer:** The Global Case Management System (GCMS) is the internal database IRCC officers use to process every application. Your GCMS notes are a copy of the entries on your own file: the officer's written reasoning, the status of each eligibility and admissibility check, a log of the documents you submitted with the officer's assessment of each, and the correspondence sent on your file. They are the only place the full reasoning behind a decision is recorded, which is why they matter far more than the refusal letter itself.

GCMS replaced older systems that some sites still name, and it covers temporary residence, permanent residence, and citizenship files alike. The notes are written by officers for other officers, so they are terse, full of shorthand, and occasionally blunt in a way official correspondence never is.

## What is inside a GCMS package?

**Short answer:** A typical package runs 10 to 50 PDF pages. It contains your application metadata, a document-by-document checklist showing what the officer accepted or flagged, free-text officer notes recording their reasoning, the status of each background check, a decision summary, and a communication log of every letter sent to you.

The parts that decide cases are the free-text notes and the document checklist. Officer notes read like internal memos. You will see entries recording that ties to the home country appear weak, that funds appear recently deposited, or that a study plan does not follow from the applicant's education history. The checklist shows which specific document triggered that conclusion.

Redactions are normal. Information about third parties, including employers, sponsors, and family members, is withheld under the exemptions in the Act. Officers are usually identified by initials or an office code rather than by name.

## How do you get GCMS notes from IRCC for free online?

**Short answer:** File a Privacy Act request through IRCC's online portal. It is free, it takes about ten minutes, and since July 13, 2022 you can file it yourself no matter what your citizenship is or where in the world you live. You do not need a Canadian representative, and you do not need to pay a service.

The confusion comes from there being two different statutes, and most guidance pointing readers at the wrong one. The Access to Information Act costs $5 and does restrict who can file. The Privacy Act, which is the correct statute for your own personal information, costs nothing and no longer restricts who can file.

| | Privacy Act request | Access to Information Act request |
|---|---|---|
| Fee | Free | $5.00 |
| Who can file | Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and foreign nationals, regardless of where they are located | Canadian citizens, permanent residents, or an individual or corporation currently in Canada |
| Use it for | Your own personal information, which is what GCMS notes are | Institutional records, policy, statistics, or another person's file with their consent |
| Legislated response time | 30 calendar days | 30 calendar days |
| Extension limit | Maximum 30 additional days | No fixed cap |

To file your own request, go to IRCC's [Privacy Act request page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/access-information-privacy/request-privacy-act.html) and choose "Apply online." Give your full name, date of birth, and your application or Unique Client Identifier number, then describe the records you want. A request phrased as "all notes, records, correspondence and electronic data held in the Global Case Management System relating to my application" captures the file without ambiguity.

If someone files on your behalf, they must include the [Consent for an Access to Information and Personal Information Request (IMM 5744)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5744.html) for every person named on the file who is 16 or older. Note that the same form is required at 18 or older on the Access to Information side. Filing by mail is still possible using form IMM 5563, sent to the Access to Information and Privacy Division, IRCC, Ottawa, Ontario K1A 1L1, but the online route is faster and gives you a tracking number.

## What are CAIPS notes, and are they still a thing?

**Short answer:** CAIPS stood for the Computer Assisted Immigration Processing System, the visa-office system IRCC used before GCMS. It has been retired. If you see a service advertising "CAIPS notes" today, they are selling you a GCMS request under an obsolete name, because the search term still has traffic.

The distinction matters in one narrow situation. If your file is genuinely old, records from the CAIPS era may sit in archived systems, and a request worded only around GCMS could come back thinner than expected. Asking for all records held about you, rather than naming a single system, avoids that.

For anything filed in the last decade, CAIPS and GCMS notes are the same request and the same result.

## How long do GCMS notes take to arrive?

**Short answer:** The legislated deadline is 30 calendar days from the day the institution receives your request. IRCC can extend that. Under the Privacy Act the extension is capped at a further 30 days, so 60 days is the practical ceiling. In practice, straightforward requests often arrive inside a month, and files that are still actively being processed take longer.

IRCC states directly on its own guidance that increases in request volume affect its ability to meet the legislated timelines. Treat 30 days as the floor rather than the expectation, and file as soon as you have a decision rather than waiting until you have drafted a reapplication.

One timing point catches people out. Requesting your notes does not pause, delay, or prejudice an application that is still open. It is a separate process handled by a separate division, and officers are not notified that you asked.

## How do you read GCMS notes once they arrive?

**Short answer:** Read the free-text officer notes first, then match each concern back to the document checklist. The refusal reason in the notes is usually stated more plainly than in your letter, and the checklist tells you which piece of evidence produced it. Everything else in the package is context.

Officer shorthand is dense but consistent. "PA" is the principal applicant. "SA" is the spouse or accompanying dependant. "IO" or "MO" refers to the immigration or migration officer. Checks recorded against eligibility, criminality, security, and medical each carry their own status, and a file can sit for months with one of them incomplete while the rest have passed.

Read the notes against the ground cited in your letter. Temporary resident visa refusals commonly turn on paragraph 179(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, which requires the officer to be satisfied you will leave at the end of your authorized stay. Study permits turn on the equivalent test in section 216. Those provisions tell you what the officer had to decide. The notes tell you why they decided it against you.

## How do you use GCMS notes in a reapplication?

**Short answer:** Treat every concern in the notes as a question you must answer with evidence. A reapplication that repeats the original package with a longer cover letter usually fails the same way. One that identifies the specific finding, rebuts it with documents that did not exist in the first file, and explains what changed tends to succeed.

Work concern by concern. If the officer wrote that funds appeared recently deposited, six months of statements showing the source of those funds addresses it. If ties to your home country were called weak, employment records, property, and dependants speak to that directly, while a letter asserting strong ties does not. If a study plan looked inconsistent, an explanation connecting the program to your existing career answers the actual objection.

Be honest about what the notes do not support. If the officer found a material misrepresentation, that is a different problem with a five-year consequence under section 40 of the Act, and it calls for legal advice rather than a quick refile.

## When are GCMS notes not enough?

**Short answer:** The notes explain a decision. They do not overturn one. If the officer made a legal error, ignored evidence in front of them, or breached procedural fairness, the remedy is an application for leave and judicial review at the Federal Court, and there is a filing deadline measured in days rather than months.

Deadlines run from the day you receive the decision: 15 days for a decision made inside Canada, 60 days for one made outside. Waiting for GCMS notes to arrive can consume that window, so if you are considering judicial review, get advice on the deadline before your notes land, not after.

There are also files where the notes disclose very little because the decision was routine. A visitor visa refused on straightforward grounds may generate two paragraphs. That absence is itself information: it tells you nothing unusual happened and the officer simply was not persuaded.

## Where should you get help reading your notes?

Request the notes yourself. They are free, the request takes about ten minutes, and nobody needs to file it for you. Paying $30 to $80 for someone to submit a free form buys you nothing you cannot do in a browser.

Where a licensed consultant earns their fee is afterwards. Reading officer shorthand against the provision the officer actually applied, deciding whether a concern is answerable with evidence or is a misrepresentation finding that needs legal advice, and rebuilding the application so the second file answers the objection rather than repeating the first. That work starts once the notes are in front of you.

Go Far Global is a licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) firm in Toronto. If you have your notes and want to know what they mean for a reapplication, [book a consultation](/book). If you are still waiting on a decision, our [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) pages show the current published figures by program.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What are GCMS notes?

GCMS notes are the records held about your file in the Global Case Management System, the internal database Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada uses to process applications. They include the officer's free-text reasoning, the status of each eligibility and admissibility check, an assessment of each document you submitted, and a log of correspondence. A refusal letter states a conclusion in a paragraph. The notes show the reasoning that produced it, which is why applicants request them after a refusal and while a slow file is pending. You have a legal right to your own notes under the Privacy Act, and requesting them costs nothing.

### What is the purpose of GCMS notes?

The notes exist for IRCC's own operations. Officers record their assessments so that any colleague picking up the file later can see what has been decided and what remains outstanding, and so the department has a defensible record of how a decision was reached. For applicants, the practical purpose is diagnostic. Because officers write for internal readers rather than for you, the notes state concerns plainly, and that specificity is what makes a targeted reapplication possible. They are also the evidentiary foundation for a judicial review application, where the question is whether the reasoning disclosed in the record was reasonable.

### Is it worth getting GCMS notes?

After a refusal, yes, and the cost of finding out is zero. Reapplying without reading the notes means guessing at the officer's concern, and a second refusal on the same ground is common. The notes replace that guess with the officer's own words. While an application is still open, the value depends on the wait: if your file is past posted processing times, the notes will show which check is outstanding, which tells you whether the delay is a security check or simple queue depth. The one situation where they add little is a recent, ordinary refusal where the letter already names a single clear ground.

### How to get GCMS notes from IRCC for free online?

File a Privacy Act request through IRCC's online portal. There is no fee under the Privacy Act, and since the Privacy Act Extension Order, No. 3 came into force on July 13, 2022, foreign nationals outside Canada can file directly rather than going through a Canadian representative. You will need your full name, date of birth, and application or client identifier number, plus a description of the records you want. Only requests under the Access to Information Act carry the $5 fee, and that is the wrong statute for your own personal information. Paid services file the same free request on your behalf.

# Canada Immigration Levels Plan 2026 to 2028: What Actually Changed

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-immigration-levels-plan-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-05-06
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The federal government tabled the 2026 to 2028 Immigration Levels Plan in November 2025 and quietly clarified the allocations through the spring of 2026.

# Canada Immigration Levels Plan 2026 to 2028: What Actually Changed

As of May 6, 2026.

The federal government tabled the 2026 to 2028 Immigration Levels Plan in November 2025 and quietly clarified the allocations through the spring of 2026. The headline number is the one most articles run with: 380,000 permanent residents per year, the same target as 2025. The headline is misleading. What changed is the composition of who fills those 380,000 seats, and the shift is significant for anyone planning a 2026 or 2027 PR application.

The previous plan tabled in late 2024 set targets of 395,000 for 2025, 380,000 for 2026, and 365,000 for 2027. The new plan holds 2026 at 380,000, holds 2027 at 380,000 (up from 365,000), and adds 2028 at 380,000. So the trajectory has flattened, but inside that envelope Ottawa has done three things that matter: it has loaded the plan toward in-Canada applicants, it has cut Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) allocations again, and it has trimmed family sponsorship without saying much about why.

If you have been following the news cycle, you have seen the budget framing about "controlled, sustainable" growth and the political pressure on housing and healthcare capacity. None of that tells you what to do with your immigration plan. Below are the real numbers, the categories that gained, the categories that lost, and the practical decisions you should make based on where you fit.

## What are the targets in Canada’s 2026 immigration levels plan?

**Short answer:** Total 2026 PR target is 380,000, economic class ~232,000 (Federal Economic ~125,000 including Express Entry, PNP ~55,000, Atlantic ~5,000, caregivers ~17,000, business pilots ~15,000), family class ~84,000, refugees and protected persons ~58,000, humanitarian and other ~6,000.

Total permanent residence target for 2026: **380,000** ([Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) Immigration Levels Plan](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/corporate-initiatives/levels.html)).

Breakdown by class (rounded):

| Category | 2026 Target | Direction vs 2025 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Economic class total | ~232,000 | Up share, flat absolute |
| Family class total | ~84,000 | Down |
| Refugees and protected persons | ~58,000 | Roughly flat |
| Humanitarian and other | ~6,000 | Down |

Inside the economic class, the most consequential numbers:

| Economic Stream | 2026 Target | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Federal Economic (Express Entry programs) | ~125,000 | In-Canada focus tightened |
| Provincial Nominee Program | ~55,000 | Cut roughly 50% from 2024 levels |
| Atlantic Immigration Program | ~5,000 | Flat |
| Caregiver and home care pilots | ~17,000 | Increased capacity |
| Federal business and economic pilots | ~15,000 | Includes community pilots, AgriFood |

The PNP cut is the single biggest line-item change. In 2024, PNP allocations totaled roughly 110,000. The 2025 plan cut that to 55,000. The 2026 to 2028 plan keeps PNP at 55,000 every year through 2028. That is a permanent halving of the most important provincial route to PR.

## Why does the in-Canada pivot matter most for 2026 PR applicants?

**Short answer:** Ottawa explicitly commits at least 40% of new 2026 PRs to come from people already in Canada on temporary status, weighting Express Entry toward Canadian Experience Class (CEC) and category-based draws, expanding home care pilots that grant PR on arrival, favouring provincial streams that target in-province temporary workers, and using the In-Canada Workers Initiative.

Ottawa has explicitly committed to having at least 40 percent of new permanent residents in 2026 come from people already in Canada on temporary status ([Canada's Immigration Levels, IRCC](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/corporate-initiatives/levels.html)). By 2027 and 2028 the share is expected to settle in the same range. This sounds like a technical detail. It is the most important shift in Canadian immigration policy since the 2021 TR to PR pathway.

In practice:

- Express Entry draws are being weighted toward Canadian Experience Class candidates and category-based draws that benefit applicants with Canadian work experience.
- The In-Canada Workers Initiative (the renamed TR to PR fast-track) processes existing PR applications from temporary residents in smaller communities, contributing to the in-Canada count without creating a new program.
- The home care pilots, which now grant PR on arrival under qualifying offers, count as in-Canada once the applicant is here on a work permit.
- Provincial nominee streams that target temporary workers already in the province are favored over streams that draw from outside.

If you are a foreign worker outside Canada hoping to apply directly for PR, the plan is telling you something. Your competitive position has weakened. The path with the highest probability now runs through getting a work permit or study permit first, building Canadian experience, then converting from inside the country.

## Which immigration categories were cut in the 2026 plan?

**Short answer:** Cuts hit PNP (110,000 in 2024 down to 55,000 holding through 2028), family sponsorship (105,000 in 2024 to 84,000 in 2026 with no fresh PGP lottery), federal humanitarian streams (about 20% reduction), and refugee resettlement capacity pulled toward in-Canada asylum processing rather than overseas resettlement.

**Provincial Nominee Program.** From 110,000 in 2024 to 55,000 in 2026, holding at 55,000 through 2028 ([Provincial Nominee Program, IRCC](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees/works.html)). Provinces have responded by tightening their streams aggressively. BC paused most non-priority PNP intake. Ontario shifted heavily to employer-driven streams in healthcare, skilled trades, and tech. Alberta is prioritizing rural and in-demand worker categories. The net effect is fewer PNP nominations available, more competitive cutoffs, and longer waiting times for nomination.

**Family sponsorship.** The combined target across spousal, parental, and dependent child sponsorship is roughly 84,000 for 2026, down from roughly 105,000 in 2024. Spousal sponsorship intake remains the largest single line in this category and is processing closer to service standard, but parents and grandparents (PGP) intake has been minimal. The PGP lottery has not run a fresh intake since 2024, and the 2026 plan does not commit to one.

**Federal humanitarian streams.** Humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) and public-policy streams are trimmed by roughly 20 percent. Expect slower processing of H&C applications and tighter approval rates.

**Refugee resettlement.** Roughly flat in numbers, but capacity has been pulled toward in-Canada asylum claim processing rather than overseas resettlement, which means private sponsorship pipelines are moving more slowly than in 2023.

## Which streams were protected or expanded in 2026?

**Short answer:** Federal economic admissions held at ~125,000 with broadened category-based draws (healthcare, trades, French speakers, STEM, education plus 2026 additions of foreign medical doctors, researchers and senior managers, transport occupations, military recruits); caregiver pilots expanded to ~17,000 with PR on arrival; Atlantic Immigration Program flat at 5,000; French-outside-Quebec targets grow each year through 2028.

**Express Entry federal economic admissions.** Held at roughly 125,000 per year ([Express Entry: How it Works, IRCC](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/works.html)). Inside that envelope, category-based draws have continued and broadened. The 2026 categories include healthcare, trades, French speakers, STEM (with cybersecurity), education, plus the 2026 additions of foreign medical doctors, researchers and senior managers, transport occupations, and military recruits with critical skills.

| Category-Based Draw Group | When Added |
| --- | --- |
| Healthcare workers | Before 2026 |
| Skilled trades | Before 2026 |
| French-language speakers | Before 2026 |
| STEM (including cybersecurity) | Before 2026 |
| Education occupations | Before 2026 |
| Foreign medical doctors | 2026 |
| Researchers and senior managers | 2026 |
| Transport occupations | 2026 |
| Military recruits with critical skills | 2026 |

If you have a strong Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) profile and fit a category, this is the stream to focus on. [Calculate your CRS score](/tools/crs-calculator) and see which [Express Entry category fits your profile](/immigration/express-entry).

**Caregiver and home care pilots.** Capacity raised to roughly 17,000 in 2026. The new home care pilots provide PR on arrival under qualifying offers, which is the strongest direct route in the system right now for caregivers and home support workers.

**Atlantic Immigration Program.** Flat at 5,000. Employer-driven, no points test, faster processing than most PNP streams ([Atlantic Immigration Program, IRCC](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/atlantic-immigration.html)). Underused relative to its potential.

**French-speaking outside Quebec.** Francophone immigration targets are protected. The express entry French-language category continues, and IRCC has set explicit francophone PR percentage targets that grow each year through 2028. If you have Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7+ in French, your odds in 2026 are materially better than in any other category.

## What does the 2026 plan mean for different applicant profiles?

**Short answer:** Applicants abroad with strong CRS plus a category fit win category-based Express Entry draws; applicants abroad with no Canadian connection should pivot to study or work permit first; in-Canada study permit holders should target CEC plus category draws; in-Canada work permit holders may benefit from the In-Canada Workers Initiative; spousal sponsorship targets remain protected.

**You are abroad with a strong CRS profile and Canadian work experience is not realistic short-term.** Your best shot is a category-based Express Entry draw or a French-language draw if you have French. Run [a current CRS calculation](/tools/crs-calculator) and map yourself against the categories. A category-based Invitation to Apply (ITA) can clear at CRS scores well below the general draw cutoff.

**You are abroad with no Canadian connection.** Reconsider the route. Direct Federal Skilled Worker draws for general candidates are infrequent and cutoffs are high. Building a profile via study permit or Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA)-supported work permit is now the more probable path to PR within three years.

**You are in Canada on a study permit.** Finishing studies, getting a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), accumulating 12 months of skilled Canadian work experience, and entering the Express Entry pool through [Canadian Experience Class](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html) plus a category-based draw is the cleanest plan. The 2026 plan favors this profile heavily.

**You are in Canada on a work permit.** If you are in a small community and your file has been sitting in PNP, AIP, caregiver, AgriFood, or community pilot inventory, the In-Canada Workers Initiative may fast-track you. Otherwise, work the existing program that fits your situation. Express Entry CEC remains the most reliable PR route for skilled workers with Canadian experience.

**You are sponsoring a spouse.** Spousal sponsorship targets are protected at the per-year level. Processing has been close to standard. Submit clean.

**You are sponsoring parents.** No new PGP intake committed for 2026. The Super Visa remains the realistic medium-term option. [Book a consultation](/appointment) if your case has a complex history.

## How does the 2026 plan compare to 2024 actual numbers?

**Short answer:** 2024 actual vs 2026 plan, total PR landings 483,000 to 380,000 (-21%), PNP 110,000 to 55,000 (-50%), Federal Economic 110,000 to 125,000 (+14%), Family class 105,000 to 84,000 (-20%), in-Canada share ~30% to 40%+ (+33% relative); the federal economic stream is the only line that grew.

A useful cross-check is to look at what IRCC actually delivered in 2024 versus what is planned for 2026.

| Metric | 2024 Actual | 2026 Plan | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total PR landings | 483,000 | 380,000 | -21% |
| PNP allocation | 110,000 | 55,000 | -50% |
| Federal Economic | 110,000 | 125,000 | +14% |
| Family class | 105,000 | 84,000 | -20% |
| In-Canada share | ~30% | 40%+ | +33% relative |

The two-year compression has been steep. The 2024 numbers are the high water mark. 2026 is roughly 100,000 fewer PRs landed, with the cuts concentrated on PNP and family. The economic federal stream is the only line that grew.

## What are the most common questions about Canada's 2026 immigration plan?

**Short answer:** Common questions: 2026 target is 380,000 holding through 2028; composition shifted to in-Canada applicants and federal economic; PNP cut to 55,000 (half of 2024); Express Entry slightly grew with broader category draws; in-Canada focus means CEC and category draws favoured plus expanded home care pilots; targets can be revised annually each November.

The six questions below cover the most common points of confusion about Canada's 2026 to 2028 Immigration Levels Plan: what the headline 380,000 target actually means, how composition shifted away from PNP and family sponsorship, what the in-Canada focus requires, whether Express Entry gained capacity, and how often the plan can change.

**What is the 2026 Canada immigration target?**
380,000 permanent residents. The target holds at 380,000 for 2026, 2027, and 2028 under the current plan.

**How does the 2026 plan compare to 2025?**
The total target is identical at 380,000. Composition shifted: more weight on in-Canada applicants and federal economic admissions, less on Provincial Nominee Program and family sponsorship.

**Are PNP allocations being cut?**
Yes. PNP allocations are 55,000 for 2026, holding at 55,000 through 2028. That is roughly half of 2024 levels. Provinces have already tightened their streams in response.

**Is Express Entry getting more spots?**
Federal economic admissions sit at roughly 125,000 in 2026, slightly higher than 2024. Inside that, category-based draws have broadened. Profiles that fit a category have meaningfully better odds than profiles that rely on the general draw.

**What does "in-Canada focus" actually mean?**
At least 40 percent of 2026 PRs are intended to come from applicants already in Canada on a work or study permit. In practice CEC and category-based draws are favored, the home care pilots are expanded, and the In-Canada Workers Initiative fast-tracks existing PR applications from temporary residents in smaller communities.

**Will the targets change again?**
The 2026 to 2028 plan is set, but each November IRCC tables a new three-year plan that can revise upward or downward. Major shifts usually require political signaling in advance. As of May 2026, no fresh adjustment has been signaled.

## What is the bottom line for 2026 immigration applicants?

**Short answer:** The 2026 plan is not a cut at the headline level, it is a redistribution: federal economic streams and in-Canada conversion are protected priorities while PNP and family sponsorship absorb most of the reduction; if you are abroad without a category fit, start with a work or study permit; PR time horizons have lengthened 6 to 18 months versus 2024.

The 2026 plan is not a cut at the headline level. It is a redistribution. Federal economic streams and in-Canada conversion are the protected priorities. PNP and family sponsorship absorb most of the reduction. If your plan was built on a 2023 or 2024 understanding of Canadian immigration, it needs updating.

The clearest practical takeaway: if you are not already in Canada and you do not fit a category-based Express Entry draw, the most reliable medium-term route now starts with a work permit or study permit. If you are already here, the federal economic streams favor your profile more than they did two years ago. Either way, the time horizon to PR for most candidates has lengthened by 6 to 18 months compared to 2024 timelines.

If you want help mapping your profile against the 2026 plan, [book a consultation](/appointment) and we will tell you what your strongest route looks like and what the realistic timeline is.

# Canada's TR to PR 2026 Pathway Is Not What Workers Were Promised

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/tr-to-pr-2026-in-canada-workers-initiative
Category: News
Published: 2026-05-06
Author: Go Far Global Team

> The TR to PR 2026 in-Canada workers initiative is the permanent residence pathway many temporary residents have waited for.

# Canada's TR to PR 2026 Pathway Is Not What Workers Were Promised

The TR to PR 2026 in-Canada workers initiative is the permanent residence pathway many temporary residents have waited for. If you have been waiting on the new TR to PR pathway, the May 4, 2026 announcement is the answer most temporary workers were dreading. After Budget 2025 floated the idea last November, after the immigration minister said in March the pathway "had already launched" without explaining what that meant, and after April's quiet reveal that the country's three largest cities would be cut out, the government finally put numbers and rules on paper.

There is no new application stream. There is no fresh intake of temporary workers who have been sitting outside the system. The TR to PR 2026 program, now branded the **In-Canada Workers Initiative**, is a one-time, two-year exercise that fast-tracks permanent residence files that have already been submitted through programs that already existed. That is the entire program.

For workers counting on a 2021-style dedicated pathway, this is a hard landing. For people who watched the press conferences and tried to figure out where they fit, the answer in most cases is that they do not. Below is who actually qualifies, who has been left out, and what your real options are if you needed this pathway and it never arrived.

## What the In-Canada Workers Initiative Actually Does

**Short answer:** The program pulls eligible files out of the existing PR backlog and processes them faster — total target 33,000 PRs across 2026/2027 with 20,000+ in 2026; eligible files must come from five buckets: Provincial Nominee Program, Atlantic Immigration Program, community immigration pilots, caregiver pilots, or AgriFood pilot; no new application form, no new intake.

The program does one thing. It pulls eligible files out of the existing PR backlog and processes them faster. It does not create a new application form. It does not open a new intake. It does not give anyone who has not already submitted a PR application a way to apply.

The total target is up to 33,000 permanent residences across 2026 and 2027. For 2026 alone the government has committed to at least 20,000 finalized cases. Between January 1 and February 28, 2026, IRCC granted PR to 3,600 workers under the initiative. That is 18 percent of the year's target with two months gone, which is roughly the pace you would expect from any normal year of file processing. It is not clear what about this is new.

To be pulled into the fast-track, your file has to come from one of five buckets:

- The **Provincial Nominee Program (PNP)**
- The **Atlantic Immigration Program (AIP)**
- The **community immigration pilots**
- The **caregiver pilots**
- The **AgriFood pilot**

If you applied through Express Entry under FSW, CEC, or FST, you are not in the program. If you applied through the family class, you are not in it. If you have a pending Quebec PR file, you are not in it. If you are a temporary worker in any of the country's three biggest cities, you are not in it either.

## Why This Looks Like Backlog Clearance, Not a New Pathway

**Short answer:** The cleanest test of a new pathway is whether it lets anyone get PR who could not before — by that test, the Initiative is not a pathway; every recipient had already applied and was going to receive PR eventually, the program just changes the queue order to clear inventory that piled up under the PNP service-standard slippage, caregiver backlogs, and community pilot transitions.

The cleanest test of whether something is a new pathway is whether it lets anyone get PR who could not get PR before. By that test, the In-Canada Workers Initiative is not a pathway. Every person who will receive PR through this initiative had already applied. They were already going to receive PR eventually. The program changes the queue order, not the queue itself.

That is meaningful when you consider the political backdrop. Canada's PR application inventory has been heavy for two years. Processing times for PNP files have stretched well past the 18-month service standard for many provinces. Caregiver pilots have a multi-year backlog. The community immigration pilot replaced the Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot in early 2025 and inherited unprocessed files. By concentrating capacity on a defined slice of these inventories, IRCC can clear them faster, hit a clean number for the public, and report a tidy result by the end of 2027.

That is a defensible operational decision. It is not a new immigration pathway. The framing matters because temporary workers spent six months reorganizing their lives around the assumption that a real route was coming. Many turned down job changes that would have moved them out of an eligible community. Many declined offers in Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal because the original signaling suggested the pathway would treat urban workers fairly. The May 4 announcement told all of those workers that the bet did not pay off.

## Who Was Left Out

**Short answer:** Major exclusions — all 41 Census Metropolitan Area workers (Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary, Ottawa, etc.), workers without a previously submitted PR application, workers in eligible programs who applied recently (front-of-queue files clear first), Express Entry FSW/CEC/FSTP applicants, and Quebec applicants who run their own selection.

The exclusions are where the disappointment is concentrated.

**Workers in Census Metropolitan Areas (CMAs).** All 41 of Canada's CMAs are out. That includes Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary, Ottawa, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, London, Halifax, Quebec City, and every other major urban centre. If your work permit is tied to an employer in a CMA, the In-Canada Workers Initiative does not exist for you, even if you have lived in Canada for five years and built your entire life here.

**Workers without a submitted PR application.** A worker who is otherwise perfectly qualified, who has a NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 job, who speaks excellent English or French, who has Canadian work experience, but who never managed to land a PNP nomination or qualify for one of the named pilots, has no way into this program. There is no direct application.

**Workers in eligible programs who applied recently.** The fast-track applies to existing inventory. If you submitted your PNP file in late 2025 or 2026, your file goes into the pool but the people ahead of you in the queue still get processed first. Practically, this initiative will mostly clear files that were submitted in 2023 and 2024.

**Express Entry applicants.** FSW, CEC, and FST applicants are not in the program at all. The fact that category-based draws have continued in parallel does not change this. Workers using Express Entry are governed by their own draws and processing times. There is no "TR to PR" door for them.

**Quebec applicants.** Quebec runs its own selection. The federal program does not touch CSQ holders or pending Quebec files.

The program rewards a narrow profile: a worker on a work permit, in a small community, with a PR file from an eligible inventory program, submitted long enough ago to be near the front of the queue.

## What You Should Actually Do Next

**Short answer:** If you do not match the eligible profile, work routes that exist — Express Entry category-based draws (foreign doctors, researchers/managers, transport, military added for 2026 with thresholds well below general cutoffs), PNP employer-driven streams targeting in-demand NOC TEER 0-3 jobs, Atlantic Immigration Program, caregiver/home care pilots with PR on arrival, or Quebec routes; status preservation via BOWP, PGWP extension, or employer-specific switches.

If you are not in the eligible profile, stop waiting on this initiative and start working the routes that actually exist. We have written separately on most of these. Quick guide:

**Express Entry.** The category-based draws launched for 2026 added foreign medical doctors, researchers and senior managers, transport occupations, and military recruits, and continue to run for healthcare, trades, French speakers, STEM, and education. CRS thresholds for category draws are running well below general draw cutoffs. If you have Canadian work experience and a competitive profile, [calculate your CRS score](/tools/crs-calculator) and check whether [an Express Entry draw category fits you](/immigration/express-entry).

**Provincial Nominee Program.** PNP allocations were cut sharply in the 2025-2027 levels plan, but provinces still have streams open and many run employer-driven streams that do not require an Express Entry profile. Most provinces have moved aggressively toward in-demand occupations and away from low-wage workers. If you have an offer in a smaller community in a NOC TEER 0-3 job, this is still your most direct route.

**Atlantic Immigration Program.** Permanent program in the four Atlantic provinces. Employer-driven, no points test, faster processing than most PNP streams. If you can secure a designated-employer job offer, this remains one of the cleanest paths to PR.

**Caregiver pilots and Home Care Worker Immigration Pilots.** The renewed home care pilots in 2025 created a more direct route for caregivers and home care workers, with PR available on arrival under qualifying offers. If you are working in Canada as a caregiver, this is worth a fresh look.

**Quebec routes.** PEQ and the regular skilled worker stream. Different timelines, different tests. If you live and work in Quebec, your route is provincial.

If your work permit is expiring soon and none of these are realistic in time, the conversation shifts to status preservation. A bridging open work permit, a PGWP extension where eligible, or a switch to an employer-specific permit can keep you in the country while you build the profile for one of the routes above. We work through this kind of triage every week. If you are in this position, [book a consultation](/appointment) and we will tell you what your real options are and what the timeline looks like.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Short answer:** Common answers — it is not a new immigration program but a fast-track for already-submitted PNP/AIP/community/caregiver/AgriFood files; the three biggest cities (Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal) plus all 41 CMAs are excluded; total target is 33,000 across 2026/2027 with 20,000+ in 2026 and 3,600 granted by end of February; Express Entry applicants are not part of it; PNP files in non-CMA queues benefit if submitted long enough ago.

**Is the In-Canada Workers Initiative a new immigration program?**
No. It does not create a new application stream. It only fast-tracks permanent residence applications that have already been submitted through the PNP, AIP, community pilots, caregiver pilots, or AgriFood pilot. If you have not already applied through one of those programs, the initiative does not give you a way to apply.

**Why is Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal not eligible?**
The government has restricted the pathway to workers living in non-CMA communities for at least two years. The stated reason is to direct PR processing toward smaller communities that face labour shortages. Practically, this excludes all 41 of Canada's Census Metropolitan Areas, which is where most temporary workers live and work.

**How many spots are there in the TR to PR 2026 pathway?**
The total target is up to 33,000 permanent residences across 2026 and 2027 combined. For 2026 alone the target is at least 20,000. Between January 1 and February 28, 2026, IRCC reported 3,600 PRs granted under the initiative.

**What if I am in Express Entry, can I be fast-tracked?**
No. Express Entry applicants are not part of this initiative. FSW, CEC, and FST processing continues under standard service standards and the regular draw schedule. [Current processing times](/immigration/processing-times) for Express Entry are governed by the stream you applied under.

**My PR application is in the PNP queue and I live in a small town. Does this help me?**
Likely yes, if your file was submitted long enough ago to be near the front of the inventory IRCC is processing. The initiative pulls eligible files out of the existing queue and finalizes them faster. It does not change the eligibility of your underlying PR application.

**What should I do if I was waiting on this program and I do not qualify?**
Reset on the routes that exist today. Express Entry category-based draws, PNP employer-driven streams, AIP, the home care pilots, and Quebec routes are still open. The faster you map your profile to a real program, the better your timeline looks. If you are not sure where you fit, [book a consultation](/appointment) and we will work through your options.

## Bottom Line

**Short answer:** The In-Canada Workers Initiative is a backlog management tool — for the small group with PR files in eligible inventory, faster processing is useful; for everyone else (especially temporary workers in Canada largest cities who built their lives here), this announcement closes a door rather than opening one; plan around the immigration system as it actually exists, not budget announcements that shift over months.

The In-Canada Workers Initiative is a backlog management tool. For the small group of applicants whose PR files are already sitting in the eligible inventory, faster processing is useful. For everyone else, including temporary workers in Canada's largest cities who built their lives here on the implicit promise of a real new pathway, this announcement closes the door rather than opening one.

Plan around the immigration system as it actually exists, not around what gets announced in a budget and shaped over six months of partial signals. Pick a real program, build the profile it asks for, and submit the application. If you need help mapping that out, [book a consultation](/appointment) with our team.

# Study Permit Document Number Canada: Where to Find It on IMM 1442

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-study-permit-number
Category: Immigration Guides
Published: 2026-05-02
Author: Maggi Issa

> If you hold a Canadian study permit, you have several different identification numbers on your immigration paperwork and figuring out which one is "the document number" takes a minute.

# Study Permit Document Number Canada: Where to Find It on IMM 1442

*As of September 3, 2026.*

The study permit document number is the number printed on the issued permit, not your application number and not your Unique Client Identifier (UCI). Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) puts it on the study permit itself (form IMM 1442). Schools, banks, and later permit forms ask for it. This page shows where it sits, how it differs from a UCI, and when you actually need it.

## TL;DR

The study permit document number is printed on IMM 1442, usually top-right, as a letter plus 9 digits (often F then nine numbers) | It is not the UCI and not the application number that starts while the file is in process | UCI format is 0000-0000 or 00-0000-0000 | IRCC does not publish a labelled diagram of the permit | You need the document number to extend, change schools, apply for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), or fill school enrolment forms

## What is a study permit number?

**Short answer:** People say "study permit number" when they mean the document number on the current study permit. It is the identifier IRCC printed on that IMM 1442. It changes if IRCC issues a new permit. It is not your UCI, which stays with you across files. It is not the application number you used while IRCC was still processing. IRCC's [study permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html) pages describe the permit. They do not host a separate "document number" explainer. Read the paper or PDF permit in front of you.

If a form asks for "document number" or "permit number," use the number on IMM 1442. If it asks for UCI or client ID, use the UCI. Mixing those two is a common reason a school portal or an IRCC form rejects the file.

## What is the IMM 1442 document number?

**Short answer:** IMM 1442 is the study permit document. The document number is the unique code IRCC printed on that form when the permit was issued. On issued permits it is typically one letter plus nine digits, for example F123456789, in the top-right block. The same string is often repeated lower on the page. IRCC has not published a public spec that locks the first letter to F for every year and every office. Treat the number on your own permit as the source, not a blog example. If you only have a PDF in your IRCC account, open that PDF. The layout matches the paper copy.

Do not pull a number from a visa counterfoil in your passport unless the form specifically asks for a visa number. A visitor visa or a study visa sticker is a different document.

| Number | Where it lives | Does it change? |
|---|---|---|
| Study permit document number | IMM 1442, usually top-right | Yes, with each new permit |
| Unique Client Identifier (UCI) | Same permit, plus other IRCC letters | No, it stays with you |
| Application number | IRCC account while the file is in process | Each application has its own |

## Where is Canada's study permit document number?

**Short answer:** Look at the top-right of the issued study permit. That is the same corner Seneca Polytechnic tells students to use when they enter permit data, and it matches the live IMM 1442 layout. If you cannot find the paper, sign in to your IRCC account and download the permit PDF. The document number is on the permit, not on the letter of acceptance you uploaded when you first applied. IRCC's [get the right documents](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/get-documents.html) page is about what you send in. It is not a map of the finished permit.

If the top-right is smudged, check the repeated number near the bottom of the same page. Do not invent a number from your UCI by deleting hyphens. Those are different identifiers.

## How is a study permit document number different from a UCI?

**Short answer:** A UCI is your unique client identifier, also called a client identification number or client ID. IRCC's help page [What is a UCI?](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=013&top=4) says it appears on official documents and has either four numbers, a hyphen, and four more numbers (0000-0000) or two numbers, a hyphen, four, a hyphen, and four more (00-0000-0000). First-time applicants who do not have a UCI yet write "Not Applicable" or "N/A," or leave the field blank if the online form blocks N/A. The study permit document number is longer, has no hyphens in the usual printout, and belongs to that permit only.

Work permits use the same document-number idea on their own IMM form. If a portal asks for a work permit document number, use [Canada work permit document number](/news/canada-work-permit-number), not the study permit code.

## When do you need a study permit document number?

**Short answer:** You need it when a form asks for the current permit's document number. Typical uses: school enrolment, a Social Insurance Number (SIN) interview, a [change of schools](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html) file, a study-permit extension, or a [Post-Graduation Work Permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html) application. Banks and landlords sometimes ask for it as well. They want the number on the permit you hold today.

If IRCC is still processing your first study permit, you do not have a document number yet. Use the application number in the account until the permit is issued. Application packages for students in Canada are listed on IRCC's [study permit application](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/information/applications/student.asp) page.

We are Go Far Global, a licensed Canadian immigration firm. If a school or IRCC form is rejecting the number you entered, [book a consultation](/book) and bring a photo of the full IMM 1442, including the top-right block.

Keep a colour scan of both sides (or the full PDF). You will need the same number again when the permit is close to expiry.

# Study in Canada from Brazil 2026: Complete Guide for Brazilian Students

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/study-canada/study-canada-from-brazil-complete-2026-guide
Category: Education
Published: 2026-05-02
Author: Maggi Issa

> Brazil is one of the fastest-growing source markets for Canadian study permits in 2026.

Brazil is one of the fastest-growing source markets for Canadian study permits in 2026. About 30,000 Brazilian students currently hold Canadian study permits, up from around 18,000 in 2022, with strong year-over-year growth driven by interest in IT, healthcare, and trades programs. The São Paulo visa office processes most Brazilian files within 6-12 weeks, faster than the global average. Brazilian applicants benefit from one of the highest study permit approval rates in Latin America (around 75-80%).

This guide covers the full pathway in 2026: which schools and programs realistically lead to PR, the proof-of-funds requirements (challenging given the BRL/CAD exchange context), São Paulo visa office timelines, IELTS vs. Duolingo for Brazilian applicants, and the post-graduation path through PGWP into Express Entry, a Provincial Nominee Program, or Quebec's PEQ. For case-specific guidance, [book a consultation](/appointment).

## Where Brazilian students actually apply

**Short answer:** Brazilian applicants favour IT/computer science, healthcare diplomas, and skilled trades — Tier 1 universities (U of T, McGill, UBC, McMaster, Western) cost $50,000 to $70,000 with selective admission; affordable Tier 2 universities (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Memorial, Regina, Brandon) run $15,000 to $25,000; most Brazilians go to Ontario, BC, and Alberta public colleges at $15,000 to $22,000; Quebec institutions (UdeM, McGill, Concordia, UQAM, CEGEPs) offer the lowest international tuition plus the PEQ pathway.

Brazilian applicants disproportionately favor three program categories: information technology and computer science, healthcare-related diplomas, and skilled trades (electrical, welding, plumbing). Patterns in our Brazilian client files:

**Universities (less common for Brazilian applicants):** University of Toronto, McGill, UBC, McMaster, Western. International tuition $50,000-$70,000 CAD per year. Selective admission, typically requiring strong ENEM scores plus IELTS/TOEFL.

**Affordable universities (growing in popularity):** University of Manitoba, University of Saskatchewan, Memorial University, University of Regina, Brandon University. Tuition $15,000-$25,000 CAD per year. Strong PR pathways through provincial nominee programs.

**Public colleges in Ontario, BC, Alberta:** Seneca, Centennial, Humber, Conestoga (Ontario), BCIT and Vancouver Community College (BC), SAIT and NAIT (Alberta), Algonquin (Ontario). Two-year diplomas at $15,000-$22,000 CAD. This is where most Brazilian applicants actually go: strong PGWP pathway, hands-on programs, lower cost.

**Quebec institutions:** Université de Montréal, McGill, Concordia, UQAM, plus CEGEPs. Quebec is a major destination for Brazilian applicants because of cultural similarities and the Quebec PEQ pathway to PR. Quebec tuition for international students is among the lowest in Canada ($16,000-$24,000 CAD per year), and Brazilian students who learn intermediate-level French gain access to the PEQ.

The 2024-2026 PGWP field-of-study update narrowed which college programs qualify. Many short-duration college programs popular with Brazilian applicants (English-as-a-second-language paired with diplomas) no longer qualify. Confirm any college program against the [PGWP-eligible list](/study-canada/pgwp-eligible-colleges-canada-2026) before depositing tuition.

## Study permit from Brazil: timeline and process

**Short answer:** São Paulo visa office covers all of Brazil, applying the 2024 PAL requirement — total realistic timeline from admission to landing is 4 to 6 months; biometrics happen at VFS Global locations in São Paulo, Rio, Brasília, Recife, or Porto Alegre; Student Direct Stream (SDS) reduces processing to 4 to 6 weeks if you meet SDS criteria.

Brazilian applicants apply through the São Paulo visa office (covers all of Brazil). The 2024 Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) requirement applies. Your Canadian school requests it from the province, and the PAL must be included with the study permit application.

| Stage | Timeline |
|---|---|
| Receive admission offer | starting point |
| Pay tuition deposit | 0-2 weeks after offer |
| School requests PAL | 1-3 weeks |
| PAL issued | 2-6 weeks after school request |
| Open IRCC online account | same day |
| Submit study permit application with PAL | 1 day after PAL |
| Biometrics at VFS Global (São Paulo, Rio, Brasília, Recife, Porto Alegre) | 1-3 weeks after submission |
| Medical exam (panel physician in Brazil) | 1-2 weeks |
| Decision | 6-10 weeks after biometrics |
| Passport submission for visa stamp | 1-2 weeks |
| Visa returned, travel | 1-2 weeks |

**Total realistic timeline: 4-6 months from admission offer to landing in Canada.** Brazilian applicants benefit from the **Student Direct Stream (SDS)**. Brazil is one of the SDS-eligible countries, which can reduce processing time to 4-6 weeks if you meet the SDS criteria (specific GIC, language test minimums, tuition fully paid).

## Proof of funds for Brazilian applicants

**Short answer:** Proof of funds runs $35,000 to $50,000 for college and $70,000 to $100,000 for university; accepted formats include a $20,635 CAD GIC at Scotiabank/CIBC/RBC, 6+ months of Brazilian bank statements (Banco do Brasil, Itaú, Bradesco, Santander Brasil, BTG Pactual), notarized parental sponsor letters with Receita Federal tax records, and education loans from Itaú, Bradesco, or Santander.

IRCC requires proof of first-year tuition plus first-year living expenses ($20,635 CAD for a single student outside Quebec, slightly different for Quebec). For a typical college student, that totals $35,000-$50,000 CAD; for a university student, $70,000-$100,000 CAD.

Brazilian applicants face a specific challenge: the BRL/CAD exchange rate has weakened significantly since 2020, making the funds requirement feel larger in BRL terms. Acceptable proof:

**GIC of $20,635 CAD** at a Canadian bank (Scotiabank StartRight is the most popular for Brazilian applicants, also CIBC, RBC). The GIC is purchased in CAD before the visa application and released to you in monthly installments after landing. For SDS applicants, the GIC is a hard requirement.

**Brazilian bank statements** showing 6+ months of consistent balances. Banco do Brasil, Itaú, Bradesco, Santander Brasil, BTG Pactual all acceptable. Visa officers in São Paulo are generally less suspicious of Brazilian bank statements than they would be for Indian or Chinese applicants. The standard 6-month consistency check applies.

**Sponsor documents from parents** if parents are funding:
- Notarized parental sponsor letter
- Parents' bank statements (6 months)
- Parents' employment letters with monthly salary
- Parents' tax records (Receita Federal Imposto de Renda)
- Real estate deeds optional but strengthens the file

**Education loans** from Brazilian banks. Itaú, Bradesco, and Santander offer Canada-bound education loans, though approval rates have tightened since 2023.

**SDS specifically requires** the $20,635 GIC plus the tuition paid in full to the school before the application. This pre-payment is the trade-off for the faster processing.

## Language tests: IELTS, Duolingo, and the SDS requirement

**Short answer:** University needs IELTS 6.5 overall (no band below 6.0), college 6.0 (no band below 5.5); SDS specifically requires IELTS Academic 6.0 in each band (or PTE 60 or TOEFL 83) and does not accept Duolingo; Duolingo English Test ($59 USD) works for non-SDS applications; PGWP requires CLB 7 (university) or CLB 5 (college) via IELTS General or CELPIP.

Most Canadian institutions require:

- **University**: IELTS 6.5 overall (no band below 6.0), TOEFL iBT 86, or PTE Academic 60
- **College**: IELTS 6.0 overall (no band below 5.5), TOEFL iBT 80, or PTE Academic 50
- **Pathway programs**: IELTS 5.0-5.5 with conditional admission

**For SDS specifically:** IELTS Academic with 6.0 in each band, or PTE Academic 60 in each component, or TOEFL iBT 83. Duolingo is **not accepted for SDS.** This is the trade-off for the faster processing.

**Duolingo English Test** is accepted by most institutions for non-SDS applications and is much cheaper ($59 USD vs. ~$1,200 BRL for IELTS in Brazil). If you don't need SDS speed, Duolingo is fine.

For the post-graduation PGWP test (November 2024 rule):
- **University graduates** need CLB 7 (IELTS General 6.0 in each band)
- **College/trades graduates** need CLB 5 (IELTS General 5.0 in each band)
- Test must be valid (within 2 years) at PGWP application time

For Brazilian applicants going to Quebec, French test requirements (TEF, TEFAQ) layer on top, especially for the PEQ pathway.

## After graduation: PGWP, Express Entry, PNP, and the Quebec PEQ

**Short answer:** PR options after PGWP — Express Entry CEC (~12 to 18 months with 1 year skilled Canadian work, CRS ~514 in April 2026), PNP graduate streams (~18 to 30 months, Manitoba and Atlantic favour trades and healthcare), Quebec PEQ with TEFAQ B2 French (~24 to 36 months, used by 25 to 30% of Brazilian-origin PR pathways), and TR to PR 2026 for non-CMA workers.

The PGWP is what makes Canadian education a PR pathway. To qualify:

1. Complete a full-time program of at least 8 months at a Designated Learning Institution (DLI)
2. Graduate from a PGWP-eligible program
3. Hold valid status throughout your studies
4. Apply within 180 days of graduation
5. Take a language test at the right CLB level

PGWP validity matches your program length, capped at 3 years.

PR pathway options for Brazilian-origin graduates:

**Path A: Express Entry CEC (~12-18 months from PGWP start to PR).** Work full-time in any skilled occupation (NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3) for 1 year, then apply through Canadian Experience Class. CEC draws cut off around CRS 514 in April 2026.

**Path B: Provincial Nominee Program (~18-30 months).** Most provinces have international graduate streams. Brazilian graduates do particularly well in Manitoba MPNP and Atlantic AIP because those programs prioritize trades and healthcare workers, exactly the categories most Brazilian college graduates fall into. PNP nomination adds 600 CRS points.

**Path C: Quebec PEQ (the Brazilian sweet spot, 24-36 months).** If you study in Quebec and pass French at intermediate level (TEFAQ B2), you can apply through the Programme de l'expérience québécoise. Brazilian applicants have a measurable advantage learning French because Portuguese and French are both Romance languages with overlapping vocabulary and grammar. About 25-30% of Brazilian PR pathways through Canadian education go through PEQ rather than Express Entry.

**Path D: TR to PR 2026.** The TR to PR 2026 pathway gives 33,000 spots but excludes the 41 Census Metropolitan Areas. If you graduated and then took a job in a non-CMA community, you qualify for [TR to PR 2026](/news/canada-tr-to-pr-pathway-33000-workers-2026).

Brazilian-origin graduates tend to receive PR within 4-6 years of starting their studies, with PEQ-track Quebec graduates often achieving PR fastest.

## Special considerations for Brazilian applicants

**Short answer:** São Paulo approves 75 to 80% of Brazilian study permits — common refusals cite insufficient home-country ties, funds genuineness (large unexplained deposits), and weak program rationale; address directly in the study plan letter with family business, return-employment, or multinational career framing; ENEM scores are accepted for most universities with notarized translation.

**Approval rates.** The São Paulo visa office approves around 75-80% of Brazilian study permit applications, one of the highest rates among Latin American countries. Common refusal reasons:

1. **Insufficient ties to home country** (the perennial visa officer concern, even though the actual policy aim is to retain skilled graduates)
2. **Funds genuineness** (sudden large deposits, inconsistent banking history)
3. **Program rationale weak** (the visa officer questions why this specific Canadian program over options in Brazil)

**The "ties to home country" framing.** Brazilian applicants should address this directly in the study plan letter. Acceptable framings: family business that requires Canadian-trained skills, plan to return to a specific Brazilian employer post-graduation, family obligations in Brazil, plan to work in a multinational that values North American education.

**ENEM scores.** Most Canadian universities accept ENEM as evidence of secondary completion, though they will request a notarized translation. Some U15 universities require additional credential evaluation through WES or ICAS.

**Visiting family during studies.** Brazilian citizens require a visitor visa to enter Canada. Visitor visa processing from São Paulo is currently 60-90 days. Apply 4-6 months before intended visit.

**Spouse and family options.** Common-law partners are recognized in Canada (12 months of cohabitation). Bringing a spouse on an open work permit is straightforward if your principal study permit is at the master's level or above; for college and bachelor-level studies, the spousal open work permit option was tightened in 2024.

## What we handle as RCICs

**Short answer:** Hire an RCIC for refusal recovery on a second application, family applications with the new 2024 spousal restrictions, PR pathway planning combining school + province + program, PEQ Quebec-system applications layered on federal IRCC, and PGWP eligibility verification on specific college programs under the 2024-2026 field-of-study rules.

Most Brazilian study permit applications can be self-managed through the IRCC online portal. Consider hiring an RCIC for:

- **Refusal recovery** if you've been refused once
- **Family applications** (spouse open work permit, children as accompanying minors, particularly the new 2024 spousal restrictions)
- **PR pathway planning**: choosing the school, province, and program combination that maximizes PR chances
- **PEQ applications**: the Quebec system is layered on top of federal IRCC and has its own paperwork
- **PGWP eligibility verification**: confirming a college program qualifies under the 2024-2026 field-of-study rules before you commit

[Book a free consultation](/appointment) to map out the right pathway before you commit to a school.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long does a study permit from Brazil take in 2026?**
São Paulo visa office processing is typically 6-10 weeks from biometrics to decision. Add 4-6 months total from admission offer to landing in Canada. Student Direct Stream (SDS) reduces processing to 4-6 weeks if you meet the SDS criteria.

**Can I apply through SDS as a Brazilian?**
Yes. Brazil is on the SDS-eligible country list. Requirements: GIC of $20,635 CAD, IELTS Academic 6.0 in each band (or PTE/TOEFL equivalent), tuition paid in full to the school. Duolingo is not accepted for SDS.

**Do I need to learn French to study in Quebec?**
You can study in English at McGill or Concordia without French. To benefit from the Quebec PEQ pathway to PR, you need TEFAQ B2 in French. Many Brazilian students take a year of French while studying to unlock PEQ.

**What is the cheapest way to study in Canada from Brazil?**
Two-year college diplomas in smaller provinces (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Atlantic Canada) at $15,000-$22,000 CAD per year tuition, plus the $20,635 CAD GIC. Total first-year cost around $35,000-$45,000 CAD. Strong PGWP eligibility and provincial nominee pathways follow graduation.

**Is the Brazilian high school diploma accepted by Canadian universities?**
Yes. The Ensino Médio diploma plus ENEM scores are accepted by most Canadian institutions. For competitive U15 programs, you may also need TOEFL/IELTS and supplementary application materials. Some universities request a credential evaluation from WES or ICAS.

**Can my Brazilian common-law partner come with me?**
Yes, if the relationship qualifies as common-law (12 months of continuous cohabitation). Common-law partners can apply for an open work permit if your principal study permit is at master's level or above. For undergraduate or college studies, the 2024 spousal restriction limits eligibility.

**Is Quebec a better choice than Ontario for Brazilian applicants?**
It depends on language goals. Quebec offers lower tuition, the PEQ pathway, cultural fit (especially in São Paulo or southern Brazil where Portuguese-French linguistic transfer is faster), and smaller Brazilian community competition. Ontario offers more program variety, larger Brazilian communities, and broader employer markets. Many Brazilian students choose Quebec for cost and PEQ access.
