# How to Apply to Canadian Universities as an International Student in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/study-canada/how-to-apply-canadian-universities-international-students
Category: Education
Published: 2026-04-28
Author: Maggi Issa

> Applying to Canadian universities as an international student requires planning, clear deadlines, and understanding the different application systems depending on which province you...

As of July 4, 2026.

Applying to a Canadian university as an international student is a sequence, not a single step, and missing one piece can cost you a whole intake. This guide walks you through choosing a school, meeting the admission requirements, hitting the deadlines, and turning your acceptance letter into a study permit.

## TL;DR

**Apply in this order: pick a Designated Learning Institution (DLI), meet the admission requirements, apply before the intake deadline, get your Letter of Acceptance, then apply for a study permit.** | Most programs have September, January, and May intakes, and you should apply roughly 8 to 12 months ahead. | You need a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) from the province for most study permit applications since 2024. | Your study permit requires proof of funds separate from tuition: CAD $22,895 in living expenses for a single applicant outside Quebec.

## How do you apply to a Canadian university as an international student?

To apply to a Canadian university as an international student, first choose a program at a Designated Learning Institution (DLI), then submit the school's application with your transcripts, English test results, and any required essays before the intake deadline. Once you are accepted, the university issues a Letter of Acceptance, which you use to apply for a study permit from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). The university admission and the study permit are two separate applications, and you must be accepted first.

## What are the admission requirements for Canadian universities?

Admission requirements vary by university and program, but international undergraduate applicants almost always need academic transcripts, proof of English or French language ability, and sometimes a statement of purpose and references. Competitive programs set higher grade and test-score thresholds.

- Academic transcripts, often with a credential evaluation for non-Canadian schooling
- English proof through IELTS, TOEFL, or an equivalent accepted test
- A statement of purpose for many programs
- Letters of reference for graduate and competitive programs
- Program-specific items such as a portfolio or entrance exam

## When should you apply to study in Canada?

You should apply roughly 8 to 12 months before your intended start date, because Canadian universities run multiple intakes and study permit processing takes time. Most schools offer a September (fall) intake, and many add January (winter) and May (spring) intakes with fewer program options.

| Intake | Typical application window |
|---|---|
| September (fall) | October to March of the prior year |
| January (winter) | June to September of the prior year |
| May (spring) | October to January |

## What is a DLI and why does it matter?

A Designated Learning Institution (DLI) is a school approved by a Canadian province or territory to host international students. You can only apply for a study permit if your Letter of Acceptance comes from a DLI, so confirming a school's DLI status is the first thing to check before you apply. Studying at a non-DLI means you cannot get a study permit, and it can also affect your eligibility for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) later.

## What happens after you get your Letter of Acceptance?

Once you have your Letter of Acceptance from a DLI, you request a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) from the province, then apply for your study permit with your proof of funds. The PAL has been required for most study permit applications since 2024, and without it IRCC will usually return the application. Your study permit file also needs financial evidence, so review the exact amounts in our guide to [study permit proof of funds](/news/canada-study-permit-proof-of-funds-2026), and budget for [tuition](/study-canada/tuition-fees-canadian-universities-international-2026) and living costs on top.

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I apply to a Canadian university from abroad?**
Choose a program at a Designated Learning Institution, submit the university's application with transcripts and English test results before the deadline, and once accepted, use your Letter of Acceptance to apply for a study permit.

**Do I need a study permit and a university acceptance separately?**
Yes. The university admission and the IRCC study permit are two different applications. You must be accepted by a DLI first, then apply for the study permit with that Letter of Acceptance.

**How early should I apply to study in Canada?**
About 8 to 12 months before your start date, so you have time for admission decisions, a Provincial Attestation Letter, and study permit processing.

**What is a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL)?**
A PAL is a letter from the province confirming you are counted under its study permit allocation. Most study permit applicants have needed one since 2024, and IRCC returns applications submitted without it when it is required.

## Getting your application in on time

Applying to a Canadian university comes down to sequence and timing: pick a DLI, meet the requirements, apply early, get your Letter of Acceptance, secure a PAL, and file a study permit backed by real proof of funds. Miss the order or the deadline and you wait for the next intake. As a licensed Canadian immigration firm, we help students line up the admission and the study permit together so nothing stalls. If you want help planning your application, book a consultation with our team.

# CELPIP Test Canada 2026: Score Chart, Booking, and CLB Conversion

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/celpip-test-canada-immigration-guide-2026
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-04-28
Author: Maggi Issa

> The CELPIP test is Canada's fastest English language test for immigration.

*Reviewed and updated May 2026 against current Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) guidance.*

# CELPIP Test Canada 2026: Complete Score Chart and Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) Conversion Guide

The CELPIP test is Canada's fastest English language test for immigration. Owned by Prometric Canada and built specifically for Canadian immigration, it's [accepted by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/language-test.html) for Express Entry, skilled worker programs, and citizenship applications. This guide covers the test format, 2026 fees, scoring, retake rules, and the CLB score you need for permanent residence.

*As of April 28, 2026.*

## What Is CELPIP?

**Short answer:** CELPIP is the Canadian English Language Proficiency Index Program, an IRCC-recognized English test administered by Prometric Canada (Paragon Testing Enterprises). It was developed at the University of British Columbia and is the fastest English test accepted for Express Entry and PR applications.

CELPIP stands for Canadian English Language Proficiency Index Program. Developed originally at the University of British Columbia, it's now administered by Prometric Canada (Paragon Testing Enterprises). Unlike IELTS, which is used globally, CELPIP is built for Canada and tests Canadian English in real-world scenarios.

The CELPIP test measures your ability to listen, read, write, and speak English. Each skill receives its own score on a scale of 1 to 12, which converts directly to a Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) level. CELPIP 8 equals CLB 8 with no conversion table needed, which saves you a step compared to IELTS.

## CELPIP General vs CELPIP-LS: Which One Do You Need?

**Short answer:** CELPIP General covers all four skills (Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking) and is used for Express Entry, Federal Skilled Worker, Canadian Experience Class, Provincial Nominee Program (PNP), and most PR streams. CELPIP-LS covers only Listening and Speaking and is used for citizenship applications. Pick the wrong one and you waste the test fee.

CELPIP comes in two versions, and picking the wrong one wastes your test fee.

**CELPIP General** is the full test covering all four skills: Listening, Reading, Writing, and Speaking. It's used for:
- Express Entry applications
- Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP)
- Canadian Experience Class (CEC)
- Skilled trades
- Permanent residence applications
- Work permits requiring language proof

**CELPIP-LS (Listening and Speaking)** tests only two skills and is used exclusively for [Canadian citizenship applications](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility.html). If you're already a permanent resident and applying for citizenship, you may use CELPIP-LS instead of taking the full test.

For immigration purposes, nearly all applicants need CELPIP General, not LS.

## What Is the CELPIP Test Format and How Long Does It Take?

**Short answer:** CELPIP General is fully computer-based and runs approximately 3 hours (plan 3.5-4 hours including check-in) in one sitting. Listening 47-55 minutes, Reading 55-60 minutes, Writing 53-60 minutes, Speaking 15-20 minutes. The test is proctored throughout at an official test centre.

CELPIP General is fully computer-based and takes approximately 3 hours. You'll complete all four sections in one sitting at an official test centre. Plan for 3.5 to 4 hours total, including check-in.

**Listening** (47-55 minutes): You listen to conversations and recorded material, then answer multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank questions. The section includes six distinct parts covering conversations, interviews, and announcements.

**Reading** (60 minutes): You read passages on various topics and answer multiple-choice questions. Topics are Canadian-focused, covering workplace scenarios, community information, and instructional texts.

**Writing** (53 minutes): You complete two writing tasks. Task 1 is an email (formal or informal, depending on the prompt). Task 2 is a longer written response covering topics like persuasive writing or narrative essays.

**Speaking** (15-20 minutes): You speak into a microphone and respond to eight different speaking tasks. You read prompts on screen and have time to prepare. Speaking tasks range from personal descriptions to opinion-based responses.

The entire test is proctored. A test administrator monitors you via camera throughout.

## How Does Your CELPIP Score Convert to a CLB Level?

**Short answer:** CELPIP scores convert directly to CLB levels: CELPIP 4 = CLB 4, CELPIP 5 = CLB 5, and so on through CELPIP 12 = CLB 12. No additional math required, unlike IELTS where General Training scores follow a separate conversion table.

Your CELPIP score converts directly to a CLB level with no additional math required. Each skill receives its own score on the 1-to-12 scale: a score of 7 maps to CLB 7, a score of 9 maps to CLB 9, and so on. Unlike IELTS General Training, where band scores require a separate conversion chart, CELPIP scores correspond to CLB levels on a one-to-one basis. Your overall CLB level is determined by your lowest score across all four skills.

| CELPIP Score | CLB Level | IELTS General Training (Approximate) |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | CLB 4 | 3.5 to 4.0 |
| 5 | CLB 5 | 4.5 to 5.0 |
| 6 | CLB 6 | 5.5 to 6.0 |
| 7 | CLB 7 | 6.5 to 7.0 |
| 8 | CLB 8 | 7.5 to 8.0 |
| 9 | CLB 9 | 8.0 to 8.5 |
| 10 | CLB 10 | 8.5 to 9.0 |
| 11 | CLB 11 | 9.0 to 9.5 |
| 12 | CLB 12 | 9.0+ |

Important: You receive a score for each skill (Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking). Your overall CLB level is your lowest score across the four skills. If you score 10 in Listening, 10 in Reading, 9 in Writing, and 10 in Speaking, your CLB level is 9 (the lowest skill). This matters for Express Entry because programs have minimum requirements in all four skills.

## How Many CRS Points Does Your CELPIP Score Earn?

**Short answer:** Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points give language the heaviest weight in Express Entry. CLB 9 in all four skills earns 32 single-applicant CRS points or 29 with spouse points per skill. CLB 10+ earns 34/32. CLB 7 earns 17/16, the minimum for [Federal Skilled Worker](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/federal-skilled-workers.html). Pushing from CLB 7 to CLB 9 typically adds 60-100 total CRS once second-language and skill-transferability bonuses are included.

CELPIP scores translate to [Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html) for Express Entry as follows:

| CLB Level | Single Applicant (all 4 skills) | With Spouse (all 4 skills) |
|---|---|---|
| CLB 5 | 15 points | 5 points |
| CLB 6 | 21 points | 9 points |
| CLB 7 | 68 points | 29 points |
| CLB 8 | 92 points | 40 points |
| CLB 9 | 124 points | 55 points |
| CLB 10 | 136 points | 59 points |

Language carries the heaviest weight in Express Entry's CRS. A single applicant with CLB 10 across all four skills earns 136 points from language alone. Education tops out at 150 points, work experience and age each cap at 100. Strong language scores move you up the pool faster than any other input you can change.

Check your Express Entry CRS score with our [CRS Calculator tool](/tools/crs-calculator).

## How Much Does CELPIP Cost in Canada in 2026?

**Short answer:** CELPIP General costs $290 CAD plus tax in Canada in 2026; CELPIP-LS costs $195 CAD plus tax. Express Rating (results in 1-2 days instead of 2-4 business days) adds $100. Pricing varies by country when booking outside Canada.

CELPIP General costs $290 CAD (plus tax) in Canada as of 2026. Pricing varies by country when booking outside Canada. When you register on celpip.ca, the fee shows in your local currency.

**CELPIP-LS** costs $195 CAD (plus tax).

**Optional add-ons:**
- Express Rating ($100): Get your results in 1 to 2 calendar days instead of the standard 2 to 4 business days
- Rescheduling ($100): Reschedule your test if you need to postpone

**Cancellation and refunds:** If you cancel 7 or more days before your test date, you receive a 50% refund of the registration fee.

Payment is accepted via credit card, debit card, prepaid Visa/Mastercard, and money orders through the CELPIP booking website.

## How Do You Book a CELPIP Test Date?

**Short answer:** Book at celpip.ca for test dates in Canada (multiple weekly dates in major cities) and in partner countries including India, UAE, Australia, and select others. CELPIP is not available in Iran; Iranian applicants typically book in UAE or Turkey.

Visit celpip.ca to find available test dates in your location. CELPIP test centres operate across Canada and in many other countries, including India, UAE, Australia, and select other locations. Iranian applicants cannot take CELPIP in Iran; the nearest options are Dubai, Istanbul, or other regional centres.

Book 4 to 6 weeks in advance if possible. Test slots fill quickly, especially in major cities.

**Important:** You cannot register for more than one test session within a 5-calendar-day period. If you want to retake the test, you must wait at least 4 calendar days between test dates.

## Is CELPIP Valid for 2 Years and What Is the Retake Policy?

**Short answer:** Minimum 4 calendar days between tests, but because you can only register one test per 5-day period the practical minimum is 5 days between bookings. Scores are valid for 2 years from the test date for IRCC purposes.

If you don't achieve the score you need, you can retake CELPIP. The minimum wait is 4 calendar days between tests. However, because you can only register for one test per 5-day period, the practical minimum is 5 calendar days between bookings.

Your CELPIP score remains valid for 2 years from the test date. For [Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/works.html), your score must be valid on the day you submit your profile and when you receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA).

## When Are CELPIP Results Released?

**Short answer:** Standard results: online in 2-4 business days. Express Rating: 1-2 calendar days for an additional $100. Both arrive electronically through your CELPIP account, and you can send official copies directly to IRCC from the same dashboard. Business days exclude weekends and Canadian statutory holidays.

CELPIP results are released faster than most English language tests accepted by IRCC. The standard scoring turnaround is 2 to 4 business days from your test date. If you need results sooner, the Express Rating option delivers scores in 1 to 2 calendar days for an additional fee of $100. Once your results are ready, CELPIP emails you a notification and you access the official score report through your CELPIP account. You can send an official copy directly to IRCC from the same portal without requesting a separate paper report.

- **Standard:** Results available online in 2 to 4 business days after your test
- **Express Rating:** Results available in 1 to 2 calendar days (additional $100 fee)

You'll receive an email notification when your scores are ready. Business days do not include weekends or Canadian statutory holidays.

## CELPIP vs IELTS: Which Test Should You Choose?

**Short answer:** CELPIP is fully computer-based with a recorded Speaking section; IELTS General Training has a paper option and a live human Speaking interview. CELPIP scores 2-4 days, IELTS 13 days. CELPIP costs $290 CAD, IELTS $339 CAD. CELPIP is Canadian-centric (vocabulary, accents); IELTS uses international English.

IRCC accepts both CELPIP and IELTS for Express Entry. The two tests differ in format, pacing, and how you'll experience the speaking section:

| Factor | CELPIP | IELTS General Training |
|---|---|---|
| Format | 100% computer-based | Paper or computer (Reading/Writing), in-person speaking |
| Duration | 3 hours | 2 hours 45 minutes |
| Listening | Computer-based | Audio on paper test or computer |
| Reading | Computer-based | Paper or computer |
| Writing | Computer-based (2 typed essays) | Paper-based handwriting |
| Speaking | Recorded to microphone | In-person interview with examiner |
| Test Accents | Canadian English | International accents (British, Australian, American) |
| Scoring Scale | 1 to 12 per skill | 0 to 9 per skill (bands with half-point increments) |
| Results Timeline | 2 to 4 business days | Up to 13 days |
| Question Types | Mainly multiple-choice, drop-down | 10+ formats (fill-in-blanks require correct spelling) |
| Cost (Canada) | $290 CAD | Varies, typically $350+ CAD |

**Advantages of CELPIP:**
- Faster results (critical if you're on a tight immigration timeline)
- Direct CLB conversion (no conversion math required)
- Computer-based speaking (no anxiety about face-to-face interviews)
- Canadian-focused content and scenarios
- Widely available in Canada with multiple test dates per week

**Advantages of IELTS:**
- More familiar format if you've studied it before
- Recognized globally (if you're considering countries beyond Canada)
- Some people find in-person speaking less intimidating than computer-based

For Canadian immigration specifically, CELPIP is faster, more convenient, and designed for the Canadian context. Many applicants choose CELPIP for these reasons.

## How Does CELPIP's AI Hybrid Scoring Work?

**Short answer:** Across 2025 and 2026, CELPIP rolled out AI-hybrid scoring for Writing and Speaking. AI algorithms produce an initial assessment which certified human raters then verify. This speeds up scoring without sacrificing accuracy and is now the standard for all CELPIP General tests.

CELPIP rolled out AI-hybrid scoring for its Writing and Speaking components across 2025 and 2026. The system uses AI algorithms to produce an initial score, which certified human raters then verify for consistency and accuracy. This hybrid approach reduces the time between your test date and results without removing human oversight from the process. Human raters specifically check for natural tone and register that confirm you understood the task prompt, not just that your sentences were grammatically correct.

Your responses are first assessed by AI algorithms, then verified by certified human raters. The hybrid system speeds up scoring while keeping accuracy intact. Human raters check for authentic "tone" and "rhythm" that confirm you understood the prompt as intended.

For Writing, CELPIP evaluates four criteria: Content and Coherence, Vocabulary, Readability, and Task Fulfillment. A common reason for score deductions in the email task is failing to distinguish formal from informal tone. An email to your manager should use different language and tone than an email to a friend.

For Speaking, the same four criteria apply: Coherence, Vocabulary, Listenability (pronunciation, rhythm), and Task Fulfillment.

The AI-hybrid system cut result turnaround. Standard results now arrive in 2 to 4 business days instead of the longer waits older scoring methods produced.

**Preparation takeaway:** Practice the formal vs informal register distinction, especially in Writing. Mismatched tone is one of the easiest ways to lose points.

## What Is the Best Strategy to Prepare for the CELPIP Test?

**Short answer:** Free prep: CELPIP practice materials on celpip.ca, YouTube channels with full lessons, and AI tools for Speaking and Writing practice. Paid prep: official CELPIP Online Prep ($60-$150), private tutors ($40-$80 per hour), and Paragon's structured prep courses. Most candidates need 4-8 weeks of preparation.

CELPIP preparation takes most applicants 4 to 8 weeks, depending on your starting English level and target score. Official preparation resources from Paragon Testing Enterprises include free sample questions on celpip.ca and paid full-length practice tests with AI-scored feedback. For a CLB 7 target, which is the minimum for Express Entry's Federal Skilled Worker Program, consistent practice in all four skills is the core requirement. For CLB 9 or higher, targeted coaching in Writing and Speaking is likely necessary, as the AI-hybrid scoring system assesses tone, coherence, and task fulfillment in detail.

**Free preparation:**
- CELPIP practice materials on celpip.ca (free listening and reading sample questions)
- YouTube channels with free CELPIP lessons
- OpenAI and other AI tools for speaking and writing practice
- Library resources on Canadian English

**Paid preparation:**
- CELPIP official paid practice tests (full mocks with AI feedback)
- Structured prep courses (e.g., ILAC, E2 Language, or language schools in your city)
- Tutoring with CELPIP-certified instructors

Start with free resources to gauge your current level. If you need CLB 7 or higher for Express Entry, aim for CELPIP 7 or above in all four skills. To be competitive with current [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) draws, score CLB 9 or higher if possible.

## Where Can You Take the CELPIP Test Outside Canada?

**Middle East:** Dubai and other UAE centres have regular CELPIP availability. This is the closest option for Iranian applicants, though any centre with reliable infrastructure works.

**Iran:** CELPIP is not available in Iran. Iranian applicants must travel to a neighbouring country to take the test. The Dubai knowledge village centre is common, with weekly slots available.

Using proxy test takers or fraudulent scores results in permanent ban from Canadian immigration and criminal charges. Your test results are verified against your identity documents at the test centre.

## How Will 2026 Express Entry Reforms Affect CELPIP Requirements?

**Short answer:** As of April 2026, IRCC is consulting on potentially lowering the minimum CLB requirement from CLB 7 to CLB 6 across all four language abilities. The consultation runs until May 24, 2026 and is not yet law. Track the IRCC consultation page for the final decision.

As of April 2026, IRCC is [consulting on changes to the Express Entry system](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry-reforms.html). The consultation runs until May 24, 2026, and is not yet law.

# WES ECA Canada 2026: 5-Year Validity, CRS Points, and Who Must Use WES

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-wes-credential-evaluation-guide-2026
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-04-28
Author: Maggi Issa

> If you're a professional from Iran, Pakistan, India, or anywhere outside Canada planning to apply for Express Entry, you'll encounter a confusing acronym early: ECA.

# WES ECA Canada 2026: 5-Year Validity, CRS Points, and Who Must Use WES

*As of August 31, 2026.*

If you studied outside Canada and you want Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for that education, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) wants an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) for immigration purposes. World Education Services (WES) is one of five designated organizations. It is not the only one, and it is not the same thing as an ECA. This guide uses the official [educational credential assessment](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/education-assessment.html) page.

## TL;DR

An ECA for immigration is required to be eligible as a Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP) principal applicant, or to claim CRS points for foreign education | The report must be less than 5 years old when you create the Express Entry profile and when you apply | Most people may use WES or four other designated organizations | Architects, some physicians, and some pharmacists must use a designated professional body instead | IRCC does not publish WES fees or WES processing times. Those come from the organization you pick

## What is an ECA, and why do you need one?

**Short answer:** An Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) is a report that says whether your foreign degree, diploma, or certificate is valid and equal to a Canadian credential. You need an ECA for immigration purposes if you completed your education outside Canada and you want to (1) be eligible as the principal applicant under the Federal Skilled Worker Program, or (2) earn CRS points for that foreign education. You can also claim points for a spouse or common-law partner's foreign education if they come with you. You do not need an ECA for a Canadian credential.

IRCC says the report does not guarantee a job in your field or a licence in a regulated occupation. If you plan to work in a regulated job, you still get licensed in the province where you settle. Put the ECA report and reference number in your Express Entry profile. Keep the original. Be ready to upload copies if you get an invitation to apply. Those rules are on the [ECA page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/education-assessment.html).

## Is WES the same as an ECA?

**Short answer:** No. An ECA is the type of report IRCC requires. WES is one organization designated to issue that report. People search "WES" and "ECA" as if they were interchangeable because WES is widely used. They are not the same. Order the product labelled for IRCC or for immigration. A course-by-course report for university admission is a different product.

IRCC accepts an ECA from any designated organization or, for some occupations, from a designated professional body. Processing times and costs vary by organization. IRCC does not set WES's price list. Check the organization you choose before you pay.

## Who can issue your ECA?

**Short answer:** Most applicants must use one of five designated organizations. Architects, some doctors, and some pharmacists must use a designated professional body when the licence rules below apply. IRCC designated WES on 17 April 2013. The full list is in the table on the [ECA page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/education-assessment.html). Occupations below use National Occupational Classification (NOC) codes.

| Who | Designated on |
|---|---|
| Comparative Education Service, University of Toronto School of Continuing Studies | 17 April 2013 |
| International Credential Assessment Service of Canada | 17 April 2013 |
| World Education Services (WES) | 17 April 2013 |
| International Qualifications Assessment Service (IQAS) | 6 August 2015 |
| International Credential Evaluation Service, British Columbia Institute of Technology | 6 August 2015 |
| Canadian Architectural Certification Board, for architect (NOC 21200) when you need a licence | 20 May 2024 |
| Medical Council of Canada, for primary medical diploma when your primary occupation is NOC 31100, 31101, or 31102 | 17 April 2013 |
| Pharmacy Examining Board of Canada, for pharmacist (NOC 31120) when you need a licence | 6 January 2014 |

NOC 21200 architects who already had a valid ECA from another designated organization before 31 October 2024 can still use that report if it remains valid. If you do not need an architect or pharmacist licence (for example a construction project manager, or a pharmacy role that is not patient-facing), a regular designated organization can assess you. Confirm licence rules with the provincial regulator.

## How long is an ECA valid for IRCC?

**Short answer:** Less than 5 years old at two moments: when you complete your Express Entry profile, and when you submit the permanent residence application. If you have an invitation, make sure the ECA will still be valid on the day you apply. If you are still in the pool, make sure it stays valid for the rest of your time in the pool. An expired ECA means IRCC will refuse the application.

If the assessment will expire before you can apply, contact the organization that issued it. They may re-issue it, depending on the type of ECA and the organization. That is IRCC's language, not a WES-only rule.

## How many CRS education points does each level earn?

**Short answer:** Points come from the Canadian equivalency on the report, not from the name on your diploma. Without a spouse, a doctoral degree is 150 CRS points, a master's or professional degree is 135, two or more credentials (one of them three or more years) is 128, a three-year or longer bachelor's is 120, a two-year program is 98, and a one-year program is 90. With a spouse the same rows are 140, 126, 119, 112, 91, and 84. Full rows sit on the [ECA page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/education-assessment.html) and the [CRS criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html).

| Canadian equivalency on the ECA | CRS without a spouse | CRS with a spouse |
|---|---:|---:|
| Doctoral (PhD) | 150 | 140 |
| Master's, or a professional degree needed to practise | 135 | 126 |
| Two or more credentials, at least one of 3+ years | 128 | 119 |
| Bachelor's or other program of 3+ years | 120 | 112 |
| Two-year program | 98 | 91 |
| One-year program | 90 | 84 |

In most cases you assess only your highest completed credential. To claim points for two or more credentials, you need an ECA for each one, and at least one credential must be three or more years. If a post-secondary credential is not equal to a Canadian credential, you can assess secondary school instead and claim high-school points.

## Do you need an ECA for a Canadian job?

**Short answer:** Not for IRCC job-offer purposes in the way people mean it. An ECA is an immigration document. Employers and regulators can ask for other assessments. IRCC is explicit: the report may help when you look for work, but it does not guarantee a job or a licence. Use Job Bank and provincial regulators for hiring and licensing. Use the ECA for [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry).

## How much does a WES ECA cost, and how long does it take?

**Short answer:** IRCC does not publish WES fees or WES turnaround times. The ECA page says processing times and costs may vary by organization, and that the organization you choose will tell you how to submit documents. Treat any dollar figure you see on a blog as stale until you confirm it on WES's own IRCC product page at the moment you pay.

What you can lock in from IRCC is the product type (immigration ECA), the 5-year validity clock, and which body you are allowed to use. Start the file early. Document shipping from some countries, including Iran, still adds weeks before the organization even starts the assessment.

## What mistakes cost people a second ECA?

**Short answer:** Ordering the wrong WES product, letting the 5-year clock run out in the pool, and assuming a master's title always maps to master's CRS points. IRCC scores the Canadian equivalency string on the report. If that string is a postgraduate diploma rather than a master's, you get diploma points.

Iranian applicants should plan for extra time on official transcripts and degree confirmation. South Asian three-year bachelor's degrees sometimes come back as a three-year bachelor's (still 120 CRS without a spouse) rather than a four-year degree. That is not a refusal. It is the equivalency. Read the report before you enter it in the profile. You cannot put two credentials in the same Express Entry education field. Add each one with Save and add.

## How should you enter the ECA in Express Entry?

**Short answer:** Enter the results and the reference number in the profile. Keep originals. Upload copies if invited. For more than one credential, fill Education history for the highest credential first, save and add, then repeat. IRCC's steps are on the same [ECA page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/education-assessment.html).

Then score yourself in the [CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator). If the equivalency is not what you expected, fix the profile before an invitation locks the numbers in.

## What questions do people ask about WES and ECA?

**Short answer:** Validity, cost, and whether WES is mandatory are the queries that send traffic to this page. WES is not mandatory unless your occupation requires a professional body and WES is not that body.

### How long is a WES report valid for Canada PR?

For IRCC, any designated ECA, including WES, must be under 5 years old at profile creation and at application.

### Is WES required for Express Entry?

No. Any of the five designated organizations can issue the ECA for most occupations. Some architects, physicians, and pharmacists must use the professional body instead.

### Can I use an expired ECA if I already have an invitation?

No. IRCC will refuse an application filed with an expired ECA. Ask the issuing organization about re-issue before you submit.

A Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) can read the equivalency against the CRS table before you submit. [Book a consultation](/book) if the report is not the credential you thought you had.

## Sources

- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Educational credential assessment](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/education-assessment.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [CRS criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html)
- Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, [Federal Skilled Worker Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/federal-skilled-workers.html)

# Co-op Work Permit Eliminated April 2026 for International Students

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-co-op-work-permit-eliminated-april-2026-international-students
Category: Study Permit
Published: 2026-04-27
Author: Maggi Issa

> On April 1, 2026, Canada eliminated the separate co-op work permit, officially the C32 permit, for international students.

# Canada Eliminates Co-op Work Permit for International Students: What Changed April 1, 2026

On April 1, 2026, Canada eliminated the separate co-op work permit, officially the C32 permit, for international students. Students pursuing mandatory work placements as part of their degree, diploma, or certificate programs at Canadian post-secondary institutions can now work under their study permit alone, provided they meet specific conditions.

The change affects hundreds of thousands of students. As of January 31, 2026, about 460,695 international students held active study permits in Canada. Many of them still do not know what the April 1 rule means for their placements, existing applications, and legal status during work-integrated learning.

Below: what changed, who qualifies, what to do if you already filed a co-op application, and the details most students miss.

## What changed when Canada eliminated the co-op work permit in April 2026?

**Short answer:** Before April 1, 2026, mandatory work placements required both a study permit and a separate C32 co-op work permit; after April 1, the study permit alone authorizes the placement, removing the second IRCC application while leaving all other student work rules unchanged.

Before April 1, 2026, the process was cumbersome. Students accepted for a mandatory co-op, internship, practicum, or mentorship placement as part of their program had to apply for two separate work permits. The first was their study permit, which allowed enrollment at a Designated Learning Institution (DLI). The second was a co-op work permit application filed separately with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). The second application could take months to process, often delaying the start of the placement.

After April 1, 2026, that second application is gone. The study permit alone now authorizes the placement. IRCC confirmed the change in its official notice: "This change simplifies the administrative process for students by requiring only one permit to complete a single study programme. It does not increase the number of students who are authorised to work or affect temporary resident volumes; it simply removes an administrative step that is no longer necessary."

The rest of the rulebook is the same. Study permit conditions, the 50% rule (work cannot exceed half the total program length), full-time enrollment requirements, and Post-Graduation Work Permit eligibility rules all remain unchanged. This is an administrative cleanup, not a loosening of student work rules.

## Who This Change Applies To: The Five Eligibility Conditions

**Short answer:** To use the study permit alone, you need a valid study permit (or pending extension), full-time enrollment at a DLI, a program of at least 6 months leading to a degree/diploma/certificate, a mandatory placement for graduation, and the R186 work authorization condition printed on your permit.

The co-op permit removal applies only to students who meet all five of these conditions at once. Miss any one of them and the old rules still apply to you.

1. **You hold a valid study permit.** Your study permit must be current. If it has expired, you must have submitted an extension application (Form IMM 5709) before it expired, and that extension application must still be pending decision.

2. **You are enrolled full-time at a Designated Learning Institution.** Full-time enrollment is required throughout the placement. Your institution must be designated by IRCC as a DLI. This applies to public post-secondary colleges, universities, and some private institutions across Canada.

3. **Your program is at least six months long and leads to a degree, diploma, or certificate.** The program must be for post-secondary credentials. Short courses, professional certifications without a formal credential pathway, and non-award-bearing programs do not qualify.

4. **The work placement is mandatory for graduation.** This is non-negotiable. Elective placements, optional work experience, and voluntary internships do not qualify. The institution must confirm in writing that the placement is required to complete the program.

5. **Your study permit has a work authorization condition printed on it.** The permit must include a remark or condition that specifically authorizes you to accept employment. Common examples printed on Canadian study permits read: "May accept employment on or off campus if meeting eligibility criteria as per R186(f), (v), or (w)" or "May accept employment only on campus if meeting criteria as per R186(f)." If your permit does not carry that language, the new rule does not cover you.

### Who Is Excluded

Even if your institution is a DLI, several categories of students still need a separate co-op work permit. These exclusions are not new; they carry over from prior rules.

- **Secondary (high school) students.** Any student in a high school program must continue to apply for a separate co-op work permit.
- **Students in ESL, French-language, general interest, preparatory, or international short courses.** These programs are not recognized for co-op authorization under the new rules.
- **Any placement that is not mandatory for graduation.** If the course or program treats the placement as optional, it does not qualify.
- **Any placement that exceeds 50% of total program duration.** If the work component takes up more than half the program timeline, it crosses the legal limit and falls outside study permit authorization.

The line that matters is between DLI-designated post-secondary programs (universities, colleges) and all other study pathways. The change covers any post-secondary DLI, not only those eligible for Post-Graduation Work Permits. PGWP eligibility is a separate question for after graduation. It does not decide whether the co-op permit change applies now.

## The 50% Rule: What Counts and What Does Not

**Short answer:** Work-integrated learning still cannot exceed 50% of your total program length: a 24-month program caps placements at 12 months; paid, unpaid, co-ops, practicums, mentorships, and clinical rotations all count, but summer jobs and freelance work outside the program do not.

The 50% rule sits at the centre of co-op authorization. It has not changed, but many students get it wrong.

Your work-integrated learning cannot exceed 50% of your total program duration. The math is simple: divide total program length by two. A 24-month program caps you at 12 months of work. A four-month program caps you at two.

What counts toward the 50%: paid placements, unpaid internships, co-ops, practicums, mentorships, clinical rotations, and any other work-integrated learning tied to your credential. The work period is measured in months, not hours. Paid and unpaid work both count.

What does not count: summer jobs outside the formal curriculum, personal projects, freelance work outside your program structure, and work experience you do on your own. The placement has to sit inside the program itself, either required or as an accepted part of the credential pathway.

Your Designated Learning Institution will confirm whether your placement counts as integrated learning and whether the duration keeps you under the 50% threshold. If you have any doubt, ask your institution's international student services office before the placement starts. Get their confirmation in writing. That written confirmation, often called a co-op letter or work placement letter, matters more than students realize.

## What Students Who Already Applied for a Co-op Permit Should Do

**Short answer:** IRCC withdraws eligible pending C32 applications automatically with no action required, but students can pull their own application to avoid delays; contact IRCC directly to confirm refund status since auto-refund is not officially confirmed.

If you filed a co-op work permit application (C32) before April 1, 2026, IRCC's stated policy is to withdraw eligible pending applications on its own. You do not need to act for the withdrawal to happen. IRCC says it will process them proactively.

You can also pull the application yourself instead of waiting for IRCC. The University of Toronto's official guidance to students reads: "you can withdraw your co-op work permit application or it may be withdrawn automatically by IRCC." If your placement starts soon and you cannot risk further delays, withdrawing yourself may be faster. Do it online through your IRCC account or by contacting IRCC directly.

### What About Fees?

IRCC confirmed that pending co-op work permit applications will be withdrawn automatically. On refunds for application fees, news outlets reported that refunds would be processed automatically. That claim is not directly confirmed in IRCC's public notice. If you paid a co-op work permit application fee and your application is withdrawn, contact IRCC directly to confirm your refund status. Do not assume the refund is automatic; verify it with IRCC yourself.

### Existing C32 Permits Issued Before April 1

If you already hold a co-op work permit issued before April 1, 2026, that permit is still technically valid. You do not need to use it. You do not need to return it to IRCC. You can rely on your [study permit](/immigration/study-permit) for the placement instead, provided your study permit carries the correct work authorization conditions. The valid C32 does not expire because the new rules took effect; it simply becomes unnecessary.

## The Co-op Letter: The Trap Many Students Miss

**Short answer:** Even without a separate permit, your DLI must still issue a written co-op letter confirming you are a full-time student in a recognized program, the placement is mandatory for graduation, the duration and dates, and that work stays within 50% of program length.

The detail most students overlook: even though you no longer need a separate co-op work permit, your institution still has to provide written confirmation that your placement is mandatory for graduation.

That letter, often called a co-op letter, work placement letter, or program confirmation letter, is the evidence your placement qualifies under the new rules. Without it, your legal status during the placement can be questioned.

Your institution's international student office or co-op office issues the letter. It should state clearly that:

- You are a full-time student enrolled in a recognized program.
- The placement is mandatory for graduation.
- The placement duration and dates.
- The placement does not exceed 50% of your total program length.

Some institutions issue this letter routinely. Others require you to request it. Do not assume your institution has sent it automatically. Contact your co-op office or international student services now and request the letter in writing. If the wording is vague ("the student may complete a placement" instead of "the placement is mandatory"), push back and ask the institution to fix it. Vague language can compromise your legal status.

Keep a copy of the co-op letter with your study permit documents. If IRCC or border officials audit you, this letter is your proof the work was authorized.

## What Did Not Change: Five Things That Stayed the Same

**Short answer:** The co-op letter requirement, R186 work-authorization remark on the study permit, 50% rule, full-time enrollment, and PGWP eligibility rules all remained unchanged; only the separate co-op work-permit application form went away.

The reform is narrow. It removes the separate application step. Most rules around it carry on untouched.

| Rule | Before April 1 | After April 1 |
|------|---|---|
| **Co-op letter from DLI required** | Yes, must confirm placement is mandatory | Yes, still required |
| **Study permit conditions must include R186 work authorization remark** | Required | Required |
| **50% rule on work vs. total program duration** | 50% maximum | 50% maximum |
| **Full-time enrollment requirement** | Must be full-time during placement | Must be full-time during placement |
| **PGWP eligibility rules** | Determined by program at PGWP-eligible DLI + other criteria | Unchanged; co-op permit elimination does not affect PGWP rules |

The 50% cap, full-time enrollment, and the requirement for a co-op letter all predate this reform. The single new thing is the removal of the separate co-op work permit application form, along with the delay it caused.

Post-Graduation Work Permit eligibility is untouched. If your program qualifies for a PGWP after graduation (typically because the DLI is PGWP-eligible and the program is at least two years long), the co-op change does not affect that. You stay eligible for a PGWP if you meet all other criteria. If your program does not qualify, this change does not make it qualify. PGWP rules sit on a separate track from co-op work authorization.

## A Note for International Students in Iran, the Middle East, and South Asia

**Short answer:** The PAL requirement for study permits in Ontario, Quebec, BC, and Alberta is untouched by this reform; current students should check their printed study permit for the R186 work-authorization remark and request a free amendment from IRCC if it is missing.

Go Far Global works with many international students from Iran, the Middle East, and South Asia studying at universities and colleges across Canada, including the University of Toronto, McGill, UBC, Concordia, University of Waterloo, Carleton University, and Toronto Metropolitan University. All of these institutions are Designated Learning Institutions, and the new rule applies to them.

If you are a new student applying for a study permit in 2026, the Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL) requirement is untouched by this reform. PAL is a study permit application requirement run by your province of study, not a co-op permit requirement. If you are applying for a study permit in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, or Alberta, you still need a PAL as part of your study permit application. The April 1 change does not touch PAL.

For current students with active study permits, the practical step is simple: pull out your printed study permit and look for the R186 work authorization remark. If the text says you may accept employment under certain conditions, you are covered. If the remark is missing, request a free amendment from IRCC before your placement starts. Do not start the placement without that confirmation. The amendment is straightforward; contact IRCC through your online account or call the IRCC call centre.

## What Is Still in Consultation (Not Yet Law)

**Short answer:** IRCC is consulting on four future changes — work during study-permit renewal queues, work while waiting for PGWP decisions, removing study-permit requirements for foreign apprentices, and standardizing work during academic breaks — but none are law yet.

IRCC has signaled four additional changes still under consultation as of April 2026. None are law, and none have a confirmed implementation date.

1. **Work authorization during study permit renewal delays.** IRCC is consulting on whether students should be allowed to work while their study permit extension sits in queue waiting for a decision.

2. **Work authorization for graduates waiting for a PGWP decision.** Some graduates are already allowed to work under specific conditions while a PGWP application is pending. IRCC is consulting on how to standardize and expand those rules.

3. **Removing the study permit requirement for foreign apprentices.** IRCC is examining whether apprentices in Canada on a work permit (rather than a study permit) should be able to access certain benefits without holding a study permit.

4. **Standardizing work authorization during scheduled academic breaks.** IRCC is consulting on when students can work during reading weeks, winter break, spring break, and summer break.

These consultations were scheduled for spring 2026, with no confirmed implementation timeline. Do not assume any of these proposals are law yet. If your situation depends on one of them, check IRCC's official website for updates.

## Critical Reminders Before Your Placement Starts

**Short answer:** Before starting a placement, verify your study permit is current or extension pending, the R186 work-authorization remark is printed on it, and your institution issued a written co-op letter confirming the placement is mandatory and within the 50% rule.

Before you begin any mandatory placement, verify three things:

1. **Your study permit is current, or you have an extension application pending.** An expired study permit without a pending extension means you are out of status and cannot legally work, regardless of the co-op change.

2. **Your study permit has the R186 work authorization condition printed on it.** Check the physical or digital copy of your permit. If the work remark is missing, the study permit alone does not authorize your placement. Request a free amendment before day one of your work.

3. **Your institution provided a written co-op letter confirming the placement is mandatory and within the 50% rule.** Request the letter now if you do not have it. Keep it with your study permit documents.

These steps take days, not weeks. Get them done now, even if your placement is months out. Starting a co-op placement without these three items in place puts you at risk of being found out of status.

If any item is missing or unclear, do not start the placement until you have sorted it out. Removing the separate permit application does not relax the underlying conditions. The conditions are identical. Only the application process changed.

## What to Do Next

If you have a study permit and a placement starting soon, check your permit now for the R186 work authorization condition. If it is not there, get a free amendment before the placement starts. Our RCIC team handles study permit amendments, PGWP applications, and study permit extensions through IMM 5709. Book a consultation at [gofarglobal.com/appointment](/appointment) if you want a consultant to verify your file before your placement begins.

- [IRCC Help Centre Q497: Designated Learning Institution Work Permit for Co-op Placements](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=497&top=15)

# Canada PNP 2026: 91,500 Nominations and a Shift in Provincial Power

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-pnp-2026-changes-91500-nominations-provincial-powers
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-04-27
Author: Maggi Issa

> On March 30, 2026, the Provincial Nominee Program underwent two critical changes that reshape how applicants move through Canada's PNP 2026 immigration system.

# Canada PNP 2026: 91,500 Nominations and a Shift in Provincial Power

On March 30, 2026, the [Provincial Nominee Program](/immigration/provincial-nominee) underwent two critical changes that reshape how applicants move through Canada's PNP 2026 immigration system.

First, the federal government allocated 91,500 PNP nominations for 2026, a 66% increase from 2025's 55,000 nominations. This number is still 17% below the 110,000 allocations available in 2024, but it signals a deliberate restart of provincial sponsorship after a year of constraint.

Second, the federal government transferred key eligibility decisions away from IRCC officers and directly to the provinces. Under Regulation SOR/2026-63, provinces now hold "sole responsibility" to evaluate whether a PNP nominee intends to reside in their province and whether they can become economically established. IRCC officers can no longer override these provincial determinations on those grounds.

This shift matters because it reduces the risk of federal rejection at the final stage. For applicants from Iran, the Middle East, South Asia, and anywhere else in the world, it means a provincial nomination now carries more weight.

## What changed in the Canada PNP 2026 nominations and provincial powers?

**Short answer:** Registered March 30, 2026, SOR/2026-63 amended IRPR Section 87(3) so provinces have "sole responsibility" to evaluate intent to reside and economic establishment — IRCC officers can no longer override these provincial determinations and must refer adverse information back to the province for a 60 to 90 day review.

The formal regulation is titled "Regulations Amending the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (Provincial Nominee Program)." It was registered March 30, 2026 (Order-in-Council P.C. 2026-278) and published in the Canada Gazette, Part II, Volume 160, Number 7 on April 8, 2026.

The regulation amended subsections 87(2), 87(3), 87(4), and references in 87(5) and 87(10) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.

The core change lives in subsection 87(3), which now reads: "The government of a province that issues the nomination certificate has the sole responsibility to evaluate, according to the provincial selection criteria that have been approved in writing by the Minister, both the foreign national's ability to become economically established in Canada and their intention to reside in that province."

That single sentence changed how PNP works.

Before March 30, 2026, IRCC officers retained independent authority to refuse a provincial nominee. Even if your province formally nominated you and said you would live there and establish economically, an IRCC officer could substitute their own judgment and reject you on those grounds. They could decide, "The province is wrong about your intent or ability." You had no appeal.

After March 30, 2026, this is no longer possible. A provincial nomination certificate is conclusive evidence on intent to reside and economic establishment. IRCC officers can verify your identity, confirm the certificate is valid, and check standard admissibility (security, criminality, health, finances). But they cannot reach a different conclusion than your province on whether you will live there or establish economically.

If an IRCC officer discovers new adverse information specifically about intent or establishment, the officer must refer it back to the nominating province. That province then has 60 to 90 days to maintain or revoke the nomination. The final say stays with the province.

For genuine applicants with real job offers or real provincial ties, this is a structural improvement. For those attempting to game the system, provinces now own that risk completely.

## 2026 Allocations by Province and Territory

**Short answer:** 2026 PNP nominations total 91,500 — Ontario 14,119, Alberta 6,403, Manitoba 6,239, British Columbia 5,254, Saskatchewan 4,761, plus Yukon, NWT, and Atlantic provinces; approximately 10,000 spaces reserved federally for French speakers and physicians; Quebec runs separately at ~50,000 immigrants per year.

Here are the official allocations for the 2026 Provincial Nominee Program:

| Province / Territory | 2025 Allocations | 2026 Allocations | Federal Reserve (50% of each) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ontario | 10,750 | 14,119 | 7,060 |
| Alberta | 6,403 | 6,403 | 3,202 |
| British Columbia | 6,214 | 5,254 | 2,627 |
| Saskatchewan | 4,761 | 4,761 | 2,381 |
| Manitoba | 4,750 | 6,239 | 3,120 |
| Yukon | 215 | 282 | 141 |
| Northwest Territories | 150 | 197 | 99 |
| Nova Scotia | (final 2025: 3,915) | ~5,236 (modeled) | 2,618 |
| New Brunswick | (final 2025: 4,250) | ~4,573 (modeled) | 2,287 |
| Prince Edward Island | (final 2025: 2,050) | ~1,704 (modeled) | 852 |
| Newfoundland and Labrador | (final 2025: 3,050) | ~2,537 (modeled) | 1,269 |

**Total PNP**: 91,500 nominations

**Federal Reserve**: Approximately 10,000 spaces within the 91,500 total, allocated to French-speaking newcomers and physicians.

**Quebec**: Separate system. Quebec operates under section 94 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and selects its own immigrants through PSTQ (Programme de l'expérience québécoise) and SWSP (Secondary Stream Worker Program). Quebec's 2026 target is approximately 50,000 total immigrants per year across all selection streams. PNP regulations do not apply to Quebec.

Ontario leads with 14,119 nominations. Manitoba jumped to 6,239 from 4,750. British Columbia's allocation dropped slightly to 5,254. Saskatchewan and Alberta held stable allocations. The Atlantic provinces and territories received smaller shares, though Nova Scotia's modeled allocation of 5,236 would represent growth if officially confirmed.

## What Changed in Each Province

**Short answer:** Ontario Express Entry streams remain suspended through 2026; BC closed Entry Level and Semi-Skilled April 23, 2026 and focuses on healthcare (31 occupations) and trades (9 occupations); Alberta added a $135 WEOI fee April 7, 2026; Saskatchewan added tech to priority sectors; Manitoba dropped hospitality/food services and added 16 skilled trades occupations; Nova Scotia consolidated 10 streams into 4.

### Ontario (OINP): 14,119 Nominations

Ontario's Express Entry-aligned streams (Human Capital Priorities, French-Speaking Skilled Worker, Express Entry Skilled Trades) remained suspended throughout 2025 and into 2026. OINP now runs primarily through Employer Job Offer streams and graduate streams.

Recent draws in April 2026 focused on the Master's Graduate stream (minimum score 61), PhD Graduate stream (minimum score 56), and regional Employer Job Offer draws across Eastern, Northern, Southwestern, and Central regions (excluding Greater Toronto Area).

Tech occupations remain eligible under specific NOC codes: 21232 (software engineers), 21230 (software developers), 21220 (cybersecurity), 21223 (database analysts), 21211 (data scientists). However, unless Ontario reactivates its Express Entry streams, these candidates must come through employer job offer routes or have a specific Ontario graduate connection.

### British Columbia (BC PNP): 5,254 Nominations

BC PNP made several cuts in early 2026. The International Post-Graduate stream closed January 7, 2026. The Entry Level and Semi-Skilled stream officially closed April 23, 2026. Tech-focused draws, which ended with the Tech Pilot in December 2024, have not resumed.

BC now focuses on healthcare (31 eligible occupations) and construction trades (9 eligible occupations). The province maintains a 35% minimum target for nominations outside Greater Vancouver, meaning at least 1,839 of BC's 5,254 allocations go to regions outside the metro area.

### Alberta (AAIP): 6,403 Nominations

Alberta's Opportunity Stream reserves 3,425 spaces. A new Dedicated Health Care Pathway reserves 500 spaces. The Express Entry Stream for Priority Sectors (construction, manufacturing, aviation, agriculture) reserves 600 spaces. These three streams account for 4,525 of Alberta's 6,403 total allocations.

Effective April 7, 2026, Alberta introduced a new $135 CAD fee for Worker Expression of Interest (WEOI). The Rural Renewal Stream eligibility criteria were modified January 1, 2026.

### Saskatchewan (SINP): 4,761 Nominations

Saskatchewan reserved 50% of its nominations (2,381 spaces) for seven priority sectors: healthcare, technology, agriculture, skilled trades, mining, manufacturing, and energy. Technology was added to this priority list in 2026 (it did not appear on the 2025 list).

Saskatchewan also reserves 750 spaces for graduates of Saskatchewan Designated Learning Institutions who are employed in priority sectors. The Innovation and Tech Talent pathway includes 32 eligible NOC codes.

A new eligibility restriction, effective in 2026, bars PGWP holders who studied outside Saskatchewan and worked in their field for fewer than six months from Saskatchewan Experience pathways.

### Manitoba (MPNP): 6,239 Nominations

Manitoba's largest change came February 4, 2026: the Hospitality and Food Services sectors were removed from the Temporary Resident Retention Pilot. In their place, 16 new skilled trades occupations were added.

Skilled Worker Overseas draws remain small and biweekly, typically issuing 46 to 72 Letters of Advice per draw. Candidates abroad applying to Manitoba face longer wait times than those within Canada.

### Atlantic Provinces

Nova Scotia consolidated 10 separate streams into 4 effective February 18, 2026: Nova Scotia Graduate, Skilled Worker, Entrepreneur, and Nova Scotia Express Entry. This streamlining reduces the number of pathways but may speed up processing for remaining streams.

New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador were still finalizing their 2026 allocations and stream-level changes as of late April. Check each province's official immigration website for confirmed details.

## The 600-Point CRS Bonus and Express Entry Integration

**Short answer:** The 600-point CRS bonus for enhanced (Express Entry-aligned) provincial nominations remains in force; on April 13, 2026, Express Entry Draw #409 issued 324 ITAs exclusively to PNP candidates with the bonus applied; base PNP nominations from suspended Express Entry provinces like Ontario do not qualify for the bonus.

The 600-point Comprehensive Ranking System bonus for an enhanced provincial nomination remains in force for 2026. IRCC continues to run dedicated PNP-only Express Entry draws for candidates with provincial nominations.

On April 13, 2026, Express Entry Draw #409 issued 324 Invitations to Apply exclusively to PNP candidates with the 600-point bonus applied. All invitees received invitations because all had met the CRS minimum (thanks to the bonus).

Not all PNP nominations are "enhanced." Only nominations issued through Express Entry-aligned streams qualify for the 600-point bonus. These provinces include:

- British Columbia (Tech Pilot closed, but some streams remain in Express Entry pathway)
- Saskatchewan (strong Express Entry alignment)
- Manitoba (Express Entry streams active)
- Atlantic provinces (Nova Scotia Express Entry stream)
- Most others with active Express Entry streams

Provinces that suspended or closed Express Entry streams (notably Ontario, throughout 2025 and into 2026) issue nominations through employer job offer and graduate streams. These are "base" PNP nominations. Candidates with base nominations apply directly to IRCC outside the Express Entry system, do not receive the 600-point bonus, and face longer federal processing.

## Processing Timelines: What to Expect

**Short answer:** Federal processing — enhanced PNP (Express Entry) about 7 months with ~13,700 queue, base PNP about 13 months with ~108,100 queue; provincial stages run 3 to 8 months depending on jurisdiction; total enhanced path 10 to 13 months versus base path 15 to 19 months.

Federal processing times depend on whether your PNP nomination is enhanced (Express Entry-aligned) or base (non-Express Entry):

| Application Type | Federal Processing Time | Current Queue Size |
|---|---|---|
| PNP Enhanced (Express Entry) | 7 months | ~13,700 applicants |
| PNP Base (non-Enhanced) | 13 months | ~108,100 applicants |

Provincial processing times vary by jurisdiction:

- Ontario: 3 to 6 months
- Alberta: 3 to 6 months
- British Columbia: 4 to 6 months
- Saskatchewan: 3 to 5 months
- Manitoba: 4 to 8 months

Total estimated timelines from application to permanent residence:

- Enhanced PNP path: 10 to 13 months total (provincial stage plus federal stage)
- Base PNP path: 15 to 19 months total

If your province has an active [Express Entry stream aligned with your occupation and experience](/immigration/express-entry), pursuing the enhanced pathway cuts your total timeline by 5 to 6 months.

## What Hasn't Changed: The Fundamentals Still Apply

**Short answer:** Express Entry CRS scoring is unchanged, provincial nomination still adds 600 points for enhanced streams, study-permit policy and the PAL requirement remain in effect, work-permit eligibility holds, and IRCC retains full control over criminality, security, and health admissibility checks.

The CRS point system for [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) applicants remains unchanged. Provincial nomination still adds 600 points if you qualify for an enhanced stream. A [CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) can estimate your current score based on age, education, work experience, and language ability.

Study permit policy is unchanged. If you're a current student, the Post-Arrival Letter of Acceptance (PAL) policy remains in effect for those with new study permits. International mobility, tuition fees, and work permit eligibility for students remain as they were.

Work permit requirements have not shifted. To pursue PNP streams in most provinces, you still need a valid work permit and a specific job offer (for employer-sponsored streams) or provincial graduation credentials (for graduate streams).

Criminality, security, and health checks remain mandatory. No regulation change removes these admissibility checks. IRCC still owns these decisions fully.

## Who This Helps and Who It Hurts

**Short answer:** The 91,500 increase and provincial-control shift help applicants with genuine provincial ties (real job offers, real graduate connections) and reduces federal-stage rejection risk; it hurts applicants targeting closed Ontario Express Entry streams, those in provinces with declining allocations like BC, and those attempting to game the system.

The 91,500 allocation increase helps applicants with genuine provincial ties. If your work offer is real, your employer relationship is real, or your graduation from a provincial school is recent, the increased allocations mean shorter wait times and higher odds of nomination.

The March 30 regulatory shift helps applicants once provinces nominate them. Rejection at the IRCC stage becomes less likely. For applicants from regions where IRCC officer bias or miscommunication has been a concern, provincial control of intent and establishment criteria is an improvement.

The increased allocation hurts applicants in provinces with declining allocations (British Columbia saw a slight decrease) or those targeting closed streams (Ontario's Express Entry streams remain suspended). It also hurts applicants trying to game the system. Provinces now own eligibility decisions fully. They face no federal override option. Bad-faith nominees face provincial investigation, not just IRCC questioning.

The shift away from Express Entry streams in Ontario hurts applicants who achieved high [CRS scores](/tools/crs-calculator) but lack a specific Ontario employer or Ontario graduation. They are shut out of the 600-point bonus path and must wait in the base PNP queue (13 months plus provincial processing).

## A Note on Diaspora Access and Tech Pathways

**Short answer:** For applicants already in Canada on study or work permits, Saskatchewan adding technology to priority sectors and Alberta Express Entry Stream for Priority Sectors (manufacturing, construction, aviation, agriculture) create practical paths for engineers, developers, and tradespeople already working in Canada.

For applicants already in Canada on study permits or work permits, the provincial allocations create opportunity. Saskatchewan's addition of technology to its priority sectors and Alberta's Express Entry Stream for Priority Sectors (which includes manufacturing and skilled trades) offer practical paths for engineers, developers, and skilled tradespeople already working in Canada.

For overseas applicants, PAL policy for new study permits remains unchanged. Obtaining a study permit, graduating, then applying through a provincial graduate stream is still viable, but timelines are 2+ years before you can even apply for PNP.

For those from Iran, the Middle East, and South Asia who have already migrated to Canada on other visa categories or study permits, the enlarged provincial allocations and the regulatory shift that strengthens provincial nominations mean your path forward is stronger than it was six months ago.

## What to Do Next

PNP rules vary widely by province and the wrong choice can cost you 12+ months. The allocation increases and the regulatory shift reduce some risks, but choosing the right province and stream requires understanding your credentials against provincial priorities.

Book a consultation to figure out which province actually fits your profile and timeline. Our RCIC team has nominated clients across all 11 PNPs and tracks every regulation change. Visit [gofarglobal.com/appointment](/appointment) to book.
