# Canadian Citizenship Processing Time Drops to 12 Months in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canadian-citizenship-processing-time-12-months-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-04-24
Author: Go Far Global Team

> After five years of ballooning wait times that pushed Canadian citizenship processing time past three years at its worst, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has...

*As of June 9, 2026.*

After five years of ballooning wait times that pushed **Canadian citizenship processing time** past three years at its worst, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has quietly rebuilt the system. The citizenship grant now processes in roughly a year, down from a 38-month peak in 2023 and finally back inside the long-promised service standard. IRCC publishes the live figure on its [processing times dashboard](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html), which is the only number you should trust month to month.

For the permanent residents currently sitting in the citizenship queue, that is the first genuinely good news since the pandemic. For the roughly 1.5 million PRs who are eligible to apply but have been holding off because of the backlog, it is a signal: the window is open again.

This article covers what actually changed, what the new **canada citizenship processing time** looks like at each stage, how to check your own file's position, the physical-presence rule that decides eligibility, and whether you should apply now or wait.

## What Is the Current Processing Time for Canadian Citizenship?

The current citizenship grant processes in about a year from application to oath, the long-standing IRCC service standard for the bulk of files. The exact figure moves month to month and is published on the official IRCC processing times dashboard. As of mid-2026 the dashboard shows roughly 12 months for a straightforward grant application, down from a 38-month peak in 2023. Files flagged for residency questions, security review, or document gaps fall outside that window and run longer. Always check the live [IRCC processing times dashboard](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) for your situation before you plan around a date, because IRCC updates it regularly and the headline number can shift.

IRCC's official dashboard breaks the journey into stages:

| Stage | Time |
|-------|------|
| Application submission to decision | ~12 months |
| Test invitation | 4 to 8 months after Acknowledgment of Receipt (AOR) |
| Citizenship ceremony (oath) | 1 to 3 months after test pass |
| **Total: submission to oath** | **~12 to 18 months** |

The headline figure is IRCC's service standard for the majority of citizenship grant applications. The 12-to-18-month range comes in because a minority of files carry security flags, residency questions, or document gaps that push them past the standard.

For context, here is what the same journey looked like in recent years:

| Year | Citizenship processing time |
|------|------------------------------|
| 2020 (pre-pandemic) | 12 months |
| 2022 | 24 months |
| 2023 (peak) | **38 months** |
| 2024 | 27 months |
| 2025 | 18 months |
| February 2026 | 14 months |
| **Mid-2026** | **~12 months** |

The 2023 peak was the largest backlog Canadian citizenship has ever had. The recovery to roughly a year in two and a half years is the single largest operational turnaround IRCC has delivered since the Express Entry launch in 2015.

## What Actually Changed to Cut the Wait?

Four reforms drove the drop. Mandatory online applications since October 2024 cut intake errors by an order of magnitude. Virtual citizenship testing replaced the in-person testing bottleneck. Virtual oath ceremonies clear far faster than in-person slots. And new processing-officer hires funded in the 2024 federal budget reached full productivity in late 2025. None of these is glamorous on its own. Together they rebuilt throughput without changing a single eligibility rule, which is why a PR who qualified in 2023 and one who qualifies today face the same requirements but very different wait times.

The four specific moves:

1. **Mandatory online applications.** As of October 2024, IRCC moved all grant applications into the citizenship portal. Paper files create three to five times more rework because of missing signatures, photo mismatches, and ID legibility issues. Forcing digital submission cut intake errors sharply. You can see the current process on the IRCC [how to apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/how.html) page.

2. **Virtual testing at scale.** Citizenship knowledge tests are now conducted online for most applicants. The in-person testing bottleneck, which required booking IRCC offices, proctored rooms, and officer availability, collapsed once the test moved to a home computer with webcam monitoring.

3. **Virtual oath ceremonies** for applicants who choose them. In-person ceremonies still run, but applicants who want to skip the wait for a physical slot can take the oath online. Virtual ceremonies clear far faster than in-person ones, which removes the last big bottleneck at the end of the file.

4. **Processing officer hires.** The federal government funded new citizenship officer roles in the 2024 budget, and those hires reached full productivity in late 2025. This is the least visible but probably the most important lever.

## How Long Does It Take to Get Canadian Citizenship After PR?

If you already hold permanent resident (PR) status and meet the physical-presence rule, expect roughly 12 months from the day IRCC receives a clean application to the day you take the oath, plus the time it takes you to first qualify. You cannot apply the moment you land. You must first accumulate 1,095 days of physical presence in Canada during the five years before you sign the application. Most PRs reach that point three to four years after landing, depending on travel. Once you submit, the processing clock runs about a year for a straightforward file. So the realistic PR-to-citizen span is closer to four to five years total: the qualifying wait plus the processing wait.

Here is the realistic **Canadian citizenship application time** to oath, step by step, once you submit.

### Months 0 to 2: Intake and Acknowledgment of Receipt (AOR)

You submit online through the portal and IRCC performs a completeness check. If your file is complete, your AOR typically arrives within 4 to 8 weeks. If your file is missing documents, the most common misses being wrong photo dimensions, an incomplete residency calculation, or missing tax records for the qualifying period, you get a letter requesting the missing items before the AOR clock starts. That alone can add two to four months.

### Months 2 to 6: Background and Residency Verification

After AOR, IRCC verifies your residency obligation (1,095 days of physical presence in Canada during the five years before applying), your tax filing history for each year you were required to file, your criminal admissibility through domestic and police checks, and your language proof at Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) level 4 in English or French. Files where residency is clean and taxes are filed move through this stage fast. The most common delays are gaps in residency evidence for applicants who travel frequently for work.

### Months 6 to 10: Test Invitation

If your background check clears, you get a test invitation by email. The test covers Discover Canada, the official civics and history study guide. Virtual tests are typically scheduled within two to four weeks of the invitation. In-person tests, for applicants who opt in, may wait four to eight weeks. After a pass, your file moves to the ceremony queue. The IRCC [after you apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/after.html) page lays out the test and ceremony steps in order.

### Months 10 to 12: Oath Ceremony

This is where most of the end-of-process wait sits. Virtual ceremonies are typically scheduled within four to six weeks of test pass. In-person ceremonies can take six to twelve weeks depending on which regional office handles your file. Total from submission to oath for a straightforward file is about 10 to 14 months.

## What Are the Physical Presence Requirements for Canadian Citizenship?

To qualify for a citizenship grant, you must have been physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days (three years) during the five years immediately before the date you sign your application, and that five-year window must include at least 730 days as a permanent resident. IRCC confirms the 1,095-day rule on its [who can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility.html) page. Time spent in Canada as a temporary resident or protected person before becoming a PR can count for up to 365 days at half-day credit. You also need to have filed taxes for at least three of the five years if you were required to file. Count carefully: a borderline application sitting exactly at 1,095 days with no buffer is the single most common reason a file slips into the slow lane.

A short worked example. Say you became a PR on January 1, 2022, after one year on a work permit. By June 2026 you have spent most of your time in Canada with a few short trips abroad. If your physical-presence total clears 1,095 days inside the five-year window ending on your signature date, you can apply. If you travel heavily for work, run the math with a margin of several weeks rather than a few days, because IRCC counts the exact days and a miscalculation triggers a request for evidence that adds months.

## How Can You Speed Up Canadian Citizenship Processing?

You can request urgent processing in narrow circumstances, and IRCC can compress a roughly 12-month file to about two to three months when you provide documentary proof. The qualifying grounds are a serious illness or death in the immediate family requiring travel on a Canadian passport, a job that mandates Canadian citizenship (defence, security, or government roles), imminent adoption travel, or the risk of losing a professional license that requires citizenship. A verbal claim of urgency is not enough. IRCC requires documents that prove the urgency, and applications without that evidence are rejected and returned to the standard queue. The full criteria are on the IRCC [urgent processing](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/how/urgent.html) page.

The most reliable way to keep a normal file fast is to submit it clean. The applications that fall outside the service standard almost always have a residency miscalculation, a missing tax year, or a photo or document quality issue that an applicant could have caught before submitting. There is no paid fast-track outside the documented urgent-processing grounds, so be skeptical of any service that promises to jump the queue for a fee.

## What Is the Current Wait Time If You Are Already in the Queue?

The queue is moving steadily, and throughput is the highest it has been since before the pandemic. Files submitted in 2024 are now finishing their final ceremony stages. Files submitted in the first half of 2025 are approaching their test invitation. Files submitted in late 2025 and early 2026 are in early background verification. If you submitted in 2024 and have heard nothing, the most common reason is a missing piece in the residency calculation rather than a system delay. Log into your IRCC secure account and check for any open messages before assuming your file is simply waiting in line.

What this means by submission cohort:

- Files submitted in **2024** are finishing their final ceremony stages
- Files submitted in **January to June 2025** are approaching their test invitation
- Files submitted in **late 2025 and early 2026** are in early background verification

If your AOR is more than six months old and no test invitation has arrived, the [check your application status](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-status.html) page explains how to confirm whether your file is progressing or stuck on an unread document request.

## How Do You Check Your Own Canadian Citizenship Wait Time?

Use three tools, ranked by how useful they actually are. First, the official IRCC processing times dashboard gives the current monthly estimate but not your queue position, so use it for realistic expectations. Second, your IRCC secure account shows your specific file status, messages, and any document requests, and you should check it weekly once your AOR is six or more months old. Third, the application status tool is the official channel for confirming where your file sits. Avoid third-party trackers, because they guess at numbers IRCC does not publish per file.

The three official tools:

1. **[IRCC processing times dashboard](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html)** for the current monthly estimate.
2. **[IRCC secure account](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/account.html)** for your specific file status, messages, and document requests. Check weekly once your AOR is six or more months old.
3. **[Check application status](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-status.html)** for the official progress channel.

For monthly breakdowns we update whenever IRCC publishes new dashboard numbers, see our dedicated **[Canadian citizenship processing time page](/immigration/processing-times/citizenship)**.

## How Long After Citizenship Until You Get a Canadian Passport?

Once you take the oath you become a citizen, but you still need to apply for a passport separately, and a first adult passport typically takes a few weeks to a couple of months to issue depending on whether you apply in person or by mail and on current passport volumes. The oath ceremony does not produce a passport automatically. You receive a citizenship certificate, then you submit a passport application with that certificate as proof of citizenship. If you need a Canadian passport for travel in 2027, build the timeline backward: submit your citizenship file in 2026, take the oath, then apply for the passport with a buffer of at least a few months. Current passport processing details are on the IRCC [Canadian passports](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-passports.html) page, which is the only source that reflects live passport wait times.

## Can You Leave Canada While Waiting for Citizenship?

Yes. You can travel outside Canada while your citizenship application is in process, as long as you keep meeting your permanent resident obligations and you are available to attend your test and oath when scheduled. Your PR status does not lapse simply because a citizenship application is pending, and IRCC does not bar travel during processing. The practical risks are timing ones: a test invitation or oath date can land while you are abroad, and missing either without rescheduling delays your file. Keep your contact details current in your IRCC secure account, watch for messages, and avoid long trips during the months when a test or ceremony invitation is likely. If you are also close to a PR card renewal, manage that separately, because a citizenship application does not extend or replace your PR card.

## What Does It Cost to Apply for Canadian Citizenship?

The citizenship grant carries a government processing fee plus a right-of-citizenship fee for adults, and the current amounts are published on the official IRCC fee schedule. Fees change, so confirm the exact figures on the IRCC [citizenship and immigration application fees](https://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/fees/index.asp) page before you pay rather than relying on any third-party summary. Minors applying for a grant pay a lower fee with no right-of-citizenship component. You pay online through the portal at the time you submit, and an incomplete or missing payment is one of the routine reasons a file is returned before the AOR clock even starts. Budget for the fee plus the cost of any documents you need to gather, such as language test results or translations, which are not part of the IRCC fee but are part of the real cost of applying.

## Should You Apply for Canadian Citizenship Now?

Apply now if you cleanly meet the 1,095-day physical-presence rule and have been waiting out the backlog, if you will need a Canadian passport in 2027, or if a pending job move favours citizenship. The window that PRs have been waiting for is open, and submitting before a new backlog builds is the smart play. Wait if your residency total is borderline at exactly 1,095 days with no margin, or if you have had travel-heavy years that need careful documentation. A borderline file that triggers a request for evidence costs more time than the few months you would spend building a buffer.

Three profiles where the answer is clearly yes:

1. **Permanent residents who cleanly met the 1,095-day rule and have been waiting out the backlog.** The window you have been waiting for is open. Submit before a new backlog builds.

2. **PRs who need a passport soon.** A first Canadian passport takes time to issue after the oath. If you want one in 2027, submit the citizenship file in 2026.

3. **PRs with pending job moves that favour citizenship.** Federal jobs, security clearances, and some regulated professions materially prefer citizens. A roughly 12-month processing time is now shorter than most hiring cycles.

Two profiles where waiting might be smarter:

1. **Applicants with borderline residency.** If you are at 1,095 days with no margin, waiting a few months to build a buffer prevents refusals that cost more time than they save.

2. **Recent travel-heavy years.** If you have spent significant time outside Canada since getting PR, your residency calculation needs tight paperwork. Apply only after you have the travel history documented.

A note for newcomers weighing a career pivot while they wait: anyone thinking about self-employment to bridge the gap should know that self-employed income does not count as qualifying work experience for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) under Express Entry. That does not affect your citizenship eligibility, which depends on physical presence rather than the type of work, but it matters for anyone also trying to keep an Express Entry profile alive.

## Common Questions About Canadian Citizenship Processing Time

Is the roughly 12-month timeline guaranteed? No. It is the service standard for the bulk of applications, not a promise. Files flagged for residency questions, security review, or document gaps take longer. Does applying as a family slow things down? No. IRCC processes family applications in parallel, but the slowest file sets the ceremony date if you want to take the oath together. What if your test invitation is late? If your AOR is more than six months old with no test invite, check your IRCC secure account for an unread message requesting a document, which is the most common cause.

A few more quick answers:

**Does your PR card need to be valid when you apply?** No. You do not need a valid PR card to apply for citizenship. You do need to prove you have met the 1,095-day physical-presence rule.

**Did the citizenship test change?** No. The test itself is unchanged: the same questions drawn from Discover Canada and the same passing threshold. What changed is how fast you reach the test after applying.

**Who can legally give you paid advice on your file?** Only a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) in good standing with the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC), a lawyer in good standing with a provincial or territorial law society, or a Quebec notary may give full paid immigration advice or represent you. Ontario paralegals are limited to advocacy before the Immigration and Refugee Board and cannot act as your full citizenship representative. Be wary of anyone outside those categories charging for representation.

## The Bottom Line

Canadian citizenship is back to its pre-pandemic service standard of about a year, with a functional queue and steady throughput. Applications submitted today land in a working system, not a broken one. If you have been waiting for the right time to apply, it has arrived. That said, a one-year timeline still rewards a clean file. The applications that fall outside the service standard almost always have a residency miscalculation, a missing tax year, or a document quality issue that could have been caught at submission.

If you are within three months of meeting the 1,095-day rule, start gathering documents now so you can submit the day you qualify. If you are considering urgent processing, assemble your supporting evidence before submitting, because the documentation requirement is strict. If you are already in the queue and unsure about your file, an RCIC review can tell you whether your delay is normal queue movement or a document gap you can fix.

Our RCIC-licensed team handles citizenship files alongside the broader [permanent residence pipeline](/immigration/permanent-residence). We can tell you honestly whether your case is ready to submit now or needs another few months of preparation.

# Canada Co-op Work Permit Eliminated April 2026: International Students Guide

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-co-op-work-permit-eliminated-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-04-24
Author: Go Far Global Team

> On April 1, 2026, IRCC scrapped the separate co-op work permit in Canada.

# Canada Co-op Work Permit Eliminated April 2026: What International Students Need to Know

*As of April 2026.*

On **April 1, 2026**, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) scrapped the separate **co-op work permit** in Canada. Post-secondary international students with a valid study permit can now complete mandatory internships, practicums, and co-op work terms **without a separate work permit application**. It is the single biggest administrative win for international students since the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) was expanded, and it quietly removes one of the most common bottlenecks in Canadian immigration.

In 2025 alone, IRCC issued nearly **120,000 co-op work permits**. Processing times routinely stretched past four months. Students missed placement start dates. Employers replaced international hires with domestic candidates to avoid the wait. Universities built entire advising teams around the paperwork. All of that is gone as of April 1.

This guide covers exactly what changed, who qualifies, what happens to co-op work permit applications already in flight, how the fee refund works, and what this signals for international student policy going forward.

## What Is a Co-op Work Permit and Why Did It Exist?

**Short answer:** Administrative code C32, a stand-alone work permit international students previously needed when their study program included a mandatory work component (co-op term, internship, or practicum). It existed because the study permit by itself did not authorize the work portion of the academic program.

A **co-op work permit**, administrative code C32, was a stand-alone work permit international students needed when their study program included a mandatory work component, which could include co-op terms, internships, clinical placements, or practicums.

The logic: a Canadian study permit only authorizes you to study. Any work in a classified job, even when required by your program, was technically work, not study, and needed its own authorization. Students had to apply for two permits, pay two application fees, and track two expiry dates.

In practice, this was paperwork duplication. Your enrolment confirmation already proved the co-op was mandatory. IRCC was processing 120,000 permits per year just to rubber-stamp that fact. The co-op work permit elimination removes the redundancy.

## What Changed on April 1, 2026?

**Short answer:** IRCC folded co-op work authorization into the study permit itself. If the work component is required to complete your program and forms part of your academic training, your study permit now authorizes you to work in that placement. No separate application, no separate fee.

IRCC folded co-op work authorization into the study permit itself. If the work component is **required to complete your program** and forms part of your academic training, your study permit now covers it. No separate application. No separate fee. No four-month processing wait.

| | Before April 1, 2026 | After April 1, 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Separate work permit needed? | Yes (administrative code C32) | No |
| Application fee | $155 CAD | $0 |
| Processing time | Up to 4 months | None (no application required) |
| Documents for employer | Study permit + co-op work permit | Study permit + DLI letter confirming mandatory co-op |

The [official IRCC notice](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/simplifying-co-op-work-permit-requirement-post-secondary-international-students.html) frames the change as "administrative simplification." There is no expansion of work authorization and no change to temporary resident volumes. This matters: it is not a loosening of rules, it is the removal of a redundant paperwork step.

## Who Qualifies Under the New Co-op Work Permit Rule?

**Short answer:** Four conditions: (1) valid study permit, (2) enrolled at a Designated Learning Institution (DLI) in a post-secondary program, (3) co-op/internship/practicum is REQUIRED to complete the program (not optional), (4) the work component is documented in your letter of acceptance or program curriculum.

The new rule applies if **all four** conditions are met:

1. You hold a **valid study permit**
2. You are enrolled at a **Designated Learning Institution (DLI)** in a post-secondary program
3. Your program requires a **mandatory work component** (co-op, internship, practicum, clinical placement, or equivalent) to graduate
4. The mandatory work component is **50% or less** of your overall program time

That 50% load limit is the hard cap. A program where work takes up more than half the total duration is no longer a study program for immigration purposes and would need a full work permit route.

"Mandatory" is the key word. Optional co-ops, voluntary internships, and work-integrated placements that are not required to graduate are not covered by the change. Those still require a work permit, though most students in that situation already qualify for the standard [24-hour-per-week off-campus work allowance](/news/international-student-off-campus-work-hours-canada-2026) without any additional paperwork.

## How Do You Apply for a Co-op Work Permit in 2026?

**Short answer:** You don't apply. Your existing study permit IS the work authorization for the mandatory placement. Bring your study permit and a DLI-issued letter confirming the co-op is mandatory; the employer can verify your authorization through IRCC's employer verification channel.

You don't. That is the entire point of the change. If you meet the four eligibility conditions above, your existing study permit is your [work authorization for the mandatory placement](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/intern.html). There is no form to fill, no portal submission, no photo to upload, no fee to pay.

What you and your employer will need on file:

- A copy of your **valid study permit**
- A **letter of enrolment** from your DLI confirming the work component is mandatory to complete your program
- Your **Social Insurance Number (SIN)**, which all temporary residents with work authorization can apply for at Service Canada
- Standard employment paperwork from your employer: employment contract, direct deposit form, T4 setup

No IRCC interaction is required for the work placement itself.

## What Happens to Co-op Work Permit Applications Already Submitted?

**Short answer:** Applications submitted BEFORE April 1, 2026: pending applications are being closed with a refund-of-fee notification. Applications submitted AFTER April 1 are not accepted. If you applied close to the cutover and got an approval, your co-op permit remains valid through its stated expiry.

This is the question dominating search traffic right now. If you applied **before** April 1, 2026, three things can be happening to your file:

### If Your Application Was Pending on April 1

IRCC is **automatically withdrawing all eligible and active co-op work permit applications** in the system. Students who were mid-process as of April 1, 2026 do not need to take any action:

- **No letter to write**
- **No cancellation form to submit**
- **No fee refund to chase**

IRCC processes the withdrawal server-side.

### Co-op Work Permit Fee Refund

Application fees paid for eligible co-op work permit applications that IRCC withdraws are **refunded automatically** to the original payment method. The refund timeline has historically been **four to eight weeks** based on similar IRCC administrative withdrawals. You will not receive an email-by-email status update, check your IRCC account and the payment card you used.

### If Your Co-op Work Permit Was Already Approved

If IRCC issued you a co-op work permit before April 1, 2026, it remains valid until its original expiry date. You do not need to replace it. You can:

- **Continue using it** alongside your study permit until it expires, or
- **Let it expire** and rely on the study permit going forward, no renewal is needed

Either approach is acceptable to IRCC and to your employer.

## Co-op Work Permit Extension: Is That Still a Thing?

**Short answer:** Not in the old sense. Extending a co-op work permit no longer applies for new cases. If your program extends beyond your study permit expiry (e.g., your co-op term shifts the graduation date), you extend the study permit itself, the work authorization follows automatically.

Short answer: no, not in the old sense. The concept of extending a co-op work permit no longer applies for new cases. If your program is extending (for example, your co-op phase starts later than your original permit anticipated), your **study permit extension** is what you renew, and your work authorization travels with it.

If you were planning to apply for a co-op work permit extension specifically (the old C32 renewal), that route is closed. Work directly on the study permit under the new rule.

## What Does the Co-op Work Permit Change Mean in Practice?

**Short answer:** For students: bring your offer letter, study permit, and DLI letter confirming the co-op is mandatory. Start the placement. No work permit required. For employers: verify the student's authorization through IRCC's employer verification channel using their study permit document number.

**For students.** Pick up your offer letter, show your study permit and your DLI's letter of enrolment confirming the co-op is mandatory, and start the placement. That is the new paper trail.

**For employers.** You were previously tracking two permits per international student: study permit + co-op work permit. You now track one. Compliance risk drops.

**For universities and colleges.** Your international student advising team likely spent significant capacity walking students through C32 applications, troubleshooting delays, and coordinating with employers during the four-month waits. That capacity is now freed for other high-impact advising. Waterloo, Toronto Metropolitan, Western, and other large co-op schools had built entire internal process guides around the old rule; those guides are now historical documents.

## What Other Changes to International Student Work Rules Are Coming?

**Short answer:** Part of IRCC's Forward Regulatory Plan 2026-2028. Three more changes in consultation: tighter restrictions on off-campus work hours (potentially reverting from 24 to 20 per week permanently), narrower PGWP field-of-study list, and PAL requirement extended to extensions filed inside Canada.

The April 1 co-op work permit elimination is the first piece of a larger package IRCC has signalled in its **Forward Regulatory Plan 2026-2028**. Three more changes are in consultation:

1. **Work authorization during study permit extension wait.** Students in implied status while waiting for a study permit extension currently lose the right to work during the gap. The proposed rule extends authorization through the decision.
2. **Work authorization during PGWP wait.** International graduates who submitted a [Post-Graduation Work Permit](/news/pgwp-post-graduation-work-permit-canada-2026) application typically wait in limbo without work status. The proposal extends implied-status work rights through the PGWP decision.
3. **Apprenticeship study permit removal.** Foreign apprentices meeting specific conditions would no longer need a study permit at all, recognizing apprenticeships as work-first rather than study-first programs.

None of those three have taken effect yet. They are in the consultation phase as of April 2026.

## How Does This Fit Into the Larger April 2026 Immigration Changes?

**Short answer:** One of eight immigration changes effective April 1, 2026. Others include: tightened Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) advertising exemptions, narrower spousal open work permit eligibility (TEER 0/1 only), revised PGWP field-of-study list, mandatory PAL for inland extensions, biometrics renewal cycle changes, and updates to the Express Entry category framework.

The co-op work permit elimination is one of [eight immigration changes effective April 1, 2026](/news/canada-immigration-changes-april-2026). The others include Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) advertising extensions, Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) delegation shifts, and tightened settlement service caps. The direction is consistent: IRCC is consolidating overlapping authorizations rather than expanding any single program. For international students, the pipeline from study permit to Permanent Residence (PR) is getting easier administratively even as competition for each PR spot is getting harder on the selection side. The [upcoming Federal High-Skilled Class replacing the Canadian Experience Class (CEC)](/news/canadian-experience-class-ending-federal-high-skilled-class) is the selection-side half of that story.

## Frequently Asked Questions

The following questions address the most common points of confusion about the co-op work permit elimination effective April 1, 2026. These answers apply to post-secondary international students at Designated Learning Institutions who hold valid study permits. If your situation is more complex, a consultation with a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) will clarify your specific options.

### What is the co-op work permit fee now?

There is no fee, because there is no separate application. The old co-op work permit application fee of **$155 CAD** no longer applies. Students who paid the fee for applications still in process on April 1 receive an automatic refund.

### Does the co-op work permit elimination extend my right to work off-campus?

No. The existing 24-hour-per-week off-campus work rule continues to apply separately. Mandatory co-op work is in addition to that allowance, not counted against it.

### If my program is at a non-DLI school, am I covered?

No. You must be enrolled at a **Designated Learning Institution**. Non-DLI enrolment disqualifies you from most student immigration benefits, including this one.

### What if my co-op placement is unpaid?

Paid or unpaid does not affect the rule. If the placement is mandatory to graduate and meets the 50% load limit, your study permit covers it.

### Does this change PGWP eligibility?

No. Your [PGWP](/news/pgwp-post-graduation-work-permit-canada-2026) eligibility still depends on completing a full program at a PGWP-eligible DLI. The co-op work permit change does not alter any PGWP criterion.

### Can I work outside the mandatory co-op placement?

Yes, subject to the standard 24 hours per week off-campus allowance when class is in session, and full-time during scheduled academic breaks.

### Does this affect my tuition or cost of living?

No. The change is purely administrative. Your program, fees, and enrolment status are unchanged.

### What if my employer or HR department asks for my "co-op work permit"?

Show them the [IRCC notice](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/notices/simplifying-co-op-work-permit-requirement-post-secondary-international-students.html) and your DLI's letter of enrolment confirming the co-op is mandatory. Most employer HR checklists are still catching up to the rule change.

## What Is the Bottom Line for International Students?

**Short answer:** For international students this is unambiguously good news. The biggest single source of paperwork delay in the student pipeline is gone. You start your co-op with your study permit, your letter of acceptance, and a DLI letter confirming the mandatory work component. No separate application, no separate fee.

For international students in Canada, this is unambiguous good news. The biggest single source of paperwork delay in the student pipeline is gone. You start your co-op with your study permit. Full stop. The $155 application fee disappears. The four-month processing wait disappears. For students in co-op programs at Canadian colleges and universities, the only authorization you need is the study permit already in hand.

For prospective students evaluating Canada vs. other destinations, the change simplifies one thing: work authorization once you are here. Study permit refusal rates have not changed. Proof of funds requirements have not changed. DLI selection still matters. [Common study permit refusal reasons](/news/study-permit-refused-canada-reasons-reapply) remain the biggest barrier at the intake stage.

## What Are the Next Steps for International Students?

If you are **currently holding a co-op work permit** approved before April 1, 2026, you do not need to switch anything. Your permit remains valid through its stated expiry date. You may continue using it alongside your study permit, or simply let it expire and rely on the study permit going forward.

If you were **in process when the rule changed**, check your IRCC account for the automatic withdrawal notification and your payment card for the fee refund.

If you are **a current or prospective student** trying to map your full pipeline from study permit to PGWP to [Canadian Experience Class replacement](/news/canadian-experience-class-ending-federal-high-skilled-class) under the new Federal High-Skilled Class, and weighing how the ongoing Express Entry changes affect your post-graduation route; a 30-minute consultation often saves months of wrong-path planning.

# Canadian Experience Class Is Ending: What Replaces the CEC in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canadian-experience-class-ending-federal-high-skilled-class
Category: News
Published: 2026-04-23
Author: Go Far Global Team

> IRCC plans to retire the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) along with the Federal Skilled Worker Program and Federal Skilled Trades Program.

# Canadian Experience Class Is Ending: What Replaces the CEC in 2026

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) plans to retire the **Canadian Experience Class (CEC)** along with the Federal Skilled Worker Program and Federal Skilled Trades Program. All three have been the backbone of [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) since the system launched in 2015. In their place, the department is designing a single unified stream called the **Federal High-Skilled Class**.

*As of April 23, 2026.*

The changes matter for anyone sitting in the Express Entry pool right now, anyone planning to submit a profile in the next 18 months, and every Canadian employer who has built recruitment around the CEC route. Here is exactly what is changing, when it is likely to happen, and what you should do before the rules shift.

## What replaces the Canadian Experience Class in the Federal High-Skilled class?

**Short answer:** Three programs become one, Federal Skilled Worker (FSW), CEC, and Federal Skilled Trades Program (FSTP) merge into the unified Federal High-Skilled Class with a single eligibility rule, Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 6 minimum across all four abilities, high school diploma verified via Educational Credential Assessment (ECA), Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) recalibrated to favour earnings and in-demand occupations, and category-based draws targeting specific occupations from the National Occupational Outlook rather than broad sectors.

| Today | Proposed under Federal High-Skilled Class |
|-------|-------------------------------------------|
| Three programs: FSW, CEC, FSTP | One unified program |
| Each program has different eligibility | Single eligibility rule for all applicants |
| Language requirements vary (CLB 5-7+) | CLB 6 across all four abilities for everyone |
| Mixed education floors | High school diploma minimum, verified via ECA |
| CRS rewards age, education, language, work experience | CRS recalibrated to favour earnings + in-demand occupations |
| Category-based draws by broad sector | Occupations identified through the [National Occupational Outlook](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/trend-analysis/job-market-reports) |

The CRS itself survives, but its inputs will be re-weighted. The **two biggest shifts** Ottawa has signalled are a move toward higher wages as a proxy for economic success, and a move away from rewarding raw Canadian work time without regard to the job's skill level.

## Why is Ottawa retiring the Canadian Experience Class?

**Short answer:** Three drivers, CEC candidates earned similar or lower wages than FSW candidates with no Canadian time so prior Canadian work proved a weak predictor of long-term earnings; the program rewarded proximity not skill, letting lower-skilled TEER-eligible workers outscore highly paid highly educated candidates; and three parallel programs created administrative drag.

The Canadian Experience Class was built on a simple idea: if you have already worked in Canada in a skilled job, you understand Canadian workplaces and are a low integration risk. That logic held up well when the program launched in 2015. Over a decade later, IRCC's own economic data tells a messier story.

Three specific frustrations drive the change:

1. **Wage outcomes didn't track Canadian experience.** Workers invited through the CEC earned, on average, similar or lower wages than Federal Skilled Worker candidates with no prior Canadian time. Ottawa now argues that prior Canadian work is a weak predictor of long-term earnings.
2. **The program rewarded proximity, not skill.** A candidate who held a lower-skilled but still TEER-eligible job for two years could out-score a highly paid, highly educated candidate with no Canadian time, regardless of which one was actually contributing more to the economy.
3. **Three parallel programs created administrative drag.** Separate eligibility rules, separate National Occupational Classification (NOC) treatment, and separate draw types forced IRCC to maintain three sets of operational guidelines. A single class collapses that overhead.

## What do we know about the Federal High-Skilled Class?

**Short answer:** New eligibility floor, 1 year skilled Canadian work OR a validated job offer (TEER 0/1/2/3), CLB 6 across all four abilities, high school diploma verified via mandatory ECA; CRS recalibrated for earnings (hourly wage bands), boosted job offer points, and in-demand occupation multiplier from the National Occupational Outlook; raw Canadian work time beyond 1 year, sibling-in-Canada bonus, and study-in-Canada bonus likely de-emphasized.

### Eligibility Floor

Every candidate, regardless of stream history, will need:
- **One year of skilled Canadian work experience OR a validated job offer** (TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3)
- **Minimum CLB 6** across all four language abilities (listening, reading, speaking, writing), in English or French
- **High school diploma or equivalent**, verified through an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA)

That last piece is a significant change. The [Canadian Experience Class today does not require an ECA](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/canadian-experience-class.html) because your Canadian experience is the proof of employability. Under the new class, every applicant, Canadian-experienced or not, completes an ECA.

### CRS Recalibration

IRCC will keep the CRS but re-weight the factors. Three signalled moves:

- **Earnings weighting.** Points tied to hourly wage bands or declared income, with higher wages scoring higher.
- **Job offer points boosted.** A validated job offer from a Canadian employer becomes a stronger CRS signal than it is today.
- **In-demand occupation multiplier.** Candidates working in or offered jobs in occupations flagged on the National Occupational Outlook receive a targeted boost.

Factors likely to be de-emphasized: raw Canadian work time beyond one year, sibling-in-Canada bonus, and potentially the study-in-Canada bonus. These have been publicly flagged as "weak predictors of economic outcomes" in the federal Forward Regulatory Plan.

### Timeline

IRCC has published this work in its [**Forward Regulatory Plan 2026-2028**](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/acts-regulations/forward-regulatory-plan/list/modernize-federal-high-skilled.html). Concrete steps:

| Stage | Expected date |
|-------|---------------|
| [Public consultations on Express Entry reforms](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry-reforms.html) | Spring 2026 |
| Draft regulations | Late 2026 or early 2027 |
| Final regulations in Canada Gazette Part II | Mid-to-late 2027 |
| First invitations under new class | Late 2027 or 2028 |

Nothing changes today. Candidates currently in the pool continue to receive Invitations to Apply (ITAs) under existing rules. Applications already submitted are grandfathered. But anyone planning their timeline around a 2027-2028 submission needs to assume the new rules apply.

## What should you do before the CEC closes?

**Short answer:** If already in the pool, stay and monitor language test expiry, annual age deductions, and 12-month profile freshness; if entering the pool, Track A submits now under current rules if you have 1 year Canadian work, Track B builds toward the new class with a validated job offer, occupation on the shortage list, completed ECA, and CLB 7 instead of CLB 6 to stay competitive.

### If You Are Already in the Pool

Stay in the pool. Your current profile continues to receive draws under CEC, FSW, or FSTP rules until the transition date. Three things to monitor:

1. **Language test expiry.** If your IELTS, CELPIP, TEF, or TCF expires before you receive an ITA, your score freezes and may disqualify you from draws you would have otherwise entered.
2. **Age deductions.** CRS age points drop annually after 30. A profile that scores 470 today may score 465 next year with no other change.
3. **Express Entry profile freshness.** Profiles expire after 12 months and must be resubmitted.

If your CRS is close to the CEC cutoff (recent draws have cleared at 507-515), focus the next 90 days on getting an ITA under current rules rather than waiting for the new system.

### If You Are Planning to Enter the Pool

Two tracks make sense.

**Track A, Submit now under current rules.** If you have one year of Canadian skilled work, submit a CEC profile immediately. Current cutoffs are high (around 515) but the pool is thinner than it was in late 2024. See our full breakdown of [how to improve your CRS score](/news/how-to-improve-crs-score-2026) for tactical tips.

**Track B, Build toward the new class.** If you do not yet have Canadian work experience and cannot get one in the next 12 months, orient your preparation toward what the Federal High-Skilled Class will reward:

- Target a validated job offer from a Canadian employer before submitting
- Make sure your occupation is on the [National Occupational Outlook](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/trend-analysis/job-market-reports) list of shortage roles
- Complete an ECA now, the three-to-four-month turnaround is a bottleneck for most applicants
- Hit CLB 7 on your language test, not just CLB 6, to stay competitive when occupation-weighted CRS goes live

### If You Are on a Work Permit

The [Post-Graduation Work Permit](/news/pgwp-post-graduation-work-permit-canada-2026) route into CEC remains viable through the transition. The mechanics of "get PGWP → bank one year of skilled Canadian work → enter CEC pool" still deliver ITAs at today's cutoffs. But bank the year fast. A candidate who qualifies in late 2026 may face the new rules before their profile gets drawn.

Provincial Nominee Programs are another route worth considering. A [Provincial Nominee Program (PNP)](/immigration/provincial-nominee) nomination adds 600 CRS points and functionally guarantees an ITA regardless of which federal program is active.

## Will CEC continue in 2026 and what are the most common questions?

**Short answer:** Common answers, applications submitted before new regulations take effect are processed under current rules; IRCC has not publicly committed to a grace period but a 2015-style short overlap window is expected; job offers are not mandatory (one year Canadian work or job offer satisfies eligibility), but offers will score higher CRS than today; category-based draws continue with more granular occupation targeting.

**Will my existing application under CEC be processed?** Yes. Applications submitted before the new regulations take effect are processed under the rules that existed at the time of submission.

**Will there be a grace period after the new class opens?** IRCC has not committed to one publicly. Based on how the 2015 Express Entry launch was handled, we expect a short overlap where CEC applications submitted during a final window are processed, but new profiles are only accepted under the new class.

**Does a job offer become mandatory?** Not mandatory. A validated job offer OR one year of skilled Canadian work experience satisfies the eligibility floor. The difference is CRS weight, offers will score higher than they do today.

**What happens to category-based draws?** They are expected to continue, but with more granular occupation targeting based on the National Occupational Outlook rather than broad sector categories like "healthcare" or "STEM."

**Should I switch to a different pathway now?** If CRS through Express Entry looks out of reach under either the current or the proposed system, [PNP programs](/immigration/provincial-nominee) and regional pilots are your realistic alternatives. Book a consultation to run the math on your specific file.

## What does the end of the Canadian Experience Class mean for applicants?

**Short answer:** CEC is not disappearing overnight but its era is ending, the Federal High-Skilled Class rewards earnings, job offers, and shortage occupations over raw Canadian seat-time; if you have CEC-eligible experience submit now while the current system rewards it; if not, build toward what the new class will measure rather than waiting for final regulations.

The Canadian Experience Class is not disappearing overnight, but its era is ending. The Federal High-Skilled Class is designed to reward earnings, job offers, and shortage occupations over raw Canadian seat-time. That is a real pivot in the philosophy of Canadian economic immigration, and it will sort winners from losers very differently than the CEC did.

If you already have CEC-eligible work experience, the smart move is to submit now, while the current system still rewards it. If you do not, build toward what the new class will measure. Either way, do not wait for the final regulations to finish preparing.

## What are your next steps before the Federal High-Skilled Class takes effect?

**Short answer:** Go Far Global RCIC team has been reviewing the Forward Regulatory Plan and rebuilding client strategy briefs to reflect both pathways simultaneously, book a free consultation to run your file against both systems and identify which one wins for your specific timeline.

Our RCIC-licensed team has been reviewing the Forward Regulatory Plan since it was published and we have been rebuilding our client strategy briefs to reflect both pathways simultaneously. If you are trying to decide whether to submit under current rules, pivot to a PNP, or pause until the new class opens, that call is worth an hour.

[Book a free consultation](/appointment) to run your file against both systems. We will tell you which one actually wins for your timeline.

# Breaking: Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver Excluded From Canada's 2026 TR to PR Pathway

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/tr-to-pr-cities-excluded-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-04-21
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab has confirmed that Canada's new Temporary Resident to Permanent Resident (TR to PR) pathway will shut out workers living in the country's...

# Breaking: Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver Excluded From Canada's 2026 TR to PR Pathway

> **UPDATE, April 23, 2026:** Portal opens in **May 2026** and accepts only 16,500 applications in the first round. Every day before the portal opens is a document-preparation day. **[Read the full TR to PR application checklist](/news/tr-to-pr-portal-may-2026-application-checklist)**.


Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab has confirmed that Canada's new **Temporary Resident to Permanent Resident (TR to PR) pathway** will shut out workers living in the country's largest cities. Speaking in an April 18, 2026 interview on the "I'm Canada" podcast, Minister Diab said the program will exclude every Census Metropolitan Area (CMA), a definition that covers roughly 84 percent of Canada's population.

For the 1.9 million temporary residents waiting on a permanent route, the location rule is the single biggest eligibility filter announced so far. If you live and work in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, or any other CMA, you will not qualify under the current design. Here is what we know, what we do not, and what you should do in the next two weeks.

*As of April 21, 2026.*

## Which cities are excluded from the TR to PR 2026 pathway?

**Short answer:** The TR to PR 2026 pathway launched in March 2026 with 33,000 PR spots across 2026-2027, but Minister Diab's April 18 statement clarified that all 41 Census Metropolitan Areas (including Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal) are excluded. Workers in any CMA cannot apply through this pathway.

The pathway [quietly launched in March 2026](/news/canada-tr-to-pr-pathway-33000-workers-2026) with 33,000 permanent residence spots spread across 2026 and 2027. Until Minister Diab's April 18 statement, the geographic rules were unclear. The new direction is blunt:

- **All 41 Census Metropolitan Areas are excluded.** That is every Canadian urban region with an urban core of 100,000 or more residents, per Statistics Canada's definition.
- **Only workers in rural and smaller communities qualify.** The federal government wants this pathway to reinforce regional populations and labour markets outside major cities.
- **Full selection criteria are still pending.** Minister Diab said the remaining details would be published "in the coming weeks" after April 18.

## Which cities are not eligible for the TR to PR pathway in Canada?

**Short answer:** All 41 Statistics Canada-defined Census Metropolitan Areas are excluded: Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary, Edmonton, Ottawa-Gatineau, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, London, Windsor, Quebec City, Halifax, Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon, Victoria, and 25 others. Only workers in smaller cities, towns, and rural communities qualify.

The CMA classification sweeps in far more than the three cities the minister named. If you work in any of the following regions, the TR to PR pathway is currently closed to you:

| Province | Excluded Census Metropolitan Areas |
|----------|-----------------------------------|
| Ontario | Toronto, Ottawa-Gatineau (Ontario side), Hamilton, Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo, London, Oshawa, St. Catharines-Niagara, Windsor, Barrie, Guelph, Kingston, Brantford, Peterborough, Belleville-Quinte West |
| Quebec | Montreal, Quebec City, Gatineau, Sherbrooke, Trois-Rivières, Saguenay, Drummondville |
| British Columbia | Vancouver, Victoria, Kelowna, Abbotsford-Mission, Nanaimo, Chilliwack |
| Alberta | Calgary, Edmonton, Red Deer, Lethbridge |
| Manitoba | Winnipeg |
| Saskatchewan | Regina, Saskatoon |
| Nova Scotia | Halifax |
| New Brunswick | Moncton, Saint John, Fredericton |
| Newfoundland and Labrador | St. John's |

A CMA is not just the downtown core. It includes surrounding municipalities with strong commuter ties. Census Canada's 2021 definition covers a population of at least 100,000 with 50,000 or more in the urban core. That is why places like Oshawa and Fredericton appear on the list even though they are not usually thought of as big cities.

## Why is IRCC limiting the TR to PR 2026 pathway to rural and smaller communities?

**Short answer:** Three drivers: housing and infrastructure pressure in the largest urban centres, persistent labour shortages in rural and small-town communities that the existing immigration system has not solved, and a political signal that federal admissions should support smaller communities rather than amplifying the urban concentration trend.

The rural focus is deliberate, not symbolic. Three pressures line up behind the decision:

1. **Housing and infrastructure.** Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver have absorbed most of Canada's recent population growth. Vacancy rates are near record lows and rents have climbed hard. Steering 33,000 new permanent residents to smaller communities takes pressure off the three markets that have the least room to grow.
2. **Regional labour shortages.** Rural Canada is losing working-age residents to urban centres. Long-term care homes, farms, food plants, trucking firms, and local hospitals outside the CMAs are the loudest voices asking Ottawa for workers. The new pathway answers that demand directly.
3. **Political math.** A program that rewards workers who stay in smaller ridings is easier to defend to provinces and to MPs outside the big three metros.

## Who can still qualify for the TR to PR 2026 pathway?

**Short answer:** Workers in Census Agglomerations (CAs) with populations between 10,000 and 99,999, plus any rural community below that threshold, remain eligible for the TR to PR 2026 pathway. The exclusion applies strictly to Census Metropolitan Areas, so smaller cities like Sudbury, Kingston, Sarnia, and Lethbridge stay in scope despite being substantial regional centres.

"Rural" for this pathway means anything outside the 41 CMAs. That is a much wider net than it sounds. You may qualify if you live and work in:

- **Census Agglomerations (CAs)** with populations between 10,000 and 99,999. Examples include Sault Ste. Marie, Thunder Bay, North Bay, Timmins, Grande Prairie, Wood Buffalo, and Prince George.
- **Rural municipalities** outside any CA or CMA. Farm country, resource towns, Atlantic fishing communities, and Prairie service centres sit here.
- **Designated communities** under existing federal rural programs, including the [Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-northern-immigration-pilot.html) and the new Rural Community Immigration Pilot.

Priority occupations signalled by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) so far match the gaps in these communities: healthcare (personal support workers, registered practical nurses, home care aides), skilled trades, agriculture and agri-food, transportation, and [care services](/immigration/work-permit).

## What TR to PR 2026 eligibility details has IRCC not yet confirmed?

**Short answer:** Open questions as of April 18: whether existing urban applicants are grandfathered, the minimum Canadian work experience threshold for 2026 (6 months, 12 months, or longer), exact National Occupational Classification (NOC) code list per priority sector, and whether telework arrangements with a non-CMA employer count even when the worker physically lives in a CMA.

Minister Diab's statement created more questions than it resolved. The full program guide has not been published. Until it lands, the following points are open:

- **Are existing urban applicants grandfathered?** Workers who applied before the CMA rule was public have no guidance yet. If you already submitted, do not withdraw. Wait for the final criteria.
- **Does relocating to a rural community count?** It is unclear whether you can move out of a CMA now and count future work time, or whether only your current or past rural employment qualifies.
- **Are there provincial caps?** 33,000 spots across the country is a small allocation. IRCC has not said whether allocations will be split by province or first-come, first-served.
- **How is "living" verified?** The program will almost certainly demand proof of rural residence, rural employment, and tax records showing genuine ties to the community.
- **What happens to dependents in a CMA?** Spouses working in a nearby CMA, or children enrolled in urban schools, may complicate eligibility. No guidance yet.

## What are my options if I live in a city excluded from TR to PR 2026?

**Short answer:** If you live in Toronto, Montreal, or Vancouver and counted on TR to PR as your backup, you need a new plan. Express Entry (with category-based draws), Provincial Nominee Programs (which can be employer-driven), and the Atlantic Immigration Program remain open to urban workers and accept applicants from any Canadian city.

If you live in Toronto, Montreal, or Vancouver and were counting on TR to PR as your backup plan, you need a new backup plan. [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) and [Provincial Nominee Programs](/immigration/provincial-nominee) are now your realistic options.

| Feature | TR to PR 2026 (post-April 18) | Express Entry | Provincial Nominee |
|---------|-------------------------------|---------------|--------------------|
| CMA workers eligible | **No** | Yes | Yes (most streams) |
| Minimum language | Likely Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 4 | CLB 7 (Federal Skilled Worker/FSW) | Varies |
| Job offer required | Work permit, rural employer | Not always | Often yes |
| Total spots | 33,000 over two years | Largest annual intake | Roughly 120,000 in 2026 |
| Typical processing | TBD (12-18 months estimated) | ~6 months | 12-24 months |

Workers in rural communities now have two advantages: they can apply through the TR to PR pathway *and* they still qualify for PNP streams that favour smaller-community employment. Urban workers lose one route but keep the others.

## What steps should I take to prepare for the TR to PR 2026 pathway?

**Short answer:** Six actions: (1) confirm your employer's municipal address against Statistics Canada's CMA list, (2) verify your NOC code falls under the priority sectors, (3) compile work-permit and Canadian work-experience evidence, (4) order language test scores, (5) prepare a relocation contingency if you live in a CMA, (6) book a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) consultation if your case is borderline.

Regardless of which route fits you, six actions protect your file right now.

1. **Confirm your CMA status.** Look up your employer's municipal address on the [Statistics Canada CMA list](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/). If it falls inside a CMA boundary, you are out for TR to PR.
2. **Document rural employment evidence.** Pay stubs, T4 slips, employer letters with the work location, and a lease or utility bill that proves you live outside a CMA.
3. **Book language testing now.** IELTS General, CELPIP, TEF Canada, or TCF Canada bookings are running four to eight weeks out. Do not wait for the full program guide.
4. **Get an Educational Credential Assessment** if you have foreign education. WES, ICES, and IQAS are each taking two to three months.
5. **Keep your work permit valid.** Renew early. If your application is close to expiry, look at a Bridging Open Work Permit.
6. **File your taxes.** The government has repeatedly flagged tax compliance as an eligibility factor. Fix any missing years now.

## What TR to PR updates should I watch for before the portal opens?

**Short answer:** Watch for four IRCC announcements: the official list of eligible occupations with NOC codes, the minimum Canadian work experience requirement, the official language proficiency threshold, and the application portal opening date with capacity details. Minister Diab said these would be released in the weeks after April 18, 2026.

Minister Diab flagged that the next wave of details is coming "in the coming weeks." Watch for four things:

- Official list of eligible occupations with NOC codes
- Minimum Canadian work experience threshold (6 months, 12 months, or 24 months)
- Official language threshold
- Whether 2026 and 2027 intake will be front-loaded or split evenly

We will update our [immigration news section](/news) the moment IRCC publishes the program guide.

## How can a licensed RCIC help me find the right PR pathway?

**Short answer:** A licensed RCIC can review your current status, map your situation against the TR to PR CMA restriction, and build a plan using Express Entry, Provincial Nominee Programs, or the rural pathway depending on where you live and work.

The CMA rule changes the math for thousands of files we are watching. If you live in a CMA, we can map your situation against [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry), [PNP streams](/immigration/provincial-nominee), and the [Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/rural-northern-immigration-pilot.html). If you live outside a CMA, we can start preparing your TR to PR file so that when the portal opens, you are at the front of the line.

The 2021 TR to PR pathway filled in a single day. With only 33,000 spots and a narrower eligible population, the 2026 program will move fast.
