# Canada's 2026–2028 Immigration Levels Plan: Every New Rule Explained

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-immigration-plan-2026-2028
Category: News
Published: 2026-04-18
Author: Go Far Global Team

> Canada stabilizes permanent resident admissions at 380,000/year while cutting temporary resident arrivals by 43%. Here's what changes for you.

Canada is admitting 380,000 permanent residents each year through 2028. That number holds steady, but everything around it is shifting.

In November 2025, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) released its [2026 to 2028 Immigration Levels Plan](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/corporate-initiatives/levels.html), and on April 8, 2026, announced plans to retire the [Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html) system as we know it. If you're applying for permanent residence, sponsoring family, coming as a student, or working in Canada, the next three years will look different than the last eleven.

Below is every material change, what it means for your situation, which pathways are getting faster or harder, and what to do now.

*As of April 2026.*

## What is in Canada’s 2026-2028 immigration plan?

**Short answer:** Canada's 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan locks permanent resident admissions at 380,000 per year (no growth from 2025), shifts the economic class share from 62% to 64% by 2028, holds family reunification near 80,000, and dramatically cuts new temporary resident admissions.

| Metric | 2026 | 2027–2028 |
|--------|------|----------|
| **Permanent resident target** | 380,000 | 380,000 |
| **Economic class share** | 62% | 64% |
| **Family reunification** | 84,000 | 81,000 |
| **New temporary residents** | 385,000 | 370,000 |
| **Study permits** | 155,000 | 150,000 |
| **Temporary workers (TFW)** | 37% fewer vs 2025 | 37% fewer vs 2025 |
| **Parents & Grandparents Program** | 15,000 | 15,000 |
| **Francophone PR (target by 2028)** | 10.5% of total | 10.5% of total |

The bigger story sits inside the 43% cut to temporary residents and the overhaul coming to Express Entry.

## What does Canada's 2026-2028 immigration plan actually do?

**Short answer:** Three explicit goals: stabilise PR admissions at sustainable levels (abandoning the earlier 500,000/year trajectory), cut temporary residents by nearly half over three years, and prioritise category-based draws over general Express Entry rounds. The plan reads as a deliberate cooldown after the 2022-2024 expansion.

The federal government has three explicit goals:

**1. Stabilise permanent residence at sustainable levels.** The earlier trajectory toward 500,000 PR/year has been abandoned. 380,000 is both the floor and the ceiling for the next three years. The government is signalling that it admitted too many people, too fast, without enough housing or services, and is pulling back.

**2. Slash temporary resident arrivals from 673,650 (2025) to 385,000 (2026) and stabilise at 370,000 for 2027–2028.** This is a 43% year-over-year cut. The target is to bring temporary residents down to less than 5% of Canada's total population by the end of 2027. If you're in Canada on a work or study permit right now, this affects your exit strategy.

**3. Rebalance immigration toward economic class and francophone recruitment.** Economic migrants will represent 64% of PR admissions by 2027 (up from 59%). Francophone immigration destined for outside Quebec will reach 10.5% of total PR admissions by 2028. Family reunification stays modest at 84,000 for 2026, declining to 81,000 by 2028.

This is a pro-economic-selection, pro-francophone, anti-temporary-resident plan rather than an anti-immigration plan.

## Why is Canada keeping permanent resident targets at 380,000?

**Short answer:** Canada is locking in 380,000 PR admissions for 2026, 2027, and 2028, with no increase and no decrease. The earlier 500,000-by-2025 trajectory was abandoned after housing affordability and infrastructure pressures peaked in 2023-2024. The economic class share is rising to 64% within this fixed total, giving more room to skilled workers and provincial nominees.

Canada is locking in 380,000 permanent resident admissions for three consecutive years. No increase, no decrease.

Why the pivot? In 2022 and 2023, the government forecast that 500,000 PR/year would be feasible and set that as a target. Housing shortages, education capacity, and healthcare strain became impossible to ignore. The Parliamentary Budget Officer released demographic analysis showing immigration alone would not solve Canada's aging population problem, and political pressure mounted.

The 380,000 figure is lower but still high by historical standards. It's also below 1% of Canada's total population in any given year, a self-imposed ceiling the government wants to respect.

For applicants, demand and competition both stay high. The number of people chasing 380,000 spots far exceeds the seats available, and Express Entry cut-offs and provincial nominee programs will remain competitive.

### Who Benefits from the PR Stabilization

- **[Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/works.html) applicants with strong profiles (Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score of 470+).** You're still in the pool. Invitations will continue regularly, though Express Entry is being restructured (more below).
- **Provincial Nominee Program candidates.** With economic class share rising to 64%, provinces have more wiggle room to nominate people. [Provincial Nominee Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html) (PNP) continues to be the path with the highest acceptance rate for mid-range profiles.
- **Francophone immigrants.** The government is directing 10.5% of total PR spots to francophones, a targeted increase. If you're an English speaker willing to reach TEF/TCF level, this is your fastest re-route to permanent residence.
- **Family class sponsorship.** Numbers are modest (84,000 for 2026), but the government is committing to process those applications consistently.

## What temporary resident reductions are in Canada's 2026-2028 plan?

**Short answer:** Canada admitted 673,650 new temporary residents in 2025 (work permits, study permits, other temporary statuses combined). The 2026-2028 plan caps new temporary resident admissions at 385,000 per year, a 43% cut. Student permits and TFWP work permits absorb most of the reduction.

The biggest shift in the plan is the collapse of temporary resident admissions.

In 2025, Canada admitted 673,650 new temporary residents (people arriving on work permits, study permits, and other temporary statuses). That number drops to 385,000 in 2026, a cut of 288,650 people in a single year.

For context, that's roughly the entire population of Ottawa no longer being allowed into Canada on a temporary basis.

### Why This Matters

**For international students:** The [study permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html) target drops from 305,900 (2025) to 155,000 (2026), a 49% cut. Your university's revenue model may have depended on 300+ international students per cohort. That is changing. Schools are already signaling they will be more selective about international applications. Scholarship funding, campus part-time job availability, and post-graduation work permit access are tightening.

**For temporary foreign workers:** [Temporary worker](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit/temporary.html) arrivals are being cut by 37% in raw numbers. Sectors like agriculture, food processing, construction, and elder care will feel this immediately. If your employer has been planning to hire you on a work permit and then transition you to permanent residence, the timeline may have shifted. You may be competing against more Canadian applicants for the same role.

**For anyone already in Canada on a permit:** If your work permit or study permit expires in 2026 or 2027, you need to know your options now. The government is pushing selected temporary residents toward permanent residence rather than extending temporary status. Line up a PR pathway before your permit expires.

### The Numbers: What's Actually Happening

The plan allocates:
- **155,000 study permits** in 2026, down to 150,000 in 2027–2028
- **Temporary foreign workers (TFW):** Approximately 60,000 in 2026–2027, down from higher historical levels
- **International mobility permits:** Another 50,000+ combined
- **Other temporary status categories:** The rest

The government is also running a one-time, two-year initiative to regularize 115,000 protected persons as permanent residents. A further 33,000 temporary workers will be transitioned to permanent status over the same period. These are not in addition to the 380,000; they are part of it.

## How is Express Entry changing under Canada's 2026-2028 plan?

**Short answer:** On April 8, 2026, IRCC announced plans to retire the current Express Entry system that has run since 2015. The three Express Entry classes (Federal Skilled Worker (FSW), Canadian Experience Class (CEC), Federal Skilled Trades (FST)) will be retired and replaced by a redesigned category-based framework, with public consultation through spring 2026.

On April 8, 2026, IRCC announced plans to retire the current Express Entry system that has defined federal high-skilled immigration since 2015.

### What's Happening

The three Express Entry classes will be retired:
- **Federal Skilled Worker Class (FSWC)**
- **Canadian Experience Class (CEC)**
- **Federal Skilled Trades Class (FSTC)**

These will be replaced with a single "Federal High-Skilled Class" featuring simplified eligibility and a recalibrated [Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/eligibility/criteria-comprehensive-ranking-system.html).

### What We Don't Know Yet

IRCC has provided minimal detail. The exact eligibility criteria, the new CRS weight distribution, the implementation date, and transition rules for people already in the pool are all TBD. The department plans to consult the public and stakeholders in Spring 2026, with further announcements expected.

It's the biggest change to Express Entry since it launched in 2015, and the details aren't public yet.

### What You Should Do Right Now

**If you don't have a profile in the pool:** Create one immediately. The current three classes remain fully operational. The government is still issuing invitations through these programs. Do not wait for details about the new class before building your profile. Use the time now to improve your language scores, education credentials, or Canadian work experience.

**If you already have a profile in the pool:** Do not withdraw it. Keep it active. The government continues to issue regular invitations through CEC, FSWC, and FSTC. You may receive an invitation under the old rules before the new system launches. If the new class has less favorable eligibility or CRS weights for your profile, you'll be grandfathered in under the old rules.

**If you're still outside Canada:** A job offer or Canadian work experience will become more valuable. The new class reportedly emphasizes job offers and in-demand occupations. Getting to Canada on a work permit first gives you optionality.

## What are the current Express Entry cut-off scores in 2026?

**Short answer:** Canadian Experience Class cut-offs sit at 507-515; Federal Skilled Worker at 730-745 (requiring higher language and education); Provincial Nominee Program draws clear around 700+ but with a +600 CRS provincial nomination bonus baked in. The general draw has been replaced by category-specific invitations.

While the long-term future is uncertain, Q1 2026 cut-offs are clear.

- **Canadian Experience Class (CEC):** 507–515 (holding high)
- **Federal Skilled Worker Program:** 730–745 (requiring higher language and education points)
- **Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) draws:** 710–802 depending on province and program
- **French-language draws:** 393–400 (the most accessible general pathway for English speakers willing to learn French)
- **Trades draws:** ~477
- **Healthcare draws:** ~467
- **First-ever Senior Managers draw:** March 5, 2026 at CRS 429 with 250 Invitations to Apply (ITAs). This is new and worth watching if you have management-level Canadian experience.

### What This Tells Us

CEC cut-offs are holding above 500. Demand for Canadian work experience is strong, and the pool of eligible CEC candidates is large.

French-language draws are much more accessible. This is intentional: the government wants to boost Francophone immigration, and they are using competitive cut-offs to incentivize language learning.

PNP cut-offs remain in the 700s+ range because each province sets its own targets and criteria. But many provinces still accept nominations at the 600 threshold with their own point bonus.

Experts are not predicting CEC cut-offs will drop below 500 before Q3 2026 at the earliest.

## How do category-based Express Entry draws work in 2026?

**Short answer:** IRCC now issues invitations by category rather than from one undifferentiated pool. The 2026 categories include healthcare, trades, French-language proficiency, transportation, agriculture, STEM, and education. Strategy: target the category that fits your profile and shifts the cut-off in your favour.

IRCC has moved away from random all-class draws and toward category-specific invitations. This changes strategy for applicants.

### Why This Matters

Rather than one weekly draw from the entire pool, IRCC now announces draw categories (sometimes just CEC, sometimes French speakers, sometimes trades, sometimes PNP-ineligible candidates). Your ability to land an invitation depends on:

1. Your profile fitting a draw category
2. Enough space in that category
3. A low enough cut-off for your CRS

### The Categories Being Drawn (2026)

- **Canadian Experience Class:** Regular draws, 250–500 ITAs
- **French speakers:** Monthly or bi-weekly, 250 ITAs, CRS 393–400 (lowest cut-offs)
- **Healthcare professionals:** Occasional, CRS ~467
- **Skilled trades:** Occasional, CRS ~477
- **STEM graduates:** Occasional (announced 2026), CRS TBD
- **PNP-ineligible candidates:** Occasional, higher CRS required
- **Senior managers with Canadian experience:** New category (2026), CRS 429

### Tactical Guidance

- If you're fluent in English but your CRS is 470–500, consider investing 6–12 months in French. TEF/TCF certification costs $400–500 and opens a dramatically more accessible draw category (CRS 393–400).
- If you have a trade designation or healthcare credentials, watch for category-specific draws. These often have lower cut-offs than the general pool.
- If your CRS is 480–510, you're likely to receive an invitation within 6–12 months if you remain in the pool and watch for your profile's category.

## How do Provincial Nominee Programs fit into the 2026-2028 immigration plan?

**Short answer:** PNP draws hold significantly lower cut-offs than federal draws when measured pre-bonus, and a provincial nomination adds 600 CRS points, effectively guaranteeing an ITA. Provincial Nominee Programs are the path with the highest success rate for mid-range CRS profiles, with provinces actively recruiting under the expanded 64% economic class allocation.

While Express Entry gets headlines, Provincial Nominee Programs (PNPs) are expanding and remain the path with the highest success rate for mid-range profiles.

### Why PNP Is Attractive

- **Lower cut-off overall:** PNP programs often accept nominations at CRS 600+, and many provinces award a provincial nomination (600 points bonus), making the total CRS post-nomination high enough to virtually guarantee a federal PR invitation.
- **No points lost to luck:** Express Entry is a draw lottery within your pool. PNP is a direct nomination if you meet criteria and the province has capacity.
- **Active provincial recruitment:** Provinces are recruiting actively for economic class immigration. With the federal economic class share rising to 64%, provinces have more headroom in their allocations.

### Active Provinces (2026)

- **Ontario Immigrant Nominee Program (OINP):** Francophone, skilled worker, and employer job offer streams. Can be slow (6–9 months).
- **British Columbia (BC PNP):** Skilled worker and international graduate pathways. Relatively accessible CRS thresholds.
- **Alberta:** Tech and healthcare focus. Growing recruitment.
- **Atlantic Canada:** Active recruitment across all four provinces (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland & Labrador, Prince Edward Island). Smaller pools, faster processing in some cases.
- **Manitoba, Saskatchewan:** Smaller programs but accepting candidates.

### What to Do

If your CRS is 450–600 and you're ineligible for Express Entry draws in the short term, apply to provincial programs in your province of choice. Treat PNP as a parallel track, not a backup.

## What does the 2026-2028 plan mean for family sponsorship?

**Short answer:** 2026 family-class admissions target 84,000 (spouses, dependent children, parents, grandparents); 2027 and 2028 target 81,000 each. Spousal sponsorship remains relatively fast at 6-12 months and is unaffected by the new plan. The [Parents and Grandparents Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/sponsor-parents-grandparents.html) is structurally constrained; [Super Visa](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa.html) remains the practical alternative for most applicants.

The government is committing to family reunification but in modest numbers.

### The Numbers

- **2026:** 84,000 family class admissions (spouses, dependent children, parents, grandparents)
- **2027–2028:** 81,000 annually
- **Parents & Grandparents Program (PGP) spots:** 15,000 annually for 2026–2028

### What This Means

Family sponsorship is alive but not expanding. If you want to sponsor a spouse or common-law partner, the process remains relatively straightforward and timelines are 6–12 months. If you want to sponsor dependent children, similar.

If you want to sponsor parents or grandparents, you're competing for 15,000 spots through the [Parents & Grandparents Program](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/sponsor-parents-grandparents.html). The application intake usually opens for a few weeks in early calendar year, and it fills quickly. If you're eligible (Canadian citizen or PR with sufficient income), you need to be ready to apply in January/February 2026.

### Income Requirements for PGP (2026)

Sponsoring parents or grandparents requires demonstrating income above the Low Income Cut-Off (LICO) for your household size. For 2026, this is approximately $39,000–$50,000 depending on family size. Two-year average income is required.

### Alternative: Super Visa

If you don't meet PGP eligibility or timelines, the Super Visa (valid for 10 years, allow stays up to 24 months per entry) is another option for bringing parents to Canada long-term without sponsoring them permanently. Super Visa holders can live in Canada repeatedly but are not permanent residents.

## Why is francophone immigration faster for English speakers in 2026?

**Short answer:** The federal government is targeting 10.5% of total PR admissions to francophones by 2028 (and 12% by 2029). With fewer French-speaking applicants in the pool, the French-language Express Entry category clears CRS cut-offs more than 100 points below CEC. Upskilling French is structurally rewarded.

The government is targeting 10.5% of total PR admissions to francophones by 2028. This is a structural advantage if you're willing to upskill in French.

### Why Francophone Immigration Is Growing

- Fewer French-speaking applicants than English-speaking globally
- Quebec workforce needs fill
- Government commitment to French language preservation
- Federal target to boost francophone economic integration outside Quebec

### Current Reality (2026)

- **French-language Express Entry draws:** 250 ITAs, CRS 393–400
- **Francophone provincial programs:** Ontario (OINP) has a francophone stream; other provinces are launching
- **Time to get TEF/TCF:** 3–6 months of study for someone bilingual at B1–B2 in both languages

### Worked Example

If your English CRS is 480 (roughly IELTS 7.0, Canadian bachelor's degree, 1 year Canadian experience) and you add French B2 (TEF 400+), your new CRS becomes eligible for a francophone draw at CRS 393–400.

This nets you an invitation 4–8 weeks after the draw announcement, instead of waiting 4–6 months (or never) in the English pool.

### Which Test to Take

- **TEF:** Faster scoring (11 days), accepted by IRCC, $450 CDN
- **TCF:** Also accepted, similar scoring timeline, slightly lower cost
- Both require a testing center; both have prep materials

For someone with working knowledge of both English and French, upskilling in French is the fastest path to Express Entry right now.

## What does the 2026-2028 immigration plan mean for your situation?

**Short answer:** Work permit holders: fewer extensions, faster pressure to transition to PR. International students: stricter PGWP rules and tighter post-grad timelines. PR-bound profiles: target a category-based draw or PNP rather than waiting for general invitations. New entrants from abroad: harder to enter on temporary status, easier through Express Entry French category.

### You're in Canada on a Work Permit

**The reality:** Your employer may have planned to hire you long-term, but the temporary resident cuts mean fewer work permit extensions and faster pressure to transition to permanent residence or leave.

**What to do:**
1. Confirm your work permit expiry date
2. If you have Canadian experience and a job offer, start an Express Entry application now (CEC stream)
3. If your employer is supportive, ask about sponsorship through the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) pathway, which can lead to PR
4. If your profile is borderline for Express Entry, explore PNP options in your province
5. Do not plan on a straightforward work permit extension beyond 2026 without a PR pathway in place

### You're an International Student Finishing Your Degree

**The reality:** Your Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) length and pathway to PR have tightened.

**What to do:**
1. Apply for your PGWP immediately after graduation (many programs have a window to apply)
2. Secure a job offer in Canada within the PGWP period if possible
3. Use the PGWP work experience to build an Express Entry profile (CEC stream)
4. If you're struggling to meet Express Entry cut-offs, explore PNP in your province
5. Consider French upskilling if your CRS is 450–480. A francophone-friendly province like Quebec (QSWP) or Ontario (francophone streams) may offer faster PR

### You're Outside Canada with a CRS of 420–470

**The reality:** You're in the pool but below the current cut-off.

**What to do:**
1. Improve language scores if they're below Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7 (IELTS 6.0). Moving from CLB 7 to CLB 8 can add 50+ CRS points
2. Pursue Canadian work experience or education (come on a work permit or study permit, then build profile)
3. Explore French certification as a CRS booster
4. Apply to PNP in a province that suits your occupation
5. Watch for category-specific draws (healthcare, trades, STEM) if your occupation qualifies

### You're Outside Canada with a CRS of 480+

**The reality:** You're eligible for Express Entry and likely to receive an invitation within 6–12 months.

**What to do:**
1. Create and activate your profile now
2. If you're below 500, confirm your profile is optimized (correct National Occupational Classification (NOC), strongest language test scores, all credentials uploaded)
3. Stay patient. Invitations are being issued regularly across categories
4. If you have French, activate that for category-specific draws
5. Have your supporting documents ready (university transcript, employment reference letters, identity documents) so you can prepare your application within 60 days of receiving an invitation

### You Want to Sponsor a Parent or Grandparent

**The reality:** 15,000 spots, thousands of eligible applicants, application window likely to open in January 2026 and fill within weeks.

**What to do:**
1. Confirm your income for 2024 and 2025 exceeds LICO for your household size
2. Gather documents: Notice of Assessment (NOA), tax returns, employment letter
3. Request sponsorship forms from IRCC when intake opens (usually announced via IRCC's website)
4. Submit within 24 hours of intake opening if possible. Many intakes fill within a week
5. If you miss the 2026 intake, consider Super Visa as a bridge for your parents to visit Canada long-term while you prepare for the 2027 intake

### You Want to Sponsor a Spouse or Partner

**The reality:** This pathway remains straightforward and relatively fast.

**What to do:**
1. Apply as soon as possible
2. Processing times are typically 6–12 months (longer if additional security checks required)
3. Ensure your spouse meets the admissibility requirements (no criminal record, no health reasons for inadmissibility)
4. Use the time while your application is processing to have your spouse gather documents and prepare for arrival
5. Spousal sponsorship is not affected by the new levels plan

## When do the key changes in Canada's 2026-2028 immigration plan take effect?

**Short answer:** April 2026: IRCC announces Express Entry retirement plan. Spring 2026 (April-June): public consultation. Mid-2026: draft replacement system published. 2027: new framework rolls out. 2028: full transition complete. Apply under the current system while it remains operational; the framework you submit under is the one your application is processed against.

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| **April 2026 (now)** | IRCC announces Express Entry retirement plan and public consultation in spring |
| **Spring 2026 (Apr–Jun)** | IRCC public consultation on new Express Entry class opens |
| **Throughout 2026** | Current Express Entry (FSWC, CEC, FSTC) remains operational; invitations continue |
| **PGP intake (Jan–Feb 2026)** | Parents & Grandparents Program application window opens (if not already closed); 15,000 spots |
| **Throughout 2026–2027** | Category-specific Express Entry draws continue (French, healthcare, trades, etc.) |
| **Late 2026 or 2027** | IRCC announces implementation timeline and detailed rules for new Express Entry class |
| **2027 or 2028** | New Express Entry class launches; transition period for existing profiles (details TBD) |
| **End of 2027** | Target: Temporary resident population drops to less than 5% of Canada's total population |
| **Throughout 2026–2028** | PR admissions remain at 380,000/year; 64% economic class by 2027 |

**What's uncertain:** The exact implementation date for the new Express Entry class, the detailed eligibility criteria, and the transition rules for people in the current pool are all TBD. IRCC will provide more detail after spring 2026 consultation.

## What questions do people ask about Canada's 2026-2028 immigration plan?

Canada's 2026-2028 immigration plan raises common questions about permanent resident targets, Express Entry changes, and what reductions to temporary residents mean for individual applicants. The plan sets 380,000 permanent residents per year through 2028, reduces new temporary residents by 43%, and replaces the current [Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html) framework with a redesigned federal high-skilled class. Below are the most common questions answered directly.

### How many immigrants will Canada let in in 2026?

**380,000 permanent residents** (this is the federal intake target). Canada will also admit **385,000 new temporary residents** (international students, temporary foreign workers, and other temporary statuses). Together, that's approximately **765,000 people arriving in Canada with official status in 2026**. This is down sharply from 2025's 1.05 million combined admissions.

### What are the changes in the IRCC 2026 plan?

The three biggest changes are:

1. **Temporary residents are being cut by 43%.** Down from 673,650 to 385,000 new arrivals in 2026.
2. **Express Entry is being retired and replaced.** The FSWC, CEC, and FSTC classes will be eliminated in favor of a single federal class (details coming in spring 2026).
3. **Economic class is rising from 59% to 64% of PR admissions.** The government is prioritizing skilled workers and people with job offers over family reunification.

### Will the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) draw go below 500 in 2026?

Unlikely before Q3 2026. Current CEC cut-offs are holding at 507–515 because demand for Canadian work experience is high and the pool is large. Experts predict CEC could see lower cut-offs later in 2026 or early 2027 as profiles accumulate Canadian experience and aging out. But a return to the 400s (pre-2023 levels) is not forecasted.

### What's replacing Express Entry?

A single "Federal High-Skilled Class" with simplified eligibility and a recalibrated CRS. The new class will emphasize job offers and in-demand occupations. Exact eligibility criteria are not yet public. IRCC will release details after spring 2026 consultation.

### When do I apply for the Parents & Grandparents Program?

Intake typically opens in January each year and fills within weeks. The 2026 window may have already closed (check IRCC.gc.ca for current status). If you missed it, prepare for the 2027 intake by confirming your income meets LICO and gathering documents now.

### Does this plan affect international student applications for fall 2026?

Yes. The study permit target has been cut by 49% (305,900 to 155,000). Universities are becoming more selective. If you're applying to Canadian schools for fall 2026, ensure your application is strong on academics and language (IELTS 6.5+). Some schools are now requiring proof of housing or increased financial requirements.

### Does this affect my visitor visa?

No. Visitor visas are a separate category from temporary residents. The cuts apply to work permits and study permits, not tourism or visiting.

### Is permanent residence getting harder in 2026?

Not harder. Staying the same. 380,000 spots for the year means demand remains high. But the pool is also large. Your competitive advantage comes from optimizing your CRS, building Canadian experience, learning French, or nominating through a provincial program.

### What if the new Express Entry class has worse odds for my profile?

You will be grandfathered under the old rules if you hold a profile in the current system before the new class launches. Do not withdraw. Keep your profile active.

### Can I still bring my spouse to Canada?

Yes. Spousal sponsorship remains available and is not affected by the new levels plan. Processing times are typically 6–12 months.

## What should you do now under Canada's 2026-2028 immigration plan?

**Short answer:** Create an Express Entry profile immediately if you qualify (the current system is operational). Target a category-based draw or PNP. If studying in Canada, confirm your program is PGWP-eligible. If on a work permit, plan your PR transition before the temporary resident cuts tighten. If planning to immigrate from abroad, build French to NCLC 7 for the lower-CRS category draws.

1. **If you're planning to immigrate:** Create an Express Entry profile immediately (free on Canada.ca). The current system is operational and invitations are being issued regularly.

2. **If you're studying in Canada:** Plan your post-graduation work permit and PR pathway now. Do not assume extensions are automatic.

3. **If you're working in Canada:** Confirm your work permit expiry and have a PR application plan for 12 months before it expires.

4. **If you're planning to sponsor family:** Gather income documents. If you want to sponsor parents/grandparents, prepare to apply during the 2026 intake (likely January).

5. **If you're a French speaker (or willing to learn):** Pursue French certification. It's the fastest CRS improvement available right now.

6. **If your CRS is 450–600:** Explore Provincial Nominee Programs in your target province as a parallel track to Express Entry.

Permanent resident numbers stay flat for the next three years while temporary residency, Express Entry, and the skills-versus-family balance shift. The sooner you act, the better positioned you will be.

# How to Improve Your CRS Score: 17 Proven Ways to Add Points in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/how-to-improve-crs-score-2026
Category: Express Entry
Published: 2026-04-18
Author: Go Far Global Team

> 17 actionable ways to boost your CRS score for Express Entry in 2026. Includes points math, 2026 draw data, and realistic routes for every score range.

# How to Improve Your CRS Score in 2026: 17 Proven Ways to Add Points

To improve your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score for Canada's Express Entry, you need to know exactly which actions add measurable points and how fast each one moves the needle. In April 2026, the Canadian Experience Class cut-off hit 515 points, the French-language stream hit 393, and category-based draws sat between 410 and 477. If you are not in a targeted category draw, your CRS score 2026 is what decides whether you receive an invitation.

Your CRS score for Express Entry is not fixed. Across the Comprehensive Ranking System's 1,200 available points, there are 17 specific actions that add measurable points to your Express Entry CRS. A provincial nomination adds 600. A language retake can add 13. This guide on how to increase your CRS score breaks down the math, the timelines, and which strategies work in 2026, plus how to calculate your CRS score before you commit to a strategy.

*As of April 18, 2026.*

This article was reviewed by Go Far Global's Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC)-Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) licensed practitioners (College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants, CICC #R515110).

## What Are the 17 Ways to Improve Your CRS Score in Express Entry?

**Short answer:** The 17 levers fall into five groups: language (4 ways: IELTS/CELPIP retake to Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 9 or 10, French test for the French stream, bilingual bonus), Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) nomination (+600), work experience (5 ways: 1-year and 2-year Canadian, foreign National Occupational Classification (NOC) stacking, skill transferability, Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) job offer +200), education (3 ways: Canadian master's, ECA, second Canadian credential), and family (3 ways: spouse inclusion, spouse language, sibling +15, spousal arranged employment).

### Language (4 Ways)

Your language proficiency is one of the first scores Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) calculates, and it's one of the fastest to improve.

**1. Retake IELTS or CELPIP to reach CLB 9**

The jump from Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 8 to CLB 9 is worth 13 additional points on the CRS (per [IRCC's CRS criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html), core human capital section). If you're bilingual in English and French, you get an extra 25-point bonus just for proving it at CLB 7+ in both languages. That's a combined 38-point swing. Most candidates can reach CLB 9 in 2–3 months of focused study. IELTS Speaking is often the bottleneck; some candidates focus there. CELPIP (Computer-based) often suits people who are comfortable with tech. Both are accepted.

**2. Push from CLB 9 to CLB 10 (or higher)**

CLB 10 adds another 9 points over CLB 9 in the core tier. CLB 11 and 12 add incrementally more. For someone already at CLB 9 (7.5+ on IELTS, or 80+ on CELPIP), an extra 2–3 weeks of targeted practice can get you to CLB 10. Worth it if you're 20 points away from the current draw cut-off.

**3. Earn a French credential (TEF, TCF, or TFI)**

If English is your first language and French your second, proving French at CLB 7 or higher opens the French-language draws, which routinely cut at 365–400 CRS. In April 2026, the French draw selected at just 393 points. For most English-speaking Canadians, this is a faster path to an Invitation to Apply (ITA) than climbing to CLB 10 in English. You don't need fluency. CLB 7 (TEF 400+, or TCF 450+) is enough. Timeline: 3–6 months to reach CLB 7 if you're a true beginner. If you already know some French, 1–2 months.

**4. Claim the Bilingual Bonus**

If you can demonstrate CLB 7 or higher in both English and French, you get a [25-point bonus](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html) just for being bilingual. Combined with the points for French itself, this can swing 40+ points. Worth pursuing in 2026, especially as IRCC's proposed reforms will emphasize language.

### Provincial Nominee Program (1 Way)

**5. Get a Provincial Nomination (PNP)**

A Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) nomination [adds 600 points to your CRS](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html) instantly. If your base CRS is 250, a PNP brings you to 850+, well above any 2026 draw cut-off. Provinces move at different speeds, and occupation eligibility varies by stream (see [IRCC's provincial nominees overview](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html)). In 2026, Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta have the most invitations, but they're also the most competitive. Manitoba and Saskatchewan are faster but favour trades or specific occupations. Quebec has its own separate program (not Express Entry). Timeline depends on the province: some process in 2–3 months; others have multi-month waits. This is your fastest route to Permanent Residence (PR) if you qualify for a provincial stream.

### Work Experience (5 Ways)

Work experience is the largest points lever after language and education. The system rewards Canadian experience heavily but also values foreign work in the right NOC codes (see [Express Entry eligibility criteria](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/become-candidate/eligibility.html)).

**6. Add One Year of Canadian Work Experience**

The CRS points for Canadian work experience jump at the 1-year mark, 2-year mark, and 3-year mark. If you currently have 0 years, getting to 1 year adds roughly 80–120 points (depending on your NOC and skill level). You work 12 consecutive months in a skilled role. Many people in the pool are on this exact timeline.

**7. Extend Canadian Work Experience to 2 Years**

If you already have 1 year, adding a second year is worth another 50–70 points. Combined with step 6, going from 0 to 2 years of Canadian work is worth 130–190 points. In 2026, with Canadian Experience Class (CEC) cuts at 507 to 515, adding 2 years of Canadian work puts you above the line, even if your language score is CLB 8.

**8. Secure Skilled Foreign Work Experience in the Right NOC**

If you're not in Canada yet and can't add Canadian experience, stacking foreign work in a high-demand National Occupational Classification (NOC) (software developers, nurses, welders, chefs) is the backup. The CRS gives you up to 15 points of transferable skills credit if your foreign work + language combo matches a target occupation. You need 2+ years in a related NOC. Timeline: depends on your current role, but people often qualify for this already.

**9. Combine Foreign Work + Language to Claim Skill Transferability Points**

The CRS has a specific "skill transferability" section worth [up to 100 points](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html). You get these if you have 2+ years of work experience in an occupation that aligns with your language level and education. For example: a Brazilian software engineer with 5 years of experience, CLB 8 English, and a bachelor's degree in computer science gets meaningful skill transferability points even before they land Canadian work. This often adds 20–40 points if your profile is filled out correctly.

**10. Pursue an LMIA Job Offer or Arranged Employment**

A valid job offer from a Canadian employer adds 200 points to your CRS. A Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) job offer carries more credibility, but the points are the same. Going from no job offer to a job offer is a 200-point jump. Timeline: highly variable. Some companies LMIA-sponsor roles in weeks; others take months. The hard part is finding an employer willing to do the legwork.

### Education (3 Ways)

**11. Earn a Canadian Master's Degree or PhD**

A master's degree earned in Canada adds 15–17 points over a foreign bachelor's (depending on how you calculate it). A Canadian graduate degree also qualifies you for a faster provincial nominee stream. You also get the 1+ years of Canadian study towards your work experience. Timeline: 1–2 years for a master's program. Not for someone targeting an ITA in the next 3 months.

**12. Get Your Foreign Credential Recognized in Canada**

If you have a degree from abroad (engineering, medicine, accounting), getting it formally assessed and recognized through a Canadian credential assessment service (WES, ICES) can add 5–15 points, depending on what you're doing with it. Recognized credentials also open provincial nominee pathways or employer sponsorships. For example, a Canadian-assessed engineering degree opens provincial engineer-in-training streams. Timeline: 2–4 weeks for the assessment report.

**13. Pursue a Second Canadian Credential (Certificate, Diploma, or Degree)**

Some people in the pool already have a bachelor's degree. Adding a diploma or certificate from a Canadian college (often 1–2 years of study) counts as "additional Canadian credential" and adds 15–17 points. Less common, but an option if you're near a draw cut-off and have the time. Timeline: 1–2 years for the program itself.

### Spouse/Family (3 Ways)

**14. Include (or Don't Include) a Spouse in Your Profile**

If you're married or have a common-law partner, adding them can increase your overall household CRS. But it can also lower your individual score if they don't have strong credentials (language, education, work experience). Run the math both ways: sometimes it's better to apply solo and have your spouse apply separately later. A profile strategy rather than a score increase, but still a legitimate lever.

**15. Get Your Spouse a Language Certificate**

If your spouse is included, improving their language score (CLB 7 from CLB 6, for example) adds a modest 15–20 points to the household CRS.

**16. Add a Sibling Nomination (15 Points)**

If you have a sibling who is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, you get 15 points on your CRS. Check your profile. If this is missing, add it immediately.

**17. Maximize Spousal Arranged Employment Bonus**

If your spouse or partner has a validated job offer from a Canadian employer, you both get bonus points (50 for your spouse, 50 for you if your spouse's offer is recognized). This is less common but worth noting. Timeline: same as a regular job offer pursuit.


## How Many CRS Points Can a Typical Candidate Realistically Add?

**Short answer:** A 30-year-old with foreign bachelor's, CLB 8 English, 3 years foreign software-developer work, and an included spouse starts at 385 CRS; retaking IELTS to CLB 9 adds 13, adding 1 year Canadian work +85, second year +70, and a PNP +600 reaches 1,153, well above any 2026 cutoff.

**Baseline Profile:**
- Age: 30 years old
- Education: Foreign bachelor's degree (assessed as equivalent)
- Language: CLB 8 in English, no French
- Work experience: 3 years foreign (software developer NOC 2175), 0 years in Canada
- Spouse: Included, CLB 6, bachelor's degree
- No provincial nomination, no job offer, no Canadian education, no sibling

**Baseline CRS Score: 385 points**

Applying the 17 strategies in sequence:

| Strategy | Added Points | New CRS Total |
|----------|--------------|----------------|
| Baseline | n/a | 385 |
| Retake IELTS to CLB 9 | +13 | 398 |
| Add 1 year Canadian work | +85 | 483 |
| Add 1 more year Canadian work (2 total) | +70 | 553 |
| Get provincial nomination | +600 | 1,153 |

In this scenario, the candidate hits the CEC cut-off (507–515) just by adding 2 years of Canadian work and improving language from CLB 8 to CLB 9. They don't need the PNP, though getting one would guarantee an ITA. The bottleneck is time. Two years of Canadian work experience takes two years.

If they also pursued French (CLB 7) instead of waiting for Canadian work, they'd hit the French-language draw cut-off (393) in just 3–6 months.


## What CRS Score Do You Need for Canada PR in 2026?

**Short answer:** IRCC held 23 draws January to mid-April 2026 issuing 65,154 ITAs: Canadian Experience Class 507 to 515, Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) 710 to 802 (rare), French Language 365 to 400 (March 18 hit 393), Skilled Trades 477, Healthcare ~467, Senior Managers 429, Physicians 169 (only 391 ITAs).

IRCC held 23 draws between January and mid-April 2026, issuing 65,154 invitations (per [IRCC's Express Entry rounds of invitations](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations.html)). The cut-offs:

| Draw Category | Cut-Off CRS | Timeline | Notes |
|---------------|-------------|----------|-------|
| Canadian Experience Class (CEC) | 507–515 | January–April 2026 | Consistent all Q1. Latest draw: April 14, 2026 at 515 |
| Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) | 710–802 | Rare in 2026 | IRCC shifted to category-based draws |
| French Language | 365–400 | Regular | March 18 draw at historic low of 393 |
| Skilled Trades | 477 | First draw April 2, 2026 | 3,000 ITAs. IRCC's first category-based pilot |
| Healthcare | ~467 | February–April | Nurses, doctors, allied health |
| Senior Managers | 429 | February 5, 2026 | IRCC's first Senior Manager draw ever |
| Physicians | 169 | February 19, 2026 | Record-low CRS; only 391 ITAs |

**Will CEC drop below 500 in 2026?** Probably not. The average CRS in the pool rose to 452 in April 2026. Most candidates sit between 491–600. Until more people improve their language or add Canadian work experience, CEC cuts will stay above 500. If IRCC issues more CEC invitations (increasing ITAs per draw from 2,000 to 3,000+), cuts could ease downward.


## Can You Get PR With Your Current CRS Score?

**Short answer:** At 300 CRS, French stream or PNP are realistic in 3 to 6 months; 400 CRS needs Canadian work or PNP; 442 is above the French cutoff (apply now if you have French); 470 is 40 to 45 points below CEC, combine 6 months Canadian work with language improvement; 530+ should already have an ITA, so check your profile for errors.

### "I have a 300 CRS. Can I get PR?"

At 300 CRS, you're below the pool. You need one of these:

1. **Get a provincial nomination (PNP):** Instantly 900+ CRS.
2. **Add 2 years of Canadian work + improve language to CLB 9:** Takes time but realistic path to 500+ (CEC cut-off).
3. **Pursue a French stream:** Prove French at CLB 7, apply to French-language draws cutting at 365–400.

Most realistic for a 300: French-language route (3–6 months) or PNP (3–4 months if you qualify).

### "I have a 400 CRS. Can I get PR?"

At 400, you're closer but still 100+ points below CEC.

1. **One year of Canadian work + CLB 9 language:** Adds ~100 points. Gets you to ~500.
2. **French stream:** Still below 400 French cut-off. Need CLB 7 French + rebalance your profile.
3. **PNP:** If you qualify, instant 1,000+.

Most realistic: Canadian work experience path (12 months) or PNP (if occupationally eligible).

### "I have a 442 CRS. Is that good?"

442 is a solid score, above average (pool average is 452). You're about 65 points below CEC. You're competitive for:

1. **Targeted draws:** If IRCC runs Healthcare, Trades, or other category draws, 442 can qualify depending on your occupation.
2. **12 months of Canadian work:** Gets you over 500.
3. **French route:** 442 is well above the French cut-off. If you can prove French CLB 7, apply to French draws immediately.
4. **Wait for CEC cut-off to drop:** If IRCC increases ITAs, cuts ease naturally.

Most realistic: French-language stream (apply now) or Canadian work experience (12 months).

### "I have a 470 CRS. Can I get PR?"

470 is competitive in 2026. You're 40–45 points below the latest CEC cut-off (515), but you're in the target zone for several tactics:

1. **Retake IELTS/CELPIP for CLB 9:** Adds ~13 points. Gets you to 483 (still below 515, but closer).
2. **Six months of Canadian work:** Adds ~40–50 points. Gets you to 510–520 (at or above CEC).
3. **Secure a job offer:** Adds 200 points. Gets you to 670+.
4. **French stream:** 470 is well above all French draws. Apply immediately if you have any French.
5. **PNP:** Instant win.

Most realistic: Combine Canadian work (6 months) + language improvement. Or fast-track with French.

### "I have a 530 CRS. How do I get an ITA?"

530 is above the April 2026 CEC cut-off (515). You should have received an ITA already, unless your profile was incomplete, your score calculation was wrong, or you're in the PNP stream. Double-check:

- Is your IELTS/CELPIP score on file and valid?
- Is your educational credential formally assessed?
- Are you claiming work experience accurately (no date gaps)?

If 530 is confirmed and you haven't gotten an ITA, contact your province's PNP office. You may have been nominated.


## What Mistakes Can Cost You CRS Points or Get Your Application Rejected?

**Short answer:** Do not claim a NOC you do not work in, backdate or pad work experience, double-count simultaneous education and work, report spouse credentials when not included, or misrepresent education credentials; misrepresentation triggers rejection plus a 5-year ban and potential permanent inadmissibility.

IRCC catches misreported data. Do not:

- Claim a NOC code you don't work in. IRCC cross-references your work history, responsibilities, and credentials. A software developer claiming NOC 0211 (managers) triggers manual review.
- Backdate or pad your work experience. IRCC requests reference letters, payslips, and tax files. Dishonesty leads to rejection and a ban on future applications.
- Double-count years of simultaneous education and work. If you worked while studying, only count the months you actually worked, not the entire year.
- Report your spouse's education or language if they're not included in your profile. Only claim points for their credentials if you're applying as a couple.
- Misrepresent your education credential. A diploma is not a bachelor's degree. A certificate is not a diploma. IRCC verifies against official transcripts.

The cost of dishonesty: application rejection, a 5-year ban on re-applying, and potential permanent resident ineligibility.


## Where Do Most Candidates Sit in the Express Entry Pool in 2026?

**Short answer:** Pool distribution: 351 candidates above 600 CRS, 11,648 between 501 to 600 (most CEC cuts fall here), 13,500+ between 491 to 500 (the densest cluster just 10 points below the 507 CEC cut-off), 15,000+ between 400 to 490, and 20,000+ below 300.

Understanding the pool is as important as understanding your own score.

- **Above 600 CRS:** Only 351 candidates. These are the anomalies: people with PhDs, multiple credentials, or provincial nominations who haven't received ITAs yet.
- **501–600 CRS:** 11,648 candidates. This is the "competitive zone" for every draw. Most CEC cuts fall here.
- **491–500 CRS:** 13,500+ candidates. The densest cluster. Just 10 points below the 507 CEC cut-off. A small improvement (one language test, a few months of Canadian work) moves people from "frustrated" to "invited."
- **400–490 CRS:** 15,000+ candidates. Below current draw cuts but above 300. These people are pursuing strategies 1–17.
- **Below 300 CRS:** 20,000+ candidates. Mostly students, recent immigrants, or people with limited credentials. They're building work experience or pursuing targeted draws.

If you're between 491–507, you're within reach of the current CEC cut-off. One small move (CLB 9 language, a job offer, or 6 months of Canadian work) could seal it.


## What Are the CRS Changes for 2026 and Beyond?

**Short answer:** IRCC announced plans in April 2026 to retire the three-stream Express Entry (FSW, CEC, FST) by late 2027 and replace it with a single Federal High-Skilled Class requiring just one year of skilled Canadian work or a validated job offer, with first invitations late 2027 to 2028.

In April 2026, [IRCC announced plans](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/consultations/2026-consultation-express-entry-reforms.html) to retire the current three-stream Express Entry system (FSW, CEC, FST) and replace it with a single "Federal High-Skilled Class" by late 2027.

**What changes:**
- The CRS framework will remain, but eligibility rules will tighten: you'll need just one year of skilled Canadian work experience (instead of CEC's current requirement) or a validated job offer.
- Language and education will be recalibrated to favour in-demand occupations based on Canada's National Occupational Outlook.
- Invitations should favour earnings potential and job offer holders more heavily.

**Timeline:** IRCC is consulting stakeholders through Spring 2026. Final rules expected in late 2027, with first invitations late 2027 to 2028.

**What this means for you now:** The current system is still active. If you get an ITA before the new class launches, you're processed under current rules. Don't wait hoping for easier rules in 2028. Improve now and apply under the system that exists today.

## What Are the Most Common Questions About CRS Score Improvement?

**How often does IRCC hold Express Entry draws?**
In 2026, IRCC is drawing multiple times per week across different categories. CEC draws happened roughly every 2 weeks. French-language draws happen every 1–2 weeks. Check [IRCC's official rounds of invitations page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations.html) for the schedule.

**Can my CRS score drop?**
Yes. Your CRS score recalculates if you turn 30 (age points drop), if your language certification expires, or if your work experience date changes. Most candidates' scores remain stable unless these life events happen. Check your profile quarterly.

**How long does it take to raise your CRS by 50 points?**
Depends on your strategy. Retaking a language test takes 2–3 months. Adding Canadian work experience takes 6–12 months. Getting a job offer can happen in weeks or months depending on the market. French language (if you already know some) can be 3–4 months. There's no single timeline.

**Is a provincial nomination still the fastest way to PR in 2026?**
Yes. A PNP is a guaranteed +600 points and bypasses all competition in the general draw. If you qualify for a provincial stream (occupation, location, or work experience), PNP is your fastest lane. Timeline: 2–4 months in provinces like Manitoba or Saskatchewan; 3–6 months in Ontario or BC.

**Does IELTS General or IELTS Academic count for Express Entry?**
Both count. IELTS General (usually easier) is accepted by IRCC. IELTS Academic is also accepted. Whichever you take, your CLB score is what matters. Don't overthink this. Just take the one that suits your comfort level.

**Will the new Express Entry replacement class change how CRS is calculated?**
IRCC hasn't released final details yet, but the CRS framework itself will likely remain. Language and education point scales may shift to favour in-demand occupations. The safest move: don't wait for 2028. Apply under the current system if you qualify now.

# Parent Sponsorship Canada 2026: PGP Intake Frozen, Super Visa Is Your Best Option

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/parent-grandparent-sponsorship-frozen-2026
Category: Guides
Published: 2026-04-12
Author: Rami Mamar

> If you were hoping to sponsor your parents or grandparents for permanent residence in Canada in 2026, that option is not available this year.

> **Update, July 15, 2026:** IRCC has now formally paused all new Parents and Grandparents Program intake, including invitations from the 2020 pool, until further notice. Read our full breakdown: [IRCC pauses parent and grandparent sponsorship](/news/ircc-pauses-parent-grandparent-sponsorship-2026).

If you were hoping to sponsor your parents or grandparents for permanent residence in Canada in 2026, that option is not available this year. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) confirmed that there will be no new Parent and Grandparent Program (PGP) intake for 2026.

*As of April 12, 2026.*

IRCC is processing only the approximately 10,000 applications submitted during the 2025 interest-to-sponsor window. No new lottery, no new expressions of interest, and no new invitations are planned for 2026.

## Why Is the PGP Frozen?

**Short answer:** The 2026 PGP freeze is part of Canada's 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan, which cut overall permanent resident targets significantly across most immigration categories. The government paused all new PGP expressions of interest and invitations, and has signalled that the Super Visa is the preferred near-term family reunification pathway for parents and grandparents while the freeze is in effect.

The freeze is part of Canada's broader strategy to reduce temporary and permanent resident volumes. The 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan cut overall immigration targets significantly, and the PGP was one of the programs affected.

The government has signaled that the Super Visa is the preferred pathway for family reunification with parents and grandparents in the near term.

## What About Applications from 2025?

**Short answer:** If you submitted an interest-to-sponsor form during the 2025 intake window and received an invitation to apply, your application is being processed. The 2026 freeze does not affect applications already in the system. Those not selected in the 2025 lottery must wait for a future intake.

If you submitted an interest-to-sponsor form during the 2025 intake window and received an invitation to apply, your application is being processed. The 2026 freeze does not affect applications already in the system.

If you submitted an interest form but were not selected in the 2025 lottery, you will need to wait for a future intake.

## What Are Your Alternatives for Bringing Parents to Canada in 2026?

**Short answer:** Three alternatives exist while the PGP is frozen. The Super Visa is the best option, allowing stays of up to 5 years per entry on a 10-year multi-entry visa with no lottery and new March 2026 income flexibility. A regular visitor visa permits stays of up to 6 months with fewer insurance requirements. The third option is to wait for a possible 2027 PGP intake, which IRCC has not confirmed.

### 1. Super Visa (Best Option)

The Super Visa allows your parents or grandparents to visit Canada for up to 5 years per entry, with a visa valid for up to 10 years. Key advantages:

- **No lottery** – apply anytime
- **Long stays** – up to 5 years per visit without extensions
- **Multiple entries** – come and go freely
- **New income flexibility** (as of March 31, 2026): hosts can qualify using either of the two most recent tax years, and the visitor's own income can supplement the host's

The Super Visa requires private medical insurance from a Canadian provider and proof that the host meets the minimum income threshold.

### 2. Regular Visitor Visa

A standard visitor visa allows stays of up to 6 months. Less ideal for long-term family reunification, but simpler to obtain and does not require medical insurance.

### 3. Wait for 2027

IRCC has not confirmed whether a PGP intake will open in 2027. Given the current levels plan's focus on reducing immigration volumes, a 2027 intake is possible but not guaranteed.

## How Much Income Do I Need for a Super Visa for My Parents in 2026?

**Short answer:** The 2026 minimum income thresholds are: 2 persons $35,377, 3 persons $43,517, 4 persons $52,843, 5 persons $59,930, 6 persons $67,592, 7+ persons $75,253. As of March 31, 2026, you can meet the threshold using income from either of the two most recent tax years, and your parent or grandparent's own income can count toward the total if you and your co-signer fall short.

The income threshold for hosting parents or grandparents on a [Super Visa](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa.html) depends on your family size. See the [full income requirements on canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/forms-documents/host-financial-support.html):

| Family Size | Minimum Income Required |
|-------------|------------------------|
| 2 persons | $35,377 |
| 3 persons | $43,517 |
| 4 persons | $52,843 |
| 5 persons | $59,930 |
| 6 persons | $67,592 |
| 7+ persons | $75,253 |

**New for 2026:** You can now qualify by meeting the threshold in either of the two most recent tax years (not just the most recent). If you and your co-signer fall short, your parent's or grandparent's own income can also count toward the total.

## What Should Iranian and Middle Eastern Families Know About the 2026 PGP Freeze?

**Short answer:** Iranian and Middle Eastern families planning PGP sponsorship should pivot to the Super Visa given the 2026 freeze. The new March 2026 income flexibility helps families with year-to-year income variation or parents holding home-country pension income. Apply 2 to 3 months before your parents' intended travel date, as Super Visa processing times vary by visa office.

Many of our clients planned to bring their parents to Canada through the PGP. With the 2026 freeze, the Super Visa is the most practical path forward. The new income flexibility rules announced in March 2026 make it easier to qualify, especially for families where income varies year to year or where parents have pension income from their home country.

If your parents are in Iran, UAE, or another Middle Eastern country, processing times for Super Visa applications vary by visa office. Apply at least 2-3 months before your parents' intended travel date.

# LMIA Changes April 2026: New 8-Week Advertising Rule and Youth Targeting Requirements

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/new-lmia-rules-april-2026
Category: Work Permit
Published: 2026-04-12
Author: Maggi Issa

> As of April 1, 2026, IRCC and ESDC have significantly changed the requirements for Labour Market Impact Assessments (LMIAs) in the low-wage stream.

As of April 1, 2026, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) and Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) have significantly changed the requirements for Labour Market Impact Assessments (LMIAs) in the low-wage stream. These changes affect employers who want to hire foreign workers, and by extension, the workers who depend on LMIA-based work permits.

## What are the new LMIA rules in April 2026?

**Short answer:** Three April 1, 2026 changes, advertising period doubled from 4 to 8 consecutive weeks across at least 3 platforms including Government of Canada Job Bank; employers must demonstrate specific Canadian youth recruitment (ages 15 to 30) through youth-targeted platforms, local educational institutions and community organizations, and documented LMIA outreach; rural TFW employers can employ low-wage TFWs up to 15% of workforce (up from 10%) until March 2027.

| Requirement | Before April 1, 2026 | As of April 1, 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Advertising period (low-wage LMIA) | 4 consecutive weeks | 8 consecutive weeks |
| Youth recruitment efforts (ages 15-30) | Not required | Required, with documented outreach |
| Rural employer TFW workforce cap | 10% | 15% (until March 2027) |

### 1. Advertising Period Doubled: 4 Weeks to 8 Weeks

Employers applying for a low-wage LMIA must now advertise the position for **8 consecutive weeks** before submitting their LMIA application, per the [updated ESDC program requirements](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers/median-wage/low/requirements.html). Previously, the requirement was 4 weeks.

The advertising must be done on at least three platforms, including the Government of Canada's Job Bank. The job posting must include the wage, location, job duties, and required qualifications.

### 2. Youth Targeting Required

Employers must now demonstrate that they made specific efforts to recruit **Canadian youth** (ages 15-30) for the position. This means:

- Posting on platforms that target young Canadians  
- Contacting local educational institutions, community organizations, or youth employment centers  
- Documenting these outreach efforts in the LMIA application

Simply posting on a job board is no longer sufficient. ESDC wants to see evidence that the employer actively tried to fill the position with young Canadians before turning to foreign workers.

### 3. Rural Exception: 15% TFW Cap (Temporary)

Rural employers participating in the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) can now employ low-wage Temporary Foreign Workers (TFWs) up to 15% of their workforce, increased from 10% ([Canada.ca: Hire a temporary foreign worker](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers.html)). This exception runs until March 2027.

## How do the new LMIA rules affect workers in Canada?

**Short answer:** LMIA processing now takes longer overall (8-week advertising plus 4 to 8 weeks ESDC processing for low-wage positions equals 12 to 16 weeks total from job posting to LMIA approval); work permit applications themselves are unchanged once the LMIA is approved; rural workers may see easier hiring under the 15% workforce cap.

### If You Are Waiting for an LMIA

The longer advertising period means LMIA processing will take longer overall. Your employer now needs to advertise for 8 weeks before even submitting the LMIA application. Combined with ESDC processing times (currently 4-8 weeks for low-wage positions), the total timeline from job posting to LMIA approval could be 12-16 weeks.

### If You Are Applying for a Work Permit

Your work permit application itself is not affected. Once your employer has an approved LMIA, the work permit process remains the same. However, the LMIA stage takes longer, so plan accordingly.

### If Your Employer Is in a Rural Area

The raised 15% cap may make it easier for your employer to hire you, as they have more room under the workforce percentage limit.

## What do employers need to do under the new LMIA rules?

**Short answer:** Four employer actions: start advertising 8 weeks before the LMIA application, document all Canadian youth outreach efforts to local schools and community organizations, use the Job Bank as one of the three mandatory platforms, and track all recruitment evidence since ESDC will review it more closely under the new rules.

1. **Start advertising early** – Begin the 8-week advertising period as soon as possible.  
2. **Document youth outreach** – Keep records of all efforts to recruit Canadian youth.  
3. **Use the Job Bank** – It remains mandatory as one of the three advertising platforms.  
4. **Track everything** – ESDC will review recruitment evidence more closely under the new rules.

## Need Help With an LMIA-Based Work Permit?

**Short answer:** Go Far Global works with both employers and workers to navigate the LMIA process, talk to our team if you or your employer need guidance on the new LMIA requirements and how they affect your work permit timeline.

If you or your employer need guidance on the new LMIA requirements and how they affect your work permit timeline, [talk to our team](/appointment). We work with both employers and workers to navigate the LMIA process.

# Canada PR Fees Increasing April 30, 2026: Submit Your Application Before the Deadline

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-pr-fees-increasing-april-30-2026
Category: News
Published: 2026-04-12
Author: Rami Mamar

> The Canada PR fee increase 2026 takes effect on April 30, 2026 at 9:00 AM ET.

# Canada PR Fee Increase 2026: New RPRF and Application Fees Effective April 30

> **See also:** For every government fee across all programs, including citizenship, work and study permits, and biometrics, read our [complete 2026 Canada immigration fee guide](/news/canada-immigration-fees-2026-complete-cost-guide).

The Canada PR fee increase 2026 takes effect on **April 30, 2026 at 9:00 AM ET**. IRCC confirmed that all permanent residence application fees rise this year, including the Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF) from $575 to $600 and economic-class principal applicant fees from $950 to $990. This is the first biennial inflation adjustment under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.

If you plan to apply for permanent residence through Express Entry, a Provincial Nominee Program, family sponsorship, or any business stream, submitting your application before April 30 keeps you at the current PR fee Canada rates. The permanent residence application fee Canada increase affects every economic and family pathway, so the savings on a typical PR application range from $25 (RPRF only) to $135 or more for families.

## New Fee Table (Effective April 30, 2026)

**Short answer:** New PR fees effective April 30, 2026 — RPRF $575 to $600 (+$25), economic-class principal applicant $950 to $990 (+$40), economic-class spouse $950 to $990 (+$40), economic dependent child $260 to $270 (+$10), family sponsorship principal $590 to $615 (+$25), family sponsorship spouse $590 to $615 (+$25), business-class principal $1,810 to $1,895 (+$85); RPRF applies to principal and spouse but not dependent children.

| Fee Type | Current | New (Apr 30) | Increase |
|----------|---------|-------------|----------|
| Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF) | $575 | $600 | +$25 |
| Principal applicant (economic class) | $950 | $990 | +$40 |
| Spouse/partner (economic class) | $950 | $990 | +$40 |
| Dependent child (economic class) | $260 | $270 | +$10 |
| Family sponsorship (principal) | $590 | $615 | +$25 |
| Family sponsorship (spouse) | $590 | $615 | +$25 |
| Business class (principal) | $1,810 | $1,895 | +$85 |

The **Right of Permanent Residence Fee (RPRF)** is charged in addition to the application processing fee. It applies to the principal applicant and their spouse or common-law partner, but **not** to dependent children.

## Who Is Affected

**Short answer:** All permanent residence applicants across Express Entry (FSW, CEC, FSTP), Provincial Nominee Program, family sponsorship (spousal and parent/grandparent), business immigration including Start-Up Visa with pending commitment letters, Atlantic Immigration Program, Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot, and Humanitarian and Compassionate grounds.

Every permanent residence applicant across all categories:

- **Express Entry** (Federal Skilled Worker, Canadian Experience Class, Federal Skilled Trades)
- **Provincial Nominee Program (PNP)**
- **Family Sponsorship** (spousal, parent/grandparent)
- **Business Immigration** (Start-Up Visa applicants with pending commitment letters)
- **Atlantic Immigration Program**
- **Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot**
- **Humanitarian and Compassionate grounds**

## What You Should Do

**Short answer:** Submit before April 30 at 9:00 AM ET if your application is ready (applications received before the deadline are grandfathered at current rates) — if your application is almost ready, prioritize completing documents now since a family of four saves roughly $75 to $120; do not rush an incomplete application since incomplete submissions get returned and you would resubmit at the new rates anyway.

### If Your Application Is Ready

Submit it **before April 30 at 9:00 AM ET**. Applications received before the deadline are grandfathered at the current fee schedule. Do not wait.

### If Your Application Is Almost Ready

You have 18 days. Prioritize completing your documents now. The savings are modest per person ($25–$85), but for a family of four applying through Express Entry, the total increase is roughly **$75–$120**.

### If You Are Still Gathering Documents

Do **not** rush an incomplete application just to beat the deadline. An incomplete submission will be returned, and you will need to resubmit at the new rates. A complete application at the higher fee is better than an incomplete one that gets rejected.

## Why Are Fees Increasing?

**Short answer:** This is an automatic biennial adjustment tied to the Consumer Price Index — IRCC is required under the regulations to adjust fees every two years to keep pace with inflation, and the last adjustment was in 2024.

This is an automatic **biennial adjustment tied to the Consumer Price Index (CPI)**. IRCC is required under the regulations to adjust fees every two years to keep pace with inflation. The last adjustment was in 2024.
