# IRCC Log In Guide: How to Track Your Canadian Immigration Application

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/how-ircc-processes-immigration-applications
Category: Guides
Published: 2026-03-09
Author: Maggi Issa

> When you submit an application to move to Canada, tracking its progress through the IRCC log in portal becomes one of your most important tools.

# IRCC Log In Guide: How to Track Your Canadian Immigration Application

> **RELATED, April 24, 2026:** Citizenship processing dropped to **12 months** in April 2026, the lowest since 2020. If you are checking your citizenship file status through GCKey, see the **[citizenship processing time guide](/news/canadian-citizenship-processing-time-12-months-2026)** for what each stage looks like.


When you submit an application to move to Canada, tracking its progress through the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) log in portal becomes one of your most important tools. IRCC processes thousands of applications daily, and their online system lets you monitor exactly where yours stands. Whether you're waiting for a work permit, study permit, or permanent residence decision, knowing how to use IRCC log in effectively can reduce stress and help you respond quickly to any requests.

As of March 9, 2026.

This guide walks you through the IRCC processing system, shows you how to use the IRCC log in portal effectively, and explains what you can expect at each stage of your application.

## How Does IRCC Process Immigration Applications?

**Short answer:** IRCC is the federal department deciding all Canadian immigration matters; applications move through completeness review, eligibility assessment, security and criminality background checks, medical exam, document verification, and final decision, with regional offices in Abu Dhabi and Beirut handling many Middle East files.

IRCC is the federal department that makes final decisions on all immigration matters in Canada. They assess whether your application meets the legal requirements for the program you applied to, conduct background checks, and verify your documents.

When you apply through IRCC, your application goes through several stages:

- Initial completeness review
- Eligibility assessment
- Background checks (security, criminality, medical)
- Document verification
- Final decision

IRCC has offices across Canada and around the world. In the Middle East, IRCC processing offices in Abu Dhabi and Beirut handle many applications from Iranian and other regional applicants. Where your application gets processed depends on the program you're applying through and where you live.

## How Do You Access the IRCC Log In Portal and Track Your Application?

**Short answer:** To access the IRCC log in portal, you need your Application Number or Unique Client Identifier (UCI), which IRCC sends to you once they confirm receipt of your application. You then create a secure online account at [canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-status.html) or link an existing application to your profile. Once logged in, the portal shows your current application status, any requests from IRCC officers for additional documents, estimated processing times, messages from officers, and a document upload tool. For Express Entry applicants, the portal also displays your current Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score and pool standing.

The IRCC log in system (officially called "Check your application status online") is your main tool for monitoring your immigration application. Here's how it works:

**Setting Up Your IRCC Account:**

To use the IRCC log in portal, you need an Application Number (also called UCI - Unique Client Identifier). You receive this when IRCC confirms they received your application. You can then create an online account or link your existing application to your account.

**What You'll See After IRCC Log In:**

Once you access your account through IRCC log in, you can see:

- Current application status (received, in progress, decision made)
- Any requests from IRCC asking for more information
- Estimated processing times for your application type
- Messages from IRCC officers
- Document submission portal

For [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) applications, the IRCC log in portal also shows your current CRS score and whether you're in an active pool. You can use our [CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) to understand what score you need and how profile changes might affect your ranking.

**Understanding IRCC Processing Timelines Through the Portal:**

The IRCC log in system shows you estimated processing times, but these are not guarantees. According to the [IRCC Help Centre](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=068&top=3), processing time starts when IRCC receives a complete application and ends when a final decision is made. [Processing times](/immigration/processing-times) vary based on:

- Your background and countries you've lived in
- Complexity of your case
- Current application volumes
- Document verification requirements

Applicants from Iran and other Middle Eastern countries often see longer IRCC processing timelines due to additional security screening requirements.

## What Happens During IRCC's Initial Assessment of Your Application?

**Short answer:** After you submit your application, IRCC first conducts a completeness review to confirm the form is filled out correctly, all required documents are included, fees are paid in full, and any non-English or non-French documents include certified translations. If your application is incomplete, IRCC sends a request through your online portal giving you 30 days to provide the missing materials. If you miss that deadline, IRCC closes your file without making a decision, and you would need to restart the process. Only after the application passes completeness review does IRCC proceed to the eligibility assessment stage.

After you submit your application, IRCC starts with completeness review. An officer checks:

- Is the application form filled out correctly?
- Are all required documents included?
- Are fees paid?
- Is everything in proper language (English or French with certified translations)?

If your application is incomplete, you'll see a request through your IRCC log in account. You have 30 days to respond. Missing this deadline means IRCC closes your application without processing it further.

Once IRCC confirms completeness, they review eligibility. For [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) applications, this includes verifying language scores, education credentials, and work experience. For [Provincial Nominee Programs](/immigration/provincial-nominee), they confirm you meet both provincial and federal requirements.

If you don't meet basic requirements, IRCC can refuse your application at this stage. Getting professional advice before applying helps avoid this outcome. If you're unsure about your eligibility, [book a consultation](/appointment) with a licensed immigration consultant.

## What Background Checks and Security Screening Does IRCC Conduct?

**Short answer:** Background checks are typically the longest phase, covering security screening (against terrorism and organized crime), criminality police records from every country lived in 6+ months in the past 10 years, medical exam, and inadmissibility review; applicants from Iran face longer timelines here.

Background checks are often the longest part of IRCC processing timelines. Through your IRCC log in portal, you might see your application status as "in progress" for months during this phase.

IRCC conducts several types of checks:

**Security Screening:**
IRCC contacts intelligence agencies to verify you have no connections to terrorism, organized crime, or hostile governments. This process takes longer for applicants from certain countries, including Iran.

**Criminality Checks:**
IRCC requests police records from every country you've lived in for more than six months in the past 10 years. Response times vary significantly by country.

**Medical Examinations:**
For most programs, you need a medical exam with an IRCC-approved doctor. Results go directly to IRCC and appear in your account status.

**Inadmissibility Review:**
IRCC checks for previous visa refusals, overstays, or immigration violations.

These checks explain why some applications take much longer than published IRCC processing timelines. For expected timelines by program, the [IRCC Help Centre](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=31&top=3) provides updated estimates. Your IRCC log in account won't show detailed progress on background checks, just that they're "in progress."

## How Does IRCC Verify Your Documents During Processing?

**Short answer:** During IRCC processing, officers may contact your universities, former employers, language testing organizations, and police authorities to confirm the accuracy of the documents you submitted. This verification step can take weeks or months, especially if third parties are slow to respond. If IRCC finds that documents were falsified or misleading, they refuse the application and may impose a ban on future applications. Applicants from Iran and some other countries may be required to provide additional document authentication because of known concerns about certain regional credentials.

A critical part of IRCC processing involves verifying submitted documents. IRCC may contact:

- Universities and colleges to confirm education credentials
- Employers to verify work experience claims
- Testing organizations to confirm language scores
- Police authorities for criminal record checks

Document fraud is taken seriously. If IRCC discovers false documents, they refuse the application and can impose lifetime bans.

For Iranian applicants, IRCC may require additional document authentication due to concerns about document fraud from certain regions. This can extend IRCC processing timelines significantly.

## What Do the Different IRCC Log In Status Updates Mean?

**Short answer:** Your IRCC log in account displays five main status messages. "Application Received" confirms that IRCC has your application and fees. "In Progress" means an officer is reviewing your file, a stage that can last several months. "Additional Documents Required" signals that IRCC needs something from you and you must respond within 30 days. "Decision Made" means IRCC has either approved or refused your application. "Closed" indicates the application was withdrawn, abandoned, or a deadline was missed. Status updates do not happen daily, so a long period of "In Progress" is normal during background checks or document verification.

Your IRCC log in account shows different status messages:

| Status | What It Means | Action Required |
|--------|---------------|-----------------|
| Application Received | IRCC has your application and fees | None; continue waiting |
| In Progress | IRCC is reviewing your file | Check portal weekly |
| Additional Documents Required | IRCC needs more information | Respond within 30 days |
| Decision Made | IRCC has approved or refused your application | Review the decision |
| Closed | Application was withdrawn or abandoned | Contact IRCC if unexpected |

Status updates don't happen daily. Your application might show "in progress" for months while IRCC waits for background check results or document verification.

## What Are the Common Issues That Delay IRCC Processing?

**Short answer:** Delays in IRCC processing usually trace back to a small set of recurring issues. Name spelling variations across passports, birth certificates, and other identity documents are a common trigger, particularly for applicants from Iran where Persian transliteration into English can produce multiple valid spellings of the same name. Missing police certificates for countries you lived in are another frequent cause. Other common delays include employers who do not respond to IRCC verification inquiries, questions about foreign education credentials, and follow-up requests after unusual medical exam results.

Several issues frequently delay applications and appear as requests in your IRCC log in account:

**Name Variations:**
If your name appears differently across documents, IRCC requests explanations. This commonly affects Iranian applicants due to Persian name transliteration issues.

**Missing Police Certificates:**
IRCC often requests additional police clearances, especially if you've traveled extensively.

**Employment Verification:**
If employers don't respond to IRCC inquiries, processing delays significantly.

**Education Credential Issues:**
Degrees from Iran may require additional verification or credential assessments.

**Medical Exam Follow-ups:**
Unusual medical results trigger additional testing requests.

## How Do You Respond to IRCC Requests Through the Portal?

**Short answer:** When a request appears in your IRCC log in account, read the full message carefully to understand exactly what officers need. Most requests give you 30 days to respond, and missing that window can result in your application being refused or closed. Submit a complete, organized response rather than sending partial documents, because incomplete answers often generate a follow-up request and add more time to your wait. Upload all documents directly through the portal, and keep digital copies of everything you submit in case you need to reference them later.

When IRCC requests additional information, you'll see it immediately after IRCC log in. Here's how to respond effectively:

1. **Read carefully:** Understand exactly what IRCC is asking for
2. **Check deadlines:** Most requests have 30-day response windows
3. **Submit complete responses:** Partial responses often trigger follow-up requests
4. **Use the portal:** Upload documents directly through your IRCC log in account
5. **Keep copies:** Save everything you submit

If you're unsure how to respond to an IRCC request, get professional help immediately. Missing deadlines or submitting incorrect information can result in application refusal.

## When Should You Seek Professional Help With Your IRCC Application?

**Short answer:** Get professional help when your portal shows no updates for months beyond normal processing, when you receive complex document requests you do not understand, when IRCC asks about discrepancies, when considering withdrawal, or when you receive a procedural fairness letter.

Consider professional assistance if:

- Your IRCC log in account shows no updates for months beyond normal processing times
- You receive complex document requests you don't understand
- IRCC asks for explanations about discrepancies in your application
- You're considering withdrawing and resubmitting your application
- You receive a procedural fairness letter

A licensed immigration consultant can review your file status, help respond to IRCC requests, and advise on next steps. [Schedule a consultation](/appointment) if you need expert guidance.

## What Are Common Questions About IRCC Log In and Processing?

**Short answer:** The most common questions about the IRCC portal concern how often to check it, what the status messages mean, and why processing is taking longer than the published estimate. Checking weekly is sufficient since IRCC does not send notifications for every status change. "In Progress" for several months is normal, as it reflects background check and document verification activity that is not visible in the portal. Timelines longer than the website estimates are common for applicants from countries with additional security screening requirements.

### How often should I check my IRCC log in account?

Check your IRCC log in account weekly. IRCC doesn't send email notifications for all updates, so regular checking ensures you don't miss important requests. However, checking daily won't make your application move faster.

### What does it mean when my IRCC log in shows "in progress" for months?

This is normal. "In progress" means IRCC is conducting background checks, verifying documents, or waiting for responses from third parties like police forces or employers. IRCC processing timelines often extend beyond published estimates due to these external factors.

### Can I log in to IRCC to check someone else's application status?

No, you can only access applications where you're the principal applicant or an authorized representative. Family members included in your application can see the same information through your account, but they cannot create separate logins for the same application.

### Why is my IRCC processing timeline longer than the website estimates?

Published processing times are averages, not guarantees. Your timeline may be longer due to complex background checks, document verification delays, missing information, or high application volumes at your processing office. Applications from certain countries, including Iran, often take longer due to additional security screening.

### What should I do if I can't access my IRCC log in account?

First, try resetting your password. If that doesn't work, contact IRCC technical support. Keep your Application Number and personal information handy. You can also submit a web form through the IRCC website to request application status updates if you cannot access your online account.

## Where Can You Get Expert Help With Your IRCC Application?

Navigating IRCC processing can be complex, especially when dealing with document requests, extended timelines, or unusual circumstances. The IRCC log in portal gives you visibility into your application status, but it doesn't explain what delays mean or how to address them.

If you're facing challenges with your IRCC application, professional guidance can make a significant difference. A licensed immigration consultant can review your file, help interpret IRCC requests, and ensure you respond appropriately to avoid refusals.

Before applying through any IRCC program, get a professional assessment of your eligibility and documentation strategy. This is especially important for applicants from Iran and the Middle East, who often face longer processing times and additional scrutiny.

# Canada Immigration Iran Special Measures 2026: Complete Guide to Changes and Lost Access

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-iran-special-measures-2026-changes
Category: News
Published: 2026-03-07
Author: Rami Mamar

> On March 1, 2026, Canada quietly renewed its canada immigration iran special measures for Iranian nationals. But this renewal is not a continuation of what came before.

# Canada Immigration Iran Special Measures 2026: Complete Guide to Changes and Lost Access

On March 1, 2026, Canada quietly renewed its **canada immigration iran** [special measures for Iranian nationals](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/iran.html). But this renewal is not a continuation of what came before. The new policy strips nearly every **immigration from iran to canada** pathway that was previously available, leaving only one option: a single work permit extension for those who already hold a valid work permit.

If you are an Iranian national in Canada, or advising one, the changes are significant. Here is what happened, what was removed, and what options remain for **iran canada immigration**.

*As of March 7, 2026.*

## How did Canada's Iran immigration special measures evolve from 2023 to 2026?

**Short answer:** Canada first introduced Iran special measures in February 2023, following the death of Mahsa Amini and the widespread protests across Iran, originally offering open work permits, study permit facilitation, visitor record extensions, fee waivers, and family inclusion as a broad humanitarian response. Each subsequent renewal has progressively narrowed the program, culminating in the 2026 revision that leaves only a single pathway.

Canada first introduced special **immigration to canada from iran** measures in **February 2023**, following the death of Mahsa Amini and the widespread protests that followed. The Iranian government's violent crackdown left many Iranians in Canada unable to safely return home.

The original policy was broad and humanitarian in scope. It recognized the danger facing Iranian nationals and offered multiple pathways to maintain legal status in Canada.

## What is the timeline of restrictions on Canada Iran special measures from 2023 to 2026?

**Short answer:** The 2023 original policy was generous and humanitarian; the March 2025 update added a February 28, 2025 arrival cutoff but kept most pathways; the March 1, 2026 revision eliminates everything except a one-time work permit extension for existing work-permit holders.

The progression from 2023 to 2026 tells a clear story of systematic narrowing for **canada iran immigration**.

### 2023 Original Policy (February 2023)

- Open work permits for Iranian nationals in Canada
- Study permit facilitation for students needing to extend or change institutions
- Visitor record extensions for those on visitor status
- Fee waivers for most application types
- No arrival-date restrictions
- Family members included in most provisions

This was Canada's most generous response, offering flexibility across almost every temporary resident category.

### 2025 Update (March 2025)

- Maintained most pathways from the original policy
- Added an **arrival cutoff**: applicants must have arrived in Canada by **February 28, 2025**
- Fee exemptions applied to applications submitted before **March 1, 2025**
- Visitor-to-worker transitions still permitted
- Student extensions still available

The 2025 update introduced time-based restrictions but kept the range of pathways intact. If you were already in Canada before the cutoff, you could still access the full suite of options.

### 2026 Revision (March 1, 2026)

- **Only work permit extensions** for existing work permit holders
- One-time benefit only (cannot be used again)
- Must hold a work permit issued before **February 28, 2025**
- Deadline: **March 31, 2027**
- No study permit facilitation
- No visitor extensions
- No status changes (visitor to worker, student to worker)
- No open work permits for new applicants
- Policy can be revoked at any time

The 2026 revision eliminates every pathway except a single work permit extension. This is no longer a broad humanitarian response. It is a wind-down measure.

## What immigration pathways were removed in 2026 and what still remains?

**Short answer:** Removed in 2026: open work permits, study-permit facilitation, visitor record extensions, visitor-to-worker and student-to-worker transitions, fee waivers, and broad family inclusion; only the one-time work-permit extension survives, and applicants must hold a work permit issued before February 28, 2025.

| Immigration Pathway | 2023 Policy | 2025 Update | 2026 Revision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open work permits | Yes | Yes (with cutoff) | **No** |
| Work permit extensions | Yes | Yes | **Yes (one-time only)** |
| Study permit facilitation | Yes | Yes | **No** |
| Visitor record extensions | Yes | Yes | **No** |
| Visitor-to-worker transitions | Yes | Yes | **No** |
| Student-to-worker transitions | Yes | Yes | **No** |
| Fee waivers | Yes | Partial | **No** |
| Family member inclusion | Yes | Yes | **Limited** |
| Arrival date restriction | None | Feb 28, 2025 | Must hold WP before Feb 28, 2025 |

## Who is still eligible for Canada's Iran immigration special measures in 2026?

**Short answer:** Eligibility under the 2026 revision requires being an Iranian national currently in Canada, holding a valid work permit that was issued before February 28, 2025, applying for a one-time extension only, submitting the application before the March 31, 2027 deadline, and satisfying standard work-permit extension requirements including a valid job offer and employer compliance. Review the [eligibility criteria on the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) Iran page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/iran.html).

The current **iran immigration to canada** policy applies to a narrow group:

- You must be an **Iranian national currently in Canada**
- You must hold a **work permit that was issued before February 28, 2025**
- This is a **one-time extension** (you cannot use this policy again for a second extension)
- You must apply **before March 31, 2027**
- Standard [work permit](/immigration/work-permit) extension requirements still apply (valid job offer, employer compliance)

If you meet all of these criteria, you can apply for a work permit extension under the facilitative public policy. The extension process is streamlined compared to standard applications, but it is not automatic.

## Who lost access to Canada's Iran special measures under the 2026 policy?

**Short answer:** Iranian students needing study-permit extensions, Iranian visitors extending stays or switching status, new arrivals after February 28, 2025, applicants seeking open work permits, and most family members previously covered now fall under standard rules without accommodations or fee waivers.

The following groups can no longer benefit from the special measures:

- **Iranian students** who needed [study permit](/immigration/study-permit) extensions or wanted to transition to work permits
- **Iranian visitors** who were using the special measures to extend their stay or switch to work or study status
- **New arrivals** who came to Canada after February 28, 2025
- **Iranian nationals seeking open work permits** (no longer available under any special measures provision)
- **Family members** who previously qualified through the broader policy provisions

For these groups, the standard immigration system now applies. There are no special accommodations or fee waivers.

## What does the 2026 policy change signal about Canada's immigration direction?

**Short answer:** The pattern is unmistakable: 2023 was a broad humanitarian response with multiple pathways, 2025 maintained those same pathways with time-based entry restrictions, and 2026 leaves only a single pathway with a fixed end date. The March 31, 2027 deadline and the "may be revoked at any time" clause together signal a structured wind-down of Canada's special immigration response to the Iranian situation.

The pattern is unmistakable. Each renewal has removed pathways and tightened eligibility:

1. **2023**: Full humanitarian response with multiple pathways
2. **2025**: Same pathways but with time-based restrictions
3. **2026**: Single pathway remaining, one-time use, with a fixed end date

This is a structured wind-down of Canada's special immigration response to the Iranian crisis. The March 31, 2027 deadline and the "may be revoked at any time" clause both signal that this will likely be the final iteration.

Iranian nationals who are currently benefiting from these measures should plan for the eventual end of this program and explore permanent immigration pathways now, while they still have valid status in Canada.

## What alternative immigration pathways are available for Iranian nationals in Canada?

**Short answer:** Alternatives include [Express Entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html) (Canadian work experience boosts your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score significantly), [Provincial Nominee Programs](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees.html) (a provincial nomination adds 600 CRS points, effectively guaranteeing an invitation to apply), Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA)-supported employer-specific work permits, family sponsorship for those with Canadian-citizen or permanent-resident relatives, and humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds for exceptional circumstances.

If you no longer qualify under the special measures, or if you want to secure a more permanent solution, several pathways remain available:

### Express Entry

Canada's [Express Entry system](/immigration/express-entry) is the primary pathway for skilled workers. If you have Canadian work experience from your time under the special measures, this strengthens your application significantly. Use our [CRS Calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) to estimate your score.

### Provincial Nominee Programs (PNPs)

Many provinces actively recruit workers in high-demand occupations. If your employer is willing to support a provincial nomination, this can add **600 points** to your Express Entry score, effectively guaranteeing an invitation. Explore [Provincial Nominee Programs](/immigration/provincial-nominee) for detailed guidance.

### Employer-Specific Work Permits

If your current employer wants to retain you beyond the special measures extension, they can apply for a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) to support a standard [work permit](/immigration/work-permit) application. Check current [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) to plan accordingly.

### Family Sponsorship

If you have close family members who are Canadian citizens or permanent residents, [family sponsorship](/immigration/family-immigration) may provide a path to permanent residence.

### Humanitarian and Compassionate Grounds

In exceptional circumstances, Iranian nationals may apply for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds, particularly if returning to Iran poses genuine risk.

## What are the key deadlines Iranian nationals need to know for the 2026 special measures?

**Short answer:** March 31, 2027 is the final deadline to apply under the [2026 work permit extension measures](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/iran.html); Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) applies standard processing times, so submit your application well before the deadline to avoid last-minute delays; the government also retains the right to revoke the policy at any time before that date.

- **March 31, 2027**: Final deadline to apply under the 2026 special measures work permit extension
- **Policy revocation risk**: The government retains the right to end the policy at any time before the deadline
- **Processing times**: Standard [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) apply, so apply well before the deadline

## How should Iranian nationals in Canada plan before the March 31, 2027 deadline?

**Short answer:** Whether you still qualify for the remaining work permit extension under Canada's Iran special measures or need to pivot to alternative immigration pathways, timing matters. The special measures are winding down toward their March 31, 2027 end date, and starting a concrete plan for permanent residence through standard Canadian immigration channels should be your immediate priority.

## What changed in Canada's 2026 Iran immigration special measures?

**Short answer:** The 2026 renewal is the most restrictive version of Canada's Iran special measures to date. What started in 2023 as a comprehensive humanitarian response with multiple open pathways has been progressively reduced to a single work-permit extension pathway, with strict eligibility requirements and a fixed end date of March 31, 2027. Iranian nationals currently in Canada should treat this as the final phase of this program.

For Iranian nationals currently in Canada, the message is clear: plan for permanent residence through standard immigration channels. The special measures are winding down, and alternative pathways offer more stable, long-term solutions.

# New Canada Immigration Minister Deputy Ted Gallivan: What It Means for Immigration System

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/ted-gallivan-new-deputy-minister-immigration-canada
Category: News
Published: 2026-03-05
Author: Rami Mamar

> Short answer: On March 4, 2026, PM Mark Carney named Ted Gallivan the new Deputy Minister of IRCC, the highest-ranking civil servant position responsible for day-to-day operations...

## New Canada Immigration Minister Deputy: Ted Gallivan Takes Charge of IRCC

**Short answer:** On March 4, 2026, PM Mark Carney named Ted Gallivan the new Deputy Minister of IRCC — the highest-ranking civil servant position responsible for day-to-day operations, budget, staffing, and executing policy direction; Gallivan was most recently interim deputy national security and intelligence advisor to the Prime Minister.

On March 4, 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a major reshuffle in the senior ranks of Canada's public service. The most significant change for immigrants: Ted Gallivan, most recently the interim deputy national security and intelligence advisor to the Prime Minister, was named the **new Canada immigration minister** deputy at Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).

The deputy minister role is the highest-ranking civil servant position in the department. Unlike the Minister of Immigration (currently Rachel Bendayan), the deputy minister is non-political. They run the day-to-day operations of IRCC, manage the department's budget, oversee staffing, and execute policy direction set by the government.

Gallivan's appointment as the **new immigration minister Canada** deputy is part of a broader shake-up that also saw Glenn Purves (from BlackRock) become Deputy Minister of International Trade, David Morrison shift to Senior Diplomatic Advisor, and Arun Thangaraj move to Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs.

## Who Is the New Immigration Minister of Canada Deputy?

**Short answer:** Gallivan holds a Concordia BA in Political Science with 35 years public service starting at the GST Interim Processing Centre — 16 years at Canada Revenue Agency rising to Assistant Commissioner of Compliance Programs Branch (2016-2021), then Executive Vice-President at the Canada Border Services Agency (2021-2025), then interim deputy national security advisor (2025-2026).

Ted Gallivan holds a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Concordia University. He started his public service career in 1991 as a summer intern at the GST Interim Processing Centre.

His career path tells a clear story: enforcement, compliance, and operational management across three key agencies that directly impact immigration.

### Canada Revenue Agency (2005 to 2021)

The **new immigration minister in canada** deputy spent 16 years at the CRA, climbing through increasingly senior roles:

- **Director, Internal Audit, Tax Operations** (2005 to 2008)
- **Director, Business Registration and Corporation Programs** (2008 to 2010)
- **Director, Summerside Tax Centre** (2010)
- **Director General, Business Returns Directorate** (2010 to 2013)
- **Deputy Assistant Commissioner, Collections and Verification Branch** (2013 to 2014)
- **Deputy Assistant Commissioner, Compliance Programs Branch** (2014 to 2016)
- **Assistant Commissioner, Compliance Programs Branch** (2016 to 2021)

His final five years at CRA were spent running the entire Compliance Programs Branch, the division responsible for ensuring Canadians and businesses follow tax law.

### Canada Border Services Agency (2021 to 2025)

In October 2021, Gallivan became Executive Vice-President of the CBSA, the agency responsible for border control, customs enforcement, and immigration enforcement at ports of entry. This gave him direct experience with the immigration system's front lines: processing arrivals, managing removals, and enforcing admissibility rules.

### National Security Advisor Role (2025 to 2026)

Before his IRCC appointment, Gallivan served as interim deputy national security and intelligence advisor to the Prime Minister, a role focused on national security coordination across government agencies.

## Who Is the New Minister of Immigration Canada Deputy Replacing?

**Short answer:** Gallivan replaces Dr. Harpreet S. Kochhar (IRCC Deputy Minister since January 2024) whose tenure oversaw the 2024 temporary resident cap reduction to 5% of population, PR target cuts from 485,000 (2024) to 395,000 (2025), study permit caps, PGWP tightening, spousal work permit restrictions, and low-wage TFWP cuts from 20% to 10% workforce cap.

Gallivan replaces Dr. Harpreet S. Kochhar, who served as IRCC Deputy Minister since January 2024. Kochhar was no stranger to the department. He had previously served as Assistant Deputy Minister of Operations at IRCC from 2017 to 2020, advising four different immigration ministers during that earlier stint.

Before returning to IRCC, Kochhar led the Public Health Agency of Canada during the COVID-19 pandemic (2021 to 2023) and served as president of the Canadian Food Inspection Agency.

### Key Changes During Kochhar's Watch (2024 to 2026)

Kochhar oversaw IRCC during one of the most significant policy shifts in recent Canadian immigration history:

- **Temporary resident cap announced**: In 2024, the government committed to reducing temporary residents to 5% of Canada's total population over three years, the first time Canada set hard targets for temporary immigration.
- **Permanent resident targets slashed**: The 2025-2027 Immigration Levels Plan cut PR admissions from 485,000 (2024) to 395,000 (2025), with further reductions planned.
- **International student cap**: IRCC introduced annual caps on [study permits](/immigration/study-permit), with a further 10% reduction in 2025 compared to 2024 targets.
- **PGWP tightening**: Post-Graduation Work Permit eligibility was narrowed to better align with labor market needs.
- **Spousal work permit restrictions**: [Work permit](/immigration/work-permit) access for spouses of international students and temporary foreign workers was restricted.
- **Low-wage TFWP cuts**: The employer cap for lower-wage temporary workers was dropped from 20% to 10% of workforce, with exemptions only for construction, healthcare, and food processing.
- **Operational modernization**: Kochhar led efforts to speed up straightforward applications and free up officers to focus on complex cases.

Kochhar's tenure will be remembered as the period when Canada reversed course on high-volume immigration and began tightening the system across every category.

## What Who Is the New Immigration Minister Canada Deputy's Background Tells Us About IRCC's Direction

**Short answer:** Gallivan compliance and enforcement background points to stronger document verification, increased TFWP and LMIA employer compliance audits, and faster removals leveraging his CBSA enforcement experience — combined with CRA-honed operational efficiency, expect "fewer immigrants but better outcomes" aligned with Carney government priorities.

Deputy minister appointments are not random. The government picks someone whose skill set matches the department's priorities. Gallivan's profile points in a clear direction.

### Expect Stronger Compliance and Verification

Gallivan spent his entire career building and running compliance systems. At CRA, he oversaw tax enforcement for five years. At CBSA, he managed the operational side of border enforcement. This is someone who knows how to build systems that catch fraud and enforce rules.

For immigration applicants, this likely means:

- **Tighter document verification**: Expect IRCC to invest more in detecting fraudulent applications, fake job offers, and misrepresented credentials.
- **Employer compliance audits**: The TFWP and LMIA system could see increased audits on employers who sponsor foreign workers.
- **Faster removals**: With his CBSA background, Gallivan understands the deportation and removal process. Enforcement of departure orders and inadmissibility findings may become more efficient.

### Operational Efficiency Over Volume

Gallivan's CRA career was defined by managing large-scale operations. The CRA processes millions of tax returns annually. That experience in high-volume processing could translate to faster application [processing times](/immigration/processing-times) at IRCC, but with a focus on accuracy over speed.

This aligns with the Carney government's stated priority: fewer immigrants, but better outcomes for those who come.

### Alignment with Carney's Immigration Vision

Prime Minister Carney has already laid out a clear immigration agenda:

- **Reduced PR targets**: 395,000 in 2025, 380,000 in 2026, 365,000 in 2027
- **International Mobility Program cuts**: Nearly halved, from 285,750 permits in 2025 to 128,700 in 2026
- **[Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) priorities**: Healthcare workers, skilled trades, scientists, researchers, and senior managers get priority
- **New doctor pathway**: A dedicated Express Entry stream for international doctors to address healthcare gaps
- **H-1B talent recruitment**: Active efforts to attract skilled workers from the United States

Gallivan's enforcement background makes him a natural fit to implement these priorities. Reducing immigration numbers while maintaining program integrity requires exactly the kind of compliance-first mindset he brings.

## What This Means for Your Immigration Application

**Short answer:** Express Entry candidates should ensure NOC code accuracy and verifiable work experience; work permit applicants face increased employer compliance scrutiny; visitor visa applicants need strong home-country ties and clear travel purpose; family sponsorship applicants need complete accurate documentation; international students should choose DLI programs aligning with labour market needs; PNP applicants may face increased federal-provincial scrutiny.

If you are applying to come to Canada or are already in the system, here is what to keep in mind:

**For Express Entry candidates**: The system continues to prioritize skilled workers in healthcare, trades, and STEM fields. CRS scores matter, but so does your occupation. Use our [CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) to check your current score and make sure your NOC code and work experience documentation are accurate and verifiable.

**For work permit applicants**: Employer compliance is likely to face more scrutiny. If your employer is sponsoring you through the TFWP or an LMIA, make sure the job offer is genuine and the employer can demonstrate a real labor market need.

**For visitor visa applicants**: Gallivan's CBSA experience means he understands admissibility from the enforcement side. Strong ties to your home country, clear travel purpose, and solid financial documentation remain critical.

**For family sponsorship applicants**: While enforcement tightening primarily affects economic streams, all [family immigration](/immigration/family-immigration) applicants should ensure their documentation is complete and accurate. Processing times may improve as IRCC modernizes its systems.

**For international students**: With study permit caps already in place, competition for spots will remain intense. Choose DLI programs that align with labor market needs to strengthen future PR pathways.

**For Provincial Nominee Program applicants**: [PNP streams](/immigration/provincial-nominee) may face increased scrutiny as the federal government works with provinces to ensure nominees meet both provincial and federal requirements.

## The Bottom Line

**Short answer:** Gallivan appointment signals the Carney government is serious about transforming IRCC from volume-focused to compliance-, enforcement-, and selectivity-focused — his 20+ years in tax compliance and border enforcement provide the tools to implement reduced immigration targets while cracking down on fraud; accuracy and genuineness in applications matter more than ever.

Ted Gallivan's appointment signals that the Carney government is serious about transforming IRCC from a volume-focused department into one that prioritizes compliance, enforcement, and selectivity. His 20+ years in tax compliance and border enforcement give him the tools to implement the government's reduced immigration targets while cracking down on fraud and misuse.

For immigration applicants, the message is clear: accuracy and genuineness in your applications have never been more important. The era of high-volume, low-scrutiny immigration in Canada is over.

# IMM 5710 Form 2026: Download and Work Permit Guide

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/imm5710
Category: Immigration
Published: 2026-03-03
Author: Maggi Issa

> Short answer: The IMM5710, officially the "Application to Change Conditions, Extend my Stay or Remain in Canada as a Worker," is the IRCC form you use to extend a work permit...

# IMM 5710 Form 2026: Download and Work Permit Guide

*As of September 4, 2026.*

IMM 5710 is Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada's (IRCC) form to change conditions, extend your stay, or remain in Canada as a worker. The official download page last updated the PDF in September 2023. You complete it on a computer in Adobe Acrobat Reader, not on a phone. The inside-Canada work-permit document list still names IMM 5710. Google's live questions about this form are answered below from those IRCC pages.

## TL;DR

IMM 5710 is the in-Canada worker form: extend, change conditions, or remain as a worker | Official PDF last updated September 2023 on the IRCC form page | Download on a computer, open in Acrobat Reader 10 or higher | IRCC gives a personalized document checklist when you apply online | Instruction guide is IMM 5553 / Guide 5553 | Restoration, if you qualify, is within 90 days of losing status

## What is the IMM 5710 form?

**Short answer:** It is the [Application to Change Conditions, Extend my Stay or Remain in Canada as a Worker (IMM 5710)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/imm5710.html). Each person who wants to apply in that stream completes their own form. The [inside-Canada work permit forms list](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit-inside/forms-documents.html) tells you to include IMM 5710, a passport photocopy, and a photo that meets visa photo specifications. It is not IMM 5707 (visitor) and not a study-permit form. Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) files filed from inside Canada also use this worker form when IRCC's checklist says so.

If you are outside Canada, this is the wrong kit. Use the outside-Canada work-permit package instead.

## How to download imm5710 form?

**Short answer:** Use the official IRCC page, on a computer. IRCC says the form may not open on tablets or phones. Click the PDF link titled Application to Change Conditions, Extend my Stay or Remain in Canada as a Worker [IMM 5710]. If it does not download, right-click and Save as. Open it in Adobe Acrobat Reader version 10 or higher, File then Open, from the folder where you saved it. The IRCC page listed the file at 846 KB and last updated September 2023. Do not fill a random "IMM 5710 2026" copy from a third-party PDF site. Those versions go stale and IRCC can bounce the file.

When you apply online, IRCC also says you receive a personalized document checklist. That online package is the one that matches your stream.

## How to complete IMM 5710?

**Short answer:** IRCC's form page tells you to read the step-by-step instructions on that same page (the "Show instructions" block) and the [instruction guide for workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5553-applying-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada-worker.html). Fill every field that applies. Sign where the form asks. The guide also covers restoration of worker status if you lost status because you overstayed (but not more than 90 days) or you changed employer, location, or type of work before you had a new permit. You still have to meet the initial requirements and other conditions. Do not leave "UCI" blank if you already have a Unique Client Identifier (UCI). First-timers who have no UCI follow IRCC's UCI help text.

| Item | What IRCC says |
|---|---|
| Form | IMM 5710 (worker, in Canada) |
| Guide | Guide 5553 |
| Checklist | Personalized in the online account; IMM 5556 is also named in the guide |
| Software | Acrobat Reader 10+ on a computer |
| Photo | Visa photo specifications on the inside-Canada list |

## How to upload imm 5710?

**Short answer:** You upload in your IRCC secure account as part of the online work-permit or extension application, on the document checklist IRCC generates. The form page is a download. The account is the upload. Convert the completed, signed PDF and keep the file size inside whatever limit the checklist shows. If a field on IMM 5710 will not flatten, IRCC's download page is telling you to use Acrobat, not a browser PDF plugin. After upload, pay the work-permit fee on the [fee list](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/information/fees/fees.asp) ($155 per person for a work permit including extensions, unless a different line applies). Incomplete uploads are how files get returned.

If an employer must pay the $230 employer compliance fee, that is their portal step, not your IMM 5710 upload. Guide 5553 says the employer pays that fee or uploads proof of exemption, and must give you the offer of employment number before you submit.

## What is the field and level of study for IMM 5710?

**Short answer:** IMM 5710 is a worker form. "Field and level of study" is a study-permit style question. It appears on some work-permit files when the job or your history is study-related, or when a school-to-work file (including some PGWP uploads) still asks education details. Fill it from your credential, not from a guess. If the personalized checklist does not ask for a study field, do not invent one. IRCC's worker guide is about extending or changing work conditions, not about picking a DLI. If you are actually changing studies, you are on the wrong form.

UBC and other schools publish PGWP walkthroughs that still point at IMM 5710. Follow IRCC's current checklist over a university PDF from last year.

## How do I submit new documents to IRCC?

**Short answer:** After you have submitted, extra documents go through the IRCC account or the webform IRCC names for your case, not by emailing a new IMM 5710 to a generic inbox. The [inside-Canada forms page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit-inside/forms-documents.html) is for the first package. Guide 5553 tells you to pay fees and use the documents on the checklist. If IRCC asks for more, they say so in the account. Sending a second full IMM 5710 unasked can duplicate the file.

We are Go Far Global, a licensed Canadian immigration firm. If status is inside the 90-day restoration window, [book a consultation](/book) before you upload. Restoration is not the same as a normal extension.

Apply before your current permit expires so you keep maintained status while IRCC processes a timely extension.

- [Guide 5553, applying as a worker](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5553-applying-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada-worker.html)

# Francophone Mobility Program 2026: LMIA-Exempt Work Permit

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/francophone-mobility-program
Category: Immigration Programs
Published: 2026-02-24
Author: Maggi Issa

> Short answer: A Canadian immigration program (LMIA-exempt code C16) that lets employers outside Quebec hire French-speaking foreign nationals without a Labour Market Impact...

# Francophone Mobility Program 2026: LMIA-Exempt Work Permit

*As of September 4, 2026.*

The Francophone Mobility work permit is open. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) lets a Canadian employer outside Quebec hire a French speaker without a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) if the language and job-offer rules are met. French speaking and listening must meet Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens (NCLC) level 5, the same band as Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) 5. The job uses the National Occupational Classification (NOC) and its Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) categories. The live hub is stamped Status Open. Applicant work-permit fee on the IRCC fee list is CAD $155. The employer pays a $230 compliance fee and uses exemption code C16.

## TL;DR

Program status: Open on the IRCC Francophone Mobility hub | Work must be outside Quebec | French speaking and listening at NCLC 5 or higher | Job offer in any NOC TEER except primary agriculture in TEER 4 and 5 | Employer: C16, $230 compliance fee, 7-digit offer number | Worker fee: $155 work permit | IRCC does not post a dedicated Francophone Mobility clock; use the processing-times tool

## Is the Francophone Mobility work permit program still open?

**Short answer:** Yes. The [Francophone Mobility work permit](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/francophone-mobility.html) page lists Status Open. It is an LMIA-exempt pathway for people who will live and work outside Quebec and who meet the language and job-offer tests. It is not a Quebec program. It is not Express Entry. It does not by itself grant permanent residence. If the hub later switches to Closed, that page is the source, not a blog. Check it before you pay fees.

The same hub points to [check if you can apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/francophone-mobility/eligibility.html) and [how to apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/francophone-mobility/apply.html).

## How to qualify for the Francophone Mobility Program?

**Short answer:** IRCC's eligibility page requires you to be destined to live and work in a province or territory outside Quebec, prove intermediate French speaking and listening (Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens, NCLC, level 5 or higher), and hold an offer of employment in any Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) category of the National Occupational Classification (NOC) except a primary agriculture occupation in TEER 4 or 5. You also need a regular work-permit eligibility path. Offers in excluded agriculture jobs do not qualify. Rules for people who applied before 15 June 2023 were tighter (NCLC 7 and TEER 0 to 3). Do not use the old grid if you are applying now.

Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) 5 is the English-scale cousin of NCLC 5. The Francophone Mobility page specifies NCLC for French speaking and listening. It does not name TEF or TCF on that eligibility text. Prove the level the way IRCC asks on the live page.

| Rule | Current (after 15 June 2023) |
|---|---|
| Where you work | Outside Quebec |
| French | NCLC 5+ speaking and listening |
| Job | Any NOC TEER except primary agriculture TEER 4 or 5 |
| LMIA | Not required if the employer uses C16 |
| Worker fee | $155 work permit (IRCC fee list) |
| Employer fee | $230 compliance fee |

## How hard to get CLB 5 in French?

**Short answer:** IRCC asks for NCLC 5 in speaking and listening, described as intermediate. That is not NCLC 7. The pre-15 June 2023 rule used a higher bar. The eligibility page does not grade "how hard" and does not list a mandatory test brand in the excerpt we checked. Intermediate speaking and listening is reachable for many people who already work in French. It is not a near-native C2. If you cannot demonstrate NCLC 5 in those two skills, this pathway is not the one. Do not guess a score. Use a result IRCC will accept, then keep the certificate with the work-permit file.

Reading and writing are not the two skills named on that eligibility paragraph. Do not assume all four skills are required unless the live page says so.

## What are the employer requirements for a Francophone Mobility work permit?

**Short answer:** Before you apply, the Canadian employer must submit the offer in the [Employer Portal](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/partners-service-providers/employer-portal.html), use exemption code C16 for Mobilité Francophone, pay the $230 employer compliance fee (or upload proof of an exemption), and give you the 7-digit offer of employment number. That number goes on your work-permit application. IRCC's eligibility page lists those employer steps. The $230 line is also on the [IRCC fee list](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/information/fees/fees.asp). The employer does not file an LMIA for this exemption.

No offer number, no complete application. Get the number in writing before you hit submit.

## How long does it take to get a Francophone Mobility work permit?

**Short answer:** The program hub links to [check processing times](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html). IRCC does not print a separate "Francophone Mobility" week-count on the program page. Use the work-permit line on the times tool for your situation (inside or outside Canada). Incomplete employer steps delay the file. Pay the $155 work-permit fee when you apply. Biometrics can add time if IRCC asks.

After a permit is issued, extending it is a new work-permit application, not an automatic renewal. Check the hub again before you extend.

## Can I get a job offer with a Francophone Mobility work permit?

**Short answer:** The permit follows a genuine job offer. You do not get the permit first and then hunt. The employer must already have submitted the C16 offer and given you the 7-digit number. Job boards that title a vacancy "Francophone Mobility" are advertising a hiring path, not a visa you can print. If you have the offer and the language proof, apply on the [how to apply](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/special-instructions/francophone-mobility/apply.html) page. A later [permanent residence](/immigration/express-entry) file, including Canadian Experience Class, is a separate program.

We are Go Far Global, a licensed Canadian immigration firm. If the employer has not paid the $230 fee or used C16, [book a consultation](/book) before you submit. A wrong exemption code is a refused work permit, not a slow one.

For the PR-side write-up of French speakers already in Canada, see [Francophone Mobility PR pathway](/news/francophone-mobility-pr-pathway-2026).

# Canada Work Permit Document Number: How to Find It in 2026

URL: https://www.gofarglobal.com/news/canada-work-permit-number
Category: Immigration Guides
Published: 2026-02-24
Author: Maggi Issa

> Find your Canada work permit document number easily with our complete guide. We explain the difference between document numbers, UCI numbers, and file numbers on Canadian work permits.

*As of May 20, 2026.* Most Canadian work permits show three different ID numbers and people mix them up constantly: the Document Number (one letter + nine digits, prefix `U`), the Work Permit Number (one letter + digits, prefix `W`), and the Unique Client Identifier or UCI (8 digits). Each serves a different purpose, and using the wrong one in an IRCC form is a top-five rejection cause for permanent residence applications.

This guide explains where each number lives on your permit, what each one is used for, and how to find them in your [Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship.html) account.

```youtube
CRxHjDSsAAw
```

## What is a Canada work permit document number?

**Short answer:** A unique alphanumeric identifier (one letter followed by nine digits) printed in the top-right corner of every IRCC-issued work permit. It identifies the specific physical permit, not the applicant, and changes each time a new permit is issued — your UCI stays the same.

The Canada work permit Document Number is a unique alphanumeric identifier printed in the top-right corner of every IRCC-issued work permit. It is one letter followed by nine digits and stays fixed for the lifetime of that specific physical permit. The Document Number identifies the permit itself, not the applicant. Each new permit you receive (after a renewal, extension, or new application) gets a different Document Number, while your underlying [IRCC Unique Client Identifier (UCI)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/account.html) stays the same.

The Document Number is what employers, the Canada Border Services Agency, and IRCC officers reference when verifying that you are authorized to work in Canada.

## Where is the document number on a Canadian work permit?

**Short answer:** In a labelled box in the top-right corner of the physical IMM 1442 permit, on the second page of the permit-and-counterfoil layout. On electronic permits the Document Number appears in the same position on the PDF served through your IRCC online account.

The Document Number sits in a labelled box in the top-right corner of the physical permit, on the second page of the permit-and-counterfoil layout IRCC ships. On electronic permits issued through the [IRCC online account](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/account.html), the Document Number appears in the same position on the PDF, usually marked "Document No." or "Document Number". If you have already lost the physical permit, you can pull the Document Number from any IRCC correspondence about the permit, or from your IRCC online account profile.

Three places to find it:

- **Physical permit:** top-right box, page 2 of the permit document.
- **Digital permit (PDF):** same position, labelled "Document No.".
- **[IRCC online account](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/account.html):** under "My Documents" or "Application History" once you sign in.

## What is the UCI and how is it different from the document number?

**Short answer:** The Unique Client Identifier (UCI) is the 8-digit number IRCC assigns the first time you interact with Canadian immigration, and it stays with you forever across every application. The Document Number changes with each new permit; the UCI does not.

| Number | Format | Where to find it | What it identifies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Document Number | One letter and nine digits | Top-right corner of the permit | The specific permit document |
| Unique Client Identifier (UCI) | Eight digits, sometimes ten | Top of the permit | You, across every IRCC application |
| Application or file number | Letters and digits | Receipts and IRCC correspondence | One specific application | If a form asks for 'UCI' or 'client ID', use the UCI.

The Unique Client Identifier (UCI) is the 8-digit number IRCC assigns to a person the first time they interact with Canadian immigration. The UCI stays with you forever, across every work permit, study permit, visitor visa, and PR application. The Document Number changes each time you receive a new permit, but the UCI does not.

If a form asks for "UCI" or "client ID," enter the 8-digit number. If a form asks for "Document Number," enter the letter-plus-nine-digits from your current permit. If a form asks for "Work Permit Number," enter the W-prefix identifier (a different field on the same permit). Confusing these is the most common cause of mismatched-identifier rejections.

| Identifier | Format | What it identifies | Changes with renewal? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Document Number | One letter + 9 digits (e.g. `U123456789`) | The specific physical permit | Yes, new permit, new number |
| Work Permit Number | `W` + digits | The work-permit application/issue record | Yes |
| UCI | 8 digits | You, the person, across all IRCC interactions | No, permanent |
| File Number | `E` / `W` / `S` / `V` / `T` + digits | A specific application submission | Each new application gets a new one |

## What is the application file number and when does it change?

**Short answer:** An IRCC-internal tracking number assigned to each submitted application, distinct from both the UCI and the Document Number. File-number prefixes follow patterns by stream (e.g., E + digits for economic class), and a new file number is assigned with every new submission.

The application file number is assigned every time you submit a new application to IRCC, and it changes with each new submission. It is used internally by IRCC to track that specific application's progress. Unlike your UCI (which is permanent), file numbers are application-specific. File-number prefixes follow these patterns:

- Economic class applications: `E` + digits (example: E099977028)
- Work permit applications: `W` + digits
- Study permit applications: `S` + digits
- Visitor record applications: `V` + digits
- Temporary resident permit applications: `T` + digits

These prefixes are application file numbers, not permit document numbers. A single applicant can have multiple file numbers active at once across different applications. Once the application closes, the file number is archived but the UCI remains.

## How do I find my work permit document number online?

**Short answer:** Sign in to your IRCC online account with GCKey or a sign-in partner, open 'View my submitted applications or profiles', and select your active work permit. The Document Number, UCI, and issue/expiry dates are listed on the document's detail page.

Sign in to your [IRCC online account](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/account.html) using your GCKey or sign-in partner credentials, then open the "View my submitted applications or profiles" section. Your active work permit document will show the Document Number, UCI, and issue/expiry dates on its detail page. The same data appears on every IRCC letter or email referencing your work permit.

Other places it appears:

- **Physical and digital permit:** top-right corner box.
- **IRCC online account profile** under "My Documents."
- **IRCC correspondence:** any decision letter, approval notice, or instruction email.
- **Employer records:** HR departments often store a copy under your I-9 equivalent file.

## What if I can't find my Canadian work permit number?

**Short answer:** Contact the IRCC Client Support Centre and verify your identity with full name, date of birth, and country of birth. A licensed RCIC or lawyer with your written authorization can also retrieve it. Lost paper permits can be reissued with Form IMM 5444.

If you cannot locate your Document Number, the fastest path is to contact the [IRCC Client Support Centre](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/contact-ircc.html). They can confirm the number after verifying your identity with your full name, date of birth, and country of birth. A licensed Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCIC) or lawyer can also retrieve it on your behalf with signed authorization. Submitting an [Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) request](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/transparency/access-information-privacy.html) returns a copy of your entire IRCC file, including all permit numbers ever issued, usually within 30 days for personal information requests.

## How does the document number affect your legal status in Canada?

**Short answer:** The Document Number is the primary identifier IRCC, employers, and CBSA officers use to confirm your authorization to work. Employers can verify your authorization through IRCC's employer-verification channel using this number, and the conditions printed on that specific permit govern your legal status.

The Document Number is the primary identifier IRCC, employers, and Canada Border Services Agency officers use to confirm you are authorized to work. When your permit is about to expire, IRCC's renewal notifications reference this number. Employers may be asked to verify your authorization independently using the Document Number, and they can confirm it through IRCC's employer-verification channels.

If your work permit is approaching expiry, file a renewal or apply for a [Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP)](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit/temporary/extend.html) at least 30 days before expiry to maintain legal status. Falling out of status by even one day creates a refusal trigger that flows through every future application. Check current [IRCC processing times](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/check-processing-times.html) before relying on a renewal landing on time.

## Why does IRCC need your document number for PR applications?

**Short answer:** IRCC uses the Document Number to verify Canadian work experience claims on permanent residence (PR) applications, especially the Canadian Experience Class and Provincial Nominee Program streams. An officer cross-checks the number against your permit history, so it must match your records exactly. Missing or incorrect Document Numbers are a common cause of incomplete-application returns.

IRCC uses your work permit Document Number to verify Canadian work experience on permanent residence applications, especially through programs like Canadian Experience Class (CEC) and [Provincial Nominee Program (PNP)](/immigration/provincial-nominee). When you claim Canadian work experience on your [Express Entry](/immigration/express-entry) profile, IRCC cross-references your Document Number against the issued permit, the National Occupational Classification (NOC) code on the permit, and the hours you have logged. A mismatched or stale Document Number flags the application for procedural review and delays processing by months.

When completing IRCC forms, double-check that you're entering the correct identifier. If the form asks for "document number," enter the U-series number (one letter, nine digits, top-right corner of your permit). If it asks for "work permit number," enter the W-series number. If it asks for "UCI" or "unique identifier," enter the 8-digit number.

Use our [CRS calculator](/tools/crs-calculator) to see how your Canadian work experience affects your Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score.

## What are the most common mistakes with work permit numbers?

**Short answer:** Confusing the UCI (8 digits) with the Document Number (one letter plus 9 digits), using an old permit's number after a renewal, omitting the letter prefix, and transposing digits when entering it on application forms. These are the top reasons IRCC returns PR applications as incomplete.

The most common errors are confusing the UCI with the Document Number, using an old permit's number after a renewal, and omitting the letter prefix. These mistakes are also the most common reasons IRCC returns a permanent residence application as incomplete. The four mistakes to avoid:

- **Confusing UCI with Document Number.** UCI is 8 digits. Document Number is one letter plus 9 digits. They are not interchangeable.
- **Using an old permit number.** Renewals produce a new Document Number. Always copy from your current permit.
- **Mixing up application file numbers with permit Document Numbers.** File numbers change with each application; Document Numbers belong to a specific physical permit.
- **Incomplete numbers.** Always include the letter prefix when providing your Document Number, `U123456789` not `123456789`.

## What happens to your document number when you renew your work permit?

**Short answer:** Every renewal or extension produces a new physical permit with a new Document Number. Your UCI stays the same. Keep every previous Document Number on file because PR applications require you to list every period of authorized employment along with its supporting permit identifier.

When you renew your work permit, IRCC issues a new physical permit with a new Document Number. Your UCI stays the same. Keep records of every previous Document Number for PR applications, because Canadian Experience Class requires you to list every period of authorized employment along with the supporting permit identifiers. The chronology of permits is what proves continuous Canadian work experience.

For renewal guidance and current requirements, visit our [work permit page](/immigration/work-permit) and our [IMM5710 work permit extension form guide](/news/imm5710), or check the official IRCC [work permit extension page](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit/temporary/extend.html).

## Do family members share the same work permit number?

**Short answer:** No. Each work permit issued to a family member carries its own unique Document Number, even when the family applied together. Spouses and dependants on open work permits or study permits each receive their own permits with their own identifiers.

No. Each work permit issued to a family member has its own unique Document Number, even if the family applied together. Spouses and dependent children who hold open work permits or study permits receive their own permits with their own identifiers. The only thing shared across a family file is the principal applicant's IRCC file number for the original application, every issued permit has a distinct Document Number and a distinct UCI per person.

For questions about [family immigration](/immigration/family-immigration) and work authorization for dependents, our team can help you understand the requirements.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the UCI the same as the work permit number?

No. The UCI is your permanent 8-digit IRCC client ID and stays the same across every application. The work permit number (Document Number, with a letter prefix and 9 digits) is specific to one issued permit and changes when you renew.

### Does my document number change when I extend my work permit?

Yes. Every renewal or extension produces a new physical permit with a new Document Number. Your UCI does not change.

### Where can I find my UCI if I never had a physical permit?

Sign in to your [IRCC online account](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/account.html). Your UCI appears at the top of your profile. If you have never created an account, your UCI also appears on the first decision letter or acknowledgement of receipt IRCC sent you.

### What do I do if my employer asks for my work permit number?

Provide the Document Number from the top-right corner of your physical permit (letter prefix + 9 digits). This is what employers use to verify work authorization. Do not give them just your UCI; that is a personal identifier, not a permit verification.

### Can I use my old work permit number on a PR application?

Only when listing prior employment periods in your work-experience history. For your CURRENT authorization, you must use the Document Number from your most recent permit. Listing an expired permit as your current authorization is a refusal trigger.

### What is the difference between the W prefix and the U prefix?

The `W` prefix is most commonly seen on work-permit application file numbers; the `U` prefix is most common on the Document Number printed on the physical permit. The exact prefix depends on the issue era and permit type. Check the label on your specific permit; whichever letter is printed is the correct one to use.
